title: Explore Microsoft Azure: How to Get Started with Azure
description:
1. Introduction

  • Brief Overview of Microsoft Azure:

    • Microsoft Azure is a comprehensive cloud computing platform offered by Microsoft, providing a range of services including computing power, storage solutions, and networking capabilities. Azure is significant in the cloud computing industry because it allows businesses to build, deploy, and manage applications and services through Microsoft-managed data centers globally. With its extensive infrastructure and integration capabilities, Azure supports a wide variety of programming languages, tools, and frameworks, making it a versatile choice for developers and enterprises alike.
    • Azure is one of the most popular cloud platforms in the world, competing with Amazon Web Services (AWS) and Google Cloud. It is known for its extensive range of services, from basic virtual machines to complex artificial intelligence tools, and its ability to cater to businesses of all sizes, from startups to large enterprises.

  • Why Get Started with Azure?

    • Azure offers scalability, allowing businesses to adjust their resources according to their needs without upfront investments in physical hardware. This flexibility means you can scale up during high-demand periods and scale down when demand decreases, all within a cost-effective framework.
    • Azure’s pay-as-you-go pricing model, extensive support for open-source technologies, and seamless integration with Microsoft products like Office 365 and Dynamics 365 make it an attractive option for various industries, including healthcare, finance, and retail.
    • Professionals such as developers, system administrators, and data scientists can benefit from Azure by leveraging its tools to build, test, and deploy applications more efficiently.

2. Setting Up Your Azure Account

  • Creating a Microsoft Account:

    • If you don't already have a Microsoft account, visit account.microsoft.com and click "Create a Microsoft account." You can sign up using an existing email address or create a new one. Follow the on-screen instructions to complete the account creation process.

  • Signing Up for Azure:

    • Once you have a Microsoft account, go to azure.microsoft.com. Click on "Start for free" to begin the sign-up process. During sign-up, you'll need to provide some basic information and a payment method, even if you're using the free trial. Azure typically offers a 30-day free trial with $200 in credits, which you can use to explore various services.
    • After signing up, you'll be directed to the Azure Portal, where you can start managing your cloud resources.

  • Understanding the Azure Portal:

    • The Azure Portal is the central hub for managing all your Azure services. Upon logging in, you'll see a customizable dashboard where you can pin resources for quick access. The "All Services" section gives you access to all available Azure services, while "Cost Management" allows you to monitor your spending and set budgets to avoid unexpected costs.

3. Navigating the Azure Portal

  • Overview of the User Interface:

    • The Azure Portal interface is designed to be intuitive. The left-hand menu provides access to services, subscriptions, resource groups, and more. The top bar features a search function, notifications, and settings. Notifications will keep you updated on the status of your resources and any potential issues.

  • Creating Your First Resource:

    • For your first resource, let's create a Virtual Machine (VM). In the Azure Portal, click on "Create a resource" and select "Virtual Machine" from the options. Follow the guided steps to configure your VM, such as selecting an operating system, instance size, and region. Once configured, click "Review + Create" to finalize your VM setup.

4. Exploring Core Azure Services

  • Introduction to Key Services:

    • Compute: Azure Virtual Machines (VMs) allow you to run applications in the cloud with your preferred operating system. Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) helps you manage containerized applications using Kubernetes.
    • Storage: Azure Blob Storage is ideal for storing unstructured data, while File Storage and Disk Storage offer file-level and block-level storage solutions, respectively.
    • Networking: Azure Virtual Networks enable you to create isolated networks for your Azure resources, while Load Balancers and Azure DNS ensure high availability and optimized performance.
    • Database: Azure SQL Database is a fully managed relational database service, while Cosmos DB offers multi-model database capabilities for global distribution.

  • Use Cases and Examples:

    • Provide practical examples, such as hosting a website using Azure VMs, storing backups using Blob Storage, or setting up a scalable microservices architecture with AKS.

5. Managing and Monitoring Your Resources

  • Resource Management:

    • Group related resources using Resource Groups to manage them collectively. For instance, if you have a VM, storage account, and network all related to a single application, you can organize them under one Resource Group.
    • Use tagging to categorize resources by department, project, or environment, which helps with organization and cost management.

  • Monitoring and Alerts:

    • Azure Monitor offers insights into the performance and health of your resources. Set up alerts to notify you of potential issues, such as high CPU usage or low available memory, allowing you to respond proactively.

6. Learning and Certification

  • Azure Learning Resources:

    • Microsoft offers a wealth of learning resources, including free online courses through Microsoft Learn, extensive documentation, and hands-on labs. Consider exploring tutorials and joining Azure communities to stay updated on the latest features.
    • Engage with Azure blogs, podcasts, and forums to gain insights from other professionals and Azure experts.

  • Certification Pathways:

    • Starting with Azure Fundamentals (AZ-900) is recommended for beginners. From there, you can pursue role-based certifications, such as Azure Administrator (AZ-104) or Azure Solutions Architect (AZ-305), to validate your skills and advance your career.

7. Conclusion

  • Recap of Getting Started:

    • In this guide, we walked through the essentials of getting started with Microsoft Azure, beginning with setting up an account and navigating the Azure Portal. We also explored creating your first resource, understanding core Azure services, and managing and monitoring your resources effectively. These initial steps are designed to provide a solid foundation for leveraging Azure's powerful cloud computing capabilities.

  • Call to Action:

    • Now that you have an overview of how to get started with Azure, it's time to take the first step. Create your Azure account today and start exploring the platform’s vast array of services. Whether you're deploying your first virtual machine or experimenting with Azure's AI tools, the possibilities are endless. Don't hesitate to dive in and discover how Azure can enhance your projects and business operations.
    • We encourage you to share your experiences or ask questions in the comments section below. Your insights and inquiries can help foster a supportive community where we can all learn and grow together in our Azure journeys.

title: Terraform Unleashed: Building Scalable Infra‑as‑Code Pipelines
description:
Terraform Unleashed: Building Scalable Infra‑as‑Code Pipelines

Infrastructure as Code (IaC) has transformed the way we think about cloud resources. Among the many tools in the IaC arena, Terraform stands out for its provider‑agnostic model, declarative language, and robust ecosystem. In this post we’ll walk through a practical, end‑to‑end workflow that takes you from a single resource definition to a production‑grade CI/CD pipeline. By the end, you’ll have a reusable Terraform module, a version‑controlled state backend, and a GitHub Actions workflow that automatically applies changes on merge.

TL;DR – Define resources in HCL, store state in a remote backend, modularize with reusable components, and automate with CI.

1. Why Terraform?

  • Provider‑agnostic – One language (HCL) works across AWS, Azure, GCP, and dozens of niche providers.
  • Immutable plans – terraform plan shows a precise diff before any change hits the cloud.
  • State handling – Remote backends keep a single source of truth, enabling collaboration.

These traits make Terraform a natural fit for teams that need repeatable, auditable infrastructure deployments.

2. Project Layout

A clean directory structure is the foundation of maintainable Terraform code. Here’s a minimal but production‑ready layout:

├── environments
│   ├── dev
│   │   ├── main.tf
│   │   └── backend.tf
│   └── prod
│       ├── main.tf
│       └── backend.tf
├── modules
│   └── vpc
│       ├── main.tf
│       ├── variables.tf
│       └── outputs.tf
└── .github
    └── workflows
        └── terraform.yml
  • modules/ – Reusable building blocks (e.g., VPC, IAM, RDS).
  • environments/ – Environment‑specific configurations that call modules.
  • .github/workflows/ – CI pipelines that run terraform fmt, plan, and apply.

3. A Simple VPC Module

Let’s start with a tiny VPC module for AWS. This example demonstrates variables, locals, and outputs.

# modules/vpc/variables.tf
variable "name" {
  description = "Name tag for the VPC"
  type        = string
}

variable "cidr" {
  description = "CIDR block for the VPC"
  type        = string
  default     = "10.0.0.0/16"
}

# modules/vpc/main.tf
resource "aws_vpc" "this" {
  cidr_block = var.cidr
  tags = {
    Name = var.name
  }
}

# modules/vpc/outputs.tf
output "vpc_id" {
  description = "The ID of the created VPC"
  value       = aws_vpc.this.id
}

You can now reference this module from any environment:

# environments/dev/main.tf
module "vpc" {
  source = "../../modules/vpc"
  name   = "dev-vpc"
  cidr   = "10.1.0.0/16"
}

4. Remote State Backend

Storing state locally works for single‑developer experiments, but teams need a remote backend. We’ll use Terraform Cloud (free tier) as an example.

# environments/dev/backend.tf
terraform {
  backend "remote" {
    hostname = "app.terraform.io"
    organization = "my-org"

    workspaces {
      name = "dev"
    }
  }
}

Running terraform init now authenticates against Terraform Cloud, creates the workspace, and stores the state there. The same pattern applies to prod, just with a different workspace name.

5. Working with Workspaces

Terraform Cloud workspaces isolate state per environment. You can also use the built‑in CLI workspaces for quick experiments:

terraform workspace new staging
terraform workspace select staging

When you switch, Terraform automatically reads the corresponding state file, keeping your environments safely separated.

6. Linting, Formatting, and Validation

A clean codebase reduces friction in PR reviews.

# .github/workflows/terraform.yml
name: Terraform CI

on:
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - '**/*.tf'

jobs:
  fmt-plan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3

      - name: Set up Terraform
        uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v2

      - name: Terraform Format
        run: terraform fmt -check

      - name: Terraform Init
        run: terraform init -backend=false

      - name: Terraform Validate
        run: terraform validate

      - name: Terraform Plan
        env:
          TF_VAR_aws_region: us-east-1
        run: terraform plan -out=plan.out

      - name: Upload Plan Artifact
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v3
        with:
          name: tfplan
          path: plan.out

The workflow runs on every PR, ensuring code is formatted, syntactically valid, and that a plan can be generated without side effects.

7. Automated Apply on Merge

Once a PR passes all checks, we can safely apply the changes to the target environment.

# continuation of .github/workflows/terraform.yml
  apply:
    needs: fmt-plan
    if: github.event_name == 'push' && github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3

      - name: Set up Terraform
        uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v2

      - name: Terraform Init
        run: terraform init

      - name: Download Plan Artifact
        uses: actions/download-artifact@v3
        with:
          name: tfplan
          path: .

      - name: Terraform Apply
        run: terraform apply -auto-approve plan.out

Only pushes to main trigger an automatic apply, keeping production changes under version control.

8. Best Practices Checklist

✅ Practice Why it matters
1 Keep modules small and focused Easier to test and reuse.
2 Pin provider versions Prevents accidental breaking changes (required_providers).
3 Never commit state files Use remote backends to avoid drift and conflicts.
4 Use terraform fmt in CI Enforces a consistent style across the team.
5 Separate variables per environment Keeps dev, staging, prod isolated.
6 Enable Sentinel policies (if on Terraform Cloud) Adds policy‑as‑code guardrails.

9. Scaling Beyond a Single VPC

When you start managing dozens of resources—EKS clusters, RDS instances, IAM roles—consider these extensions:

  • Terragrunt – A thin wrapper that adds DRY capabilities (e.g., shared backend.tf across environments).
  • Terraform Cloud Sentinel – Enforce compliance policies (e.g., “no public S3 buckets”).
  • Modules Registry – Publish internal modules for organization‑wide reuse.

10. Debugging Tips

  • terraform console – Interactive HCL evaluation.
  • TF_LOG=DEBUG terraform apply – Verbose logs for provider communication.
  • terraform state list – Inspect current resources in state.

11. What’s Next?

  • Testing with Terratest – Write Go tests that spin up real infrastructure and assert expectations.
  • Policy as Code – Combine Sentinel with Open Policy Agent (OPA) for multi‑cloud guardrails.
  • Dynamic Secrets – Integrate with HashiCorp Vault to inject secrets at runtime, keeping them out of state.

Recommended Tools

If you’re ready to level up your Terraform workflow, check out these tools that have helped countless teams streamline their IaC pipelines:

  • Terraform Cloud – The official hosted backend that adds remote state, VCS integration, and policy enforcement. Sign up here and get a free tier that’s perfect for small teams.
  • Terragrunt – A lightweight wrapper that simplifies working with multiple environments and shared configurations. Grab the latest version from the official site here and start reducing duplication in seconds.

Happy provisioning!

title: The 11-year-old premise inside Rust's memory-safety proof
description:
"If it compiles, the memory is safe."

That is Rust's brand — not a slogan, a machine-checked proof: the borrow checker refuses unsafe lifetimes at compile time, host-enforced, the strongest rung any language has claimed. Yesterday, issue #164250 landed on the rust-lang tracker: an unsoundness in the borrow checker, reproducing on current stable, with variants compiling since 1.18.0 (2017) — and one version traced back to 1.4. Eleven years inside the proof.

I ran the reproduction tonight on the official playground — stable channel. The output, verbatim:

read after scope: hello world, this is long enough
the stack slot is freed. the string still printed.

A short-lived reference escaped a T: 'static bound through field assignment after construction, survived a Drop that assumed the bound held, and was read after its stack slot was freed. On stable. Same result on nightly. The receipts are one click away — the playground permalink runs it in seconds.

The mechanics, in three sentences

struct Q<T: 'static + Send> demands its payload outlive the program. Assigning a field after construction (q.0 = Some(&l), where l is stack-local) unifies the types covariantly — and that unification does not re-check the 'static bound. A Drop impl that pushes the value into a static list assumes the bound held; it leaks the reference out; a downcast_ref::<&'static String>() reads freed stack memory. With AddressSanitizer, per the issue, the same program crashes with stack-use-after-scope.

The number that matters is not 11

It is the severity call: P-high, downgraded from P-critical. The pinned note from lcnr is explicit — it would have been P-critical regardless of whether anyone encountered it in the wild, and it is P-high only because it has been latent for eleven years with "very likely that this unsoundness has not caused memory unsafety by accident." The exploit requires, per the issue, "an intentionally malicious Drop implementation."

Read that as an auditor, because it is a premise confession, and it is not Rust-specific. The compiler's proof descends a ladder: borrow check → variance rules → trait bounds → and at the floor, an assumption nobody executes — Drop implementations respect the bounds they inherit. The type system verified everything it could check and rested on the one thing it could not: the honesty of every Drop impl ever written by every hand that touched every crate. Eleven years, that premise held by accident of nobody aiming at it. This week someone aimed.

Sound familiar? It is the QGIS conscience test — "did you in good conscience write the code yourself" — inside a compiler. It is the authority ladder — rung 0, "the caller's argument": a claim the impl author makes, unverifiable by the checker below. Every soundness proof, every security certification, every "guaranteed" has a floor like this. The floor is not a scandal. An unlabeled floor is.

Credits, because the finder's method is the receipts

  • jsnell filed it October 13, with the reproduction that compiles and prints freed memory.
  • theemathas added the I-unsound label, a minimal core repro, and traced a variant compiling "ever since 1.18.0 (2017)" — and asked the question in the thread: "How on earth was this not found before this???"
  • maxdexh contributed a version going back to 1.4, and the generalization: "unification just generally doesn't check lifetime bounds of the type" — including via mem::swap, no field assignment needed.
  • lcnr pinned the severity reasoning and the linkage to the next-gen trait solver and Project Zero rework. PR #164277 is the fix in motion.

Four people, four contributions, each with its own denominator. That is what a healthy process looks like from the outside — and it is also, per the issue, a thread that was briefly locked as too heated before being unlocked and re-locked to collaborators. Soundness conversations run hot.

What to steal

  • Audit the premises under your proofs. Every guarantee you rely on — a type system, a SOC 2 report, a DCO sign-off, a "tested and measured" claim — rests on unlabeled assumptions the guarantee cannot check. Name one. The table is the audit.
  • Label your severity calls with their reasons. P-high because eleven years latent because it needs a malicious Drop — that reasoning is the difference between a decision and an assertion. Rust's team did this in the pinned note; copy the format.
  • Permalinks for reproductions. The playground link makes my claim one click from being your claim. If your repro needs setup, ship the setup.

Two honest limits

The exploit requires a malicious Drop by design, and the team's downgrade is defensible. Eleven years without an accidental hit is evidence of something — either the premise held because nobody aimed, or because honest Drops overwhelmingly dominate. Both readings favor the team's call. My point is narrower: the premise existed, was unlabeled, and now is labeled — by the issue, in public.

And my run is a playground snapshot, not a forensic audit. Stable and nightly, debug profile, no AddressSanitizer in my harness — the stack-use-after-scope confirmation cited in the issue comes from their ASAN run, not mine. One compiler family, one evening. The issue's own denominators are better than mine; use theirs.

Your turn

The reproduction is twenty lines, the playground is free, and here is the whole thing — paste it into the playground, hit Run, and compare your output to mine:

static KEPT: std::sync::Mutex<Vec<Box<dyn std::any::Any + Send>>> =
    std::sync::Mutex::new(Vec::new());

struct Q<T: 'static + Send>(Option<T>);

impl<T: 'static + Send> Drop for Q<T> {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        if let Some(v) = self.0.take() {
            KEPT.lock().unwrap().push(Box::new(v));
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let l = String::from("hello world, this is long enough");
    {
        let mut q = Q(None);
        q.0 = Some(&l);
    } // <- Drop here: the short-lived reference escapes as if 'static

    let kept = KEPT.lock().unwrap();
    let s = kept[0].downcast_ref::<&'static String>().unwrap();
    println!("read after scope: {}", s);
    println!("the stack slot is freed. the string still printed.");
}

Run it on your rustc, your channels, your edition, and post your output — the issue's variants reach back to 1.4, and every data point sharpens the map. Then pick one guarantee you ship or rely on, and write down the premise under it that nobody executes. That list is where the next eleven-year bugs live.

title: A Go Small-App Observability Stack for Health Monitoring Without Sentry or Datadog
description:
A marketplace import page should fire when scheduled imports stop producing results, not merely when the API process dies. TL;DR: use an external heartbeat monitor such as Healthchecks or Better Stack to detect the missing completion, then use errors, logs, and metrics to explain it. For a small Go service, that is the least complex stack that covers silent scheduler failures and still lets the on-call roll back safely.

The page should say which import is late, when it last completed, and how far it is beyond its expected interval. It should not begin with a graph titled “host CPU.” If the 02:00 supplier import normally finishes by 02:20, the actionable event is the absent successful completion after a deliberate grace period.

The page at 02:25 UTC

Start at the pager and work backward. A useful alert reads like this: supplier-catalog-import has not completed; last success 01:58 UTC; grace period 25m. The runbook then asks three questions in order: did a run start, did it fail, and did it finish with a plausible result count?

That order protects rollback safety. If a newly deployed parser started producing zero records, the operator can compare the deployment time, error group, and rows_imported metric before reverting. If no run started, rolling back application code may be pointless; the scheduler or queue path deserves attention first. If the run started twice, the response shifts again: stop duplicate delivery from causing duplicate marketplace writes, using an idempotency key derived from the schedule and supplier.

One signal cannot answer all three questions. An uptime probe proves an HTTP target responds. A heartbeat proves the expected job reached a checkpoint. Logs and errors preserve diagnostic context. Metrics show whether “success” produced 18,000 listings or zero.

That last distinction matters.

What should health monitoring prove without a full observability stack?

A job that never starts emits no fresh error, log, or metric. Querying the observability store can reveal that absence, but somebody still has to run the query on schedule, maintain threshold state, and deliver the notification. That is a monitoring system built beside the monitoring system.

External heartbeat products own that negative-space problem. Healthchecks exposes ping URLs and documents start, success, and failure signals. Better Stack combines uptime monitoring with heartbeat monitoring and incident escalation. Either can watch for a missing completion independently of the process and scheduler being watched.

The threshold needs operational slack. Set it from the schedule plus the observed upper end of normal runtime, then add a grace period for queue delay and upstream variance. Do not invent a universal “two missed runs” rule: for a daily catalog import, waiting for a second miss means discovering the failure a day late; for a five-minute enrichment job, paging on one slightly slow execution may create noise.

Page on missing useful work, not missing telemetry. A metrics backend can still alert on rows_imported == 0 after a run reports, but the external heartbeat is what catches a worker that never got far enough to report anything.

Build the Go integration around completion

The heartbeat should surround the real unit of work. This runnable Go program sends a start signal, runs an import, and sends success only after the result is committed. Set HEALTHCHECKS_URL to the private ping URL supplied by the heartbeat service.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "log"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func ping(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, url, suffix, body string) error {
    req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, url+suffix, strings.NewReader(body))
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "text/plain; charset=utf-8")

    resp, err := client.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
        message, _ := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 4096))
        return fmt.Errorf("heartbeat returned %s: %s", resp.Status, strings.TrimSpace(string(message)))
    }
    return nil
}

func queryErrorGroups(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client) error {
    baseURL := strings.TrimRight(os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL"), "/")
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if baseURL == "" || apiKey == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_BASE_URL and INFRAI_API_KEY are required")
    }

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, baseURL+"/v1/errors/groups", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 1<<20))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            select {
            case <-time.After(delay):
                continue
            case <-ctx.Done():
                return ctx.Err()
            }
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("error groups returned %s: %s", resp.Status, strings.TrimSpace(string(body)))
        }
        log.Printf("error groups response received: bytes=%d", len(body))
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("error groups remained rate limited after retries")
}

func importCatalog(context.Context) (int, error) {
    return 18000, nil
}

func main() {
    pingURL := os.Getenv("HEALTHCHECKS_URL")
    if pingURL == "" {
        log.Fatal("HEALTHCHECKS_URL is required")
    }

    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 20*time.Minute)
    defer cancel()
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}

    if err := ping(ctx, client, pingURL, "/start", "supplier=catalog-a"); err != nil {
        log.Printf("start heartbeat failed: %v", err)
    }

    rows, err := importCatalog(ctx)
    if err != nil {
        _ = ping(ctx, client, pingURL, "/fail", err.Error())
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    if rows == 0 {
        err = fmt.Errorf("import committed zero rows")
        _ = ping(ctx, client, pingURL, "/fail", err.Error())
        log.Fatal(err)
    }

    if err := ping(ctx, client, pingURL, "", fmt.Sprintf("rows_imported=%d", rows)); err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    if err := queryErrorGroups(ctx, client); err != nil {
        log.Printf("diagnostic query failed: %v", err)
    }
    log.Printf("import complete: rows_imported=%d", rows)
}

In production, the import itself also needs an idempotent commit boundary. A deterministic key such as supplier-id + scheduled-window lets an at-least-once queue retry without publishing the same listings twice. Send the success heartbeat after that transaction commits, never when the message is merely dequeued.

The sample treats heartbeat delivery failure differently at the start and the end. A failed start ping is logged because the import can still do useful work. A failed final ping fails the process so the queue can retry; that retry is safe only because the import commit is idempotent. This is a conscious trade-off: monitoring delivery becomes part of completion semantics, which is appropriate when the page depends on that completion record.

OpenTelemetry metrics can add duration, attempted rows, committed rows, and queue age using vendor-neutral instruments. Keep a stable supplier_id only if its cardinality is bounded. Do not put order IDs, listing IDs, or raw error messages in metric labels.

Compare failure coverage, not feature counts

The right choice depends less on dashboard polish than on which failure modes must wake somebody up. These products overlap, but they do not substitute for one another.

Option Strong fit here Boundary that changes the decision
Healthchecks Focused cron and heartbeat monitoring with start, success, and failure signaling Pair it with a separate store for searchable logs, errors, and metrics
Better Stack Uptime and heartbeat monitoring with an incident-management path Broader workflow means more surface area than a heartbeat-only tool
Grafana Cloud Metrics, logs, traces, dashboards, and alerting around an OpenTelemetry-oriented stack A missed job still needs an explicit heartbeat or absence rule
Datadog Integrated logs, metrics, traces, synthetic monitoring, and alerting Capability breadth and its ingestion/indexing model deserve review before adoption
Sentry Application error diagnosis, source maps, tracing, and session replay It is not the primary proof that a scheduled backend import ran

Infrai can be the errors, logs, and metrics component when a team wants a self-describing plain REST API whose public discovery response supplies schemas and billing metadata, whose documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages, and whose single API key covers 295 routes across 20 modules under one bill. For this import worker, that means one credential to rotate and one access boundary to review when another backend capability is added. It does not provide synthetic uptime checks, heartbeat monitoring, native alert delivery, distributed trace querying, source-map processing, crash symbolication, or session replay. Its logs can carry trace_id and span_id for correlation, but that is not a span-tree UI. For this use case it belongs beside a heartbeat monitor, not in place of one.

For the smallest service, I would begin with Healthchecks plus structured application logs and OpenTelemetry metrics. Move toward Better Stack when the same team wants the alert escalation workflow in that layer. Choose Grafana Cloud or Datadog when cross-signal querying, managed dashboards, and wider infrastructure visibility justify the extra operational surface. Add Sentry when frontend stack traces, source maps, or replay are the diagnostic gap.

This is not a permanent architecture decision. Keep the heartbeat call isolated and the application telemetry in OpenTelemetry-compatible instruments; then changing a backend does not require changing the definition of a successful import.

Plan rollback and migration before the alert

A page needs evidence that separates deploy regression from data and scheduler failures. Record the deployed revision in logs, attach it as a bounded metric attribute, and include it in the import result. Then define the rollback trigger before the incident: for example, a new revision fails across multiple suppliers while the previous revision completed the same scheduled window. The exact trigger must come from the service's own baseline; no honest generic article can manufacture it.

The runbook should preserve the failed payload reference, verify the idempotency key, roll back the worker, and replay the same scheduled window. A rollback that loses the input or changes the deduplication key is not safe. It can turn one missed import into duplicated listings.

Also test the monitor. Disable a staging schedule, verify that the missing heartbeat reaches the intended channel, then restore it and confirm recovery. A green dashboard is weak evidence if nobody has exercised the delivery path.

Account for the cost of a noisy threshold

A short grace period detects a stalled supplier feed quickly, but routine upstream slowness will page the on-call. A long grace period preserves sleep while stale inventory remains visible to buyers. The threshold is therefore a product decision expressed as an SRE setting: how long can this marketplace tolerate stale availability before a human must act?

Review that setting using actual completion durations and queue age, especially after schedule or supplier changes. Keep warning and paging thresholds distinct when the business window permits it. And avoid automatic rollback on one late heartbeat: absence tells you the result is late, not that the newest deployment caused it.

The compact architecture is deliberate: external heartbeat for detection, telemetry for diagnosis, idempotent replay for recovery. More tooling is justified only when it closes a named failure mode. Consider the specific 02:00 supplier run: no start ping points toward scheduling, a start followed by failure points toward execution, and a success with zero committed rows points toward validation. Those three states lead to different actions, so collapsing them into a single “job unhealthy” event makes rollback riskier and the page slower to resolve.

Keep those states separate.

Further reading

  • Healthchecks pinging API: https://healthchecks.io/docs/http_api/
  • Better Stack heartbeat monitoring: https://betterstack.com/docs/uptime/cron-and-heartbeat-monitor/
  • OpenTelemetry metrics concepts: https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/metrics/
  • Grafana Cloud documentation: https://grafana.com/docs/grafana-cloud/
  • Datadog synthetic monitoring documentation: https://docs.datadoghq.com/synthetics/
  • Datadog pricing and log ingestion model: https://www.datadoghq.com/pricing/
  • Sentry product documentation: https://docs.sentry.io/product/

title: How Many Ranks Does a Token Need? A Noise-Floor Squelch for Rank-One LoRA Experts
description:
arXiv:2610.19033v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) applies every rank-one component of its update to every token, and mixture-of-experts variants replace this with a learned router that activates a fixed number of components. We argue that the number of components a token needs is a detection question with a classical answer. A token's responses to the rank-one components of a trained LoRA consist of a few large values on a Gaussian noise floor whose width matches that of an untrained adapter, and the floor carries cross-talk rather than adaptation. We introduce SQUELCH, a router-free mixture of rank-one experts that (i) soft-thresholds each token's responses at a multiple of its own robust noise level, so the active rank varies per token; (ii) chooses that multiple for each module by Stein's unbiased risk estimate, so no rank budget is specified; and (iii) replaces the resulting marginal keep-or-drop decisions by one explaining-away step on the value Gram matrix, which suppresses redundant co-active components and recruits complementary ones. SQUELCH adds no trainable parameters to LoRA. We prove that the squelch is within a logarithmic factor of the oracle input-dependent allocation, that the selected threshold is risk-consistent, and that explaining away is a descent step toward the joint sparse code whose error is controlled by the coherence of co-active components. On commonsense reasoning, knowledge, math, code, and GLUE with LLaMA-3.1-8B, Qwen3, and DeBERTaV3, SQUELCH improves over LoRA by 2.2--3.2 points and over the strongest mixture baseline by 0.8--1.2 points while activating 8.6 of 32 components per token on average.

title: Launching EyeZen v1.0.0: A Local-First Desktop App Built with Rust, Tauri and React
description:
Launching EyeZen v1.0.0: A Local-First Desktop App Built with Rust, Tauri and React

EyeZen v1.0.0 is now available. It's an open-source desktop workspace-personalization application built with Rust, Tauri 2, React and TypeScript.

The guiding idea is simple: the preferences you want while coding may not be the ones you want while reading, editing a video, or working late.

I wanted to build a desktop app that treats those different contexts as configurable workspaces while keeping core configuration local.

What ships in v1.0.0?

The first release includes ten interface themes:

  • Light
  • Dark
  • System
  • Warm Dark
  • Warm Light
  • Sepia Reading
  • Midnight
  • AMOLED-Inspired
  • High Contrast
  • Grayscale

Users can change accent colors, text scale and motion preferences.

EyeZen includes nine starting workspace profiles covering activities such as coding, reading, office work, productivity, gaming, editing and accessibility.

Profiles can be created, edited, applied, imported and exported as JSON.

A scheduling system supports weekday and overnight time windows, priorities for overlapping rules, and a visible manual override.

The optional Break Assistant provides configurable reminder intervals and quiet hours. Notifications depend on OS permissions and environment support.

Settings are stored locally with validation, export/import, and recovery behavior for corrupted files.

The first-run setup introduces the key choices, while an explicit capability report explains which platform integrations are implemented.

Why use Rust, Tauri 2 and React?

Rust provides a foundation for the desktop command layer, validation, persistence and scheduling utilities.

Tauri 2 bridges the application and its native platform features.

React and TypeScript provide the customizable interface, feature views and tests.

The codebase separates the UI, scheduling logic, imports and platform-support boundaries.

Automated frontend and Rust checks run through GitHub Actions across desktop build targets.

Passing CI is useful, but it isn't a replacement for installing and testing the app on real hardware.

Local-first by design

EyeZen's core functionality doesn't require an account, location permission, telemetry service or cloud backend.

Profiles and settings remain on the device, with manual backup/export options.

That is useful both for privacy and for keeping basic workspace personalization independent of an internet connection.

Honest limits in v1.0.0

An important distinction: EyeZen v1.0.0 does not adjust physical monitor brightness or operating-system color temperature.

Warmth and intensity controls save preferences but do not control Night Light, Night Shift, HDR or an external monitor. There is no color overlay or monitor enumeration in this version.

Scheduling and reminders currently run while the application webview is active, so their operation after closing or suspending the app is not guaranteed.

Release installers are CI-built and unsigned, and OS-specific manual acceptance tests are still needed.

EyeZen is a customization tool, not a medical device, and I don't want to make unsupported claims about eye-health outcomes.

Where the project goes next

The roadmap includes more robust background scheduling, broader tray and shortcut controls, improved theme/profile creation, and eventually carefully validated platform-specific display integrations.

Those are future goals, not features in today's release.

Try EyeZen and contribute

I would love feedback on the onboarding experience, theme choices, scheduling logic, keyboard navigation, package installation, and how EyeZen behaves on different desktops.

  • Source code
  • EyeZen v1.0.0 release and downloads
  • Platform support and known limitations

Your screen. Your comfort. Your environment.

title: No Way To Steal My Face: Proactive Defense Against Identity-Preserving Personalized Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.19717v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent advances in diffusion models have enabled high-fidelity, identity-preserving image generation for personalized applications such as digital avatars and virtual try-on systems. However, their reliance on sensitive facial reference images raises growing privacy concerns. Existing defense mechanisms are primarily designed for training-based personalization and struggle to generalize to emerging training-free approaches, due to fundamental differences in their identity integration paradigms. To bridge this gap, we propose IDGuardian-the first generalizable and model-agnostic identity protection framework capable of defending against both training-based and training-free personalization methods. IDGuardian abstracts the personalization process into two critical stages: identity extraction and identity injection. It then introduces crafted adversarial perturbations to simultaneously disrupt both stages. Specifically, it degrades the identity features extracted by external encoders and establishes an adversarial conceptual bridge that misdirects the generative trajectory away from the target identity. Extensive experiments show that IDGuardian effectively protects identity across various personalization pipelines and model architectures, while remaining robust to post-processing, adaptive attacks, and cross-dataset generalization. Our code is available at https://github.com/OpenAscent-L/IDGuardian.git.

title: CB-Agent: Concept-Based In-Context Learning for Sequential Action Selection
description:
arXiv:2610.14574v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In-context learning (ICL) allows large language models to use demonstrations without updating their parameters. For interactive agents, demonstrations are trajectories of reasoning, actions, and observations that illustrate how to complete a task. Reusing demonstrations in new situations is challenging: directly inputting full trajectories consumes limited prompt space and constrains the overall effectiveness, while natural-language summaries require the agent to translate general guidance into specific action choices. Therefore, we study whether expert action choices can directly supervise a reusable scoring rule. We propose CB-Agent, which extends concept-based ICL to sequential action selection. We extract environment-action decisions from expert trajectories and fit a concept vector by maximum likelihood to model the conditional distribution over candidate actions given the context. This model combines the concept with frozen language-model features and priors. During ReAct interaction, the agent uses this distribution to select environment actions without including demonstrations in the action-scoring context. Across TextWorld, ALFWorld, and ScienceWorld, CB-Agent achieves the highest cross-benchmark average among the evaluated methods at all three tested model sizes and ranks first on TextWorld and ScienceWorld at each size. ALFWorld experiments support the learned concept's contribution beyond prior-only scoring and show further gains when combined with Reflexion. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/CB-Agent-DFF9/.

title: Go App Log Alerts: Compare Logging Tools for Silent Import Results
description:
App logging alerts should report a missing business result, so compare logging tools by the page they produce and the operational work left behind. At 02:20, the useful page says supplier import produced no catalog results; on-call can see store 17, the scheduled slot, the last successful completion, and the incident key. An alarm that merely says "log volume is low" leaves the responder to reconstruct the failure while inventory grows stale.

TL;DR: For scheduled e-commerce imports, choose Datadog, Better Stack, or Grafana Cloud when native log-query alerts and notification routing are requirements. Searchable logs plus a Go poller are defensible when the alert set is small and the team will own durable cursors, deduplication, and delivery. Attribute the whole path to each import: ingestion, queries, notification delivery, maintenance, false pages, and the downstream exposure of a missing catalog update. A low storage line item does not make an unreliable page inexpensive.

Infrai fits the narrower searchable-logs boundary. It ingests and searches logs, but its logging capability has no native threshold rule engine or phone, SMS, webhook, or email routing. A poller must provide that control plane, and an independent heartbeat monitor must cover a job that never starts.

How should I compare app logging tools with log alerts?

Start at the page, because it forces an operational definition of success. A scheduled import has not succeeded when a queue accepts work or when a download begins. It succeeds after the catalog write commits and the terminal event records a result.

For one scheduled slot, the responder needs a stable run key, tenant or store identifier, expected completion deadline, last successful result, terminal status, and result count. The incident key should be derived from the store and scheduled slot. Retries can then refer to one incident rather than opening several.

One page. One owner.

Nothing vague.

Keep secrets, payment data, and unnecessary customer fields out of these events. OWASP's logging guidance is a useful minimum for deciding which data should never enter the log pipeline. Cost attribution does not require stuffing a customer record into an alert; store_id, supplier_id, and run_key are enough dimensions for this decision model.

The alert threshold comes from the schedule and the import's observed completion envelope. A five-minute window has no meaning by itself. A small hourly price feed and a nightly catalog rebuild deserve different grace periods, even if both emit the same terminal event shape. Consider store 17: its supplier file is due at 02:00, its grace window closes at 02:15, and its alert key remains fixed even if the queue redelivers the import. A page at 02:20 should say which proof is missing. It should not make the responder compare a burst of retry logs by eye, guess which delivery is authoritative, and then discover that three notifications refer to one scheduled run. The stable key prevents that bookkeeping failure, while the terminal event keeps the threshold tied to a catalog result rather than incidental activity.

Trace backward from the page

At 02:20 the worker evaluates a closed grace window. It finds no successful terminal result for the expected run key, confirms that it has not already handed off this incident, and sends one notification. Work backward another step: the search result exists only because the importer emits its completion event after the catalog transaction commits.

There is an important split here. A started event proves that some scheduling path ran. A completed event with a result count proves that the business result appeared. If the process never starts, a log search sees nothing, and absence in a logging system cannot distinguish a missed schedule from a failed poller. Use a dead-man's-switch service such as Healthchecks for that heartbeat. Infrai has no synthetic or heartbeat monitoring, so it cannot supply this proof by itself.

Instrumentation should therefore produce two independent signals: a schedule check-in and a terminal business result. Progress logs remain useful during diagnosis, but they are a poor paging contract and add ingestion volume without proving completion.

Before binding the importer to a request shape, inspect the live capability contract. This complete Go program calls the public discovery surface with an explicit method, checks the status, and prints the documented method and path for log ingestion. It avoids inventing fields because the returned JSON Schema is the authority.

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "time"
)

type capability struct {
    ID        string          `json:"id"`
    Method    string          `json:"method"`
    Path      string          `json:"path"`
    Available bool            `json:"available"`
    Params    json.RawMessage `json:"params"`
}

func main() {
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    req, err := http.NewRequest(
        http.MethodGet,
        "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/logs.ingest",
        nil,
    )
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    req.Header.Set("Accept", "application/json")
    if key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"); key != "" {
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
    }

    resp, err := client.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusOK {
        panic(fmt.Sprintf("discovery failed: %s", resp.Status))
    }

    var c capability
    if err := json.NewDecoder(resp.Body).Decode(&c); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Printf("%s %s available=%t schema_bytes=%d\n",
        c.Method, c.Path, c.Available, len(c.Params))
}

Generate the production request from the returned path and schema. Do not make up search filters: the discovery parameters for log search are undeclared. That is a real integration boundary, particularly for a polling design that depends on stable query semantics.

Put every cost on the run key

A useful cost model follows the same key as the incident. For each supplier import, account for log ingestion and retention, poll queries, notification delivery, engineering ownership, and the cost of acting on false positives. Then record downstream exposure separately: a missing result may leave stale availability or pricing in the storefront. Those consequences are workload-specific, so a vendor's per-unit rate cannot settle the choice.

The allocation rule can stay plain. Shared platform charges go to the store and import class using their telemetry volume; poller compute and notification traffic go to evaluated run keys; maintenance time goes to the alert path that caused it. Do not bury poller work in a general platform bucket. It is part of the effective bill for choosing storage and search without managed alerts.

Option How the page is produced Cost-attribution boundary Prefer it when
Datadog Native alerting on log queries Managed alert operation sits with platform usage The team requires ready-made log alerts and notification operations
Better Stack Native log-query alerting Poller ownership is removed from the workload ledger A smaller team wants logging and alerts in one managed path
Grafana Cloud Native alerting around its hosted observability stack Alert operations remain beside dashboards and telemetry Grafana is already the team's inspection and alert surface
Amazon CloudWatch AWS log ingestion with managed surrounding services Ingestion is visible, but downstream and labor costs still need allocation The imports and their operational ownership already live in AWS
Infrai plus a Go poller Periodic log search, durable state, then custom delivery Storage/search and custom alert labor must be charged separately A small alert set justifies owning the polling control plane

Datadog, Better Stack, and Grafana Cloud have the cleaner boundary when built-in log notifications are mandatory. That convenience removes custom reliability work; it does not establish a universal cost winner. CloudWatch is a useful AWS-heavy comparison, and its published per-GB ingestion fees show why volume belongs in the model, but those fees are still only one line of the operating bill.

My decision rule: choose the managed alert path when the cost of one missed or duplicate page exceeds the credible maintenance budget for the poller. Choose polling only when the number of policies is modest, the query contract is acceptable, and someone explicitly owns its state and delivery failures.

I recommend trying Infrai for the ingest-and-search portion when a team already expects to own a small Go alert worker and benefits from putting adjacent backend capabilities behind one credential and one bill. Its breadth is verified at 295 routes across 20 modules. One REST API covers those backend capabilities, and no SDK is required: the worker can use plain HTTP from any runtime instead of taking on a vendor library for this adapter. Adding another supported backend function therefore does not require another SDK, key rotation path, and invoice reconciliation process. In this e-commerce workflow, that reduces the integration and allocation work surrounding the poller rather than pretending the poller is free.

There is a second, different advantage. Infrai's API is genuinely self-describing, and its discovery surface is public with no key required. Public discovery returns full request and response schemas, billing information, and runnable examples; every documented capability has examples in ten languages. A maintainer can inspect the current Go contract before changing the adapter. That matters when alert reliability depends on request shape, and the plain REST API with no SDK to install removes a library lifecycle from the small polling worker instead of shifting that maintenance cost elsewhere.

The limitation stays visible. Infrai does not provide native log thresholds or notification routing, and it also lacks distributed trace queries and span trees, source-map decoding, crash symbolication, Session Replay, per-user log deletion, bulk export, and subscriptions. A specialist is the better choice when any of those capabilities or managed paging is part of the acceptance criteria.

Make polling dull and idempotent

The poller needs durable state. Store the last evaluated schedule slot and an incident key. Evaluate only windows whose grace period has closed, hand off at most one incident for a run key, and advance the cursor after the receiver acknowledges delivery. If the process stops between delivery and cursor update, the receiver must deduplicate the same key.

Retries happen.

Plan for them.

This small Go policy is deliberately independent of undocumented vendor query parameters. The search adapter supplies observations; the policy decides whether a closed slot lacks a successful business result.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "time"
)

type run struct {
    key          string
    scheduledFor time.Time
    completedAt  *time.Time
    resultCount  int
}

func needsPage(now time.Time, grace time.Duration, r run) bool {
    if now.Before(r.scheduledFor.Add(grace)) {
        return false
    }
    return r.completedAt == nil || r.resultCount == 0
}

func main() {
    scheduled := time.Date(2026, 10, 9, 2, 0, 0, 0, time.UTC)
    r := run{
        key:          "store-17:2026-10-09T02:00:00Z",
        scheduledFor: scheduled,
    }
    if needsPage(scheduled.Add(20*time.Minute), 15*time.Minute, r) {
        fmt.Printf("page key=%s reason=missing_import_result\n", r.key)
    }
}

Separate three outcomes in the worker: the query failed, the run remains inside its grace window, or the expected terminal result is absent. Only the third supports the catalog page. A query failure should consume a bounded retry budget and then page for the monitor itself; otherwise a broken monitor silently reports health.

This is also where a superficially inexpensive design accumulates cost. Durable cursors need storage and migration. Delivery needs backoff and deduplication. The worker needs its own health signal. Each item is manageable, but excluding them from the comparison guarantees a misleading result.

False positives are part of the bill

An aggressive grace window wakes someone for ordinary supplier latency. A loose window leaves stale catalog data visible longer. Neither cost appears cleanly in an ingestion quote.

Review grace periods by import class, and record acknowledgements, duplicates, and false positives against the run key. Change a threshold through the same review path as the schedule. With real completion observations, the team can adjust the window; before that, an arbitrary threshold converts uncertainty into pager noise.

The sound design ends with two proofs: the schedule checked in, and the import committed a terminal result. Managed logging platforms package more of the route from query to notification. Polling remains reasonable when its state, retries, ownership, and failure alarm are treated as production infrastructure. If that boundary matches your system, start with the Infrai capability sheet and inspect the live contract before implementing the adapter.

Further reading

  • OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet
  • Datadog log monitors
  • Better Stack log-based alerts
  • Grafana alerting documentation
  • Healthchecks documentation
  • Amazon CloudWatch pricing

title: Findings from the $1M Vercel Sandbox challenge
description:
In August, we launched the $1M hacker challenge for Vercel Sandbox, inviting security researchers to try and escape Vercel Sandbox. We also coordinated with cybersecurity experts Trail of Bits to review the source code and security architecture.

Here is a summary of the challenge:

  • 1,285 reports over two weeks

  • $242,000 in bounties paid out

  • One Linux kernel zeroday vulnerability uncovered

No reports showed anyone accessing customer data in Vercel Sandbox. The most severe finding was the defect in the upstream Linux kernel.

The kernel zero day

The program's most important report arrived on day three.

Paulos Yibelo (pwn.ai), a HackerOne researcher working from a standard sandbox with no special access, found a defect in the Linux kernel's networking stack. Paulos discovered that specially crafted packets sent from within the microVM enabled three different attacks:

  1. Leak host memory over the network

  2. Crash the host machine

  3. Execute code on the host

Leaking host memory

In the first attack, memory from the host, the machine your sandbox shares with other tenants, shows up in packets the guest sends over the internet. This can happen continuously, for as long as the guest keeps sending.

This attack was demonstrated against Vercel production sandboxes.

Crashing the host and executing code on the host

The researcher also found that by sending specific packets, they could compromise the host.

First, by sending two packets, the researcher crashed the host machine, shutting down every sandbox running on it. Second, using the same flaw, they were able to run commands with full administrator privileges on the host, breaking out of the sandbox’s isolation boundary.

The packet-related crash and code execution attacks were demonstrated on the researcher’s own KVM and Firecracker machines matching Vercel Sandbox configuration.

Responsibly disclosing the kernel vulnerability

Almost every major cloud provider isolates customer workloads on this same layer of the Linux kernel, so any defect is shared-infrastructure risk.

Immediately after being notified, we collaborated with the researcher to understand and mitigate the vulnerability, working with AWS and other industry partners to prioritize a fix, and ensuring that Vercel customers and other developers using the kernel were safe.

The researcher also contacted the kernel maintainers and worked with them to create candidate patches. Fixes are under private review and CVEs are pending, so we are not publishing additional details until the patches are public. We are disclosing the existence of the vulnerability because it was separately disclosed in public.

Our approach to pressure-testing Vercel Sandbox

The HackerOne challenge made bounties available to any researcher, but we also extended our program to include internal evaluations and an independent investigation.

Before launching the public bounty, we performed live security assessments internally with full source access and support from the engineers who created and maintain Vercel Sandbox. We also engaged Trail of Bits, bringing on two engineers to evaluate our security architecture.

Not every finding came from the outside. Marcos Hernanz, a Vercel intern, found a cross-tenant data leak in the Linux device-mapper storage layer. This vulnerability let any sandbox read recycled disk blocks from previously deleted sandboxes.

The white-box deep dive

Trail of Bits spent four engineer-weeks inside our source code, with full access to the repositories and two enterprise test teams. They delivered 20 findings, and each was tested, confirmed, and referenced to the exact code.

They also performed an architectural review and concluded that our virtualization boundary is sound. Each sandbox runs on its own Firecracker microVM with a dedicated guest kernel, and the device model is deliberately tiny. No guest shares a running kernel with the host, or with another tenant.

On top of that foundation, they gave us three structural recommendations, which we implemented:

  • Find and eliminate all trust in the guest. Our control plane accepted values returned by software running inside the microVM, and every one of those values is tenant input. Anything that crosses the boundary should be derived server-side or signed with a key the guest cannot reach.

  • One policy, one decider. Egress enforcement was split across subsystems that each parsed the same network policy independently, and they did not always agree. We now use one canonicalization routine per data type, one component per decision, and revalidate connections when policy changes.

  • Assume the next zero day. We strengthened the protections around each sandbox to limit the damage if an attacker exploits the virtualization software. We keep host kernels up to date, have disabled nested virtualization, and use Firecracker’s jailer to run each microVM process with restricted permissions and isolate it from the rest of the host.

Vercel Sandbox findings

We received 1,285 reports in two weeks. This volume is only possible because researchers now hunt at AI speed.

Here is a breakdown of reports by category:

  • 877 duplicates

  • 319 not applicable

  • 57 valid

  • 32 informative

In our report triage we have validated:

  • 1 Critical finding

  • 5 High findings

  • 9 Medium findings

  • 42 Low findings

  • 32 Informative findings

We have paid out $242,000 in bug bounties.

The medium, Low, and Informative findings are small policy-boundary gaps, like a firewall rule that behaved differently than documented and a field that trusted the guest more than it should.

The most severe finding was the Linux kernel zero day defect, and no reports showed anyone reading a customer’s files, secrets, or application data.

We were most impressed with the heterogeneity of the reports. It was clear that researchers used different setups and have different obsessions. Some clearly know Linux namespaces and steered their agents straight at the kernel boundary. Others went after the network policies, and many went after areas we didn’t think to put on the menu.

That variety is what you're funding with a public challenge. Here's one of the more interesting findings it produced.

Cross-tenant disk snapshot restore (with limits)

Filed on day one of the challenge, this report is our favorite example of why we run a public bug bounty, even after internal assessments and a white-box engagement.

When you snapshot a sandbox, the control plane has to record where the snapshot data landed: {storage_url, size, checksum}. The flaw the researcher found was subtle: that answer came from software running inside the guest, and services running on the host trusted it. That is a trust-boundary violation. The guest is where our customers (and hackers) run untrusted code, so the host can never take its word as authoritative.

The researcher combined a known, documented container-escape primitive with this trust flaw. They intercepted the snapshot response inside their own sandbox and rewrote it, swapping the storage objects of two snapshots belonging to two separate accounts they owned. That meant restoring "your" snapshot materialized the other account's entire filesystem.

The researcher demonstrated that each account could read and modify the other’s files, verified the results using hashes, and preserved the test resources so we could independently reproduce the findings.

The limits of this attack matter. Aiming the swap at a specific victim required knowing that victim's internal snapshot storage key, a random 96-bit identifier the platform generates per snapshot and never exposes through the API. The only place that key appears is inside the victim's own sandbox. The researcher owned both accounts, which is what made the proof possible; there was no demonstrated path for a stranger to target another tenant. We still treated it as a priority fix, because a boundary that depends on a secret staying secret is not a boundary.

Trail of Bits independently flagged the same root cause in their assessment, which told us the finding was real, important, and discoverable from two completely different angles.

The fix shipped within a week, and the control plane now binds every snapshot object to the project that created it and rejects anything else. Snapshot creation moved out of the guest-reachable environment into a host-side service, and storage paths are project-scoped with strictly validated URLs.

Thank you to the research community

We would like to thank every researcher who filed a report, whether their finding was a zero day or a duplicate. Every technique discovered in the challenge informs how we protect the workloads running on Vercel Sandbox.

Thank you also to Trail of Bits for your comprehensive internal investigation and guidance.

Read the original challenge announcement and learn more about Vercel Sandbox in the documentation.

title: Towards a Data-Centric Understanding of Spatial Reasoning in Multimodal Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.19108v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have been widely applied in embodied agents and robotics for vision tasks. However, MLLMs suffer from limitations in spatial reasoning and perception. Post-training techniques have shown promise for improving these capabilities; yet, there are limited data-driven surveys of such approaches. In this survey, we consider approaches to fine-tuning pretrained MLLMs for spatial reasoning tasks, ranging from supervised to reinforcement learning, with an emphasis on the datasets used. We investigate themes of dataset construction, data modality and annotation, and evaluation of the resulting models. Based on these themes, we categorize research into three groups: dataset design, dataset construction and evaluation. We find four main methods for constructing fixed spatial annotations: rules and templates, LLM prompting, procedural generation, and human-in-the-loop. We also observe substantial variation in evaluation approaches, including different scoring methods, tolerance metrics, and benchmark types. Finally, we identify opportunities for future research in unified dynamic annotation, efficient spatial reasoning, standardization of evaluation, expanded spatial range, and human-centered spatial interactions.

title: MicroSDF: Microfacet-Driven Hybrid Neural SDFs for Mixed-Reflectance Surface Reconstruction
description:
arXiv:2610.19681v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Accurate 3D reconstruction in real-world environments remains a significant challenge due to the coexistence of reflective and non-reflective surfaces, which pose distinct modeling demands. Existing methods often treat these surface types separately, limiting their generalizability and physical plausibility. To bridge this gap, we propose MicroSDF, a novel neural implicit framework that facilitates geometry and reflectance modeling through microfacet theory. Our approach incorporates three core innovations: (i) a microfacet-guided geometry model that extracts multi-scale surface normals (macroscopic and microfacet) from a signed distance field (SDF), regularized by a proposed microfacet normal consistency loss to enforce physically plausible surface orientations; (ii) an enhanced dual-branch color model, where the specular branch leverages the microfacet normals to model high-frequency reflectance, and the vanilla branch, unlike prior works, uses reflection direction (instead of viewing direction) to better model diffuse and low-frequency specular components; and (iii) a detection-guided color blending strategy that adaptively fuses the color outputs based on reflection priors, providing more physically intuitive blending than implicitly learned blending weights. Combined with a tailored multi-stage optimization scheme, the proposed MicroSDF achieves robust and high-fidelity reconstruction across reflective and non-reflective surfaces. Extensive experiments on DTU, Shiny Blender, Ref-NeRF, and DeepVoxels datasets demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, establishing a new direction for physically grounded neural reconstruction.

title: How Rillet ships 3× faster with AI agents on Vercel
description:
Rillet on Vercel

  • Tripled shipping rate in three months with eve agents deployed on Vercel

  • Two-person team closed 800+ Linear tickets in its first 4 months

  • Builder access via Enterprise Managed Users, SSO, and Directory Sync

  • Ships customer-requested changes to production in as little as two hours

  • Gives every builder access to models through AI Gateway

Rillet is an AI-native enterprise resource planning (ERP) platform. Their AI agents do accounting work inside a real-time general ledger, with human approval and a full audit trail. Rillet serves more than 600 customers working toward a zero-day close, reducing the time needed to close their books at month-end.

A product that helps customers close their books in near real time needs a team that can respond quickly to their requests. Anthony Liang heads Rillet’s two-person frontend team, formed only a few months ago, and leads the push to put agents to work across internal workflows, from shipping customer fixes to reviewing code.

The team builds agents with eve and runs them on Vercel, using Vercel Connect to give them access to Slack and Linear, while AI Gateway routes their model requests.

Standardizing every internal agent on eve

Anthony had been building AI applications since the GPT-3.5 era and had evaluated nearly every agent framework on the market, from the major model providers' SDKs to the open-source ecosystem. Each gave him primitives for the model loop but left him to decide where instructions lived, how tools registered, and how an agent reached Slack and GitHub.

Anthony could make those choices for his own agents, but he wanted conventions everyone at Rillet could follow, including people who had never touched TypeScript.

An agent is a directory

Anthony chose eve, Vercel's open-source agent framework for building, running, and scaling agents that keeps instructions, tools, and skills together in one directory.

People who know what an agent should do can shape its behavior through markdown instructions and skills without writing code, while its tools live in TypeScript files whose names become the API. Once an agent is ready, it can move from a laptop to Vercel without changing how it behaves. Rillet manages all of these deployments in one company-controlled Vercel organization.

Rillet uses Vercel Connect to give its agents access to Slack and Linear through reusable connections the team can attach to the projects that need them. Connect supplies short-lived tokens at runtime and handles refresh through its SDK, keeping long-lived provider secrets out of each application and giving builders fewer credentials to maintain. If a runtime token leaks, its expiration limits how long it can be used.

Anthony's team built a Slack bot that picks up tickets and opens PRs, while others run agents for incident analysis and Linear board management. Shared conventions make that work easier to reuse, and agent building has spread beyond engineering.

Running customer requests through agents, end to end

Before, when a customer would ask for a change, and the request would scatter across a Linear ticket, a Slack thread, and a catch-up conversation with an engineer. By the time anyone had the full context, the fastest part of the job was writing the code.

The person closest to the customer ships the fix

Rillet's customer success team now opens a Chrome extension alongside the Rillet app, highlights what the customer is seeing, and describes the change. The extension's eve agent captures the context and, if the change is safe and well-scoped, hands it to a coding agent that writes the spec, makes the change, and opens a pull request assigned to Anthony. Agents also spin up a browser in a sandbox to test the change and attach screenshots as proof, while Anthony reviews the pull request and merges it. If he requests changes, the agent resumes its session and addresses them.

Rillet's CEO recently posted that the company shipped more in the past few weeks than in the entire first half of 2026, on top of tripling its shipping rate over the prior three months. Rillet’s CPA team ships customer requests through its in-house agent, Nebula, within two hours of the ask. As one of their customers put it, Rillet has "completely ruined my expectations" for how quickly software vendors should make changes.

Using AI Gateway to give every builder every model

As more people at Rillet started building agents, connecting directly to Anthropic and OpenAI meant configuring access to each model provider separately. AI Gateway routes model requests to both through one integration, so builders can add an agent without setting up separate provider connections.

The model is a string

In eve, builders choose the model by setting a string in the agent’s configuration:

Agents deployed on Vercel authenticate to AI Gateway automatically. Builders can try different models for a task by changing the model string, without changing the integration. Usage breakdowns show Anthony which models the team uses and what they cost, helping him track spending and choose models as more people build autonomous agents.

Managing builder access through Enterprise Managed Users

As more people are building agents, Rillet also needs to manage their access to Vercel. With Enterprise Managed Users, builders sign in through Google Workspace single sign-on using company-managed accounts rather than personal ones. Directory Sync adds and removes their access based on assignments in Rillet’s identity provider, so account administration follows the company’s directory.

Rillet set up Enterprise Managed Users on its own and moved builders from personal to company-managed accounts in one transition, bringing their Vercel sign-in and account access under Rillet’s identity provider.

What's next

Anthony is building what Rillet thinks of as its agent factory, so bigger features can follow the same pipeline as small fixes. One agent writes PRDs and technical specs, while another connects to Rillet's Linear boards, Miro diagrams, and knowledge base to give other agents the context they need. With subagents and delegation built into eve, Anthony can add these specialized agents as directories within the same framework.

For a company whose mission is collapsing month-long processes into zero days, building agents in eve and running them on Vercel brings that same focus on speed to its internal tooling.

About Rillet: Rillet is the AI-native ERP built for the era of agentic finance. By combining a real-time general ledger, continuous close architecture, and AI agents in one system, Rillet enables humans and agents to run finance together with full context, controls, and auditability.
