title: PCAD-31-02 in Code: Validation Checks and Safe sqlite3 Queries Behind 30 of the 48 Items
description:
The Python Institute PCAD-31-02 exam has 48 items, and 30 of them come from two syllabus blocks: Data Acquisition and Pre-Processing (14) and Programming and Database Skills (16). If you can clean a messy file, validate it, move it into a database with safe queries and read the result back into pandas, you have practised the skills behind 62.5% of the exam.

This post does all of that in one small script you can run. Every output shown below was produced by running it with Python 3.12 and pandas 3.0.6, using only sqlite3 from the standard library for the database part.

What does the PCAD-31-02 exam look like?

PCAD (Certified Associate Data Analyst with Python) is the associate-level data exam of the OpenEDG Python Institute. The figures below come from the official PCAD certification page, read on 15 October 2026.

Item Value
Exam code PCAD-31-02, active since July 15, 2025 (PCAD-31-01 retired July 14, 2025)
Questions 48 single-select and multiple-select items, some scenario-based
Time 60 minutes, plus the NDA screen
Passing score 75%
Price Exam from $195; exam with retake from $225; practice test $49
Delivery Online through OpenEDG Testing Service (TestNow)
Prerequisites None formal; PCAP and PCED (or equivalent) recommended
Validity 6 years

How are the 48 items split across the five blocks?

The Python Institute publishes the split in the PCAD-31-02 exam syllabus, last updated July 15, 2025. Each item is worth up to one point, and the raw score is normalized to a percentage.

Block Items Weight
1. Data Acquisition and Pre-Processing 14 29.2%
2. Programming and Database Skills 16 33.3%
3. Statistical Analysis 4 8.3%
4. Data Analysis and Modeling 9 18.8%
5. Data Communication and Visualization 5 10.4%

Note what that means for your study plan. Blocks 1 and 2 are the bulk, but 30 of 48 is still below the 75% pass mark, so the statistics, pandas and charting blocks cannot be skipped. The script below covers the large blocks; it also touches objective 4.1.1 (cleaning with pandas) on the way.

Why load every column as text first?

Objective 1.2.2 asks you to identify erroneous data before you fix it. If pandas guesses types on load, a bad value can silently change a whole column's type, and you lose the chance to see which rows were wrong. Loading with dtype=str keeps the raw values so the cleaning step decides what each one means.

Here is a small order file with the problems the syllabus lists by name: stray spaces, mixed case, a thousands separator, a missing value written as text, a negative amount, a duplicate row, a date in the wrong format and five spellings of yes and no.

import io
import sqlite3

import pandas as pd

pd.set_option("display.width", 120, "display.max_columns", 10)   # print tables in full

RAW = """order_id,customer,country,amount,paid,order_date,ship_date
1001,  Ana Lima ,BR,120.50,yes,2026-09-01,2026-09-03
1002,ben okafor,NG,"1,080.00",Y,2026-09-02,2026-09-01
1003,Chen Wei,CN,n/a,no,2026-09-02,2026-09-05
1004,Ana Lima,br,-15,TRUE,2026-09-03,2026-09-04
1004,Ana Lima,br,-15,TRUE,2026-09-03,2026-09-04
1005,Dara Singh,IN,64.00,0,03/09/2026,2026-09-06
1006,Ben Okafor,NG,310.00,1,2026-09-04,2026-09-07
1007,Chen Wei,cn,89.90,yes,2026-09-05,2026-09-05
1008,Dara Singh,IN,455.00,N,2026-09-06,2026-09-09
1009,ana lima,BR,72.25,y,2026-09-07,2026-09-08
"""
df = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(RAW), dtype=str)
print(len(df), "rows")   # 10 rows

Which cleaning steps does Block 1 name, and what do they look like?

Objective 1.2.4 lists them in one sentence: string manipulation, format standardization, boolean normalization, case normalization and string-to-number conversion. Each one is a single line in pandas.

BOOL = {"yes": True, "y": True, "true": True, "1": True,
        "no": False, "n": False, "false": False, "0": False}

df = df.drop_duplicates()
df["customer"] = df["customer"].str.strip().str.title()
df["country"] = df["country"].str.strip().str.upper()
df["amount"] = pd.to_numeric(df["amount"].str.replace(",", ""), errors="coerce")
df["paid"] = df["paid"].str.strip().str.lower().map(BOOL)
for col in ("order_date", "ship_date"):
    df[col] = pd.to_datetime(df[col], format="%Y-%m-%d", errors="coerce")
df["order_id"] = df["order_id"].astype(int)
print(df.dtypes)

order_id               int64
customer                 str
country                  str
amount               float64
paid                    bool
order_date    datetime64[us]
ship_date     datetime64[us]
dtype: object

The key argument is errors="coerce". As the pandas.to_numeric reference explains, it turns a value that cannot be parsed into NaN instead of raising an exception. That is what you want during cleaning: the bad value becomes a marker you can count and report, not a crash halfway through a file.

The same idea applies to dates. Passing an explicit format means 03/09/2026 becomes NaT rather than being guessed as March 9 or September 3. Whether that date was day-first or month-first is a question for the data owner, not for the parser.

What do type, range and cross-field checks look like in pandas?

Objective 1.3.1 names three kinds of validation: type, range and cross-field. Build each check as a boolean column, then keep the rows where no check fired. A table of named checks is easier to report to a stakeholder than a chain of filters.

checks = pd.DataFrame({
    "amount_not_numeric": df["amount"].isna(),            # type
    "order_date_unparsed": df["order_date"].isna(),       # type
    "amount_not_positive": df["amount"] <= 0,             # range
    "shipped_before_order": df["ship_date"] < df["order_date"],  # cross-field
})
bad = checks.any(axis=1)
print(checks[bad].set_axis(df.loc[bad, "order_id"]))
clean = df[~bad]
print(len(clean), "rows pass")

          amount_not_numeric  order_date_unparsed  amount_not_positive  shipped_before_order
order_id
1002                   False                False                False                  True
1003                    True                False                False                 False
1004                   False                False                 True                 False
1005                   False                 True                False                 False
5 rows pass

Two details are worth knowing for the exam. First, a comparison with NaN or NaT is always False, so a missing amount does not trip the range check; that is why the type check exists separately. Second, the duplicate of order 1004 was already gone, because drop_duplicates() ran before validation. Removing or imputing a row is a decision with consequences, and objective 1.2.4 asks you to discuss imputation against exclusion. Here exclusion is the honest choice: there is no sensible value to invent for a missing order amount.

How do Python types map to SQLite columns?

Objective 2.4.5 is about converting data types between SQL and Python. The sqlite3 module documentation lists exactly five Python types that go into SQLite without help: None, int, float, str and bytes.

Python value SQLite storage What to do
None NULL Nothing
int INTEGER Nothing
float REAL Nothing
str TEXT Nothing
bool INTEGER (0 or 1) Store as int(value)
datetime or pandas Timestamp No date type Store as ISO 8601 text

SQLite has no boolean and no date storage class. The SQLite page on datatypes and type affinity says booleans are stored as the integers 0 and 1, and dates as ISO 8601 text, a real number or an integer. Here is what happens if you skip the conversion:

con = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
con.execute("""
CREATE TABLE orders (
    order_id   INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    customer   TEXT    NOT NULL,
    country    TEXT    NOT NULL,
    amount     REAL    CHECK (amount > 0),
    paid       INTEGER NOT NULL,
    order_date TEXT    NOT NULL
)""")
first = clean.iloc[0]
try:
    con.execute("INSERT INTO orders VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)",
                (first["order_id"], first["customer"], first["country"],
                 first["amount"], first["paid"], first["order_date"]))
except sqlite3.ProgrammingError as e:
    print("ProgrammingError:", e)

ProgrammingError: Error binding parameter 6: type 'Timestamp' is not supported

So convert each row explicitly and insert the batch with executemany. The with con: block commits on success and rolls back on an exception, and the CHECK constraint in the table is a second line of defence for the range rule:

rows = [
    (int(r.order_id), r.customer, r.country, float(r.amount),
     int(r.paid), r.order_date.strftime("%Y-%m-%d"))
    for r in clean.itertuples(index=False)
]
with con:
    con.executemany("INSERT INTO orders VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)", rows)
print(con.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders").fetchone())   # (5,)

try:
    with con:
        con.execute("INSERT INTO orders VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)",
                    (1010, "Eve Park", "KR", -5.0, 1, "2026-09-08"))
except sqlite3.IntegrityError as e:
    print("IntegrityError:", e)   # CHECK constraint failed: amount > 0

Why does the exam keep asking about parameterized queries?

Two Block 2 objectives, 2.4.4 and 2.4.6, come back to the same point: never build SQL by pasting values into a string. The demonstration takes four lines.

name = "x' OR '1'='1"
unsafe = f"SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE customer = '{name}'"
print(con.execute(unsafe).fetchone())        # (5,)  every row matched
print(con.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE customer = ?", (name,)).fetchone())   # (0,)
print(con.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE customer = :who",
                  {"who": "Ana Lima"}).fetchone())   # (2,)

The f-string version closes the quote early and turns the filter into a condition that is always true. With a ? placeholder the driver sends the value separately from the SQL text, so the quote characters are just part of a name that matches nobody. The third line shows the named style, :who with a dictionary, which reads better once a query has several parameters.

How do you get query results back into pandas?

Objective 2.4.1 lists the clauses the exam expects you to combine: SELECT, FROM, JOIN, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY and LIMIT. The query below uses all of them, with a LEFT JOIN so that an order from a country missing in the lookup table is kept and labelled rather than dropped.

con.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE countries (code TEXT PRIMARY KEY, region TEXT NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO countries VALUES ('BR', 'Americas'), ('NG', 'Africa'), ('IN', 'Asia');
""")
QUERY = """
SELECT COALESCE(c.region, 'Unmapped') AS region,
       COUNT(*)                       AS orders,
       ROUND(SUM(o.amount), 2)        AS revenue,
       MIN(o.order_date)              AS first_order
FROM orders AS o
LEFT JOIN countries AS c ON c.code = o.country
WHERE o.paid = :paid
GROUP BY region
HAVING COUNT(*) >= :min_orders
ORDER BY revenue DESC
LIMIT 5
"""
summary = pd.read_sql_query(QUERY, con, params={"paid": 1, "min_orders": 1})
print(summary)
print(summary.dtypes)

     region  orders  revenue first_order
0    Africa       1   310.00  2026-09-04
1  Americas       2   192.75  2026-09-01
2  Unmapped       1    89.90  2026-09-05
region             str
orders           int64
revenue        float64
first_order        str
dtype: object

The params argument of pandas.read_sql_query passes values to the driver, so the placeholder rule still holds. Look at the last dtype, though: first_order came back as text, because that is how SQLite stored it. Add parse_dates=["first_order"] to the call and the column comes back as datetime64. The round trip from Timestamp to text and back is exactly the kind of conversion objective 2.4.5 has in mind.

The Chen Wei order lands in "Unmapped" because CN is not in the lookup table. With an INNER JOIN that paid order would vanish from the revenue total without any warning, which is a classic scenario question.

Is there a short video on preparing for PCAD?

This three-minute video from the EduSum channel gives preparation tips for the PCAD exam. It is about study habits rather than code, so it pairs well with the hands-on script above.

What should you practise after this script?

Run the script, then break it on purpose. Add a row whose paid value is maybe and see what map() produces; it gives NaN, and the column is no longer boolean. Then write a validation check for it. That loop of breaking the data and then catching the break is a fast way to learn Blocks 1 and 2.

To track the rest of the syllabus objective by objective, this PCAD-31-02 syllabus breakdown with exam details lists every block and topic on one page.

For Blocks 3 to 5, write small scripts of the same kind: a bootstrap of the mean with NumPy, a linear and a logistic regression with a train and test split, and one Matplotlib chart with labelled axes, a title and a legend.

When you want to see how the scenario items are phrased, work through these PCAD sample questions with answers and note which block each one belongs to.

Frequently asked questions

1. How many questions are on the PCAD-31-02 exam, and what score do I need to pass?

The exam has 48 single-select and multiple-select items, and you have 60 minutes plus the NDA screen. You pass with a cumulative score of at least 75%.

2. How much does the PCAD exam cost?

The Python Institute lists the exam from $195, the exam with a retake from $225, the exam with a practice test from $215 and all three from $245. The practice test alone is $49.

3. Is PCAD-31-01 still available?

No. PCAD-31-01 was retired on July 14, 2025, and PCAD-31-02 has been the active version since July 15, 2025. Use the PCAD-31-02 syllabus when you study.

4. Do I need PCAP or PCED before taking PCAD?

There are no formal prerequisites. The Python Institute recommends PCAP and PCED, or equivalent knowledge, plus field-specific skills.

5. How long is the PCAD certification valid, and when can I retake a failed exam?

The certification is valid for 6 years. After a failed attempt you must wait 15 days before you can take the exam again.

Issue

Starting with GKE version 1.36, the default engine for kube-dns is CoreDNS. For Pod IP DNS queries in the <a-b-c-d>.<namespace>.pod.cluster.local format, CoreDNS returns NXDOMAIN if the specified <namespace> does not exist. The legacy kubernetes/dns implementation skipped checking the existence of the namespace provided in the <namespace> segment in these queries.

Queries in the <a-b-c-d>.<namespace>.pod.cluster.local format are not part of the Kubernetes DNS specification. We can't guarantee that uses outside of those specified in the DNS spec will remain consistent across releases.

title: Beyond Aggregate Accuracy: Item-Level Transitions in Prompt Optimization
description:
arXiv:2610.19084v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Automatic prompt optimization (APO) uses feedback from model responses to improve prompts automatically. However, its effectiveness is usually measured through overall scores, which do not reveal which questions become correct, which previously correct answers become wrong, or whether improvements extend to unseen questions. We introduce Reflective Feedback-Driven Prompt Optimization (RFDPO), a tool that tracks recoveries (incorrect to correct), regressions (correct to incorrect), and churn (all changed outcomes). RFDPO uses this feedback to guide subsequent revisions and records prompt changes throughout optimization. We evaluate RFDPO across five benchmarks covering law, knowledge, instruction following, mathematics, and privacy, using GPT-5 as the optimizer and GPT-4o-mini and GPT-4.1 Mini as solvers. Our results show that overall accuracy can hide substantial changes: in five of nine configurations, churn was at least five times the absolute net change, and a single-item net change concealed up to 17 changed outcomes. Average validation gains were 7.9 percentage points, compared with 5.2 points on held-out tests. In a controlled ablation on LegalBench-Hearsay, item-level feedback reduced churn by 40% ($p=0.024$) while maintaining similar net gains. These findings motivate reporting recovery, regression, churn, and performance on unseen data alongside overall accuracy.

title: Do Vision CIL Methods Transfer to Protein? A Diagnostic Benchmark of Frozen Protein Encoders
description:
arXiv:2610.18879v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Protein function annotation operates over an expanding label space, making class-incremental learning (CIL) a natural framework for incorporating newly discovered functions without full retraining. Yet existing CIL methods have been developed largely in vision and have not been systematically evaluated over frozen protein representations. We conduct a controlled benchmark of nine representative CIL methods across five sequence-, structure-, and sequence--structure-based protein encoders and two enzyme function datasets at different scales, while keeping the encoders frozen and evaluation settings consistent across representations. We find that no method transfers reliably across encoders, and that these failures persist across alternative phase constructions. Diagnostic analyses reveal that this instability arises from weak gradient-based stability signals, substantial heterogeneity in embedding geometry, and covariance assumptions whose appropriate capacity changes with both dataset scale and encoder. These findings suggest that the representation itself should be treated as a central component of continual-learning design rather than a passive feature extractor. More generally, reliable protein CIL will require encoder-aware methods that adapt their statistical assumptions and capacity to the geometry of the representation on which they operate. Code is available at https://github.com/zygao930/ProteinCIL.

title: Microsoft Decision-1 now available on AI Gateway

The model can answer yes/no questions, choose among named categories, or score an input against an ordered set of criteria. Multiple questions can share the same input in one request. Choice and score answers include probabilities for each option, so your application can decide when to act or send an uncertain result for review.

Call Decision-1 through the AI SDK decision API, the OpenAI-compatible Decisions API, or the TypeSafe-compatible API. You only need an AI Gateway API key, with no separate Azure account or deployment.

To get started, use microsoft/microsoft-decision-1 as the model name in your requests:

title: AI Gateway adds confidence-based decision fallbacks
description:
AI Gateway can now escalate a decision request to a fallback model when the primary model's answer trips a confidence condition you set.

Conditions can be combined, so an escalation can depend on more than one signal. The plain model names you already list in models keep catching outright errors, so existing fallbacks are unaffected. Confidence conditions cover Choice and Score questions. Boolean questions escalate on a probability range instead.

Set the fallback by adding one conditional object to providerOptions.gateway.models. Requests without it keep their existing behavior.

Leave out question and the condition checks every question of the matching type, so { confidenceBelow: 0.6 } escalates when any Choice or Score answer falls below 0.6.

Because a triggered fallback runs a second decision, it bills both stages.

Learn more in the decision fallbacks documentation, or see them in practice for mapping CSV columns and flagging UI copy for translation review.

title: Shaping Latent Mixture-of-Experts: From Expert Geometry to Layerwise Capacity Allocation
description:
arXiv:2610.14644v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Fine-grained mixture-of-experts (MoE) models commonly increase expert count by narrowing each expert, treating expert shape as a by-product of routing granularity. LatentMoE moves expert computation into a lower-dimensional space, exposing the input dimension and intermediate width of each expert as explicit design choices. We show that an expert's local Jacobian rank is jointly bounded by these two dimensions, and that balancing them maximizes the rank ceiling at fixed per-expert parameters. Controlled shape sweeps across model scales and routing granularities consistently favor near-square experts. We further use layerwise intrinsic dimension (ID) to guide capacity allocation across depth, co-varying the number and shape of experts while keeping per-layer parameter count, activated FLOPs, and communication volume constant. Compared with layer-homogeneous baselines, our ID-guided allocation achieves lower validation loss and stronger downstream performance. These results establish expert shape and layerwise allocation as practical design axes for MoEs.

Sandbox memory observability in the CLI

Sandbox observability data is also available through the Vercel CLI via the vercel metrics command under vercel.sandbox.memory_used_bytes. Run the command in a linked project for project-specific data, or append --all to see aggregate data across all projects in your team.

The CLI returns:

  • The reporting period

  • The measurement interval

  • The project the sandbox is associated with

title: October 08, 2026
description:
Cloud SQL for MySQL

Feature

Cloud SQL for MySQL now supports the innodb_cloudsql_managed_buffer_pool_tuneup_pct database flag.

Managed buffer pool automatically adjusts the InnoDB buffer pool size to reduce out-of-memory events. When instance memory usage remains at or below 70% for 10 minutes or longer after prior reductions, Cloud SQL increases the buffer pool size. You can now use the innodb_cloudsql_managed_buffer_pool_tuneup_pct flag to change this 70% threshold to a different percentage. Increase the threshold to restore the InnoDB buffer pool size when baseline usage exceeds 70%, or decrease it to preserve additional RAM allocation for memory spikes.

This flag requires the Cloud SQL maintenance version MYSQL_VERSION.R20260726.00_05 or later. For more information, see Enable managed buffer pool.

Feature

Cloud SQL for MySQL supports blue-green deployments (Preview).

Blue-green deployments let you update databases—such as performing major version upgrades from MySQL 8.0 to 8.4 and staging hardware or configuration modifications—while minimizing downtime. During a blue-green deployment, Cloud SQL creates a separate staging environment (green) that mirrors your existing production environment (blue) and maintains continuous logical replication from blue to green. You can test application compatibility and performance on the green environment without affecting production traffic, and then trigger a switchover to the green environment with minimal application downtime.

For more information, see About blue-green deployments in Cloud SQL.

Gemini Enterprise: Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 in AI developer tools

Administrators can enable Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5 (claude-opus-5-5) and Anthropic Claude Sonnet 5.5 (claude-sonnet-5-5) for AI developer tools (Antigravity 2.0, Antigravity CLI, and Antigravity for IDEs). Third-party models are turned off by default:

  • In-console Terms of Service consent flow: Administrators can opt in to Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 directly in Gemini Enterprise > Settings > AI developer tools > Antigravity authorized models in the Google Cloud console without a separate Anthropic account or onboarding. For more information, see Configure AI developer tools settings.
  • Location availability: Third-party model inference is available in the global, us, and eu locations (in-country regions aren't supported). For a list of countries and regions that can access the model, see Anthropic's Supported countries and regions.
  • Consumption billing: Third-party model usage is billed as consumption on your Cloud Billing account and counts toward your project's spend cap, which covers all models. Overages must be turned on before you can enable a third-party model. For more information, see Configure overages and the Cloud Billing SKUs for Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5 and Anthropic Claude Sonnet 5.5.
  • Thinking levels: Developers sign in with their existing Gemini Enterprise license and select Claude Opus 5.5 or Claude Sonnet 5.5 in the model picker at a thinking level of Low, Medium, High, or Max (for example, Claude Opus 5.5 (High)). Medium is the default.

Google Cloud Contact Center as a Service

Announcement

Google Cloud CCaaS 6.19

We've released version 6.19 of Google Cloud CCaaS.

The timing of the update to your instance depends on the deployment schedule that you have chosen. For more information, see Deployment schedules.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where agents could be assigned more concurrent chats than their configured maximum limit when multiple chat offers arrived almost simultaneously.

  • Fixed an issue where calls were unevenly distributed among available agents on skills-based queues.

  • Fixed an issue where supervisor-initiated sign-outs silently discarded mandatory interaction dispositions during an agent's wrap-up period.

  • Fixed an issue where an agent's corporate email address and internal ID were exposed in the browser's network metadata during a virtual agent to human escalation.

  • Fixed an issue where voice calls were incorrectly routed back to the virtual agent queue instead of the intended destination.

  • Fixed an issue where inbound callers experienced a 2-second delay when connecting to an agent.

Looker 26.20 will roll out to Looker (original) and Looker (Google Cloud core) instances on the following schedule:

  • Expected final deployment and download available: Sunday, October 25, 2026

Looker 26.20 is expected to include the following changes, features, and fixes.

Breaking

Custom TopoJSON URL validation is updated to improve security. This change is isolated to Google Maps rendering in preview. Existing dashboards and Looks with the Google Maps Enhancements preview feature enabled that use custom TopoJSON files may be impacted.

Feature

The Gemini in Looker admin page has been restructured to allow Looker admins to selectively enable Conversational Analytics features and capabilities. Enablement for generally available Conversational Analytics features is now organized under the follow settings:

  • Conversational Analytics (Conversations page): Enables access to the Conversations page for data agents with Explores and direct chats with an Explore.
  • Dashboard agents: Enables default data agents on user-defined and LookML dashboards.
  • Additional options: Allows Conversational Analytics data agent creators to enable the Advanced Analytics feature for all conversations with their data agent. To use Advanced Analytics, you must also enable whichever Conversational Analytics toggle corresponds to the content that you are querying (Conversational Analytics (Conversations page) or Dashboard agents). If both the Conversational Analytics (Conversations page) and Dashboard agents toggles are turned off, then Advanced Analytics cannot be enabled. If either Conversational Analytics (Conversations page) or Dashboard agents is enabled, Advanced Analytics can be enabled, but it is turned off by default.

The Conversational Analytics (Conversations page) and Dashboard agents settings inherit the enablement state of the Conversational Analytics setting in previous versions of Looker.

Conversational Analytics preview features can still be enabled selectively under the Enable Trusted Tester Features setting.

(Note: This item was added on October 14, 2026.)

Feature

Conversational Analytics data agents for both user-defined dashboards and LookML dashboards are now generally available.

(Note: This item was added on October 14, 2026.)

Feature

You can now apply themes to Looks in addition to internal dashboards.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where duplicating a scheduled plan could fail to retain the custom message value. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

Table visualizations now proportionally scale left-pinned columns during automatic sizing, which prevents unnecessary horizontal scrollbars. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where enabling subtotals on table visualizations did not automatically disable the Cell Visualizations option. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where previews for Looker charts in Slack integrations could fail to be displayed. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where editing and saving a dashboard could cause the dashboard to reload indefinitely, forcing users to refresh the page. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where table cell visualizations that included both positive and negative values could display unwanted scrollbars and hide value labels. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where the BigQuery JDBC driver could fail to properly parse certain data types, such as BYTES, STRUCT/RECORD, and nested ARRAY structures. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where linked filters on a dashboard could fail to display autocomplete suggestions even when a parent filter is selected. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

The System Activity query_metrics Explore has been updated to ensure that phase timings (such as connection acquisitions, execution runtimes, and optimistic pivot fallback retry loops) are successfully captured for queries that fail or time out. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

The System Activity Dashboard Diagnostics dashboard has been updated to fully support statistics, tile run counts, and performance recommendations for LookML dashboards. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where the color palette popover in visualization settings failed to dynamically reposition when it expanded, causing controls to overlap or truncate. This feature now performs as expected.

Breaking

When you set up a connection, self-service modeling will now be available only if a role that grants create_self_service_from_table also selects it through that role's model set.

Fixed

The opacity for the comparison bar in short KPI visualizations has been reduced to increase legibility.

title: Free MCP Server Hosting: What Zero Dollars Actually Gets You
description:
We build a cloud whose agents operate it over MCP, so we spend a lot of the week talking to servers we wrote. Every one of those servers is hosted, always-on, and billed by the hour. But before any tool of ours is hosted, it lives on a laptop, behind a tunnel, answering calls from an agent on the same desk. That stage is free, it is where everyone should start, and this post is about how much you can get done there before you pay anything.

The short version for anyone searching this exact question: yes, you can host an MCP server for free. Run it on a machine you already own, use the free tier of a managed platform, or use serverless if your tools keep no state. Each is genuinely free and each breaks in a way you can predict. We have hit all three breaks, from both sides: as the people hosting the tools, and as the platform that inherits them when they grow.

Path What it costs Where it breaks Who it suits
Your machine behind a tunnel $0 The machine sleeps, reboots, loses wifi; the tool is up only while you are Development and solo experiments
The free tier of a managed platform $0, the platform carries the idle hours One instance, a memory ceiling, sometimes a request cap A first real tool, before a teammate depends on it
Serverless, stateless tools only $0 per call and response No state and no held connections; most MCP servers do not qualify Pure call-and-return tools

The rest of this post is about where each of those breaks, because that is the part the table cannot tell you.

The tunnel stage, and why it ends

Your laptop can be an MCP server tonight. Start the process, put a tunnel in front of it, point your agent at the URL, and you have a hosted server for zero dollars. We still develop this way; nothing beats editing a tool and watching the agent pick up the change seconds later.

It ends the first time the tool is useful to someone who is not you. A tunnel only works while the machine is awake, and the machine is yours: it sleeps when you sleep, it reboots when an update lands, it loses the wifi exactly once, at the worst moment. A remote MCP server is only remote if it stays up. The lesson is not that tunnels are bad. It is that shared usefulness and shared uptime are the same requirement, and a laptop cannot provide either.

Free tiers are real, read the edges

The managed path costs nothing on a free tier, and we want to defend free tiers for a moment, because we run one. A free tier that carries one small always-on service costs the platform almost nothing and makes the platform useful enough that you stay. That is the whole trade, and it is a fair one.

What the edges look like, from our side of the fence: one instance, a memory ceiling, sometimes a request cap. One small MCP server is a lightweight process speaking HTTP, and it fits. What does not fit is the day two agents call at once, or the day your tool needs a database next to it and you start gluing vendors together for state that should live on the same platform.

If your tools keep no state at all, a serverless function is another zero-dollar route, and for a pure request-and-response tool it is a good one. Most MCP servers do not qualify: they hold connections open and remember things between calls, which fights the request-and-forget model. We tried the stateless-only shape ourselves and kept running back to a real process.

The math that hides under "free"

An always-on service, however small, is 730 metered hours a month. It answers twice a day and meters around the clock. Free tiers pay that slice for you because it is the cheapest loyalty program ever invented, and honestly, it works.

We wrote before about what an always-on VM actually costs once it is billed by the hour, and the punchline was a customer spending 84% of a real bill on one VM that never slept. Scale-to-zero exists because of stories like that. Free tiers are the same instinct pointing the other direction: the platform carries the idle hours so your first tool costs nothing. Neither model is charity. Both are fine, as long as you know which side of the meter you are standing on.

The day to stop being free

It is not a resource threshold, it is a trust threshold. You will notice one of these three things: you check that the server is up before you check your email, because a teammate's agent depends on it now. A workflow treats its downtime as an incident. Or a second process appears because one instance became a queue.

Any one of those means the tool has outgrown the free stage, and the move is smaller than people fear. On Scalix Run the free-tier deploy and the paid deploy are the same command, same URL, one setting changed:

scalix-cloud run deploy --name mcp-server \
  --image registry.scalix.world/my-org/mcp-server:v1 \
  --port 8080 \
  --min-instances 1

You change a plan, not an architecture, and the URL your agents already know does not move. That matters more than the price. Re-pointing every agent that trusts your server is the real cost of outgrowing a host.

Where we land

Start free, on the machine or the tier, and mean it: the free stage is where your tool earns the right to exist. Then let the trust signals, not the invoice, tell you when to move. Start on the free tier, and if you want to see client configs for MCP servers we host ourselves, they are public at scalixworld/scalix-cloud-mcp.

title: The Lifecycle of LLM-as-a-Judge: Building, Aligning, and Monitoring at scale
description:
By Emma Yanyang Kong, JJ Tan, Ishan Gupta, Lars Olds, Claire Campbell, David Fagnan, Ratna Kavuri, Rohan Gosain, Veli Balin, Minsu Jang, Louis Garcia

Introduction

Any team generating text with an LLM at scale hits the same problem. You cannot evaluate everything manually. You don't know which outputs are great, which are mediocre, and which are harmful, because you simply cannot read them all. The standard solution is LLM-as-a-Judge, a second model that scores the first model’s output as a proxy for human raters. It is fast, cheap, and easy to deploy. However, it introduces a new and critical question: Who evaluates the evaluator? Furthermore, if the judge drifts, quietly degrading and starting to approve bad output, nothing downstream will flag it.

This post is about how we solve that problem, by building, aligning, and continuously monitoring LLM judges so they stay trustworthy over time. Our core principle is simple: An LLM judge must never operate alone. It has to be anchored in human judgment. We keep a human-in-the-loop (HITL) at every phase of the lifecycle. Humans define what “good” means, create the labeled benchmark datasets to train and validate the judge, monitor its behavior while it runs in the system, and review and approve any updates before they’re rolled out.

We believe:

A reliable LLM judge is not a static artifact. It has a lifecycle.

It needs to be built against trusted human labels, aligned with human preference and reasoning, run under human-set policy, and maintained as the data and usage pattern shift. Each of these stages has human owners. In the sections below, we walk through these four phases, the key design decisions in each, and the lessons we’d share with a team building their own LLM judge, using one concrete task as our running example: recommendation explanations.

A recommendation explanation is a short natural-language message that accompanies a recommended item, and it shapes how users perceive and trust a recommender system. In our work, an explanation is human-readable evidence for why a title was recommended based on what the member has previously watched, shown on the title’s detail page, which is the screen a member reaches by selecting a title from the homepage. We focus on similarity-based explanations, which connect a recommended title to one reference title the member has interacted with via shared attributes such as genre and tone. For example,

A funny, heartfelt holiday romance about love and new beginnings, much like “My Secret Santa.”

Quality matters here because a misleading or poorly grounded explanation erodes the very trust the explanation is meant to build.

Everything that follows comes out of a series of controlled, user-facing online experiments we ran on the explanation feature, including a month-long experiment on the Netflix mobile app. In these tests we used an LLM to generate explanations, hundreds of thousands a week across a constantly changing catalog. Manually reviewing them at this scale isn’t feasible, so we deployed a second LLM to evaluate them.

What counts as a good explanation is specific to our task. However, the way we build, align, and monitor the LLM judge for evaluating explanations should be reusable and generalizable across different tasks.

The Lifecycle at a Glance

Figure 1 summarizes the four phases of our LLM-judge lifecycle and the data flow connecting them.

We start with Birth: Benchmark Data Creation, where human experts craft hard or near-boundary examples and human raters label them with pass/fail decisions and written rationales. We augment this with LLM-generated gray-area examples to build a richer benchmark dataset.

Next, in the second phase of Training: LLM Judge Development, we tune the LLM judge to align with human labels and rationales from the Birth phase, using self-reflection to identify mismatches between the judge and humans, and updating the rubrics based on those mismatches and anchor examples. We iterate in this phase until our metrics show that the judge is sufficiently aligned with human raters.

In the third phase, Deployment, we integrate the judge into the explanation generation system as both a gate and a critic. The LLM generator writes explanations, and the LLM judge scores them and either passes them through or blocks them and supplies a rationale that the generator can use for self-refinement and retries. Passed explanations are served to members, and low-quality explanations are gated.

Finally, in the last phase, HITL Alignment & Drift Monitoring, we keep the judge aligned with humans over time. “Human-in-the-loop” here means a person is directly involved in the decision, not just reviewing outcomes after the fact. We benchmark the judge against trained raters, and a human approves every change before it is rolled out to the system. During each test we sampled a set of explanations each week (both passed and gated, with a bias toward newer items), had human raters review them with labels and rationales, and compared the judge against these human ratings. If drift exceeded a threshold, we triggered retraining and benchmark data augmentation. This closes the loop by feeding new human-labeled data and updated signals back into the benchmark and development phases.

System components

Four automated components appear across all phases, alongside the human roles that define, validate, and supervise them.

  • Generator: produces the explanation text, optionally using prior judge rationales and traces as part of its prompt for revision.
  • Judge: evaluates an explanation and returns a pass/fail label together with a written rationale. In the deployed pipeline, it acts as both a guardrail (gating bad outputs) and a critic (providing feedback for self-refinement).
  • Reflector: revises the Judge’s rubric when the Judge makes mistakes. It updates the rubric based on mismatched examples, human rationales, and anchor examples. It tunes the rubric and does not directly evaluate explanations.
  • Meta-Judge: checks whether the Judge failed an explanation for the right reason by comparing the Judge’s rationale against a human rater’s rationale.
  • Human experts and raters: the experts who define the quality criteria; the raters whose labels and written rationales the Judge is tuned and measured against; the reviewers who monitor the Judge while it is running and explicitly approve any changes before they were rolled out.

Phase I, Birth: Establishing Ground Truth

Everything downstream depends on knowing what “good” means, so this is the most human-intensive phase. Our internal writing experts define the must-have criteria an explanation must satisfy, author detailed labeling guidelines, and hand-craft tricky adversarial examples. Those same guidelines do double duty. They’re both the rulebook for human raters and the seed rubric for the LLM judges we tune later.

Why we built our own benchmark

Off-the-shelf LLM-judge benchmarks focus on general-purpose text evaluation and miss what makes our task specific. Explanations are short, item-specific, and context-dependent (each one is tied to a target title and one or two reference titles the member has watched). We also care about alignment to our own editorial bar, not just generic language quality. As a result, we built our own custom benchmark from three complementary sources:

  • Expert-crafted adversarial cases: hand-authored pass/fail examples with known failure modes, the kind of edge cases nothing else reliably produces.
  • Boundary examples: LLM-synthesized explanations that are deliberately pushed near the pass/fail boundary, then rated by humans. These capture the ambiguous cases that sampling from live traffic rarely surfaces on its own.
  • Real sampled explanations: explanations sampled from the output of our LLM generator during test runs.

Two details that mattered

  • The benchmark is not frozen. A monitoring pipeline (Phase IV) appends a fresh batch of human-rated explanations on a weekly cadence, so over the course of a test the benchmark tracked the current catalog and new usage patterns instead of going stale.
  • Every “fail” label carries a free-text rationale explaining why the explanation failed. This looks like a small bookkeeping detail, but it is actually critical for the next phase, since those rationales are what we use to tune and audit the judge’s reasoning.

Phase II, Training: Aligning the Judge to Humans

The failure mode: right answer, wrong reason

There is a failure mode that does not show up in label-agreement metrics at all. A judge can agree with humans on the label, passing when they would pass and failing when they would fail, while reaching the right verdict for the wrong reason. On a dashboard it looks perfectly aligned. But as soon as you ask it to explain a rejection, which our pipeline does to steer self-revision, it can return misleading guidance.

We therefore care about not just label agreement but also reasoning alignment. In our setup, the Judge is always asked to output:

  • a label (e.g., PASS/FAIL), and
  • a short natural-language rationale for that label.

Here is an illustrative example. The member watched a musical, a family fantasy with a young heroine and a well-known ensemble cast. We recommend an adventure movie that is also a family fantasy with a young heroine, which is why the recommender paired them. But it shares neither the songs nor the ensemble cast.

The label (FAIL) is correct, and the stated reason is reasonable at first glance. But it turns out to be incomplete in a way that simple label agreement cannot detect, as we show below.

Reasoning-Aligned Rubric Tuning

We tune each criterion’s LLM Judge with a procedure we call Reasoning-Aligned Rubric Tuning (RART). As introduced in the system components above, the Judge, Meta-Judge, and Reflector are distinct components. The Judge scores an explanation against a rubric and gives a rationale, the Meta-Judge compares that rationale against a human-written one, and the Reflector edits the rubric text itself. RART is how the three are combined into a training loop.

Every Judge is a fixed prompt template parameterized by a rubric, so tuning it does not mean retraining the underlying model. Instead we iteratively refine the rubric text until the Judge’s behavior matches human labels and human rationales. At iteration i, the Judge is conditioned on the current rubric text and maps an explanation to a pair, a label and a rationale.

At a high level, each RART iteration proceeds as follows.

  1. Score the training data with the current rubric.
  2. Evaluate weighted alignment metrics on a held-out validation set. If all per-criterion metrics exceed their thresholds, stop.
  3. Otherwise, construct an error-driven focus set of misaligned examples and hand it to the Reflector, which proposes a revised rubric.

The key difference from a standard loop is how we define a “mistake.” Most self-improvement loops look only at label disagreements. RART adds a second class of error. The Meta-Judge examines the cases where the Judge and a human both said fail and compares the Judge’s stated reason against the human’s rationale. When the two diverge, that is a right answer, wrong reason error, and it is also fed to the Reflector. Concretely, the focus set handed to the Reflector is the union of two error classes:

  • Label mismatches: examples where the Judge’s label differs from the human’s.
  • Right label, wrong reason: examples where the Judge and the human both said FAIL, but the Meta-Judge finds their two rationales don’t match.

So the Reflector revises the rubric from both ordinary label errors and right label, wrong reason errors. That second term is the core of RART. The Judge is pushed not only to match human decisions but to justify them in a way the Meta-Judge recognizes as aligned with human reasoning.

Returning to the earlier example, the LLM Judge said FAIL and a human said FAIL, so a label-only check would register agreement. Placing the two reasons side by side shows what that check misses.

RART routes it into the focus set, so the next rubric revision has to account for it.

Since the Meta-Judge is an LLM too, we checked it against humans first. Trained human raters labeled a sample of agreed-fail rationale pairs, and the Meta-Judge matched their verdicts on nearly all of them.

Alignment metrics

We run one Judge per criterion, each with its own rubric, tuned and scored on its own. So everything below is measured per criterion on held-out data. For each one we track three metrics.

  • Specificity (fail-recall): how often the Judge correctly rejects bad explanations. This is the one we care about most, because a bad explanation that slips through the gate is a trust hazard.
  • Recall (pass-recall): how often it correctly passes good explanations, which keeps coverage high and revision cost low.
  • Reasoning agreement: on the explanations both reject, how often they reject for the same reason.

Each criterion’s Judge gets its own three, and one can be healthy while another slips. That is also why the gate is strict. An explanation has to pass every must-have criterion to be eligible to serve.

Ablation: does the reasoning signal help?

To isolate the impact of the reasoning signal, we compare RART to an otherwise identical loop that uses only label disagreements. We call this baseline vanilla: same Reflector, same Judge, same data, but no Meta-Judge and no use of human rationales.

Figure 2 shows the result. On two of the three must-have criteria, vanilla and RART land in the same place, because the starting rubric was already near ceiling and the metrics had very little room to gain. On the third criterion, the vanilla (label-only) method degrades. The Reflector in the vanilla loop rewrites the rubric into degenerate forms, and specificity and reasoning agreement fall with every iteration, ending up worse than the rubric it started from. RART stays stable on that same criterion and lifts both, with a small recall gain as well. The reason is that a vanilla (label-only) optimizer can reach the right label through unsound reasoning, and unsound reasoning doesn’t generalize to new data. Anchoring the signal on the rationale prevents that. Reasoning alignment helps where there is headroom and doesn’t hurt where there isn’t.

Phase III, Deployment: Putting the Judge to Work

Once deployed, the judge sat inside the generation pipeline, gating and critiquing explanations as they were produced during our tests.

Two roles for one judge

Once we align the LLM Judge with humans, we reuse it in two distinct roles for every generated explanation:

  • Role 1, the gate. The Judge scores each explanation against the must-have criteria and rejects anything that fails.
  • Role 2, the critic. When an explanation fails, we don’t just throw it away. The Judge’s free-text reason gets appended to the Generator’s prompt, and the Generator tries again.

The second role turns the pipeline into a generate → judge → revise loop, with the Judge’s critique steering each revision.

Bounded retries, and why we drop rather than serve

We cap the retries. Each revision costs another round of generation and judging, and the gains flatten quickly. Figure 3 shows what the loop actually buys, on 1,000 generated explanations run through as many as 12 revisions with four generators. Every curve climbs, which is the Judge’s critique doing its job, but the steep part is early, and the gap between generators is obvious. Revision amplifies a capable generator rather than rescuing a weak one. In our test runs we used a budget of 3 retries with our strongest generator, and an explanation still failing after that was dropped rather than served.

That “drop rather than serve” rule is deliberate. The two outcomes aren’t symmetric. A bad explanation is a trust hazard, while a missing explanation just forgoes an opportunity. When in doubt we’d rather show nothing, and most explanations cleared the bar within the retry budget.

Do judge-approved explanations help members?

Passing the Judge proves an explanation is good by our standards, but it doesn’t prove that judge-approved explanations are useful to members. To test that connection, we ran a one-time controlled experiment on the Netflix mobile app, explanations vs. no explanations on the title detail page, over roughly a month, with the pipeline generating and judging hundreds of thousands of explanations a week during the period.

Members who saw explanations shifted their viewing toward titles they hadn’t watched before, and more of their browse sessions ended in a meaningful play. Both effects were statistically significant, and we saw no member-initiated takedowns or escalations about explanation quality during the test. The result worth carrying over isn’t the size of that effect. It’s that offline agreement with our raters was necessary for these explanations to work but never sufficient to show they help members. Only the online A/B test could establish that judge-aligned explanations are not just quality-compliant but genuinely useful.

Phase IV, Monitoring: Keeping the Judge Aligned

A judge that’s well aligned at launch won’t stay that way. The catalog shifts, and so does what counts as high quality. The lifecycle has to close the loop.

The weekly human review

For each week a test was running, we pulled roughly 300 generated explanations for human review, stratified across the Judge’s decisions (served, revised, dropped) and weighted toward newer catalog items, where drift is most likely. The stratification stayed fixed week to week, so successive weeks were comparable. A panel of at least three raters reviewed each explanation, and the majority label was our ground truth. Those labels did two jobs. They told us whether judge-human agreement was slipping, and they grew the benchmark.

Setting the bar with human disagreement

The panel also tells us how much the raters disagreed with each other, which turns out to be the right yardstick for the Judge. Rather than hold it to a fixed threshold, we score the Judge and each rater against the same majority label and ask that the Judge fall within the raters’ own spread.

Take one criterion and one of its metrics, M. That week’s sample gives one value M(J) for the Judge and a set of per-rater values M(H) for the three or more raters on the panel. We require

so the Judge must score no worse than two standard deviations below the average rater. A harder week widens human disagreement and widens the band with it, so the Judge isn’t penalized for difficulty the humans also felt.

Falling below the band on any metric-criterion pair is a drift event, which triggers re-tuning (back to Phase II) on the augmented benchmark. A re-tuned rubric never goes live automatically. Someone on the team reads the proposed changes and signs off before it reaches the running pipeline, and we keep the previous rubric for instant rollback.

What human review catches that metrics can’t

Beyond asking whether the Judge still agrees with human raters, the weekly review answers a second question. Are the current guidelines still asking for the right things?

In the weekly review process, reviewers surfaced issues that did not show up in Judge–rater agreement. An explanation can use accurate attributes and still overstate how similar two titles really are. A single vague adjective (“exciting”, “fun”, “emotional”) can technically satisfy the rubric while saying almost nothing. Sometimes the reference itself is the problem, something the member wouldn’t think of as a comparable title at all, so the comparison lands oddly no matter how the attributes line up. Some genres show the same problem at scale. Stand-up specials can share similar metadata tags but differ completely in tone and cultural context, so a comparison may look justified on paper, not be bad enough for a rater to fail, and still land poorly with members. And some explanations meet every must-have criterion while still reading like generic “word soup” that does not help the user much.

When recurring patterns kept appearing, we updated the Phase I guidelines, which seed both the raters’ instructions and the judges’ rubrics, so one revision updates both sides. Other times we added product rules outside the Judge, for example by blocking certain title types from being used as references.

Drift detection catches a judge that has stopped agreeing with people. Only the continued human review tells us when our definition of a “good explanation” is too narrow or incomplete. We need both.

  • Drift detection keeps the Judge aligned with the current rubric.
  • Continuous human review keeps the rubric aligned with what actually works for members.

What We Learned

Five lessons we think transfer to any team shipping an LLM judge:

  1. Invest in the benchmark before the judge. A modest, rationale-annotated benchmark beats a large label-only one. Those written rationales are exactly what make reasoning-aligned tuning possible. You can’t correct a judge’s reasoning if you never wrote down the human’s.
  2. Tune on reasoning, not just labels. A judge can reach the right verdict for the wrong reason, which looks fine on a dashboard but gives misleading feedback and doesn’t hold up on new data. In our ablation, the label-only loop degraded a rubric that the reasoning-aware loop kept stable.
  3. One aligned judge can serve many roles. Reusing the same judge as both gate and critic amortizes the alignment cost and keeps production behavior consistent across roles. Alignment is the expensive part, so get one judge right and use it more than once.
  4. Plan for monitoring from day one. A recommender platform’s items and members never stop changing, so an LLM judge, like any ML model, has to be watched and re-tuned if needed, not shipped and forgotten.
  5. Keep people in the loop by design, not by exception. Automating evaluation is not the same as delegating responsibility for it. In our lifecycle, humans set the standard (Phase I), supply the rationales the judge is aligned to (Phase II), decide the conservative default of dropping rather than serving a doubtful output (Phase III), and review a standing sample of live decisions and approve every rubric change before it ships (Phase IV). These checkpoints are much harder to retrofit once a judge is already making decisions on its own. The standing review also tells us what our rubric is missing, not just when our judge has slipped.

Taken together, the judge extends the reach of our reviewers, and those reviewers are the basis for trusting the judge. That relationship is what makes it responsible to run this system at scale. An automated evaluator that no one audits provides no assurance about the decisions it is making.

Acknowledgements

This post summarizes our research paper, “The Lifecycle of LLM-as-a-Judge for Large-Scale Recommendation Explanations,” which has the full methodology, metrics, and ablations.

Our thanks to the internal human writers and review experts who defined what a good explanation is and keep those guidelines current; to our Human Data Operations team and the raters they train and calibrate, whose labels and written rationales are what the judges are aligned to; and to the engineers across the team who built and operate the pipeline; and to our UI engineering partners, who built the member-facing surfaces that bring these explanations to the homepage.

The Lifecycle of LLM-as-a-Judge: Building, Aligning, and Monitoring at scale was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: Backpropagating Verifier Rewards Through Continuous Flow Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.19080v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has substantially improved the reasoning of autoregressive and discrete-diffusion language models. Language models that generate continuous token embeddings are emerging as a strong alternative, but RL post-training for them remains understudied. We propose \method{}, a post-training framework for continuous flow language models. Such a model denoises token embeddings over multiple steps and decodes them into discrete tokens only at the last step. To obtain pathwise gradients, which backpropagate through continuous actions and have much lower variance than REINFORCE, we introduce a critic that estimates the value of intermediate token embeddings, bypassing the non-differentiable decoding step. The critic must also keep track of the value function as the policy changes; to this end, we design a critic that predicts a value from every token representation and improves policy optimization. Across four reasoning tasks, \method{} reliably improves a continuous flow language model through RL post-training and outperforms baseline methods of the same type.

I am very pleased to announce that, after a long hiatus, Perseid 0.1.0, a set of utilities for versioning PostgreSQL database schemas, has been released.

  • Git repository: https://codeberg.org/perseas/perseid
