title: What To Do When a Free LLM API Says 429 (A Field Playbook)
description:
What To Do When a Free LLM API Says 429 (A Field Playbook)

Every free LLM API says yes right up until the moment it says no. The no arrives as an HTTP 429, usually forty requests into a demo or halfway through a batch job, and most tutorials end the story at "add a retry loop." Here is what actually works when you are building on free tiers, provider by provider and layer by layer.

First, find out which limit you hit

A 429 is not one problem, it is four. Free tiers meter you on several axes at once, and the fix depends on which one fired:

  • Requests per minute (RPM): you are asking too often. Smoothing helps, capacity does not.
  • Tokens per minute (TPM): a few long prompts ate the whole minute. Shorten contexts, cap max_tokens.
  • Requests per day (RPD): you are done until the reset. No code fix exists, only spreading work across days or providers.
  • Concurrency: two in-flight requests when the tier allows one. Queue, do not parallelize.

Read the response body and headers before you touch your code. Groq sends x-ratelimit-remaining-requests (daily) and x-ratelimit-remaining-tokens (per minute) plus retry-after, so the 429 tells you which window is empty and when to come back. The Gemini API returns 429 RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED and names the violated window in details[].quotaId, with retryDelay set for per-minute limits; its daily quotas reset at midnight Pacific. OpenRouter free-model caps jump from a small daily allowance to a larger one once the account has purchased credits, and its error text and x-ratelimit-reset-requests header say which window closed. Some providers, sadly, send nothing: if a 429 comes back bare, treat every window as closed and back off to the hour.

Then, retry like it means something

Three rules that cover most cases:

  1. Honor retry-after when present. It is the provider telling you the truth; guessing is worse.
  2. Exponential backoff with jitter when it is not: 1s, 2s, 5s, 10s, plus random offset, capped at a few minutes. Retrying a daily cap in a loop accomplishes nothing, so stop after 3 to 5 attempts and surface the error.
  3. Count tokens, not requests. A retry loop tuned for RPM will still fail when TPM is the real wall, because the retry itself burns more tokens per minute.

Then, stop depending on one well

One provider's free tier is one quota pool. The structural fix is to treat free tiers as a pool of pools:

  • Keep several OpenAI-compatible keys (Gemini, Groq, NVIDIA NIM, OpenRouter, Cloudflare Workers AI, Cerebras and others each publish their own caps) and fail a request over to the next provider when one window closes. Because all of them speak the OpenAI chat format, your client code does not change, only the base URL and key.
  • Route by limit shape, not just availability. A nightly summarization job wants RPD headroom (Groq's daily allowances, or Gemini's daily caps). An interactive prototype wants RPM smoothness. A one-shot extraction can burn a per-token-limited tier without hurting anything.
  • Watch the terms. Several free tiers (Cohere's trial key, Mistral's La Plateforme free tier) are explicitly for evaluation, not production. OpenRouter's terms prohibit reselling API access. Read them before you build a product on top.

Hand-rolling this means a provider abstraction, a per-provider window tracker, a queue, and health checks for every one of them, which is most of a side project by itself. If you would rather not own that layer, there are routers that do it: I build FreeLLMAPI, an open-source, self-hosted router that keeps your provider keys, handles 429s and retries with backoff, falls back to other providers and models, and exposes one OpenAI-compatible endpoint at the end. The same job can be done by hand with the playbook above; the router just means you write it once and self-host it.

And log the shape of your traffic

Whatever you choose, log per-request: provider, model, latency, status, and the rate-limit headers. A week of logs tells you which window you actually bump, and that single fact decides whether you need smoothing, shorter prompts, a second provider, or honestly, the $5 paid tier. Most "we need more quota" problems turn out to be "one long prompt repeated in a loop" problems. The 429 is information. Read it before you reroll the key.

title: StatusCake, BetterStack, UptimeRobot, Healthchecks: Go API Uptime Trade-offs Explained
description:
TL;DR: Use StatusCake, Better Stack, or UptimeRobot for outside-in API checks and production notifications. Add Healthchecks for scheduled jobs that can fail by never starting. For a small EU-hosted B2B SaaS comparing an experiment across tenant cohorts, keep application metrics and structured logs as a separate evidence ledger for outcomes, dependency failures, latency, and attributable cost.

Do not ask one green check to prove all three things. Endpoint reachability, scheduled arrival, and experiment economics run on different clocks. The operating rule is straightforward: the uptime vendor pages a human, the heartbeat catches silence, and internal evidence decides whether the experimental schedule is worth keeping.

Begin with the failure clock

Imagine three cohorts: control, hourly, and batched. Each scheduled reconciliation run needs a stable run ID, a privacy-safe tenant reference, its cohort, outcome, elapsed time, dependency status, and attributable cost. Cost is the primary decision axis, but it cannot stand alone. A cohort with lower recorded cost because half its jobs never started is corrupted evidence, not a winner.

An HTTP probe can show that /healthz responds now. It cannot establish that the 02:00 reconciliation happened, nor can it explain why one cohort generated more failed dependency calls. A dead-man check covers the missing start. Logs and metrics cover the work that did start.

Use Google's four golden signals—latency, traffic, errors, and saturation—as the service-health frame, then attach cost to the experiment record. Keep liveness cheap and narrow. If a cohort aggregation query becomes part of the health handler, a slow analytics workload can manufacture an availability incident.

Two deadlines belong in the runbook: the probe timeout and the latest acceptable job arrival. Write them before rollout. Missed is missed.

Should API uptime use StatusCake, BetterStack, UptimeRobot, or Healthchecks?

StatusCake, Better Stack, UptimeRobot, and Healthchecks overlap at the edges, but their useful roles differ. For EU hosting, verify processing locations, retention, subprocessors, and contractual terms directly; a selectable EU probe does not prove that every event and notification stays in one jurisdiction.

Product Best role in this runbook Boundary to verify
StatusCake Public HTTP endpoint checks from selected locations Probe coverage, escalation channels, and retention for the chosen plan
Better Stack Endpoint checks near an incident and on-call workflow Data processing terms and fit with the real escalation rota
UptimeRobot Direct endpoint monitoring for a small operating team Check interval, notification routes, and team access controls
Healthchecks Dead-man checks for cron, queue, and reconciliation jobs It does not replace outside-in API availability monitoring

There is no universal winner. Run the same drill against the notification path the team will actually depend on: force an unhealthy endpoint, delay it beyond the configured timeout, and omit one expected heartbeat. Pick the product whose detection and acknowledgement path works under those conditions. Add Healthchecks whenever “nothing ran” is itself an incident. A five-minute check interval, for example, creates a different operating promise from a one-minute interval; use the value configured in the selected plan and write that exact delay into the runbook rather than assuming “uptime monitoring” implies instant detection.

Datadog Synthetic Monitoring and Grafana Cloud Synthetic Monitoring are credible alternatives when either platform already anchors the wider monitoring estate. Their broader surface may be useful, but it adds operational scope that a small service should choose deliberately. Product count is not resilience.

Keep notification and evidence separate

The external vendor owns detection and delivery. The service owns truthful health responses. The experiment pipeline owns cohort evidence. This division is plain enough to use during a page and precise enough for a postmortem. It also prevents a common accounting trap: when the endpoint stays green but a scheduled batch never begins, the absence belongs to the heartbeat timeline; when the batch begins twice after queue redelivery, the duplicate belongs to the run ledger. Both can affect the same cohort total, but they need different detectors and different remediation.

Keep those clocks separate.

Infrai can provide a lightweight internal layer for recording incidents and working with health-related logs and metrics, but it is not a full uptime platform. It has no built-in threshold rules or phone, SMS, and webhook alert routing, and it does not perform synthetic probes or heartbeat monitoring. Those limits make the external monitor the production notification system.

Infrai provides a single API key and unified billing across backend services, so a team does not have to juggle dozens of keys or reconcile dozens of invoices at month end. That matters when cost attribution already consumes engineering attention. The API is genuinely self-describing, and the discovery surface is public with no key required. The verified catalog contains 295 routes across 20 modules.

Keep the boundary sharp. Logs can carry trace_id and span_id, but there is no distributed trace query or span tree. There is no source-map decoding, Electron minidump symbolization, or Session Replay. The log API also has no per-user deletion route or bulk export/subscription interface, so do not send personal data when an opaque tenant reference is sufficient. Retention and cold-storage configuration are not exposed. This is not suitable as the primary uptime system; choose StatusCake, Better Stack, or UptimeRobot when notification routing is required, and Healthchecks when missed schedules are the risk. That trade-off is more important than catalog breadth.

There is one more integration constraint: filter parameters for log search and metric query are not clearly declared in discovery. Do not invent them. Inspect the current contract, test the behavior away from production, and treat any unresolved query semantics as a dashboard design input rather than an assumption.

Inspect the reporting contract safely in Go

Because search and query filters are not declared clearly enough to reproduce here, the safe minimal example reads the live metric-reporting contract instead of guessing a payload. It uses an environment key, an explicit method, response checks, and bounded 429 retries. The base address is assembled only to keep this independent comparison unlinked.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "log"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        log.Fatal("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }

    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    baseURL := "https://api." + "infrai." + "cc/v1"
    url := baseURL + "/discovery/metrics.report"

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, url, nil)
        if err != nil {
            log.Fatal(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            log.Fatal(err)
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            log.Fatal(readErr)
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            log.Fatalf("discovery failed: status=%d body=%s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return
    }
    log.Fatal("discovery remained rate limited after four attempts")
}

Validate the returned request schema before reporting an aggregate. Any eventual write retry needs a stable idempotency key derived from the scheduled run ID, so delivery cannot count the same completion or cost twice. The platform specifies a 24-hour default deduplication window for idempotent capabilities.

The run ID must cross the queue boundary unchanged. Standard queues are at-least-once systems, so the consumer—not the scheduler—owns deduplication. That reflex prevents a notification retry from becoming an accounting error.

Verify, then make rollback boring

Before assigning real experiment traffic, use staging with the production notification configuration. Return a healthy response, force a 503, delay the response past the chosen timeout, and intentionally omit a scheduled heartbeat. Confirm that primary and backup recipients can acknowledge each event and that duplicate notifications do not trigger duplicate remediation.

Then run one item for each cohort. Verify the outcome, dependency status, duration, and attributed cost land under the intended cohort; repeat one run ID and confirm it is not counted twice. This is a small test matrix, but it probes the dangerous boundaries instead of admiring a green dashboard.

Rollback is a scheduling operation: stop new assignments to hourly and batched, preserve in-flight run IDs, and send new tenants to control. Do not rewrite old labels or delete inconvenient failures. Afterward, verify the public probe and the control heartbeat independently before comparing cohort totals again.

Restored availability gets the service back; preserved evidence makes the experiment defensible.

References

  • Google SRE Book: Monitoring Distributed Systems
  • StatusCake uptime monitoring documentation
  • Better Stack uptime monitoring documentation
  • UptimeRobot help center
  • Healthchecks documentation
  • Datadog Synthetic Monitoring documentation
  • Grafana Cloud Synthetic Monitoring documentation

title: How I Built a 100% In-Browser Instagram Chat Analyzer (Zero Cloud Uploads)
description:
Direct messages contain our most intimate conversations, jokes, memories, and photos. Yet, when searching for tools to visualize chat history or generate Spotify Wrapped-style stats for group chats, virtually every existing tool asks for your Instagram login or forces you to upload your sensitive ZIP archives to their cloud servers.

I wanted to change that. I built Stats Insta — a completely free, 100% client-side Instagram Chat Analyzer where your data never leaves your device.

In this article, I will share the engineering challenges behind parsing multi-megabyte JSON exports in the browser, decoding escaped Unicode emojis, computing deep conversational metrics, and generating 9:16 Instagram Story cards directly from the DOM.

🔒 The Architecture: 100% Client-Side Privacy

The core philosophy behind Stats Insta is Local-First Processing:

  1. Zero Server Uploads: The application does not have a backend parsing server or database for chat messages.
  2. Native HTML5 FileReader: When a user drops a message_1.json file, the browser reads the file directly into client-side RAM using FileReader.readAsText().
  3. Session-Only Memory: Once you refresh or close the browser tab, the data is instantly garbage-collected by the browser engine.

You can verify this in Chrome DevTools (F12 > Network Tab): dropping a 50MB conversation file triggers 0 network POST requests.

⚙️ Technical Challenge 1: Decoding Instagram's Unicode Escapes

When Meta exports your message history in JSON format, emojis and special characters are not stored as standard UTF-8 strings. Instead, they are encoded as escaped byte sequences (e.g., \u00e2\u009d\u00a4 for a red heart).

If rendered directly in React, emojis appear as garbled characters (Mojibake). To resolve this, I implemented an in-memory Unicode normalization pipeline:

const decodeUnicode = (unicodeString: string): string => {
  try {
    return decodeURIComponent(
      unicodeString.replace(/\\u([0-9a-fA-F]{4})/g, "%u$1")
    );
  } catch (error) {
    return unicodeString;
  }
};

This converts raw escaped sequences into native browser-rendered emojis at runtime without lagging the main thread.

📊 Technical Challenge 2: Calculating Deep Conversational Metrics

Simple message counts are boring. People care about the hidden dynamics of their friendships. We compute several unique behavioral metrics in browser memory:

1. The "Night Owls" Tracker (12:00 AM – 4:59 AM)

We parse the Unix millisecond timestamps (timestamp_ms) on each message and isolate activity occurring in the late-night window:

const hour = new Date(msg.timestamp_ms).getHours();
if (hour >= 0 && hour <= 4) {
  nightOwlCounts[msg.sender_name] = (nightOwlCounts[msg.sender_name] || 0) + 1;
}

This immediately reveals who stays awake sending reels and memes while everyone else is asleep.

2. The Conversation Starter Algorithm

Who puts in the effort to keep the conversation alive? We sort the timeline chronologically and scan for silence gaps exceeding 12 hours:

const TWELVE_HOURS_MS = 12 * 60 * 60 * 1000;
if (lastTimestamp === 0 || msg.timestamp_ms - lastTimestamp > TWELVE_HOURS_MS) {
  starterCounts[msg.sender_name] = (starterCounts[msg.sender_name] || 0) + 1;
}
lastTimestamp = msg.timestamp_ms;

3. The Swear Jar

We scan message strings against a local tokenized dictionary of 100+ global curse words and slang to generate a friendly group chat leaderboard of who has the dirtiest mouth.

📱 Technical Challenge 3: Generating 9:16 Instagram Story Wrapped Cards

People love sharing aesthetic visual summaries with their friends. To make the tool virally shareable, I built an in-browser Story Card generator that renders a 1080x1920 (9:16 Full HD) graphic using HTML5 Canvas:

  • Glassmorphism gradient backgrounds with radial glowing orbs
  • Rounded progress bars showing conversational dominance percentages
  • Dynamic badges and highlights
  • 1-Click Native Share: On mobile devices, we invoke the Web Share API (navigator.share({ files: [pngFile] })), which opens the native iOS/Android share sheet directly into Instagram Stories!

🚀 Try It Live & Explore the Code

The project is completely free to use, and I have published detailed guides on understanding Meta's export architecture:

  • 🌐 Live Application: https://stats-insta.vercel.app/
  • 📘 Guide: How to Open & Read Instagram message_1.json Files
  • 📙 Guide: Activity Heatmaps & Peak Texting Hours

I would love to hear feedback from the DEV community! What other client-side analytics or visual metrics would you like to see added?

title: I Turned 44 Blog Posts Into a Frontend Roadmap You Have to Pass
description:
It's Sunday night, the interview is on Thursday, and the frontend roadmap in your other tab has more topics than you have evenings. You're sure about half of them and fairly sure about the rest.

The roadmap can't tell you which "fairly sure" is real. It only knows what you ticked.

So test the topics before you read them. Here's what that looks like for HTML: ten questions drawn at random, seven right to pass, and the whole stage counts as cleared.

No account and no reading, just ten questions. Here's why that beats a checkbox, and how it works.

What you'll learn

By the end of this article you'll be able to:

  • Explain why a frontend roadmap you tick yourself overstates what you know, using a 2006 study of re-reading versus testing
  • Compare seven well-known frontend roadmaps and courses on price, sign-up, checks, skipping and certificates
  • Use checkpoints to skip the stages you already know and find the gaps you don't
  • Compute learning progress from quiz attempts instead of storing it
  • Tell when this path is the wrong tool, and what to use instead

Who this is for

You've shipped frontend code for a year or more, in Vue or React, and you want to find out quickly what you actually know: for an interview, a promotion or your own peace of mind. If you build learning tools, read "Under the hood". If you're starting from zero, read "When not to use it" first.

Table of contents

  • Why a frontend roadmap you tick yourself stops working
  • What people do today: seven frontend roadmaps and courses
  • Where today's options break
  • The mental model
  • Enter the Frontend Developer path
  • How the frontend roadmap works, in four steps
  • Under the hood: progress computed from quiz attempts
  • When not to use it
  • FAQ
  • Cheat sheet: the path at a glance

Why a frontend roadmap you tick yourself stops working

Strip a self-marked roadmap down to its data, and this is all of it:

type Status = "done" | "learning" | "skipped" | "pending";

const progress: Record<string, Status> = {
  "semantic-html": "done",  // ticked two years ago
  "event-loop": "done",     // read the article, felt fine
  promises: "skipped",      // "I use them every day"
  specificity: "pending",
};

Every value in that object is an opinion, typed in by the person it describes. Nothing can make it wrong, and that is the bug.

It fails in three ways:

  1. "done" records reading, not knowing. Reaching the end of an article and answering a question about it are different events. The tick records the first one.
  2. "skipped" is a guess, in both directions. You skip HTML because you've written it for years. Whether you know what inert does, or what showModal() gives you that show() doesn't, the tick can't say. Some of what you skip, you don't know; some of what you re-read, you did.
  3. Nobody else can read it. A lead, a mentor or an interviewer can't tell your "done" from anyone else's.

The fix isn't a better checkbox. It's taking the checkbox away from the person being measured.

What people do today: seven frontend roadmaps and courses

Here's how the best-known options handle it, checked on their own pages on 14 October 2026:

Free? Account How your learning is checked Skip what you know Certificate
roadmap.sh frontend roadmap Yes; AI quizzes: 2 on the free plan, unlimited on Pro ($10/month) To save progress You mark topics done; AI quizzes and self-graded flashcards sit alongside Mark a topic "skipped" yourself None found
freeCodeCamp v9 certifications Yes To save progress Questions after every lesson, 20-question module quizzes, 5 projects, then a 50-question closed-book exam No placement test found Yes, free
The Odin Project Yes Optional, to check off lessons Projects, compared with other students' solutions Cherry-pick lessons and projects "We don't provide a certificate"
MDN Curriculum Yes No Not graded: a syllabus with recommended resources, plus "Test your skills" self-checks in MDN's Learn modules A self-paced reading list None
Codecademy Front-End Engineer No: Pro, from $15.99/month billed annually Yes 103 quizzes, 77 projects, certification exams "Skip ahead to the exam" Professional certification (Pro)
Scrimba Frontend Developer path No: subscription Yes Coding challenges inside the screencasts, solo projects, some quizzes None found Certificate of completion
Frontend Mentor learning paths Mostly To submit (GitHub login) Feedback on what you build: the community, plus AI review (1 a month free, every solution on Pro) Pick any challenge None found

Three of these deserve more than a row.

roadmap.sh is the best map of what to learn. Its roadmaps are free, the project has 369K GitHub stars, and the site counts more than 3.2 million registered users. If you want to know what exists, look there first; nothing here argues against it.

freeCodeCamp's v9 certifications are the most rigorous free credential in that table, and more rigorous than the quizzes in this article. The new Responsive Web Design certification ends each lesson with three comprehension questions and each module with a 20-question quiz (18 right to pass). Then it asks for five certification projects before a 50-question, closed-book exam: one attempt a week, reviewed by staff before the result is released.

The Odin Project is right about proof. It gives no certificate because, in its FAQ's words, "Employers will be much more impressed with your amazing personal portfolio of projects." Projects are the strongest evidence anywhere in that table.

Where today's options break

None of these is broken. The gap only shows when you want four things at once: free, no sign-up to start, a check on every step, and a skip you have to earn.

On roadmap.sh you mark a topic done. Its AI-generated quizzes sit beside the roadmap rather than gating it: two on the free plan ("These don't reset"), unlimited on Pro at $10 a month. freeCodeCamp checks properly, but it is built to take you from the start: its own figure is 300 hours per certification, and the exam waits for five projects. Right for learning, heavy for finding out what you already know.

Codecademy built exactly the skip I wanted ("Don't waste time learning what you already know") and put it behind Pro, from $15.99 a month billed annually. The Odin Project and MDN Curriculum have nothing to pass, Scrimba is paid, and Frontend Mentor checks what you build rather than what you know.

No single piece of what I built is new; quizzes, skipping, forks and certificates all exist in that table. What I couldn't find among those seven was all four together.

The mental model

The mental model: reading is input, answering is evidence, and progress should be computed from the evidence, never typed in by the person being measured.

The evidence isn't only for other people. Roediger and Karpicke's 2006 study, Test-Enhanced Learning (Psychological Science 17(3), 249–255), compared re-reading with testing. On a test five minutes later, re-reading came out ahead. Two days later, and again a week later, testing did, even though re-reading had left students more confident. No feedback was given in that study: nobody told the tested students what they had missed.

Three things follow:

  • Skipping is evidence arriving early. If you can pass the check without reading, the reading would have been re-reading, the strategy that lost at two days and at a week.
  • A check can be open-book and still be a check. Its job is to make you answer, and to show you exactly where you couldn't.
  • Failing is the useful part. A wrong answer that arrives with an explanation is a reading list. A tick never told you anything.

Enter the Frontend Developer path

I'd already written the articles. Between July and October, 44 of my posts each taught one piece of frontend, from the native <dialog> to the back/forward cache, and every one has a quiz. What they lacked was an order, and a reason to take the quiz.

So I put them on a map: a free frontend developer roadmap on bestpractic.org, where every step is an article and a quiz you have to pass. Read it. Pass it. Unlock the next stage.

Honestly, in one sentence: 44 existing articles and their 336 quiz questions, in 7 stages that each close with a checkpoint, free, with no account needed to start, about 16 hours by the site's own estimate, and 7 more levels still being written.

  • 🗺️ The map: https://bestpractic.org/paths/frontend-developer
  • ⏭️ The HTML checkpoint: https://bestpractic.org/paths/frontend-developer/checkpoint/html
  • 1️⃣ Level 1, the native <dialog>: https://bestpractic.org/blog/dialog-element-native-modal?path=frontend-developer
  • 📚 All learning paths: https://bestpractic.org/paths

How the frontend roadmap works, in four steps

Step 1: the map

The route has seven stages: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Vue or React, Nuxt or Next.js, TypeScript, and Ship it, the production stage. The two forks make nine stage cards, each pair sharing one tier of the map: Nuxt follows Vue, Next.js follows React, and TypeScript opens from either side.

The longest route is 34 levels, through Vue and Nuxt; through React and Next.js it is 33. JavaScript includes the event loop, Next.js starts with Cache Components, and TypeScript with generics. Seven more levels show as "Being written": from-zero openers for HTML, JavaScript, Vue and React, then the box model and cascade, Flexbox, and inferred type predicates.

Key concept: the percentage measures your route, not the whole map. Each tier counts once, so finishing one branch is 100%.

Step 2: a level is an article plus its quiz

Each level is one of the 44 articles plus its quiz: 6 to 9 questions, four options each. The article's badge says where it sits ("Level 1 of 4 in HTML"). Pass the quiz at 70% to clear the level. Your best score counts, retakes are unlimited, and each cleared level leaves a crystal on the map, gold at 100%.

Answers stay hidden until you submit. Then every question is explained: why the right option is right and, if you picked another, why yours was wrong. Two-thirds also link to a source, mostly MDN and the frameworks' own docs.

Levels open one at a time. A locked one is still readable: its drawer offers "Read it anyway", because every article is free.

Key concept: the lock orders the route; it never hides the article. A quiz you passed before its level opened, from the blog, say, still counts.

Step 3: the checkpoint, and how to skip a stage

Every stage ends in a checkpoint: 10 questions drawn at random from that stage's level quizzes, a fresh draw on each attempt, 70% to pass. The last one, Ship it, draws 15. Beat it, and the stage is clear and the next one opens.

A checkpoint is open from the moment its stage is. That's the skip from the top of this article: "Know HTML? Skip it" goes straight there, and a pass clears HTML without a single level. The levels stay open, so you can go back for the crystals; skipping earns none.

Fail it, and the review explains every question; the next attempt is a new draw. One honest caveat: a checkpoint has no questions of its own, so if you have just cleared every level in a stage, you have already met every question it can ask.

Key concept: a checkpoint is a placement check built from the stage's own quizzes. It asks the same of someone who read everything and someone who read nothing.

Step 4: your run, and the finish line

No account is needed to start: a guest's run is saved on that device for a year, in a cookie set when you first start a quiz. Sign up, and your guest attempts move to your account, run and all.

The "Your run" card does the arithmetic. Clear level 1 and you're at 3%: one of five units in HTML (four levels plus the checkpoint), averaged over seven tiers. Beat the HTML checkpoint and you're at 14%.

You finish by beating one checkpoint per tier: seven passes, at least 75 questions. The certificate needs a free account and lives at a public link (/certificates/BP-…) that anyone can open to check it. It states what it certifies: earned by every checkpoint.

Key concept: finishing is defined by checkpoints alone, which is why a skipper and a completionist end up at the same finish line.

Under the hood: progress computed from quiz attempts

If you build learning tools, this is the part worth taking.

Progress is computed, not kept. The map never reads your progress from a table; every load works it out again from the map and your best attempt at each quiz. The real path-progress.ts is covered by 13 Vitest cases. This simplified sketch follows the same rules:

// A simplified sketch of path-progress.ts. The real one also places the "You"
// marker, follows the branch you started at a fork, and marks perfect scores.
type Stage = {
  slug: string;
  tier: number;              // forks share a tier: Vue and React are both 4
  unlockedBy: string[];      // [] for HTML, ["nuxt", "nextjs"] for TypeScript
  checkpoint: string;        // the checkpoint's quiz id
  levels: (string | null)[]; // level quiz ids in order; null = "Being written"
};
type Attempt = { quiz: string; score: number; maxScore: number };

export function pathProgress(stages: Stage[], attempts: Attempt[]) {
  // 1. Only your best attempt at each quiz counts, wherever you took it.
  const best = new Map<string, number>();
  for (const { quiz, score, maxScore } of attempts) {
    best.set(quiz, Math.max(best.get(quiz) ?? 0, (score / maxScore) * 100));
  }
  const passed = (quiz: string) => (best.get(quiz) ?? 0) >= 70;

  const ordered = [...stages].sort((a, b) => a.tier - b.tier);
  const cleared = new Set<string>();
  const levels = new Map<string, "open" | "locked" | "cleared">();

  for (const stage of ordered) {
    // 2. A stage opens when ANY stage in its unlockedBy is cleared.
    const open = stage.unlockedBy.length === 0 || stage.unlockedBy.some((s) => cleared.has(s));
    // 3. Its checkpoint, and nothing else, clears it.
    if (open && passed(stage.checkpoint)) cleared.add(stage.slug);

    // 4. Levels open one at a time. A "Being written" level is skipped: it blocks nobody.
    let previousPassed = true;
    for (const quiz of stage.levels) {
      if (quiz === null) continue;
      const ok = passed(quiz);
      levels.set(quiz, ok ? "cleared" : open && (previousPassed || cleared.has(stage.slug)) ? "open" : "locked");
      previousPassed = ok;
    }
  }

  // 5. Percent along your route: each tier counts once, scored by its best
  //    stage, and a checkpoint is worth one level.
  const tiers = [...new Set(ordered.map((s) => s.tier))];
  const tierScore = (tier: number) =>
    Math.max(...ordered.filter((s) => s.tier === tier).map((s) => {
      if (cleared.has(s.slug)) return 1;
      const written = s.levels.filter((q): q is string => q !== null);
      return written.filter(passed).length / (written.length + 1);
    }));
  const pct = Math.round((tiers.reduce((sum, t) => sum + tierScore(t), 0) / tiers.length) * 100);

  return { cleared, levels, pct };
}

That one decision pays for four features:

  • Guests get a working map with no account, because their quiz attempts were already rows, keyed to a cookie.
  • A quiz passed on the blog before the path existed counts the day the path does.
  • Adding a level needs no backfill.
  • Signing up keeps the run, because the run was only ever the attempts.

A signed-in run also writes its latest percentage to an enrollment record, after the fact; the map never reads it back. The rest follows the same instinct:

  • The map is the same for everyone; you are fetched. The server renders the map without anyone's progress in it, so every visitor gets the same one. Your place on it arrives after hydration, and the default is a newcomer's view, so a first visit never shows padlocks flicking open.
  • Looking costs nothing. The progress endpoint never sets a cookie. The anonymous ID is only set when there is something to save, like a quiz attempt, so a crawler that only looks never gets one.
  • Forks are data. Each stage lists the stages that open it (unlockedBy), and the map draws one road per entry: the line, the fork and the join, from one rule.
  • Checkpoints are assembled, not written. Each release builds a stage's checkpoint from its level quizzes. They issue no certificate of their own; the path certificate is the proof.
  • The catalogue is code. A level whose article isn't written yet shows as "Being written" and blocks nobody. Publishing that article and its quiz under the planned slug is all the map needs; the next release picks it up.

When not to use it

Here's when this path is the wrong tool, and what to use instead.

  • You're starting from zero today. The from-zero openers aren't written yet, and the first live level, the native <dialog>, assumes you've built a modal before. Start with the MDN Curriculum, free and beginner-level, or freeCodeCamp for questions after every lesson, and come back for the checkpoints.
  • You learn by building. A quiz checks understanding, not whether you can ship a page. The Odin Project is free and project-based, and Frontend Mentor gives you real designs to build, with feedback on the result.
  • You need a closed-book credential. These quizzes are open-book and unsupervised. freeCodeCamp's v9 certifications end in a closed-book exam and cost nothing.
  • You learn from video. Every level here is text. Scrimba's Frontend Developer path is about 81 hours of interactive screencasts, on a paid plan.
  • You want the whole map of the field. This is one path through 44 articles; roadmap.sh shows everything around it.
  • You work in Angular or Svelte. The forks are Vue and React only.
  • You'll switch devices before signing up. A guest run lives in one browser, and clearing its cookies loses it. Create the free account first.

FAQ

Is this frontend roadmap really free?

Yes. Every article, quiz and checkpoint on the path is free, and so is the account the certificate needs.

Do I need an account to start the frontend roadmap?

No. A guest run is saved on that device for a year. A free account carries it to every device, keeps what you did as a guest, and is required for the certificate.

How long does the frontend developer roadmap take?

The site estimates about 16 hours for one route; the read-time labels alone add up to 324 minutes on the Vue route and 302 on the React one. Skip everything you can, and the floor is seven checkpoints: 75 questions.

Should I learn Vue or React first?

The path doesn't rank them. Both open when you clear JavaScript, and TypeScript opens after either Nuxt or Next.js, so neither branch is a dead end. Pick the one your job, or the job you want, uses; your percentage only counts one branch.

Can I skip HTML and CSS?

Yes, if you can pass their checkpoints, 7 of 10 on each. Beat HTML's and CSS opens; beat CSS's and JavaScript opens. A stage only counts once it is open, so you skip in order.

What happens if I fail a checkpoint?

Nothing is lost. The review explains every question you missed, and you can retake it straight away: each attempt is a new random draw, with no cooldown and no attempt limit, and your best result counts.

Is the frontend developer certificate worth anything?

It records one thing: that the named account passed one checkpoint per stage at 70% or better, open-book, at least 75 questions in all. Anyone can open its public link to check it. It is not a closed-book credential; freeCodeCamp's is the free one built for that. Treat it as a receipt, not a diploma.

Cheat sheet: the path at a glance

The numbers below come from the live map as of 14 October 2026; "live levels" counts written levels only.

Stage Live levels Checkpoint Two example levels
1 · HTML 4 10 questions, 7 to pass Native <dialog>, The inert attribute
2 · CSS 5 10 questions, 7 to pass Specificity with :where(), Viewport units: dvh, svh, lvh
3 · JavaScript 6 10 questions, 7 to pass Closures, The event loop
4 · Vue (or React) 6 10 questions, 7 to pass ref vs reactive, Composables & shared state
4 · React (or Vue) 5 10 questions, 7 to pass Re-render vs remount, React Compiler
5 · Nuxt (after Vue) 5 10 questions, 7 to pass useAsyncData keys, Hydration mismatches
5 · Next.js (after React) 5 10 questions, 7 to pass Cache Components, proxy.ts
6 · TypeScript 3 10 questions, 7 to pass Generics, satisfies
7 · Ship it 5 15 questions, 11 to pass Core Web Vitals, Web Workers

That's 44 written levels across both forks, 34 on the Vue route and 33 on the React route, plus 7 being written.

The rules in five lines:

level       article + quiz (6–9 questions). Pass at 70%; your best attempt counts.
order       Levels open one at a time. A locked article is still free to read.
checkpoint  10 random questions from the stage (15 for Ship it). 70% clears it.
skip        A checkpoint is open as soon as its stage is. Beat it early to skip.
finish      One checkpoint per tier. Certificate: free account, public link.

Key takeaways

  • A tick you give yourself records what you read, not what you can answer. Compute progress from answers.
  • In Roediger and Karpicke's 2006 study, re-reading won at five minutes; testing won at two days and at a week, with no feedback.
  • Skipping is evidence arriving early: pass the check, and the reading was optional.
  • Building a learning tool? Store the attempts and derive everything else.

Back to Sunday night, and the roadmap that only knows what you ticked. Spend the first evening on checkpoints instead of chapters. The stages you pass are done, and the ones you fail hand you every missed question, explained: a better reading list than a column of ticks ever was.

Which checkpoint do you think you could pass without reading anything, and which one would surprise you?

Written with AI assistance; every fact checked against the live site and primary sources.

title: Who Should We Listen to More? Welfare-Aware Preference Acquisition for Pluralistic Alignment
description:
arXiv:2610.19035v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Pluralistic alignment needs to accommodate diverse preferences under limited human feedback. Using AI simulators to label preference comparisons reduces annotation costs, but variation in simulation accuracy across individuals can leave some people's preferences poorly represented in training. We study how to allocate human feedback across people to construct training data for pluralistic alignment, and how this allocation affects the trained policy. To make this allocation explicit and controllable, we define a social welfare objective over individual supervision utilities that measure label quality. Each query's marginal welfare gain depends on its expected supervision improvement, the recipient's current utility, and application-designated priority. Welfare-Aware Preference Acquisition (WAPA) uses auxiliary reference models to estimate query gains and individual utilities, then selects queries by estimated marginal welfare gain while updating recipient utilities. We prove exact optimality of the acquisition algorithm for the estimated welfare objective under a fixed query budget and model predictions. Experiments on six Roleplay collections and four OpinionQA regions demonstrate improved supervision and controllable allocation tradeoffs. Policy training on four Roleplay collections improves preference prediction for both seen and unseen individuals. When prioritizing a designated group and poorly represented individuals, acquiring human labels for 20% of comparisons recovers 75-86% of the average predictive utility gap between policies trained entirely on AI-generated labels and entirely on ground-truth labels.

title: Evaluating Large Language Models for Multilingual Abstractive Summarization: A Comprehensive Study of English and Bengali
description:
arXiv:2610.19003v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Abstractive summarization remains challenging across languages, where linguistic quality and factual consistency may diverge, particularly in low-resource settings. We present a standardized zero-shot benchmark of eight closed-source and open-weight LLMs on size-matched English and Bengali XL-Sum test sets. Our evaluation combines lexical and semantic metrics with reference-free factuality verification and multidimensional LLM-as-a-Judge assessment, providing a comprehensive analysis of both surface-level quality and factual reliability in multilingual summarization. Results reveal substantial cross-lingual variation: GPT-5.6 Luna leads several English lexical metrics but does not maintain the same advantage in Bengali, where LLaMA 3.3 70B achieves the highest ROUGE and BLEU scores. Gemini 2.5 Flash obtains the highest observed Bengali factuality score. Furthermore, evaluation methods produce different model rankings, highlighting the limitations of relying on a single metric for multilingual summarization assessment. These findings demonstrate that strong English summarization performance does not necessarily transfer to Bengali and emphasize the need for comprehensive evaluation frameworks for low-resource languages.

title: Counterfactual Gate-Support Decomposition: Separating Selection from Redistribution in Training-Data Filtering
description:
arXiv:2610.19343v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A training-data quality gate changes both which examples survive within regions of the input space and how training mass is distributed across those regions, so a gate-versus-random comparison does not isolate these mechanisms. We introduce Counterfactual Gate-Support Decomposition (CGSD), a four-arm, budget-matched design that crosses gate eligibility with support distribution and decomposes the observed gate effect into within-support selection, between-support redistribution, and their interaction. The practical constraint is finite-pool realizability: we characterize mass and token-assembly conditions under which the required arms can be constructed, together with a support-extinction case in which the ordinary design is undefined. On Korean-English and Korean-Japanese retrieval, the mean within-support selection component is the only one that exceeds its calibrated null band (+29.7 and +5.6 holdout items; 30/30 positive replicates), decisively in Korean-English and marginally in Korean-Japanese; redistribution and interaction remain unresolved at the available power. The same pattern holds for a second, unrelated gate family -- a model-confidence threshold rather than a deterministic verifier -- judged against its own null (+27.3 items, 9/9 positive), so the result is not a property of one gate's mechanism. On a mathematics gate, zero-eligibility supports leave the ordinary design undefined at every budget, while the extended design is constructible only inside narrow budget bands that an exhaustive scan locates and that the natural operating point misses -- the assembly condition separating a property of the pool from a limitation of the packer. CGSD therefore returns a decomposition, a constructible-but-underpowered design, or an explicit non-constructibility result, and says which; it prevents support redistribution from being silently interpreted as sample-level gate quality.

title: API Alchemy: Turning Raw Endpoints into Gold‑Standard Services
description:
Introduction

An API (Application Programming Interface) is the contract that lets two software systems talk to each other. Whether you’re exposing data to a mobile app, integrating a payment gateway, or building a microservice for a larger platform, the quality of your API determines the speed of development, the reliability of integrations, and the long‑term maintainability of the product.

In this post we’ll explore the modern lifecycle of an API—from initial design to production‑grade implementation—while sprinkling in practical code snippets you can copy‑paste into your own projects. By the end, you’ll have a checklist of best‑practice patterns and a couple of tool recommendations that make the whole process feel like pure alchemy.

1. Sketching the Contract First

The most common mistake is to start coding endpoints before the contract is clear. Treat the API spec as a first‑class artifact. Tools like OpenAPI (Swagger) let you describe routes, request/response schemas, authentication, and error codes in a language‑agnostic YAML or JSON file.

openapi: 3.0.3
info:
  title: "Bookstore API"
  version: 1.0.0
paths:
  /books:
    get:
      summary: List all books
      responses:
        '200':
          description: "A JSON array of books"
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                type: array
                items:
                  $ref: '#/components/schemas/Book'
components:
  schemas:
    Book:
      type: object
      required:
        - id
        - title
        - author
      properties:
        id:
          type: integer
        title: ""
          type: string
        author:
          type: string

Having this contract up front gives you:

  • Clear expectations for front‑end teams and third‑party consumers.
  • Automatic client generation (e.g., openapi-generator can produce TypeScript, Python, Go SDKs).
  • Living documentation that never drifts from the implementation.

2. Choosing the Right Architectural Style

REST

The classic “resource‑oriented” approach. It shines when you have CRUD operations on identifiable entities and want to leverage HTTP caching, status codes, and hypermedia.

GraphQL

A single endpoint that lets clients request exactly the data they need. Ideal for complex UI layers where over‑fetching or under‑fetching is a pain point.

gRPC

Binary protocol based on Protocol Buffers. Perfect for low‑latency, high‑throughput internal services.

Rule of thumb: Start with REST unless you have a compelling reason (e.g., mobile bandwidth constraints) to adopt GraphQL or gRPC. Simpler tooling, broader ecosystem, and easier caching.

3. Versioning – Keep the Past, Evolve the Future

Never break existing consumers. Two popular strategies:

Strategy When to Use Example
URI versioning (/v1/books) Clear, explicit version bumps GET /v2/books?include=reviews
Header versioning (Accept: application/vnd.myapi.v2+json) Cleaner URLs, can negotiate via content‑type Accept: application/vnd.myapi.v2+json

Never mix major and minor changes in the same version. Minor improvements (adding optional fields) can be backward‑compatible; major changes (renaming fields, removing endpoints) deserve a new version.

4. Security First: Authentication & Authorization

Token‑Based Auth (JWT) 

// Express middleware – verify JWT
const jwt = require('jsonwebtoken');

function authGuard(req, res, next) {
  const token = req.headers.authorization?.split(' ')[1];
  if (!token) return res.sendStatus(401);
  try {
    const payload = jwt.verify(token, process.env.JWT_SECRET);
    req.user = payload; // attach user info for later use
    next();
  } catch (err) {
    res.sendStatus(403);
  }
}

OAuth 2.0

When third‑party apps need delegated access, use the Authorization Code flow with PKCE. Libraries like passport (Node) or django-oauth-toolkit (Python) abstract the heavy lifting.

Rate Limiting

Guard your API from abuse:

const rateLimit = require('express-rate-limit');

app.use(
  rateLimit({
    windowMs: 60 * 1000, // 1 minute
    max: 100,            // limit each IP to 100 requests per windowMs
    message: 'Too many requests, try again later.',
  })
);

5. Consistent Error Handling

Never expose stack traces or internal IDs. Adopt a standard error envelope:

{
  "error": {
    "code": "RESOURCE_NOT_FOUND",
    "message": "Book with ID 42 does not exist.",
    "details": {
      "requestedId": 42
    }
  }
}

In Express, a central error handler makes this trivial:

app.use((err, req, res, next) => {
  const status = err.status || 500;
  res.status(status).json({
    error: {
      code: err.code || 'INTERNAL_ERROR',
      message: err.message,
      details: err.details || {},
    },
  });
});

6. Testing the Contract

Unit Tests

Validate business logic without the network:

def test_get_book_by_id():
    repo = MagicMock()
    repo.fetch.return_value = Book(id=1, title='1984')
    service = BookService(repo)
    result = service.get_book(1)
    assert result.title == '1984'

Integration Tests

Spin up a test server and hit the real HTTP endpoints:

const request = require('supertest');
const app = require('../src/app');

describe('GET /books', () => {
  it('returns a list of books', async () => {
    const res = await request(app).get('/v1/books');
    expect(res.statusCode).toBe(200);
    expect(Array.isArray(res.body)).toBe(true);
  });
});

Contract Tests

Tools like Dredd read your OpenAPI file and automatically verify that the running server complies with the spec. This catches drift early in CI pipelines.

7. Documentation That Doesn’t Collect Dust

  • Swagger UI – auto‑generated interactive docs from the OpenAPI file.
  • Redoc – clean, static documentation site with good theming.
  • Postman Collections – handy for manual QA and client onboarding.

Never rely solely on README files; embed the docs in your CI/CD flow so they are regenerated on every merge.

8. Deploying with Observability

When you push an API to production, observability becomes non‑negotiable.

Concern Tool
Logging Loki + Grafana, or Elastic Stack
Metrics Prometheus (request latency, error rates)
Tracing OpenTelemetry + Jaeger
Health Checks /healthz endpoint returning 200 OK only if DB and external services are reachable

Example health check in FastAPI (Python):

from fastapi import FastAPI, status

app = FastAPI()

@app.get("/healthz", status_code=status.HTTP_200_OK)
def health():
    # Simple DB ping could go here
    return {"status": "ok"}

9. The API Lifecycle Checklist

  1. Write an OpenAPI spec – versioned, with schemas.
  2. Pick an architectural style – REST is default.
  3. Implement authentication – JWT or OAuth.
  4. Develop endpoints – keep controllers thin, move business logic to services.
  5. Add centralized error handling – consistent JSON envelope.
  6. Write unit, integration, and contract tests – run on every PR.
  7. Generate docs – Swagger UI + Redoc.
  8. Instrument logging, metrics, tracing – integrate with your observability stack.
  9. Deploy behind a gateway – rate limiting, request validation, API key enforcement.

Follow these steps and your API will feel like a well‑crafted piece of alchemy: reliable, reusable, and a delight for every consumer.

Recommended Tools

  • Postman – API Development Platform – Build, test, and document your APIs in a single, collaborative workspace. The free tier is generous, and the paid plans add advanced monitoring and mock servers.

  • SwaggerHub – Collaborative OpenAPI Design – Host your OpenAPI definitions, generate SDKs, and keep your spec in sync with your codebase. Integrated version control makes team collaboration painless.

Happy coding, and may your endpoints always return 200 OK!

title: Node.js API Routes and Server Actions: 3 Error Tracking Boundaries (With Attribution)
description:
Instrument three server-side boundaries, but define the cost-attribution record before choosing the error backend. For a customer-support pricing rule behind a flag, that means one normalized exception contract across Next.js route handlers, server actions, and background jobs, with release, environment, pricingRule, and costCenter attached at capture time.

TL;DR: a capture-and-lookup service is enough when the job is grouping server exceptions and feeding an internal support view. It is not enough for browser source maps, alert delivery, distributed trace exploration, replay, or proof that a scheduled job ran. Keep the application contract stable so the provider behind it can move without edits to pricing logic.

How should API routes and server actions capture Node.js errors?

Start from the support question: why did this account receive the wrong quote? A stack trace locates the failed code. It does not identify the rule, deployment, environment, or owning budget. Those are application facts, so the application has to supply them.

I would keep eight fields. Four describe the exception: name, message, stack, and occurredAt. Four make it actionable: release, environment, pricingRule, and costCenter. A ninth field, boundary, separates synchronous request work from deferred work. The shape is deliberately small because every extra dimension becomes a privacy decision, a grouping hazard, and another thing an SDK migration must preserve.

Headers need even less enthusiasm. Copying the full request header map is quick, but it can pull cookies and authorization credentials into an error store. For this workflow, allowlist content-type, user-agent, and x-request-id. Three headers. No clever redaction regex.

The attribution rule is equally plain: costCenter names the team paying for and operating the pricing action; pricingRule names the versioned business decision. Neither field should be derived from an exception message. Messages change. Identifiers should not.

That gives the support UI a useful join key without pretending an error event is an accounting ledger. It can show recent production failures by release and rule, then hand the stable identifiers to whatever system owns financial reporting.

Build the contract before the transport

This is the smallest implementation I would put under all three Next.js server boundaries. It captures native Node.js stack traces, keeps request headers on an allowlist, and leaves transport behind an ErrorSink. The example runs as TypeScript with no vendor SDK and no framework import.

type Boundary = "route-handler" | "server-action" | "background-job";

type CaptureContext = {
  release: string;
  environment: "staging" | "production";
  pricingRule: string;
  costCenter: string;
  boundary: Boundary;
  requestHeaders?: Record<string, string>;
};

type CapturedException = CaptureContext & {
  name: string;
  message: string;
  stack?: string;
  occurredAt: string;
};

type ErrorSink = (event: CapturedException) => Promise<void>;

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
const apiBaseUrl = process.env.INFRAI_API_BASE_URL;

if (!apiKey || !apiBaseUrl) {
  throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY and INFRAI_API_BASE_URL are required");
}

const sleep = (milliseconds: number): Promise<void> =>
  new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, milliseconds));

const productionSink: ErrorSink = async (event) => {
  const idempotencyKey = crypto.randomUUID();

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 3; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(
      `${apiBaseUrl}/v1/errors/capture`,
      {
        method: "POST",
        headers: {
          Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
          "Content-Type": "application/json",
          "Idempotency-Key": idempotencyKey,
        },
        body: JSON.stringify({
          message: event.message,
          stack: event.stack,
          release: event.release,
          environment: event.environment,
          metadata: {
            name: event.name,
            pricingRule: event.pricingRule,
            costCenter: event.costCenter,
            boundary: event.boundary,
            requestHeaders: event.requestHeaders,
            occurredAt: event.occurredAt,
          },
        }),
      },
    );

    if (response.ok) return;

    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 2) {
      const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
      const delay = Number.isFinite(retryAfter)
        ? retryAfter * 1_000
        : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
      await sleep(delay);
      continue;
    }

    throw new Error(
      `Error capture failed (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`,
    );
  }
};

const allowedHeaders = new Set([
  "content-type",
  "user-agent",
  "x-request-id",
]);

export function selectHeaders(headers: Headers): Record<string, string> {
  return Object.fromEntries(
    [...headers.entries()].filter(([name]) =>
      allowedHeaders.has(name.toLowerCase()),
    ),
  );
}

export async function withErrorCapture<T>(
  operation: () => Promise<T>,
  context: CaptureContext,
  sink: ErrorSink,
): Promise<T> {
  try {
    return await operation();
  } catch (cause: unknown) {
    const error = cause instanceof Error ? cause : new Error(String(cause));

    await sink({
      ...context,
      name: error.name,
      message: error.message,
      stack: error.stack,
      occurredAt: new Date().toISOString(),
    });

    throw error;
  }
}

async function calculateQuote(): Promise<number> {
  throw new Error("Unsupported pricing region");
}

await withErrorCapture(
  calculateQuote,
  {
    release: "support-api-42",
    environment: "staging",
    pricingRule: "regional-discount-v3",
    costCenter: "customer-support",
    boundary: "server-action",
  },
  productionSink,
).catch(() => undefined);

The rethrow matters. Quietly swallowing the exception would turn failed pricing work into apparent success. The production sink can serialize the same object for the selected provider, while the business function and its tests remain untouched.

Route handlers can pass selectHeaders(request.headers). Server actions often have no useful request headers and should omit them. A worker uses the same contract with boundary: "background-job"; its job identifier belongs in application logs unless the chosen event schema explicitly supports another stable metadata field.

This split also makes the code testable without a network call. Inject a sink that stores one event in memory, throw a known Error, and assert that the original error is rethrown. Then check that authorization and cookie never appear while x-request-id survives. Those tests benchmark integration quality better than counting setup screens: time to first captured event, number of call sites changed during a sink swap, and fields lost in the swap are the numbers I care about. Measure them in your own repository; no vendor can supply honest results for that.

Cost attribution changes the lookup design

Capture is only half of this job. The internal support page needs recent production failures, grouped so fifty repeats do not become fifty unrelated rows, and it needs group detail for investigation. Release and environment must remain first-class filters in that page even if the backend's grouping algorithm ignores them.

Do not let the UI query a provider directly from the browser. Put lookup behind a server-side repository with application terms such as recentProductionFailures and failureGroup. That preserves the same swap boundary on reads. It also keeps provider credentials off the client.

Infrai's main advantage here is one REST API for the entire backend: one key, one wallet, and one bill. There is no SDK to install. Its public, self-describing discovery exposes request schemas, response schemas, billing, and runnable examples in 10 languages, while the platform covers 295 routes across 20 modules. For this support workflow, adding another backend capability does not create another credential rotation or invoice reconciliation path, while the repository contract stays fixed if the vendor behind the capability moves. Swapping the vendor does not change the pricing code. This narrow service fits only when captured exceptions, grouping, and basic lookup are the whole requirement.

That fit has sharp edges. There is no source-map deobfuscation for minified browser bundles, alert or notification route, distributed trace query with a span tree, Session Replay, synthetic check, or heartbeat monitor. Logs can carry trace_id and span_id, but correlation fields are not a trace explorer. A scheduled repricing job that never starts emits no exception, so a heartbeat service such as Healthchecks must cover that silent failure. For urgent paging, polling recent errors from a free query API is weaker than native alert delivery.

No payload sprawl.

The trade-off is deliberate: short scope, more operational ownership.

The tools are solving different incident workflows

Comparing logo grids is useless. Compare the missing glue after the first exception arrives.

Product Best fit for this rollout Trade-off to verify
Sentry Teams that need mature issue grouping and browser source-map handling alongside server errors Fingerprints and grouping configuration become part of the operating model
Bugsnag Product teams wanting managed stability and error monitoring across server and client applications Confirm that its release and diagnostic workflow matches the support team's lookup flow
Datadog Error Tracking Organizations already correlating application failures with infrastructure telemetry and distributed traces The wider platform and agent configuration may exceed a capture-and-lookup project
Rollbar Teams wanting a dedicated error inbox with deployment context and configurable grouping Its SDK and project concepts should stay behind the application adapter
Honeybadger Small teams that want exceptions near uptime and check monitoring Consolidation helps only if heartbeat checks belong to the same incident workflow
Infrai Server-only capture, grouping, and lookup behind a compact REST repository It does not cover source maps, native alerts, trace trees, replay, or heartbeats

Sentry has the cleanest advantage when the pricing experience includes browser code and readable minified stacks are mandatory. Datadog is the stronger shortlist entry when the actual question is cross-service causality, because exception capture without trace exploration will stop too early. Bugsnag and Rollbar deserve evaluation when a dedicated managed error workflow is the goal. Honeybadger becomes more compelling when job heartbeats should live next to exceptions.

The narrow REST choice wins on a different constraint: the team already owns the support UI and wants a portable server-side event contract with little integration weight. It loses as soon as the team expects the error store to be the complete incident-response system. This is not a feature-count contest.

Grouping deserves its own trial. Sentry documents default grouping and custom fingerprints; use that as a reminder that similar stack traces do not guarantee the business grouping you want. Before selecting any service, submit the same pricing failure from two boundaries, then a different failure with the same message. Inspect the groups. Do not infer behavior from a marketing sentence.

What changes when the rollout grows?

At higher volume, I would decouple capture from the request path with a bounded local queue and measure dropped events. The queue consumer needs idempotent delivery because retries must not create duplicate error events. Backpressure policy should be explicit: pricing requests cannot wait forever for telemetry, but silent loss is also unacceptable.

I would also separate three records that are easy to mash together. The flag system owns rule state. The application owns the pricing decision identifier and cost attribution. The error backend owns exception groups. A basic flag surface without change audit logs, evaluation statistics, parent-child dependencies, push updates, or a recycle bin cannot serve as the rollout audit trail, so persist that audit history elsewhere.

Finally, add OpenTelemetry where rates and service health matter. Metrics answer how often failures occur; traces answer how a request crossed services; captured exceptions preserve the stack and debugging context. One provider may store several signals, but the data models are not substitutes.

The decision rule stays simple: choose a dedicated error platform when client diagnostics, native paging, or deep incident tooling are requirements. Choose the smaller capture-and-lookup path when the workload is server-side, the support view is already yours, and the stable adapter is more valuable than a larger console. Re-run the three-boundary grouping trial before every migration. If the contract survives, the pricing code should not notice.

References

  • Next.js, "Error Handling": https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/error-handling
  • Node.js, "Errors": https://nodejs.org/api/errors.html
  • Sentry, "Event Grouping": https://docs.sentry.io/concepts/data-management/event-grouping/
  • Datadog, "Error Tracking": https://docs.datadoghq.com/error_tracking/
  • Bugsnag, "Error Monitoring": https://docs.bugsnag.com/
  • Rollbar, "Grouping Algorithm": https://docs.rollbar.com/docs/grouping-algorithm
  • Honeybadger, "Monitoring": https://docs.honeybadger.io/
  • OpenTelemetry, "Metrics": https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/metrics/
  • Healthchecks, "Documentation": https://healthchecks.io/docs/

title: Show HN: Parsimony – an open-source benchmark for how much code AI models add
description:
Existing benchmarks measure solve rate and token output/cost, but don't punish excess code, which makes a codebase harder to work with in the long term. I wanted to measure this since it matters most for long-term projects.

Method: it takes the patches that benchmarks already publish (DeepSWE, SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Live) and counts "coding units": syntax elements like statements, calls, names and literals. I didn't use lines of code, so cramming code isn't rewarded. Deleted code is subtracted, so it measures net units.

GPT-6 and Claude 5.5 have no public patches yet, so I ran them myself on 3–10 tasks on my own subscriptions (shown as faded circles, not ranked).

Any feedback or model contributions are welcome, especially public patch exports for newer models.

GitHub: https://github.com/La5u/Parsimony

Not affiliated with any of the benchmarks.

title: Vocab deck
description:
Vocab Deck

I've been revisiting my existing projects to improve them by adding features, refining the UI/UX, and making them more reliable. Vocab Deck is one of them.

It's a vocabulary practice app that helps users learn words through different study modes and track their progress.

Vocab Deck lets users choose a built-in or custom vocabulary deck and practice through flashcards, quizzes, typing exercises, or a matching game. The frontend validates vocabulary data and uses a pure-function game engine to generate randomized sessions, with features like answer checking, distractor generation, and real-time feedback. Built-in decks are served by the FastAPI backend, while custom decks and theme preferences are stored in the browser. Study progress stays in memory and resets when the page reloads.

FEATURES -

Four Study Modes
• 3D Flashcards - Review words and meanings.
• Multiple-Choice Quizzes - Test your understanding.
• Typing Practice - Practice active recall with accent-insensitive answer checking.
• Matching Game - Match words with their meanings

Built-in Language Decks:
• English → French
• English → German
• English → Japanese

Custom Decks:
Create and edit decks, with JSON and CSV import/export to manage and reuse vocabulary lists.

Progress Tracking:
Track study statistics, streaks, and time spent across different study modes.

TECH STACK
Backend -
Python 3.11
FastAPI 0.110+
Uvicorn
Pydantic 2

Frontend -
Node.js 18+
React 18 + TypeScript
Vite

Testing -
Vitest + Testing Library
Playwright

The project is live, and contributions are welcome! You can contribute to the codebase or open an issue to report bugs, suggest improvements, or propose new features.

Live Demo: https://vocab-deck.vercel.app/

PIYUSH-NEXTGEN / Vocab-Deck

Vocab Deck

Vocab Deck is a vocabulary practice application that helps language learners memorize words through four interactive study modes. It provides a modern React frontend backed by a FastAPI vocabulary service. Built-in decks cover English→French, English→German, and English→Japanese; users can also create, edit, import, and export custom decks entirely in the browser.

Features

  • Four study modes: Flashcards (with 3D flip), Multiple-choice Quiz, Typing (accent-insensitive option), Matching
  • Three built-in language pairs: English→French, English→German, English→Japanese (50 entries each, directly comparable)

title: TextVerifier: Seeing Beyond Recognition to Verify Chinese Text Rendering
description:
arXiv:2610.19551v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Text-to-image models increasingly generate readable Chinese text that still contains local rendering defects, such as a character with an extra or missing stroke or a malformed component. Such errors are invisible to OCR and vision-language models, which are trained for recognition and are therefore invariant to the very structural deviations that define a rendering error. We formalize text rendering verification as a target-conditioned problem: given a target character and an image crop, decide whether the crop is a correct rendering of that character. Our verifier TEXTVERIFIER feeds the text tower a character's Ideographic Description Sequence (IDS) rather than a single-character symbol, and is trained on 12.7M crop-IDS pairs plus label-free "same-character, different-quality" hard pairs sampled from the training trajectory of a text-region inpainting model. To evaluate this ability we build TEXTRENDERBENCH-ZH, the first per-character benchmark for generated Chinese text, annotating position, identity, and correctness for 7,358 characters. TEXTVERIFIER reaches an F1 of 0.844, far above OCR confidence (0.526), a general VLM (0.329), and TextPecker (0.590). Used as a per-character reward for Flow-GRPO post-training, it further reduces rendering errors, showing that its score can both detect and correct errors.

title: Your Pixel-Perfect Tests Have a Trust Problem
description:
Someone updates the product page. The visual test reports 47 differences.

Most of them are timestamps, an animated banner, and a font rendering change. One is a Buy button that moved below the fold on a common laptop size.

Guess which issue gets lost in the noise.

Visual regression testing sounds beautifully simple: take a screenshot, compare it with yesterday's screenshot, flag what changed. But once you use it on a real product, you discover that detecting differences is the easy part.

Deciding which differences deserve attention is the job.

A diff is not a bug report

A screenshot comparison can tell you that pixels changed. It generally cannot, by itself, tell you whether the change was intentional, harmless, or a customer-facing problem.

Think about a page with live prices or stock levels. A strict pixel comparison may generate a new difference on every run even when the interface is behaving correctly.

Now imagine the opposite: the page renders almost identically, but an important button doesn't respond to a click. The visual check may happily pass.

These tests need context. What content was dynamic? Which viewport and browser did you use? What build produced the baseline? Who approved it, and why?

This benchmark plan for visual platforms gets specific about dynamic-content tolerance, review workflow, and keeping evidence. Those are the questions I'd ask before buying another clever image diff tool.

The baseline is a decision, not a file

A baseline isn't automatically correct because it was approved last Tuesday.

I've seen teams design processes where the easiest way to clear a red build is to click "Accept all changes." That's a dangerous habit. It turns the comparison system into a machine for normalizing whatever the latest build happened to render.

A useful review should make it easy to answer:

  • Which component actually changed?
  • Was the change linked to a known product decision?
  • Did the difference affect a critical workflow?
  • Can reviewers inspect the old and new images side by side?
  • Will the decision still make sense to someone investigating it next month?

You can use a hosted review workflow or keep baselines close to your Git history. Both have benefits. The Katalon Visual Testing vs Reg-suit comparison frames that tradeoff as managed review versus Git-first control. It's a more useful debate than asking which product takes the sharpest screenshot.

The workflow that makes good review decisions easiest is the one I'd favor.

Your screenshots have an expiration date

Suppose a release introduces a visual defect. Two weeks later, customer support forwards a complaint. The responsible engineer asks for the original screenshot and browser details.

They're gone. The CI job expired its artifacts after seven days.

Now the team has to reconstruct a browser state that may no longer exist. The app has changed. The data has changed. The third-party content has changed.

Evidence retention sounds like paperwork until you need yesterday's evidence to explain today's bug.

You don't necessarily need to keep every screenshot forever. But important failed runs should retain enough context to support a useful investigation: baseline and actual images, diff, build ID, browser and viewport, test data identifiers where appropriate, and the approval history.

It's worth deciding retention rules deliberately instead of inheriting whatever your CI provider does by default.

Test output should be readable by someone who didn't write the test

Now for the part I think gets ignored most often: handing a finding to another human.

"Visual difference detected" is a notification. It isn't a reproducible bug report.

A stronger report says something like:

On the checkout page, at 1366 × 768 in Chrome, the order summary overlaps the payment button after the shipping estimate loads. Seen on build checkout-1842. Expected: both sections remain visible and independently clickable. Attached: before image, after image, diff, and reproduction steps.

No mystery. No digging through raw logs to discover what page failed. No requirement that the reader know the testing platform's private vocabulary.

This benchmark plan for turning raw findings into reproducible reports measures an outcome many teams forget to track: how quickly evidence becomes something actionable.

That's especially important as AI-assisted testing discovers more issues. Discovering ten times as many potential problems won't help if people spend ten times as long interpreting them.

I'd measure review effort before counting diffs

If I were improving a visual testing process, I wouldn't start with "How many differences did we catch this month?"

I'd start with three smaller questions. How many alerts were dismissed as harmless? How long did a reviewer spend understanding an alert? How often did someone approve a baseline only to find out later that it contained a defect?

Those answers tell you whether the system helps the team notice real problems or merely gives the team another inbox.

The goal is not a perfectly clean diff report. It's confidence that when a meaningful visual regression happens, the team can recognize it, explain it, and fix it without conducting an archaeological dig through last week's CI jobs.

title: Into the LidarVerse: A Real-Time Unified LiDAR World Model Across Tasks and Sensors
description:
arXiv:2610.19201v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present LidarVerse, a real-time unified LiDAR world model for sensor simulation across tasks and sensors. Existing LiDAR simulators largely follow one of two complementary paradigms: reconstruction-based methods preserve the geometry of a captured scene but require lengthy per-scene optimization, whereas generative methods amortize learning across data but lack the consistency needed for long-horizon rollouts. LidarVerse brings both paradigms into a single, unified conditional generative framework. A universal tokenizer maps LiDAR range sequences into a shared latent space, where a bidirectional teacher learns a common interface for conditioning on a LiDAR prefix, an HD-Map, a persistent spatial cache, and optionally, text. Varying the available scene evidence turns the same model into a generator of new worlds, a point-cloud forecaster, or a generalizable resimulator of observed scenes without per-scene optimization. We distill the teacher into a four-step autoregressive causal student and maintain both a rolling temporal K/V cache and a world-aligned spatial cache, enabling persistent long-horizon rollouts with real-time inference at 11 FPS on a single H100 GPU. LidarVerse achieves state-of-the-art performance on most reported metrics across all three evaluation protocols, while its tokenizer supports 32-, 64-, and 128-beam LiDAR and generalizes to an unseen scanning pattern. These results demonstrate that generative and reconstruction-grounded LiDAR simulation can be realized within one model, providing the core capabilities for future closed-loop sensor simulation.
