The December 16, 2024 release note for enhanced per-environment proxy limits stated that the maximum number of API base paths per Apigee organization is 3000. That number is incorrect. The maximum number of API base paths per organization is 6,000 for both Apigee and Apigee hybrid.

For optimal performance, Apigee recommends using no more than 3,000 API proxy basepaths per environment or environment group. This is a recommendation, not an enforced limit.

For more information, see Limits and Enhanced per-environment proxy limits.

Fixed

CodeMender updates (v0.10.0)

This release introduces updates to CodeMender:

  • Impact-aware PR delta scanning: Added --diff and --staged flags to cm find to audit modified pull request hunks and 1-hop neighbor files while suppressing pre-existing vulnerabilities.
  • SARIF report export and CI gating: Added SARIF v2.1.0 export (--format sarif, --output) and severity-based CI gating (--fail-on) to cm report to integrate scan results into CI/CD pipelines and code scanning tools.
  • Adaptive hybrid deep scanning: Added --deep and --deep-workers flags to cm find to combine deterministic file pruning, parallel package-batched analysis, and post-triage verification for higher vulnerability recall and precision.
  • Custom workspace directory: Added support for the CM_HOME environment variable to override the default ~/.codemender directory for configuration, local state (state.db), backups, and artifacts.
  • Bug fixes:
    • Required build and test validation (build.command) to succeed during cm fix before marking a patch as applied and a finding as fixed.
    • Stabilized vulnerability fingerprints across multiple scans and bound cm verify directly to the target finding ID to prevent duplicate findings.
    • Restored the configured session model automatically when reconnecting to an active session with cm session resume.
    • Updated cm verify to add .exploit to .gitignore before execution so cancelled verification sessions do not leave untracked proof-of-concept scripts.

For more information, see the CodeMender documentation.

Google Kubernetes Engine

Feature

GKE ambient networking is now available in Preview through an allowlist.

GKE ambient networking provides a simplified, sidecarless deployment model for a service mesh with Layer 4 capabilities. By moving proxy functionality to node-level components integrated into GKE Dataplane V2, ambient networking reduces resource overhead, eliminates workload restarts for proxy updates, and simplifies mesh lifecycle management.

The Preview release supports single-cluster Layer 4 mesh capabilities using the Gateway API, which includes mutual TLS (mTLS), service discovery, Layer 4 traffic management, and Layer 4 telemetry.

For more information, see Ambient networking overview and Prepare GKE ambient networking.

Knowledge Catalog

Feature

Knowledge Catalog support for importing dbt metadata is now generally available and includes the following updates:

  • You can import metadata from dbt Cloud job runs using the dbt Cloud interface, the dbt platform CLI, or the dbt Administrative API and webhooks.
  • You can generate and import metadata artifacts from dbt Core 2.x and dbt Fusion in addition to dbt Core 1.x.
  • You can import entry links (--include-entry-links and --skip-bigquery-link) to capture dbt lineage and semantic relationships and link materialized dbt nodes to physical BigQuery tables, and search related BigQuery entries using the lookupEntryLinks method.
  • You can configure dbt metadata import jobs and search or view imported dbt entries using the Google Cloud console, the Google Cloud CLI, or the Dataplex REST API.

For more information, see Import metadata from dbt Core.

Feature

Data products now support configuring a default IAM role in an access group. The default role, once configured, is automatically granted on all packaged and supported assets in the data product. Data product owners can override the default role for individual assets. In addition, the assets table in a data product now shows the permission state of each asset (Applied, Failed, or Unsupported).

For more information, see Create data products and Manage data products.

Announcement

This dialog notifies users that authorizing the connection allows Looker to access data on their behalf, and that privileged Looker users—such as administrators and developers—may have visibility into their data (for example, when an administrator runs queries by using another user's active OAuth token during a sudo session).

title: WinARDet: Compressed Window Auto-Regression for Long-Horizon Vision-Language Grounding
description:
arXiv:2610.19419v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: MLLM-based detectors formulate vision-language grounding as autoregressive coordinate generation, yet in dense scenes, they often collapse into a box repetition loop, repeatedly emitting identical boxes until the decoding budget is exhausted. We trace this failure to historical-answer attention takeover: Under full-history autoregression, repeated coordinate tokens in the growing answer history attract disproportionate attention, crowding out the attention sinks needed to attend to new visual evidence. % To break this loop, in this paper, we propose \textbf{Compressed Window Auto-Regression} (WinAR). This new mechanism partitions a long answer sequence into consecutive generation windows and restricts full token-level autoregression to the current window only while compressing each previous window into a fixed set of latent tokens that condition subsequent decoding. This design reduces the repeated exposure to raw historical coordinates that triggers the attention takeover, yet preserves cross-window dependencies essential for coherent multi-object generation. On RSDense, which contains 200-2,000 objects per image, our model WinARDet improves RexOmni F1-score (IoU=0.5) from 32.16 to 39.36 over the baseline, while reducing the redundancy rate from 35.48% to 13.00%. WinARDet also generalizes across decoding strategies and output formats, including parallel box decoding and polygon generation, providing a practical paradigm for long-horizon vision-language grounding across scene densities.

title: DecisionRobust: Benchmarking Robustness for JEV Style Decision Models Across Text and Vision
description:
arXiv:2610.19118v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Emerging decision models such as JEV provide typed interfaces that map task instructions and observations directly to choices, judgments, and scores. As these models are increasingly used for automated decision-making, understanding their reliability under adversarial manipulation becomes critical. We introduce DecisionRobust, a benchmark for systematically evaluating the robustness of decision models across textual and visual inputs. Our benchmark covers practical decision-making scenarios and a diverse suite of attacks, including semantics-preserving text perturbations, image perturbations, and prompt injection in both modalities. We curate evaluation sets through external validity checks and cross-model candidate selection. We evaluate 30 model configurations on text tasks and 17 on vision tasks, including 24 and 12 held-out models, respectively, that are excluded from candidate selection. Our experiments reveal several key findings. First, attacks expose vulnerabilities beyond the models used for construction and selection, although optimized image perturbations transfer weakly to many targets even with multiple surrogates. Second, relative model robustness varies across tasks and attack types, and resistance to input perturbations does not necessarily imply resistance to prompt injection. Third, label-consistency checks substantially reduce measured attack success across text and image settings, highlighting the importance of validating apparent failures. The benchmark is available at https://yifan-lan.github.io/DecisionRobust/.

title: Scaling Cheap Synthetic Pretraining Improves Indoor Radio-Map Prediction
description:
arXiv:2610.19015v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Real measurements are too limited to train an accurate indoor pathloss predictor that works across a wide range of buildings. Large-scale synthetic pretraining offers a way forward, but real building layouts are also scarce, and accurate ray-tracing simulators are slow, expensive, and often proprietary. We address both problems by introducing a generator that automatically creates diverse indoor layouts and a fast, open-source approximate ray tracer that computes radio maps for them. Using this pipeline, we generate 128M synthetic samples, pretrain ResNet-101 and Swin-T encoder-decoders, and fine-tune them on high-quality benchmark data. Despite simulator mismatch, our ResNet-101 model reduces error by 15% on average relative to the best known methods across five indoor radio-map prediction tasks and improves transfer on a small real-measurement dataset. Both architectures show predictable data-scaling trends: power laws fitted on 2M-16M samples predict the mean normalized downstream RMSE at 32M-128M with 3.33% mean absolute percentage error for ResNet-101 and 7.10% for Swin-T. These results show that pretraining on large amounts of cheap simulated data can improve indoor radio-map prediction, even when real measurements and high-quality simulations are limited.

title: Your Cloud App Is Live. Can You Tell When Something Goes Wrong?
description:
Your application is deployed. The page loads, the API responds, and your latest release looks successful.

But what happens an hour later?

An endpoint starts slowing down. Requests fail intermittently. Storage usage keeps growing.

The next cloud skill worth learning is monitoring: understanding what your application is doing after deployment.

Start with three questions

Before creating a dashboard, decide what you need to know:

  1. Is the application available?
  2. Is it responding quickly enough?
  3. Are users experiencing errors?

These questions give your monitoring a purpose.

For a small API, start by tracking request volume, response time, and error rate. Add infrastructure metrics, such as CPU usage, where they help explain application behavior.

Understand metrics, logs, and traces

These tools answer different questions:

  • Metrics show patterns over time, such as rising response times or a sudden increase in failed requests.
  • Logs record events that can help explain what happened during a failure.
  • Traces follow requests across components, helping you identify where time was spent or an error occurred.

Imagine your API becomes slow.

A response-time metric shows when the slowdown started. Application logs reveal repeated database timeouts. A trace helps identify the database call responsible for the delay.

You can introduce these tools gradually as your project grows.

Make alerts useful

An alert should point to something you can investigate or act on.

For a learning project, consider alerts for:

  • Repeated failed health checks.
  • A sustained increase in server errors.
  • Response times exceeding your chosen threshold.
  • Spending approaching your budget.

Choose thresholds based on your application’s normal behavior. Too many noisy alerts make it harder to notice the ones that matter.

For each alert, write a short note: what it means, where to investigate, and what recovery steps to try.

Practise a controlled failure

Use a test environment to stop your application deliberately.

Check whether your monitoring detects the failure. Inspect the logs, restore the service, and verify that it becomes healthy again.

Record what you learned in your project README.

Deploying an application is a milestone. Knowing how to detect and recover from a failure builds confidence in running it.

title: How Do LLMs Understand Legal Philosophy? Diagnosing Legal-Philosophical Reasoning in LLMs
description:
arXiv:2610.19427v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Legal reasoning is a fundamental capability for large language models (LLMs) to complete legal AI tasks such as legal judgment prediction. In legal practice, this reasoning is shaped by legal philosophy: a judge's view of the nature and sources of law guides how legal materials are interpreted and applied, so judges working from the same statutes and precedents can reach different judgments. Existing research has largely overlooked whether LLMs can understand legal philosophy and apply it in legal reasoning, an ability we call \textit{legal-philosophical reasoning}. To fill this gap, we introduce LePhilBench, a benchmark for evaluating the legal-philosophical reasoning of LLMs that comprises two benchmarking tasks and a dataset. The two tasks evaluate how well LLMs understand legal philosophy and how well they apply it in legal reasoning, respectively. The dataset is manually and meticulously constructed. Its test set contains 220 U.S. Supreme Court opinions. A law professor designed fourteen annotation questions on legal philosophy, and three law-trained annotators with formal training in jurisprudence answered all fourteen questions for every opinion, yielding 9,240 legal-philosophical labels. LePhilBench takes the first step toward exploring legal-philosophical reasoning in LLMs.

title: Your Test Didn't Flake. Your UI Moved While Nobody Was Looking.
description:
A test clicks Save. The app saves the record. A green toast appears, hangs around for two seconds, and blocks the next button.

The test fails.

Someone adds a three-second sleep. The test passes. Everyone moves on.

Two weeks later, the toast takes four seconds to disappear on a busy CI machine. Same failure. Different Monday.

I think this is one of the most expensive habits in frontend testing: treating every unpredictable UI event as a timing problem. Sometimes the timing is fine. The application has changed which element is actually available for interaction.

A small UI change can be a big state change

Modern apps throw a surprising amount of stuff at a browser: notifications, loading masks, drawers, dropdowns, permission prompts, confirmation dialogs, and third-party widgets. Any of these can alter where focus goes or which control is on top.

Imagine this sequence:

  1. A user changes a billing address.
  2. A confirmation dialog opens.
  3. Clicking Confirm triggers a loading overlay.
  4. A toast slides across the bottom of the page.
  5. The test tries to click Continue.

If Continue is behind the toast, clicking it isn't a legitimate user action at that moment. Retrying the same coordinates is no better. A useful test should wait for an actionable state, then locate the button again.

This is why I like the idea behind this benchmark for testing toast interference and modal stacking. It separates completing the flow from recovering sensibly when the interface gets noisy. Those are different abilities.

A test that passes after twenty silent retries isn't automatically better than one that fails immediately with a screenshot showing the obstruction.

The DOM can be ready while the experience isn't

React and Next.js introduce a variation of the same problem. The server sends HTML. The browser paints it. Hydration begins. Something changes.

The button you found on the first render might be replaced, disabled, or wired to behavior only after hydration. This creates a particularly irritating failure: everything looks fine in the screenshot, but the click happens at the wrong stage.

Blanket rules such as "fail the build for every hydration warning" are tempting. They also make it hard to distinguish a harmless discrepancy from a broken purchase button.

A more useful approach is to reproduce the mismatch, identify the affected component, and assert the interaction the user actually needs. There's a focused walkthrough of testing React and Next.js hydration mismatches without treating every warning as fatal.

The key question isn't whether the console is immaculate. It's whether the page ended up usable and correct.

Focus bugs are the quiet cousin of click bugs

Custom comboboxes are a great trap for overconfident tests. You type into the box, see an option, click it, and assume the widget works.

Now try the same thing without touching the mouse.

Does Arrow Down move the active option? Does Escape close the list? Does focus remain where it should? Does aria-activedescendant point to a real option? Does Enter choose the highlighted item rather than the first item in the DOM?

A click-only test can happily pass through a component that fails for keyboard users. The combobox and typeahead testing guide is worth using as a checklist when you're dealing with custom widgets.

I'd add one rule: check the resulting value and focus state, not merely whether a dropdown was visible.

Please stop screenshotting every pixel

The same mistaken obsession with implementation details shows up in layout testing.

A grid can reflow because content grows, a font changes, or the viewport narrows. That doesn't necessarily mean the user experience is broken. Meanwhile, a footer button can become inaccessible with only a tiny visible change.

For CSS subgrid and intrinsic sizing, I'd rather assert things like:

  • Key elements don't overlap.
  • Important controls remain inside the viewport or reachable by scrolling.
  • Text isn't clipped.
  • Reading and tab order still make sense.

Use screenshots for visually meaningful regressions, not as the only definition of correctness. The practical examples in this piece on testing CSS subgrid and layout reflows make that distinction nicely.

A better way to debug the next "flaky" failure

When the next intermittent click failure appears, resist the immediate urge to increase a timeout. First find out what was actually on screen. Was the button covered? Was it disabled? Did the page re-render? Where was keyboard focus? Which state was the app in immediately before the action?

Then create a small, repeatable version of the problem. Force the toast to appear. Delay the hydration step. Stack the dialogs. Navigate with the keyboard.

A test that fails consistently under a known bad state is easier to fix than a test that passes inconsistently after a random sleep.

The funny part is that teams often spend more time arguing about locator syntax than asking whether the element was genuinely available to the user. The second question is usually where the bug lives.

title: Can LLMs Access their World Knowledge for Event Prediction?
description:
arXiv:2610.19021v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent work has questioned whether large language models (LLMs) can be useful for temporal event prediction. Despite vast pretrained world knowledge, LLMs often underperform simpler specialized models. We ask whether this knowledge is truly inaccessible, or whether current methods fail to present event prediction in a form LLMs can use. We argue for the latter and show that LLMs become effective event forecasters when the interface is designed around two choices. The first grounds each event in a natural-language description, and the second separates event semantics from the prediction space to prevent semantic bias from label associations. To test this, we introduce DescribeEvent, a benchmark of ~150K events across seven datasets and six domains with event-level descriptions. We find that capable LLMs substantially benefit from descriptions and symbolic labels, outperforming description-free variants and non-LLM baselines, while weaker models gain little. These results suggest that accessing LLM world knowledge for event prediction is an interface problem, and that event descriptions offer a practical way to elicit the knowledge LLMs already encode.

title: Our header is 48 pixels tall, every page offsets by 56, and the root layout renders no header at all
description:
notifio.app is the marketing site for a desktop app that watches rental search pages and alerts you when a new listing appears. The site is 38 URLs. Its header is one component, 70 lines, and the three most interesting things in it are a pair of pointer-events classes, a number that is wrong on purpose, and the fact that app/layout.tsx does not render it.

The layout renders fonts and a JSON-LD block, and then stops

Here is everything inside <body> in the root layout:

<body className="bg-[#0a0a0a] text-[#fafafa] antialiased font-sans">
  {/* Who is behind this site, in the form a crawler reads. */}
  <script type="application/ld+json" dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ ... }} />
  {children}
</body>

No nav. No footer. Both are imported and rendered by each page:

$ grep -rl --include="*.tsx" "<Nav" src | wc -l
15

Fifteen files, each opening with the same three lines. The App Router's whole pitch is that shared chrome belongs in a layout, so this needs a reason, and the honest one is a shape rather than a rule: a layout wraps every route under it, and opting out of a layout means moving a route into a different segment. Putting the header in the page means a page that should not have one simply does not import it.

Today, all fifteen import it. The payment success page imports it, the maintenance page imports it, and so the opt-out I am describing is currently used by nothing, which makes the duplication a cost with a hypothetical benefit. The part that keeps it from being a real problem is that fifteen files is not 38 pages: one of them is ArticleLayout, which renders all eight long-form pages, the five listed at notifio.app/guides plus three audience pages, and two more are dynamic routes covering the fifteen entries at notifio.app/alerts and the five at notifio.app/compare. The number of files that would need editing to change the chrome is fifteen; the number of pages is 38.

If I were starting again I would put it in the layout and use a route group for anything that needs to escape. I am writing down the trade rather than the conclusion, because the version in the repo works and has never once been the reason a change was hard.

Two classes so a transparent header does not eat clicks

The header is fixed, full width, and centres its contents:

<div
  className={`fixed top-0 inset-x-0 z-50 flex justify-center pointer-events-none transition-all duration-300 ease-out ${
    scrolled ? "pt-3 px-4" : "pt-0 px-0"
  }`}
>
  <nav className="pointer-events-auto w-full ...">

pointer-events-none on the outer div, pointer-events-auto on the nav inside it. This is the entire reason the design works.

Once scrolled, the nav is a rounded pill with max-w-6xl and 12px of padding above it. The outer div is still the full width of the viewport and roughly 60 pixels tall, sitting at z-50 above everything. Without those two classes, that invisible rectangle swallows every click and hover in the top strip of the page, including the ones aimed at the gap either side of the pill. Nothing in the UI tells you why. You just find a dead zone at the top of a page, usually on a wide monitor, usually weeks later.

The pair is the smallest fix available: the container keeps its layout job and gives up its hit-testing job, and the one child that needs to be clickable takes hit-testing back. Worth remembering as a shape, because every floating or inset fixed element has this problem: a fixed positioning container is as clickable as it is wide, not as wide as it looks.

The scroll state is a boolean, and that is a throttle 

const [scrolled, setScrolled] = useState(false);

useEffect(() => {
  const onScroll = () => setScrolled(window.scrollY > 20);
  window.addEventListener("scroll", onScroll, { passive: true });
  return () => window.removeEventListener("scroll", onScroll);
}, []);

No requestAnimationFrame, no debounce, no IntersectionObserver sentinel. The listener runs on every scroll event, which during a trackpad flick is a lot of events, and it reads window.scrollY each time, which is a layout read.

What it does not do is re-render. setScrolled(false) while the state is already false is a no-op as far as the rendered output goes, because React bails out when the next state is identical to the current one. The component re-renders when the value flips, so a long scroll down the pricing page produces one state change rather than four hundred. The derived class strings change at exactly the moment the appearance is supposed to change, and the CSS transition does the 300ms of work between the two states.

That leaves the cost of the handler itself, which is why { passive: true } is there: it promises the browser that this listener will never call preventDefault, so scrolling is not blocked waiting to find out. A boolean threshold plus a passive listener is enough for this. The version with a rAF-throttled handler and a ref holding the last value is more code that produces the same pixels.

The one thing I would change: the handler never runs on mount. Load the page already scrolled, which happens on a refresh or when following a link to an anchor, and the header renders in its unscrolled state until you move. One extra onScroll() call before the addEventListener fixes it, and it is a genuine bug rather than a trade.

The number 56, seventeen times

The nav's inner row is h-12, which is 48 pixels. When scrolled it gains pt-3, 12 more, for 60. Every page then pushes its content down by this:

<main className="pt-14">

pt-14 is 56 pixels. Not 48, not 60, in between.

$ grep -rn --include="*.tsx" "pt-14" src | wc -l
16
$ grep -rn --include="*.tsx" "100vh-56" src | wc -l
2

Fifteen of those sixteen pt-14 matches are a page clearing the header, the sixteenth is the footer's own padding, and the two calc matches are this, on the success and maintenance pages:

<main className="pt-14">
  <section className="flex min-h-[calc(100vh-56px)] items-center justify-center px-6 py-20">

The same constant written twice in two notations, in two files, for pages whose single card is supposed to be vertically centred in whatever is left under the header. Seventeen places that know how tall the header is, and the one match that is not about the header at all is the footer, which is its own small hazard: the string is not searchable for the thing it means.

The defensible part is that the header is position: fixed, so it is out of flow and the gap under it has to come from somewhere. The indefensible part is the value. 48 and 60 are both real heights depending on scroll position, 56 is neither, and the reason it works is that pages have 80 pixels of their own top padding under it so an 8 pixel error is invisible.

A CSS variable, --nav-height, set once and used by both the component and the pages, would make the relationship explicit and let the two states disagree honestly. The reason it has not happened is the reason most of these do not: nothing has gone wrong yet. Writing it down is the cheap half of fixing it.

Three links out of 38 URLs 

<Link href="/alerts">Sites</Link>
<Link href="/pricing">Pricing</Link>
<Link href="/download">Get Notifio</Link>

That is the whole menu, with no mobile variant because three short links fit. The hub pages for guides and comparisons are not in it, which is deliberate: the header carries the path a visitor is on, which is "what does it watch", "what does it cost", "give me the app". Everything else is reachable from the footer, which has its own set of trade-offs that I wrote up in the footer post, and from in-page links.

The one detail in the markup worth copying:

<Image src="/icon-light.svg" alt="" width={18} height={18} priority className="opacity-90" />
Notifio

alt="" on the logo, because the word "Notifio" is right there in the same link as text. An alt="Notifio" here makes a screen reader announce the brand twice for one link. The priority is because this is the only image above the fold on every route.

What the component is, in total

A fixed container that does not take clicks, a pill inside it that does, one boolean of state, three links, and a hardcoded offset repeated in every page. The interesting work in a site header is almost never the markup. It is the two classes that keep an invisible rectangle from stealing input, and the constant that quietly knows how tall everything is.

The 38 URLs it sits on are mostly generated rather than written, which is a different post: our sitemap is 38 URLs and only ten of them are typed out by hand. The app the header is advertising is at notifio.app/download.

title: Learning to Select Features with Manifold Deep Unfolding PCA
description:
arXiv:2610.19436v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Unsupervised feature selection (UFS) is of great significance in image processing and pattern recognition. Nevertheless, existing model-based methods often rely on manually tuned hyperparameters, while deep learning-based methods generally require massive training data. To address these issues, this paper proposes an efficient manifold deep unfolding feature selection network (MDUFS-Net). Technically, we first incorporate the $\ell_{2,0}$-norm into the classic principal component analysis (PCA) framework, then unfold the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM)-based iterative algorithm into an end-to-end trainable network, thereby enabling automatic parameter learning. Moreover, a manifold optimization strategy is developed to improve the numerical robustness. On this basis, we further extend MDUFS-Net into an enhanced variant called MDUFS-Net+ by introducing the $\ell_{0}$-norm for more discriminative feature representations. Extensive experiments validate that our proposed MDUFS-Net and MDUFS-Net+ outperform state-of-the-art methods in the UFS task, with promising performance in clustering. Our code is available at https://github.com/xianchaoxiu/MDUFS.

title: Taste is not a design methodology
description:
It has become our favorite answer to AI-generated sameness. The reality is good products come from judgment built on facts, and the agency to use them when the room prefers opinions.

Ask Rick Rubin what he does and he’ll tell you he has “no technical ability” and knows nothing about music. In a 2023 interview with Anderson Cooper, the producer said artists pay him for confidence in his own taste.

https://medium.com/media/1f83a53654c7bc936b099303acddda54/href
“The confidence I have in my taste and my ability to express what I feel has proven helpful for artists.” — Rick Rubin

Everyone now wants that job.

Just typing this makes me squirm because I believe the field should be research and data driven as much as it can be. With humans even.

“Taste is the new moat” might be the industry’s favorite sentence of 2026: artificial intelligence made competent screens cheap, so the one thing left to sell is the judgment to pick the good one. A ProductLed interview in January went further, telling builders not to validate before they build. It’s about 45 minutes in.

I decided not to show the video inline because it adds fuel to the fire and their use of typography isn’t to my taste.

It’s come up with couple of authors I follow — The taste paradox by Nicole Alexandra Michaelis is a good read over at UX Collective, and Xinran Ma had a interview recently about it in UX — and it’s in the zeitgeist.

My point is that it’s the wrong word.

The moat crowd is right that judgment matters; they’re wrong about where it comes from:

  • Taste is a preference. It comes from what you’ve seen and who you admire, and two people with different taste can disagree with no way to settle it.
  • Judgment is a claim you can check. It rests on principles research has tested, plus evidence about your users, so it can be explained, taught, and shown wrong.

Judgment needs agency too, because someone has to raise those facts when the most senior voice would rather trade opinions. What Nicole Alexandra Michaelis and Xinran Ma are talking about Judgement i.e. experience they can back with facts and experience.

The short rule: if you can’t name the fact or research behind a call, it’s still an opinion, which is otherwise known as taste.

Admit taste is an opinion

In 2001, researchers in Bordeaux and Montpellier gave a panel of 54 tasters a white wine colored red with an odorless dye. The panel described it with the vocabulary of red wine.

Nothing had changed but the color, and that was enough to overwrite their noses.

That’s the trouble with treating taste as a standard: it’s an opinion that feels like a fact. Two skilled designers can look at the same screen, reach opposite conclusions, and neither can prove the other mistaken.

Taste feels like perception, but a lot of it is expectation. Apple Music is probably the best example, it’s Apple, but still a challenging application to use established as fact.

For example, I like driving Audi TTs. A lot.

The proportions, the way one sits on a highway on-ramp, the complete impracticality of the back seat, the beautifully designed cockpit, the race to 110 miles per hour in California.

That last part is just storytelling, really.

I don’t expect any of that to be anyone else’s taste, and nothing is wrong when it isn’t, because my taste in cars only has to satisfy only me. A product has to work for thousands of people who never met me for it to be profitable, and that’s where a preference stops being enough.

My expectation is that Audi TT’s are designed for my taste, and it doesn’t fail me, ever.

Design has its own version of the wine study.

In 1995, Masaaki Kurosu and Kaori Kashimura of Hitachi had people rate 26 ATM layouts and found that how usable a layout looked tracked its beauty far more than its inherent usability. The field now calls this the aesthetic-usability effect, and it cuts both ways.

Generative tools make this worse because they turn out polished screens by default, so every option in the review looks finished. That’s the blind spot in the moat argument: the less polish costs, the less polish can tell you.

It reminds me of a conversation I had with Scott Jenson — Generative AI makes a lot of beautifully just above average screens. I made that argument they’re still better than a lot of portfolios I have seen, even if the screens have less depth.

This is why “does it have taste?” makes a weak review question: it has no failure condition other than an opinion.

Ruiqi Zhou called taste unfalsifiable in a February essay named Taste Is the New Moat — And That’s the Problem. It’s a great read, and points out that a standard you can never fail works more like a status marker, and status markers reward whoever already holds status. Usually, that’s product management.

Build judgment on laws that have held for centuries

User experience borrowed its foundations from people who ran experiments, and they had computers in only some cases.

Here are examples:

  • Paul Fitts showed in 1954 that the time to hit a target depends on its size and distance using fighter cockpits for research, and William Edmund Hick showed that decision time climbs as options pile up. Both findings have held up for seven decades.
  • Jakob Nielsen and Rolf Molich developed heuristic evaluation in 1990, and the ten heuristics are still the default checklist. Each turns an opinion into a checkable claim, like a button too small for a thumb.
  • Dieter Rams and his ten principles took what could have stayed personal taste and wrote it down where other people could use it, which is why teams still audit work against them fifty years on.

They are normative rather than experimental, but a checklist can be argued with. I keep plain-language summaries of Fitts’s Law, Hick’s Law, Nielsen’s heuristics, and Rams’s principles on ux-guidelines.com, a reference site I maintain. Every law has conditions, and knowing them is part of judgment.

Hick’s Law describes a choice among equally likely options, and a 1985 study of its exceptions found cases where adding choices barely slowed people down. Fitts measured people tapping a stylus between two targets, not a thumb stretching across a phone.

A law applied outside its conditions is just another opinion with a citation.

Principles don’t settle everything.

At Microsoft, Ronny Kohavi’s team reported that only about a third of well-run experiments improved the metric they were designed to move. The laws tell you what’s likely, and testing tells you what happened.

User research earns its place next to the laws for the same reason.

A law is general and your users are specific, so only watching them shows which steps they repeat and where they give up. Teresa Torres makes the cadence the point, defining continuous discovery as weekly contact with customers by the team building the product, rather than a study that lands after the decision.

Test beauty with the people who will use it

None of this means beauty is decoration. The same aesthetic-usability effect explains why users forgive attractive products, and appearance shapes trust and first impressions.

Don Norman gave the effect a mechanism in Emotional Design: a positive mood broadens thinking and makes people more forgiving of small friction. Jony Ive’s teams built the most admired hardware of their era and also shipped the butterfly keyboard, which Apple settled a class action over for $50 million in 2022 after years of complaints.

Taste operating at that altitude still needed someone to check whether the thing worked.

The mistake is assuming the designer’s eye can stand in for the audience’s. Nielsen Norman Group showed the same five screenshots to 229 adults aged 18 to 25 and 228 aged 35 and older,

The results?

  • The younger group rated the flat designs slightly more attractive.
  • The older, slightly less attractive.

Whose taste was right? Each group’s, for itself.

Beauty is in the eye of the beholder, especially in enterprise software, where the person who admires the demo is rarely the one who lives in the product eight hours a day.

Beauty is a user outcome, so measure it like one.

That’s where the line between fact and opinion falls here. What users report about a screen is a fact about your audience, while a design lead’s verdict is one more opinion, however practiced the eye behind it. The survey used a modified version of the Microsoft Desirability Toolkit, which asks people to pick words that describe what they see from a fixed list.

Score task success and time on task separately from those ratings, so a polished prototype can’t inflate the verdict on whether the thing works.

Teach the principles before the portfolio

In 2009, two researchers who had spent careers on opposite sides of this argument wrote a paper together. Daniel Kahneman had documented how judgment fails, while Gary Klein had defended expert intuition in the field.

Their joint answer on when intuition deserves trust came down to two conditions:

  • The environment has to be regular enough to learn about who they’re designing for
  • The person needs a real chance to learn it

Design taste rarely gets that chance. A designer ships a screen, moves on to the next project, and never finds out whether the choice helped anyone.

Confidence grows with years, but accuracy only grows with feedback.

Tell a designer two years out of school to trust their taste, after a portfolio course, maybe an internship, and very few closed loops between a decision and its outcome. What they have is exposure to showcase sites and admired apps, which produces taste that matches the feed, not the user.

Principles are the shortcut experience can’t hand out, and they come with standing. A junior designer who knows Hick’s Law can push back on a longer menu in her first critique, and a new hire who has studied the heuristics can flag a missing undo before anyone senior does.

Facts give people the agency that seniority usually keeps for itself.

Give everyone the agency to argue from facts

Taste has a politics problem.

When the standard is taste, the taste that counts usually belongs to the most senior person present. Ron Kohavi named it in a 2008 Stanford talk, Listen to Your Customers not to the HiPPO: the HiPPO is the highest-paid person’s opinion.

A taste culture is a HiPPO culture with better typography.

The fix isn’t to ban taste from the room, it’s to stop one person from owning it without evidence.

Everybody on a team has taste, and the new designer’s is worth as much as the vice president’s, which is exactly why it makes a poor standard: nothing decides whose version wins except rank. Facts don’t work that way, since a law or a session recording says the same thing no matter who reads it out.

Taste cultures have a patron saint they misappropriated: Steve Jobs.

He told BusinessWeek in 1998 that designing by focus group is hard. People, he said, “don’t know what they want until you show it to them.” It gets quoted as permission to skip research, though the same answer described watching trends and studying Apple’s installed base.

But even he met his match in Paul Rand.

When Steve Jobs needed a logo for NeXT in 1986, he hired Rand, whom he openly called the greatest living graphic designer. The friction came immediately: Jobs asked for a few options, and Rand refused, saying he would solve the problem and Jobs would pay him, and if he wanted options he could hire someone else.

Jobs agreed to the terms and the $100,000 fee. Rand returned with one design, the tilted black cube, presented in a hand-bound booklet that walked Jobs through the reasoning until the logo felt inevitable.

Jobs loved it, and later admitted that you don’t hand a genius a menu.

Because of this, Apple did research all the time and that gave Jobs credibility to make judgement calls. Those that claim they have the same truly understand the company, nor how to combine taste with judgement.

Even Steve Jobs’ famous 2x2 Matrix Strategy is rooted in science — Paradox of Choice.

The larger problem is survivorship bias, another old law. We remember the founder whose certainty paid off and forget the rooms where the same certainty sank the product with dollar amount attached to it.

Agency with receipts is the fix.

Session notes, retention data, and a heuristic all lose to a senior “that feels off,” unless the team agrees that facts outrank opinions.

With that agreement in place, the quietest person in the room can win by naming the law a design breaks or the data point it ignores. Peter Merholz argues that design executives earn that standing by making design their secondary concern.

The fair counterargument belongs to Doug Bowman, Google’s first visual designer.

In 2009 he left and explained why in Goodbye, Google: a team was testing 41 shades of blue, and he had been asked to prove whether a border should be three, four, or five pixels wide.

His complaint went past the trivia: with nobody senior who understood design, he argued, the company ran out of reasons for its decisions, and data became “a crutch for every decision” that kept anything daring from shipping.

$200 million later. Hard to argue that as an outcome.

Measuring everything is its own way of dodging judgment, so decisions slow to the test calendar, and designers who could settle a border width from a principle leave for places where that counts, as Bowman did.

Aim evidence at the choices that change what users can do. A corner radius needs no significance test, since a law settles it faster.

Choose facts over opinions

Judgment is knowing which facts apply, and where they stop applying: a law, a heuristic, a published study, or research on your own users. Where taste says “this feels right,” judgment points out that the target is too small to tap reliably and that Fitts showed why in 1954.

Agency is saying that out loud in the review, even when it cuts against the most senior opinion in the room.

Judgment tells you which facts matter, and agency is using them when the room prefers an opinion.

The new reality:

  • Generative tools can produce fifty layouts before my morning coffee.
  • Judgment cuts the pile fast, dropping the ones with targets too small to hit, menus too long to scan, and flows that ask people to hold too much in their heads.
  • What’s left goes to research, where users settle what the principles can’t.

Teams that run interviews and usability sessions on a schedule build a store of facts they can reach for in any review, and teams that skip them are left with preferences and a deadline. Dan Maccarone spent a year rebuilding his studio’s process around these tools and found that it didn’t make the work faster, which he counts as the point: what changed was where the thinking had to happen.

Rubin’s approach works because a record has no task to fail. A designer who borrows that job description claims the authority without the conditions that make it hold.

Judgment also improves in a way taste doesn’t, if somebody writes the call down. Jeff Gothelf formalizes that in the Lean UX canvas: state what you believe will happen, then name the evidence that would tell you whether you were right. It’s the equivalent of the Change My Mind meme, and it’s brilliant.

Picture two designers.

  • One moves a filter panel above the results because Hick’s Law favors fewer competing choices on the way to what people came for, predicts lower search abandonment, and checks the numbers six weeks after launch.
  • The other spends the same six weeks studying award-winning screen shots.

Only the first one learned something new about their users, and only their judgment got sharper.

Conclusion

Taste isn’t going away, and it isn’t the real enemy.

Opinions shape style, brand voice, and the small choices no principle covers. The trouble starts when an opinion gets treated as a fact and wins arguments it hasn’t earned.

The moat story is half right.

Artificial intelligence does make average output cheap, and plenty of products will look alike because of it. The scarce skill isn’t picking the prettiest variation, it’s knowing which ones break what the field already knows, which ones deserve a test, and what the result means for the next decision.

The wine panel in Bordeaux wasn’t foolish; its members were human, and so are we. That’s the whole reason design has laws and methods at all.

Human perception drifts toward what it expects to see, and principles are how a field keeps itself honest across decades of new tools.

So learn the laws, read the research carefully, and give your team the agency to use both. Then let your users decide the rest. Judgment you can explain, backed by the nerve to raise it, will outlast taste you can only defend, and teams built on it will ship the products everyone else ends up copying.

Action Items

  • Ask “what fact supports this?” instead of “does it have taste?” In critiques, every significant call should rest on a principle, a study, or something your users did. If nobody can name one, label the call an opinion and flag it for testing.
  • Teach the laws before the look. Give junior designers Fitts’s Law, Hick’s Law, cognitive load theory, and Nielsen’s heuristics before mood boards. Principles hand them decades of feedback, and the standing to use it.
  • Make it safe to push back with facts. Say plainly that a cited principle or data point outranks a job title, and back the junior designer who uses one against you. Agency that gets punished once rarely shows up twice.
  • Test where the facts run out. Brand feel, new interaction patterns, and cases where two laws conflict all need research. Run a usability session, a few interviews, or a first-click test that week, and log the prediction behind it. Leave the border widths alone.

Taste is not a design methodology was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: September 14, 2026
description:
Agent Platform Workbench

Apigee hybrid

Announcement

hybrid v1.17.0

On September 14, 2026 we released an updated version of the Apigee hybrid software, 1.17.0.

  • For information on upgrading, see Upgrading Apigee hybrid to version v1.17.

Note: This is a minor release: The container images used in minor releases are integrated with the Apigee hybrid Helm charts. Upgrading to a minor via the Helm chart automatically updates the images. No manual image changes are typically needed. For information on container image support in Apigee hybrid releases, see Apigee release process.

Feature

Model Context Protocol (MCP) support

Apigee hybrid now supports Model Context Protocol (MCP), an open protocol that lets agentic AI applications use your APIs as tools through managed MCP endpoints. Apigee hybrid routes, authorizes, and secures these MCP tool calls the same way it manages your other APIs, so you don't need to run or maintain your own MCP servers.

MCP support is an optional feature that is not enabled by default. You must explicitly enable it in your Apigee hybrid configuration.

For more information, see Model Context Protocol (MCP) overview, Enable MCP for Apigee hybrid, and the MCP quickstart.

Feature

Root CA certificate rotation

Apigee hybrid v1.17.0 lets you rotate the root certificate authority (CA) certificate that anchors trust for TLS communication between your runtime components. You can now replace the root CA before it expires, without downtime.

For more information, see Rotate the root CA.

Feature

TLS 1.3 support

Apigee hybrid v1.17.0 adds support for TLS 1.3, a newer version of the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol that offers faster connection handshakes and stronger security than earlier TLS versions.

For information about configuring TLS on the ingress gateway, see Configuring TLS and mTLS on the Apigee ingress gateway.

Feature

Forward proxy support for AI policies

Apigee hybrid v1.17.0 adds forward proxy support for AI policies, such as the Model Armor and semantic caching policies. Outbound calls from these policies can now be routed through an HTTP forward proxy.

For more information, see Configure a forward proxy, Get started with the Model Armor policies, and Get started with semantic caching policies.

Feature

Semantic cache Private Service Connect (PSC) endpoint support

Apigee hybrid v1.17.0 adds Private Service Connect (PSC) endpoint support for semantic caching. The semantic caching policies can now reach their backing services over a Private Service Connect endpoint, which keeps that traffic on your private network.

For more information, see Configure semantic caching over Private Service Connect.

Feature

Semantic cache distance measure support

Apigee hybrid v1.17.0 adds support for non-default Vertex AI Vector Search distance measures in the SemanticCacheLookup policy. A new optional <DistanceMeasureType> element accepts DOT_PRODUCT_DISTANCE (the default, and the existing behavior), COSINE_DISTANCE, SQUARED_L2_DISTANCE, and L1_DISTANCE. The policy compares <Threshold> in the direction the declared measure implies, so declaring a non-default measure requires re-tuning the threshold in the same edit.

For more information, see SemanticCacheLookup policy.

Feature

Reduced service account permissions

Apigee hybrid v1.17.0 reduces the Google Cloud IAM permissions that Apigee service accounts require. Service accounts that use Cloud Storage now require only the storage.objects.get and storage.objects.create permissions rather than the broader Storage Admin (roles/storage.admin) role. The Cassandra components also no longer run with the privileged: true security context.

For more information about service accounts, see Create service accounts.

Various security and CVE fixes are included in this release.

This extension requires PostgreSQL 17 or later and is supported on PostgreSQL release R20260712.01_06 or later.

Compute Engine

Feature

For more information, see Gemini model versions and lifecycle.

This release introduces updates to CodeMender:

  • Network stream resilience: Improved CLI session stability with automatic reconnection and transient error recovery during long-running scans and remediation workflows.

Anthropic's Cyber Verification Program (CVP) is available in Preview on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. CVP enables verified organizations to use supported Claude models (Claude Opus 4.7, Claude Opus 4.8, Claude Sonnet 5, and Claude Opus 5) for legitimate defensive cybersecurity tasks with default dual-use restrictions lifted.

GoogleSQL is optimized for broad data exploration, statistical aggregation, and deep-dive ad hoc investigations. title: Vercel CDN no longer caches responses with Vary: Cookie
description:
Vercel CDN no longer caches origin responses when Vary includes Cookie.

Vary tells a cache which request headers may change the response. Because cookies often contain visitor-specific values, varying by Cookie can create many cache entries that are rarely reused. The response is still served normally but isn't stored for future requests.

You can identify these responses by checking the x-vercel-cache header and Runtime Logs. The header is set to MISS, and Logs show vary_key_denied:cookie as the cache reason.

If Logs show vary_key_denied:cookie for a route you expect to be cached, check the Vary header returned by your origin:

  • If the response is the same regardless of cookies, remove Cookie from Vary. Vercel CDN can then cache it if it meets the other caching requirements.

  • If the response depends on cookies, keep Cookie in Vary and use Cache-Control: private to prevent personalized responses from being stored in the shared CDN cache.

Caching behavior for other supported Vary headers is unchanged.

Learn more about high-cardinality headers and the vary_key_denied cache reason.

title: Similar Models, Broken Odds: Where Luce's Axiom Fails in Chatbot Arena
description:
arXiv:2610.19095v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Chatbot Arena ranks language models with the Bradley-Terry model, which gives each model one score and so assumes Luce's choice axiom. Choice theory predicts where this fails: near-copies are told apart more decisively than their scores imply. On 1.8 million Arena votes, votes between versions of one model are 1.37 times as decisive as Bradley-Terry predicts, between sizes of one generation 1.26 times and between models of one lab 1.12 times; a release a year later gives consistent multipliers, and the effect survives alternative tie treatments, prompt subsets and topics, and timing checks. How alike two models' answers are worded and formatted tracks the effect. A correction with four to six parameters predicts held-out votes better than Bradley-Terry and than models with hundreds of parameters, mostly by modelling ties; frozen and carried to new releases in a test fixed in advance, its gains are concentrated in ties, and better head-to-head odds are not established. The leaderboard order barely moves. With language-model judges and three-answer menus, a near-copy takes votes mostly from its twin when choices are pooled over prompts (log-odds shift +0.10, 95% interval 0.05 to 0.16); within a prompt the shift is smaller and clear for two of four judges.

title: 5 Common Reasons Why GBase Database(GBase 8s) Cannot Connect After Installation
description:
Your GBase Database(GBase 8s) instance is online, but dbaccess or a remote client still cannot connect. Before reinstalling the database, check these five common causes: incorrect sqlhosts configuration, firewall restrictions, port conflicts, server name mismatches, and client connection settings.

This troubleshooting guide explains what to check first and how to narrow down GBase Database(GBase 8s) connectivity issues efficiently.

1. Incorrect Hostname in sqlhosts

Typical symptom: Local connections work, but remote connections fail.

The sqlhosts file defines connection information for a database server, including its server name, connection protocol, host, and port.

For example:

gbase01 onsoctcp 192.168.1.100 9088

If the configuration uses localhost or 127.0.0.1, remote clients may be unable to reach the intended network endpoint.

What to check:

  • Verify the hostname or IP address in the relevant sqlhosts entry.
  • Confirm that the address is reachable from the client machine.
  • Check that the server is listening on the expected interface and port.

Use the actual network address and connection settings for your environment. Avoid changing configuration or restarting the instance until you have identified the cause.

2. Firewall Blocking the Database Port

Typical symptom: The GBase Database(GBase 8s) instance is online, but remote connections time out.

A running database does not guarantee that network traffic can reach it. The operating system firewall, network firewall, or cloud security rules may block the database listener port.

Check the firewall status and test connectivity from the remote client:

systemctl status firewalld

nc -vz 192.168.1.100 9088

Replace the example IP address and port with your actual server settings.

If the connection is blocked, review the applicable firewall rules and allow only the required source addresses and destination port. Avoid disabling the firewall as a troubleshooting shortcut.

3. Database Port Conflict

Typical symptom: The instance fails to start correctly, or the expected database port is unavailable.

Another service may already be using the configured port.

Check which process is listening:

ss -lntp | grep ':9088'

Alternatively, use lsof if it is installed.

If a conflict exists, identify the process before taking action. Do not stop an unrelated service simply because it occupies the port.

Depending on your environment, you may need to resolve the conflict or configure GBase Database(GBase 8s) to use an available port. Ensure that the server configuration and client connection entries remain consistent.

4. Server Name Mismatch Between onconfig and sqlhosts

Typical symptom: The instance appears to be running, but client connections fail with a server name or connection configuration error.

GBase Database(GBase 8s) uses instance configuration and connection definitions that must agree with the intended server name.

Review the relevant settings:

grep -E 'DBSERVERNAME|DBSERVERALIASES' \
  "$GBASEDBTDIR/etc/onconfig.gbase01"

cat "$GBASEDBTSQLHOSTS"

The exact configuration file names depend on your installation.

Verify that the server name requested by the client corresponds to a valid server configuration and that the associated connection protocol, host, and port are correct.

Do not change instance identifiers blindly. Confirm the active configuration before making adjustments.

5. Client-Side sqlhosts Misconfiguration

Typical symptom: The database is accessible from the server itself, but a remote application or client cannot connect.

The client may be using a different sqlhosts file or an outdated connection definition.

Check the active environment and client configuration:

echo "$GBASEDBTSQLHOSTS"

Then inspect the file referenced by that variable and verify the server entry.

For remote connections, confirm that:

  • The client uses the correct database server name.
  • The hostname or IP address is reachable.
  • The protocol and port match the server configuration.
  • Client environment variables and driver settings are appropriate for the installed version.

A correct server-side configuration cannot compensate for an incorrect client connection definition.

Quick GBase Database(GBase 8s) Diagnostic Script

This basic script checks instance status, the expected listening port, and the configured sqlhosts file.

#!/bin/bash

echo "=== GBase Database(GBase 8s) Diagnostics ==="

echo
echo "1. Instance status"
if command -v onstat >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    onstat - 2>&1 | head -5
else
    echo "onstat not found; check the database environment."
fi

echo
echo "2. Listening port"
if command -v ss >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    ss -lnt | grep ':9088' || echo "Expected port not found."
else
    echo "ss command unavailable."
fi

echo
echo "3. sqlhosts configuration"
if [[ -n "${GBASEDBTSQLHOSTS:-}" &&
      -r "$GBASEDBTSQLHOSTS" ]]; then
    cat "$GBASEDBTSQLHOSTS"
else
    echo "sqlhosts path is unset or file is unreadable."
fi

echo
echo "4. Firewall status"
if command -v systemctl >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    systemctl is-active firewalld 2>/dev/null ||
        echo "firewalld inactive or unavailable."
fi

echo
echo "5. Next step"
echo "Test connectivity from the actual client."
echo "Review database and client logs for detailed errors."

Save the script as check_gbase_connection.sh and run it under an account with the appropriate permissions.

This is a preliminary diagnostic tool, not a complete connection test. Replace port 9088 with the actual configured port. A listening port alone does not prove that database authentication or SQL queries will succeed.

Final Thoughts

When GBase Database(GBase 8s) cannot connect after installation, start with the instance state, then check the listener, network connectivity, sqlhosts, and client configuration. Use the exact error message to narrow down the cause before changing settings.

The key takeaway: An online database instance is only the first step. Reliable connectivity requires consistent server configuration, an accessible network endpoint, and correctly configured clients.

Systematic troubleshooting is usually more effective than reinstalling GBase Database(GBase 8s) without identifying the underlying problem.

title: Mitigating Video Hallucinations via Attention-Guided Representation Perturbation
description:
arXiv:2610.19728v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Video large language models (Video LLMs) often generate responses unsupported by the input video. Contrastive decoding (CD) can mitigate these hallucinations, but its effectiveness depends on how the negative branch weakens visual evidence. Existing methods rely on predefined perturbations or masking guided by question reconstruction, offering limited control over the model's visual reliance during answer generation. We introduce Attention-guided Representation Perturbation for Contrastive Decoding (ARP-CD), a training-free framework for constructing contrastive negatives directly in representation space. ARP-CD uses the attention mass assigned to visual tokens at the answer-prediction position to guide bounded gradient updates of the language model's input visual hidden states. These updates reduce visual attention and produce a negative input, whose predictions are contrasted with those of the original branch throughout generation. Experiments across four Video LLMs and four benchmarks show that ARP-CD outperforms representative training-free baselines in most model--benchmark settings, reducing hallucinations while improving general video understanding. Further analyses show that attention-guided perturbation directions improve negative quality and that the resulting negatives provide effective contrastive references for correcting the original predictions.

title: Why don't Graph Transformers attend to the same token?
description:
arXiv:2610.19324v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In large language models (LLMs), attention concentrates heavily on the first token. This 'attention sink' is believed to protect deep models against over-mixing. Even though graph transformers face a related pressure, we find that a SoTA graph transformer, GRIT, rarely forms sinks on molecules, and that it sinks less when trained on larger graphs, the opposite of the trend in LLMs. In principle, a graph can prevent sinks: we prove and show empirically that its symmetry and locality limit the attention any node can receive. On molecules, however, with distinguishable atoms and global attention, neither limit prevents sinks; what stops them lies in the model. We find that the attention scoring function is the main cause. Replacing GRIT's gated logit with a dot product raises its sink rate from 0.09 to 0.68 on identical graphs. In Graph Transformers using dot-product attention, removing the sink gives about the same error as removing a random node, while GRIT's most-attended nodes matter to its predictions. Attention sinks are therefore a property of dot-product attention rather than of Transformers. In our experiments, they form when dot-product scoring has a distinguishable node to concentrate on.

title: Should SLMs be in the Driver's Seat? A Study of Local Models as Interpreters in Cloud-Written Agent Programs
description:
arXiv:2610.14209v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The most accurate agents executing user-provided tasks are driven by large, cloud-hosted models, which solve them by reading the private data of the user. Agents powered by models small enough to run on edge devices keep that data local, but yield far worse results. A third option is to have cloud models write a program that devices execute: the data stays local, but as the program is written before any data is seen, it fails whenever a step depends on interpreting content that appears only at run time. We explore an intermediate architecture, in which the cloud-written program defers bounded questions over user data to a small local model through an ordinary function call. On AppWorld this improves the success rate of a code-only agent in all six combinations of backbone model and test partition we evaluate, by up to 14.9pp, recovering a substantial part of the gap to a cloud-hosted ReAct loop while keeping user data on the device.

title: Kandinsky S2V 1.0: Audio-Driven Avatar Video Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.19290v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present Kandinsky S2V 1.0, an open family of speech-to-video models for controllable audio-driven human animation, comprising Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Lite (2B parameters) and Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Pro (21B parameters). From a single reference image, a speech waveform, and a text prompt, the models generate long-form 25 FPS video in which lip motion, expression, pose, and gesture follow the speech. The architecture draws text and audio conditioning from one Qwen2.5-Omni model and adds a reference-aware three-scale visual memory. Training starts from the Kandinsky 5.0 Video foundation models [1] and combines mixed reference-memory layouts with an area-adaptive face loss. The training corpus contains 1.17M single-speaker clips selected by active-speaker detection, with captions generated directly in English and Russian. A side-by-side human evaluation against the strongest open-source baseline and two proprietary commercial models shows that Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Pro performs comparably to or better than these models on average and is also preferred for lip synchronization. On common speech to video benchmarks, Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Lite and Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Pro rank among the top performing models according to mean rank over five reported metrics. Beyond the base models, we provide {\pi}-Flow distilled variants of both Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Lite and Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Pro. The distilled Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Pro model generates video in 16 sampling steps without classifier-free guidance, achieving a 5.4 times end-to-end speedup over the base model, while matching or exceeding it on nearly all reported benchmark metrics. To accelerate open research and deployment in speech-to-video generation, we release the code, model checkpoints, and diffusers integration under the MIT license.

title: Outcome-Routed Distillation and Reinforcement Learning for Diffusion Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.19271v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: On-policy distillation provides dense supervision on the student's own samples, but its targets still come from the teacher. Verifier reinforcement learning (RL) instead uses an outcome signal, but it provides no direct constraint on capabilities outside the verifier. Combining the two is difficult for diffusion language models (dLLMs), because bidirectional denoising makes the policy likelihoods required by ratio-based RL unreliable.
  We develop a likelihood-free pipeline for a mixture-of-experts dLLM. Each rollout group is routed by verifier outcome. Mixed groups use ratio-free, group-centred REINFORCE. If every student rollout fails but a teacher succeeds, the model receives dense KL supervision on the student's denoising canvases. All other groups are skipped. A KL term anchored to the distilled checkpoint limits changes outside the verifier reward.
  The tool-calling teacher succeeds on only 18.6% of the training prompts. At 24 denoising steps, distillation exceeds the teacher by 6.77 percentage points, and routing improves the distilled checkpoint by a further 18.31 points. Routing lowers reasoning-trace accuracy by 0.71 points but raises direct-answer accuracy on the same items by 13.21 points. The anchored arm restores trace accuracy. Its tool-calling score differs by -0.16 points, with a confidence interval that includes zero, although this comparison also removes a small fallback distillation route. A domain-conditional recipe retains a 16.37-point tool-calling gain; a second seed gives 18.23 points and reproduces both preservation results, but the math result is seed-dependent. We pre-registered every arm and evaluated each comparison on paired items in a single sweep on one machine.

title: Demystifying On-Policy Distillation: Where Does the Teacher's Advantage Live?
description:
arXiv:2610.19145v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) is increasingly studied as a cheaper alternative to reinforcement learning, yet it remains a form of knowledge distillation (KD) that relies on teacher supervision. We revisit OPD from the KD perspective by asking where the teacher's advantage lies along student-generated trajectories. Controlled token flips at teacher-student disagreements directly measure the accuracy gained from teacher corrections. Single-token flips yield a modest average gain on selected failed trajectories, whereas repeated flips raise accuracy from 28.4% to 74.5%, close to the teacher's 76.9%. Gains continue to accumulate with more flips, but mass- and KL-based selection outperform random flips by 15-18 percentage points at counts of similar magnitude. Selective intervention remains useful after OPD, but greater argmax agreement does not consistently improve accuracy across model pairs. We advocate training schedules that learn more valuable teacher corrections while maintaining distributional stability. Controlled flips and fork-resolution analysis evaluate OPD beyond accuracy by measuring which teacher preferences the student acquires and what further correction can recover.

title: Equal-information evaluation of credit assignment in modular financial reinforcement learning
description:
arXiv:2610.14750v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Credit assignment in modular financial reinforcement learning is difficult to evaluate because an attributed signal may improve a component loss without adding decision-relevant information or improving economic outcomes. We propose an evaluation framework combining equal-information reconstruction controls, fixed-utility comparisons and prespecified downstream guardrails. The framework is instantiated in an attribution-guided modular trading architecture and tested in three controlled studies covering update allocation, supervision-target representation and portfolio risk control. We find that residual-based allocation is exactly reproduced by an ordinary loss-budget control under the disclosed interface; direct shortfall supervision improves component prediction but fails decoded-outcome preservation; and component-wise critic supervision worsens risk-condition certainty equivalent and drawdown relative to scalar supervision under fixed utility. These results identify three distinct evaluation failures: redundant attribution signals, representation-induced prediction trade-offs, and misalignment between component supervision and downstream risk outcomes. A preserved historical engineering case further shows why module-level learning claims require run-level provenance. The contribution is a reusable methodology for evaluating credit assignment in expert systems operating under partial observability, delayed feedback and economic risk constraints.

title: Reducing the Gap Between Spatial and Space-Filling Curve Neighbors in 3D Point Cloud Segmentation
description:
arXiv:2610.19530v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As a lightweight and highly accurate method for nearest-neighbor search in 3D point clouds, approaches based on space-filling curves (SFC) have been proposed. However, due to the inherent properties of SFC, a gap arises between proximity relationships along the SFC and those in the original Euclidean space. In this study, we propose a loss function that reduces the influence of this gap. Specifically, we compute the distances between adjacent points along the SFC and train the model to optimize feature similarity between pairs of points that are distant from each other in the original 3D space. We incorporate the proposed method into a high-performing 3D point cloud segmentation model and evaluate its effectiveness on three datasets. The results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms conventional methods on both indoor and outdoor point cloud datasets.

title: PMO-Dock: Benchmarking Docking, Specificity, and Generalization in Molecular Optimization
description:
arXiv:2610.19011v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The Practical Molecular Optimization (PMO) benchmark standardized evaluation in molecular optimization, but it is built on simple property-based oracles that do not capture structure-based drug design. As the field has moved to docking-based objectives, evaluation practice has become unstandardized, and different methods report results on different docking tasks, often without a shared protocol for fair comparison or sample-efficiency constraints. To address this, we introduce Practical Molecular Optimization for Docking (PMO-Dock), a benchmark and protocol for docking-based optimization consisting of 25 tasks covering hit generation, lead optimization, and a new specificity task requiring strong on-target binding while penalizing off-target interactions. The protocol separates model development from final evaluation: validation tasks are used for hyperparameter tuning, and test tasks are held out for final evaluation and are not used during development. Evaluation on the test tasks is done under a strict oracle budget to reflect realistic drug-discovery settings. We benchmark four diverse high-performing methods spanning different optimization paradigms, Saturn (reinforcement learning), GenMol (discrete diffusion), Genetic-guided GFlowNet, and ChemLlama (LLM-based evolutionary search). Our results show no universally best method across tasks, additional analyses of hyperparameter transfer (cross-task and cross-category) and sensitivity show that transfer is often limited and varies by method, motivating method-dependent selection strategies. This benchmark provides a concrete standard for evaluating generalization to unseen tasks and sample efficiency under a limited test-time oracle budget.

title: Theoretical and Practical Advances in Hierarchical Bayesian Deep Learning Methodology
description:
arXiv:2610.19074v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reliable uncertainty quantification remains an important challenge in AI. Hierarchical Bayesian methods provide a principled framework for this by representing unknown quantities through posterior distributions. Joint inference of neural-network parameters and prior hyperparameters is challenging for conventional Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods due to strong dependencies. In this work, we introduce the multilevel particle marginal Metropolis-Hastings (MLPMMH) method, which combines pseudo-marginal inference for the hyperparameters with coupled sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) across hierarchy of network-width truncations for conditional parameter inference. The hierarchy is induced by a trace-class neural network (TNN) prior with width-dependent decay, motivated empirically by the compressible structure observed in trained neural-network parameters. Under standard multilevel coupling assumptions, we establish that MLPMMH achieves mean-square error (MSE) $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^2)$ at expected computational cost $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-2})$, and verify the predicted rate on a Bayesian regression problem. To address larger-scale applications, we further introduce S-MLPMMH, a practical approximation that replaces the exact sampling components with a PCA-based hierarchy and scalable Bayesian Monte Carlo. Experiments on MNIST demonstrate competitive predictive performance and uncertainty quantification while exploiting the parallel structure of the approximation. Software has been made publicly available at https://github.com/submission-code-anon/mlpmmh-anon.

title: Decoupled Drift-Diffusion World Models for Consistent Future Frame Prediction
description:
arXiv:2610.19212v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: World models of visual information predict future image frames conditioned on given action sequences. This predicted scene evolution is driven by deterministic changes such as controlled motion on a robot platform, as well as stochastic changes such as rendering of manipulated objects or previously occluded regions. Our key insight is that the spatial location of these stochastic changes is itself learnable. We leverage this insight by jointly regressing both the deterministic next-state prediction and the spatial uncertainty map, then using the uncertainty map to guide a conditional diffusion process. We propose Decoupled Drift-Diffusion World Model (D3WM), which uses a transformer trained with a Gaussian negative-log-likelihood objective to produce both the deterministic next-state prediction and a spatial map of heteroscedastic aleatoric uncertainty. The learned uncertainty map then provides a structured spatial gate for a conditional diffusion model: deterministic regions are anchored to the predicted state, while uncertain regions, such as disocclusions or dynamic textures, are sampled by the diffusion process. We frame this decomposition under a variance-gated stochastic differential equation that separates deterministic drift from stochastic diffusion. D3WM shows improved results over competitive baselines in two distinct types of action spaces: robotic tabletop manipulation and camera motion.
