title: 371 translations crash their Android apps: a census of 1.26 million strings on F-Droid
description:
Made with AI agents by MV2 of Munim, Inc. Every number below comes from code and data you can rerun: android-translation-crash-census (code Apache-2.0, data CC BY 4.0).

When an Android app calls getString(R.string.files_left, n), the translation for the user's language goes to java.util.Formatter. If a translator typed %1$ where the English says %1$s, or wrote 50% without escaping it, the call throws. English never breaks, so the developer never sees it. Only people using that language do.

How often does that happen in practice? Searches of GitHub, arXiv and the web turned up single-project fixes (Commons, Firefox for Android, ConnectBot, OsmAnd) but no measurement across apps. The census makes one.

What was checked

  • Every source repository behind F-Droid's index: 4,476 repositories for 4,667 apps, latest commit, read in 11 minutes on 4 cores.
  • 3,755 have Android string resources. 1,703 have translations of strings with printf placeholders.
  • That is 1,262,958 translations. Each one, and its English source, was formatted with OpenJDK 21's real java.util.Formatter, using arguments of the types the English string expects.
  • For repositories with a failing translation, the census also reads the Kotlin and Java code to see whether anything formats that string with arguments. A broken string nobody formats can't crash.

What it found

  • 371 translations in 98 repositories throw with the arguments the English string expects.
  • 238 of them, in 66 repositories, are strings the app's own code formats. Those are the crashes users can actually hit. That count is after two corrections made by reading rows by hand (below).
  • About 1 in 3,400 formatted translations crashes. It's concentrated: ownCloud's Uyghur file alone has 47 reachable crashes (% 1 $ s instead of %1$s), and Cashiro and Wikimedia Commons follow. Most affected apps have one to four.
  • The exceptions are UnknownFormatConversionException 251, MissingFormatArgumentException 48, FormatFlagsConversionMismatchException 48, IllegalFormatConversionException 20 and IllegalFormatFlagsException 4.

Two false positives the census found in itself

The first run reported 382 crashes, 250 of them reachable. Reading the rows against each app's code took 12 out of the reachable 250, and 11 out of the 382:

  • %t and Long. Four Cashiro strings use %t where the English has %d. %t rejects the Integer the census passed but accepts the Long the app passes, so they print the wrong text instead of crashing.
  • Markup that is text. Wikipedia writes some English strings in CDATA: <![CDATA[... attributed to %1$s. <a href="%2$s">Learn more</a>.]]>. To Android that link is plain text, so the app formats it with two arguments and passes it to Html.fromHtml. The checker removed every <...> before reading placeholders, so the %2$s in the href disappeared from the English. Translations whose link markup was itself broken kept their %2$s, and looked like they read an argument the app never passes. They show a broken link, but they don't throw. That is six rows in Danish, Indonesian, Portuguese, Romanian and Russian. Five more were in values-qq, translatewiki.net's notes for translators, which no device loads. All 11 are gone from the totals above, and 8 of them were in strings the code formats.

The real JVM agreed with the static check on all of these, because both read the same extracted text. Checking the checker against a JVM doesn't catch a mistake in what you feed them both. Census 0.3.1 fixes the extraction (only real XML elements lose their markup), and a full re-run will list every row that changes.

The mistakes, by kind

A small rule-based classifier names the mistake behind the first placeholder Formatter can't use. For the 242 reachable rows left after the Wikipedia correction (238 after %t):

Kind Example Rows Repos
malformed index % 1 $ s, %$1s 50 5
stray percent (%1$d%), 电量 %1$d % 45 26
conversion missing %1$ musikspelare, Wideo (%1) 43 18
flag mismatch Mesaj:% s 34 14
argument not passed a Russian few form reading %2$d 27 14
conversion letter in another script %1$с, %1$دم, %1$δδ 26 6
wrong type %g or %t for %d 10 5
unknown Latin conversion %1$DH, %2$vs 7 4

A stray % is the most widespread mistake (26 repositories). The malformed index is the biggest cluster, but it is almost all one Uyghur file. Turkish % s makes up 22 of the 34 flag mismatches: the space between % and s is read as a flag.

The kind I didn't expect: the placeholder letter itself gets translated. Russian %1$с (a Cyrillic es, not an s), Bulgarian %1$дмлн. for %1$dM, Arabic %1$دم (dal for d), Greek %1$δδ. To a reader each looks fine. To Formatter, с is an unknown conversion. It's narrower than I expected: 26 reachable rows in 6 apps, and in 14 of them the letter looks like or transliterates the Latin one.

Every route shipped one

The hand-checked cases came through Crowdin, Transifex, translatewiki.net, Lokalise, Weblate, and files edited straight in the repository. All of those platforms have placeholder checks of some kind. A check that warns but doesn't block isn't enough once a release script pulls translations in automatically. (A per-platform crash rate is the next thing the census measures.)

A static check you can run in CI

The census compares the real JVM with a static check, the java-format rule in l10n-guard (Python, standard library only, Apache-2.0). Of the 371 JVM crashes it called 364 errors and the other 7 warnings, and it called nothing an error that the JVM accepted. Both share the text-extraction mistake above, which the next l10n-guard release fixes.

python l10n_guard.py android app/src/main/res/values/strings.xml app/src/main/res/values-ru/strings.xml

It exits non-zero on an error, so it can gate a pull request that brings in translations.

Android Lint's StringFormatInvalid catches many of these too, but only in builds that run lint after the translations land.

Reporting them

The census files nothing by itself. Each case was checked by hand against the project's current code before anything was reported, and only to projects whose rules allow AI-assisted reports. Mastodon and AnkiDroid don't, so they weren't reported; their rows are in the data for their translators.

So far:

  • Tallybook merged the fix for 9 Turkish strings (#397). The maintainer reproduced the crash on an emulator and found a path I had missed: one of the strings crashes the Utility settings screen as soon as it opens, and has since 2019.
  • ownCloud acknowledged the 55 broken Uyghur strings (#5018).
  • Open: Homer Audio Player 2 #26 (Chinese battery indicator), Shader Editor #294 (a Russian plural reading an argument it never gets), FadCam #360 (Italian and Greek strings in video deletion and export).

Limits

  • Only the latest commit of each default branch was read, so a translation may already be fixed on its platform.
  • Code use is pattern-matched. Strings looked up by name at runtime count as unused, so the reachable count is a floor in that sense. So is leaving out the 190 translations that throw only if the app passes text: reading code shows some of those do crash.
  • It can also overcount, as the two corrections above show. Both were found by reading rows by hand, and more may exist.
  • Verdicts come from OpenJDK 21. Android's Formatter is the same code for these cases, but edge cases can differ by API level.
  • I reproduced nothing on a device. One maintainer did, on an emulator.

If you maintain an app in the data, findings.csv links every row to the exact line at the commit read.

This article and the census were made with AI agents working for MV2 of Munim, Inc. The numbers were checked against the published data.

title: Unlocking Go: A Deep Dive into the Language that Powers Modern Cloud Apps
description:
Introduction

If you’ve been watching the cloud-native wave for the past few years, you’ve probably heard the name Go (or Golang) tossed around a lot. From Docker and Kubernetes to HashiCorp’s suite of tools, Go has become the lingua franca of infrastructure software. But what makes Go so compelling for developers building high‑performance, maintainable services? In this post we’ll explore Go’s core philosophy, walk through practical code examples, and highlight best‑practices that will help you write production‑grade Go code.

Why Go?

Go was created at Google in 2007 by Robert Griesemer, Rob Pike, and Ken Thompson. Their goal was simple: a language that feels like a scripting language but compiles to fast, native binaries. The design principles are:

  • Simplicity – a small standard library, minimal syntax, and a single, opinionated way to do things.
  • Concurrency as a first‑class citizen – goroutines and channels provide lightweight parallelism.
  • Fast compilation – sub‑second build times keep the feedback loop tight.
  • Static typing with type inference – catch bugs early while keeping code readable.

These goals translate into tangible benefits for cloud‑native development: quick iteration, low overhead binaries, and reliable concurrency.

Getting Started: Hello, World! 

package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    fmt.Println("Hello, World!")
}

Compile with go build -o hello . and run ./hello. The binary is self‑contained – no runtime dependencies needed.

Structuring a Go Project

A typical Go module looks like this:

myapp/
├─ go.mod          # module definition
├─ cmd/            # entry points (main packages)
│   └─ server/main.go
├─ internal/       # private packages
│   └─ handler/
│       └─ handler.go
└─ pkg/            # reusable libraries (optional)
    └─ config/
        └─ config.go
  • go.mod declares the module path and dependencies. Run go mod init github.com/yourname/myapp to create it.
  • Keep business logic inside internal/ – this prevents other modules from importing it unintentionally.
  • Use cmd/ for the executable(s) that wire everything together.

Concurrency Made Easy: Goroutines & Channels

Go’s concurrency model is built around goroutines (lightweight threads) and channels (typed pipes). Here’s a classic example that fetches URLs concurrently:

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io/ioutil"
    "net/http"
    "sync"
)

func fetch(url string, wg *sync.WaitGroup, ch chan<- string) {
    defer wg.Done()
    resp, err := http.Get(url)
    if err != nil {
        ch <- fmt.Sprintf("%s: error %v", url, err)
        return
    }
    body, _ := ioutil.ReadAll(resp.Body)
    resp.Body.Close()
    ch <- fmt.Sprintf("%s: %d bytes", url, len(body))
}

func main() {
    urls := []string{"https://golang.org", "https://dev.to", "https://github.com"}
    var wg sync.WaitGroup
    ch := make(chan string, len(urls))

    for _, u := range urls {
        wg.Add(1)
        go fetch(u, &wg, ch)
    }
    wg.Wait()
    close(ch)

    for result := range ch {
        fmt.Println(result)
    }
}

Key takeaways:

  • go fetch(...) launches a goroutine instantly.
  • sync.WaitGroup ensures the main routine waits for all workers.
  • The buffered channel collects results without blocking the workers.

Error Handling – The Go Way

Go eschews exceptions; errors are explicit values. This makes failure paths clear and testable.

func readFile(path string) ([]byte, error) {
    data, err := os.ReadFile(path)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("read %s: %w", path, err)
    }
    return data, nil
}

func main() {
    if _, err := readFile("/nonexistent"); err != nil {
        log.Fatalf("Fatal error: %v", err)
    }
}
  • Wrap errors with %w to retain the original cause – errors.Is and errors.As can later inspect it.
  • Use log.Fatalf for unrecoverable errors in simple tools; in libraries, return the error up the stack.

Testing & Benchmarking

Go ships with a built‑in testing framework. A typical test file ends with _test.go:

package math

import "testing"

func Add(a, b int) int { return a + b }

func TestAdd(t *testing.T) {
    got := Add(2, 3)
    if got != 5 {
        t.Fatalf("expected 5, got %d", got)
    }
}

func BenchmarkAdd(b *testing.B) {
    for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ {
        Add(i, i)
    }
}

Run go test -v ./... for verbose output, and go test -bench=. ./... to execute benchmarks. The testing package also supports table‑driven tests, subtests, and coverage reporting (go test -cover).

Dependency Management with Modules

Since Go 1.11, modules are the default. Add a third‑party library with:

go get github.com/spf13/viper@v1.15.0

The go.mod file will now contain:

module github.com/yourname/myapp

go 1.22

require (
    github.com/spf13/viper v1.15.0 // indirect
)

Run go mod tidy to prune unused dependencies and ensure reproducible builds.

Deploying Go Binaries – From Docker to Serverless

Because Go produces static binaries, containerization is straightforward:

FROM golang:1.22-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN go build -o server ./cmd/server

FROM alpine:latest
COPY --from=builder /app/server /usr/local/bin/server
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["server"]

The final image is only ~15 MB. For serverless platforms like AWS Lambda, use the aws-lambda-go library and compile with GOOS=linux GOARCH=amd64.

Best Practices Checklist

✅ Practice
✅ Keep functions small (ideally < 30 lines)
✅ Prefer composition over inheritance – use interfaces
✅ Use context for cancellation & deadlines
✅ Run go vet, staticcheck, and golint in CI
✅ Document exported symbols with GoDoc comments
✅ Avoid global variables – inject dependencies
✅ Write table‑driven tests for edge cases

Conclusion

Go’s blend of simplicity, performance, and first‑class concurrency makes it a natural fit for modern cloud‑native services. By embracing Go’s idioms – explicit error handling, lightweight goroutines, and a strong standard library – you can ship reliable binaries fast and keep your codebase maintainable.

Ready to give Go a spin? Clone the starter repo, run go test ./..., and watch your first binary fire up in seconds. Happy coding!

title: Adaptive Observation Control for Active Visual Recognition
description:
arXiv:2610.19624v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Visual recognition models usually process a fixed view under a fixed computation budget, although images often benefit from different scales and amounts of spatial evidence. Active vision can adapt by observing a coarse scene and then selecting informative fixations, but the public AdaptiveNN-DeiT-S pipeline still fixes both field of view and observation count. We extend this fixed-step recognizer with a controllable observation interface that adapts both the field of view and the number of fixations to the input. Specifically, the model predicts a per-fixation scale that sets its field of view, refines each selected crop with optional scale-gated foveation and a residual high-resolution detail-token branch, and uses label-grounded stop heads for input-dependent early termination. Experiments across fine-grained benchmarks, full ImageNet-1K, and ImageNet-A/R-derived classification splits show that the interface remains competitive with fixed-step references while exposing a controllable observation budget. The same checkpoint enables threshold-controlled accuracy-compute trade-offs without per-threshold retraining. On sequential ImageNet-1K, the learned stop rule outperforms fixed-step truncation of the same checkpoint, sustaining 81.9% top-1 using 2.45 of the four focus steps and exceeding three-step truncation at lower cost. On each benchmark, a variant combining scale control and detail-token fusion achieves the highest accuracy among the tested component-added non-exit variants. Our code is available at https://github.com/GZHU-DVL/LI-Dikai.

title: The Attention Trap: When Good Software Design Works Against the People Using It
description:
The Attention Trap: When Good Software Design Works Against the People Using It

What behavioral science reveals about engagement loops, digital habits, and the responsibility of developers.

The software that doesn't want you to leave

You open an app to check one thing: whether a package shipped, what time the game starts, a reply from a friend. You find it in seconds. Then a post below it catches your eye, and another below that, and when you next look at the clock twenty minutes have gone somewhere you never decided to send them.

Nothing malfunctioned. The feed did precisely what it was built, tuned and measured to do, and those twenty minutes were logged somewhere as a small engineering success.

Software can be excellent at meeting its engagement objectives while producing experiences that conflict with what its users wanted from their time. What happens when software succeeds at keeping us engaged but fails to respect our original intentions?

Engagement in itself is not the problem. Reading a long essay, learning a language or a video call with family are engagement too. The useful distinction is between engagement a person would endorse on reflection and engagement they drift into and later regret.

Public conversation tends to land on the individual. In a July 2026 segment of NPR's TED Radio Hour, journalist Nayeema Raza proposed that three pre-internet habits could help people slow down and break the screen cycle. Personal habits matter, but every habit plays out in an environment, and on a screen that environment is written by developers. This essay looks at that side of the glass.

The architecture of engagement

Almost every feature associated with compulsive use began as a fix for a real problem. Infinite scrolling removed the friction of pagination on small touchscreens. Autoplay spares someone watching a series from reaching for the remote. Notifications tell you a person needs you. Recommenders find the few relevant items among millions. Streaks help people keep up practice they chose.

What these features share is that they remove a decision point. A paginated list ends, and the end is a natural moment to ask whether you want more. Each convenience shortens the distance between continuing and never having decided at all.

Reviewing 43 papers, Monge Roffarello, Lukoff and De Russis catalogued eleven types of what they call attention-capture damaging patterns, infinite scroll and autoplay among them. They distinguish deceptive designs, which mislead, from seductive ones, which deceive no one and simply make continuing the path of least resistance. Most engagement features are of the second kind, which is why intent is a poor guide to their effects.

In a survey of 120 YouTube users, Lukoff and colleagues found that autoplay and recommendations primarily undermined people's sense of agency, while search and playlists supported it. That is self-reported perception, not measured harm, but it shows that one product can contain features that hand control to the user and features that quietly take it back.

Underneath the interface sits the objective function. A ranking model trained on watch time or click-through rate learns to serve whatever produces those signals. Kleinberg, Mullainathan and Raghavan formalized the difficulty in a theoretical model in which users have an impulsive in-the-moment self and a long-term self with different preferences, while the platform observes only behavior. In their model, raising engagement improves welfare along some directions of design change and lowers it along others, and engagement data alone cannot reveal which. It is a model rather than an empirical finding, but it names the core problem: behavioral data measures what people do, not what they wanted.

What behavioral science actually tells us

The science here is more interesting and less alarming than the popular version.

Habits. Wood and Rünger's review describes habits as responses that, through repetition in stable contexts, come to be triggered by cues rather than deliberate goals. They are an efficient default mode of action, with a curious side effect: people tend to infer from how often they do something that they must have intended it. Software that sits one tap away in every idle moment is well positioned to become such a cue.

Uncertain rewards. Since Skinner's operant conditioning research, psychologists have known that behavior rewarded intermittently tends to persist longer than behavior rewarded every time. A feed mixes things you care about with things you do not, in an unpredictable order, which is why HCI researchers, Rixen and colleagues among them, have discussed partial reinforcement as a plausible explanation for scrolling's pull. It is a plausible hypothesis built on an analogy to laboratory findings, not an established mechanism of feed use.

Dopamine and the word "reward." In 1997, Schultz, Dayan and Montague showed that the activity of dopamine neurons in monkeys matched a reward prediction error, the quantity at the heart of temporal-difference learning algorithms. That paper bridged machine learning and neuroscience, and it has been stretched far beyond what it shows. The signal it describes concerns learning, the updating of expectations, rather than pleasure, and nothing in those recordings establishes that every notification releases dopamine in your brain.

The shared vocabulary causes its own confusion. In a recommender trained with reinforcement learning, "reward" is a number an engineer chose, such as a click or seconds watched, and "learning" means updating parameters. In psychology and neuroscience, the same words describe how organisms' behavior and neural activity change with experience. The mathematics overlaps; the mechanisms differ. What genuinely connects them is the behavioral loop: the system learns what you respond to while you learn what the system delivers. Two learners, coupled through an interface.

Attention. The experimental evidence on interruptions is clearer. In a laboratory study, Stothart, Mitchum and Yehnert found that merely receiving a call or text notification, without answering it, impaired performance on an attention-demanding task. In a randomized field experiment with 237 smartphone users, Fitz and colleagues found that people whose notifications were batched three times a day felt more attentive, productive and in control, and reported better mood, than controls. Hourly batching did little, and no notifications at all brought more anxiety and fear of missing out. The lesson concerns timing and dose, not abolition.

Self-regulation. In an experience-sampling study of 205 adults, Hofmann, Vohs and Baumeister found that desires for media use, along with work, brought about the most self-control failure. A randomized experiment by Allcott, Gentzkow and Song offers stronger evidence. Temporarily paying people to use social media less reduced their use even after the payments stopped, consistent with habit formation, and letting people set limits on their own future use reduced it substantially, suggesting they wanted to use less than they did. Through their economic model, the authors estimate that self-control problems account for 31 percent of social media use: a model-based estimate, but resting on an experimental pattern that is hard to dismiss.

The trouble with "addiction." None of this licenses calling ordinary use an addiction. Reviewing the literature, Panova and Carbonell found insufficient support for smartphone addiction as a disorder and proposed "problematic use" instead. Kardefelt-Winther and colleagues warned that the behavioral-addiction label is being stretched until it pathologizes ordinary leisure.

"Screen time" deserves similar caution. Across three large datasets, Orben and Przybylski found that digital technology use explained at most 0.4 percent of the variation in adolescent well-being; Twenge, Haidt and colleagues contested that reading, and the debate remains open. Meanwhile, a meta-analysis by Parry and colleagues found that self-reported media use correlates only moderately with logged use, and problematic-use scales even more weakly. Total minutes is a blunt instrument. What people do, why, and whether it crowds out the rest of their lives tell us far more.

Why willpower is only part of the equation

If behavior were purely a matter of resolve, interface design would be irrelevant. The Fitz study is a quiet rebuttal: participants did not become more disciplined; their environment changed, and their experience changed with it.

A useful way to see this is to count actions. In a continuous feed, continuing costs nothing, while stopping requires a decision nothing in the interface prompts. In a batched design, continuing costs one deliberate action and stopping costs none. Neither forces anything; they differ in which choice is the default.

A field study by Rixen and colleagues shows how rarely the app itself provides the exit. Tracking 46 participants' social media sessions for a week, they found that most reasons for ending a session had nothing to do with the app: a waiting task, sleep, food, another person. Sessions spent mainly scrolling were rated less positively than those spent mainly posting or watching stories, though individual differences mattered far more than session content.

It is tempting to conclude that friction is the answer. The evidence is more modest. A large meta-analysis of choice-architecture interventions by Mertens and colleagues, subsequently corrected by its authors, reported an average effect, but a reanalysis by Maier and colleagues found no evidence of an overall effect after correcting for publication bias, a disagreement still unresolved. In HCI, Monge Roffarello and De Russis's meta-analysis of digital self-control tools reported a small-to-medium effect on reducing time spent, but noted that the evidence comes mostly from short experiments, often without control groups, that cannot show whether the change lasts. Friction is a design variable worth testing, not a cure.

Two ways to build a content feed

Imagine two versions of the same feed, showing the same posts in the same order. The content is identical. Only the shape of the experience differs.

In Version A, continuous scrolling, new posts appear automatically as the reader nears the bottom of the page. There is no page two, no final post, no visible edge. Reaching the end of what has loaded is never an event, because more has already arrived. The feed never asks whether you want to continue; continuing is simply what happens next. If the reader stops, the decision has to come entirely from them, made against the momentum of the interface.

In Version B, intentional continuation, the feed shows a limited batch of posts, perhaps ten, followed by a visible stopping point: a short note that the batch is finished, a count of how many posts have been seen so far, and an option to load more. Nothing prevents the reader from continuing. The next batch is a single tap away. But the end of the batch becomes a moment, and continuing becomes a choice rather than a default.

That is the essential difference. Version B does not force anyone to stop, impose a time limit or hide content. It restores the kind of decision point that a paginated list or the last page of a magazine once supplied without anyone noticing. In the terms of the previous section, it changes which action costs effort: in Version A, stopping requires initiative; in Version B, continuing does, if only slightly.

Both designs offer access to exactly the same information. What changes is the behavioral environment surrounding it, and the research reviewed above suggests that cues, defaults and stopping points shape behavior in ways that willpower alone does not explain.

This comparison is an illustration, not evidence. Nothing here shows that Version B improves well-being, reduces regret or changes long-term habits. Those are empirical questions, best answered by testing designs like these with real users and measuring the outcomes that matter to them.

Can we measure success differently?

Teams optimize what they measure. Time spent, session length and daily active users are cheap to collect, hard to dispute and tied to revenue. As the Kleinberg model makes explicit, they cannot distinguish a person who stayed because the product was valuable from one who stayed because leaving took effort.

Complementary signals get closer. Task completion asks whether someone who arrived to do something did it. Satisfaction and perceived control, gathered in brief in-product surveys, capture whether the time felt worthwhile. Notification usefulness shows in how often notifications are opened deliberately rather than dismissed or disabled. Voluntary return, sessions started without a prompt, separates a pull the user generates from one the system generates. Reported regret asks directly whether a session was time well spent.

None of these is easy. Surveys suffer from low response rates and selection bias, and regret is colored by mood. Users genuinely disagree: one person's relaxing evening of scrolling is another's lost one. And any metric that becomes a target can be gamed, a well-being metric included.

The practical approach is to treat these as guardrails, not replacements. When an experiment raises session length, check task completion and reported control in the same arms. A change that adds time while lowering perceived control is a different result from one that raises both, even if the headline dashboard cannot tell them apart.

The responsibility of developers

It would be convenient to blame engineers, and wrong. Developers usually implement requirements set elsewhere, under deadlines, against targets and business models they did not choose. Most infinite feeds were built by people trying to make a product feel smooth.

But engineering responsibility has never been limited to intent. We expect developers to consider security risks nobody asked about and accessibility needs missing from the ticket. An interface's behavioral consequences belong in the same category.

In practice that means asking a slightly different question in design review: not only what a feature makes possible, but what it makes easier, more automatic, or harder to interrupt. Engineers can flag metrics that reward behavior users would not endorse. Designers can make stopping points visible. Product managers can propose guardrails. Organizations, which set the incentives, carry the largest share, because individual conscience is a poor substitute for goals that don't penalize doing the right thing.

Designing for the freedom to leave

Engagement and autonomy are not opposites; the best software earns long sessions because people choose them. The problem begins when a system becomes better at keeping people than at serving them, and our metrics cannot tell the difference.

Behavioral science offers no villain here and no simple fix, only a quieter observation: people act within environments, and much of their environment is now made of code. Those who write it are deciding, whether they intend to or not, where the exits are and how easy they are to find.

If we can design software that makes people want to stay, can we also design software that respects their decision to leave?

title: What Breaks in Multi-Image Schema Application? Factorial Oracle Interventions Reveal an Instance-Information Bottleneck
description:
arXiv:2610.19611v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Modern vision-language models can accept multi-image contexts, but aggregate accuracy rarely reveals where a multi-image reasoning pipeline fails. We study a controlled schema-application task in which a model must locate two target characters in a 16-image sequence, identify their visual attributes, consult an item-specific visual codebook, and compose two ordered nonce code names. We introduce a within-item 2-by-2 factorial Oracle design: Oracle-A supplies a verified textual schema, Oracle-B supplies a verified ordered target-appearance representation, and both interventions retain the original images and final question. Across 72 new items and 1,188 analyzed model responses, Oracle-B increased strict exact accuracy by 54.6 percentage points (95% confidence interval: 46.3 to 63.0) and outperformed Oracle-A by 60.6 points (Holm-adjusted p-value no greater than .0002). An auxiliary retrieval diagnostic reached only 49.1% ordered-appearance accuracy even after removing code-name generation. Providing both Oracle sources yielded 100% accuracy across all models. These results localize the dominant recoverable deficit to upstream ordered instance recovery rather than primarily to downstream schema use and composition.

title: Frame Evidence:A Benchmark for Reference Frames and Visual Evidence in Multi-Image Spatial Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2610.19564v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A spatial answer depends on the reference frame specified in language and its supporting visual evidence. Item accuracy alone obscures whether correctness persists when either changes. We introduce Frame Evidence, a benchmark of 320 matched triplets and 960 Chinese multiple-choice questions from captured and rendered scenes. One family compares three grounded reference frames over fixed images. The other pairs image deletion annotated as insufficient with answer-preserving addition. Joint metrics require correct answers across all three frames and paired evidence variants. Across 20 configurations on 288 held-out questions, GPT three-shot reaches 50.00\% item accuracy, but the best three-frame group accuracy is 5/48 (10.42\%), reached by GPT two-shot. Few-shot prompting and task-specific adaptation improve item accuracy without consistently improving joint correctness. Input controls show where images support matched success, while repeated executions reveal answer instability beneath similar scores.

title: Chatbots Are Lazy Design: Building an 'Invisible UI' with In-Browser SLMs & WebGPU
description:
☕ Deep Dive (18 min read) — Grab a coffee. We are skipping the AI hype to dissect real architecture, runnable WebGPU code, UX failure modes, and why the bottom-right floating chat bubble is an interface dead-end.

⚡ TL;DR & Quick Links

  • 🚀 Try the Live WebGPU App: invisible-ui-demo.vercel.app (Chrome 113+, Edge, Brave, Safari 18+)
  • 💻 GitHub Repository: github.com/QuentinMerle/invisible-ui-demo
  • 💡 The Core Thesis: Slapping a chat bubble onto a webpage offloads navigation friction back onto the user. By executing a Small Language Model (SmolLM2-360M) directly on the user's GPU via WebLLM, we can infer user intent from passive interaction cues (dwell time, cursor trajectory, text highlighting) to adapt UI workflows in real time— at 0 ms network latency, $0.00 cloud inference cost, and 100% GDPR privacy.
  • ⚠️ The Big UX Lesson: An interface mutating under the user's eyes feels like a bug. The winning pattern isn't aggressive morphing—it's Explicit Assent (the "Sommelier" model).

Table of Contents

  1. The Flaw of the Conversational Paradigm
  2. The PoC Architecture & Hard Constraints
  3. Demo 1 — LiquidStore: Detecting Intent Without Asking
  4. What Failed on the First Try: The Scroll-Only Trap
  5. The UX Uncanny Valley: Does Anyone Want Their Screen Mutating?
  6. Demo 2 — Auto-Hydrating Form: Killing the 12-Field Checkout
  7. Conference Slides vs. npm Reality: The In-Browser SLM Trap
  8. The FinOps Breakdown: Why Frontier Models Are an Anti-Pattern
  9. WebMCP: Making Pages Speak to Autonomous Agents
  10. What This Changes for Product Analytics and A/B Testing
  11. Key Takeaways & Run It Locally

In my previous article (Implementing Client-Side AI in E-commerce: WebLLM and Privacy-First Architecture), I focused on the plumbing: proving that running an LLM directly in the user's browser via WebGPU is viable—with zero server roundtrips, zero token bills, and absolute client-side privacy.

The plumbing worked. But once WebLLM was running in the browser, a practical product question emerged: what do we actually build with it in a real interface?
Right now, the industry's default reflex is almost always the same: a floating chat bubble in the bottom-right corner.
Yet anyone who has tried purchasing a complex product through a conversational widget knows the friction. Try configuring a camera with a bot: it asks vague questions, you type paragraphs, it misinterprets your constraints, you correct it, the viewport jumps around, and six messages later your cart is still empty. Two well-designed faceted filters would have solved the problem in thirty seconds.
The chatbot hadn't simplified anything. It replaced a clear visual workflow with slow text ping-pong, dumping the cognitive effort back onto the user.
Slapping a text box over an existing interface and praying an LLM guesses what someone wants is simply lazy design.

1. The Flaw of the Conversational Paradigm

Chatbots are fundamentally passive. They sit there waiting for input, assuming the user:

  1. Knows exactly what they want,
  2. Knows how to articulate it into a prompt,
  3. Actually wants to hold a conversation with an e-commerce website. In reality, users don't want to chat with an online store. They want to find what they need and check out.

Good interface design does the opposite of a chatbot: it removes friction before the user has to ask for help.

So I wanted to test an alternative thesis:

If a language model can run locally on the client's GPU, why wait for the user to type? Why not use an ultra-lightweight Small Language Model (SLM) to infer intent from micro-interactions (dwell time, cursor velocity, text selections) and adapt the interface dynamically—without a single keystroke?
Technically, it runs beautifully. But in practice, it surfaced an unexpected UX challenge.

2. The PoC Architecture & Hard Constraints

The constraint: everything must execute strictly on-device. Zero backend servers, zero cloud APIs, zero telemetry leaving the browser.
Not out of ideological purity, but out of technical necessity: if an interface requires an HTTP roundtrip to adapt in real time, network latency (300ms–1500ms) instantly kills the physical feel of the UI.

  • Frontend: React 19 + Vite + Tailwind CSS
  • Compute Engine: @mlc-ai/web-llm running over WebGPU
  • Model: SmolLM2-360M-Instruct-q4f16_1-MLC (~190 MB download, ~376 MB VRAM footprint)
  • Agent Protocol: WebMCP (navigator.modelContext)

3. Demo 1 — LiquidStore: Detecting Intent Without Asking

The Scenario: A product page for a high-end dual-boiler espresso machine. Two distinct buyer personas visit this page:

  1. The Tech-Obsessed Barista: Hunts for technical specs (bars of pressure, dual-boiler architecture, PID temperature precision).
  2. The Aesthetic Lifestyle Buyer: Drawn to countertop presence, copper finishes, kitchen styling, and ambient vibe.

A static, one-size-fits-all page serves neither well.

The Mechanics

A custom React hook (useImplicitIntent) aggregates three layers of interaction signals:

  • IntersectionObserver for viewport presence.
  • pointerover listeners for cursor dwell.
  • selectionchange events for highlighted text.

A 400ms ticker accumulates weighted scores inside a useRef (zero React re-renders) before triggering an arbitration.

Golden Architectural Rule: Never call an LLM as your first line of defense. Plain, deterministic JavaScript handles the heavy lifting first.

// Simplified logic from useImplicitIntent.js
const scores = { expert: 0, lifestyle: 0 };
// 400ms ticker — accumulates within a ref, zero re-render overhead
interval = setInterval(() => {
  visibleElements.forEach(({ profile, ratio }) => {
    scores[profile] += ratio * 0.35; // Macro: passive viewport presence
  });
  if (hoveredProfile) {
    scores[hoveredProfile] += 0.95;  // Micro: active cursor attention
  }
  const delta = Math.abs(scores.expert - scores.lifestyle);
  if (delta >= 2.8) {
    commitLockIn(scores);            // Decisive heuristic -> early lock-in (zero LLM needed)
  }
}, 400);
// Fallback after 6 seconds of active exploration:
commitLockIn(scores);

When the behavioral signal is clear (delta >= 1.5), pure JS resolves the persona instantly. Zero inference needed.
When the signal is ambiguous—the visitor spent equal time reading technical tolerances and browsing lifestyle galleries—the local model (SmolLM2-360M via WebLLM) steps in as a neutral arbiter:

async function callLocalModel(scores) {
  const response = await engine.chat.completions.create({
    messages: [
      {
        role: "system",
        content: "You are a strict binary classifier. You only answer with \"expert\" or \"lifestyle\"."
      },
      {
        role: "user",
        content: `Behavioral scores — expert: ${scores.expert.toFixed(2)}, lifestyle: ${scores.lifestyle.toFixed(2)}.
Decide which persona dominates.
Answer STRICTLY with one of these two words: "expert" or "lifestyle".`
      }
    ],
    temperature: 0.1,
    max_tokens: 10
  });
  const raw = response.choices[0].message.content.trim().toLowerCase();
  return raw.includes('expert') ? 'expert' : 'lifestyle';
}

The prompt is minimal, and the task is strictly binary. SmolLM2-360M resolves this arbitration in under 100ms on WebGPU.

4. What Failed on the First Try: The Scroll-Only Trap

My initial prototype tracked everything using IntersectionObserver. It was a complete failure.

An IntersectionObserver only fires when an element crosses a visibility boundary. The moment an engaged user stops scrolling to read a paragraph, the API stops firing entirely. Stationary dwell time was simply ignored.
More fundamentally, scrolling is merely a macro signal. An element can easily occupy 60% of the viewport while the user is looking at another tab or reading the top navigation.
The true proxy for visual attention on desktop computers is the cursor. Eye-tracking literature consistently demonstrates an approximate 75% correlation between mouse trajectories and gaze fixations.

To capture a dependable signal, we had to fuse three measurement tiers:

  1. The Macro Signal (Scroll / Viewport): Baseline weight (0.35 per 400ms tick) proportional to the section's visible ratio.
  2. The Micro Signal (Cursor / Hover): When the pointer enters an annotated element ([data-profile]), weight jumps to 0.95—nearly 3x passive visibility. Lingering over "9.0 BAR" or "PID ±0.5°C" is an active intent signal.
  3. The Engagement Signal (Text Highlighting): If a user selects a technical term ("Dual boiler"), the engine applies an immediate +1.2 boost. Text selection is the strongest deliberate analytical gesture on the desktop web short of an explicit click.

5. The UX Uncanny Valley: Does Anyone Want Their Screen Mutating?

Once the pipeline was hooked up, I started testing it. My immediate reaction as a user was visceral:
Having an interface reshape itself while you are reading feels terrible.

When a headline morphs mid-sentence, when the CTA button changes colors unexpectedly, or when review cards swap places with technical specs without a click, your brain does not think "Wow, intelligent AI!"

Your brain thinks:

  • "Wait, did I accidentally click something?"
  • "Is my browser glitching?"
  • "Where did the paragraph I was reading go?"

This is the Uncanny Valley of UI design. It directly violates Jakob Nielsen's foundational heuristic: User Control and Freedom.
In our prototype, the first safety net was a 6-second observation window backed by an irreversible commit lock-in. The engine observes the opening seconds, locks its decision permanently, and stops. No jitter, no flip-flopping.
Yet for production software, a timer isn't enough. Three far more graceful architectural patterns emerge:

Pattern A: The Intent Passport (Cross-Page Transition)

The golden rule: the page currently being viewed NEVER shifts by a single pixel. The engine monitors behavior on the product page. When the user navigates forward—clicking "Add to Cart" or navigating to checkout—the destination page renders directly in its tailored state. The human mind expects a fresh layout upon navigation; it rejects one shifting under its gaze.

Pattern B: Below-the-Fold Progressive Enrichment

Never mutate anything inside the active viewport. If the user is reading the hero section, the engine may reorganize technical spec tables or customer reviews located further down the page. When the user scrolls down, the content feels organically tailored without any visual jump.

Pattern C: Explicit Assent (AI Proposes, the Human Decides)

This is the pattern we implemented in the live PoC.
Instead of forcibly swapping components, the SLM works silently in the background. Once intent is resolved, it surfaces a discrete contextual badge floating at the bottom:

⚙️ "Looks like you're analyzing engineering specs. [Switch to Workshop View]"

✨ "Interested in premium finishes and aesthetics? [Explore the Copper Edition]"

The user clicks if they want. If ignored, the badge gently fades away without interrupting their flow.

The Restaurant Analogy

Model Analogy What the User Experiences
The Chatbot A lazy waiter handing you a blank sheet of paper: "Write down what you want to eat." Cognitive load. The user must articulate everything from scratch.
Direct Morphing An overzealous waiter snatching your plate mid-chew and swapping it for another dish without warning. Disorientation & rejection. "Wait, what just happened? Did the site break?"
Explicit Assent An attentive sommelier. Having observed your entrée choice, they step forward quietly: "If you enjoy crisp minerality, this vintage pairs beautifully with your dish." Perceived value & comfort. The user feels understood while retaining complete autonomy.

6. Demo 2 — Auto-Hydrating Form: Killing the 12-Field Checkout

Mobile checkout abandonment sits around 85%. Tedious input forms remain the primary culprit.

The Approach: At checkout, the user encounters a single input area:

"Paste your email signature or any unstructured address text."
The user pastes a messy corporate email signature containing a name, title, direct phone number, multi-line office address, and two emails.

Quentin Merle
Staff AI Engineer | Vibrisse Studio Inc.
42 Sugar Maple Road, Suite 300, Saint-Odilon, QC G0S 1M0
Direct: +1 (581) 555-0194 | quentin@vibrisse-studio.dev

In ~400ms to 700ms on local WebGPU, SmolLM2-360M extracts the fields, populates the form inputs, and renders visual confidence indicators:

  • Green indicator: High confidence extraction (Name, Street, Postal Code).
  • Amber highlight: Ambiguous field (e.g., distinguishing between a personal mobile and a corporate switchboard number), inviting the user's eye to verify before paying.

The Privacy Moat: The extracted payload (names, home addresses, phone numbers) never leaves the browser. No third-party API or backend server ever sees the data transit. This eliminates GDPR/PIPEDA liability for address parsing.

7. Conference Slides vs. npm Reality: The In-Browser SLM Trap

On tech conference slides, the theoretical darling for this task is Google's FunctionGemma 270M: an ultra-compact model purpose-built for function calling and tool_calls.

Once you leave the slides and install @mlc-ai/web-llm, you run straight into a wall:

  1. No official WebGPU binary exists for FunctionGemma 270M in MLC-AI's model registry. Google released gemma-2-2b-it, but no ready-to-run 270M WebGPU build.
  2. The in-browser function calling trap: In WebLLM's source (functionCallingModelIds), native support for the OpenAI tools schema is restricted to Hermes-2-Pro (7B/8B) or Hermes-3 (3B). Forcing a mobile shopper to download 2 GB to 4.5 GB of weights into their browser cache just to parse a shipping address is a non-starter.

The Engineering Solution: Grammar-Constrained Outputs (XGrammar)

The practical production pattern does not rely on multi-gigabyte models with conversational function calling layers. It pairs Grammar-Constrained Generation (Structured Outputs) with an ultra-lightweight SLM.
WebLLM embeds @mlc-ai/web-xgrammar. Instead of hoping the model doesn't hallucinate conversational filler, WebGPU constrains token-by-token sampling at the logits level. Generating invalid JSON becomes mathematically impossible.
With SmolLM2-360M-Instruct-q4f16_1-MLC:

  • Download size: ~190 MB
  • VRAM footprint: ~376 MB
  • Cold start: ~3 seconds on WebGPU (subsequent loads are instant via Cache API / IndexedDB) 
// Structured extraction via local WebLLM with JSON grammar constraint
const response = await engine.chat.completions.create({
  messages: [
    { 
      role: "system", 
      content: "You are a strict JSON extractor. No conversation, output only a valid JSON object matching the requested shipping schema." 
    },
    { 
      role: "user", 
      content: `Extract shipping fields from this raw text:\n"""${rawText}"""` 
    }
  ],
  temperature: 0.1,
  max_tokens: 350
});
const shippingData = JSON.parse(response.choices[0].message.content.trim());

8. The FinOps Breakdown: Why Frontier Models Are an Anti-Pattern

A common pushback is: "WebGPU isn't on 100% of devices yet. Can't we just call an LLM API in the cloud?"
Yes. But this is where teams fall into the Frontier Model Trap, defaulting to gpt-6 or claude-5-5-sonnet.

For micro-UI tasks, that is both an architectural mistake and a FinOps disaster:

  1. A sledgehammer for a thumbtack: Binary classification or address extraction requires zero world knowledge or complex multi-step reasoning. A 360M model achieves >98% accuracy on these tasks.
  2. The economic reality: Calling frontier models costs $2.50 to $15.00 per million tokens, with Time-To-First-Token (TTFT) latency between 800ms and 2,500ms. On an e-commerce platform with 200,000 monthly visitors, your bill explodes into thousands of dollars just to adapt a few buttons!
Dimension WebGPU Local (SmolLM2-360M) Edge Micro-API (Groq / Gemini Flash-Lite) Frontier Cloud (GPT-4o / Claude Sonnet)
Inference Cost $0.00 (Zero bill, infinite scale) ~$0.00005 / request (negligible) ~$0.01 / request (FinOps anti-pattern)
Network Latency 0 ms (on-device WebGPU) 80 to 150 ms (Global edge) 800 to 2,500 ms (ruins real-time UX)
Privacy / GDPR 100% on-device (Zero transit) Encrypted transit to provider Encrypted transit to provider
Device Reach Modern WebGPU browsers 100% of browsers (via Edge Worker) 100% of browsers
Server Footprint 0% (Compute offloaded to client) Minimal (Stateless Edge Worker) Minimal (Stateless Edge Worker)

If you must support legacy devices without WebGPU, deploy a lightweight Serverless Edge Function (Cloudflare Worker or Vercel Edge) routing to a micro-model (gemini-2.0-flash-lite or llama-3.1-8b on Groq). Never call AI APIs directly from client code to avoid leaking API credentials.

9. WebMCP: Making Pages Speak to Autonomous Agents

There is a second half to this story.
WebMCP (Web Model Context Protocol) is an emerging standard under incubation within the W3C Machine Learning Community Group (accessible via Chrome Origin Trials). The core idea: rather than forcing external AI agents to scrape the DOM and guess CSS selectors, the webpage formally exposes its semantic tools via navigator.modelContext.

// Exposing structured capabilities directly to external AI agents
navigator.modelContext.register({
  name: "switch_product_profile",
  description: "Adapt the product page layout based on the requested user profile",
  parameters: {
    profile: { type: "string", enum: ["expert", "lifestyle", "general"] }
  },
  handler: ({ profile }) => {
    setIntent(profile);
    return { success: true, appliedLayout: profile };
  }
});

When a user browses with an autonomous agent (Claude in Chrome or Gemini in Android), the agent can execute switch_product_profile({ profile: "expert" }) cleanly. No brittle scraping.

  • For humans (implicit): In-browser SLMs observe passive interaction cues and adapt the UI seamlessly.
  • For AI agents (explicit): Autonomous agents query and manipulate the page cleanly via WebMCP.

10. What This Changes for Product Analytics and A/B Testing

Traditional A/B testing splits traffic blindly across a heterogeneous population: 5,000 visitors to Variant A, 5,000 to Variant B. Three weeks later, Variant B converted 3% better. But for whom? The technical buyers? The lifestyle buyers? The signal is drowned in aggregate noise.

Behavioral telemetry inverts this paradigm.
Micro-dwell telemetry, hover trajectories, and scroll cadences qualify visitor intent within the first five seconds of their session.
Testing becomes conditional:

  • An experimental "Technical Spec Deep-Dive" variant is served exclusively to visitors whose expert score crossed the confidence threshold.
  • The test cohort is smaller, but vastly more homogeneous: statistical significance is reached in days rather than weeks.
  • Hypotheses become surgical: "For verified technical personas, does displaying the pump pressure curve before the pricing block lift checkout conversion?" A chatbot gathers zero signal until the user actively types. An invisible UI qualifies and measures engagement from the very first second.

11. Key Takeaways & Run It Locally

Running a Small Language Model locally in the browser isn't an experimental novelty—it is viable production infrastructure today.

  • SLMs belong behind the scenes: Small models shine as silent intent routers and data extractors, not conversational chatbots.
  • Respect the user: Propose, never impose. Explicit assent beats aggressive real-time morphing every single time.
  • Zero-cost scale: Offloading micro-inference to client-side WebGPU cuts server bills to zero and guarantees uncompromising client privacy.

Run the Code Locally 

# Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/QuentinMerle/invisible-ui-demo.git
# Enter project directory
cd invisible-ui-demo
# Install dependencies
npm install
# Launch Vite dev server
npm run dev
  • Live Demo: invisible-ui-demo.vercel.app
  • GitHub Repo: github.com/QuentinMerle/invisible-ui-demo

☕ Curious to hear your thoughts: What's your take on in-browser SLMs vs. conversational bots? Have you experimented with WebGPU or intent-driven UI patterns? Drop your feedback, critiques, and intuitions in the comments below!

🍁 Proudly engineered from the Beauce region (Quebec) by Quentin Merle at Vibrisse Studio.

title: How to Build a Benchmark That Actually Measures Taste
description:
arXiv:2610.14707v2 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Expert-aligned "taste" benchmarks should reward craft judgment, not the ability to game the test. We introduce TasteBench, a pairwise good-vs-bad benchmark across visual, brand, book, and tech items under a frozen rubric with expert-only gold (panel n>=3; percent agreement >=0.60 primary gate; weak engagement labels train/analysis-only), together with a control protocol that separates craft judgment from test-gaming. Applying the protocol to a Round-1 pilot (primary_human_expert; three biological human experts; n=250 pairs) surfaces and quantifies three validity threats: two construction artifacts that inflate the trivial-baseline layer, and a difficulty ceiling that inflates every score. (1) Position: the preferred item is slot A with probability 0.956, so an always_item_a policy scores 0.956 (fair chance 0.5). (2) Lexical leakage: a filename token cue scores 0.912. (3) Difficulty ceiling: craft domains show near-ceiling human agreement (book/brand/tech 1.0), and even under A/B randomization (eval_assignment_seed7; gold_side_A ~0.47) all five VLM cards reach 1.0 on craft, with only visual separating (~0.84-0.91; a post-hoc hard subset, n=107, leaves craft at 1.0). The protocol (expert-only gold, a weak-label firewall, side randomization at construction, filename scrubbing, and hard filters) makes each artifact measurable and, for the two construction artifacts, correctable; we release a reference eval harness and a side-randomization tool, and show the tool removes the position skew (0.916 to 0.495/0.505). The result is a calibrated view of what the benchmark does and does not yet measure: position and leakage are fixable, whereas the craft-domain ceiling is a pair-difficulty limit that Round-2 must address. We do not evaluate engagement, era/circle conditioning, or calibration here, and we claim no general taste SOTA.

title: Your AI Agent Is Smart. So Why Shouldn't You Trust It?
description:
Why AI Agents Should Preview Changes Before Executing Them

Because understanding a request and safely executing it are two different things.

Imagine building an AI assistant that manages calendar events.

A user asks:

“Clear my Tuesday and move everything to next week.”

The AI understands the instruction. It identifies the events and proposes new dates. Everything seems fine.

But should the application immediately update the calendar?

Not necessarily.

AI Agents Can Make Real Changes

Modern AI assistants can do much more than answer questions. They can modify records, create tasks, delete information, and trigger workflows.

That makes them powerful. It also means mistakes can have real consequences.

What if the assistant moves an important meeting? What if the user meant only personal tasks? What if the proposed schedule conflicts with another commitment?

Even when an AI generates a reasonable plan, executing it without review can lead to unexpected results.

The Human-in-the-Loop Pattern

At ByDesign, AI scheduling follows a preview-first approach.

Instead of immediately applying generated changes, the application presents a proposed schedule for the user to review.

The workflow looks like this:

User Request → AI Generates a Plan → Preview Changes → User Reviews → Accept and Schedule

The user can inspect the proposed changes before they are applied. This creates a clear separation between generating a plan and committing changes to persistent data.

The AI can suggest what should happen, while the user remains in control of whether those changes should be applied.

Why This Pattern Matters

Human-in-the-loop design provides three important benefits.

1. Transparency

Users can see what the AI intends to change before those changes take effect.

2. Control

Users can review the proposed schedule, identify mistakes, and adjust the plan before accepting it.

3. Trust

Important changes are not silently applied. Users have a clear opportunity to understand and approve the outcome.

ByDesign also includes undo behavior and confirmation for destructive actions, helping users recover from mistakes and make important changes more deliberately.

The Bigger Lesson

Not every AI action needs manual approval. Low-risk actions may be handled automatically when the user has clearly authorized them.

However, when an AI agent can modify important user data, it is worth considering whether an action should be previewable, reversible, or explicitly confirmed.

The right approach depends on the impact of the action, the user's intent, and the consequences of getting it wrong.

A reliable AI agent isn't one that acts without hesitation. It's one that knows when to ask.

Explore ByDesign

title: Mastering Go: From Zero to Scalable Services in 2024
description:
Mastering Go: From Zero to Scalable Services in 2024

Go (often called Golang) has been quietly taking over the backend landscape for the past few years. Its clean syntax, built‑in concurrency primitives, and zero‑dependency binaries make it a perfect fit for everything from tiny CLI tools to massive, distributed systems. In this post we’ll walk through the language fundamentals, show you how to spin up a production‑ready HTTP service, and sprinkle in some best‑practice patterns you can adopt right away.

TL;DR – By the end of this article you’ll have a working Go HTTP server, a test suite, and a Dockerfile ready for deployment on any cloud provider.

Why Go Still Matters in 2024

Feature What It Means for You
Compiled, statically typed Fast startup, predictable performance, and early‑catchable bugs.
First‑class concurrency Goroutines + channels let you write concurrent code without the mental overhead of locks.
Standard library Batteries‑included HTTP, JSON, crypto, and more – no external dependencies needed.
Built‑in tooling go fmt, go vet, go test, and go mod are ready out of the box.
Cross‑compilation One binary runs anywhere – perfect for Docker and serverless.

If you’re still on the fence, remember that companies like Google, Uber, Dropbox, and Cloudflare ship critical services written in Go. The ecosystem is mature, and the language’s roadmap is steady – a safe bet for long‑term projects.

Getting Started: Your First Go Program

Create a directory for the project and initialize a module:

mkdir hello-go && cd hello-go
go mod init github.com/yourname/hello-go

Now add a simple “Hello, World!” server:

// main.go
package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "log"
    "net/http"
)

func helloHandler(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    fmt.Fprintln(w, "👋 Hello, Go!")
}

func main() {
    http.HandleFunc("/", helloHandler)
    log.Println("🚀 Server listening on :8080")
    log.Fatal(http.ListenAndServe(":8080", nil))
}

Run it with go run . and visit http://localhost:8080. You should see the greeting.

Key takeaways:

  • package main tells the compiler this is an executable program.
  • func main() is the entry point, just like int main() in C.
  • The standard library’s net/http makes a web server a few lines of code.

Structuring a Real‑World Service

In production you’ll want a clearer separation of concerns. Let’s refactor the above into a small, testable service.

/cmd
  /server
    main.go
/internal
  /handler
    hello.go
    hello_test.go

/cmd/server/main.go

package main

import (
    "log"
    "net/http"

    "github.com/yourname/hello-go/internal/handler"
)

func main() {
    mux := http.NewServeMux()
    mux.HandleFunc("/", handler.Hello)

    log.Println("🚀 Starting on :8080")
    log.Fatal(http.ListenAndServe(":8080", mux))
}

/internal/handler/hello.go

package handler

import (
    "fmt"
    "net/http"
)

// Hello is a plain‑old‑function handler – easy to test.
func Hello(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    fmt.Fprintln(w, "👋 Hello from a structured Go app!")
}

/internal/handler/hello_test.go

package handler

import (
    "net/http"
    "net/http/httptest"
    "strings"
    "testing"
)

func TestHello(t *testing.T) {
    req := httptest.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "/", nil)
    w := httptest.NewRecorder()

    Hello(w, req)

    resp := w.Result()
    body := w.Body.String()

    if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusOK {
        t.Fatalf("expected %d, got %d", http.StatusOK, resp.StatusCode)
    }
    if !strings.Contains(body, "Hello") {
        t.Fatalf("unexpected body: %s", body)
    }
}

Run the test suite with go test ./.... The output should be PASS.

Embracing Concurrency with Goroutines

A common Go idiom is to launch background work as a goroutine. Let’s add a simple health‑check that runs every 10 seconds and logs the current time.

package main

import (
    "log"
    "time"
)

func healthTicker() {
    ticker := time.NewTicker(10 * time.Second)
    for t := range ticker.C {
        log.Printf("🩺 Health check at %s", t.Format(time.RFC3339))
    }
}

func main() {
    go healthTicker() // fire‑and‑forget
    // ... start HTTP server here
}

Because goroutines are cheap (they start in a few kilobytes of stack), you can spawn thousands without exhausting resources. Just remember to coordinate shutdowns with context.Context to avoid orphaned goroutines.

Dependency Management with Go Modules

Go modules have become the de‑facto standard for dependency handling. Adding a third‑party library is as easy as:

go get github.com/gorilla/mux@v1.8.0

Your go.mod now records the exact version, and go.sum stores cryptographic checksums to ensure reproducible builds.

// Using gorilla/mux for richer routing
package main

import (
    "log"
    "net/http"

    "github.com/gorilla/mux"
)

func main() {
    r := mux.NewRouter()
    r.HandleFunc("/users/{id}", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
        vars := mux.Vars(r)
        fmt.Fprintf(w, "User ID: %s", vars["id"])
    }).Methods(http.MethodGet)

    log.Println("🚀 Listening on :8080")
    log.Fatal(http.ListenAndServe(":8080", r))
}

Modules also make it trivial to vendor dependencies for environments where external network access is restricted – just run go mod vendor.

Containerizing the Service

Docker is the lingua franca of modern deployments. Here’s a minimal Dockerfile that builds a static binary and runs it on Alpine:

# Build stage
FROM golang:1.22-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN go build -o server ./cmd/server

# Runtime stage
FROM alpine:3.20
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /app/server .
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["./server"]

Build and run:

docker build -t hello-go .
docker run -p 8080:8080 hello-go

Your service now runs in a ~15 MB container – perfect for cost‑effective cloud VMs.

Observability: Logging and Metrics

Production services need visibility. The standard log package works, but structured logging makes downstream analysis easier. A popular choice is zap:

go get go.uber.org/zap@v1.26.0

package main

import (
    "go.uber.org/zap"
)

func main() {
    logger, _ := zap.NewProduction()
    defer logger.Sync()
    logger.Info("🚀 Server starting", zap.Int("port", 8080))
}

For metrics, expose a Prometheus endpoint:

import (
    "github.com/prometheus/client_golang/prometheus/promhttp"
)

func main() {
    http.Handle("/metrics", promhttp.Handler())
    // other routes…
}

Now you can scrape /metrics with any Prometheus server and set alerts based on request latency, error rates, etc.

Deploying to the Cloud

With a static binary and Docker image, you have a lot of options: managed Kubernetes, serverless platforms, or simple VPS instances. Below are two reliable providers that make Go deployments painless.

Recommended Tools

  • Kinsta – Kinsta offers managed cloud hosting with automatic Docker support, daily backups, and a global CDN. Their Go‑ready environments let you spin up a container in seconds, and the built‑in monitoring tools pair nicely with the observability setup we discussed.

  • DigitalOcean – If you prefer a more hands‑on approach, DigitalOcean’s Droplets and App Platform give you full control over the VM or Kubernetes cluster. Their straightforward pricing and extensive tutorials make it a go‑to for startups looking to scale without breaking the bank.

Both services provide generous free tiers or credits for new accounts, so you can experiment without upfront costs.

Wrapping Up

Go’s simplicity is deceptive – underneath the clean syntax lies a powerful runtime that can handle high‑throughput workloads with minimal effort. By mastering modules, testing, concurrency, and containerization, you’ll be ready to ship production‑grade services that scale effortlessly.

Give the code snippets a spin, tweak the health‑check logic, and push your Docker image to your favorite cloud. In the Go ecosystem, the next step is always just a go get away.

Happy coding!

Feel free to leave comments or share your own Go stories below. Let’s build a faster, safer web together.

title: GBase Database(GBase 8s) Character Set Troubleshooting: Fix Chinese Garbled Text
description:
Chinese garbled text is a common issue when working with GBase Database(GBase 8s). The cause may be incorrect database locale settings, client encoding mismatches, terminal configuration, or data that was already corrupted during insertion. This guide covers practical checks to help identify and troubleshoot character encoding problems.

1. Understand Common Character Encoding Problems

Before changing any configuration, identify the symptom.

  • Chinese text displays as question marks (**????**): The original characters may have been lost during data insertion or conversion.

  • Chinese text displays as unreadable symbols: The client and database may be interpreting the same bytes differently.

  • Only one application has the problem: The issue may be related to that application's connection or encoding configuration.

  • Chinese text displays correctly in one tool but not another: Compare the client environments before changing database settings.

The key is to determine whether the problem occurs during storage, transmission, or display.

2. Check GBase Database(GBase 8s) Locale Settings

Start by checking the environment variables used by the database installation and client tools.

echo "$GBASEDBTDIR"
echo "$LANG"
echo "$LC_ALL"
echo "$CLIENT_LOCALE"
echo "$DB_LOCALE"

These values help identify the current environment configuration. Their availability and expected values depend on the installation and client setup.

You can also inspect the database environment using the relevant GBase Database(GBase 8s) monitoring commands available in your version.

Before changing locale settings, verify the database's existing locale and the locale expected by the application. Do not assume that changing an environment variable will convert existing data or repair text that was stored incorrectly.

3. Check the Client and Terminal Encoding

If Chinese text looks incorrect in a command-line session, check the terminal environment first.

locale
echo "$LANG"

Confirm that the terminal, client application, and database connection use compatible character encodings.

If the problem occurs only in one terminal or database client, test the same query using another client. This helps distinguish a display issue from a database storage issue.

4. Test Chinese Data

Use a small test table in a non-production database to check whether Chinese characters can be inserted, stored, and retrieved correctly.

CREATE TABLE charset_test (
    id INTEGER,
    name VARCHAR(100)
);

INSERT INTO charset_test VALUES (1, '中文测试');

SELECT * FROM charset_test;

If the returned text is incorrect, compare the result across different database clients.

Before running this test, confirm that the target database supports the intended characters and that your session is configured appropriately. Use an existing test table if you do not have permission to create tables.

A successful test does not necessarily prove that all existing data is correct. It only helps narrow down the problem.

5. Check Application and JDBC Connections

For Java applications, review the JDBC connection configuration and the encoding settings supported by your specific GBase Database(GBase 8s) driver.

For example, a connection URL may look like this:

jdbc:gbasedbt-sqli://192.168.1.100:9088/mydb:GBASEDBTSERVER=gbase01

Verify the correct JDBC URL format, connection properties, and supported character set settings against the documentation for your installed GBase Database(GBase 8s) driver. Do not copy connection properties from another driver or version without verification.

If command-line clients display Chinese correctly but a Java application does not, focus on the application's connection configuration and data handling before modifying the database.

6. Quick Troubleshooting Checklist

When troubleshooting Chinese garbled text in GBase Database(GBase 8s), check these items in order:

  1. Confirm the database locale and supported character set.

  2. Review CLIENT_LOCALE, DB_LOCALE, and related environment settings where applicable.

  3. Check the terminal and client application's encoding.

  4. Compare query results across different clients.

  5. Test inserting and retrieving Chinese text in a test environment.

  6. Review application and JDBC driver configuration.

  7. Determine whether existing data was already corrupted before attempting any conversion or repair.

Avoid changing locale settings on a production system without understanding the impact and preparing a recovery plan.

Conclusion

Troubleshooting character encoding issues in GBase Database(GBase 8s) starts with identifying where the problem occurs: storage, connection, or display. Check locale settings, compare client behavior, and test with a small amount of Chinese text before making changes.

A systematic approach helps isolate the cause while reducing the risk of disrupting existing data or production services.

title: A Hybrid Kinematic GCN and Elastic Transformer for Efficient Indian Sign Language Recognition
description:
arXiv:2610.14680v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Sign Language Recognition (SLR) presents complex challenges due to variable signing speeds and spatial intricacies. Specifically, Indian Sign Language (ISL) requires precise modeling of its inherently bimanual nature and is bottlenecked by the scarcity of large-vocabulary benchmarks and the inability of standard models to handle irregular signing velocities. To address this, a structurally-aware hybrid framework for efficient, gloss ISL recognition is proposed. To minimize computational redundancy, an entropy-driven SVD sampler that dynamically extracts informative keyframes is used. Because this subsampling creates irregular physical time gaps, the proposed architecture employs a Continuous Dual Positional Encoding paired with a distance-aware Elastic Transformer to preserve natural signing rhythm. Spatially, a Kinematically-Conditioned Adaptive GCN explicitly models bimanual geometry using unified bone-joint features. To validate our framework, a 120-class, 9,453-video native ISL dataset is created. Augmented by Physical Node Dropout and ArcFace optimization to mitigate subject-specific memorization, our framework achieves a competitive 89.8% accuracy, establishing a strong baseline for complex sign language modeling.

title: Refined Topology-Pass Scheduling: Damped Trust-Region Compensation for Dynamic k-NN Graphs in SE(3)-Equivariant Structure Prediction
description:
arXiv:2610.19246v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Equivariant structure-prediction pipelines alternate coordinate updates with the construction of a k-nearest-neighbour (kNN) graph whose membership is a discrete, piecewise-constant function of the coordinates. Rebuilding that graph at every block boundary (PB) is the expensive part of an epoch, whereas reusing one frozen graph (F) is fast but leaves a topology gap. We study a two-pass design in which the cheap pass records a small amount of state (margins, kNN radii, measured per-boundary displacements) and a second pass compensates conservatively. We formulate the choice of the graph-construction basis as a damped fixed-point iteration whose unique fixed point is exactly PB, and derive (i) exact non-flip certificates with the two-sided constant $m_i/4$ and one-sided constant $m_i/2$, (ii) the minimum-variance (BLUE) replay gain $\gamma^*$ and the resulting feasibility crossover, (iii) an $\ell_\infty$ trust-region projection that preserves convergence, and (iv) an analytic near-tie spacing law $E[m] \approx r_k/(3k)$ that matches measurements to 1\%. Three compensation levels are implemented in C++ (L1: frozen set with live geometry; L2: margin-gated local repair; L3: damped, projected basis) and validated under a matched-conditions protocol (identical seed, MSA depth and trajectory family, only the topology mode differs). L2 reproduces the PB edge set exactly ($D = 0.0000$ at every boundary), L1 stays within 0.6% and L3 interpolates monotonically: L2 reproduces the PB edge set exactly when the trust region is removed, and L3 interpolates between the frozen and the PB topology. The recorded trajectory itself yields a measured $1.5\times$ Pass-1 and $1.76\times$ epoch speed-up with no measurable loss gap. An open-source implementation of the runtime and of all the experiments reported here is available at https://github.com/AlbertHuang96/ProteinPredictMachineLearning.
