title: A 3% zoom hid a one-pixel rounding gap for 372 cards, then cut the first letters off the 373rd
description:
A while ago I wrote about
putting a real screenshot at the top of 372 practice test cards:
a dev-only capture route, a crop script, and a manifest the build generates so a
card can never point at a file that is not there.

This post is what happened when a second kind of content needed the same
treatment, which is the point at which you find out which of your decisions were
decisions and which were coincidences.

The frame, and the arithmetic in it

The screenshot does not sit flush at the top of the card. It sits inset, like
the screen of a handheld console, with the card acting as the case around it:

<div className="shrink-0 p-2 pb-0">
  <div className="bg-muted ring-border relative aspect-[16/10] overflow-hidden rounded-[12px] ring-1">
    <div className="absolute -inset-px">
      <Image src={src} alt={alt} fill sizes={sizes} className="object-cover" />
    </div>
    {badge && <div className="absolute top-2.5 right-2.5 shadow-sm">{badge}</div>}
  </div>
</div>

The radius is not a taste choice, it is subtraction. The card is
rounded-[20px]. The frame around the screen is p-2, so 8px. A rounded corner
inset by 8px only stays parallel to its parent if its own radius is 8px smaller:
20 - 8 = 12, hence rounded-[12px]. Use the same radius for both and the inner
corner looks tighter than the outer one; use a bigger one and the gap between
the curves visibly fattens at 45 degrees. This is the single most common
giveaway in nested rounded rectangles and it costs one subtraction to get right.

The aspect ratio is 16/10 because that is the capture ratio, so the box and
the image agree and object-cover has nothing to crop. I did try a shorter box
on phones, on the theory that a card is mostly text. It cut off the bottom strip
of the screen, which in most of our tests is where the answer controls live, so
the screenshot stopped showing the thing it was there to show.

The bug the extraction exposed

Look at that inner wrapper again:

<div className="absolute -inset-px">

A negative one pixel inset on every side, so the image overhangs its box by a
pixel all round and gets clipped by overflow-hidden. It used to be this:

className="scale-[1.03] object-cover"

Both exist to solve the same real problem. At some card widths the browser
rounds the image's layout box a fraction short of its container and leaves a
one-pixel grey sliver down the right edge. A 3% scale buries the sliver under
overflow, and for 372 game screenshots it was invisible and fine.

Then the same component rendered an assessment centre exercise, whose brief
panel starts hard against the left edge of the screen, and 3% of 1280 pixels is
about 19 pixels of horizontal zoom. The first letters of the panel went missing.

The two fixes look equivalent and are not. A scale is proportional, so it costs
you a percentage of the content at every edge, and the percentage you need is a
guess about rendering you cannot measure. A one-pixel bleed is absolute: it
covers exactly the sub-pixel rounding that caused the problem and nothing else.
I had reached for the proportional fix because it was one class, and it survived
only because no content was near enough to the edge to notice.

The general version, which I keep relearning: a fix sized in percent for a
problem measured in pixels works until the content changes.

Extracting it

Both surfaces now render the same component:

export function CardScreenshot({ src, alt, sizes, badge }: {
  src: string;
  alt: string;
  sizes: string;
  /** Pinned to the screen's top right corner. */
  badge?: ReactNode;
}) { /* ... */ }

Four props, and the choice of which four is the whole design. src and alt
are obviously the caller's. sizes is too, and it has to be, because
next/image needs a sizes string that describes the card's width at each
breakpoint and the two grids are different:

// game cards, three columns from lg
sizes="(min-width: 1024px) 400px, (min-width: 768px) 50vw, 100vw"
// exercise format cards, two columns from sm
sizes="(min-width: 896px) 440px, (min-width: 640px) 50vw, 100vw"

A shared component that guessed sizes for its callers would silently serve one
of them the wrong image width forever, and next/image gives you no warning
because it has no idea how wide your card is.

What is deliberately not a prop: the padding, the ratio, the radius, the ring,
the bleed, the badge position. Those are the frame. If a caller needed a
different one of those, it would not be this component.

The docstring carries the constraint the component cannot enforce:

The card must be overflow-hidden rounded-[20px]: the screen's corners are the
card's 20px less the 8px frame, so the curves run parallel.

That is a contract a type cannot express, so it is written where whoever breaks
it will be looking.

916 is not a round number

Generalising the capture script meant turning its constants into a record with
one entry per content type:

const TARGETS: Record<'game' | 'exercise', Target> = {
  game: {
    viewportHeight: 800,
    headerHeight: 64,
    footerHeight: 0,
    // ...
  },
  exercise: {
    // The e-tray's three panes run the full width, so a 16:10 trim would cut
    // text off both edges. 916 is 800 plus ExerciseContainer's h-14 header and
    // the workspace's 60px "Finish & score" bar, which leaves an area of exactly
    // 1280x800 to keep whole between them.
    viewportHeight: 916,
    headerHeight: 56,
    footerHeight: 60,
  },
};

Games capture at 1280x800 and the default crop takes a 16:10 box from the middle
of the play area. That works because most games are roughly centred.

An e-tray exercise is three panes side by side across the full width. Trimming
it to 16:10 from the centre would cut text off both edges, so these captures use
the mode that keeps the whole area and pads it instead. But "the whole area" has
to actually be 16:10 to avoid padding bars, and the area is the viewport minus
the chrome. So the viewport height is derived backwards from the area you want
to keep: 800 for the content, plus 56 for the header, plus 60 for the bottom
action bar, is 916.

Which means footerHeight had to exist as a concept at all. The game target has
footerHeight: 0 and the crop maths is the same for both:

const bottom = viewport.height - target.footerHeight;
const areaHeight = bottom - header;

Three fields and two subtractions where there used to be two constants. Adding a
second target to a script written for one is almost always this: the constants
you hardcoded were not wrong, they were just unnamed.

The ids are not the filenames

One detail worth a paragraph because it bit me. The generated manifest lists the
captures that exist:

/**
 * Exercises with a card screenshot at public/exercises/screenshots/<id>.webp.
 * Generated by `pnpm tsx scripts/game-screenshots.ts manifest`; do not edit by hand.
 */
export const EXERCISE_SCREENSHOTS: ReadonlySet<string> = new Set([
  'etray-product-launch',
  'group-discussion-scenarios',
  'intray-office-manager',
  'presentation-board-strategy',
  'roleplay-difficult-client',
  'written-recommendation-report',
]);

Four of those six do not match the source file they are defined in.
etray-marketing-launch.ts exports an exercise whose id is
etray-product-launch; written-consulting-report.ts is
written-recommendation-report. The files were named during drafting and the
ids were named for the reader.

Generating the manifest from the output directory rather than from the content
library is what makes that harmless. The capture is written as <id>.webp, the
manifest is read back from the filenames, and the card looks up its own id. At
no point does anything have to know what the file on my disk is called. Had I
written the list by hand from the content folder, four of the six would have
pointed at nothing.

And one line of selection logic

The public page shows one captured scenario per format:

/**
 * One captured scenario per format for the top of its card, the first in
 * library order, so the e-tray card shows the free sample. A format with no
 * capture keeps its icon.
 */

"The first in library order" is doing real work there. The library is ordered
with the free sample first, so the card for the format you can try without an
account shows the scenario you would actually get. And a format with no capture
is not broken, it keeps the icon treatment, which is also why the card's radius
is conditional: rounded-[20px] with a screenshot, rounded-xl without, because
the nested radius arithmetic only applies when there is something nested.

The game cards are live now, so you can see the frame on any provider page, for
example Aon's, where the cards lead with a
capture of the test they open. The exercise cards on the
assessment centre practice page
still show icons at the time of writing; the six captures above go out with the
next deploy. The free e-tray scenario on that page runs in full without an
account either way.

title: NavAble: A Large-Scale Dataset and Synthetic Data Generation Pipeline for Blind Navigation
description:
arXiv:2610.19330v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reliable recognition of accessibility-critical objects (e.g., audible pedestrian signals, door-activation buttons, and handrails) is essential for assistive navigation technologies that support safe, independent mobility for blind and low-vision (BLV) users. Yet these categories are underrepresented in existing large-scale vision datasets, and the few datasets that include them suffer from limited class coverage, inconsistent annotations, and poor diversity. We introduce NavAble, a large-scale dataset spanning 11 accessibility-critical object classes, combining 41K curated open-source images with 8K newly collected, densely annotated real-world images. To extend scale and diversity, we develop a synthetic data generation pipeline that renders high-fidelity 3D assets across 37 environments under diverse styles and viewpoints, yielding 452K frames with rich ground-truth annotations from 565 assets. The pipeline minimizes manual effort by combining automated web image crawling, VLM-based filtering, SAM 3D-based asset generation, and convenient camera trajectory configuration, enabling large-scale data generation at a diversity unattainable through manual collection. Experiments show that fine-tuning existing segmentation models on the NavAble Dataset achieves reliable accessibility-object segmentation (>80% mIoU on our held-out test set). We also demonstrate the effectiveness of synthetic data augmentation, which yields up to +3.5 mIoU over real-world-only fine-tuning. Beyond benchmark evaluation, validation on egocentric data from two mobility-assistive robots demonstrates improved perception reliability in real-world navigation scenarios. Together, NavAble establishes a scalable foundation for BLV navigation perception, directly addressing the data scarcity and embodiment gaps. The dataset and pipeline are publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/NavAble/NeurIPS_2026_BLV.

title: Controllable Diverse Sampling through Pullback Directions
description:
arXiv:2610.14294v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Conditional diffusion models can generate high-quality images that align closely with a given prompt. However, samples generated from different random seeds may remain visually similar, limiting creative exploration. Existing approaches can increase variation, but often require additional optimization or sampling overhead, while stronger perturbations may introduce distortions that degrade image quality or prompt alignment. We propose a training-free method that leverages the local pullback geometry induced by the mapping from the conditioning-embedding space to the image space to identify directions of maximal output sensitivity. By steering different sampling trajectories along these directions, we encourage distinct generations while maintaining consistency with the conditioning signal. Experiments on MS-COCO and BrushNet show the efficacy of the method in improving diversity on prompt-conditioned image generation and inpainting.

title: Pre-Trained Language Models as Zero-Shot Tools for Social Science Research
description:
arXiv:2610.19048v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Record linkage and demographic inference from names are routine demands in social science. Most approaches to these problems require labeled training data that are difficult or costly to acquire. I show that pre-trained language models perform both tasks accurately without requiring task-specific training. For record linkage, I introduce EnsembleLink, an algorithm that uses pre-trained embeddings alongside string-based scorers to retrieve a short list of candidates and then identify the likeliest matches. EnsembleLink matches or exceeds the performance of most prior approaches while generalizing across scripts and formats that those methods are unable to handle. For ethnicity inference from names, I show that large language models (LLMs) achieve up to 83.8% accuracy on U.S. voter files, compared to 78.0% for name-supplemented BISG. Open-weight models offer reproducible implementations that approach these models in accuracy. Moreover, LLMs are able to infer group membership for religious, caste-based, and other ethnic group categories outside of the United States, and reduce bias in downstream estimates of geographic racial gaps. Where pre-training encodes the world knowledge required by each task, task-specific labels add less information.

title: PassThrough: Catch Shoot Expenses Before They Disappear
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge: Week 2 — Side Hustle

What I Built

PassThrough helps freelance photographers and videographers turn shoot expenses into invoice-ready lines.

Parking, travel, props, and rush prints are easy to forget when the job is over. Upload a receipt, attach it to a shoot and client, review the extracted fields, then approve the costs that are billable. Only approved, billable expenses appear in the CSV export.

The model suggests the merchant, date, total, currency, and a short expense description. It does not approve anything or send an invoice. The freelancer checks the source receipt and corrects the fields first.

The person I built this for is a working photographer or videographer who regularly fronts small production costs. Recovering even a few missed expenses could justify paying for a small tool like this. I have not tested that willingness to pay with a customer yet; that is the next thing I need to validate.

Demo

Try PassThrough

The public demo is deployed with Backboard configured. Use sample receipts only: the Render free service can lose stored data after a restart or deploy, and this version is not for sensitive client documents.

Code

PassThrough on GitHub

How I Built It

The app uses Python, FastAPI, SQLite, and a small HTML/CSS/JavaScript interface. Backboard sends receipt images and scanned PDF pages to the configured open-weight Qwen3.5 9B model through OpenRouter. Searchable PDF text is extracted locally, then sent for model processing.

After extraction, ordinary code validates the date, currency, and positive amount. The user reviews each field and decides whether it is billable. The CSV contains only approved billable lines.

flowchart LR
  A[Receipt photo or PDF] --> B[PassThrough web app]
  B -->|Image or scanned page| C[Backboard]
  B -->|Searchable PDF text| C
  C --> D[Qwen3.5 9B via OpenRouter]
  D --> E[Suggested receipt fields]
  E --> F[Human review and code validation]
  F --> G[Workspace expense list]
  F --> H[Approved invoice-line CSV]

Each browser profile gets a separate workspace using a private cookie, and database queries scope receipts to that workspace. This is not account authentication: people sharing one browser profile share its workspace. On local runs, receipt files and records stay in the local data directory. On the hosted demo, they are stored by the Render service and may be ephemeral.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

I chose an open-weight model because receipt extraction is a narrow job where I want to be able to change the model without rebuilding the whole product around one proprietary model API. Backboard gives this web demo a hosted way to run the configured model, while leaving the model choice visible and replaceable.

There is a real tradeoff: this is not local inference. Receipt images and scanned pages go to Backboard, and searchable PDF text is sent there too. Hosted inference is easier to demo than asking every freelancer to install a vision model, but it adds provider cost and means the public version is not suitable for confidential receipts. A local inference option would be a separate piece of work, not a feature I’m claiming today.

Prize Categories

  • Best Use of Backboard
  • Best Use of Render

title: Artificiality's First Exam: An LLM-Referenced C-test for Supraintelligence
description:
arXiv:2610.14005v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Under the accelerated pace of AI development, any benchmark whose difficulty is calibrated with humans or current AI systems becomes circular, or saturates soon. How can we then evaluate machines that may become more capable than the current machines and the people who write the tests? One answer to the question hinges on inverse problems, inductive inference questions for which difficulty depends on the complexity of the underlying mechanism, given the observations and the previous knowledge. Levin's Kt, a computable variant of Kolmogorov complexity, puts a theoretical upper bound to that difficulty, balancing the simplest representation encoding for the mechanism and the logarithm of the time steps to run that mechanism. Previous tests derived from Levin's Kt, such as the original C-test, are based on minimalistic Universal Turing Machines (UTM), capable of very limited representations and no previous knowledge. Reasoning large language models (LLM) are UTMs that capture a compendium of human culture as knowledge, using prompts as natural language programs. This paper presents the first test based on Levin's Kt with LLMs as representational machines. Fresh test items can be produced at high difficulties, estimated in a ratio scale measured in bits, before any human or frontier model can solve them. We formalise the measure, devise a lightweight generation and certification pipeline, explore the effect of the power of the reference machine and the gap between examiner and examinee. We produce a first battery of certified items administered to twelve LLMs. The resulting agent characteristic curves decrease with difficulty, down to the uncharted high-difficulty region, the supra-intelligence window of items we can certify, yet beyond generations of frontier intelligence.

title: How Inner Optimizers Shape Replica Scaling
description:
arXiv:2610.19064v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Training large language models (LLMs) across geographically distributed and poorly interconnected compute pools or data centers has become a topic of significant interest. This has led to increased study of local optimization methods such as DiLoco for LLMs, especially those that use local (or inner) adaptive or preconditioned optimizers, which are critical for high-performance LLM training. However, a central challenge remains: it is well known that increasing the number of model replicas (replica scaling) while fixing the total training budget leads to monotonically decreasing performance. Existing work has empirically demonstrated that the choice of inner optimizer (Muon v.s. AdamW) can significantly improve this trend, but offers only limited explanation of the performance difference. In this work, we consider a range of inner-optimizers and identify two important factors that impact replica scaling: (1) the covariance structure of the pseudo-gradients and (2) the impact of batch size on the pseudogradient's noise scale. Based on these insights, we theoretically and empirically demonstrate that whitening-based pre-conditioning is a powerful inner-optimizer desideratum. Our empirical evaluation extends the results to reveal that whitening-based inner-optimizers achieve strong replica scaling (for 8-96 replicas), with performance relative to DP improving as parameters and data are scaled.

title: Netflix Stratum Media Processing: Automated Container Right-Sizing
description:
By Violetta Pidvolotska and Naveen Mareddy

Stratum is Netflix’s internal serverless media processing platform, shaped by over a decade of experience developing large-scale distributed systems. It powers a wide range of media workloads — including encoding, packaging, inspection, and quality scoring — behind playback, advertising, studio workflows, AI embeddings, and more.

Engineers develop Stratum functions by packaging application code and OS dependencies into OCI images. Stratum then schedules these containers as batch jobs on Netflix’s Titus compute platform, with upstream services triggering function executions.

Every day, Stratum manages hundreds of thousands of containers across bursty, high-throughput, and latency-sensitive workloads. As Netflix’s core media processing platform, this load needs to scale as new content formats enter the catalog, such as podcasts, live events, sports, ads, or regional ingests like TF1 in France.

To request resources for these functions, owners specify their CPU, memory, disk, and network limits as YAML configuration, as shown below:

functionName: VideoEncoder.encodeV1
resources:
  numCpus: 8
  memoryInMB: 18000
  diskSizeInMB: 50000
  networkInMbps: 1000

Maintaining optimal values manually is challenging amidst evolving Netflix infrastructure, EC2 instance upgrades, and application-level changes. Consequently, configs are often over-provisioned upfront or slowly drift away from their ideal values over time. Mis-sized configurations are a universal pain of large-scale serverless platforms, causing additional cognitive load for function builders and operational costs for platform owners.

In this post, we share how we built the Stratum Resource Tuner (SRT) — an automated system that safely right-sizes running containers in production without human intervention. We will walk through real-world examples, our safety architecture, and what we learned when an automated change went wrong.

The Challenge: Over-Provisioning

When engineers write a new Stratum function, they typically copy a resource YAML from an existing function or size it for the absolute worst-case scenario. Once running in production, engineers rarely revisit these configurations until a failure occurs, prompting them to over-provision resources out of an abundance of caution.

Manual resource tuning does not scale for the following reasons:

  • High Operational Friction: Downsizing requires days of manual metric monitoring and trial-and-error testing, diverting valuable engineering cycles away from other high-impact work. If a cut goes too far, engineers face production incidents — making manual tuning a high-risk, low-reward task.
  • Continuous Infrastructure & Codec Evolution: Cloud providers regularly upgrade their hardware. A resource allocation that was optimal on an older hardware generation quietly becomes inefficient on newer hardware. At the same time, Netflix continuously advances media standards and improves encoding algorithms (such as AV1, AV2, and spatial audio). An allocation tuned for one codec might not be optimal when an improved algorithm is released.
  • Dynamic Workload Evolution: As Netflix expands into new media types — such as streaming video podcasts, sports, interactive AI-adapted ad formats, and major broadcaster integrations like TF1 in France — media processing footprints can change unpredictably, rendering static container resource limits imprecise.
  • Rising Industry Hardware Costs: Driven by massive global AI infrastructure demand, server hardware and DRAM prices continue to climb, making idle container memory significantly more expensive to waste.
  • Compounding Platform Scale: At Netflix scale, even minor over-provisioning multiplies exponentially across hundreds of thousands of daily container executions, compounding wasted capacity across the entire Stratum platform.

To understand the scale of the challenge, we analyzed historical usage across Stratum’s workloads. The telemetry confirmed our hypothesis: over-provisioning was frequent, wasted compute was compounding, and the sustainable path forward required a fundamental re-evaluation of how resource configurations are managed.

Meet the Stratum Resource Tuner

To address the challenges listed above, we built the Stratum Resource Tuner (SRT) to automatically right-size Stratum containers. Our north star is to ensure that users never have to manually specify the resource configurations. We started with a handful of high-throughput workloads with relaxed latency requirements, which account for the majority (70%–80%) of resource usage.

As a quick note on terminology, we use “right-sizing” and “tuning” interchangeably in this post. “Downsizing” means decreasing resource limits, while “upsizing” means increasing them. Since our goal is to optimize for cost, this post focuses on downsizing.

Automatic right-sizing is not enabled by default. Function owners must manually opt in on a per resource type basis (e.g., CPU, memory, network, or disk). Once enrolled, SRT operates without a human in the loop across five steps:

  1. Collect resource usage metrics across all executions of that function.
  2. Generate a recommendation for each resource type (e.g., CPU or memory).
  3. Verify the recommendation through experiments.
  4. Apply or reject the recommendation based on the results of experiments.
  5. Monitor post-apply metrics, watching for anomalies after applying the recommendation.

“Recommendation” is a key construct in SRT and serves as the primary unit of operation. As SRT executes its steps, it promotes the recommendation through several stages:

  • CREATED: A scheduled workflow generated the recommendation.
  • EVALUATING: Recommendation verification is running, and SRT is analyzing the results.
  • APPLIED: All experiments passed, and SRT automatically rolled out the recommended configuration.
  • REJECTED: At least one experiment failed, leaving the function configuration untouched.
  • MONITORED: SRT monitors the recommendation during a post-apply soak period to verify stability.

The sections below examine each of these stages in detail. To illustrate the flow, we will follow the real-world lifecycle of the VideoEncoder.encodeV1 function — a high-throughput video encoding function whose over-provisioned memory and CPU footprints were successfully tuned.

Note that all operational thresholds and safety limits discussed below are fully configurable per function to accommodate varying workload characteristics and risk tolerances.

Metrics Collection

To make these recommendations possible, we need a solid metrics collection mechanism. Every Stratum container reports its function execution metadata, infrastructure dimensions, and resource utilization (CPU, memory, disk, and network) at sub-minute resolution.

These metrics flow through Keystone, Netflix’s real-time event streaming platform, and land in two separate datastores:

  • Execution summaries store: Stores execution-level summary metrics indexed in Elasticsearch for fast point lookups, serving as our short-term datastore for querying and inspecting individual runs.
  • High-resolution long-term store: Stores raw, high-resolution usage metrics in Iceberg tables. While slower to query, it serves as our long-term datastore, holding months of history for resource utilization trend analysis.

One record is written per execution, which is represented as a span. Here is how these records look for a single span of our VideoEncoder.encodeV1 function.

In Elasticsearch, the record captures the high-level summary of the completed span, identified by tags.stratum.spanId:

{
  "tags.stratum.spanId": "38536313f65f060a",
  "tags.functionName": "VideoEncoder.encodeV1",
  "tags.stratum.phase": "run",
  "tags.stratum.success": true,
  "tags.stratum.retriedWithMoreResources": false,
  "tags.stratum.function.execDurationSecs": 26,
  "tags.cpuCount": 8,
  "tags.memoryInMB": 18000,
  "tags.diskInMB": 50000,
  "tags.networkInMbps": 1000,
  "tags.titusTaskId": "06e1a7c0-2502-4a54-905f-b13a1e786107",
  "tags.instanceType": "r7a.24xlarge",
  "tags.nf.region": "us-east-1",
  "ts": 1780743028000
}

In Iceberg, the record contains the same metadata, but adds the sub-minute resource utilization timeseries tracked during that span:

{
  "span_id": "38536313f65f060a",
  "function_name": "VideoEncoder.encodeV1",
  "phase": "run",
  "success": true,
  "start_epoch_secs": 1780743002,
  "end_epoch_secs": 1780743028,
  "runtime_secs": 26,
  "cpu_requested": 8,
  "memory_mb_requested": 18000,
  "disk_mb_requested": 50000,
  "network_mbps_requested": 1000,
  "titusTaskId": "06e1a7c0-2502-4a54-905f-b13a1e786107",
  "instance_type": "r7a.24xlarge",
  "tags.stratum.retriedWithMoreResources": false,
  "env": "prod",
  "resource_usage": [ 
   { "cpu_usage": 1.13, "memory_mb": 3701.37, "disk_mb": 20120.4, "net_in_mb": 221.09, "net_out_mb": 0.12 },
   { "cpu_usage": 2.25, "memory_mb": 3584.09, "disk_mb": 25410.1, "net_in_mb": 0.02, "net_out_mb": 0.05 },
   { "cpu_usage": 4.16, "memory_mb": 6750.79, "disk_mb": 30400.5, "net_in_mb": 165.90, "net_out_mb": 0.38 },
   ... 
  ]
}

Recommendation Generation

A scheduled Conductor workflow runs daily, reading the past month of usage data from Iceberg and generating recommendations for every function and resource type. The workflow also generates recommendations for functions that have not opted into automatic right-sizing to preview potential savings.

Each recommendation is saved in the recommendations datastore, enabling us to query and filter recommendations by function, resource type, or status on an ad hoc basis.

For each function and resource type, the workflow applies the following generation logic:

  • Filter by workload type: We only tune high-throughput workloads. This focuses our efforts on right-sizing, which yields the most meaningful fleet-wide savings.
  • Aggressively tune CPU and network: We target p99 usage with no extra headroom. CPU and network are compressible resources; if a container occasionally hits these limits, the function might execute slightly slower.
  • Conservatively tune memory and disk: We target p99.9 usage and include a safety buffer. Running out of physical memory or disk space causes hard failures — such as Out of Memory (OOM) or Out of Disk (OOD) crashes — making a protective margin essential.
  • Apply safeguards to changes: We discard recommendations if the absolute reduction is too small to justify operational effort. For memory and disk, we clamp the maximum reduction allowed in a single cycle to 15% — a safety limit introduced after learning from early production runs.

The workflow creates new recommendations in the CREATED state. If a recommendation already exists in this state for a given function and resource type, SRT overwrites it with updated calculations. Once a recommendation advances past the CREATED state, its recommended_value and stats fields become immutable. Subsequent daily runs generate a new recommendation with a unique ID instead of modifying the existing record.

Here is how these recommendations look across resource types in their initial CREATED state for our VideoEncoder.encodeV1 function:

  • CPU recommendation
{

  "function_name": "VideoEncoder.encodeV1",
  "env": "prod", "resource_type": "CPU",
  "current_value": 8, "recommended_value": 4,
  "status": "CREATED",
  "resource_cost_usd_per_hour": ***,
  "stats": {
    "usage": { "p99": 4.16, "p999": 4.57 },
    "execution": {
      "total_fn_executions": 748762182,
      "success_fn_executions_pct": 99.75,
      "total_fn_exec_runtime_hr": 88102723
    },
    "window": { "start": "2026-05-05T00:00:00Z", "end": "2026-06-05T00:00:00Z" }
  },
  "experiment_inputs": null,
  "experiment_workflow_execution_id": null,
  "outcome_message": null,
  "finalized_at": null
}
  • Memory recommendation (15% reduction in one step)
{
  "id": "2edb734a-6184-4f5e-8ffa-23004bd665d7",
  "function_name": "VideoEncoder.encodeV1",
  "env": "prod", "resource_type": "MEMORY_MB",
  "current_value": 18000, "recommended_value": 15300,
  "status": "CREATED",
  "resource_cost_usd_per_hour": ***,

  "stats": {
    "usage": { "avg": 5296.43, "p99": 6750.8, "p999": 7820.3 },
    "execution": {
      "total_fn_executions": 748762182,
      "success_fn_executions_pct": 99.75,
      "total_fn_exec_runtime_hr": 88102723
    },
    "window": { "start": "2026-05-05T00:00:00Z", "end": "2026-06-05T00:00:00Z" }
  },
  "experiment_inputs": null,
  "experiment_workflow_execution_id": null,
  "outcome_message": null,
  "finalized_at": null
}

As the recommendation moves through its lifecycle, SRT populates the remaining parameters.

When proceeding to the verification stage, SRT transitions the recommendation status to EVALUATING, records the target experiment settings, and links the active workflow execution tracking the experiment.

Finally, once verification runs complete, the status changes to APPLIED or REJECTED, storing the outcome details and completion timestamp for analysis.

Retry with More Resources

We take a conservative approach to generating recommendations, prioritizing system stability over extreme efficiency. Because recommendations rely on historical usage data, they cannot always anticipate sudden spikes or novel workload profiles when functions encounter heavy, unseen requests.

To handle these unexpected spikes, we developed a fail-safe mechanism. A watcher process running in each tuned container tracks memory and disk usage during function execution. If the container exceeds the pre-set thresholds, 85% for non-cached memory usage or 95% for disk usage, the watcher flags the execution as high risk, cancels execution, and re-queues the task onto a larger container:

new_container_size = original_container_size * 1.5

This 1.5 multiplier only applies to memory and disk dimensions.

This “retry with more resources” mechanism serves as our safety net: larger container configurations are applied only when retrying tasks to self-heal from edge cases. Although these infrequent retries incur additional compute costs and latency, they allow us to keep day-to-day configurations highly optimized without having to size for rare, costly outliers up front.

For our VideoEncoder.encodeV1 function, if a heavy run causes memory usage to exceed the 85% threshold (15,300 MB) within its current 18,000 MB container, the system aborts the execution and reruns it on a 27,000 MB container.

While we prefer to trigger retries based on actual OOM or OOD events rather than pre-set thresholds, technical constraints in our current architecture make true event detection challenging. Using pre-set thresholds serves as a reliable stopgap while we develop improved detection capabilities.

SRT automatically enables the retry mechanism for any function opted into memory or disk right-sizing. Each Stratum container reports retry events, which flow into Elasticsearch and Iceberg alongside standard performance telemetry.

Recommendation Verification

Every recommendation must pass a two-stage verification process managed by a Conductor workflow before rollout. During this EVALUATING stage, SRT executes two distinct experiment types:

  1. Synthetic experiment: A low-cost, low-risk test to catch obvious regressions before production rollout.
  2. Production experiment: A live evaluation that validates changes across diverse production workloads to increase confidence.

A recommendation advances to production testing only after passing the synthetic experiment. When an opted-in function has multiple pending recommendations, SRT prioritizes and evaluates the candidates with the highest estimated savings first.

Synthetic experiment:

  • Runs in a test environment isolated from production traffic.
  • Sets up two clusters: one for the current and one for the recommended config.
  • Replays identical request sets across both clusters simultaneously without splitting traffic, exposing both configurations to 100% of test requests.
  • Typically runs for 1–2 hours.
  • Runs to completion without early termination checks.

Production experiment:

  • Runs in production on real user traffic, split three ways:
    ◦ ~90% remains on the main cluster (current production config).
    ◦ ~5% goes to a baseline cluster (current production config).
    ◦ ~5% goes to an experimental cluster (recommendation config).
  • Evaluates recommendations against a similarly sized baseline cluster rather than the main cluster to preserve comparable traffic profiles.
  • Typically runs from one day to one week, depending on traffic volume.
  • Fails fast: cancels the experiment early if regressions are detected.

The Stratum platform executes other experiments alongside SRT experiments. To avoid over-splitting traffic, SRT experiments run at lower priority and yield resources to active, higher-priority experiments.

Traffic arrives in irregular bursts separated by multi-day or multi-week lulls. The verification pipeline accommodates these variable arrival patterns rather than expecting steady traffic.

Back to our VideoEncoder.encodeV1 memory recommendation (18,000 MB → 15,300 MB), verification is triggered with:

{
  "recommendationId": "2edb734a-6184-4f5e-8ffa-23004bd665d7",
  "syntheticExperiment": { "numberOfExecutions": 3000 },
  "productionExperiment": {
    "enabled": true,
    "maxContainers": 20, // max containers shift to baseline & experimental clusters
    "upGateTimeoutMinutes": 10080, // time to wait for traffic to start flowing
    "maxRunDurationMinutes": 1240, // max time to run the experiment once traffic starts
    "minSamples": 500 // min executions needed on both clusters before evaluating
  }
}

Both verification stages evaluate recommendations against two sequential checks, terminating immediately if either fails:

  • Retries with more resources: Restricts memory and disk downsizes to a maximum 1% retry threshold over the experiment duration.
  • Execution time: Compares median runtimes to prevent outlier distortion, permitting up to a 10–15% slowdown relative to baseline, depending on workload, and is configurable by function.

If a recommendation passes both verification stages, SRT updates its status to APPLIED and rolls out the configuration to the main production cluster. If a check fails at any point, SRT marks the recommendation as REJECTED and preserves the existing configuration. SRT sends notifications for both outcomes.

For VideoEncoder.encodeV1, both stages passed cleanly:

{
  "outcome": "APPLIED",
  "syntheticExperiment": {
    "result": "SUCCESS",
    "samples": { "baseline": 3000, "experimental": 3000 },
    "medianExecutionSecs": { "baseline": 59.0, "experimental": 59.0 },
    "slownessIncreasePct": 0.0,
    "retryRatePct": { "baseline": 0.0, "experimental": 0.0 }
  },
  "productionExperiment": {
    "result": "SUCCESS",
    "samples": { "baseline": 50361, "experimental": 49790 },
    "medianExecutionSecs": { "baseline": 196.0, "experimental": 198.0 },
    "slownessIncreasePct": 1.0,
    "retryRatePct": { "baseline": 0.0, "experimental": 0.0 }
  }
}

The recommendation moved to the APPLIED state, permanently setting the memory allocation for VideoEncoder.encodeV1 to 15,300 MB. We observed similarly clean results for the CPU recommendation, which reduced CPU allocation from 8 cores to 4.

Post-Apply Monitoring

Passing verification experiments does not mark the end of the recommendation lifecycle. Updated function code, modified input parameters, or underlying changes in the compute environment (Titus/EC2) can alter production behavior over time. To ensure configuration safety and foster feature adoption, we instituted continuous post-apply monitoring for applied changes.

We monitor metrics for 90 days across two rolling time windows: a 30-minute fast window and a 24-hour slow window. Each window maintains specific alert thresholds: a 3% retry rate over 30 minutes or a 2% rate over 24 hours triggers an automated notification.

At steady state, workloads exhibit baseline retry rates around 0.1%, with rates up to 2%–3% falling within acceptable operational variances. Most applied recommendations remained stable over the past three months.

VideoEncoder.encodeV1 has operated on its tuned configuration for months without breaching thresholds. However, VideoEncoder.encodeV2 presented a challenging edge case: a 50% memory reduction passed all verification checks and ran stably for two weeks before an unexpected traffic shift drove retry rates above 60%.

Because early versions lacked automated rollback capabilities, engineers manually triaged exception cases. This incident highlighted the need for automated mitigation, prompting us to construct self-healing rollback functionality.

Today, the two auto-revert windows look like this:

  • Last 30 minutes: 3% retries warn us; 10% triggers an auto-revert.
  • Last 24 hours: A 2% retry rate triggers both an alert and an automatic revert.

Breaching an auto-revert threshold immediately restores the function configuration to its pre-recommendation baseline.

We intentionally maintain straightforward revert logic — restoring the last known stable configuration rather than attempting dynamic resource adjustments during an incident.

The VideoEncoder.encodeV2 incident also reshaped our recommendation generation rules for memory and disk allocations. Rather than applying full target reductions immediately, SRT now applies smaller, incremental 15% step changes, advancing only after confirming stability at each step. Additionally, we introduced a global kill switch to disable automated right-sizing across all functions in case of unexpected issues or side effects.

Additionally, we enforce a mandatory cooldown period — typically one week — before initiating new experiments on a function. Pausing adjustments allows us to observe performance across diverse production traffic patterns, identifying potential risks before applying subsequent recommendations.

Where Are We Today

Oversized containers and config drift don’t have to be an accepted tax of running serverless workloads at scale. By building the Stratum Resource Tuner, we transformed manual, risk-averse resource sizing into an automated, self-healing pipeline. Through real-world workloads and hard lessons from unexpected spikes, we’ve proven that continuous right-sizing can safely deliver significant gains in infrastructure efficiency.

We initially focused on right-sizing high-throughput video encoding workloads, aiming for an initial 5% reduction in overall Stratum compute costs. For instance, VideoEncoder.encodeV1 achieved a 50% reduction in CPU usage and 40% in memory usage without compromising performance or retry rates.

However, edge cases like VideoEncoder.encodeV2 highlighted key lessons: large single-step reductions can introduce hidden risks, and manual incident response slows recovery. These insights led us to enforce stricter safety guardrails in the Stratum Resource Tuner, including capping memory and disk reductions at 15% per cycle and adding automated rollbacks when retry thresholds are breached. Guided by these safeguards, re-tuning VideoEncoder.encodeV2 yielded a stable 20% memory reduction with zero subsequent incidents.

Looking ahead, our key priorities include:

  • Expand SRT beyond high-throughput encoding workloads to support a wider variety of functions and workload types.
  • Further tune the resources in regions with constrained resource availability.
  • Move from reactive alerts to proactive, automated upsizing for under-provisioned functions.
  • Experiment with intentional upsizing for latency-sensitive workloads to evaluate performance gains and reduce function execution time.
  • Upgrade our failure signals for OOM/OOD events from lagging indicators to leading indicators to improve tuning precision.

If solving problems like this sounds exciting, we are hiring in our Warsaw office. Check out open roles here.

Credits

Special thanks to Olof Johansson, Jakub Karczewski, Adam Mazur, Ethan Mathieu, Rosanna Lee, Ameya Vasani, Jean Barkhuysen, Paul Hieromnimon, and Adithya Prakash.

Netflix Stratum Media Processing: Automated Container Right-Sizing was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: PII Redaction for Web Scraping: A Practical Python Pipeline
description:
TL;DR:

  • Remove unnecessary personal fields before storing scraped records.
  • Detection and redaction are separate operations with different failure modes.
  • A redaction middleware reduces data exposure; it does not establish GDPR compliance by itself.

A scraping pipeline can collect contact details even when its business task only needs organization names or product descriptions. Those details may enter logs, storage, embeddings, and model prompts before anyone notices them. The useful place to reduce exposure is immediately after extraction and before those downstream systems receive the record.

This tutorial implements a small middleware with Presidio. It uses synthetic contact information, a narrow pattern-based detector, and an explicit storage allowlist. The example is intentionally limited so you can see which entities it recognizes and which responsibilities remain outside the code.

Pipeline at a Glance

The pipeline runs acquisition, extraction, detection, redaction, validation, and storage in that order. Acquisition returns page content. Extraction selects business fields. The privacy stage then examines the selected text and removes recognized contact details before the storage stage receives anything.

Keep this boundary close to extraction. If raw HTML is logged upstream, a later redaction function cannot remove the copy already written to your logs. Treat raw captures as restricted diagnostic material when they may contain personal data, and give them a separate retention policy.

The Scrapeless Web Unlocker guide describes a URL acquisition path. Your middleware remains responsible for the field-level decisions after acquisition.

Identify Fields You Need to Keep

Define the allowed business fields before selecting a detector. If your task needs an organization name, category, and public description, do not persist contact emails merely because the page includes them. An allowlist makes that decision visible in code.

Also distinguish redaction from pseudonymization and anonymization. Removing a matched substring is a text transformation. Replacing a value with a stable token may still let records be linked. An anonymous result requires a broader assessment of whether a person can be identified from the remaining data and available context.

The pseudonymization discussion in the EDPB consultation guidelines explains why replacing an identifier alone does not settle whether a record can be attributed to a person. Whether a particular workflow has an appropriate legal basis, notice, retention policy, or transfer arrangement depends on its circumstances. The middleware below does not answer those questions.

Detect PII with Presidio

Presidio separates recognition from text transformation. Its regular-expression tutorial shows how PatternRecognizer accepts patterns with entity types and scores.

Install the analyzer and anonymizer:

python -m pip install presidio-analyzer presidio-anonymizer

This starter uses pattern recognizers directly. It does not load a language model or claim to identify names, addresses, or all phone formats. Add suitable recognizers and evaluate them against your actual language and data distribution before expanding the scope.

Redact, Tokenize, or Quarantine Records

The following program processes synthetic data, redacts two supported patterns, and writes only approved fields. The example.com email address and phone format are demonstration inputs, not scraped personal information.

import json
from pathlib import Path

from presidio_analyzer import Pattern, PatternRecognizer
from presidio_anonymizer import AnonymizerEngine
from presidio_anonymizer.entities import OperatorConfig

recognizers = [
    PatternRecognizer(
        supported_entity="EMAIL_ADDRESS",
        patterns=[Pattern(
            name="email",
            regex=r"[A-Za-z0-9._%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\.[A-Za-z]{2,}",
            score=0.8,
        )],
    ),
    PatternRecognizer(
        supported_entity="PHONE_NUMBER",
        patterns=[Pattern(
            name="demo_us_phone",
            regex=r"\b\d{3}-\d{3}-\d{4}\b",
            score=0.7,
        )],
    ),
]
engine = AnonymizerEngine()
allowed_fields = {"organization", "description", "source_url"}


def detect(text):
    found = []
    for recognizer in recognizers:
        found.extend(recognizer.analyze(
            text=text, entities=recognizer.supported_entities
        ))
    return found


def clean_record(record):
    cleaned = {}
    for key, value in record.items():
        if key not in allowed_fields:
            continue
        if not isinstance(value, str):
            raise TypeError("This schema permits string fields only")
        cleaned[key] = engine.anonymize(
            text=value,
            analyzer_results=detect(value),
            operators={"DEFAULT": OperatorConfig("replace", {
                "new_value": "<REDACTED>"
            })},
        ).text
    if any(detect(value) for value in cleaned.values()):
        raise ValueError("Recognized contact data remains")
    return cleaned


synthetic = {
    "organization": "Example Research Lab",
    "description": "Contact sample.person@example.com or 202-555-0143.",
    "source_url": "https://example.com/",
    "raw_contact": "sample.person@example.com",
}
result = clean_record(synthetic)
assert "raw_contact" not in result
assert "sample.person@example.com" not in result["description"]
assert "202-555-0143" not in result["description"]
Path("clean-record.json").write_text(
    json.dumps(result, indent=2), encoding="utf-8"
)
print(result["description"])

The synthetic demonstration prints:

Contact <REDACTED> or <REDACTED>.

The Presidio anonymizer supports different transformations. Choose them deliberately. A reversible transformation needs key management and access rules; a stable replacement can preserve relationships that you may not want to retain.

If a required business field becomes unusable after redaction, quarantine the record for review instead of restoring the removed personal value automatically. Store a reason code without copying the sensitive substring into that reason.

Apply the Middleware to Scrapeless Output

Run the middleware after your parser maps the acquisition response into the declared record schema. Pass only the extracted fields to clean_record, rather than treating every HTML attribute as an approved business field.

For a page fetched through Scrapeless Web Unlocker, the sequence is: check the API envelope, verify page identity, parse the selected content, clean each record, and then export accepted records. A browser session follows the same storage boundary after its extraction step.

Some personal information lives outside body text. Query parameters, document names, images, and free-form metadata need their own treatment. If a URL can identify a person, do not assume it is safe merely because your current contact regex does not match it.

Validate Missed Entities and Retention Rules

A detector needs both positive and negative test cases. Positive cases check that supported personal values are removed. Negative cases check that normal product identifiers, dates, and technical strings are preserved. Include nonstandard formatting and the languages present in your real data.

The final detector call in the code confirms that its own recognized patterns are absent. It cannot detect an entity type the recognizer never supported. Document that scope so the check is not presented as a complete privacy assessment.

Keep raw captures out of routine logs. Record counts, entity types, reason codes, and schema outcomes instead of raw snippets. Define who can review quarantined records and when diagnostic captures are deleted. Apply the same controls to embeddings and model inputs, because those are additional downstream copies.

Conclusion

A practical privacy boundary starts with collecting and storing fewer fields. Add detection and redaction for the fields you still need, test the recognizers on realistic examples, and keep raw diagnostics separate. The software can enforce those decisions consistently once the decisions have been made.

FAQ

Does replacing matched emails make a dataset anonymous?

No. Other fields and contextual information may still identify a person. Anonymity depends on the complete dataset and use context.

Does this code recognize names and addresses?

No. It recognizes its configured email pattern and one demonstration phone format. Additional entity types need their own recognizers and evaluation.

Why use an allowlist as well as a detector?

An allowlist prevents unnecessary fields from reaching storage. Detection handles supported personal values inside fields that remain allowed.

Is a privacy middleware enough for GDPR compliance?

No. The workflow also needs decisions about its purpose, legal basis, transparency, retention, security, and other applicable obligations.

Only collect data you are authorized to access, and review applicable terms and privacy requirements. This article provides technical information, not legal advice.

title: Token Utility for On-Policy Distillation via Local Trust-Region Optimization
description:
arXiv:2610.18883v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Token-selection methods for on-policy distillation (OPD) prioritize student-visited positions using diverse signals, including uncertainty, teacher-student disagreement, and mismatch direction. We instead derive token importance from the distillation objective itself: how much can each position's loss decrease under an equal local KL budget on the student's predictive distribution? The answer is the utility $s_t=g_t^\top F_t^\dagger g_t$, where $g_t$ is the logit gradient and $F_t$ is the categorical Fisher matrix. For reverse-KL it equals the student-weighted variance of the student-teacher log-probability ratio, and for forward-KL it equals the Pearson $\chi^2$ divergence, so the appropriate utility follows from the choice of objective. On shared training checkpoints, several independently motivated criteria, including student entropy, KL disagreement, and TIP, concentrate their importance on nearly the same positions as the derived utility at a 50\% selection fraction, while diverging at stricter fractions and for direction-specific criteria. We instantiate the utility as Fisher Utility Weighting (FUW), a continuous, mean-normalized token weighting. Across seven mathematical reasoning benchmarks and three Qwen3 student-teacher pairs, FUW improves over matched uniform OPD under both reverse-KL (1.35-4.0 macro points) and forward-KL (1.08-2.71 macro points), and is competitive with existing selective methods using a single closed-form score derived from the training objective.

title: Java var, Records and Sealed Classes Explained Simply
description:
Java has a reputation for being wordy, and for a long time it earned it. To store a simple pair of numbers, I had to write a class with two fields, a constructor, two getters, equals, hashCode and toString. That's around forty lines for something that is just "x and y." And a line like this made my eyes tired:

Map<String, List<Integer>> scores = new HashMap<String, List<Integer>>();

Modern Java fixed a lot of this. In this post, we'll learn three features that make code shorter and safer:

  • var (local variable type inference), so you stop repeating types.
  • record classes, which give you data classes in one line.
  • sealed classes, which let you say exactly which classes may extend yours.

At the end, we'll combine all three in one small program. If you read the post about streams, you'll notice that these features fit with them very well.

A quick note on versions, because each feature arrived at a different time: var came in Java 10, records are final in Java 16, sealed classes in Java 17, and the pattern-matching switch that I use with sealed types is final in Java 21. Any recent LTS version has all of them.

Unless I show a full class, the snippets go inside a main method. Records and other types are declared outside it.

Part 1: var (local variable type inference)

What is var?

var lets the compiler work out the type of a local variable from the value on the right side. This is called LVTI, short for Local Variable Type Inference.

var name = "Asha";
var count = 10;
var prices = new ArrayList<Double>();
var scores = new HashMap<String, List<Integer>>();

The long line from the start of this post becomes much shorter, because the type was already written on the right side. Why say it twice?

var is NOT dynamic typing

This is the most common misunderstanding. var doesn't make Java behave like JavaScript. The variable still has one fixed type, chosen at compile time:

var name = "Asha";
System.out.println(name.toUpperCase());

name = 5;

Output:

ASHA

and then a compile error on the last line:

incompatible types: int cannot be converted to String

name is a String forever. You can call String methods on it, and you can't put a number in it.

Behind the scenes

The compiler simply replaces var with the real type while compiling. The bytecode is exactly the same as if you had written the type yourself, so var has no cost at run time.

   var count = 10;                       -->   int count = 10;
   var names = new ArrayList<String>();  -->   ArrayList<String> names = new ArrayList<String>();

   The type is worked out when you COMPILE. Nothing changes when the program RUNS.

Where you can use it

var works for local variables, in several places:

var message = "Hello";                          // normal local variable

for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) { }                 // classic for loop

for (var n : List.of(1, 2, 3)) { }              // enhanced for loop

BiFunction<Integer, Integer, Integer> add =
        (var a, var b) -> a + b;                // lambda parameters (Java 11+)

Where you can't 

   var x;                  error: cannot infer type (no initial value)
   var x = null;           error: cannot infer type (the value is 'null')
   var f = () -> 1;        error: cannot infer type (lambda needs a target type)
   var a = {1, 2, 3};      error: cannot infer type (array initializer needs a type)

   Also NOT allowed: fields, method parameters and return types.

The compiler can only infer a type when the right side makes it clear. In all these cases, there's nothing (or not enough) to infer from. Also, var is only for local variables, so it can't be used for class fields or in method signatures.

A gotcha: the diamond 

var list = new ArrayList<>();
list.add("a");
list.add(1);

System.out.println(list);

Output:

[a, 1]

With a normal declaration, List<String> list = new ArrayList<>(); tells the compiler to use String for the diamond <>. With var, there's no target type, so the compiler picks ArrayList<Object>, and the list accepts anything. Write new ArrayList<String>() when you use var.

Another small thing to know: var list = new ArrayList<String>(); has the type ArrayList<String>, not List<String>. If you want your variable to use the interface type (a good habit), write it out: List<String> list = new ArrayList<>();.

Is var a good idea?

It depends on readability:

  • Good: the type is obvious from the right side. var users = new ArrayList<User>(); and var reader = new BufferedReader(...); need no extra explanation.
  • Not good: the right side hides the type. In var result = process(data);, a reader has to look up process to learn what result is.

A good rule: use var when it removes repetition, and use the explicit type when it adds information. And since the type is no longer visible, choose clear variable names.

Part 2: Records

The problem: so much code for plain data

Here is a simple class that just carries two numbers:

class PointClass {
    private final int x;
    private final int y;

    PointClass(int x, int y) {
        this.x = x;
        this.y = y;
    }

    int getX() { return x; }
    int getY() { return y; }

    @Override
    public boolean equals(Object o) {
        if (this == o) return true;
        if (!(o instanceof PointClass)) return false;
        PointClass other = (PointClass) o;
        return x == other.x && y == other.y;
    }

    @Override
    public int hashCode() {
        return Objects.hash(x, y);
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "PointClass[x=" + x + ", y=" + y + "]";
    }
}

That's a lot of text, and every line is boilerplate (code you write only because the language requires it). A record does the same in one line:

record Point(int x, int y) { }

Point p = new Point(3, 4);

System.out.println(p);
System.out.println(p.x());
System.out.println(p.equals(new Point(3, 4)));
System.out.println(p.hashCode() == new Point(3, 4).hashCode());

Output:

Point[x=3, y=4]
3
true
true

Two points with the same values are equal, even though they are different objects. Records compare by value, not by identity.

What the compiler writes for you

The list in the parentheses, (int x, int y), is called the record's components. For them, the compiler generates:

   record Point(int x, int y) { }
            |
            |   the compiler expands it into roughly this:
            v
   final class Point extends java.lang.Record {
       private final int x;
       private final int y;

       Point(int x, int y) { ... }         // the "canonical" constructor
       int x() { return x; }               // accessors: note, NO "get" prefix
       int y() { return y; }
       boolean equals(Object o) { ... }    // compares all components
       int hashCode() { ... }
       String toString() { ... }           // Point[x=3, y=4]
   }

You can verify the hidden parts yourself:

System.out.println(Point.class.getSuperclass());
System.out.println(java.lang.reflect.Modifier.isFinal(Point.class.getModifiers()));

Output:

class java.lang.Record
true

So a record is a real class. It's final (nobody can extend it), and its parent is java.lang.Record. (Behind the scenes, the generated equals, hashCode and toString are wired up with the same invokedynamic mechanism we saw with lambdas.)

Validation with a compact constructor

What if you want to reject bad values? Write a compact constructor. It has the record's name but no parentheses. It runs before the fields are set:

record Age(int value) {
    Age {
        if (value < 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Age cannot be negative");
        }
    }
}

System.out.println(new Age(25));

try {
    new Age(-1);
} catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
    System.out.println("Error: " + e.getMessage());
}

Output:

Age[value=25]
Error: Age cannot be negative

You can also adjust a value in the compact constructor by reassigning the parameter. And records can have their own methods and static helpers:

record Person(String name, int age) {
    Person {
        name = name.trim();
    }

    String greeting() {
        return "Hi, " + name;
    }

    static Person of(String name) {
        return new Person(name, 0);
    }
}

System.out.println(new Person("  Asha ", 25));
System.out.println(Person.of("Ravi").greeting());

Output:

Person[name=Asha, age=25]
Hi, Ravi

The rules of records

  • A record is implicitly final and can't extend another class (it already extends Record).
  • It can implement interfaces, and it can be generic, like record Pair<A, B>(A first, B second).
  • The component fields are private final. You can't add extra instance fields, and there are no setters.
  • You can add methods, static methods and static fields.
  • Any extra constructor must call the canonical one with this(...).

A trap: records are shallowly immutable

The fields can't be reassigned, but if a field holds a changeable object, that object can still change:

record Team(String name, List<String> members) { }

var members = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Asha"));
var team = new Team("Core", members);

members.add("Ravi");
System.out.println(team);

Output:

Team[name=Core, members=[Asha, Ravi]]

The team changed even though we never touched the record! The fix is a defensive copy in the compact constructor:

record SafeTeam(String name, List<String> members) {
    SafeTeam {
        members = List.copyOf(members);
    }
}

var members = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Asha"));
var team = new SafeTeam("Core", members);

members.add("Ravi");
System.out.println(team);

Output:

SafeTeam[name=Core, members=[Asha]]

Now the record keeps its own unchangeable copy.

Records work nicely with streams

Because the accessors are plain methods, they fit method references:

record Student(String name, int marks) { }

List<Student> students = List.of(
        new Student("Asha", 88),
        new Student("Ravi", 72),
        new Student("Meera", 95));

students.stream()
        .filter(s -> s.marks() > 80)
        .map(Student::name)
        .forEach(System.out::println);

Output:

Asha
Meera

Records are ideal for small data carriers: results that return several values, map keys, DTOs (objects that carry data between layers) and test data.

Part 3: Sealed classes

The problem: inheritance is too open

Normally, if you write interface Shape, anyone can implement it, anywhere, at any time. That's flexible, but sometimes it's a problem. Imagine you want to say "a Shape is only a Circle or a Rectangle, nothing else." With normal inheritance, you can't say that, and the compiler can never be sure it has seen every possible shape.

A sealed class or interface solves this. It lists exactly which classes may extend or implement it, using the permits keyword:

sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Rectangle { }

record Circle(double radius) implements Shape { }
record Rectangle(double width, double height) implements Shape { }

   Normal hierarchy:    Shape  <---  anyone can extend it (unknown subclasses)

   Sealed hierarchy:    Shape  <---  ONLY Circle and Rectangle
                                     the compiler knows ALL the cases

If another class tries to join the family uninvited:

final class Triangle implements Shape { }

class is not allowed to extend sealed class: Shape (as it is not listed in its 'permits' clause)

The three choices for a subclass

Every class that is permitted by a sealed class must declare what happens next in the family, with one of three keywords:

  • final: no more subclasses. The family ends here.
  • sealed: it restricts its own subclasses again, with its own permits list.
  • non-sealed: it opens the hierarchy back up, so anyone may extend it. 
sealed class Vehicle permits Car, Truck, Bike { }

final class Car extends Vehicle { }

sealed class Truck extends Vehicle permits Pickup { }
final class Pickup extends Truck { }

non-sealed class Bike extends Vehicle { }

              Vehicle  (sealed)
             /    |     \
          Car   Truck    Bike
        final  sealed   non-sealed
                  |
               Pickup
                final

Records are automatically final, which is why they pair so well with sealed interfaces. A few more rules:

  • A permitted subclass must directly extend the sealed class.
  • It must be in the same module (or the same package, if your project doesn't use modules).
  • If all the subclasses are in the same file as the sealed class, you can leave out permits, and the compiler works it out.

The payoff: exhaustive switch

Because the compiler knows every possible subtype, a switch over a sealed type doesn't need a default:

static double area(Shape shape) {
    return switch (shape) {
        case Circle c    -> Math.PI * c.radius() * c.radius();
        case Rectangle r -> r.width() * r.height();
    };
}

System.out.println(area(new Circle(1)));
System.out.println(area(new Rectangle(3, 4)));

Output:

3.141592653589793
12.0

(This pattern-matching switch needs Java 21 or newer.) The best part comes later. Imagine you add a Triangle to the permits list but forget to update area. The code stops compiling:

the switch expression does not cover all possible input values

The compiler found the bug for you, long before a user would. That's the real value of sealed types: when the set of cases changes, every place that must handle them is flagged.

In Java 21 and newer, you can even take a record apart inside the case:

case Circle(double radius)             -> Math.PI * radius * radius;
case Rectangle(double width, double height) -> width * height;

A practical example: success or failure

A common use is a result type that is either a success or a failure:

sealed interface Result permits Success, Failure { }
record Success(String data) implements Result { }
record Failure(String error) implements Result { }

static String describe(Result r) {
    return switch (r) {
        case Success s -> "OK: " + s.data();
        case Failure f -> "Error: " + f.error();
    };
}

System.out.println(describe(new Success("saved")));
System.out.println(describe(new Failure("timeout")));

Output:

OK: saved
Error: timeout

Behind the scenes

The permits list is stored inside the .class file. When a class is loaded, the JVM checks it, so the rule is enforced both by the compiler and at run time. You can even read it with reflection:

System.out.println(Shape.class.isSealed());

for (Class<?> c : Shape.class.getPermittedSubclasses()) {
    System.out.println(c.getSimpleName());
}

Output:

true
Circle
Rectangle

Sealed vs enum vs final

These three often get confused:

  • final means no subclasses at all.
  • enum means a fixed set of objects (like MONDAY, TUESDAY), each created once.
  • sealed means a fixed set of types, and each type can have many objects, usually with different data (a Circle has a radius, and a Rectangle has a width and height).

Putting it all together

Let's use everything in one small program: a tiny calculator that models expressions as a sealed hierarchy of records, walks them with a switch, and uses var for the local variables.

sealed interface Expr permits Num, Add, Mul { }
record Num(int value) implements Expr { }
record Add(Expr left, Expr right) implements Expr { }
record Mul(Expr left, Expr right) implements Expr { }

public class Calculator {
    static int eval(Expr e) {
        return switch (e) {
            case Num n -> n.value();
            case Add a -> eval(a.left()) + eval(a.right());
            case Mul m -> eval(m.left()) * eval(m.right());
        };
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var expr = new Add(new Num(2), new Mul(new Num(3), new Num(4)));

        System.out.println(eval(expr));
        System.out.println(expr);
    }
}

Output:

14
Add[left=Num[value=2], right=Mul[left=Num[value=3], right=Num[value=4]]]

Look at how each feature helped:

  • Records gave us four tiny data types in four lines, and a readable toString for free.
  • Sealed told the compiler that Expr is only Num, Add or Mul, so eval needs no default.
  • switch with patterns unpacked each case without casts.
  • var kept the long type name out of main.

Try adding a Sub record to the permits list, and watch the compiler point at eval.

Which one should I use?

  • var or the explicit type? Use var when the right side already shows the type (new ArrayList<String>(), a constructor call, a clearly named factory). Use the explicit type when it helps the reader, or when you want an interface type like List<String>.
  • Record or class? Use a record for plain, unchangeable data carriers: DTOs, map keys, multiple return values, test data. Use a class when you need changeable state, inheritance, hidden internal data or behavior that doesn't revolve around the data. Many frameworks that need changeable, proxied objects (such as JPA entities) don't fit records.
  • Sealed, enum or open interface? Use an enum for a fixed set of constants. Use a sealed hierarchy for a fixed set of types that carry different data. Use a normal open interface when other people should be able to add their own implementations (a plugin system, for example).
  • Records and sealed together? This is a great combination for modeling "one of several shapes of data," like results, events, commands and expressions.

Common mistakes

  1. Using var when the type becomes unclear. If a reader can't tell what the variable is without hunting, write the type. Also remember var list = new ArrayList<>() gives you ArrayList<Object>.
  2. Thinking var makes Java dynamic. The type is fixed at compile time. You can't assign a different type later, and you can't use var for fields, parameters or return types.
  3. Assuming records are fully immutable. If a component is a list or another changeable object, it can still change. Make a defensive copy in the compact constructor, and remember that you can't add instance fields or setters.
  4. Using the wrong accessor name. A record's accessor is p.x(), not p.getX(). And equality is based on values, so two records with the same data are equals.
  5. Forgetting what a permitted subclass must say. Each one has to be final, sealed or non-sealed, and it must sit in the same module (or package). Otherwise, the code won't compile.
  6. Adding a default branch to a switch over a sealed type. It silences the compiler's exhaustiveness check. When you add a new subtype later, it falls into default without any warning. Leave default out so the compiler can protect you.

Quick recap

  • var lets the compiler infer the type of a local variable. The type is still fixed at compile time, and the bytecode is the same as if you'd written it out.
  • var needs an initial value that shows the type. It can't be used for fields, parameters, return types, null or lambdas without a target type. Use it when it removes repetition, not when it hides the type.
  • A record is a one-line data class. The compiler generates the final fields, canonical constructor, accessors like x(), and equals, hashCode and toString. It's implicitly final, extends java.lang.Record and can't have extra instance fields.
  • Use a compact constructor for validation, and make a defensive copy of changeable components.
  • A sealed class or interface lists its allowed subclasses with permits. Each one must be final, sealed or non-sealed.
  • Sealed types give you an exhaustive switch with no default, so the compiler tells you when you forget a case.
  • Records plus sealed interfaces plus pattern-matching switch is a powerful modern-Java pattern.

Try it yourself

Here's a small practice idea: model a payment system. Create a sealed interface Payment permits Card, Upi, Cash, with a record for each, such as Card(String number, int amount), Upi(String id, int amount) and Cash(int amount). Write a method fee(Payment p) that returns a different fee for each, using a switch with no default. Use var for your local variables in main.

For a bonus experiment, add a new record NetBanking to the permits list, and read the compiler error on your switch. Then handle the new case and see it compile again.

If this helped, or if you spotted something I should fix, tell me in the comments. I'm still learning too.

That wraps up this two-part series on modern Java.

title: Structure-Preserving Document-Level Data Augmentation via Discourse Parsing
description:
arXiv:2610.19497v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Data augmentation (DA) plays a vital role in improving model performance in low-resource or limited-supervision scenarios within Natural Language Processing (NLP). Existing DA methods, such as synonym replacement and back-translation, have demonstrated effectiveness on the word or sentence level; however, they frequently neglect discourse-level coherence and logical flow, which are essential for complex tasks dependent on inter-sentential relationships. In this paper, we propose a structure-preserving document-level data augmentation framework based on large language models (LLMs) and document-level discourse structure parsing. Our approach identifies rhetorical relations between sentence pairs and extracts key phrases, which are then replaced with semantically coherent but topically shifted content while preserving the original discourse structure. Experimental results on text summarization and question answering show that the proposed augmented data provides complementary supervision and improves combined-data training across the evaluated tasks. Comparisons with a standard RST parser and controlled ablations further support the proposed discourse representation.
