title: REWIND: Uncertainty-Guided Trajectory Repair for Test-Time Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2610.19561v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: An early mistake in the generated reasoning can constrain all subsequent reasoning. Repeated-generation methods, like MCMC-based approaches, attempt to improve output quality by sampling multiple generations, but their effectiveness can be limited by randomly selecting where to regenerate. On MATH500 with Qwen2.5-Math-7B, we find that incorrect responses have substantially higher mean token entropy than correct responses, with an average within-question relative increase of approximately 112%, suggesting that entropy can signal reasoning errors. Motivated by this finding, we introduce REWIND, a training-free controller that uses entropy dynamics to propose targeted suffix regenerations. Across three model families and five benchmarks, REWIND outperforms all baselines, with gains of 0.51-10.00 percentage points over the strongest baseline. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of targeted, uncertainty-guided trajectory repair across models and tasks. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/rewind-D310.

title: Remember, Revisit, Revise: Scaffold Memory for Long-Horizon 3D Geometry
description:
arXiv:2610.19674v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Geometry foundation models estimate camera poses and 3D scene structure from video sequences, but maintaining consistent reconstructions over long horizons remains challenging. Feed-forward models process long sequences as independent, fixed-length frame windows and align their predictions, causing pose and reconstruction errors to accumulate across windows. Streaming models retain information from past frames to inform future predictions, but cannot revise earlier estimates when later observations reveal errors. To address this, we introduce Scaffold MemOry for Revision (SMORE), a framework equipping frozen geometry foundation models with a revisable external memory for long-horizon inference. Inspired by hippocampal associative memory in biological brains, which links spatial context with sensory experience, SMORE associates where an observer is with what it observes, enabling past observations to be stored, retrieved, verified against new evidence, and revised when inconsistencies are detected. We evaluate SMORE with eight competitive geometry models on five datasets spanning camera pose estimation, multi-view depth estimation, 3D point-cloud reconstruction, simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM), and novel view synthesis. Across all evaluated models, SMORE consistently improves long-sequence pose estimation, reduces multi-view depth error by up to 58%, reduces Chamfer distance for 3D point-cloud reconstruction by up to 43%, and achieves average trajectory error as low as 2.9 cm in long-horizon SLAM. By retaining corrected poses and observations, SMORE further improves the fidelity and spatial consistency of large-scale 3D scene reconstruction. These results establish revisable external memory as a flexible interface for extending pretrained geometry models beyond fixed-context prediction toward iterative, error-correcting inference over long visual sequences.

title: Building Retrieval Architecture for Developer Changelog Tracker — 5 Python Ranking Signals
description:
When a changelog bot cites the wrong release, the root cause is usually a trust-boundary mistake, not a weak language model. Short answer: use staged retrieval with explicit collections, bounded queries, and traceable source context, then choose ranking signals you can evaluate. Keep region, retention, and deletion policy beside the index design; an AI runtime cannot grant contractual residency for a specialist data store.

The retrieval contract comes before ranking

For a B2B SaaS developer changelog tracker, write the user-visible answer first: “What changed in package X, and when?” Turn that sentence into a contract with required fields: canonical URL, release timestamp, package, version, source region, and a citation span. A result that matches the words but lacks a timestamp is not a valid answer.

I model each chunk with immutable source_id, published_at, updated_at, and deleted_at metadata. The collection is private to the application tenant. Deletions are events, not a cleanup task: remove the record from the collection when the upstream page disappears, and re-index changed content deliberately so an old chunk cannot outrank the current release.

The first stage gathers candidates from lexical web search or a vector collection. The second stage scores them with signals that mirror the contract:

  • lexical overlap for package and version tokens;
  • semantic similarity for paraphrased release notes;
  • recency, with a bounded decay rather than an unreviewed “newer is always better” rule;
  • source authority, such as the maintainer’s canonical feed;
  • metadata completeness and citation-span availability.

That is the trap.

For the orchestration layer, Infrai is worth testing when a team wants a self-describing REST surface: its public discovery endpoint exposes capability schemas and runnable examples, so a Python service can inspect a new retrieval capability without installing another SDK. Keep the tenant's durable records in the system that owns your residency and deletion agreement; the routing layer does not replace that boundary.

How should a Python changelog tracker rank retrieval signals?

Start with a small labeled set: 50–100 real questions, two acceptable citations per question, and a reviewer decision for “stale but relevant.” Measure recall@k for candidate generation and citation precision for the final answer. I would not ship a new weighting because it feels right; I would ship it when the eval harness shows fewer unsupported citations without pushing latency past the product budget. Your mileage may vary because release cadence and tenant vocabulary change the labels.

A simple, inspectable score is often enough for the first iteration:

from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from math import exp


@dataclass
class Candidate:
    text: str
    lexical: float
    semantic: float
    authority: float
    published_at: datetime
    has_citation_span: bool


def rank(candidates: list[Candidate], now: datetime | None = None) -> list[Candidate]:
    now = now or datetime.now(timezone.utc)

    def score(item: Candidate) -> float:
        age_days = max((now - item.published_at).total_seconds() / 86400, 0)
        recency = exp(-age_days / 180)
        citation = 1.0 if item.has_citation_span else 0.0
        return (
            0.30 * item.lexical
            + 0.30 * item.semantic
            + 0.20 * recency
            + 0.15 * item.authority
            + 0.05 * citation
        )

    return sorted(candidates, key=score, reverse=True)

The exact weights are provisional. Log every component, the selected source_id, and the final citation so a failed answer can be replayed. A 429 from a provider is a control-flow event: back off, honor Retry-After, and keep the user request bounded by a deadline.

A bounded two-stage request in Python

The following example keeps discovery and retrieval separate. It searches the public web for candidate release notes, then queries a named vector collection for internal copies. It uses one timeout budget and exponential backoff; no provider key is embedded in the source.

import os
import time
from typing import Any

import requests


BASE_URL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"


def post_json(path: str, payload: dict[str, Any], deadline: float) -> dict[str, Any]:
    key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
    headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {key}", "Content-Type": "application/json"}
    delay = 0.5
    while True:
        remaining = deadline - time.monotonic()
        if remaining <= 0:
            raise TimeoutError("retrieval deadline exceeded")
        response = requests.request(
            method="POST",
            url=f"https://api.infrai.cc/v1{path}",
            headers=headers,
            json=payload,
            timeout=min(remaining, 8.0),
        )
        if response.status_code == 429:
            retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
            wait = float(retry_after) if retry_after else delay
            time.sleep(min(wait, max(remaining, 0)))
            delay = min(delay * 2, 8.0)
            continue
        if not response.ok:
            raise RuntimeError(f"retrieval failed ({response.status_code}): {response.text}")
        return response.json()


def retrieve(question: str) -> tuple[dict[str, Any], dict[str, Any]]:
    deadline = time.monotonic() + 10.0
    web = post_json("/web/search", {"query": question}, deadline)
    vector = post_json(
        "/vector/query",
        {"collection": "tenant-changelog", "query": question, "limit": 20},
        deadline,
    )
    return web, vector


if __name__ == "__main__":
    web_results, vector_results = retrieve("Python 3.13 deprecation in package acme-sdk")
    print({"web": web_results, "vector": vector_results})

The payload fields should be checked against the current discovery schema before production rollout. The important architectural property is the boundary: web results are candidates, while the tenant collection supplies durable metadata and citation context. Keep raw documents in a storage system whose region, retention, deletion API, and processor terms meet your contract; route only the minimum text needed for ranking.

Infrai is a practical fit when a team wants this wiring behind one plain REST API and a self-describing discovery surface: GET /v1/discovery exposes capabilities, schemas, and runnable examples, so adding a retrieval stage does not require installing another SDK. The same key and consistent interface across backend capabilities also reduce integration bookkeeping. That is an operational benefit, not proof that the service is your data processor of record.

Where the alternatives fit

No single backend wins every trust review. Here is the decision I would put in an architecture record:

Option Strength for changelog retrieval Boundary or trade-off
Elasticsearch Mature lexical ranking, filters, and self-managed deployment choices You own cluster operations, patching, and residency configuration
OpenSearch Open-source distribution with familiar inverted-index and vector features Compatibility and managed-service terms vary by provider
Pinecone Managed vector index with a focused operational surface Confirm region, retention, and deletion guarantees for your tenant contract
Weaviate Hybrid search and schema-oriented objects More platform concepts to govern when the bot needs only a narrow index
Infrai Self-describing REST discovery plus a single integration surface for web and vector stages A specialist search or storage provider may be better for contractual residency controls

The catch is important: stick with a regional Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Pinecone, or Weaviate deployment when legal or procurement requires a processor agreement and deletion evidence that your chosen runtime does not provide. Infrai should be the option to try for the retrieval orchestration layer when transparent discovery and a consistent HTTP integration matter; it should not be used as a substitute for a specialist provider's residency contract.

Ship the eval gate with the index

Before rollout, replay the labeled questions after every re-index. Check that deleted release notes no longer appear, that an updated page has one canonical chunk, and that each answer can point to a source span. Set hard limits for candidate count, query time, and retries; a slow upstream source must not block the user flow.

The eval set should include awkward cases: a package with two releases on the same day, a changelog edited after publication, a superseded security notice, and a question whose answer is “no matching release.” Record the query, candidate IDs, score components, selected span, and policy version. That trace lets a reviewer distinguish a ranking error from a missing document, and it gives you a concrete regression test when the ingestion job changes.

I have found the most useful dashboard is small: recall@20, citation precision, stale-result rate, deletion lag, and p95 retrieval time. Do not collapse those into one vanity score. A bot can improve recall while quietly returning older citations, which is a trust regression even if the language model sounds fluent.

I'm not sure a single global recency half-life will survive every ecosystem. Keep it configurable, record the version of the ranking policy, and inspect misses by package and release age. I've seen enough retrieval reviews to know that a tidy score can hide a messy contract. The useful artifact is a trace, not a confidence adjective; don't ship on confidence wording alone.

If this boundary fits your system, start by checking the vector discovery and retrieval guidance and verify the live schema before wiring it into production.

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401

title: Your voice agent sounds right. Did it place the right order?
description:
Here is a Hinglish call to a restaurant voice agent:

caller:  Do paneer wrap... actually ek hi karo. Bina pyaaz. Aur ek mango lassi.
agent:   2 Paneer Wrap add kar diya. Paneer Wrap 1 kar diya. Paneer Wrap No onion kar diya.
         1 Mango Lassi add kar diya. Aur kuch?
caller:  Bas itna hi, thanks.
agent:   Aapka order: 1 Paneer Wrap, No onion; 1 Mango Lassi. Order place ho gaya, shukriya!

The agent read back one wrap without onion. This is what it committed:

Field Expected Actual Result
Submitted orders 1 1 Pass
Paneer Wrap quantity 1 2 Fail
Paneer Wrap · Onion No onion With onion Fail
Mango Lassi quantity 1 1 Pass

A transcript-based test, or an LLM judge reading the conversation, passes this call. The customer gets two wraps with onion.

What I built

IndicOrderBench is an open-source benchmark and CI gate for voice ordering agents. It compares the committed backend state against each scenario's acceptable end states, in English and Hinglish, instead of grading the words the agent said.

The single-file HTML report from the fixed reference agent. The failing run of the same scenario is the one that catches the wrong order.

The hard failures it targets aren't accent or latency. They're mid-sentence corrections ("two... actually one"), modifiers ("no onion"), cancellations and duplicate submissions, especially in code-mixed speech where number words and negations don't look like English.

pip install indicorderbench

iob demo --out demo-out     # buggy vs fixed reference agent, no network, no keys
iob run starter --agent builtin:correct --tag smoke --trials 3

A run writes results.json (every transcript, tool call and backend snapshot), junit.xml for any CI system, and a single-file report.html that opens from file://. The exit code is non-zero when an agent change starts placing wrong orders, so the build fails before a customer sees it.

You can connect your agent in-process from Python, or over an HTTP adapter. The sandbox backend hands you JSON-schema tool definitions to give your LLM.

Scope

It's small and deterministic on purpose: reproducible runs, no API keys for the demo. It's an early benchmark, not a leaderboard of production systems.

Repo (Apache-2.0): https://github.com/Lingikaushikreddy/indicorderbench
PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/indicorderbench/

If you've seen a voice agent fail in a way this doesn't cover, open an issue with the transcript. Scenarios are easy to add.

title: ScienceBuddy-PV: A Verifier-Governed Recursive Improvement Protocol for Panvascular Intervention Research
description:
arXiv:2610.14523v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: ScienceBuddy-PV adapts the ScienceBuddy recursive-in-recursive design to panvascular intervention research through a structured evidence ledger, device-vessel ontology, abstention contract and retained failure bank. Recursive harness optimization and outer-loop model learning, including reinforcement learning, are specified but not executed. We audit a fixed component, rather than the complete agent system, using separate ARCADE syntax and stenosis tasks (1,000 training, 200 validation and 300 test images per task). A shared task-masked convolutional model was trained once per representation setting; its parameters and the heuristic support gate were then held fixed, with the stenosis threshold selected on validation data. On the locked test sets, syntax Dice was 0.475 (95% CI 0.459-0.490) and stenosis Dice was 0.231 (95% CI 0.214-0.249). Stenosis pixel AUROC was 0.957 and AUPRC was 0.180 at prevalence 0.00975. The gate accepted 76.7% of stenosis-frame outputs versus 100% for a score-only comparator. In a constructed mask audit, it accepted 44.3% of reference candidates and rejected 55.7%, exposing the cost of abstention. Acceptance does not establish correctness or clinical safety. This public-data component audit makes support and abstention measurable and provides a reproducible protocol for future collaborative agent studies. It does not demonstrate recursive improvement, patient-level validity or clinical device recommendations.

title: Scheduling Stale-Reservation Webhooks — Follow-Up Tasks One Hour Later, Queue or Cron
description:
Short answer: put each reservation's one-hour follow-up in a delayed queue message, then make the consumer idempotent; use cron for a periodic sweep, not for one cron row per reservation.

That choice follows the delivery guarantee you actually need. A reservation is an event with a due time, not a recurring calendar rule. When the hold expires, the worker should re-check the reservation state, emit the webhook if it is still stale, and record that it did so. The scheduling mechanism only gets the work near the right time.

What should a Node.js team schedule for a one-hour webhook hold?

Think in two clocks. The first is the business clock: expires_at = created_at + 3600. The second is the delivery clock: when a worker receives a message and can make the follow-up request. A delayed message joins those clocks without creating a scheduler object for every row. A cron sweep can also work, but it introduces a scan interval and another place to coordinate locks.

The timer is not the business decision.

For a reservation that was created at 12:00, publish an event with a 3,600-second delay. At 13:00, the consumer loads the reservation and checks a version or state transition. If the customer already confirmed payment, the message becomes a no-op. If the hold is still open, the consumer sends the webhook using a stable event id and commits the completion before acknowledging the message.

That last sentence matters more than the word “delayed.” Standard queues are at-least-once. A retry can deliver the same message twice, so the webhook side effect needs a unique key such as reservation_id:hold-expired:v3. Delivery is not exactly-once just because the timer looked precise.

Here is the smallest publish boundary. The request body fields shown are the queue contract used by this example; the public discovery record is the place to verify the current schema before shipping.

import json
import os
import time
import requests

BASE = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"


def publish_expiry(queue_name: str, reservation_id: str) -> dict:
    body = {
        "queue": queue_name,
        "message": {
            "reservation_id": reservation_id,
            "event_id": f"{reservation_id}:hold-expired:v3",
        },
        "delay_seconds": 3600,
    }
    for attempt in range(5):
        response = requests.post(
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/publish",
            headers={
                "Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['INFRAI_API_KEY']}",
                "Content-Type": "application/json",
                "Idempotency-Key": body["message"]["event_id"],
            },
            json=body,
            timeout=10,
        )
        if response.status_code == 429 and attempt < 4:
            retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
            time.sleep(float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2**attempt)
            continue
        if not response.ok:
            raise RuntimeError(response.text)
        return response.json()
    raise RuntimeError("unreachable")

The retry loop is intentionally boring. It honors Retry-After, uses an idempotency key, and surfaces non-429 responses instead of treating every HTTP response as success. A one-hour delay is below the seven-day delayed-message limit, and the message is small enough to stay well below the 256KB body cap.

Queue messages, cron sweeps, and specialist schedulers

The comparison is less about brand names than failure boundaries. Before looking at the alternatives, Infrai is a concrete fit for the trigger-and-buffer slice: its public discovery endpoint exposes schemas and runnable examples. Infrai gives this flow one key and one bill for queue, cron, and adjacent backend capabilities instead of another credential rotation path; its one platform spans 295 routes across 20 modules, so the same convention can cover a storage reference or an observability hook without another SDK family. That removes integration friction without changing the reservation state machine.

Here is how I would evaluate the common choices for this reservation flow:

Option Best fit Delivery and operating trade-off
Delayed queue message One follow-up per webhook event Natural per-event delay; at-least-once consumption requires idempotent handling
Cron plus database sweep Holds longer than seven days or a recovery pass Fewer delayed messages, but every run scans due rows and must claim them safely
Celery beat/worker Python teams already operating Celery Mature task routing, with broker and worker operations to own
BullMQ Node.js teams invested in Redis Good queue ergonomics, but Redis durability and topology become part of the design
Temporal Multi-step workflows, timers, and joins Strong workflow model, with a larger platform and programming model than this job needs

Creating a cron entry per reservation is the awkward middle. It turns a one-off event into scheduler configuration, creates cleanup work when a reservation is canceled, and makes a burst of reservations look like a burst of schedule mutations. Cron is still useful: one job every five minutes can sweep long waits, repair missed records, or enqueue work after an outage. It just should not be the primary row-level timer here.

The catch is that a queue is not a workflow engine. There is no native DAG, debounce, throttle, or fan-out join in this boundary. If expiry must wait for three independent services and then aggregate their results, Temporal or Airflow is a better fit. If your team already has Redis and BullMQ expertise, that operational context can outweigh a hosted REST surface. Your mileage may vary when the queue is not the largest integration cost.

How do delivery limits change the Node.js design?

The seven-day delay ceiling defines a clean split. For a 30-day reservation, write expires_at to your database and let a recurring cron sweep claim due rows, then publish ordinary queue messages. In PostgreSQL, FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED is a practical way to let several sweep workers claim different rows without holding a global lock. The queue remains the execution buffer; the database remains the source of long-lived time.

Large webhook bodies need the same separation. Store the payload in private object storage and put only a reference, reservation id, and event id in the message. A 256KB message cap and a 30-day maximum retention make a queue a poor archive. Acknowledgement deletes the message, and there is no Kafka-style replay or multiple consumer-group history to rescue an underspecified audit trail.

Cron has edges too. A cron task can run for at most 900 seconds and calls a public HTTP URL; it does not host your application code. For a long reconciliation, have cron trigger a queue publish and let workers do the work. A paused cron does not replay missed triggers, and trigger timing has second-level jitter. Those are acceptable properties for a sweep, not guarantees for a payment ledger.

I once assumed “the timer fired” meant “the follow-up happened.” It did not. The useful audit record was the reservation state transition and the idempotency key, not the scheduler's run log, whose stored output is limited to the first 4KB. Keep those records in your database. In a real incident review, I would want to answer which worker claimed the row, which downstream status code arrived, and whether a retry reused the same event id; a timestamp in a cron dashboard cannot answer all three, so the database record and webhook receipt belong in the same trace.

That is the operational boundary.

Where does a single REST boundary help?

Infrai is a reasonable option when the queue and cron are only two pieces of a small backend. Its public discovery surface describes a capability's method, path, schemas, and runnable examples, so a team can inspect the scheduling contract before installing an SDK. The practical advantage is one plain REST API and one credential boundary: swapping the service behind a capability does not force a rewrite of the reservation code's interface. The supporting benefit is that queue and cron can share that same key and billing boundary while the application stays in Python, Node.js, or another language.

I would recommend trying Infrai for the trigger-and-buffer portion when you want a self-describing HTTP contract, have a public worker endpoint, and do not need workflow joins or replayable streams. Keep a specialist queue or workflow platform when those semantics are the product requirement, not incidental infrastructure. Infrai does not make an internal endpoint public, and it does not remove the need for consumer idempotency.

The decision rule is short: delayed queue messages for one-off holds, cron for recurring sweeps and long horizons, and a workflow engine for dependencies. Measure the state transition, not just the scheduled timestamp.

If that boundary matches your system, start with the queue capability discovery and verify the request schema before wiring the producer.

References

  • Infrai capability index
  • Infrai queue discovery
  • Celery introduction
  • BullMQ guide
  • Temporal documentation
  • PostgreSQL SELECT documentation

title: From Existing Methods to New Research Ideas: Two Perspectives on Recursive Self-Improvement
description:
arXiv:2610.14625v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) offers a route to AI systems that participate in their own continued development. Recent methods allow language agents to retain changes to their parameters, memory, skills, and code for subsequent execution and improvement. We examine how these methods can inform new research ideas through two complementary perspectives. First, we introduce a unified taxonomy with nine design dimensions organized into four groups: update targets, update organization, update schedule and scope, feedback and selection. This taxonomy places existing methods in a shared design space, where examining individual dimensions and their interactions can inspire new research ideas. Second, we examine how existing RSI methods draw on traditional deep learning, for example through optimization, regularization, data augmentation, continual learning, and adversarial learning. We develop further ideas by examining more specific learning mechanisms and drawing on evolutionary computation. We also review how existing benchmarks assess self-improvement under online, offline, and offline-to-online settings. Together, these perspectives help researchers develop new RSI research ideas from existing designs and learning mechanisms. RSI papers and resources are available at https://prism-shadow.github.io/awesome-rsi/.

title: Historical-Feature Residual Adaptation for Sequential Screening
description:
arXiv:2610.19315v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Sequential screening policies must use acquired feedback effectively under a fixed experiment budget. We study acquisition-time residual adaptation: a small ranking correction built from fixed historical features and anchored to base scores recorded before feedback is revealed. The interface accepts a history-conditioned scorer and a candidate feature table; its primary instantiation augments AssayFormer's ten-dimensional representation with 64 historical directions while retaining the pretrained model. In retrospective evaluation on 20 official-test screens from 15 recorded sources, a comparison fixed before target-outcome access increased source-macro fraction of hits recovered from 22.58% to 28.61%, exceeding all six prespecified comparators. A same-feature ordinary ranking head achieved 25.73%. Supplementary strong logistic, rank-fusion, and unprojected controls achieved 26.42%, 26.02%, and 26.78%, respectively. A separate model-independent pilot on 13 reused development screens reconstructs the features without AssayFormer assets. Across three seeds, residual adaptation improves random-forest hit recovery from 28.87% to 31.27%, while logistic recovery changes from 30.22% to 29.78%. The results show effective pretrained-policy adaptation and useful transfer to an independent nonlinear base, with gains that depend on the base model.

title: Node.js GDPR-Friendly App Logging: Hosted Services, Deletion, Retention, and Export APIs
description:
The least complex workable design is to keep personal data out of operational logs, attach a pseudonymous subject reference when correlation is unavoidable, and send the re-identification map to a system built for deletion. Short answer: for an EU-facing logistics app, use a mature hosted log service when per-user erasure, retention controls, or bulk export are hard requirements. A centralized ingest-and-search API can cover ordinary debugging, but it should not become the system of record for data-subject workflows unless those controls exist.

The page arrives at 02:17: “dispatch-agent completion rate below threshold.” On-call can see that 73 route-planning jobs started, 69 completed, and four have no terminal event. They can also see each AI loop's duration and attributed model cost. What they must not need to see is a driver's name, email address, street address, or raw prompt. The useful incident key is agent_run_id; the compliance liability is everything copied around it.

That distinction determines the architecture before vendor selection does.

What should have fired before the completion-rate page?

The earlier signal is not “many errors.” It is an age invariant: every accepted planning job must reach exactly one durable terminal state within the service-level window. A job can fail without emitting an exception, and a worker can disappear after acknowledging work. Error-count alerts miss both cases.

The alert path therefore starts with a scheduler or queue monitor that knows which jobs should exist. Infrai has no alert or notification route and no synthetic or heartbeat monitoring, so a team using its centralized log ingest and search must pair it with a heartbeat service such as Healthchecks or run its own polling alert. It also does not provide distributed trace queries or a span tree; trace_id and span_id in logs are correlation fields, not a tracing backend.

This matters during triage. The page should contain a runbook link, the violated invariant, the evaluation window, and a query key. It should not dump the last prompt into a notification. An operator first checks the authoritative job state, then uses agent_run_id to find the corresponding log events and cost records.

No log line is proof that a job completed.

The database transition is.

How should I compare GDPR-friendly hosted app logging services?

There are two defensible architectures for this workload. Both need the same invariants: retries cannot create a second logical job; every run has one stable identifier; cost and latency attach to that identifier; and personal data is excluded or tokenized before it crosses the logging boundary.

Shape Operational invariant Good fit Boundary that decides it
Specialist observability stack The logging vendor owns search, retention policy, compliance export, and subject-deletion workflow Regulated production logs and established audit pipelines Choose only after verifying deletion granularity, export completeness, EU processing terms, and retention configuration
Split control plane The job database owns identity and completion; a narrow log API receives pseudonymous events; a separate monitor pages on missing work Moderate log volume and teams minimizing backend integrations The log store must remain disposable because it is not the erasure or archive authority

The first shape is the conservative choice when logs may contain personal data. Evaluate Datadog, Better Stack, Axiom, and Elastic against a written test plan rather than a feature-page checklist: create a subject's events, change retention, delete that subject's records, export the required interval, and preserve evidence that the workflow ran. The supplied requirement is the judge. A product that cannot pass the deletion test is unsuitable even if its search is excellent.

The second shape can deliberately include Infrai for everyday ingest and search. One key. One wallet. One bill. Infrai provides one API key and consolidated billing across 295 routes in 20 backend modules, replacing the pile of vendor credentials and invoices that otherwise needs reconciling at month end. It directly reduces credential sprawl in a small on-call rotation. Infrai's API is genuinely self-describing, and its public discovery surface requires no key; it returns request and response schemas, billing information, and runnable examples. That is useful when a team wants to validate an integration before adding it to the dispatch path.

Teams running moderate-volume, pseudonymized logistics logs should try Infrai for the search-and-debug slice when consolidating backend credentials and integration surfaces matters. Keep compliance deletion and archival outside that slice. There is no per-user log deletion API, no bulk export or subscription API, and no exposed retention configuration entry point. Those are design boundaries, not backlog assumptions.

Instrument the AI loop at the state transition

Instrument four moments: accepted, model call finished, terminal state committed, and abandoned-by-deadline. The model-call event records latency_ms and cost_usd returned by the AI surface, associated with agent_run_id. Do not derive cost by scraping prose from a log message. Infrai specifies per-call cost, vendor, latency, cache status, and request ID metadata on its native envelope; its OpenAI-compatible surface also exposes cost and latency metadata.

The application is Node.js, but the operational probe below is Go because a static runbook binary is easy to execute from a bastion or a scheduled diagnostic job. It calls the real log search route without inventing filters: the route's discovery parameters do not declare any. The probe reads the key from the environment, sets the HTTP method, retries a 429 using Retry-After when present, and returns non-success bodies to the operator instead of printing a false green result.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

const searchURL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/logs/search"

func retryDelay(header string, attempt int) time.Duration {
    if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(header); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
        return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
    }
    return time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
}

func searchLogs(client *http.Client, key string) ([]byte, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, searchURL, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            time.Sleep(retryDelay(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"), attempt))
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("log search returned %s: %s", resp.Status, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("log search remained rate limited after 4 attempts")
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
        os.Exit(2)
    }
    body, err := searchLogs(&http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}, key)
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    fmt.Println(string(body))
}

This probe is diagnostic, not the alert itself. Since no search filters are declared in discovery, it deliberately sends none; pretending that a convenient agent_run_id parameter exists would make the runbook brittle. In production, cost_usd and latency_ms must come from model response metadata, while the terminal outcome must come from committed application state. The ingestion-side allowlist should admit fields such as event, agent_run_id, shipment_ref, latency_ms, cost_usd, outcome, and occurred_at, while rejecting email, driver_name, address, prompt, and response. A random shipment_ref can be resolved through the separately controlled application database when access is authorized; deleting that mapping breaks the link without pretending the log vendor has performed per-user erasure.

Retries need the same discipline. A worker retries with the original agent_run_id; the database enforces one terminal transition; duplicate telemetry is tolerated and deduplicated downstream by event identity. This is the idempotency reflex that prevents an observability retry from looking like a second paid model run.

How the hosted options differ at this boundary

Datadog is the broad-suite candidate: evaluate it when logs need to sit beside metrics, traces, and an established incident workflow. Axiom is the focused analytical candidate for teams that want to interrogate event data and should be tested against the same deletion and export script. Better Stack is the candidate when logs and on-call workflow need to be assessed together. Elastic deserves a place when control over the storage and operating model outweighs the work of running or managing the stack.

Those are evaluation lanes, not claims that every plan or deployment mode supplies the required GDPR control. Product behavior, region availability, retention limits, and APIs change. Record the exact plan, region, and API tested in the data-protection impact assessment, then rerun the test before renewal.

Infrai occupies a narrower lane. Centralized ingest and search cover routine debugging, and its 295 routes across 20 modules can consolidate credentials beyond logging. The trade-off is sharp: it has no per-user deletion, bulk export, subscription, native alert notification, synthetic monitoring, source-map decoding, crash symbolication, or Session Replay. If any of those is part of the acceptance criteria, select a specialist that demonstrates it or build an explicitly owned adjacent system.

This is why the comparison cannot be reduced to query speed or price. The relevant cost is the amount of operational state the team must own when a driver invokes a data right or an auditor requests a bounded export.

Thresholds create their own incident load

Set the missing-job threshold from the contractual completion window, queue delay, and a measured safety margin. Do not copy a percentile from a web-performance guide into a batch workflow. A logistics planner that normally takes minutes and a synchronous customer request have different failure semantics.

Start the alert in shadow mode. Count pages that would have fired, label each as actionable or expected delay, and only then enable paging. A threshold that catches every slow run but wakes someone for normal carrier API variance is not conservative; it spends attention until the real silent failure is ignored.

There is a second false positive to avoid. Search lag is not job failure. Page from the scheduler or durable job state, then use logs as evidence. If the logging service is unavailable, the agent loop should continue and the shipper should retry with bounded storage; observability must not become a new dependency in the dispatch path.

The final decision rule is plain: choose the specialist-stack shape when deletion, retention configuration, or export must be performed inside the log platform. Choose the split control plane when logs are pseudonymous, moderate in volume, and operational search is the goal. In both cases, prove the alert from the state machine and prove the GDPR workflow with test data before production traffic arrives.

Further reading

  • Datadog data security and privacy documentation
  • Better Stack logs documentation
  • Axiom documentation
  • Elastic data lifecycle management documentation
  • Healthchecks documentation
  • ClickHouse documentation
  • Core Web Vitals definitions and percentile guidance
  • Infrai app logging comparison guide

If this split boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai app logging guide and verify the discovery schema before wiring the shipper.

title: Four pay-per-result YouTube and Google News scrapers on Apify (no API key)
description:
I built four small data tools on Apify that return YouTube and Google News data as JSON, without an API key or quota. You pay per result delivered, and nothing else. Here is what each one does and how to call it from Python.

The four tools

  1. YouTube Transcript Extractor - timestamped transcripts for videos, playlists and channels, with optional chunks sized for RAG. Videos without captions are reported and not charged. $0.004 per transcript. https://apify.com/xargaar_tools/youtube-transcript-extractor-batch
  2. YouTube Comments Scraper - comments (and optionally replies) with author, likes, reply count and publish time. $0.0015 per comment. https://apify.com/xargaar_tools/youtube-comments-scraper-fast
  3. YouTube Search Scraper - search results with title, channel, views, duration, publish date and thumbnail, with upload date and duration filters. $0.002 per video. https://apify.com/xargaar_tools/youtube-search-video-scraper
  4. Google News Scraper with Full Article Text - news results for a keyword, language and country, with the full article text pulled from the publisher page when it can be extracted. $0.003 per headline, $0.01 per article with text. https://apify.com/xargaar_tools/google-news-scraper-article-text

YouTube blocks datacenter IPs, so the YouTube tools run through a residential proxy by default. That cost is already in the per-result price.

Calling one from Python 

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient("YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN")
run = client.actor("xargaar_tools/youtube-comments-scraper-fast").call(run_input={
    "startUrls": ["https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dQw4w9WgXcQ"],
    "maxCommentsPerVideo": 50,
})
for item in client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items():
    print(item["likes"], item["author"], item["text"][:80])

Swap the Actor name and input to use the others. Every Actor has an input form in the Apify console if you prefer clicking to coding.

What I tested

I ran each Actor on Apify's platform before publishing. Transcripts: 11 of 12 test videos returned a transcript, a private video was reported cleanly instead of failing the run. Comments: 45 comments from one video, replies mode, and a channel URL across two videos. Search: two queries returned 80 videos, and the date and duration filters changed the results as expected. News: 10 results, 6 with full article text.

Known limits

  • Comments come back in YouTube's top-comments order. A "newest first" sort is not supported yet.
  • The search tool applies one filter per query (upload date or duration).
  • News articles behind paywalls or bot protection return the headline data without full text.

If something breaks or you need a field that is missing, open an issue on the Actor page and I will look at it.

Xargaar Tools builds small, pay-per-use data tools.

title: HyrCap: Hybrid Rank-Calibration of Action Proposals for Temporal Event Understanding
description:
arXiv:2610.19526v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Temporal action detection in long untrimmed videos suffers from inaccurate localization and low-quality proposals, especially with sparse annotations and ambiguous boundaries. For open-ended video understanding and LLM-driven event analysis, reliable proposals connect temporal localization, event annotation, and semantic understanding. However, conventional temporal action detection (TAD) pipelines lack explicit modeling of proposal localization quality, cross-representation support, and inter-proposal relations. We propose Hybrid Rank-Calibration of Action Proposals (HyrCap), a proposal-centric query-based TAD framework for temporal event understanding. Hybrid combines complementary video features with different localization cues, while Rank-Calibration adjusts proposal ranking confidence to reflect localization reliability and candidate competition. HyrCap treats dense query-based predictions as an over-complete temporal event hypothesis space. Cross-Representation Consensus Calibration, Localization Quality Estimation, and Proposal Redundancy Suppression improve proposal ranking reliability, localization quality, and candidate discrimination. Inspired by LLMs' capabilities in fine-grained semantic recognition, event description, and reasoning, we introduce HyrCap for Semantic Action Understanding, using calibrated proposals for standard TAD and as inputs to LLM-based semantic understanding. We define a staged evaluation protocol to separately measure event localization, segment-level semantic understanding, and combined event understanding performance. Experiments on public benchmarks show that HyrCap achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple metrics and provides a finer-grained paradigm and evaluation protocol for query-based event segmentation and annotation.

title: Apple is testing a black and white icon for Apple Music in iOS 18.2
description:
Apple Music is refreshing its visual identity by replacing its 13-year-old red icon with a black-and-white design, as observed in iOS 27.2 beta 4.

The update introduces a slightly tilted logo, oval-shaped notes, a drop shadow, and dark mode variants, alongside removing red accents from widgets and the app interface.

The new icon retains the classic note shape, but is slightly tilted to the left, has more oval notes, and a subtle shadow. The company also created a dark version with a white design on a black background, as well as options with a transparent or colored appearance. Along with removing the red color from the icon, Apple also removed red from the widgets on the home screen, and changed the interior color of the app from red and pink to blue.

Reactions from users on social media have been mostly negative. Many have called the new look boring and uninteresting, arguing that the change was unnecessary, although there have also been some users who found the change positive.

As the app is still in the testing phase, Apple reserves the right to change its mind before the final version is released.

title: Weighted Ensemble Sampling for Rare-Event Estimation in Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.19202v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Rare but severe failures of large language models can become practically significant at deployment scale. Estimating their probabilities with direct Monte Carlo sampling is highly inefficient, while proposal-based methods typically require auxiliary learning of an additional proposal distribution. We introduce \textbf{Weighted Ensemble (WE)}, a training-free framework for rare-event estimation in language models. WE samples exclusively from the original language model and improves upon direct Monte Carlo by periodically reallocating the sampling budget toward prefixes that appear more likely to reach the target rare event. To guide this reallocation without learning a separate proposal distribution, we exploit internal LLM representations as prefix-level signals and empirically validate their effectiveness. We provide a theoretical analysis of the proposed algorithm. Experiments on safety-related tasks spanning both small-scale and modern large-scale LLMs demonstrate that WE improves the efficiency and reliability of rare-event probability estimation.

title: LAMP: 3D Source-Aware Lighting Estimation at Multiple Points
description:
arXiv:2610.19266v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Existing illumination estimation methods primarily recover lighting distributions for rendering, but typically leave the contributions of individual physical light sources at specific scene locations implicit. We address this gap by leveraging the scene understanding capabilities of vision-language models (VLMs) to connect local illumination with its physical sources. We introduce LAMP, a framework for point-conditioned, source-aware illumination reasoning from a single RGB image with marked query points. LAMP constructs a shared inventory of active light sources, ranks contributing sources for each query, and predicts their 3D query-to-source directions. We supervise these relationships using procedurally controlled indoor scenes, reusing independently rendered source responses to derive contribution targets across lighting configurations and obtaining exact directions from source and query positions. On the Infinigen test set, fine-tuning Qwen3-VL-8B increases dominant-source 3D PCK@0.5m from 0% to 70.6%, with 94.5% of directions within 12.5 degrees of ground truth among correctly localized sources. Combined with a lightweight network predicting dense RGB irradiance, LAMP achieves probe-rendering quality comparable to prior lighting-estimation methods while additionally localizing individual physical sources in 3D and explicitly attributing local illumination to them.

title: MySQL GROUP_CONCAT with ORDER BY, SEPARATOR and DISTINCT (Tested on 8.4)
description:
To join several rows into one string per group in MySQL, use GROUP_CONCAT() with GROUP BY. The order and the separator go inside the brackets: GROUP_CONCAT(subject ORDER BY subject SEPARATOR ', '). Add DISTINCT straight after the opening bracket to drop duplicates. Two things catch people out: NULL values are skipped silently, and the result is cut off at group_concat_max_len, which is 1,024 bytes by default, with only a warning to tell you.

I ran every query in this post on MySQL 8.4.6 on 11 October 2026, with the default sql_mode (which includes ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY), and pasted the real output under each one. Everything below is copy-and-paste ready: create the two tables, insert the rows and run each query in order. If you run your queries from PHP, my guide to PDO fetch() and fetchAll() shows how to read the results back.

The sample tables

The examples use two small tables: students and the subjects they’ve taken, with an optional score. I’ve deliberately included a duplicate (Chloe took Biology twice), a NULL score and a row with a NULL subject, because that’s where GROUP_CONCAT behaves in surprising ways.

CREATE TABLE students (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(40), class VARCHAR(10));
CREATE TABLE subjects (student_id INT, subject VARCHAR(40), score INT NULL);

INSERT INTO students VALUES
  (1,'Ayesha','10A'), (2,'Ben','10A'), (3,'Chloe','10B'), (4,'Dev','10B');

INSERT INTO subjects VALUES
  (1,'Maths',91), (1,'Physics',84), (1,'English',77),
  (2,'History',68), (2,'Maths',73),
  (3,'Biology',88), (3,'Maths',NULL), (3,'Biology',90),
  (4,NULL,NULL);

Basic GROUP_CONCAT: one row per group

GROUP_CONCAT() is an aggregate function, like COUNT() or SUM(). The MySQL aggregate function reference describes it simply as “return a concatenated string”. You group the rows, and it glues each group’s values together.

SELECT s.name, GROUP_CONCAT(sub.subject) AS subjects
FROM students s
JOIN subjects sub ON sub.student_id = s.id
GROUP BY s.id, s.name
ORDER BY s.id;

+--------+-----------------------+
| name   | subjects              |
+--------+-----------------------+
| Ayesha | Maths,Physics,English |
| Ben    | History,Maths         |
| Chloe  | Biology,Maths,Biology |
| Dev    | NULL                  |
+--------+-----------------------+

Notice three things. The default separator is a comma with no space. The order inside each list isn’t guaranteed; here it happens to follow insertion order, but you shouldn’t rely on that. And Dev’s only subject is NULL, so his whole result is NULL.

GROUP_CONCAT with ORDER BY and SEPARATOR

To control the order of values inside each string, put ORDER BY inside the function call. To change the separator, add SEPARATOR after it. Both are part of GROUP_CONCAT’s own syntax, separate from the query’s outer ORDER BY.

SELECT s.name,
       GROUP_CONCAT(sub.subject ORDER BY sub.subject SEPARATOR ', ') AS subjects
FROM students s
JOIN subjects sub ON sub.student_id = s.id
GROUP BY s.id, s.name
ORDER BY s.id;

+--------+-------------------------+
| name   | subjects                |
+--------+-------------------------+
| Ayesha | English, Maths, Physics |
| Ben    | History, Maths          |
| Chloe  | Biology, Biology, Maths |
| Dev    | NULL                    |
+--------+-------------------------+

The outer ORDER BY s.id sorts the rows of the result. The inner ORDER BY sub.subject sorts the values within each string. You’ll often want both.

Ordering by a different column

The inner ORDER BY doesn’t have to use the column you’re concatenating. Here I list each student’s subjects best score first, with the score in brackets and a pipe as the separator:

SELECT s.name,
       GROUP_CONCAT(CONCAT(sub.subject, ' (', sub.score, ')')
                    ORDER BY sub.score DESC SEPARATOR ' | ') AS best_first
FROM students s
JOIN subjects sub ON sub.student_id = s.id
GROUP BY s.id, s.name
ORDER BY s.id;

+--------+------------------------------------------+
| name   | best_first                               |
+--------+------------------------------------------+
| Ayesha | Maths (91) | Physics (84) | English (77) |
| Ben    | Maths (73) | History (68)                |
| Chloe  | Biology (90) | Biology (88)              |
| Dev    | NULL                                     |
+--------+------------------------------------------+

Look closely at Chloe. Her Maths entry has disappeared. Its score is NULL, CONCAT() returns NULL if any argument is NULL, and GROUP_CONCAT skips NULL values. That leads us to the biggest gotcha.

Why NULL values disappear from GROUP_CONCAT

The MySQL manual states that, unless otherwise stated, aggregate functions ignore NULL values, and GROUP_CONCAT follows that rule. If every value in a group is NULL, the result is NULL rather than an empty string.

SELECT s.name, GROUP_CONCAT(sub.subject) AS subjects, COUNT(*) AS rows_in_group
FROM students s
LEFT JOIN subjects sub ON sub.student_id = s.id
WHERE s.id = 4
GROUP BY s.id, s.name;

+------+----------+---------------+
| name | subjects | rows_in_group |
+------+----------+---------------+
| Dev  | NULL     |             1 |
+------+----------+---------------+

There’s one row in the group, but its subject is NULL, so the concatenated result is NULL. Two fixes:

  • Default for the whole result: wrap it in COALESCE(GROUP_CONCAT(sub.subject), 'none'), which returned none for Dev in my test.
  • Keep NULL items visible: use COALESCE() or IFNULL() on the value inside, for example GROUP_CONCAT(CONCAT(sub.subject, ' (', COALESCE(sub.score, '-'), ')')), so Chloe’s Maths stays in the list instead of vanishing. In my test that returned Biology (90) | Biology (88) | Maths (-). Note that NULL scores sort last with DESC, which is usually what you want.

GROUP_CONCAT DISTINCT: removing duplicates

Put DISTINCT first inside the brackets to keep only unique values. You can combine it with ORDER BY and SEPARATOR:

SELECT s.name,
       GROUP_CONCAT(DISTINCT sub.subject ORDER BY sub.subject SEPARATOR ', ') AS subjects
FROM students s
JOIN subjects sub ON sub.student_id = s.id
WHERE s.id = 3
GROUP BY s.id, s.name;

+-------+----------------+
| name  | subjects       |
+-------+----------------+
| Chloe | Biology, Maths |
+-------+----------------+

Biology now appears once. If duplicate rows are a symptom of bad data rather than a legitimate repeat, fix the table instead; my post on deleting duplicate rows in MySQL covers safe ways to do that.

Custom separators: no separator, new lines and more

Any string literal works as a separator, including an empty one and escape sequences:

SELECT class,
       GROUP_CONCAT(name ORDER BY name SEPARATOR '')   AS squashed,
       GROUP_CONCAT(name ORDER BY name SEPARATOR '\n') AS one_per_line
FROM students
GROUP BY class;

+-------+-----------+--------------+
| class | squashed  | one_per_line |
+-------+-----------+--------------+
| 10A   | AyeshaBen | Ayesha
Ben   |
| 10B   | ChloeDev  | Chloe
Dev    |
+-------+-----------+--------------+

The new-line version breaks the text table, which is exactly what you want when you’re building a plain-text email or a CSV cell. Other separators I find handy are ' | ' for readable reports and ';' for exporting to spreadsheets that treat commas as column breaks.

The 1024 limit: group_concat_max_len and truncated results

This one causes real bugs in production. GROUP_CONCAT results are capped by the group_concat_max_len system variable. On my MySQL 8.4.6 server, SELECT @@group_concat_max_len; returned 1024. When a result is longer, MySQL cuts it off and raises a warning, but the query still succeeds, so your application never notices.

To demonstrate, I set a tiny limit of 20 bytes:

SET SESSION group_concat_max_len = 20;
SELECT GROUP_CONCAT(name ORDER BY id SEPARATOR ', ') AS names FROM students;
SHOW WARNINGS;

+----------------------+
| names                |
+----------------------+
| Ayesha, Ben, Chloe,  |
+----------------------+
+---------+------+---------------------------------+
| Level   | Code | Message                         |
+---------+------+---------------------------------+
| Warning | 1260 | Row 4 was cut by GROUP_CONCAT() |
+---------+------+---------------------------------+

Dev was silently dropped, and the string even ends with a stray separator. Raising the limit for the session fixes it:

SET SESSION group_concat_max_len = 1000000;
SELECT GROUP_CONCAT(name ORDER BY id SEPARATOR ', ') AS names FROM students;

+-------------------------+
| names                   |
+-------------------------+
| Ayesha, Ben, Chloe, Dev |
+-------------------------+

Practical advice:

  • Run SET SESSION group_concat_max_len = ... right after connecting, in the same connection that runs the query. It only lasts for that session.
  • If you can’t predict the size, check warnings (warning code 1260) or compare the result length with the limit.
  • If the list could be huge, ask whether you need one string at all. Fetching the rows and joining them in PHP or Python is often simpler and has no cut-off.

Top N per group with GROUP_CONCAT

MySQL’s GROUP_CONCAT has no LIMIT clause inside the brackets (MariaDB added one, MySQL hasn’t), so a common trick is to order the list and then keep the first N items with SUBSTRING_INDEX():

SELECT s.name,
       SUBSTRING_INDEX(GROUP_CONCAT(sub.subject ORDER BY sub.score DESC SEPARATOR ','), ',', 2) AS top2
FROM students s
JOIN subjects sub ON sub.student_id = s.id
WHERE s.id = 1
GROUP BY s.id, s.name;

+--------+---------------+
| name   | top2          |
+--------+---------------+
| Ayesha | Maths,Physics |
+--------+---------------+

SUBSTRING_INDEX(str, ',', 2) returns everything before the second comma. It breaks if the values themselves contain your separator, so pick one that can’t appear in the data. For anything more complex, a window function such as ROW_NUMBER() in a subquery is more robust.

GROUP_CONCAT vs JSON_ARRAYAGG

If the result is going to code rather than a human, consider JSON_ARRAYAGG(), which the MySQL manual lists as returning the result set “as a single JSON array”. You get proper quoting for free, so commas inside values can’t break your parsing:

SELECT s.name, JSON_ARRAYAGG(sub.subject) AS subjects_json
FROM students s
JOIN subjects sub ON sub.student_id = s.id
WHERE s.id IN (1, 2)
GROUP BY s.id, s.name
ORDER BY s.id;

+--------+---------------------------------+
| name   | subjects_json                   |
+--------+---------------------------------+
| Ayesha | ["Maths", "Physics", "English"] |
| Ben    | ["History", "Maths"]            |
+--------+---------------------------------+

In PHP you can json_decode() that column straight into an array. The trade-off: JSON_ARRAYAGG doesn’t accept an ORDER BY inside the brackets. When I tried JSON_ARRAYAGG(name ORDER BY name) on MySQL 8.4.6, it failed with syntax error 1064. Use GROUP_CONCAT when the order of items matters, or sort the array in your application code after decoding it.

Error 1055 and ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY

Because MySQL 8.4 enables ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY by default, every non-aggregated column in your SELECT must be in the GROUP BY or depend on it. Grouping by the primary key s.id while selecting s.name is fine, since the name depends on the id. But this query fails:

SELECT s.class, s.name, GROUP_CONCAT(sub.subject)
FROM students s
JOIN subjects sub ON sub.student_id = s.id
GROUP BY s.class;

ERROR 1055 (42000): Expression #2 of SELECT list is not in GROUP BY clause and contains
nonaggregated column 'gc_demo.s.name' which is not functionally dependent on columns in
GROUP BY clause; this is incompatible with sql_mode=only_full_group_by

Each class has several names, so MySQL can’t pick one. Either add s.name to the GROUP BY or aggregate it too, for example GROUP_CONCAT(DISTINCT s.name). Don’t switch the SQL mode off to make the error go away; it’s protecting you from random results.

When not to use GROUP_CONCAT

GROUP_CONCAT is brilliant for display: a tag list next to a blog post, a comma-separated list of products in an order summary, or a quick report you paste into a spreadsheet. It’s a poor fit when you need to filter, count or join on the individual values later. Searching inside a concatenated string with LIKE '%Maths%' is slow and matches partial words, and storing comma-separated lists in a column breaks the basic rule of one value per field. Keep the data in proper rows and only concatenate at the very end, in the query that feeds the page.

Using GROUP_CONCAT safely from PHP

If any part of the query comes from user input, such as a class name from a dropdown, bind it with a prepared statement rather than gluing it into the SQL string. My guide to PHP PDO prepared statements shows the pattern. GROUP_CONCAT itself is just another column in the result; you read it with fetch() like any other value and explode(', ', $row['subjects']) if you need an array back.

FAQ

How do I use ORDER BY inside GROUP_CONCAT?

Put it inside the brackets, after the column: GROUP_CONCAT(subject ORDER BY subject ASC). It sorts the values within each concatenated string. The query’s outer ORDER BY sorts the result rows separately.

How do I change the GROUP_CONCAT separator?

Add SEPARATOR as the last part inside the brackets: GROUP_CONCAT(subject SEPARATOR ', '). The default is a comma with no space. Use SEPARATOR '' for no separator or SEPARATOR '\n' for one value per line.

Why is my GROUP_CONCAT result cut off?

It has hit group_concat_max_len, which was 1,024 bytes by default on my MySQL 8.4 server. MySQL truncates the string and raises warning 1260. Run SET SESSION group_concat_max_len = 1000000; before the query.

Why does GROUP_CONCAT return NULL?

Every value in that group was NULL, and aggregate functions ignore NULLs. Wrap the call in COALESCE(GROUP_CONCAT(col), '') to get an empty string or a default label instead.

How do I remove duplicates in GROUP_CONCAT?

Add DISTINCT straight after the opening bracket: GROUP_CONCAT(DISTINCT subject ORDER BY subject SEPARATOR ', ').

Can I limit the number of values in GROUP_CONCAT?

Not with a LIMIT inside the function in MySQL, but you can order the values and keep the first N with SUBSTRING_INDEX(GROUP_CONCAT(col ORDER BY score DESC), ',', N). For complex cases, use ROW_NUMBER() in a subquery.

What is the difference between GROUP_CONCAT and JSON_ARRAYAGG?

GROUP_CONCAT returns a plain string with your chosen separator and supports ORDER BY and DISTINCT inside the call. JSON_ARRAYAGG returns a JSON array with proper quoting, which is safer to parse in code.

title: Unlocking Structured Pruning for Reasoning Language Models via Attention-Preserving MLP Trimming
description:
arXiv:2610.19121v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Structured pruning reduces LLM inference costs by removing model components to produce smaller dense models. However, existing methods can cause reasoning performance to collapse on long-form reasoning tasks such as AIME. We propose \textit{LayerTrim}, a training-free structured pruning method that identifies redundant decoder layers and selectively trims their MLP features while preserving attention and decoder depth. LayerTrim is the first training-free structured pruning method designed to preserve long-form reasoning without gradients or recovery training. Across three reasoning language models and five benchmarks, LayerTrim outperforms existing structured pruning methods in most evaluated settings, improving average accuracy by up to 21.4 percentage points over RESP. On \texttt{Qwen3-14B}, LayerTrim achieves 1.24$\times$ faster prefill and 19.7\% lower peak GPU memory than the dense model, while better preserving reasoning ability. It also achieves the shortest average generation length among evaluated pruned models, while retaining the highest average accuracy. These results demonstrate that LayerTrim improves reasoning efficiency through both structural compression and reduced token generation.

title: PsyMemBehav: Psychology-Informed and Memory-Grounded Two-Level Identity-to-Action Reasoning for Social-Media Behavior Simulation
description:
arXiv:2610.14570v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) support social simulation, but faithfully reproducing real users requires grounding both structured platform decisions and language in sparse, noisy behavioral evidence. We introduce PsyMemBehav, which maps psychology-informed profiles and retrieved memories to target-first platform behavior through two-level identity-to-action reasoning. To support this approach with comprehensive behavioral traces, we construct a dataset PsyMemBehav-bench from 5.57M observed behaviors of 5,862 real users (approximately 950 per user) across Reddit, Bluesky, and Twitter. Each recorded engagement is modeled as target selection followed by Comment, Like, or Repost and optional response generation. PsyMemBehav combines 41-dimensional user descriptors, top-5 BM25 memories, reverse-CoT supervision, and rubric-guided DPO over complete reasoning-action trajectories. Experiments show that PsyMemBehav 27B ranks first in 11 of 12 reported individual-level metrics, improving average response quality over GPT-5.4 from 54.28 to 59.68 (9.95% relative), and obtains the lowest group-level MAE (0.081) and MSE (0.009) among simulated systems. These results support evidence-grounded user modeling for observed-thread continuation; the benchmark remains conditional on recorded engagement and does not model no-action decisions.

title: A share link should stop working when the person who made it loses access
description:
Most apps that let you share a record by link store the link as a random token plus the record ID. Someone opens the link, the server finds the token and shows the record. The app saves who created the link, but nothing checks that person again.

This breaks when the creator's own access changes. A contractor shares a project doc with a client, then the contract ends and an admin removes them from the workspace. The link they made still opens the doc. The same thing happens when someone moves to another team and loses a folder, or when a doc is moved into a restricted space after the link was made.

Treat the link as acting for its creator. When someone opens it, check that the creator can still read the record right now, and that the link's level (view, comment or edit) is no higher than what the creator has today. If either check fails, return the same error you'd return for an unknown token, so whoever holds the link can't tell the record still exists.

When you deactivate a user, list the links they created and show them to the admin doing it. Some are fine to keep, like a public pricing sheet, and the admin can hand those to someone who still has access.

To test it, create a link as a regular user, remove that user from the workspace, then open the link in a private window. If the record loads, your links don't check their creator.

title: Deep Generative Models for Phylogenetic Inference with Complex Evolutionary Processes
description:
arXiv:2610.19053v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Inference of phylogenetic trees from sequences plays a central role in understanding evolutionary relationships, with applications ranging from tracking pathogen spread to reconstructing the history of life. Conventionally, practitioners obtain posteriors over trees using likelihood-based methods like MCMC. However, likelihoods are only available for simple evolutionary models with restrictive assumptions. For realistic evolutionary models, inference using conventional methods is prohibitively expensive, inaccurate, or even impossible. In practice, practitioners settle for using as flexible a conventional method as possible, even though they expect it is misspecified. In principle, we could use simulation-based inference: simulate tree and sequence data from an evolutionary model and train a neural network to predict the posterior over trees given sequences. However it is a mathematical challenge to represent and train complex posterior distributions over trees. Here we present a flexible family of conditional generative models over trees. Our models iteratively build trees using three natural paradigms -- top-down, middle-out, or bottom-up -- and are trained using a discrete diffusion framework. For real and synthetic datasets of up to $65$ taxa and $>10^5$ tokens, our models recover MCMC posteriors much more accurately than the previous state-of-the-art simulation-based method Phyloformer 2. Finally, we compare to IQ-Tree, a popular flexible-but-misspecified conventional method. Our models match its tree estimates on simple data, but on more realistic data, our method is reliably more accurate.

title: AWS Lambda durable functions increases durable operation and checkpoint payload limits
description:
Starting today, AWS Lambda durable functions increases the maximum number of durable operations per execution from 3,000 to 30,000, and the maximum checkpoint payload size from 256 KB to 1 MB. Higher operation limits let you safely do more work in a single execution including expanding iterative loops, polling for longer time periods, and building more complex rollback paths that run when a step fails. At 1 MB, checkpoint payloads match the maximum payload size of asynchronous Lambda invocations, and integration services such as Amazon SQS, and Amazon EventBridge, so a workflow can persist a full event from any of these sources in a single operation.

AWS Lambda durable functions helps you build resilient multi-step applications and AI workflows that execute for up to one year, with built-in checkpointing, automatic retries, and waits that suspend execution without incurring compute charges. Every durable operation counts toward the per-execution limit, including each step attempt, each poll of a wait-for-condition, and each branch of a parallel or map operation. With 30,000 operations, a single execution has more room to coordinate complex, multi-step workflows, iterate across thousands of items, or poll an external system for weeks, without exceeding checkpoint limits.

An agentic application can reason over thousands of model and tool calls, and with 1 MB checkpoints it persists larger conversation histories, model responses, and outputs from tools directly in the checkpoint instead of writing to external storage. For state larger than 1 MB, the JavaScript and Python SDKs include a FileSystem serializer that writes the payload to an Amazon EFS or Amazon S3 Files mount and checkpoints a pointer instead.

 The new limits apply in all AWS Regions where AWS Lambda durable functions is available. To learn more about these service limits, see the AWS Lambda developer guide.

arXiv:2610.14487v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generative recommendation models based on autoregressive decoding have been adopted as alternatives to classical ranking-based systems. While their modeling flexibility has been widely studied, their resilience to data poisoning remains largely unexplored. In this work, we ask: how susceptible are generative recommenders to conditional targeted poisoning? Under a realistic setting where an adversary can inject limited malicious interactions and query a recommendation API as a black box, our empirical study shows that generative recommenders are vulnerable: injecting fewer than 1% synthetic interactions significantly increases the likelihood of promoting malicious targets under the trigger. To characterize this vulnerability, we analyze the synthesis of malicious interactions from two perspectives: (i) decoding alignment and (ii) prefix popularity. We observe that short, context-aligned prefixes that are both common under the model's induced transition dynamics and strongly linked to a frequent trigger consistently amplify targeted promotion. Motivated by this analysis, we develop AlignPoison, a black-box framework that discovers and samples context-aligned prefixes from API outputs. We conduct experiments on benchmarks in unimodal and multimodal generative recommendation settings. Results show that these prefixes outperform competitive baselines, improving ASR lift by up to 16.3 percentage points and highlighting a decoding-dependent, context-sensitive poisoning vulnerability in generative recommendation models.

title: GBase Database(GBase 8s) Character Set Migration: From en_US.8859-1 to zh_CN.utf8
description:
Configuring the correct character set is essential when deploying GBase Database(GBase 8s) for applications that store Chinese data. If your database currently uses en_US.8859-1, you may encounter character conversion issues when inserting or retrieving Chinese text. This guide explains how to check locale settings, understand configuration limitations, and plan a safe character set migration in GBase Database(GBase 8s).

Why Does Character Set Configuration Matter?

Character set configuration affects how GBase Database(GBase 8s) stores, interprets, and exchanges text data. The single-byte encoding 8859-1 cannot represent Chinese characters directly.

For applications that require Chinese support, a compatible locale such as zh_CN.utf8 may be appropriate, provided it is supported by your GBase Database(GBase 8s) version and operating system.

Before making changes, understand three important concepts:

  • DB_LOCALE: Defines the database locale and influences character data handling.
  • CLIENT_LOCALE: Controls locale-related behavior on the client side.
  • Operating system locale: Determines which locales are available to database utilities and applications.

These settings serve different purposes. Changing a client locale does not automatically convert existing database data, and modifying instance configuration does not necessarily change the locale of an existing database.

Method 1: Check the Current Locale Configuration

Before changing anything, inspect your GBase Database(GBase 8s) environment and verify which locales are available on the server.

echo "$GBASEDBTDIR"
locale -a
onstat -

The locale -a command lists the locales available on the operating system. Check whether a UTF-8 Chinese locale is installed and note its exact name, since naming conventions vary between Linux distributions.

Next, inspect the relevant GBase Database(GBase 8s) configuration files and identify the current locale settings.

Do not immediately modify onconfig and restart the instance. First, confirm which parameters are supported by your installed version and determine whether your goal is to change the client environment, configure a new database, or migrate an existing database.

Important: Changing DB_LOCALE in an instance configuration file should not be treated as a method for converting an existing database from en_US.8859-1 to zh_CN.utf8.

Method 2: Migrate Existing Data to a UTF-8 Database

If an existing GBase Database(GBase 8s) database uses en_US.8859-1, migration to a separately prepared target database may be necessary.

The migration process should preserve both the database structure and the original data while ensuring that Chinese characters are converted correctly.

Step 1: Back Up the Source Database

Before migration, create a complete backup using a supported backup method for your GBase Database(GBase 8s) environment.

Verify that the backup is usable and prepare a rollback plan. Do not perform character set migration directly on your only production copy.

Step 2: Prepare the Target Database

Prepare a target database using a locale configuration supported by your GBase Database(GBase 8s) version.

Because database creation syntax and locale capabilities can differ by version, follow the applicable product documentation rather than assuming that a generic CREATE DATABASE statement can specify any desired character set.

Confirm the target database locale before proceeding.

Step 3: Export the Source Data

Where supported, use the database export utilities to export the source database schema and data.

For example:

dbexport old_db

Check the command output and exported files to confirm that the operation completed successfully. Review the export format and determine whether character conversion is required before importing the data.

Step 4: Import Data into the Target Database

Use a migration procedure supported by your installed GBase Database(GBase 8s) version to load the schema and data into the prepared target database.

Review table definitions, indexes, constraints, stored procedures, and other database objects during migration.
