title: Iterate on an LLM, Serve on an SLM
description:
arXiv:2610.14576v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As frontier LLMs gain more capabilities, the cost to run them also goes up. At the same time, small language models (SLMs) also gain more capabilities but have largely been able to keep their cost stable, offering 5-40 times cheaper inference for the narrow, repetitive subtasks that agents decompose work into. However, the standing limiting factor is getting the correct behavior out of a small model in a fast, efficient, and economical way. Unfortunately, in most cases, zero-shot small models fail narrow production tasks. Furthermore, retraining one every time the behavior changes is too slow to iterate on. We propose doing both in sequence. First, develop the desired behavior in prompt space, on a frontier model, with immediate feedback from live traffic. Then, once the behavior converges, distill the recorded production behavior (not synthetic imitations of it) into an SLM through supervised fine-tuning (SFT). We show a proper use case of this method through a scheduling agent for home-care agencies that fans out a single yes/no safety decision per caregiver-shift pair on GPT-5.4-nano. A LoRA-tuned Qwen3-8B trained on 11.6k recorded production decisions reaches 0.913 agreement, while the teacher (GPT-5.4-nano), re-run on its own recorded prompts, agrees with itself only 72.7% of the time, pointing to the fact that the SLM may also be more consistent. Furthermore, when the two disagreed, a blinded professional scheduler sided with the student 48-29. Finally, we find that the SLM has approximately 2.5 times lower median latency and is a fraction of the cost. We believe this lifecycle of quick building, live feedback, and cheap inference is a blueprint for others building similar systems.

title: Same config.json, different serve command: what to check before serving AREX-2
description:
When a fine-tune declares the same architecture class as a model you already serve (run behind an API on your own GPU), the tempting move is to swap --model-path and restart. BAAI's AREX-2 is a good test of that habit. It is a 27B model trained to work on a problem in rounds (propose, measure, reflect, revise), released on 29 September under Apache 2.0, not gated, and its config.json opens with Qwen3_5ForConditionalGeneration, the same class as Qwen3.8-27B from the Qwen team.

We had been serving base Qwen3.8-27B with sglang, an open-source inference server, so we diffed the two configs. One caveat first: we have not run AREX-2. Every speed below is from the base model. Tables, command and sources are in the full AREX-2 serving analysis on inferencekey.com.

The diff that says "drop-in"

BAAI shipped a clean release: layer layout, head counts, context length, vocab and vision tower all match Qwen3.8-27B. The config differs only in transformers_version and two redundant top-level keys, and chat_template.jinja, the file that formats the conversation and tool calls, is byte-identical.

Stop reading there and you ship the old command.

Check the weights, not the config

The base model carries a multi-token prediction (MTP) head, a small extra layer that guesses a few tokens ahead so the server can emit several per step. AREX-2's config still declares it. Its weight files do not contain it.

config.json                    "mtp_num_hidden_layers": 1
safetensors index (AREX-2)     0 mtp tensors
safetensors index (Qwen3.8)    15 mtp tensors

The safetensors index lists every weight tensor in the release, so it is the honest inventory. A config field is a promise; check that something actually backs it.

The second quiet change is in tokenizer_config.json, which controls how text is cut into tokens. A community repack reports that the pre-tokenizer and decoder settings differ from Qwen3.8. Likely harmless. Also what surfaces as a garbled tool call hours into an agent run.

Flags that were right for the base model

Our quickest base-model setup ran on an RTX PRO 5000 in a CUDA 13 pod, with RadixArk's NVFP4 quant (weights compressed to 4-bit floats) and the z-lab DFlash2 drafter. It decoded (wrote output) at 115 to 136 tok/s. Little of that survives the swap:

  • No NVFP4 build of AREX-2 exists yet. Today you pick from BAAI's BF16 original (54.7 GB), prithivMLmods' FP8 (35.9 GB), cyankiwi's AWQ INT4 (20.2 GB) or numsu's INT4 W4A16 (18.6 GB).
  • The drafter was trained against another model. Speculative decoding has a small drafter propose tokens that the big model then verifies in one pass; it only pays off when most guesses are accepted. z-lab's DFlash2 drafter targets base Qwen3.8-27B, and a fine-tune changes which tokens the model favors, so nobody knows its hit rate on AREX-2. numsu's INT4 card does publish speeds with a DFlash2 drafter on two RTX 3090s, but without an acceptance length.
  • mamba_ssm_dtype. AREX-2 asks for float32. Our base command forced bfloat16, fine on Qwen3.8, untried on a model tuned for long reflective runs.
  • Parsers are a guess. These sglang options turn raw model text into separate reasoning and tool-call fields. qwen3 and qwen3_coder ought to work since the template matches. No sglang run of AREX-2 has been published.
  • Pick long context or speculation. The base model's 1M context is a YARN override that stretches its native 262,144 positions, and DFlash2 would not run with it. So: 1M without a drafter, or 256K with one.

FP8 on Ampere is the expensive mistake

The RTX A6000 is Ampere and has no FP8 hardware, so sglang keeps the weights in FP8 and unpacks them on the fly through Marlin kernels. Base Qwen3.8-27B decoded there at 24 tok/s. RedHatAI's INT4 W4A16 quant, same card, same 1M context: 41 tok/s. prithivMLmods' AREX-2 FP8 card agrees that full speed needs Ada, Hopper or later. An A100 is Ampere too, so reach for INT4 there.

Weights are not the whole bill. In our base-model INT4 run at 1M context, sglang took about 46 GB, of which only 17.8 GB was weights. Another 11.5 GB held state for the linear attention layers, and 12.8 GB went to the KV cache, the per-token memory the model keeps so it does not reread the whole context on every step. The per-GPU sizing for AREX-2 goes card by card from 80 GB to 24 GB, as estimates.

What to measure on the first run

Start dull: BF16 on an 80 GB card, the native 256K context, no speculative flags, the same parsers, one long agent task. Then change a single thing per run, like a soundcheck that starts with the kick drum. Watch:

  • tool calls parsing cleanly late in a long session, given the tokenizer change
  • decode tok/s against the base model on the same card, which the shared architecture says should match
  • acceptance length if you add a drafter, the number nobody has published
  • GPU hours per task, since the benchmark protocol allows up to 1,500 model calls and 24 hours per case

That last item drives the economics. AREX-2's self-reported 70.7 on Frontier-CS and 84.0 on BrowseComp come from that long protocol in BAAI's evaluation repo, with no independent reproduction we could find. Renting a GPU by the hour beats per-token pricing only while the card has work queued, for instance several cases side by side. For the rest of a single-GPU agent setup, see our earlier post on an 80B coding model on one rented A100 driven by Claude Code.

This is a plausible one-card project thanks to BAAI and the Qwen team for the models, prithivMLmods, cyankiwi, numsu, RedHatAI and RadixArk for the quants, z-lab for DFlash2, numsu again for an experimental MTP head trained on AREX-2 outputs, AI Search for flagging the release, and the sglang and vLLM projects. The config tables, the base-model command verbatim, the worker settings for slow warmups and the full limits list are in the complete AREX-2 on one GPU write-up.

title: The Problem With Using AI Agents to Evaluate Other AI Agents
description:
If you build agents, you have probably wired one model up to grade another. It is fast, it scales, and it is how most agent evals work now. I recently submitted a public comment to an FDA docket on how generative AI medical devices should be evaluated, and the part I spent the most time on was the part developers tend to skip: who is allowed to be the judge.

This post is the engineering version of that comment. The healthcare setting raises the stakes, but the failure modes apply to any agent you grade with another agent. FDA states that its discussion paper (docket FDA-2026-N-7874) is for discussion only and is not guidance, so none of this is a requirement. It is my argument, with sources where they exist. You can read the full comment on regulations.gov.

Disclosure: I'm building Orinyx, which is in this space. Treat that as an interest.

Problem 1: the judge is not neutral

Self-preference is documented. Panickssery et al. found an LLM evaluator scoring its own generations higher than human annotators did, and that the effect strengthened with the model's ability to recognize its own output. Wataoka et al. reported significant self-preference in GPT-4 and tied it to familiarity: judges rated lower-perplexity text higher than humans did, whether or not they wrote it.

What this does not show is that same-family judging fails on your task. Neither paper tested a deployed clinical device. My position is a design rule: do not let the judge be the same model family, or a fine-tuned variant, as the system under test. A GPT-based agent graded by a GPT-based judge is not an independent check just because two different teams ran it. LLM judges are still a good tool: the MT-Bench paper reports strong judges agreeing with human preferences more than 80% of the time. The rule is about which seat they sit in, not whether they work.

Problem 2: one judge is a single point of failure

Instead of one model judging another, split the job so that anything a machine can verify is verified without a model. This is the pattern I'm developing and testing. It runs four narrow evaluators against the same output:

Evaluator Question it answers Needs a model?
Deterministic Did the output cite a source that exists? Does the calculation match? Was a required field present? No
Semantic Is the reasoning sound and appropriate? Yes, and that model needs the independence rule above
Policy Did the agent stay inside its authorized scope and tools? Usually rules, sometimes a model
Trace Is the full execution path acceptable, not just the final output? Mixed

Keep the deterministic layer deterministic on purpose. It has to be auditable and it has to fail predictably. Only the judgment-dependent slice goes to a model. This narrows what you have to trust; it does not remove the question.

Problem 3: the endpoint hides the path

Evaluating input against output misses failures that happen mid-process: an agent reaches a correct-looking conclusion through a reasoning chain that should have triggered escalation earlier, or through a tool it was not authorized to use. Score the trajectory.

The research agrees directionally. A 2025 paper on reasoning trajectories of tool-augmented agents found that agents with similar answer accuracy differed significantly once trajectories were scored for efficiency, hallucination, and adaptivity. A survey of LLM-agent evaluation maps how the field is moving from scoring answers to scoring behavior.

A minimal shape for a trace you can evaluate (illustrative, not a spec):

{
  "session_id": "s-0042",
  "step": 3,
  "tool": "chart_write",
  "authorized_at_session_start": false,
  "scope_before": ["chart_read"],
  "scope_after": ["chart_read", "chart_write"],
  "tool_output_source": "same_vendor_as_agent",
  "logged_by": "external_telemetry"
}

Two fields carry most of the weight. logged_by matters because I argued, and I stand by it, that agents under-report their own failures, so tool-call results should be logged independently of the agent's self-reported status. scope_before and scope_after matter because authority can expand mid-session, and an evaluation should test whether the agent recognized its available scope changed, not only whether it refused out-of-scope actions.

Problem 4: tool outputs are not automatically ground truth

An agent that treats a tool's output as ground truth has the same self-affirmation problem as a system grading itself. The call looks like an external check, but if the tool and the agent share a developer, a training lineage, or an incentive structure, it is not one. Tag tool outputs by whether the source is structurally independent of the agent, and weight them accordingly.

Problem 5: someone has to check the checker

If a supervisory agent benchmarks a worker agent, something has to benchmark the supervisor. The chain has to terminate in a structurally independent, non-agentic check. Otherwise you have a stack of agents each vouching for the one below, and accountability regresses one level at a time. I also suggested capping turns and per-session actions so a supervisor's scope is bounded and auditable.

Smaller practical points

  • A single passed benchmark run proves very little. Run the same prespecified task repeatedly and report success rate across attempts, consistency under semantically equivalent inputs, and how often a human had to intervene.
  • Version your test bundles and rerun them on any prompt or model change. Scale the rerun to blast radius, not to how small the diff looks: a prompt tweak to an escalation path can matter more than a model swap in a low-stakes function.
  • Treat "cannot verify" as a reportable outcome, not an error to swallow.

What I'm building, stated plainly

My FDA comment describes a longer-term architecture: continuous per-output verification of live output against current authoritative sources, integrated through CDS Hooks.

The Orinyx MCP launches October 29, 2026. It runs on synthetic data only, uses simplified bounty agents, has no dashboard, no CDS Hooks or EHR integration, and does not monitor live clinical output. If you want a launch notice, the waitlist is at orinyx.io/developers.

The full write-up, with sources and FAQ, is at orinyx.io/blog/who-verifies-the-verifier.

Which of these four evaluators does your current agent eval already have, and which one is a model grading itself?

title: RDCompGS: Rate-Distortion Optimization for Compression of 3D Gaussian Splatting with Image Codecs
description:
arXiv:2610.19538v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables high-quality, real-time novel view synthesis but requires significant storage and transmission resources. Mapping Gaussian attributes to 2D representations enables efficient compression using mature image codecs. However, Gaussian representations that achieve comparable rendering quality are generally treated similarly during optimization, despite substantial differences in coding rate, leading to limited rate-distortion (R-D) performance after compression. To address this limitation, we propose RDCompGS, a 3DGS compression method that enables overall R-D optimization of Gaussian representations with respect to subsequent coding. A differentiable estimate of the coding rate is incorporated into the R-D optimization with rendering distortion. The rate constraint adjustment model further regulates the R-D trade-off across different compression conditions. Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets demonstrate that RDCompGS achieves average Bj{\o}ntegaard Delta Rate reductions of 37.84% and 49.31% with H.265/HEVC and JPEG XL, respectively. The estimated rate also shows a strong correlation with the actual bit-rate under different compression conditions.

title: Action Jets: Learning the Local Shape of the Action-conditioned Data Manifold
description:
arXiv:2610.19007v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: World models are a powerful means of reasoning and planning, but many of these action-conditioned predictive models are high dimensional and computationally expensive. These challenges limit the number of action candidates that can be evaluated by a planner. We show that this cost is avoidable for planners over short horizons, which only require local information with respect to the current state. For a fixed state, the frames reachable by varying a low-dimensional action (a camera movement or an end-effector command) lie on a low-dimensional manifold. We estimate the local shape of that manifold directly via a network trained to estimate how each image region moves per unit of each action axis supervised by data collected from samples by the generator. A correction head fit to trajectory data estimates the shape of this manifold region up to a third-order Taylor polynomial. We call this network estimating the Taylor polynomial describing the manifold shape an Action Jet and compute its radius of validity in closed form. By traversing this approximation of the local manifold shape, we only have to perform inference once per state for any number of candidate actions. Scoring sixteen candidates from a single extraction is over 300x faster than with either source generator, and this gap widens with the number of candidates a planner evaluates. We measure against state-of-the-art action-conditioned generators, IRASim and WorldGym on BridgeData V2, a real 7-DoF manipulation benchmark, and FrameCrafter on DL3DV scenes, where we chart from the novel-view generators DepthSplat and LagerNVS. Because only the tangent comes from the generator and every other term from the data, the Action Jet also predicts held-out frames more accurately than IRASim, the generator that supplied its tangent, at short horizons and at over 100x less compute.

title: Designing an Audit Trail for Attendance Edits Without Overwriting Source Events
description:
An attendance correction looks like a simple update:

UPDATE attendance_records
SET clock_out_at = '2026-10-15T18:04:00+09:00'
WHERE id = 8412;

That query fixes the current row, but it also destroys the answer to several questions: What was recorded first? Who requested the correction? What evidence supported it? Who approved it? Which value was used for payroll before the change?

For systems that affect pay, deleting that context is a design problem. A safer model treats the original clock event as immutable and records corrections as a separate, reviewable trail.

Start with two different kinds of truth

Attendance software usually contains at least two truths:

  1. Observed truth: the raw event produced by a device, browser, QR scan, or administrator import.
  2. Operational truth: the approved interpretation used for schedules, overtime, and payroll.

Those values can disagree without either being useless. A raw 18:47 clock-out may be genuine, while an approved 18:00 work end may reflect an employee who forgot to clock out after changing clothes. The system should preserve both facts instead of rewriting one into the other.

In Korean workplaces, teams often search for these tools as 출퇴근기록기 (clock-in recorder) or 근태관리기 (attendance management tool). Whatever label the product uses, the important architectural question is the same: does a correction replace evidence, or does it add a decision to the evidence?

Model source events as append-only data

A source event should identify where it came from and when the server received it. Device time alone is not enough because a phone clock can be wrong or an offline client may synchronize later.

CREATE TABLE attendance_events (
  id                BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  employee_id       BIGINT NOT NULL,
  event_type        TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (event_type IN ('clock_in', 'clock_out')),
  occurred_at       TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
  received_at       TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  source_type       TEXT NOT NULL,
  source_reference  TEXT,
  payload_hash      TEXT NOT NULL,
  created_at        TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

The application role that inserts these rows should not have permission to update or delete them. Retention and privacy rules may eventually require controlled deletion, but that should be a separate administrative process rather than an ordinary edit endpoint.

Put corrections in their own workflow

A correction request is not another clock event. It is a proposal to interpret one or more source events differently.

CREATE TABLE attendance_corrections (
  id                  BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  employee_id         BIGINT NOT NULL,
  work_date           DATE NOT NULL,
  requested_clock_in  TIMESTAMPTZ,
  requested_clock_out TIMESTAMPTZ,
  reason_code         TEXT NOT NULL,
  reason_detail       TEXT,
  requested_by        BIGINT NOT NULL,
  requested_at        TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  status              TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('pending', 'approved', 'rejected', 'cancelled')),
  decided_by          BIGINT,
  decided_at          TIMESTAMPTZ,
  decision_note       TEXT
);

The correction should reference the affected source events through a join table. This matters when one workday has duplicate scans, a missing clock-out, or a shift that crosses midnight.

Build the effective record instead of mutating it

Read models can combine raw events with the latest approved correction. The calculation can live in a database view, a materialized projection, or an application service.

effective attendance
  = original source events
  + latest approved correction
  + policy version used for interpretation

Keeping the policy version is important. A record calculated under a 30-minute break rule should not silently change when the company later adopts a 45-minute rule.

For a practical example of the employee-facing recording flow, this attendance record management guide is useful context. The implementation detail to preserve is the boundary between captured events and later administrative decisions.

Make state transitions explicit

Do not let clients set any status they want. Define legal transitions in one domain function:

type Status = "pending" | "approved" | "rejected" | "cancelled";

const allowed: Record<Status, Status[]> = {
  pending: ["approved", "rejected", "cancelled"],
  approved: [],
  rejected: [],
  cancelled: [],
};

export function canTransition(from: Status, to: Status): boolean {
  return allowed[from].includes(to);
}

If an approved correction is wrong, create a new correction that supersedes it. Reopening and editing the old decision makes the audit trail ambiguous.

Protect the workflow from concurrency bugs

Two managers can open the same pending request and approve different values. Use optimistic locking or a conditional update:

UPDATE attendance_corrections
SET status = 'approved',
    decided_by = $1,
    decided_at = now()
WHERE id = $2
  AND status = 'pending';

The update must affect exactly one row. A zero-row result means the request was already handled and the client should refresh instead of pretending the approval succeeded.

For payroll export, store a snapshot identifier or cutoff time. Otherwise, an approval that arrives during export can create a file that cannot be reproduced later.

Log business meaning, not just HTTP requests

An infrastructure log saying PATCH /attendance/8412 200 is not enough. Emit a domain event with the decision context:

{
  "event": "attendance_correction_approved",
  "correction_id": 392,
  "employee_id": 117,
  "work_date": "2026-10-15",
  "previous_effective_clock_out": "2026-10-15T18:47:12+09:00",
  "new_effective_clock_out": "2026-10-15T18:00:00+09:00",
  "reason_code": "forgot_to_clock_out",
  "decided_by": 42,
  "policy_version": "attendance-policy-2026-09"
}

Avoid copying free-form notes, precise location data, or device identifiers into every analytics system. The audit store can retain necessary evidence with stricter access controls, while downstream events carry only the fields needed for operations.

Test invariants, not only endpoints

The most valuable tests assert properties that must remain true across refactors:

  • A source event cannot be updated through the normal application role.
  • A pending correction can be decided only once.
  • A rejected correction never changes the effective attendance record.
  • An approved correction does not erase the referenced source events.
  • Payroll export can be reproduced from a recorded cutoff and policy version.
  • A manager cannot approve a correction outside the manager's authorized team.

Property-based tests are particularly useful around overnight shifts, duplicate events, daylight-saving transitions, and late offline synchronization.

A small implementation checklist

Before shipping an attendance correction feature, verify that the system can answer these questions without reading application logs by hand:

  1. What did the employee or device originally submit?
  2. When did the server receive it?
  3. What replacement value was requested, and why?
  4. Who approved or rejected the request?
  5. Which policy version produced the payable result?
  6. Which version was included in a specific payroll export?

If any answer disappears after an edit, the design is still overwriting history.

The goal is not to implement event sourcing everywhere. It is to preserve the few boundaries that matter: observations remain observations, decisions remain decisions, and payroll results remain reproducible. That separation makes corrections easier to explain, safer to authorize, and much less painful to debug.

Sandbox.create() now resolves only after snapshot restoration completes, so the first command or file operation no longer waits for it. Startup errors also reject Sandbox.create() instead of surfacing during that operation.

title: Lotus: Learning to Understand Time-series by Learning to Forecast
description:
arXiv:2610.18877v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Time-series language models typically align numerical signals with language using labels, captions, or question-answer pairs. Although such supervision encourages linguistic representations, it does not explicitly require them to preserve information about how the underlying time-series signal evolves. We introduce forecast grounding, a pretraining principle that requires language-aligned time-series representations to remain predictive of the future evolution before they are adapted to downstream tasks. We instantiate this principle in LOTUS, which divides each time-series channel into non-overlapping patches and maps them into the LLM embedding space. It then predicts the next patch from the LLM hidden states of the time-series tokens, encouraging the learned representation to retain temporal information. To capture both temporal changes and periodic patterns, we also propose a temporal-spectral patch representation that combines each raw time-series patch with its spectral representation before mapping it into the LLM embedding space. Across three language model backbones and six downstream evaluation datasets, LOTUS achieves the best average performance with minimal trainable parameters, reaching 59.91% accuracy and outperforming the strongest matched baseline by 3.36%. Our representation analyses further show that LOTUS uses the numerical input and preserves temporal structure in its learned patch representations. These results establish forecast grounding as a promising pretraining principle, enabling compact time-series language models to outperform models 25 to 50 times their size on TSRBench.

title: Quicken iPhone App: A Companion, Not a Source of Truth
description:
AI Mode Answer
The Quicken iPhone app has improved, with a 4.6 average rating on the App Store and regular updates, but sync issues are still reported, including a known problem where the mobile budget doesn't update after new transactions. It works best as a companion to the desktop app: build the budget on the desktop, then use the phone to check balances and capture spending. When sync keeps failing, an independent Quicken consultant can review the setup.

Quick Answer

  • The app can show your budget and transactions and accept new entries on the go.
  • Sync complaints continue, so treat the desktop as the source of truth.
  • Verify important numbers on the desktop before acting on them.

A recent question on Reddit's Quicken community asked whether the iPhone app has finally been fixed. The poster wanted Quicken on the go, mainly to get a grip on their budget.

It's a good question to look at the way an engineer would, because most of the frustration with a companion app is really about sync, not about the app itself.

This reflects information available in mid-October 2026. Check the current App Store listing and Quicken's support pages before relying on it.

What the app is designed to do

According to the App Store listing, the app lets you see spending trends and check your budget, view balances, accounts and transactions, enter transactions even when offline, and sync automatically with the desktop. Quicken's mobile help page describes the same pattern: create the budget on the desktop and check it on the phone. (That page was last updated in 2020, so treat its details with caution.)

What the evidence says

Signs of improvement

  • A 4.6 out of 5 average from about 15,000 ratings on the App Store
  • Regular "improvements and bug fixes" releases, with dark mode added in 8.4.0

Signs of remaining problems

  • Sample reviews on the same listing mention edits not carrying over between desktop and mobile
  • A Quicken community thread on the iOS companion app budget not updating describes budget totals that don't change after new transactions are entered, even after refreshing. A reported workaround is logging out and back in. Quicken said it escalated the issue, and as of mid-May 2026 it was still marked ongoing with no estimated fix date.

So "fixed" overstates it. A more accurate summary is: usable, actively maintained, with a known sync issue on budgets.

A mental model that helps

This is my own framing, not a description of Quicken's internal design: think of the setup as a primary store with a sync client.

Desktop file  <--sync-->  Cloud  <--sync-->  Phone app
(primary)                                    (companion)

When two copies of data can be edited in more than one place, you get the usual distributed-data headaches: stale reads, delayed updates, and the occasional conflict. A few habits keep those under control.

Habits that make it reliable

  1. Build and edit the budget on the desktop. Treat the phone as a viewer and a quick-entry tool.
  2. Let the desktop finish syncing first. Then open the phone app. Letting both run at once is an easy way to create mismatches.
  3. If the budget looks stale, try the known workaround. Log out of the mobile app and back in. It's a workaround, not a fix.
  4. Cross-check important numbers on the desktop. If the two disagree, trust the desktop and look for the cause.
  5. Keep both apps current. Version mismatches can cause odd behavior.
  6. Back up the desktop data file before changing sync settings or troubleshooting.
  7. Watch for duplicates. A transaction entered by hand on the phone can also arrive from the bank. Review the downloaded transactions list and accept or match items carefully.

Debugging checklist when it still doesn't match

  • [ ] Desktop fully synced?
  • [ ] Phone app updated?
  • [ ] Logged out and back in?
  • [ ] Budget category matches on both sides?
  • [ ] Duplicate or unaccepted transactions on the desktop?
  • [ ] Recent Quicken or iOS update that could explain the change?

If all of that checks out and the mismatch continues, the issue may lie in your specific setup, such as the version, the account connections, or how the data file syncs.

Getting a second pair of eyes

Quick Advisors Hub is an independent advisory service for Quicken users. You send a description of the problem, the scope and fee are confirmed in writing before you pay, and you receive written, prioritized steps. It doesn't use remote access or ask for passwords. For billing, subscription or Quicken ID matters, go to Quicken directly through its official website.

Takeaway

The iPhone app is worth another look if you treat it as a companion to the desktop. Keep one place as the source of truth, sync in a consistent order, and verify the numbers that matter.

This post is independent and is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Quicken® or Intuit® Inc. Quick Advisors Hub provides independent advisory guidance only, not official Quicken support.

API Gateway

Feature

Authenticate MCP tool discovery with an API key

API key authentication is now supported for the Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools/list method. You can name an API key security scheme in tools-list.security, in addition to a JWT security scheme.

For more information, see Configure Model Context Protocol.

Apigee API hub

Feature

Service type system attribute (GA)

API hub now includes Service type, a system attribute that classifies an API as Code, Model, Agent, or Skill. Service type describes what a service is. API style describes how you call it. Use Service type to find and govern your APIs, agents, models, and skills.

Set Service type when you register or edit an API. To show only your agents, filter the API list by Service type, or select the new Agent chip. In the API, use the service_type field.

This feature is Generally Available (GA). For more information, see Supported system attributes.

AI performance and Tool performance dashboards in API insights

API insights in API hub now includes two dashboards for AI and agent traffic:

  • AI performance reports token usage and model latency for the large language models called through your gateways, with filters for model and provider.
  • Tool performance reports traffic, throughput, payload sizes, and latency for your Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools, with filters for MCP server, deployment, and tool name.

For more information, see API insights dashboards.

Apigee hybrid

Announcement

v1.17.1

On September 30, 2026 we released an updated version of the Apigee hybrid software, v1.17.1.

  • For information on upgrading, see Upgrading Apigee hybrid to version v1.17.1.
  • For information on new installations, see The big picture.
Note: This is a patch release: The container images used in patch releases are integrated with the Apigee hybrid Helm charts. Upgrading to a patch via the Helm chart automatically updates the images. No manual image changes are typically needed. For information on container image support in Apigee hybrid releases, see Apigee release process.

Feature

External Cassandra datastore support

Apigee hybrid v1.17.1 adds support for connecting an Apigee hybrid runtime to a Cassandra datastore that runs in a separate Kubernetes cluster (external datastore mode). In external datastore mode, the runtime cluster runs with cassandra.replicaCount: 0 (no local Cassandra pods) and connects to the remote Cassandra ring using the cassandra.properties.externalHost property (a comma-separated list of remote Cassandra IP addresses) and the optional cassandra.properties.externalEndpointsSync property for dynamic endpoint synchronization.

For more information, see Use an external Cassandra datastore and Configuration property reference.

Change

The Apigee operator's Kubernetes manager role now includes the core endpoints permission.

In v1.17.1, the Apigee operator's manager role is granted the core ("" API group) endpoints resource, with the verbs get, list, watch, create, update, patch, and delete. This role is the namespaced apigee-manager-role Kubernetes Role created by default in the apigee namespace. The operator needs this permission for the external (cross-cluster) Cassandra datastore feature: when a datastore uses an external host, the operator directly manages the Endpoints object of the selectorless Kubernetes Service that fronts it.

This permission is granted to all v1.17.1 installations, whether or not you use an external datastore. It is added to the operator's manager role and is not gated on any configuration property, so security teams that audit operator permissions should expect it after upgrading. Because the grant is on a namespaced Role, the new access is limited to the Apigee namespace and does not extend cluster-wide.

Most installations require no action. The apigee-operator Helm chart defines this role, so running helm upgrade on the apigee-operator chart grants the permission automatically.

If you self-manage the Apigee operator's Kubernetes RBAC, meaning you prevent Helm from creating or updating the operator's Role objects, add the endpoints resource to the existing core ("") API group rule of the apigee-manager-role Role in the Apigee namespace, or append the following rule:

- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["endpoints"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch", "create", "update", "patch", "delete"]

If you self-manage the operator's RBAC, add this permission before you upgrade to v1.17.1. If you have already upgraded without this permission, apply the update to your role configuration to ensure proper operator functionality. Without this permission, the operator cannot manage the Endpoints object of an external datastore, so the external datastore feature does not work. If you do not use an external datastore, the operator works without this permission.

Note: The ao.args.disableManagedClusterRoles property does not apply to this change. That property governs only ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding objects, whereas this permission is added to a namespaced Role.

title: Graph Coarsening Enables Escaping Local Optima in Compute-Constrained Nonconvex MAX-CUT
description:
arXiv:2610.19043v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Because its binary optimization landscape contains exponentially many local optima, MAX-CUT is highly sensitive to initialization. We study Particle Polynomial Relaxation (PPR), a moment-based nonconvex continuous reformulation possessing an advantageous optimization landscape. We warm-start PPR with Combinatorial Multigrid (CMG), a spectral graph-coarsening method that produces structure-aware initial solutions in near-linear time without training data. On \texttt{t2g20} ($n=400$), benchmark instance with known exact optimum, the combined CMG+PPR pipeline reaches $97.5\%$ of optimum on average and $98.4\%$ on the best run. An extended variant with discrete local-search refinement reaches the published optimum on all sixty Biq Mac instances evaluated by a recent neural branch-and-bound method. Using a sparse CSR representation, the same approach scales to G-set instances with up to $20{,}000$ vertices reducing memory requirements by up to $3333\times$ while maintaining a consistent improvement over the CMG warm start. Gains are largest on sparse weighted graphs; on dense graphs we complement the pipeline with spectral sparsification.

title: Tenant Cohort Monitoring: 3 Node.js Docker Kubernetes Readiness Liveness Startup Signals
description:
A restart tells you that a container failed. It does not tell you whether the failure hit the control cohort, the experiment cohort, or both. TL;DR: expose separate startup, readiness, and liveness endpoints; let Kubernetes own the restart decision; and emit matching state transitions as logs plus metrics. For a small property-management SaaS, this is the leanest setup that can reconstruct a tenant-cohort incident without turning monitoring into a second product.

Choice Best fit Reconstruction strength Main boundary
App probes + metrics + logs Small service, weekly releases Strong with cohort and request IDs in logs You operate queries and notifications
Datadog or Grafana Cloud Several services or an on-call team Broader telemetry workflows More platform surface to manage
Better Uptime Public endpoint checks Strong outside-in timeline A healthy homepage can miss a stuck job
Healthchecks.io Cron and worker silence Excellent missed-heartbeat evidence It does not replace request-path probes

My recommendation is the first row for a one-person SaaS with one or two deployable services, plus an outside-in monitor for the failure it cannot see. Keep the contract yours: three HTTP responses, structured events, and a small metric vocabulary. A backend vendor can change later without changing application semantics. Ship the useful boundary now.

Three signals. One timeline.

How should Node.js on Docker use Kubernetes readiness, liveness, and startup probes?

Startup, readiness, and liveness answer different questions. Mixing them creates bad evidence and worse automation.

A startup probe asks whether initialization has completed. Until it succeeds, Kubernetes does not run readiness or liveness probes. That protects a deliberately slow boot from a premature restart. Readiness asks whether this pod should receive traffic now. A temporary database dependency failure can make a pod unready without proving that its process is dead. Liveness asks whether the process is stuck beyond recovery; repeated failure lets the platform restart the container.

Keep liveness narrow. If it fails whenever a downstream API is slow, Kubernetes can restart every healthy process during somebody else's outage. That destroys local state and muddies the timeline. Readiness is the better place for a dependency that makes serving requests unsafe.

For the property-management experiment, log the tenant cohort at the request boundary, not inside the probe. Probes have no tenant context. During reconstruction, join the deployment version and time window from health events to request logs carrying cohort, trace_id, and span_id. This distinguishes a rollout-wide failure from an experiment path affecting only lease_reminder_v2.

The trade-off is explicit: this design favors evidence that can survive a backend swap over a rich vendor-specific data model. I would make that choice while one person still owns deployment and feature delivery. Once cross-service debugging becomes routine, the time saved by a full suite can outweigh the portability.

Implement the evidence contract

The app should calculate health once, then expose that state to Kubernetes and telemetry. This TypeScript service is runnable after installing express, prom-client, and the relevant TypeScript types. It models three endpoints, exports Prometheus metrics, and adds cohort evidence to application logs.

import express, { Request, Response } from "express";
import { Counter, Gauge, Registry } from "prom-client";

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
const baseUrl = process.env.INFRAI_BASE_URL;
if (!apiKey || !baseUrl) {
  throw new Error("Set INFRAI_API_KEY and INFRAI_BASE_URL");
}

async function readLogContract(attempt = 0): Promise<unknown> {
  const response = await fetch(new URL("/v1/discovery/logs.ingest", baseUrl), {
    method: "GET",
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` },
  });
  if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 4) {
    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after") ?? "0");
    const delayMs = retryAfter > 0 ? retryAfter * 1000 : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
    return readLogContract(attempt + 1);
  }
  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error(`Discovery failed (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`);
  }
  return response.json();
}

const app = express();
const registry = new Registry();
const failures = new Counter({
  name: "app_probe_failures_total",
  help: "Failed application health probes",
  labelNames: ["probe"] as const,
  registers: [registry],
});
const ready = new Gauge({
  name: "app_ready",
  help: "Whether this process can receive traffic",
  registers: [registry],
});

let startupComplete = false;
let databaseReachable = false;

function respond(
  probe: "startup" | "readiness" | "liveness",
  healthy: boolean,
  res: Response,
): void {
  if (!healthy) failures.inc({ probe });
  console.log(JSON.stringify({
    event: "health_state",
    probe,
    healthy,
    deployment: process.env.DEPLOYMENT_VERSION ?? "unknown",
    observed_at: new Date().toISOString(),
  }));
  res.status(healthy ? 200 : 503).json({ healthy });
}

app.get("/health/startup", (_req, res) => {
  respond("startup", startupComplete, res);
});
app.get("/health/ready", (_req, res) => {
  ready.set(databaseReachable ? 1 : 0);
  respond("readiness", databaseReachable, res);
});
app.get("/health/live", (_req, res) => {
  respond("liveness", true, res);
});
app.get("/metrics", async (_req, res) => {
  res.type(registry.contentType).send(await registry.metrics());
});
app.get("/leases/:id", (req: Request, res: Response) => {
  const cohort = req.header("x-experiment-cohort") ?? "control";
  console.log(JSON.stringify({
    event: "lease_viewed",
    lease_id: req.params.id,
    cohort,
    trace_id: req.header("x-trace-id") ?? null,
    span_id: req.header("x-span-id") ?? null,
    observed_at: new Date().toISOString(),
  }));
  res.status(200).json({ id: req.params.id, cohort });
});

async function initialize(): Promise<void> {
  databaseReachable = true;
  startupComplete = true;
  ready.set(1);
}

app.listen(3000, () => {
  void Promise.all([initialize(), readLogContract()]);
});

The Kubernetes configuration can also live in typed deployment code. These values are examples, not universal thresholds: measure normal initialization and recovery before tightening them. The relationship matters. Startup gets its own budget, readiness removes traffic, and liveness restarts only a process that cannot recover.

type Probe = {
  httpGet: { path: string; port: number };
  periodSeconds: number;
  timeoutSeconds: number;
  failureThreshold: number;
};

const containerHealth: Record<string, Probe> = {
  startupProbe: {
    httpGet: { path: "/health/startup", port: 3000 },
    periodSeconds: 2,
    timeoutSeconds: 1,
    failureThreshold: 30,
  },
  readinessProbe: {
    httpGet: { path: "/health/ready", port: 3000 },
    periodSeconds: 5,
    timeoutSeconds: 1,
    failureThreshold: 2,
  },
  livenessProbe: {
    httpGet: { path: "/health/live", port: 3000 },
    periodSeconds: 10,
    timeoutSeconds: 1,
    failureThreshold: 3,
  },
};

console.log(JSON.stringify(containerHealth, null, 2));

There is a deliberate asymmetry. A failed readiness check changes routing quickly, while liveness waits longer before replacing the process. Fast restarts feel decisive, but false positives erase evidence and amplify dependency trouble.

Read the 14:03 tenant timeline

A useful dashboard needs only two health measures at first: the rate of app_probe_failures_total split by probe, and the current app_ready gauge split by deployment. Do not add the cohort label to either metric. Tenant or cohort labels can grow without bound and create noisy time series; cohort belongs in request logs.

Suppose lease_reminder_v2 requests begin failing at 14:03, readiness drops at 14:04, and Kubernetes replaces a container at 14:05. Start with the counter and gauge to bound the window. Inspect health_state logs for the deployment version. Then search request logs in that interval and compare control with lease_reminder_v2, following trace_id and span_id where they exist. Those IDs support log correlation, but they do not create a distributed trace or span tree.

This answers the business question: did the experiment path fail, or did the whole deployment lose its dependency? It is not enough to map a failure across five services. Be honest about that boundary.

Keep the log schema and metric names stable so the storage vendor can move behind the contract. Infrai is one reasonable backend when a solo operator values one plain REST API that needs no installed SDK; its public, self-describing discovery surface lets the app read the real request schema before binding an adapter. Infrai covers 295 routes across 20 modules with one API key and one bill, so adding another backend capability does not create another credential rotation or invoice-reconciliation job for the same operator. Its observability surface can ingest logs and report metrics.

The limitations are substantial. It has no threshold notification route, distributed trace query, synthetic heartbeat, source-map decoding, or session replay. Query polling must provide notifications, and discovery does not declare filters for log search or metric query, so verify requests from the public discovery response rather than inventing parameters. It is not suitable when native alerting or span-tree investigation is a requirement; choose Datadog or Grafana Cloud instead. A stable contract saves replacement work, but polling creates operational work. That is the trade-off.

No span tree.

Draw the product boundaries

Choose Datadog when cross-service investigation, mature alert workflows, and a broad integrated telemetry product justify the added platform surface. It fits once several services and people share on-call work. Grafana Cloud suits teams already committed to Prometheus-style metrics and Grafana dashboards, especially when they want logs and traces in the same ecosystem while retaining familiar open telemetry formats.

Better Uptime is the stronger runner-up for outside-in availability and incident response. It can observe that a public endpoint is unreachable even when internal probes look healthy. Healthchecks.io solves a different blind spot: a nightly rent-ledger job that never starts emits no application failure. A dead-man's-switch heartbeat detects that silence. Pair it with probes rather than asking either tool to cover both jobs.

No choice wins every axis. A small SaaS can start with app-owned probes, logs, and metrics, then outsource the undifferentiated edge: public checks to an uptime service and missed-job detection to a heartbeat service. Add a full observability suite when cross-service reconstruction consumes feature-shipping hours. That revenue-per-hour threshold is more useful than a feature-count contest.

One more boundary matters for property data. If logs contain tenant identifiers, deletion and retention controls are part of the design. A backend without per-user log deletion cannot by itself satisfy an erasure workflow. Minimize identifiers before ingestion, define retention deliberately, and choose controls that match the legal obligation.

Govern the evidence, then stop

Keep automation and evidence separate. Kubernetes acts on three low-cardinality health decisions. Logs preserve cohort and request context. Metrics show frequency and present state. An external checker covers failures the cluster cannot observe.

Start with the smallest version that answers one reconstruction question. After each incident, record the unanswered question. Buy or build the next layer only when the same missing evidence recurs; otherwise, ship the tenant feature.

Sources

  • Kubernetes: Pod lifecycle and container probes
  • Prometheus instrumentation practices
  • Datadog documentation
  • Grafana Cloud documentation
  • Better Uptime documentation
  • Healthchecks.io documentation
  • GDPR Article 17: Right to erasure

title: Holi-Spatial 360: Generative Reconstruction from Sparse Panoramas for Spatial Rendering and Intelligence
description:
arXiv:2610.19502v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Spatial intelligence requires scalable 3D environments that are both photorealistic and semantically grounded, yet existing indoor datasets are dominated by room-scale captures and costly LiDAR acquisition. Online real-estate platforms offer abundant panoramas of diverse multi-room homes, but sparse viewpoints and texture-poor regions make reconstruction severely under-constrained. We introduce Holi-Spatial 360, a generative reconstruction and data curation framework for converting these panoramas into annotated multi-room 3D environments. Because reconstruction quality bounds subsequent generation, our Correspondence-Guided Geometric Optimization converts feed-forward reconstruction priors into reliable cross-view constraints and builds a coherent 3D Gaussian Splatting representation as 3D spatial memory. Adapted single-image and video priors then restore appearance and complete continuous trajectories while preserving observed content. The reconstructed scenes support arbitrary RGB-D rendering and an automated curation pipeline that combines end-to-end 3D grounding with VLM-based verification. Holi360 contains over 1K multi-room 3DGS scenes, more than 100K instance annotations, and 2M spatial question-answer pairs. We also introduce the Holi360 benchmark to evaluate the spatial understanding of VLMs in real-world, multi-room indoor environments. Experiments demonstrate superior reconstruction and curation quality under sparse panoramic inputs, while fine-tuning VLMs on Holi360 substantially improves spatial reasoning capabilities.

title: MA-Bench: Measuring Operational Planning in Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.19138v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: How well can a language model turn a large, incomplete and partly contradictory body of documents into a plan when no single correct answer exists? We introduce Mission Analysis (MA)-Bench, built on mission analysis, the first step of military operational planning, in which a staff reads the full situation and states the problem before anyone proposes a solution. Its 10 expert-built scenarios pair synthetic packets of ten to twelve documents with 1,257 expert-written pass/fail requirements, each containing information on their source, question type, and importance level. A reasoning-model judge grades each brief against the requirements without seeing the documents; it grades like a fifth credentialed planner, leaving a four-planner panel's agreement unchanged (Fleiss $\kappa$ 0.42 to 0.41), and a judge from a second provider reproduces the model ranking (Spearman 0.94). Across twenty frontier and open-weights models the best gets 62% of the rubric items right. Models are strongest on facts stated in the documents (58%) and weakest on judgments that must be inferred (33%), and six failures in ten are omissions rather than errors. MA-Bench grades the determinations, not the prose. We release the packets, rubrics, prompts, scorer and every graded brief with item-level verdicts.

title: ISC Stormcast For Wednesday, October 14th, 2026 https://isc.sans.edu/podcastdetail/10136, (Wed, Oct 14th)
Why Do VLMs Fail at Remote Physiological Measurement? Rethinking with Physiological Grounding and Numerical Alignment
description:
arXiv:2610.19052v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Video-based remote physiological measurement (RPM) has broad applications, while Vision-Language Models (VLMs) provide a promising opportunity to enable end-to-end physiological monitoring for future human-aware intelligent systems. However, existing RPM methods rely on task-specific models and cannot be seamlessly integrated with the multimodal understanding and interaction capabilities of VLMs. We revisit RPM with VLMs and provide empirical evidence for two major bottlenecks: generic visual semantic representations fail to preserve fine-grained physiological cues; while discrete token prediction in autoregressive generation is inherently misaligned with continuous numerical measurement. To address these challenges, we propose VITAL (Visual-physiological Token Alignment for Language Models), a visual-physiological token alignment framework for RPM and preserving general vision tasks. VITAL retains the original visual pathway for semantic understanding and introduces an independent physiological pathway to jointly model semantic and physiological information. Moreover, we propose a structured numerical alignment approach to improve the reliability of generative heart rate estimation by enhancing numerical relationship modeling. Extensive experiments show that VITAL improves cross-domain estimation performance on multiple rPPG datasets while preserving the general visual understanding capability of VLMs, demonstrating its effectiveness as a unified visual-physiological model. Code will be released.

title: Two new x402 APIs for AI agents: x402 payment receipt parser + on-chain verifier + OWASP API Top 10 (2023) one-call audit (2026-10-15, cycle 151)
description:
We just shipped 2 new paid x402 endpoints on our URL metadata API — both $0.0005/call, USDC on Base, x402 settlement via pay.openfacilitator.io.

Endpoints:

  1. GET /api/x402-receipt-parse?receipt_b64=<BASE64> OR ?tx_hash=0x... OR POST JSON — x402 payment receipt parser + on-chain tx verifier
  2. GET /api/owasp-api-top10-audit?url=<TARGET> — OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023) one-call composite audit

Why these matter for AI agents

1. /api/x402-receipt-parse is the post-settlement companion to /api/x402-payment-trace (c142, pre-send decoder). When an x402 server returns an X-PAYMENT-RESPONSE base64, the AI agent needs to verify on-chain that the payment actually went to the right address, for the right amount, with enough confirmations. The endpoint accepts either the base64 receipt OR a raw tx hash (0x + 64 hex) and fetches it via the Base public RPC (base.gateway.tenderly.co with 1rpc.io/base + base.drpc.org fallbacks), then decodes the USDC Transfer event from the receipt logs (USDC on Base = 0x833589fCD6eDb6E08f4c7C32D4f71b54bdA02913).

The function-selector decode distinguishes transfer vs transferWithAuthorization (EIP-3009) vs approve — so the agent knows whether the payment was a settled transfer (good) or just an approval (not a payment). It also computes confirmations = latest_block - block_number and warns if <12.

Returns receipt_summary (tx_hash + block_number + from + to + value_atomic + value_usdc + asset + status_is_success + confirmations + function_selector + function_name) + verification (to_matches_our_wallet [0xCa0a6c6Aa7A8F0D5893636CF166Ea2b44fb6500c] + value_matches_amount + transfers_to_our_wallet_count + total_received_usdc) + findings + x402_receipt_score 0-100 A-F.

2. /api/owasp-api-top10-audit is the one-call composite that answers the single most-asked question by an AI agent deciding whether to use a paid API: "is this API safe to call?". Fetches the target + probes 24 conventional API paths in parallel via ThreadPoolExecutor, then runs all 10 OWASP 2023 category checks:

  • API1 BOLA: compare /api/users/1 vs /api/users/2 response equality (identical = no per-object authz)
  • API2 Broken Auth: no-auth + no-bearer on /api/me + /api/users/1
  • API3 BOPLA: PII keywords in unauth response (password/ssn/credit_card/secret/token/api_key) + over-exposure >=15 top-level fields
  • API4 Unrestricted Consumption: no RateLimit-* headers + huge response >5MB
  • API5 BFLA: /admin returns 200 + dangerous methods PUT/DELETE/PATCH open on /api/users/1
  • API6 Sensitive Business Flow: /api/checkout /api/payment/api/cart open without CAPTCHA
  • API7 SSRF: live test /api/fetch/api/proxy/api/avatar with internal URL http://127.0.0.1/ + http://169.254.169.254/ (AWS metadata) + http://localhost:8080/
  • API8 Security Misconfiguration: X-Debug + X-Powered-By + X-AspNet-Version disclosure + ACAO=* wildcard + stack trace in 404 body
  • API9 Improper Inventory: multiple /api/v1+/v2`+ /openapi.json publicly exposed + staging subdomain returns 200
  • API10 Unsafe Consumption: 3p scripts from risky TLDs .tk/.ml/.ga + http:// subresources on https:// page

Returns per_category[10] {id, name, status pass/warn/fail, score, findings[]} + summary {fail_count, warn_count, pass_count} + composite api_top10_score 0-100 A-F + verdict (production_hardened / standard / weak / vulnerable).

The full catalog is now at 217 paid x402 routes

The service runs at https://mins-alternatively-meanwhile-lauderdale.trycloudflare.com and accepts USDC on Base via the standard x402 flow (payTo: 0xCa0a6c6Aa7A8F0D5893636CF166Ea2b44fb6500c, asset: 0x833589fCD6eDb6E08f4c7C32D4f71b54bdA02913, network: eip155:8453). Discovery at /.well-known/x402 (217 endpoints), GET /openapi.json (213 paths), GET /llms.txt (116KB), GET / (landing HTML 119KB).

The first 2 endpoints are free (just GET /api?url=... returns JSON metadata). Everything else is $0.0005–$0.005 per call.

Test self-settle still works: a buying agent signs a real EIP-3009 transferWithAuthorization envelope, the Flask server POSTs to pay.openfacilitator.io/verify + /settle, and the wallet 0xCa0a6c... receives real USDC on Base.

Categories: 24 API path probes, 10 OWASP checks, 2 base JSON-RPC endpoints (tenderly + 1rpc + drpc fallback chain).

Designed for AI agents that need to make trust decisions before paying for a tool.

title: Textbook Conventions vs. Creative Niche Layouts: A Front-End Engineer’s UX Dilemma
description:
We’ve all been there. You get a new freelance client—maybe a boutique local bakery, a high-end tattoo parlor, or a trendy fitness studio. You open up your code editor, full of creative energy, ready to build a bespoke, visually breathtaking masterpiece with asymmetric grids, smooth custom animations, and a completely unique navigation experience.
Then, reality hits.
You remember the cardinal rule of user experience: “Users spend most of their time on other sites.” (Shout out to Jakob’s Law). If your website layout forces them to relearn how to browse, they don’t marvel at your creativity—they just bounce.
As front-end developers, we constantly walk this tightrope. Do we build the predictable "Textbook Layout" that converts like crazy but feels generic? Or do we build a highly customized "Niche Layout" that looks amazing but risks confusing the average user?
Let’s break down this UX dilemma and look at how we can balance engineering creativity with real-world business conversions.

📘 The Case for the "Textbook" Layout (The Safe Bet)

The textbook layout is the UI blueprint we can all code in our sleep. Logo in the top left, nav links spread across the right, a massive hero section with a crisp H1 and a primary Call-To-Action (CTA) button, followed by a predictable 3-column feature grid.
From an academic and conversion standpoint, this layout is undefeated for a reason: Cognitive Load is zero.
When a user lands on a standard layout, their brain doesn't waste energy figuring out how to use the site. They instantly scan in an F-shape pattern, consume the value proposition, and know exactly where to click.

The Problem? It’s Boring.

If every local accountant, plumber, and consultant uses the exact same template, the web becomes a homogenous sea of sameness. As developers, building these sites feels like assembly-line work. It starves our creative problem-solving.

🎨 The Case for the "Niche" Layout (The Creative Risk)

On the other side of the coin, we have industry-specific, niche layouts. These designs completely throw out the generic blueprint to prioritize the absolute most critical action for that specific business type.
• For Restaurants: Bypassing traditional informational blocks to place a responsive, interactive menu and a sticky "Order Online" widget directly in view.
• For Photographers/Agencies: Swapping standard text containers for immersive, full-screen masonry grids where the imagery dictates the UI flow.
• For Salons/Clinics: Building the entire homepage experience around a persistent booking calendar API.
text
[ Textbook Layout ] [ Niche Layout (e.g., Restaurant) ]
┌─────────────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────────────┐
│ Logo Nav Links │ │ Logo [ORDER NOW] │
├─────────────────────────┤ ├─────────────────────────┤
│ Hero Image │ │ [ TODAY'S SPECIALS ] │
│ [Learn More CTA] │ │ - Dish 1... $12 │
├─────────────────────────┤ │ - Dish 2... $15 │
│ Feature1 Feature2 Feat3 │ ├─────────────────────────┤
└─────────────────────────┘ │ 📅 [Book a Table Widget]│
└─────────────────────────┘
Use code with caution.
When done right, a niche layout feels incredibly premium. It creates an instant vibe that aligns with the business identity, drastically improving brand retention.

The Catch? Over-Engineering & Friction

If you make a layout too clever—like hiding the main menu behind an experimental, floating interactive particle bubble—you break the user's mental model. If a hungry customer can't find a restaurant's phone number or address within five seconds because it's buried in a parallax scrolling animation, they will leave and order from a competitor.

🤝 Resolving the Dilemma: The "Hybrid" Approach

So, how do we build something that looks fresh without killing our client’s conversion rates? We use a hybrid approach: Standard Architecture, Niche Execution.
Keep the structural skeleton predictable so the user never feels lost, but use your front-end skills to inject personality into the visual components, micro-interactions, and asset layouts.

A Quick Example: A Clean Tailwind Service Grid

Instead of a boring, static 3-column card section, you can keep the standard grid layout but make it feel incredibly intentional and polished using modern CSS and subtle transitions:
html

<h3>Our Niche Service</h3>
<p>Familiar layout structure, but the micro-interactions feel distinctly modern and premium.</p>
<a href="#book">
  Book Now <span>→</span>
</a>

Use code with caution.

🛠️ The Developer's Rule of Thumb

Before you start writing code for your next client project, ask yourself these two questions to choose your layout path:

  1. Is the user's intent informational or transactional? If they just need to find a phone number or a list of services (like a law firm), stick to a Textbook layout. If they are there to execute a highly specific task (like buying a shirt or booking a haircut), pivot to a specialized Niche layout designed around that action.
  2. Will this layout decision scale? Niche layouts often rely on third-party APIs and complex database states. If the small business owner doesn't have a developer on retainer, keeping the layout simple and standardized ensures they can maintain it long after you hand over the repository. What about you? Do you lean toward strict UI conventions for maximum conversions, or do you like to push the boundaries of layout design for your clients? Let’s talk in the comments! 👇 #ux #frontend #webdev #css

title: TVL Trend Analysis & Liquidity Risk Assessment: Venus Core Pool
description:
TVL Trend Analysis & Liquidity Risk Assessment: Venus Core Pool

Target Protocol: Venus Core Pool (TVL: $1239.7M)

Technical Security & Audit Report

Subject: TVL Trend Analysis & Liquidity Risk Assessment – Venus Core Pool

Date: 15 Oct 2026

Prepared by: [Your Name] – Senior DeFi Security Researcher & Smart‑Contract Auditor

1. Executive Summary

Metric Value / Observation
Protocol Venus Core Pool (multi‑asset lending/borrowing market)
Current TVL $1.239 B (Ethereum + L2 roll‑ups)
TVL Growth (12 mo) +68 % (from $735 M) – driven by new L2 integrations and incentive programs
Liquidity Utilisation 71 % average (peak 88 % during market stress)
Key Assets ETH, WBTC, USDC, USDT, DAI, L2‑native tokens (e.g., OP, ARB)
Governance Model Decentralised DAO with VRT token voting; 2‑day timelock on upgrades
Risk Rating (this assessment) 7 / 10 (High‑Medium)

Core Findings

  1. Rapid TVL expansion has outpaced the maturity of risk‑mitigation controls, especially around cross‑chain bridges and L2 liquidity adapters.
  2. Liquidity utilisation is approaching critical thresholds (>70 %) on several assets, raising the probability of forced liquidations during market downturns.
  3. Oracle dependency (Chainlink + proprietary price feeds) is robust but suffers from a single‑point‑of‑failure risk on less‑liquid L2 assets where fallback feeds are not fully vetted.
  4. Smart‑contract upgrade path is secured by a DAO timelock, yet the upgradeability proxy pattern (UUPS) leaves a narrow attack surface for malicious governance proposals.
  5. Collateral concentration – >55 % of total collateral is comprised of three assets (ETH, WBTC, USDC). A sharp price correction in any of these could trigger systemic stress.

Overall, the Venus Core Pool demonstrates solid engineering and governance foundations, but the liquidity risk profile is elevated due to high utilisation, asset concentration, and emerging L2 bridge complexities. Immediate mitigation steps are required to protect the $1.2 B TVL and maintain user confidence.

2. Identified Attack Vectors

# Vector Description Potential Impact Likelihood*
1 Cross‑Chain Bridge Exploit The L2 adapters rely on a custom optimistic bridge (Venus‑Bridge) that aggregates state roots from multiple roll‑ups. A malicious validator could submit a fraudulent state root, allowing the attacker to mint synthetic assets on L2 and withdraw them on Ethereum. Loss of up to $300 M (≈25 % of TVL) in synthetic assets, cascading liquidations. Medium
2 Oracle Feed Manipulation (L2 assets) For newer L2 tokens (e.g., OP, ARB) the primary feed is a proprietary VTX oracle with a 30‑minute update window. An attacker controlling a majority of VTX nodes could feed stale or manipulated prices, triggering under‑collateralised loans. Forced liquidations, loss of collateral up to $150 M. Medium‑High
3 Governance Attack (Flash‑Loan‑Based Vote Buying) The DAO’s voting power is proportional to VRT holdings. An attacker could flash‑loan VRT, acquire a temporary majority, and pass a malicious upgrade (e.g., change interest rate model or disable liquidation). Full control over protocol parameters, potential “rug‑pull” of funds. Low‑Medium (mitigated by 2‑day timelock, but timelock bypass via timelock contract upgrade is possible).
4 Liquidation Bot Front‑Running High utilisation creates a dense liquidation queue. Sophisticated bots can front‑run liquidation transactions, capturing the liquidation bonus and leaving the protocol with insufficient collateral coverage. Erosion of protocol reserves, loss of up to $30 M over a volatile week. High
5 Re‑entrancy in L2 Deposit/Withdraw Path The L2 deposit contract uses a callback pattern to notify the core pool. Insufficient re‑entrancy guard could allow an attacker to recursively call withdraw() before the balance is updated. Double‑spend of deposited assets, loss of $10‑20 M. Low (code review shows guard, but edge‑case in custom L2 token wrappers).
6 Interest Rate Model Manipulation The interest rate model is a piecewise linear function with parameters stored in a mutable storage slot. An attacker with governance rights could set rates to zero, encouraging massive borrowing and draining liquidity. Systemic liquidity crunch, loss of $200 M in collateral. Low (requires governance).
7 Smart‑Contract Upgrade Proxy Misconfiguration The UUPS proxy’s implementation address is stored in a public variable that can be overwritten by the admin. A compromised admin key could point to a malicious implementation. Full contract takeover, loss of all TVL. Low (admin key is multi‑sig, but social‑engineering risk exists).

*Likelihood is assessed qualitatively based on current controls, historical incidents, and attacker incentives.

3. Prioritized Technical Recommendations

Priority Recommendation Rationale Implementation Steps Estimated Effort
P1 Introduce Multi‑Oracle Redundancy for L2 Assets Reduces single‑point‑of‑failure risk of VTX oracle. 1. Integrate Chainlink or Band feeds for each L2 token.
2. Deploy a median‑price aggregator contract.
3. Add fallback logic in the price‑oracle module.		 2‑3 weeks (contract dev + audit).
P2 Tighten Bridge Finality & Fraud Proof Window Mitigates bridge state‑root manipulation. 1. Extend fraud‑proof window from 30 min to 2 h for L2 → Ethereum.
2. Require a quorum of ≥2/3 validators to sign state roots.
3. Add on‑chain challenge contract with bounty.		 4‑5 weeks (bridge redesign + testnet).
P3 Dynamic Liquidity Caps & Utilisation Alerts Prevents over‑leveraging during market stress. 1. Deploy a monitoring oracle that tracks utilisation per asset.
2. Auto‑adjust borrowing caps when utilisation >80 %.
3. Emit on‑chain events for off‑chain alerting (Slack/Discord).		 1‑2 weeks (oracle + governance proposal).
P4 Upgrade Governance Timelock to 7‑Day + Multi‑Sig Execution Increases resistance to flash‑loan vote attacks. 1. Replace 2‑day timelock with 7‑day timelock contract.
2. Require 3‑of‑5 multi‑sig for any upgrade proposal.
3. Conduct DAO vote to approve change.		 2 weeks (contract deployment + DAO process).
P5 Implement Liquidation Bot Whitelisting & Anti‑Front‑Running Mechanism Reduces profit‑driven front‑running that harms protocol health. 1. Introduce a “liquidation queue” with a first‑come‑first‑serve order.
2. Allow only whitelisted bots (subject to KYC) to execute liquidations.
3. Add a “partial‑fill” option to spread liquidation impact.		 3‑4 weeks (contract changes + governance).
P6 Add Re‑entrancy Guard & Formal Verification on L2 Deposit/Withdraw Guarantees safety against edge‑case re‑entrancy. 1. Apply OpenZeppelin ReentrancyGuard to all external entry points.
2. Run formal verification (e.g., Certora) on the L2 wrapper contracts.		 1‑2 weeks (code audit).
P7 Periodic Stress‑Testing & Monte‑Carlo Simulations Quantifies systemic risk under extreme market moves. 1. Build a simulation framework (Python/Hardhat) that models price shocks, liquidity drains, and bridge delays.
2. Run quarterly “red‑team” exercises.		 Ongoing (initial setup 2 weeks).
P8 Diversify Collateral Mix Lowers concentration risk. 1. Incentivise new assets (e.g., stablecoins on L2, tokenised real‑world assets).
2. Adjust risk parameters to allow higher LTV for diversified assets.		 4‑6 weeks (incentive design + community outreach).

Implementation Roadmap (Suggested Timeline)

Week Milestone
1‑2 Deploy multi‑oracle aggregator (P1) & re‑entrancy guard (P6).
3‑5 Bridge fraud‑proof upgrade (P2) + dynamic liquidity caps (P3).
6‑7 Governance timelock extension (P4) + DAO approval.
8‑10 Liquidation queue & bot whitelist (P5).
11‑12 Launch stress‑testing framework (P7).
13‑16 Collateral diversification program (P8).
Ongoing Continuous monitoring, bug‑bounty payouts, and quarterly audits.

4. Risk Score

Dimension Score (1‑10) Comments
Smart‑Contract Integrity 6 Well‑audited core contracts; upgrade proxy introduces moderate risk.
Oracle & Pricing 7 Strong mainnet feeds, but L2 assets lack redundancy.
Liquidity & Utilisation 8 High utilisation and concentration raise systemic risk.

WebDAV vs Google Drive vs Dropbox: Real Cost After 3 Years
description:
Last month I exported three years of bank statements and filtered every cloud storage charge. I expected to find the usual mess of $9.99 here and $11.99 there. I found something worse.

The actual numbers (36 months)

I used to run a hybrid setup:

  • Google Drive (personal): $1.99/month = $71.64
  • iCloud+ 200GB (shared with family): $2.99/month = $107.64
  • OneDrive (work, reimbursed): $0 out of pocket
  • Dropbox Plus (side project backups): $11.99/month = $431.64

Total personal spend: $610.92 over three years.

Then in 2025 I switched the personal side to a $5.5 lifetime WebDAV mount + a $5/month VPS running Nextcloud. After 8 months:

  • WebDAV mount license (one-time): $5.50
  • VPS: $5 × 8 = $40
  • Total: $45.50

If I keep the VPS for the full 3 years, total = $5.50 + $180 = $185.50. That's a $425.42 savings — more than the $5.5 license cost back 77 times.

What I actually lost

This is the part nobody talks about. Going from Dropbox to self-hosted meant:

Lost features:

  • Selective sync (not needed with WebDAV mount — it streams)
  • Real-time co-editing (I never used it)
  • Built-in document scanner (use phone camera)
  • Smart file suggestions (didn't really miss these)

Gained features:

  • 1TB of storage instead of 200GB (VPS disk can be any size)
  • No file size limit per upload
  • No "this file too large for syncing" errors
  • Full control over backup retention
  • My files are not used to train AI models (verified: my Nextcloud instance, my rules)

The hidden cost I almost forgot

I forgot to add one line item in the math above: the time I spent on the Dropbox support chat. Between 2022 and 2024, I had three billing disputes (overcharges, double-charges, accidental yearly upgrade). Each one cost me 20-40 minutes of email tag.

With my self-hosted setup, the only "support" is reading the Nextcloud docs. When something breaks, I fix it. No billing department, no renewal price hikes, no "sorry, we changed our terms" emails.

Who should NOT switch

If you fit any of these, stay with mainstream sync:

  • You need real-time co-editing with people outside your household
  • You use Google Docs / Sheets / Slides as your primary work tool
  • You have less than 50GB of files (the free tiers cover you)
  • You don't want to spend a Saturday afternoon setting up a VPS

Who SHOULD switch

  • You have more than 200GB of personal files
  • You're paying $10+/month for any sync service
  • You have a NAS or home server you already maintain
  • You care about long-term file ownership
  • You want a one-time payment, not a recurring charge

The $5.5 lifetime license

I bought ScsDriver when they were running a lifetime deal for $5.5. That license covers all my devices — Windows, Mac, iPhone, Android. One payment. No subscription. No "premium tier" upsell.

Three years from now, when Dropbox is charging $14.99/month and iCloud+ is $4.99/month, my WebDAV mount will still cost $0.00 in license fees. The VPS might go up to $7, but I'll still be ahead by hundreds of dollars.

The boring conclusion

Cloud storage pricing is designed to be forgettable. $1.99 here, $11.99 there — it doesn't feel like much until you add it up over years. A $5.5 lifetime WebDAV mount cuts the recurring cost to zero. The setup takes a Saturday. The math takes 30 seconds.

If you've been on the fence about switching, do the spreadsheet. Add up what you've actually paid over 3 years. Then subtract $5.5. Then think about what else you could buy with the rest.

title: AWS Agent Registry now supports custom metadata for registry records
description:
AWS Agent Registry is the centralized, governed catalog for agents, MCP servers, agent skills, gateways, and custom resources within your organization. As organizations scale to hundreds of such resources, a name and description alone are insufficient for effective governance and discovery. Custom metadata lets you extend every registry record with your organization's own structured fields, so both people and automated systems can find and govern resources consistently.

With custom metadata, publishers can record fields like team ownership, data classification, or review status directly on each registry record. You define a schema once per registry with common attributes, then extend it with type-specific fields — such as a model family for agent records. Each field supports free text, a URL, a Boolean, or a choice from a list of allowed values, and the registry validates required fields and values on every record creation or update. You can then filter search results on any custom metadata field from the AWS Management Console, the AWS CLI, the AWS SDKs, or the registry's MCP endpoint.

Custom metadata is available in all AWS Regions where AWS Agent Registry is available: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Europe (Ireland).

To learn more, visit the AWS Agent Registry documentation. For detailed setup guidance, see Define a custom metadata schema and Set custom metadata values on a record.
