title: HiPPT: Physiology-Grounded Wearable PPG Representation Learning via Multi-Scope Text Alignment
description:
arXiv:2610.14489v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reusable wearable PPG representations should capture local pulse morphology and broader physiological regularities. Existing pretraining objectives, however, usually apply supervision at the recording or pair level, overlooking that different concepts become reliable over different scopes of waveform evidence. We propose HiPPT, a physiology-grounded framework that matches each supervision source to its appropriate evidence scope. We construct a PPG-Text corpus of over 4 million wrist-worn recordings from 202K users, pairing recordings with waveform-derived morphology and metadata-derived context descriptions. HiPPT combines record-level morphology alignment, which grounds individual recordings in pulse characteristics, with cross-recording context alignment, which aggregates recordings sharing the same metadata tuple to capture context-consistent regularities. Waveform-guided text modeling further recovers masked contextual concepts from PPG patch representations, providing fine-grained waveform-text supervision. Across six downstream tasks spanning blood pressure, vascular stiffness, physiological attributes, and cross-dataset heart-rate estimation, HiPPT achieves the best result on the primary linear-probing metrics. The aligned space also supports zero-shot profiling of age group, sex, and BMI category, individually and jointly, with performance improving as more recordings are aggregated. These results show that evidence-scope matching yields transferable and semantically accessible wearable PPG representations. Code and pretrained weights will be released.

title: Healthtech Metering in Go: Provision a Scoped API Key with a Setup Script
description:
TL;DR: A setup job should mint a credential restricted to one customer-usage writer, place it in a secret store without printing it, authenticate with the stored value, and fail unless the returned subject, tenant, and scopes exactly match the request. For a healthtech meter, that identity check matters more than a green “secret written” response: the invoice pipeline must be able to show which workload was allowed to append usage for which customer account, while the credential itself stays out of logs and build artifacts.

Treat bootstrap as a small security transaction with an explicit commit point. Provisioning is not complete when a key exists. It is complete only after the key has crossed into the secret store, the setup process has discarded its plaintext copy, and an authenticated probe proves that the stored value represents the intended machine identity. This framing also forces failure handling into the design: before the commit point, any partial key is untrusted and must be removed; after it, rotation becomes an ordinary lifecycle operation with a known owner and version.

How should a setup script provision and verify a scoped API key?

Imagine the incident review, without inventing an incident: a healthtech platform receives one usage event for customer clinic-042, the event later contributes to a metered invoice, and the audit trail says only that “CI” wrote it. The dashboard is green. The useful questions are less comfortable: which subject authenticated, which tenant boundary applied, which scopes were effective, and did the same credential have permission to read patient data or alter invoices?

If those answers cannot be recovered without exposing the key, the bootstrap design has already failed its primary decision axis: auditability of access. The invariant is straightforward: a credential used to append billable usage must resolve to one stable workload subject, one expected account boundary, and the smallest effective scope set. An environment name such as production is context, not identity.

No identity, no commit.

I would page on repeated identity-verification failures, unexpected subjects, or broader scopes. I would not page merely because a rotation occurred. A rotation is expected state change; an accepted credential that cannot prove its owner is the event that threatens attribution.

Model the handoff before choosing an API

There is no universal API-key provisioning protocol, so keep vendor routes outside the safety logic. The core needs three adapters: a provisioner that returns a secret once, a store that accepts bytes under a versioned name, and an identity endpoint that reports the authenticated principal. That separation lets a team replace an account API or secret backend without weakening the checks that decide whether bootstrap succeeded.

For the example meter, request only an append permission for a single tenant. Do not grant a generic admin scope because setup is convenient. Do not reuse the deployment credential either; deployment and usage submission produce different audit questions and deserve different subjects.

Boundary Required evidence Reject when
Provisioning requested subject, tenant, and scope set the request is ambiguous or overbroad
Secret write versioned secret reference, not plaintext the destination is mutable without version evidence
Authentication returned subject, tenant, and effective scopes any field differs from the request
Audit request ID and secret version the record contains the key or its hash

Do not log a key fingerprint as a consolation prize. A stable fingerprint becomes another correlator, is unnecessary for the decision above, and can encourage teams to treat possession evidence as identity evidence. Log the non-secret subject, tenant, scope set, secret version, and request ID instead. OWASP's secrets guidance recommends centralized storage, least privilege, rotation, expiration where possible, and care to prevent secrets from reaching logs.

That is enough evidence.

Make the verification path executable

The following program is deliberately adapter-driven. Its in-memory implementations make the example runnable with go run, while production adapters would call an account control plane and a secret manager over authenticated, encrypted connections. The safety function does not know their URLs.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "crypto/rand"
    "encoding/base64"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "slices"
)

type Request struct {
    Subject string
    Tenant  string
    Scopes  []string
}

type Identity struct {
    Subject string
    Tenant  string
    Scopes  []string
}

type Provisioner interface {
    Create(ctx context.Context, request Request) ([]byte, error)
    Revoke(ctx context.Context, credential []byte) error
}

type SecretStore interface {
    Put(ctx context.Context, name string, value []byte) (version string, err error)
    Get(ctx context.Context, name, version string) ([]byte, error)
    Delete(ctx context.Context, name, version string) error
}

type Authenticator interface {
    WhoAmI(ctx context.Context, credential []byte) (Identity, error)
}

func bootstrap(ctx context.Context, request Request, name string,
    p Provisioner, store SecretStore, auth Authenticator) (string, error) {

    credential, err := p.Create(ctx, request)
    if err != nil {
        return "", fmt.Errorf("provision credential: %w", err)
    }
    committed := false
    defer func() {
        if !committed {
            _ = p.Revoke(ctx, credential)
        }
        clear(credential)
    }()

    version, err := store.Put(ctx, name, credential)
    if err != nil {
        return "", fmt.Errorf("store credential: %w", err)
    }

    stored, err := store.Get(ctx, name, version)
    if err != nil {
        _ = store.Delete(ctx, name, version)
        return "", fmt.Errorf("read stored version: %w", err)
    }
    defer clear(stored)

    identity, err := auth.WhoAmI(ctx, stored)
    if err != nil {
        _ = store.Delete(ctx, name, version)
        return "", fmt.Errorf("authenticate stored credential: %w", err)
    }
    wantScopes := append([]string(nil), request.Scopes...)
    gotScopes := append([]string(nil), identity.Scopes...)
    slices.Sort(wantScopes)
    slices.Sort(gotScopes)
    if identity.Subject != request.Subject || identity.Tenant != request.Tenant ||
        !slices.Equal(gotScopes, wantScopes) {
        _ = store.Delete(ctx, name, version)
        return "", errors.New("verified identity does not match requested boundary")
    }

    committed = true
    return version, nil
}

type memoryBackend struct {
    value    []byte
    request  Request
    version  string
}

func (m *memoryBackend) Create(_ context.Context, request Request) ([]byte, error) {
    raw := make([]byte, 32)
    if _, err := rand.Read(raw); err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    m.request = request
    return []byte(base64.RawURLEncoding.EncodeToString(raw)), nil
}

func (m *memoryBackend) Revoke(_ context.Context, _ []byte) error { return nil }

func (m *memoryBackend) Put(_ context.Context, _ string, value []byte) (string, error) {
    m.value = append([]byte(nil), value...)
    m.version = "1"
    return m.version, nil
}

func (m *memoryBackend) Get(_ context.Context, _, version string) ([]byte, error) {
    if version != m.version {
        return nil, errors.New("unknown version")
    }
    return append([]byte(nil), m.value...), nil
}

func (m *memoryBackend) Delete(_ context.Context, _, _ string) error {
    clear(m.value)
    m.value = nil
    return nil
}

func (m *memoryBackend) WhoAmI(_ context.Context, credential []byte) (Identity, error) {
    if !slices.Equal(credential, m.value) {
        return Identity{}, errors.New("unauthorized")
    }
    return Identity(m.request), nil
}

func main() {
    backend := &memoryBackend{}
    request := Request{
        Subject: "ci-usage-writer",
        Tenant:  "clinic-042",
        Scopes:  []string{"usage:append"},
    }
    version, err := bootstrap(context.Background(), request,
        "healthtech/clinic-042/usage-writer", backend, backend, backend)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Printf("bootstrap verified: subject=%s tenant=%s secret_version=%s\n",
        request.Subject, request.Tenant, version)
}

The compensating path deserves scrutiny. If storage or verification fails, the program deletes the untrusted stored version and attempts revocation. Production code should use a short, separate cleanup context so cancellation of the main setup context does not prevent cleanup; it should also emit a non-secret request ID for reconciliation. The example keeps one context to expose the transaction shape without pretending that generic adapters share retry semantics.

This sample requires Go 1.21 because it uses clear and the slices package.

One subtle limit remains: Go's clear reduces accidental retention in these byte slices, but it cannot promise that no copy exists elsewhere in a runtime, transport, or backend. The stronger controls are architectural: never place the returned value in command arguments, environment dumps, formatted errors, test snapshots, or shell tracing; restrict the setup runner; and make the secret short-lived enough that rotation is routine.

Test the identity mismatch, not only the happy path

A useful test changes the returned identity after the secret write. Make the fake authenticator return clinic-024, add usage:read, or replace ci-usage-writer with a human subject. Each mutation must make bootstrap fail and trigger deletion plus revocation. Also test a store that acknowledges Put but cannot read the exact version back; “latest” is a race-prone reference when two setup jobs overlap.

Test logs too. Feed a recognizable canary credential through every error path, capture process output, and fail the test if the canary appears. This is where a bland success metric stops helping. The check should distinguish these states: provisioning never happened, provisioned but not stored, stored but not authenticated, identity mismatch, cleanup incomplete, and verified.

Retries require idempotency at the adapter boundary. If the provisioning service accepts an idempotency token, derive a new opaque token for one bootstrap attempt and persist its non-secret request ID. If it does not, reconcile by requested subject and tenant before creating another credential, then revoke superseded credentials after a verified replacement exists. Never infer success from an earlier process exit code alone.

Know when a static key is the wrong primitive

This pattern applies when the target service accepts an API key and the CI system must bootstrap it. It does not make a long-lived bearer secret ideal. When both ends support workload federation or another short-lived, audience-bound mechanism, prefer that design: the pipeline exchanges an existing workload identity for temporary access instead of storing a reusable credential. OAuth 2.0 defines bearer-token handling, and RFC 8707 defines resource indicators that can restrict where an access token is intended to be used; neither specification turns an arbitrary API key into a federated identity.

The decision is operational. Static bootstrap is defensible when its scope is narrow, its owner is machine-specific, rotation and revocation are tested, reads from the secret store are auditable, and the authenticated service can report effective identity. The limitation of this pattern is the reusable bearer secret: it is a poor fit when the service cannot expose identity, when all keys inherit account-wide permissions, or when a CI runner cannot keep secret output out of logs. The trade-off is extra setup and rotation work in exchange for compatibility with services that do not accept workload federation; that reason disappears as soon as both sides can exchange a workload identity for short-lived, audience-bound access.

Prefer federation then.

Before enabling the usage writer, run one synthetic event against a non-billable test tenant, verify the authenticated subject in the access record, and confirm that a forbidden operation is actually denied. Then alert on identity drift and cleanup failures, not on dashboard color. The final artifact is evidence of a bounded principal, not evidence that a string was copied successfully.

Sources

  • https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Secrets_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6750
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8707

title: Verifier-Grounded Agentic RL for Provably Correct Code
description:
arXiv:2610.19298v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning for code usually rewards passing tests, which a model can do while remaining wrong on the inputs the tests do not cover. A program verifier instead decides whether a program satisfies a formal specification for all inputs. Language models are almost always paired with verifiers at inference time only, and turning a verifier into a reward raises two difficulties. It reports only acceptance or rejection, which gives no gradient when every attempt fails, and a policy can cheat it, most simply by telling it to assume what the proof was supposed to establish. We build an agentic environment and reward that address both. The reward reads the verifier's diagnostics rather than its verdict, scoring a candidate by the weighted fraction of proof obligations it discharges, extended with hidden probes from a reference proof's annotations. An integrity audit outranks the verifier, rejecting any candidate that alters the specification or assumes what it was meant to prove. The model works as an agent against a live verifier over many turns, with a separately trained proof specialist as a frozen collaborator. Across Qwen3 models from 1.7B to 14B and a 35B Qwen3.6 mixture-of-experts model, held-out verification on code generation rises from 66.1% to 93.5% on DafnyBench and from 56.3% to 100% on SWE-Proof. This reward leads every other training signal we compare, including a binary pass-or-fail reward trained under otherwise identical settings, with the widest margin on code generation. When the agent must also deliver the repository patch, graded by each project's withheld tests, the fraction of held-out issues it resolves rises from 59.6% to 72.5%. Evaluated unchanged on three verification suites withheld from training, the checkpoints improve on all of them, including one whose language and verifier are absent from training.

title: Designing clear search results for a healthcare directory.
description:
A healthcare directory should help people answer three questions quickly: What kind of provider is this? Where are they located? How can I contact them?

Make results easy to compare

Use a consistent order for each result: provider name, specialty or service, city, address, and contact options. Distinguish individual professionals from clinics and other organizations so visitors understand what they are opening.

Keep descriptions short in search results. Detailed information belongs on the profile page.

Make the next action clear

Use specific labels such as “View profile,” “Call,” and “Get directions.” If online booking is unavailable, avoid a button that suggests an appointment can be reserved.

A phone number should remain readable even when it is also clickable. This helps people who want to copy it or call from another device.

Explain empty results

When a search returns nothing, keep the search terms visible and suggest a practical next step, such as removing a location filter or trying a broader specialty.

Avoid silently replacing the requested location with unrelated results.

Check the mobile experience

Review long provider names, addresses, and translated labels on a narrow screen. Contact buttons should remain easy to identify, and opening a result should preserve a clear way back to the search.

These are design suggestions, not findings from a completed usability study.

GjejeMjekun is a healthcare directory in Kosovo where users can search for providers by name, specialty, or location. It provides a concrete setting for considering these design questions. I share it as a project I like; I do not work for or represent it.

title: Your Mentee Has Been Put on a Performance Plan
description:
Your mentee joins the call and does not turn the camera on. After a minute of small talk they say it. Their manager gave them a performance improvement plan yesterday. Sixty days, four written goals, a meeting every Friday. They sound embarrassed to be telling you, and a little afraid of what you will think.

The first thing they need from you is not advice. It is evidence that this conversation is still safe. Say so plainly. Thank you for telling me. This does not change how I see you, and we will work out what to do together.

Then help them read the document properly, because most people only read it once, in shock. Go through each goal and ask the same questions. What exactly would count as meeting this? Who decides? Is there a number, a deadline, an example of what good looks like? Vague goals are common, and a vague goal cannot be met on purpose. Encourage them to ask their manager, in writing and in a calm tone, to make each one concrete.

Be honest about what a plan can mean. In some companies it is a genuine attempt to help someone recover. In others it is mostly paperwork on the way to an exit. You probably cannot tell which from the outside, and neither can they yet. So help them prepare for both without despair. Work hard on the goals as if recovery is possible, and quietly update the CV as if it might not be. Neither one undermines the other.

Help them build a weekly rhythm. A short written note to the manager each Friday, before the meeting, listing what they did against each goal. That record helps them think clearly, and it means the final judgement rests on facts rather than impressions.

Watch their health as well as their work. Sixty days under scrutiny is exhausting, and people on plans often stop sleeping, stop asking questions and start hiding small mistakes, which makes everything worse.

Know your limits. You are not their lawyer, their manager or their HR representative. If something seems unfair, point them to the people who can actually act on it.

And whatever happens at day sixty, stay. People remember who kept turning up while things were going badly.

– Asael Shinder

title: HowTo: AI Pair Programming with IBM Bob
description:
AI pair programming becomes much more valuable when it goes beyond asking an AI assistant to generate an entire application from a single prompt. A better approach is to treat AI as a development partner that works alongside you throughout the engineering process, from understanding requirements and planning the solution to implementation, testing, refactoring, and documentation.

That's the approach explored in this AI Pair Programming with IBM Bob tutorial. Instead of relying on one-shot code generation, the tutorial demonstrates a structured workflow for building a FastAPI To-Do API while keeping the developer involved in important decisions and validation.

Start with Requirements, Not Code

Before generating anything, the workflow begins by defining what the application should actually do. Clear requirements give Bob the context needed to understand the intended functionality instead of making assumptions about the solution.

This is an important shift in AI-assisted development. The goal isn't to write the longest prompt possible. The goal is to give the AI enough relevant context to understand the problem and expected outcome.

Plan Before You Implement

Once the requirements are established, Plan mode can be used to turn them into a structured implementation approach.

This gives the developer an opportunity to review the proposed direction before code is generated. Missing requirements, assumptions, or architectural decisions can be identified and refined while they are still part of the plan rather than after they have become implementation.

AI makes implementation faster, but that makes good planning even more valuable.

Move from Plan to Working Code

After reviewing the plan, Agent mode can help translate that plan into an implementation.

In the tutorial, this process is used to build the FastAPI application. But generated code isn't treated as the final result. The developer remains part of the loop by reviewing the implementation and validating whether the application matches the original requirements.

The workflow looks like this:

Developer defines intent
        ↓
Bob creates a plan
        ↓
Developer reviews decisions
        ↓
Bob implements
        ↓
Developer and Bob validate

That's much closer to pair programming than simply asking an AI tool to "build this for me."

Keep the Context Focused

Another important lesson from the tutorial is context management.

Long AI conversations can accumulate requirements, experiments, failed approaches, code snippets, and unrelated information. Eventually, all of that context can begin influencing later work.

Using fresh context windows for focused stages of development helps keep the implementation aligned with the current objective.

For larger projects, this becomes increasingly important. Good AI pair programming isn't only about providing more context. It's about providing the right context at the right time.

Refactor Instead of Stopping at "It Works"

Getting an application to run is only one stage of software engineering.

Once the initial implementation is working, IBM Bob can assist with reviewing and refactoring the code to improve its structure and overall quality.

AI-generated code shouldn't automatically be considered finished simply because it executes successfully. Just like human-written software, it should be reviewed, improved, tested, and validated before being treated as complete.

Generate Tests and Validate the Application

Testing becomes another part of the collaborative workflow.

The tutorial demonstrates using Bob to generate unit tests and validate application behavior. Rather than separating testing from implementation, testing becomes part of the same development cycle.

The workflow therefore evolves naturally from generation into verification:

Generate → Review → Refactor → Test → Validate

This helps shift AI-assisted development away from pure code generation and toward complete engineering outcomes.

Document What You Built

Documentation is frequently postponed until the end of a project or skipped entirely.

With an AI pair-programming workflow, documentation can become part of the development process itself. After the implementation stabilizes, Bob can help create technical documentation based on the completed work.

That means future developers receive more than a repository full of code. They also gain context around what was built and how the application is structured.

Take the Application to Docker

The tutorial completes the journey by building and running the application with Docker.

This demonstrates that AI pair programming doesn't need to end when the source code has been generated. The workflow can continue through testing, documentation, packaging, and running the application.

The Complete AI Pair-Programming Workflow 

Requirements
    ↓
Plan
    ↓
Review
    ↓
Generate Code
    ↓
Validate
    ↓
Refactor
    ↓
Test
    ↓
Document

What I like about this workflow is its structure.

The developer doesn't disappear from the process, and Bob isn't treated as a one-click code generator. Instead, both contribute differently. The developer provides requirements, intent, judgment, feedback, and validation, while Bob helps accelerate the implementation-heavy parts of the process.

That's ultimately what makes AI pair programming different from simple AI code generation.

The most effective workflow isn't necessarily the one that generates the most code from the fewest prompts. It's the one that helps you move from an idea to a well-planned, reviewed, tested, and documented implementation while staying in control of the engineering decisions.

title: VLX-Go: Robust Embodied Tracking through Multi-Stage Learning and On-Policy Refinement
description:
arXiv:2610.19361v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Embodied visual tracking requires a robot to identify a designated target from visual observations and control its own motion to follow that target through an environment. Following an isolated person is a comparatively simple demonstration of embodied visual tracking, but following the intended person among distractors remains challenging. Existing methods exhibit a substantial drop in success from single-target to distractor tracking, motivating a focus on the shared spaces that person-following robots must navigate. We present \method{}, a vision--language waypoint policy built around the hypothesis that visual and language representations should be aligned before tracking-specific motion is learned. The policy combines complementary frozen visual encoders, multiscale temporal context, a transformer backbone, and a lightweight head for robot-centric waypoint prediction. Its training progresses through vision--language alignment, multimodal reasoning mid-training, and tracking specialization on 19,532 oracle episodes. Compared with 41.54\% distractor-tracking success for our earlier OmTrackVLA model, the complete multi-stage recipe achieves 55.80\%. We then explore on-policy refinement using filtered oracle labels for states visited by the policy. This preliminary study adds 2.42 percentage points of distractor-tracking success, reaching 58.22\%, while reducing collision rate by 1.99 pts. The final policy records the highest distractor- and ambiguous-tracking success rates among the compared methods. These results support staged multimodal learning as a promising direction for tracking among distractors and motivate further study of on-policy refinement for person following in shared spaces.

title: MagicGarment: Benchmarking Single-Image Standalone 3D Garment Reconstruction
description:
arXiv:2610.19623v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Single-image 3D reconstruction has advanced rapidly, yet standalone garments remain challenging due to thin-shell geometry, open boundaries, and layered structures. Existing datasets and evaluation protocols provide limited support for systematic evaluation in this setting. We introduce MagicGarment, a benchmark for single-image standalone 3D garment reconstruction with 1,518 professionally constructed assets across 17 composite garment types, aligned multimodal annotations, and a unified evaluation protocol. We further establish a garment-aware reference baseline by adapting a pretrained image-to-3D backbone at two levels: Grounded Semantic Refinement (GSR) provides garment-focused visual conditioning, while Flow-Time-Route LoRA (FTR-LoRA) adapts the frozen 3D generative backbone using flow-timestep, token-routing, and expert-load information. Experiments demonstrate MagicGarment's benchmark utility and the effectiveness of garment-aware adaptation. Project page: https://1019538157.github.io/MagicGarment/.

title: Mastering Rust: A Practical Guide to Safe, Fast Systems Programming
description:
Introduction

Rust has taken the software development world by storm, promising memory safety without a garbage collector and performance on par with C and C++. If you’ve been curious about why Rust is becoming the go‑to language for systems programming, embedded development, and even web services, this article will walk you through the core concepts, practical code snippets, and best practices to get you productive fast.

Pro tip: The best way to learn Rust is by writing small, focused programs that exercise the language’s ownership model. The examples below are designed to be copy‑and‑paste ready.

Why Rust?

Feature Traditional Languages Rust
Memory safety Manual malloc/free → bugs Ownership + Borrow Checker
Data races Hard to avoid in multithreaded code Compile‑time guarantees
Zero‑cost abstractions Often hidden runtime cost Abstractions compile down to efficient machine code
Modern tooling Varies by ecosystem cargo, rustfmt, clippy

Rust’s ownership model eliminates many classes of bugs that plague C/C++ developers, while its zero‑cost abstractions let you write expressive code without sacrificing speed.

Getting Started with Cargo

Cargo is Rust’s built‑in package manager and build system. Create a new project with:

cargo new hello_rust --bin
cd hello_rust
cargo run

You’ll see:

   Compiling hello_rust v0.1.0 (/path/to/hello_rust)
    Finished dev [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 0.45s
     Running `target/debug/hello_rust`
Hello, world!

Cargo handles dependencies, builds, testing, and publishing to crates.io—all from the command line.

Ownership, Borrowing, and Lifetimes

At the heart of Rust lies ownership. Every value has a single owner; when the owner goes out of scope, the value is dropped. Borrowing lets you reference data without taking ownership, and lifetimes ensure those references remain valid.

Example: Moving vs Borrowing 

fn main() {
    let s = String::from("Rust");
    takes_ownership(s); // s is moved here
    // println!("{}", s); // ❌ compile error: value borrowed after move

    let t = String::from("Lang");
    let len = calculate_length(&t); // borrow immutably
    println!("The length of '{}' is {}", t, len);
}

fn takes_ownership(some_string: String) {
    println!("Got: {}", some_string);
    // some_string is dropped here
}

fn calculate_length(s: &String) -> usize {
    s.len()
}

The compiler enforces these rules at compile time, preventing dangling pointers and double frees.

Error Handling: Result and ? Operator

Rust distinguishes between recoverable (Result<T, E>) and unrecoverable (panic!) errors. The ? operator propagates errors succinctly.

use std::fs::File;
use std::io::{self, Read};

fn read_file(path: &str) -> io::Result<String> {
    let mut file = File::open(path)?; // Propagates error if file not found
    let mut contents = String::new();
    file.read_to_string(&mut contents)?;
    Ok(contents)
}

fn main() {
    match read_file("Cargo.toml") {
        Ok(text) => println!("File contents:\n{}", text),
        Err(e) => eprintln!("Error reading file: {}", e),
    }
}

Concurrency Made Safe

Rust’s type system guarantees that data races are impossible at compile time. Let’s spawn threads that share read‑only data.

use std::thread;

fn main() {
    let numbers = vec![1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
    let handles: Vec<_> = numbers
        .chunks(2)
        .map(|chunk| {
            thread::spawn(move || {
                let sum: i32 = chunk.iter().sum();
                println!("Chunk sum: {}", sum);
            })
        })
        .collect();

    for h in handles {
        h.join().unwrap();
    }
}

Because each thread receives its own chunk slice (&[i32]), the borrow checker ensures no mutable aliasing occurs.

Building a Simple HTTP Server with hyper

Rust excels at networking. Below is a minimal HTTP server using the popular hyper crate.

# Cargo.toml
[dependencies]
hyper = { version = "0.14", features = ["full"] }
tokio = { version = "1", features = ["full"] }

use hyper::{Body, Request, Response, Server};
use hyper::service::{make_service_fn, service_fn};
use std::convert::Infallible;
use tokio::runtime::Runtime;

async fn handle(_: Request<Body>) -> Result<Response<Body>, Infallible> {
    Ok(Response::new(Body::from("Hello from Rust!")))
}

fn main() {
    let rt = Runtime::new().unwrap();
    rt.block_on(async {
        let make_svc = make_service_fn(|_conn| async {
            Ok::<_, Infallible>(service_fn(handle))
        });

        let addr = ([127, 0, 0, 1], 3000).into();
        let server = Server::bind(&addr).serve(make_svc);

        println!("Listening on http://{}", addr);
        if let Err(e) = server.await {
            eprintln!("server error: {}", e);
        }
    });
}

Run cargo run, and visit http://127.0.0.1:3000 to see the response. This tiny server showcases async/await, Tokio’s runtime, and zero‑cost abstractions—all hallmarks of Rust.

Testing and Benchmarking

Rust ships with a built‑in test harness. Write unit tests in the same file:

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn test_calculate_length() {
        let s = String::from("test");
        assert_eq!(calculate_length(&s), 4);
    }

    #[test]
    #[should_panic]
    fn test_panic() {
        panic!("this test should panic");
    }
}

Run with cargo test. For performance, use the criterion crate to write reliable benchmarks.

Deploying Rust Applications

When you’re ready to ship, compile a statically linked binary:

cargo build --release
# Binary located at target/release/your_project

The resulting executable can be deployed to any Linux server without needing a runtime. Containerizing with Docker is also straightforward:

FROM rust:latest AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN cargo build --release

FROM debian:buster-slim
COPY --from=builder /app/target/release/your_project /usr/local/bin/your_project
CMD ["your_project"]

Community and Learning Resources

  • The Rust Book – the official guide, free online.
  • rustlings – interactive exercises that solidify fundamentals.
  • crates.io – discover reusable libraries, from serde (serialization) to actix-web (web frameworks).
  • Discord & Reddit – vibrant communities ready to help newcomers.

Conclusion

Rust’s blend of safety, speed, and modern ergonomics makes it a compelling choice for a wide range of projects—from low‑level system utilities to high‑throughput web services. By mastering ownership, leveraging Cargo, and embracing async patterns, you’ll write robust code that compiles with confidence.

Recommended Tools

When you’re ready to host your Rust services, consider reliable cloud providers that offer excellent performance and developer‑friendly pricing.

  • Kinsta provides managed cloud hosting with a focus on speed and security. Their platform supports Docker containers and custom binaries, making Rust deployments a breeze. Check out their plans at Kinsta for a seamless experience.

  • DigitalOcean offers flexible droplets and Kubernetes clusters that are perfect for scaling Rust applications. Their straightforward pricing and extensive documentation help you get a production‑grade environment up and running quickly. Learn more at DigitalOcean.

Happy coding in Rust!

title: Go Logistics Queue 2026: Publish Per Waiter Under Burst Recovery
description:
Short answer: send a small recipient-specific delta when a customer may see only their own queue position; send a whole-queue snapshot only to an authorized display that genuinely needs the entire ordered set. For a small SaaS, the least complex defensible design is usually a versioned delta plus a periodic or on-demand snapshot for repair. Every update carries a monotonically increasing queue version, clients reject older versions, and a detected gap triggers resynchronization.

The page says customer queue display stale, and the on-call sees an apparently healthy publisher beside a growing count of clients whose acknowledged version trails the current queue version. That is the useful symptom. A page based only on publish errors arrives too late, because a successful publish says nothing about whether the customer view converged.

The publisher was green.

This distinction drives the message-size comparison. A snapshot can repair state in one delivery but repeats data that most recipients neither need nor should receive; per-recipient deltas keep the hot path small but require explicit gap detection. Do the byte arithmetic with encoded messages, then choose the smallest disclosure boundary that still meets the recovery SLO.

Should a queue publish one message per waiter?

A logistics dispatch session is a state machine. A shipment request joins a queue, changes position, becomes ready, or leaves. The customer-facing display needs to converge on an authorized projection of that state. If one subscriber misses version 418, version 419 may still arrive, and a green publish counter can coexist with a wrong screen.

The signal that should fire earlier is version lag, measured at the receiving edge: current_queue_version - last_applied_version, grouped by session and bounded by the service-level objective. Transport acknowledgements help diagnose the path, but they do not prove that the UI applied the state. Define the SLO in terms of visible convergence, such as the proportion of active displays that apply the current authorized version within the chosen time window. The target and window must come from the product's tolerance for stale queue positions; there is no honest universal number.

Start with three counters: produced versions, applied versions, and resynchronizations. Add a histogram for convergence time and a gauge for connected displays by session. Do not put customer IDs into metric labels. High-cardinality identity belongs in sampled traces or structured logs with suitable access controls and retention.

One trap is paging on a single late client. A browser in the background, a device losing radio coverage, or a closed tab can all stop acknowledging progress without indicating a service-wide failure. Page on an SLO-burning cohort; retain per-connection lag for diagnosis. Otherwise the alarm measures client churn and trains the on-call to ignore it. The limitation of this cohort view is equally plain: aggregation can hide one customer who has been stale for a long time, so the dashboard still needs a longest-lag view even when that view does not page anyone.

Message size is multiplication, not a payload contest

Compare encoded bytes over the same observation window. Let S be encoded snapshot bytes, D encoded recipient-delta bytes, N connected recipients, C queue changes, and R snapshot repairs. Ignoring shared framing for a moment, whole-queue fan-out costs roughly C * N * S; recipient deltas cost roughly C * N * D + R * S. Add transport framing, authentication metadata, retries, and compression as measured terms rather than intuition.

For a capacity-planning example, suppose a test fixture has 80 waiting customers. Its encoded authorized snapshot is 6,400 bytes and its encoded per-recipient position update is 120 bytes. With 80 connected customers and 10 queue changes, the payload arithmetic is 5,120,000 bytes for repeated snapshots versus 96,000 bytes for deltas, before repairs and framing. These are illustrative inputs, not benchmarks. Serialize your actual schema because field names, identifiers, timestamps, and encoding choices change the result.

The ratio is informative; the absolute result decides capacity.

Eighty recipients matter.

Decision concern Recipient delta Authorized snapshot
Normal-path bytes Scales with the changed projection Scales with the full authorized projection
Recovery Needs gap detection and a snapshot fetch or push Replaces prior state when accepted
Ordering Version check is mandatory Version check is still mandatory
Privacy boundary Can disclose one customer's projection Must be filtered for the display's authorization
Server work More projections or routing keys Larger serialization and filtering work
Client work Apply a transition Replace and render state

Compression does not settle the architecture. It may reduce repeated fields in snapshots, but the sender still constructs the authorized payload and the receiver still handles it. Measure compressed and uncompressed sizes with representative data, then preserve hard limits for both. The trade-off is workload-dependent: a slowly changing, publicly visible depot board can make snapshots the simpler choice, while a private customer view with frequent position changes makes whole-queue publication inappropriate. Recipient deltas are not suitable when clients cannot preserve a version or request repair; snapshots are not suitable when their contents exceed the recipient's authorization boundary.

Instrument the version contract

The useful instrumentation sits beside the state transition. A message needs a session identifier, a queue version, a type, and the smallest authorized payload required for that recipient. This Go sketch shows application semantics, not a transport guarantee:

package queue

import (
    "errors"
    "fmt"
)

type Update struct {
    SessionID string `json:"session_id"`
    Version   uint64 `json:"version"`
    Kind      string `json:"kind"`
    Position  int    `json:"position,omitempty"`
}

type View struct {
    SessionID string
    Version   uint64
    Position  int
}

var ErrVersionGap = errors.New("queue version gap")

func Apply(view View, update Update) (View, error) {
    if update.SessionID != view.SessionID {
        return view, errors.New("session mismatch")
    }
    if update.Version <= view.Version {
        return view, nil // Duplicate or reordered old delivery.
    }
    if update.Version != view.Version+1 {
        return view, fmt.Errorf("%w: have %d, received %d", ErrVersionGap, view.Version, update.Version)
    }
    if update.Kind != "position_changed" {
        return view, errors.New("unsupported update kind")
    }

    view.Version = update.Version
    view.Position = update.Position
    return view, nil
}

Old duplicates become harmless, while a forward gap becomes observable and recoverable. The resync path returns an authorized snapshot with a version; the client replaces local state only when that version is newer. A reconnect begins the same way. The end-to-end claim should remain modest: the display converges under the retry and repair policy you test.

No version, no guarantee.

Persisting the state transition and publishing its notification in unrelated operations creates an ambiguity: either the state commits without an event, or an event escapes before the state does. A durable change record processed asynchronously can close that gap, provided its retry behavior and retention meet the recovery objective. Test the crash points around commit, publication, acknowledgement, and client application.

Test disorder deliberately. Duplicate version 418, deliver 419 before 418, disconnect after receipt but before acknowledgement, expire retained events, and reconnect from an older snapshot. Also test authorization changes during a session. A whole-queue payload cached under yesterday's access decision is a data exposure, not a harmless stale view.

Delivery guarantees belong in the buy-versus-build review

A managed transport can remove socket operations from the on-call queue; a self-hosted path can offer tighter control over retention, placement, and protocol behavior. Neither choice removes the application version contract. Ask where acknowledgement occurs, how long replay remains possible, what ordering scope exists, what happens under subscriber backpressure, and which side owns reconnect storms.

Operating question Managed path Self-hosted path Decision evidence
Who pages for saturation? Service boundary may absorb part of it Platform team owns the full path Documented responsibility and drill results
Can retention meet repair time? Constrained by the offered contract Configurable within team capacity Tested maximum disconnect window
How is lock-in contained? Adapter and export paths matter Protocol and storage choices still create coupling Recovery exercise using the abstraction
What is the real cost? Usage plus integration and incident work Compute, storage, upgrades, and on-call load Same traffic model and staffing assumptions

WebRTC data channels are one standards-based option for peer-to-peer data exchange, and the W3C specification defines their behavior and API surface. That does not make a peer mesh the default for a customer queue: topology, authorization, discovery, and recovery remain system responsibilities. Apply the same encoded-byte and convergence tests to any transport.

The deployment gate should include a shadow calculation of both message shapes against production-like fixtures, a load test with synchronized reconnects, and a rollback rule tied to convergence rather than publisher throughput alone. Capacity must include headroom for repair traffic. If every client requests a snapshot after a brief network interruption, the recovery path can become the largest burst in the system.

Set the alert where action changes

Use recipient deltas for routine customer updates when authorization is narrow and changes are frequent. Use a versioned snapshot for initial load, verified gaps, and displays authorized to render the whole queue. If a client cannot implement version checks and repair, repeated snapshots may be simpler, but account for disclosure and fan-out before accepting that simplicity.

Then tune the page. An alert threshold below the normal tail of client behavior creates noise, interrupts sleep, and consumes the same engineering capacity needed to improve recovery. A threshold that waits until many displays are stale protects the pager while abandoning the SLO. Start from the error-budget burn that requires human action, validate it during disconnect and reconnect drills, and keep lower-severity signals on a dashboard for trend work.

False positives have a concrete cost: an engineer investigates transport health while the underlying event is a backgrounded browser or a session that has already ended. Filter inactive sessions, distinguish disconnected from connected-but-behind, and require enough affected traffic to justify a page. The final architecture is credible only when its alert points to an action the on-call can take.

References

  • W3C, WebRTC 1.0: Real-Time Communication Between Browsers: https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/

Further reading

  • https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/

title: MonoMIP: Multi-Height Inverse Perspective Mapping for Monocular 3D Object Detection
description:
arXiv:2610.19071v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Monocular 3D object detection methods increasingly rely on depth-guided transformers, but they operate entirely in the perspective image plane where spatial relationships are distorted by foreshortening. We propose MonoMIP, a dual-decoder framework that adds complementary 3D geometric reasoning through Bird's-Eye View (BEV) features constructed via Multi-Height Inverse Perspective Mapping. We perform IPM at K elevation planes spanning ground to rooftop, producing an ordered stack of height-conditioned metric BEV features that reduces above-ground misprojection and exposes depth-dependent appearance variation across planes. A BEV decoder with multi-scale deformable attention aggregates this multi-height evidence per query, while a depth-guided 3D decoder provides complementary perspective-space predictions. Without extra training data, MonoMIP attains 25.84% Moderate AP3D|R40 on KITTI val and 21.66% on the official test set for Car, outperforming recent published monocular methods on both the KITTI and Waymo benchmarks.

title: Whose Data, Whose Benchmark? A User-Centric Framework for Auditing Evaluation Resources
description:
arXiv:2610.19268v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Benchmarks shape how model capabilities are measured and interpreted, yet their scores can obscure whose conventions, contexts, and judgments define successful performance. We introduce a user-centric audit framework that distinguishes users who contribute benchmark content from those whose needs evaluation results are intended to represent. The framework operationalizes seven dimensions across benchmark content, metadata, documentation, and scoring procedures. Across 16 resources, we find that American-centered conventions account for 62.4-94.4% of matched signals in 11 text benchmarks, while geographic visibility in five image-text resources is concentrated and strongly associated with national GDP share (mean Pearson r = 0.780; Spearman p = 0.778). Documentation reveals a systematic source-target gap: all 16 resources operationalize source-user context, but none operationalize target-user context. Paired scoring experiments further show that meaning-preserving answer variants reduce DROP exact-match accuracy from 100.0% to 33.3%, while TruthfulQA exhibits metric-dependent reductions in reference similarity. Our framework and documentation checklist make user assumptions auditable, clarifying what benchmark scores represent and where evaluation claims are supported.

title: Joint Discrete and SE(3) Diffusion for Protein Interface Design
description:
arXiv:2610.14699v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The design of high-affinity, target-specific protein binders is central to the development of modern therapeutics. However, existing protein-generation methods remain limited in this setting, as many generated designs fail to simultaneously achieve geometric and physicochemical complementarity at binding interfaces. To address this challenge, we introduce PIDiff, a physicochemically enhanced multimodal diffusion framework for protein-protein complex design. PIDiff jointly designs target-conditioned protein sequences and structures by coupling diffusion in discrete sequence space with diffusion on the continuous (SE(3)) structural manifold. At its core, PIDiff employs PIFormer, a novel architecture that interleaves geometry-aware invariant point attention with global sequence self-attention. We further curate PIBench, a protein-protein complex dataset with diverse target scaffolds derived from the Protein Data Bank (PDB). We first pretrain PIDiff on PIBench and subsequently fine-tune it for two therapeutically relevant applications: minibinder design and antibody design. PPFrame consistently outperforms baseline methods across sequence design success rate, structure binding energy, and sequence-structure co-designability on all tasks.

title: CAFE: Confining Feature Distillation to Language-Routed Adapters for Compact Multilingual Automatic Speech Recognition
description:
arXiv:2610.19134v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Feature distillation is usually expected to add to logit distillation. We find that this expectation does not hold for two common feature losses in compact multilingual automatic speech recognition (ASR), and analyze why through their gradients. The gradient of a projection-based loss is orthogonal to the task gradient, while that of Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA), a similarity-based loss, is weakly aligned with it. CKA lowers the word error rate (WER) on non-English languages, but at the expense of data-rich English. Three loss-level remedies (one trained, two probed) all fall short, and the CKA gradient overlaps with the subspace English uses in the shared encoder by 97.5% to 99.5% (about 81% by chance). Guided by this diagnosis, we propose CAFE (Confined-Adapter Feature distillation), which confines the CKA gradient to adapters that English bypasses, addressing the trade-off in the parameters rather than in the loss. On the Open ASR Leaderboard, CAFE lowers the average WER from 8.55% to 8.02%, beats an adapter-only capacity control at 8.51%, and makes English more stable across checkpoints. At 254M parameters, it trails the 0.6B teacher by 2 WER points and is competitive with much larger models across 48 test sets in 24 languages. We use 564k hours of training data and state-of-the-art models to keep the findings relevant to practice.

title: Deleting a user's data from backups: crypto-shredding with one key per person
description:
A user asks you to delete their data. You delete the row. Then you remember the replica, last month's backup, the S3 export someone made for analytics, and the log line with their email in it. You can't edit most of those.

Crypto-shredding is the standard way out: encrypt each person's data under their own key, keep the keys in one small keystore, and "delete" a person by destroying their key. The ciphertext can stay wherever it is. Without the key it's noise.

I built a small library for this called aegis-shred: a Rust core, a Python package and a CLI.

from aegis_shred import MasterKey, Vault

vault = Vault.open("keys.db", MasterKey.from_env("AEGIS_MASTER_KEY"), create=True)
blob = vault.seal("user-42", b"alice@example.com", context=b"users.email")  # store anywhere
vault.unseal(blob, context=b"users.email")   # b'alice@example.com'
vault.shred("user-42")                       # erase user-42, everywhere, at once
vault.unseal(blob, context=b"users.email")   # raises aegis_shred.Shredded

How it works 

master key (from your secret manager)
  └─ wraps one data key per subject ───── keystore (SQLite file)
        └─ HKDF → one key per sealed object
              └─ AES-256-GCM, chunked (STREAM)
                    └─ sealed blob/file ── your database, S3, backups, …
  • seal creates the subject's key on first use and returns a self-describing blob. The blob names a random key id, never the user.
  • unseal checks every chunk. A modified byte, a reordered or missing chunk, truncation, or a different context all fail.
  • shred deletes the wrapped key in one transaction, writes a tombstone and a hash-chained audit entry, and returns a receipt. From then on, in every process, that user's blobs raise Shredded.
  • The keystore stores subjects only as HMAC(index_key, subject_id), so the keystore and audit log don't list your users either.

The context argument binds a blob to where it lives, so a ciphertext copied from one column into another won't decrypt.

Large files are streamed in 64 KiB chunks with constant memory, and the output file only appears if every chunk verifies.

Install 

pip install aegis-shred          # prebuilt wheels for Linux, macOS, Windows
cargo add aegis-shred            # Rust library
cargo install aegis-shred-cli    # the aegis command

Honest limits

This is v0.1, alpha. The byte format is specified and versioned, every guarantee has a test, and a second independent implementation in Python runs in CI. But there has been no independent security audit. Read the threat model in the repo before relying on it.

Whether crypto-shredding satisfies GDPR Art. 17, CCPA or India's DPDP Act for your situation is a question for your lawyers. The library gives you the mechanism and an audit trail, not legal cover.

Repo (MIT OR Apache-2.0): https://github.com/Lingikaushikreddy/Aegis

Feedback on the threat model and the file format is the most useful thing you could send me.

Configure a timestamp attribute

You can configure timestamp attributes in the dashboard or via the CLI.

In the Vercel dashboard, open Flags, select Entities, and create or select an entity. Add an attribute and set its data type to timestamp.

Or define the attribute with the CLI:

Whether you configure the attribute in the dashboard or CLI, your application must provide its value when evaluating a flag. The entity and attribute names must match your configuration, and the value must be a Unix epoch timestamp in milliseconds.

This Flags SDK example passes the current time as system.time. Date.now() returns the required value in milliseconds. Keeping it inside dedupe() ensures that every flag evaluated during the same request uses the same time:

Add a targeting rule

In the dashboard, open the flag and add a targeting rule using the timestamp attribute. The rule compares the value from your application with a date and time you choose.

Rules support is after, is at or after, is before, and is at or before. The date and time picker uses your local timezone.

To add a time-based targeting rule with the CLI, use after, at-or-after, before, or at-or-before:

title: SAGE: Pushing 2-Bit Vector-Quantized LLMs toward Real-World Usability
description:
arXiv:2610.14745v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Extreme low-bit weight-only quantization is an effective approach to reducing the deployment costs of large language models. Below 3 bits, scalar quantization often suffers severe accuracy loss, while vector quantization (VQ) better preserves accuracy through more expressive joint encoding. However, existing VQ methods still exhibit substantial degradation on real-world tasks, and two design challenges remain underexplored: (1) protecting sensitive weight channels within jointly encoded vectors; and (2) allocating a fixed bit budget among representation components, such as direction and radius, to suit different weight matrices. To address these challenges, we propose SAGE: Split Adaptation and Grouping by Energy for weight-only vector quantization. First, Energy-Stratified Grouping (ESG) couples channel grouping with activation-weighted fitting, grouping channels from different energy tiers within each subvector to prioritize sensitive channels. Second, Adaptive Bit Split (ABS) balances direction-codebook capacity and radius precision per matrix, selecting the split with the lowest activation-weighted reconstruction error under a fixed budget. Across benchmarks covering knowledge, mathematics, code generation, instruction following, and tool use, SAGE achieves state-of-the-art performance in the 2-bit quantization setting. On Qwen3-30B-A3B, it retains 95.3% of the BF16 model's average benchmark score. With our custom-designed CUDA kernel, SAGE delivers up to a 2.55-fold non-streaming end-to-end speedup over FP16. The code is available at https://github.com/Zincwolf/sage.

title: Reels-RSI: Program-Level Self-Improvement for Code-Rendered Explainer Videos
description:
arXiv:2610.14495v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Explainer videos -- a worked geometry problem, why the sky is blue, how a dynasty fell -- are usually one more target for pixel video generation. We argue they are a different kind of artifact: a program (script, storyboard and per-frame animation code) that a deterministic renderer turns into frames. A program can be read, diffed, tested and audited; pixels can only be watched. Reels-RSI is an open-source reel director for any agent harness; its self-improvement happens at the program level rather than in weights or prompts. Every revision pass is logged with a code snapshot; a retrospective pairs each check finding with the diff that fixed it and proposes lessons; a lesson that a static check can catch is compiled into a rule with a must-fail and a must-pass example, so the memory is unit-tested; and a rule learned today runs over everything made before it. A bounded, benchmark-gated step lets an agent rewrite the director's playbook, kept only when blind pairwise judgments on held-out topics prefer it; nothing enters memory without a human decision. Across 111 reels -- a field study, two playbook evolutions, a 2x2 memory ablation, a weaker director, a 48-reel learning curve and a judge-reliability study -- we find that the rule learned in the field caught four latent defects in frames authored before it existed and none after; that rules are an audit for a strong director (eight unguarded reels, no violation) and a guard for a weaker one (thirty violations unguarded versus five); that lessons shorten revision loops but do not compound or move the judge; and that the first rewrite's 11--1 verdict was a position bias in our vote design (judges pick the second-shown reel 62--81% of the time), masking scripts that traded thirteen facts for craft. We document four failure modes of the preference signal, which check caught each, and the fixes. Code, rules, lessons and data are public.

title: Building a 12-axis political quiz with Vite, TanStack Start and Cloudflare Workers
description:
Most political quizzes squeeze you onto one line, left vs right, or a two-axis compass. I wanted something that keeps questions apart: you can want a strong welfare state and still distrust central government, or love new technology and be socially traditional. So I built The 12 Axes, a free quiz that scores you on twelve independent axes, in English, Spanish and Portuguese.

The statements and the scoring model come from the open-source 12Axes quiz (MIT). My part was the product around it: a fast, server-rendered site with shareable results and no accounts. Here is how it fits together.

The stack

  • Vite for the build and dev server.
  • TanStack Start (with TanStack Router) for file-based routes, server rendering and typed search params.
  • Cloudflare Workers to serve every page from the edge. The quiz itself has no backend at all.

There is no database. Everything a result needs fits in the URL.

Scoring in a dozen lines

Each statement belongs to one axis and points toward one of its two poles. Answers run from -2 (strongly disagree) to +2 (strongly agree). An axis score is the average answer, flipped for statements that point the other way and mapped to 0-100%:

export function scoreQuiz(items: QuizItem[], answers: (number | undefined)[]) {
  const sums = new Array(12).fill(0);
  const counts = new Array(12).fill(0);
  items.forEach((item, i) => {
    const answer = answers[i];
    if (answer === undefined) return;
    sums[item.axis] += answer * (item.level < 4 ? 1 : -1);
    counts[item.axis] += 1;
  });
  return sums.map((sum, axis) =>
    counts[axis] ? Math.round(50 + (50 * sum) / (2 * counts[axis])) : 50
  );
}

A skipped axis stays at 50, the neutral middle, rather than breaking the result.

A result that fits in 24 characters

Twelve scores from 0 to 100 need two base-36 digits each, so a whole result is a 24-character string:

export const encodeScores = (scores: number[]) =>
  scores
    .map((s) => Math.min(100, Math.max(0, Math.round(s))).toString(36).padStart(2, '0'))
    .join('');

That string goes in the result URL as ?r=. Sharing a result is sharing a link: the result page rebuilds every score, match and chart from those 24 characters, so nothing is stored anywhere. Decoding validates strictly (/^[0-9a-z]{24}$/, every value ≤ 100) and anything else falls back to an empty state. TanStack Router's typed search params make this pleasant: the route declares the param, and the page component gets a typed value.

Matching ideologies and historical figures

Two kinds of matches are shown, and both use root-mean-square distance:

  • Ideologies are defined on four classic dimensions (economy, power, diplomacy, culture), so they are compared on the four matching axes. Match = 100 minus the RMS gap.

  • Historical figures have a position on up to twelve axes. Many took no stand on some of them; Aristotle had no view on biotechnology. Skipping those axes would favour figures with few known positions, because they get compared on less. So an unknown axis counts as a fixed gap of 28 points, and a figure needs at least six known axes to be ranked at all.

One bug worth sharing: I had entered one axis backwards for twenty figures, and every match still looked plausible. Now a unit test pins the direction of every axis with figures whose positions are unambiguous. Plausible-looking output is the hardest kind of wrong to notice.

Progress that survives a reload

The full test has 288 statements, so losing your place hurts. Progress lives in localStorage and is restored on load. Answers never leave the browser, which is also why there is no sign-up.

A share card made from the DOM

The share card is a normal React component styled like the rest of the site. To share it as an image, it is rendered off-screen and turned into a PNG in the browser. On phones that support the Web Share API with files, the share sheet gets the image directly:

if (navigator.canShare?.({ files: [file] })) {
  await navigator.share({ files: [file], url, title });
}

Elsewhere you get a download button. Building the card as a component, not a canvas drawing, means it uses the same fonts, translations and layout code as the page.

Three languages, one set of routes

English lives at /, Spanish at /es/ and Portuguese at /pt/. Every page renders hreflang alternates and a canonical URL. Each language also gets its own Open Graph image, so a link shared in a Spanish group chat shows a Spanish preview.

Running on Cloudflare Workers

The Worker's fetch handler is a thin wrapper around the TanStack Start handler. It is also where redirects belong:

  • the old launch domain 301s to the same path on the new one;
  • plain http:// 301s to https://, with a 308 for anything other than GET/HEAD so a request body is never silently turned into a GET.

Both live in a pure function with unit tests, including one that feeds each redirect target back in and expects no further redirect. A redirect loop on the edge is not something you want to discover from Search Console.

Deploys are one wrangler deploy. The custom domain, TLS and caching come with Workers.

SEO for a quiz site

A few things mattered more than I expected:

  • Server-render everything crawlable, including FAQ answers inside collapsed panels: hidden="until-found" keeps them in the HTML while staying collapsed.
  • A sitemap with real lastmod dates and an IndexNow ping after each content change, so Bing and other IndexNow engines hear about new pages without waiting for a crawl.
  • An explainer page per axis, so the site answers "what does this axis mean" and not just "take the quiz".

Try it

The quick test takes 60 statements, about six minutes: 12axes.site. I'd love to hear which axis surprised you, and whether the historical-figure match felt fair.

title: Evidence-Anchored Overdose Death Prediction from Death Investigation Reports
description:
arXiv:2610.19556v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Confirmation of overdose deaths in the United States is often delayed due to the complexities of certifying drug-involved deaths. Death investigation reports represent a rich but underutilized data source that could be used to predict whether a death is a suspected overdose (i.e., a death preliminarily identified as an overdose prior to the final cause and manner of death determination). We present an automated framework that classifies suspected overdoses from death investigation reports, while producing supporting explanations guided by expert knowledge. Through an expert-guided design process, we investigate 1) what type of explanations are best for model prediction performance, and 2) which architecture is better suited for this task: pipeline models that rationalize first and then predict, or self-rationalizing models that jointly predict and rationalize? Our experiments show that a pipeline model with explanations grounded in the input death investigation reports outperforms the other settings. Our best model also outperforms a rule-based system currently in deployment by 15%, while allowing expert interventions for final decisions.

title: No Bootstrap, No Principal: The Day My Audit Log Became Fiction
description:
My v0.1.0 series couldn't talk about authorization, because there wasn't any. v0.2.0 shipped RBAC-lite, scoped API keys, and an encrypted secret vault on HivePlane — and the first thing the field test taught me is that attribution has a cold-start problem.

I shipped a control plane with roles, permissions, and an audit trail — and for an hour, none of it was reachable, because there was no way to mint the first API key.

This is the article about the prerequisite for every governance claim I made in the earlier series: a principal. Without one, your audit log is fiction.

The cold start

The finding was D-10. RBAC was wired. /auth/login existed. Scoped keys were implemented. And the entire model was unreachable end-to-end, because there was no HTTP bootstrap to mint the first admin key. The roles existed; nobody could assume one.

The fix was a dev-grade env admin key — boot the first principal from the environment, then issue scoped keys from there:

# the first principal has to come from outside the API
export HIVEPLANE_AUTH__ENABLED=true
export HIVEPLANE_AUTH__ADMIN_KEY=$(openssl rand -hex 32)
# now you can POST /keys to issue scoped, tenant-bound keys

The lesson is that authn is the admission gate for the operators. Until there's a principal, every "who did this" question is unanswerable, and every other governance feature is theater.

The audit log that named the wrong person

Then I found the worse one. Pause, resume, stop, kill-switch, quarantine — every privileged operator action — was attributed to a client-supplied actor field. The caller put --operator alice in the request. The audit log recorded alice. Any caller could sign an action as anyone.

tip: A who column populated by the request body is a confession that you don't know. The actor must come from the authenticated principal, not the payload. A client-supplied actor is repudiation by construction.

Findings #560, #561, and #541 were all the same shape: the action was real, the attribution was a string the caller chose. The fix is that the principal resolves the actor; the field is read-only. You can attribute an action to yourself. You cannot attribute it to someone else.

The endpoints that had no permission at all

Then the field test found the gaps RBAC was supposed to cover and didn't:

  • #537 — registry mutation endpoints had no permission checks. A viewer could DELETE /workloads.
  • #526 — destructive immune-system endpoints (quarantine, kill-switch) were ungated.
  • #563 — pause/resume/stop had no permission gate; a viewer could stop any run.
  • #566 — the UI session secret shipped a hardcoded public default.

A role system that doesn't gate the destructive verbs is a role system in name only. The fix is server-side authorization on every privileged action: approve, promote, kill-switch. A viewer cannot approve. A viewer cannot stop. A viewer cannot delete a workload. The 401/403 is the product.

HMAC-first, not bearer-first

The one I didn't see coming was #515. With auth enabled, GitHub and Alertmanager webhooks got 401 before the HMAC signature was verified. The bearer-first model broke event ingest from ≥3 sources — which is a release gate. Triggers are the autonomy layer; if they can't authenticate, the fleet doesn't run itself.

The fix is that webhook ingest is HMAC-first, not bearer-first. The signature is verified before any bearer token is required; the trigger source is trusted by its HMAC, not by a login. Autonomy and authorization have to coexist, or you've secured the plane against its own purpose.

What I learned

Bootstrap the first principal, or none of it exists — the env admin key is the admission gate for operators. Attribution comes from the principal, never the payload: a client-supplied actor is repudiation by construction. Gate the destructive verbs — a viewer who can delete a workload doesn't have a role, they have root. And webhooks are HMAC-first: bearer-first auth breaks event ingest, and autonomy and authorization have to coexist or you've secured the plane against its own purpose.

The v0.2.0 field test asserts per-tenant budget/policy/key isolation with a viewer who cannot approve, and a secret that never appears in logs/traces/agent context (verified by test). Full evidence in the field-test report; the auth bootstrap and key-rotation runbook is at docs/runbooks/auth-bootstrap-and-key-rotation.md.

References

  • HivePlane — pip install hiveplane==0.2.0
  • Field test report (36/36)
  • Auth bootstrap & key rotation runbook
  • Secrets, RBAC & access audit design
  • Secrets, RBAC & access audit (User Guide)

Open your audit log. Pick one privileged action. Is the who populated by the authenticated principal — or by a field the caller wrote? If it's the second, your audit log is a story someone else is telling you.

title: CedarDB brings its new online data management service
description:
CedarDB, a startup born from the Umbra research project at the Technical University of Munich, is bringing its PostgreSQL-compatible database to the cloud.

The platform is optimized for running high-speed analytical queries alongside daily transaction processing without additional memory overhead.

The move into the cloud marks a new phase for the team as they look to help enterprises query long-term transaction data using natural language.

According to Sichert, large companies have systems with many years of transaction data, but these cannot always quickly answer analytical questions formulated in everyday language.

CedarDB has been in development for about ten years and began as a research project at the Technical University of Munich, called Umbra. It was designed to run quickly without requiring more processors, more computing power, or more memory.

It is also compatible with PostgreSQL, which means customers don't have to rebuild their applications to use it, which reduces the cost of migration, according to Sichert.

READ ALSO

Eight US states take legal action against OpenAI over minors' safety

In May 2025, the company announced the free CedarDB Community Edition and CedarDB Enterprise, which is installed on customer premises. At the same time, it announced initial funding of 5,3 million euros, approximately $6 million.

CedarDB had been testing its online service with users on a waitlist. On October 14, 2026, it announced on stage at TechCrunch Disrupt that CedarDB Cloud is available to a limited number of users. The fully managed online version is expected to help the company reach more users beyond large enterprises.

In June, Databricks introduced LTAP, an architecture that aims to combine transactional, analytics, dataflow, and day-to-day operations data using a common data copy. Sichert sees the move as a sign that there is demand for CedarDB’s approach. However, it’s not yet clear how much of an impact it will have on the market.

CedarDB currently has 14 employees and plans to serve the first users of the online service with these. Sichert estimates that the company will need a larger team if it gains more traction. In that case, it will seek a new round of funding.
