title: DevSecOps in Practice: Securing Java and Spring Boot Delivery Pipelines
description:
DevSecOps is often described as "shifting security left," but in practice many teams still experience security as a gate at the end of the pipeline. A scanner runs, a report lands in a shared folder, and a developer discovers three weeks later that a critical dependency has been waiting to be fixed the whole time. The goal of DevSecOps is not to add more gates. It is to make security a property of the delivery pipeline itself, so that the safe path is also the fastest path.

This article walks through the practices I use when building Java and Spring Boot services in regulated environments. It covers how to automate dependency and secret scanning, how to enforce policy as code, how to harden container images, how to protect the runtime, and how to make the whole system produce evidence that auditors and incident responders can rely on.

What DevSecOps Actually Means

DevSecOps extends DevOps by treating security as a shared responsibility across development, operations, and security teams. Three ideas make it work:

  1. Automate the checks. Manual reviews do not scale to dozens of deployments a day. Every check that can be automated should be.
  2. Fail fast, but with useful feedback. A build that fails with a clear explanation and a suggested fix is far more useful than a report generated next month.
  3. Make the secure path the default. Templates, base images, and shared pipeline stages should be secure out of the box, so that teams do not need to remember every rule.

The rest of this article applies these ideas to concrete stages of the delivery pipeline.

Stage 1: Secure Coding Feedback in the IDE

The earliest feedback comes from the developer's own environment. Static analysis plugins for IntelliJ IDEA or VS Code can flag common issues such as SQL built with string concatenation, unsafe deserialization, or hardcoded credentials as the developer types. These tools are useful, but they only help if the team agrees on a shared rule set. Commit a configuration file to the repository so that everyone runs the same rules.

The most common class of vulnerabilities in Java services is still injection. Compare these two approaches:

// Vulnerable: user input concatenated into SQL
public List<Customer> findByEmail(String email) {
    String sql = "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE email = '" + email + "'";
    return jdbcTemplate.query(sql, customerRowMapper);
}

// Safe: parameter binding
public List<Customer> findByEmail(String email) {
    return jdbcTemplate.query(
            "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE email = ?",
            customerRowMapper,
            email);
}

A static analysis rule can detect the first pattern automatically. Make it a blocking check in the pipeline rather than a warning that everyone learns to ignore.

Stage 2: Secret Detection Before the Commit Leaves the Machine

Secrets in source control are one of the most common causes of breaches, and they are expensive to clean up because the history of the repository keeps them alive. Prevent them at three points:

  • Pre-commit hooks that scan staged changes for API keys, tokens, and private keys.
  • Pipeline scanning on every push, using a dedicated secret scanner such as Gitleaks or TruffleHog.
  • Repository-level protection that blocks pushes containing known secret patterns.

A simple pre-commit configuration with Gitleaks looks like this:

# .pre-commit-config.yaml
repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks
    rev: v8.18.4
    hooks:
      - id: gitleaks

When a secret is detected, the response should be rotation first and cleanup second. Assume the credential is compromised, rotate it in the secrets manager, and then remove it from history if needed.

Applications should never read secrets from files in the repository. Load them at runtime from a secrets manager such as AWS Secrets Manager, Google Secret Manager, OCI Vault, or HashiCorp Vault:

@Configuration
public class DatabaseConfig {

    @Bean
    DataSource dataSource(
            @Value("${db.url}") String url,
            @Value("${db.username}") String username,
            @Value("${db.password}") String password) {
        HikariDataSource ds = new HikariDataSource();
        ds.setJdbcUrl(url);
        ds.setUsername(username);
        ds.setPassword(password);
        return ds;
    }
}

In this example, the password is resolved from the environment or from a secrets integration at startup. The value never appears in a file under version control. Spring Cloud Config, the AWS Secrets Manager integration, or the Vault Spring integration can supply these properties without changing application code.

Stage 3: Dependency and Supply Chain Scanning

Most of the code running in a typical Spring Boot service was written by someone else. That is an advantage, but it also means that a single vulnerable transitive dependency can expose your entire system. Dependency scanning should happen on every build.

The OWASP Dependency-Check Maven plugin is a common choice for Java projects:

<plugin>
    <groupId>org.owasp</groupId>
    <artifactId>dependency-check-maven</artifactId>
    <version>10.0.4</version>
    <executions>
        <execution>
            <goals>
                <goal>check</goal>
            </goals>
        </execution>
    </executions>
    <configuration>
        <failBuildOnCVSS>7</failBuildOnCVSS>
        <suppressionFiles>
            <suppressionFile>owasp-suppressions.xml</suppressionFile>
        </suppressionFiles>
    </configuration>
</plugin>

The failBuildOnCVSS setting stops the build when a dependency has a high-severity known vulnerability. Suppressions should be explicit, reviewed, and time-limited. A suppression without an expiration date tends to become permanent.

Beyond scanning, three supply chain practices reduce risk:

  • Pin versions. Use explicit versions in the build file and review updates instead of accepting floating ranges.
  • Generate an SBOM. A Software Bill of Materials, produced with CycloneDX for example, lets you answer quickly whether a newly disclosed vulnerability affects any of your services.
  • Verify artifacts. Sign container images and build artifacts, and verify signatures before deployment.

Stage 4: Static and Dynamic Analysis in the Pipeline

Static Application Security Testing (SAST) analyzes source code for vulnerability patterns. Dynamic Application Security Testing (DAST) probes a running application from the outside. Both have a role, and both produce noise if they are configured carelessly.

For SAST, focus on rules that map to real risk in your context, such as injection, broken authentication, path traversal, and insecure deserialization. Triage new findings on every pull request, and track the trend over time rather than fixating on the total count.

For DAST, run a baseline scan against a deployed test environment on a schedule, and run a more thorough scan before major releases. Keep the scan credentials limited to test accounts with the minimum necessary permissions.

Stage 5: Container Hardening

Containers package your application together with its operating system libraries, and each layer can carry vulnerabilities. Harden the image in three ways.

Use minimal base images. A distroless or slim Java runtime image contains far fewer packages than a full operating system image, which means fewer vulnerabilities to patch.

FROM maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-21 AS build
WORKDIR /workspace
COPY pom.xml .
RUN mvn -B dependency:go-offline
COPY src ./src
RUN mvn -B -DskipTests package

FROM gcr.io/distroless/java21-debian12:nonroot
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /workspace/target/payments-service.jar app.jar
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0", "-jar", "/app/app.jar"]

This multi-stage build keeps the build tools out of the final image, and the nonroot variant of the distroless base runs the process as a non-root user.

Scan the image. Run Trivy or Grype against the built image in the pipeline, and fail the build on critical vulnerabilities that have a fix available.

Set runtime restrictions. In Kubernetes, configure the pod to run as non-root, drop Linux capabilities, and mount the root filesystem as read-only where possible:

securityContext:
  runAsNonRoot: true
  allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
  readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
  capabilities:
    drop:
      - ALL

Stage 6: Policy as Code

Security rules that live only in a document are difficult to enforce consistently. Policy as code expresses those rules in a form that the pipeline and the cluster can evaluate automatically. Open Policy Agent (OPA) with Rego, or Kyverno for Kubernetes, are common choices.

A simple example is a rule that rejects any deployment without resource limits, which protects other tenants from a runaway service. In Kyverno, a policy might look like this:

apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-resource-limits
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Enforce
  rules:
    - name: check-limits
      match:
        any:
          - resources:
              kinds:
                - Pod
      validate:
        message: "CPU and memory limits are required."
        pattern:
          spec:
            containers:
              - resources:
                  limits:
                    memory: "?*"
                    cpu: "?*"

The advantage of policy as code is that it is versioned, reviewed, and tested like any other code. When a policy changes, the change is visible in history, and the same rule applies in every environment.

Stage 7: Runtime Protection and Observability

No pipeline catches everything, so the system needs to detect and respond to suspicious behavior at runtime. Three capabilities matter most.

Structured security logging. Log authentication failures, authorization denials, and sensitive actions in a structured format, with a correlation identifier. Make sure that logs never contain tokens, passwords, or full personal data.

@Component
public class SecurityEventLogger {

    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger("security");

    public void authorizationDenied(String principal, String resource, String action) {
        log.warn("event=AUTHZ_DENIED principal={} resource={} action={} correlationId={}",
                principal, resource, action, MDC.get("correlationId"));
    }
}

Rate limiting and abuse detection. Limit login attempts and sensitive endpoints, and alert on unusual patterns such as many denials from one client in a short window.

Runtime threat detection. Tools such as Falco can detect unexpected process execution, shell access in containers, or writes to sensitive paths, and send alerts to the security team.

Connect these signals to your incident response process. An alert that nobody reads provides no protection.

Stage 8: Evidence and Compliance

DevSecOps is not complete until you can prove that your controls work. Compliance frameworks such as PCI DSS, SOC 2, and ISO 27001 require evidence, and the most efficient evidence is the kind the pipeline generates automatically:

  • Build logs showing that scans ran and their results
  • Records of who approved each deployment and when
  • Policy evaluation results for each release
  • Access reviews generated from identity provider data
  • Vulnerability management metrics, such as mean time to remediate by severity

Store this evidence in a system that the delivery team cannot silently modify, and retain it according to your regulatory requirements. When an auditor asks how a control works, the answer should be a link to the pipeline definition and a sample of its output, not a meeting to reconstruct what happened.

Measuring DevSecOps Maturity

Metrics keep the program honest. Useful measures include:

  • Mean time to remediate critical vulnerabilities, by service
  • Percentage of services with automated scanning in their pipeline
  • Secret detection rate before and after pre-commit hooks were introduced
  • Deployment failure rate caused by security policy, which shows whether the controls are too strict or too loose
  • Exception count and age, to ensure suppressions do not accumulate

Review these metrics regularly with both engineering and security leadership. The goal is to improve the system over time, not to produce a perfect score on day one.

Common Pitfalls

Several patterns undermine DevSecOps programs in practice:

  • Scanning without action. A dashboard full of unresolved findings trains teams to ignore security signals. Set clear ownership and service-level targets for remediation.
  • Too many blocking rules at once. Introducing dozens of strict gates on the first day causes teams to find workarounds. Start with the highest-impact checks and expand gradually.
  • Security as a separate team's pipeline. If developers cannot see or fix the findings themselves, the feedback loop is too slow. Give teams direct access to results and guidance.
  • Ignoring the human path. Developers under deadline pressure will choose the fastest route. Make sure the secure route is also the easiest one.

Key Takeaways

  • DevSecOps makes security a property of the delivery pipeline, not a separate phase at the end.
  • Automate secret detection, dependency scanning, and static analysis, and make the critical checks blocking.
  • Keep secrets out of source control and load them from a secrets manager at runtime.
  • Harden container images with minimal bases, non-root execution, and image scanning.
  • Express security policy as code so it is versioned, reviewed, and enforced consistently.
  • Monitor runtime behavior and connect alerts to a real response process.
  • Generate compliance evidence automatically from the pipeline itself.
  • Measure progress with metrics that reveal both the strength of controls and the friction they create.

DevSecOps works best when it feels like an improvement to the delivery process rather than an obstacle to it. Start with one pipeline, add secret detection and dependency scanning this week, and expand from there. Each automated check removes a class of risk without asking anyone to remember a rule.

title: Loss Curvature as a Sampling-Free Proxy for Memorization in Diffusion Models
description:
arXiv:2610.19042v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Understanding the mechanism behind why diffusion models memorize their training data remains an open question in generative modeling. In this paper, we examine this question from two perspectives: (a) the model-level perspective concerning the onset of memorization in a model during training, and (b) the sample-level perspective concerning the proclivity of an individual sample to be memorized by a given model. We show that the so-called input loss curvature, or the Frobenius norm of the Hessian of the diffusion model's training loss, is an effective metric for quantifying both perspectives on memorization. In particular, we empirically demonstrate that input curvatures averaged across training and validation samples can identify when a model is likely to start regurgitating its training data when tracked over training time. However, this metric is not sufficient for measuring an individual sample's likelihood of being memorized. To address this perspective, we introduce a counterfactual definition of memorization in diffusion models, extending the analogous notion from supervised learning proposed by [Feldman, 2019]. We prove that this counterfactual memorization is controlled by the input curvature of the leave-one-out model, thus establishing a direct theoretical link between a sample's local loss landscape and its generation likelihood. We validate our derived bounds through several empirical experiments and show that input-dependent curvature provides a proxy for memorization.

title: A CSS mutation test for your Ionify pilot
description:
A shorter rebuild is useful when the page shows your latest change. This Ionify lab checks one visible result—a border changing from 2px to 6px—while keeping local engine state. Use a disposable, supported app and retain your normal styling packages.

Add an unmistakable rule

In a stylesheet already imported by the app:

.build-lab-card {
  border: 2px solid #b77928;
  padding: 1rem;
}

Apply the class to an element you can easily find. Build with pnpm exec ionify build and inspect the production output through your normal static preview server.

Now change only the border width to 6px. Build again without deleting the local engine state. Check the element's computed border width in the browser. Record the result, not just the time.

Which styling path did you try, and did the production border reach 6px?

Exercise the real styling path

If your app uses CSS Modules, repeat with a property in an imported module. If it uses a preprocessor or generated utility CSS, make a change that that pipeline must observe. Do not assume the plain-CSS result covers it.

Ionify's public setup describes CSS/CSS Modules support. Sass and Less still require their compiler packages. Tailwind and PostCSS need their normal packages and configuration. Follow the current configuration reference for the version under test.

Optional: record enough to debug 

Project / report key:
Stylesheet mechanism:
Exact build command:
Starting state / state retained:
Changed source and value:
Expected computed style:
Actual production computed style:
Engine and styling package versions:
Config files involved:
Was a service worker or browser cache active?
Evidence: redacted screenshot or public reproduction URL

If the style is stale, first confirm the browser is serving the output you just built. Preserve the failure before clearing caches so the reproduction still explains what happened.

The purpose is a reliable edit-to-check loop. No style change needs to become a migration argument; it just needs to reach the app correctly.

title: Actionable Meta-Requirements for AI Robustness Auditing
description:
arXiv:2610.14356v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI-enabled systems must remain dependable when the conditions under which they operate change (e.g., due to input perturbations, distribution shifts, or changes in external dependencies). This makes robustness auditing of such systems important for judging whether the available evidence is sufficient to support a defined robustness conclusion. However, designing an AI robustness auditing framework is challenging. A key unresolved issue is determining the requirements such a framework should support; these requirements have not yet been consolidated. We address this gap through meta-requirements: higher-order requirements specifying what a class of auditing frameworks should support. In design science research, literature and domain experts are common sources of meta-requirements; accordingly, we derive the initial set from literature and validate and refine it with practitioners. Our systematic literature review retained 74 of 2,890 records and derived 43 meta-requirements across 16 categories. We evaluated them with 128 practitioners, obtaining 5,504 ratings and 586 substantive comments. Overall, 81.20% of ratings indicated agreement or strong agreement. In particular, 41 of the 43 literature-derived meta-requirements were classified as strongly supported. Practitioner feedback refined the requirements and identified an additional requirement concerning external components and supply chain dependencies. The final set comprises 44 meta-requirements across 16 categories, of which 43 received quantitative validation. These meta-requirements can help organizations implement AI robustness auditing frameworks, assess existing frameworks for completeness, and refine them.

title: Long-horizon Video Generation with Slot Memory Addressed By Region Tokens
description:
arXiv:2610.19257v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Memory for long-horizon video generation must satisfy two competing requirements: it must remain bounded so generation can continue indefinitely, while still recovering what was observed at a place when the camera returns, regardless of how long ago it was seen. Reconstruction-based memories provide spatial recall by caching and reprojecting explicit geometry, but require growing storage and depend on estimated 3D structure. Recurrent memories keep a constant-size state, but retention is governed by temporal recurrence, causing old observations to fade with time. We introduce SMART, a slot memory addressed by region tokens, which combines bounded storage with spatially addressed recall. SMART stores content in a constant-size slot recurrence whose writes are addressed by the observing camera and whose reads are queried by the rendering camera, without constructing an explicit 3D representation or maintaining a growing cache. Consequently, recall is conditioned on inter-view geometry rather than on recency. Each read additionally provides a confidence estimate that conditions a chunk-causal diffusion transformer, allowing it to selectively trust retrieved content while relying on its generative prior elsewhere. On long trajectories in Memory Maze and Minecraft, SMART maintains high-fidelity recall far beyond its training horizon while using constant memory and per-step cost.

title: Build in public
description:
While building ShopPilot AI, I’ve been working on a function that checks availability for a requested product color and size.

“Out of stock” and “that variant doesn’t exist” need different answers.

I defined three cases to test:
• The variant exists and has stock.
• The variant exists but has zero stock.
• There’s no matching variant.

The interesting part was the third case.

JavaScript’s .find() returns undefined when nothing matches, so I need to handle that before reading the variant’s stock.

This is a small function, but it’s helping me connect JavaScript fundamentals, TypeScript, and testing to a real customer question.

I’m learning how to use TDD for this logic: define the expected behavior with a failing test, implement it, then refactor.

My main lesson so far: a useful test starts with a clear requirement.
Before checking whether the code works, I need to decide what it should do.

title: Integrating Netflix’s Foundation Model into Personalization applications
description:
Authors: Divya Gadde, Ko-Jen Hsiao, Dhaval Patel and Moumita Bhattacharya

The motivation for building the Netflix Foundation Model for personalization was laid out in this previous blog post. The Netflix homepage is powered by several specialized models and it requires significant time and resources to maintain and continue innovating on these individual models. Therefore, we decided to centralize member preference learning and have one powerful model learned from comprehensive user interaction histories and content data at a large scale and have this model distribute its learnings to other models.

The previous two blog posts(1, 2) focus on the development of the Foundation Model and here we talk about how we integrate the Foundation Model into various applications. We found that there is extensive literature focused on the training and inference of large-scale transformer-based models. However, there remains a significant gap in practical guidance and research on how to effectively and efficiently integrate large models into existing production systems. At Netflix, we experimented with 3 distinct integration approaches — embeddings, subgraph and fine-tuning. The motivation for trying different approaches stems from varying application needs. Specifically, different teams have different latency requirements, tech stack constraints and different appetites for leveraging the full power of a large foundation model.

In this blog, we go over the 3 approaches we experimented with and which are now used in production for different use cases. Each integration approach has its own set of motivations, tradeoffs, complexities and learnings. The following sections go into the details of each of these integration approaches.

Embeddings from Foundation model

Transformer style foundation models naturally lend themselves to generating comprehensive user profile and item representations. Our approach for generating embeddings includes getting the hidden state of the last user event as the profile embedding and weights from the item tower as item embeddings.

Netflix has an elaborate set up for refreshing the embeddings every day. First, the Foundation Model is pre-trained from scratch every month. Then, the monthly pre-trained model is fine-tuned everyday based on the latest data. The daily fine-tuning also expands the entity id space to include the newly launching titles. After the daily fine-tuned model is ready, we run batch inference to refresh the profile and item embeddings and publish them to the Embedding Store.

An important part of this setup is the embedding stabilization technique (paper). When the pretraining job retrains the model from scratch, the embedding spaces between different runs are completely different due to the random initialization in the model. In addition, the embeddings start to drift when the daily job fine-tunes on the latest data, despite the daily fine-tuning job warm-starting from the previous day’s model. Therefore, it is important to map the embeddings generated everyday into the same embedding space, so that downstream models can consume pre-computed embeddings as features.

This embedding approach relies heavily on the Embedding Store, which is a feature store specializing in embeddings built by the platform team at Netflix. The embedding store makes producing and consuming embeddings easy by taking care of versioning and timestamping the embeddings. The Embedding Store also provides various interfaces to access the embeddings offline and online.

This approach is often the initial and most straightforward way for applications to interact with the Foundation Model. Embeddings can serve as powerful features for other models or for candidate generation, helping to retrieve appealing titles for a user or facilitate title-to-title recommendations. Integrating embeddings as features into existing pipelines is generally well-supported and offers a low barrier to entry. Compared to other integration approaches, using embeddings from the Embedding Store is expected to have a relatively smaller impact on training and inference costs.

However, this approach also has some cons. The time gap between embedding computation and downstream model inference can lead to staleness, impacting the freshness of recommendations. This may prevent applications from fully unlocking the benefit of the Foundation Model, especially for use cases requiring real-time adaptability.

Overall, the default starting point for leveraging the Foundation Model is through its profile and item embeddings via the Embedding Store, provided that the embeddings’ freshness and stability meet application-specific needs. While embeddings may not leverage the full power of the Foundation Model, they offer a good initial step.

Our biggest learning from working on this approach is that embeddings are a low cost and high leverage way of using the Foundation Model. A resilient embedding generation framework and embedding store are essential for updating the embeddings daily and serving them to application models. We found this infrastructure to be so valuable that we stepped up our investment here to build a near-realtime embedding generation framework. This new framework also enables us to update the embeddings based on user actions during the session, making the embeddings and our downstream models more adaptive. Although the near-real time framework cannot be used for very large models, it represents an important direction for addressing embedding staleness and adaptiveness of recommendations.

Foundation Model as a Subgraph

This approach involves using the Foundation Model as an input to the downstream model i.e. the Foundation Model decoder stack is a subgraph of the application model’s full model graph and hence the name “subgraph integration”. The Foundation Model subgraph processes raw user interaction sequences and outputs representations that are then fed into the downstream model graph.

Applications can fine-tune the Foundation Model subgraph as part of their own training process, potentially leading to better performance than just using static embeddings. In this approach, there is no time gap or staleness between the Foundation Model inference and the application model’s inference, ensuring that the most up-to-date learnings are used. This approach also allows applications to leverage specific layers from the Foundation Model that may not be exposed through the Embedding Store, uncovering more application-specific value.

However, the subgraph approach comes with some complexities and trade-offs. To use the Foundation Model as a subgraph, application models need to generate all the features necessary for the subgraph as part of their feature generation process. This can add time, compute and complexity to their feature gen jobs. Merging the Foundation Model as a subgraph also increases the application model size and inference time. To alleviate some of these complexities, the Foundation Model team provides some reusable code and jobs that make the feature generation more compute efficient. To optimize the inference performance, we split the subgraph and ensure it only runs once per profile per request and is shared by all items in the request.

Overall, the subgraph approach allows for a deeper integration and enables the applications to harness the full power of the Foundation Model. But it can also make the application’s training code more complex, requiring a trade-off between metric improvement, compute cost, and time. Therefore, we would reserve this approach for high impact use cases where the increase in metric wins compensate for the cost and complexity.

Fine-tuning Foundation Model and use directly

This approach is similar to fine-tuning LLMs with domain specific data. In the previous blog post, we described how the Foundation Model is trained on a next-token prediction objective, with the tokens being different user interactions. Different interactions are of different importance to various surfaces on the Netflix website. For example, for the ‘Trending now’ row, recent interactions on trending titles might be more important than old interactions. Hence, the Foundation Model can be fine-tuned on more product specific data and then the fine-tuned model can be used to directly power the product. During fine-tuning, application teams can choose to do full parameter fine-tuning or freeze some layers. They can also choose to add a different output head with a different objective. We built a fine-tuning framework to make it easy for application teams to develop their own custom fine-tuned versions of the Foundation Model.

This approach offers the ability to adapt the Foundation Model to application’s specific data and objectives, making it optimized for their use case. A side benefit of this integration approach is that it provides a de facto baseline for new models/applications. Instead of coming up with a new model stack and spending months on feature engineering, new applications can directly utilize fine-tuned foundation models. However, this approach can lead to more models and pipelines to maintain across the organization.The latency and Service Level Agreements (SLAs) of the fine-tuned model must be carefully optimized for the specific application use case.

Conclusion

We are continuing to innovate on these integration approaches over time. For example, the Machine Learning Platform team is working on near-real time embedding inference capabilities to address the staleness issues with the embedding approach. We are also working on a smaller distilled version of the Foundation Model to reduce the inference latency of the subgraph approach. We also provide a fine-tuning framework to make it easy to fine-tune and leverage the Foundation Model. We also continue to refine and standardize the APIs used in these approaches to make it easy for application teams to use them. Overall, these three integration patterns provide a comprehensive framework for how Netflix applications can interact with and extract value from the Foundation Model.

Acknowledgements

We thank our stunning colleagues in the Foundation Model team for developing and continuing to innovate on the Foundation Model. We thank our colleagues in the AIMS applications teams for driving the integrations and their valuable feedback and discussions. We also thank our Machine Learning Platform team for building and supporting the infra components to get these approaches up and running in production.

Contributors to this work (name in alphabetical order): Davis Shepherd Inbar Naor Jin Wang Jonathan Indig Kevin Zielnicki Luke Wang Mario Garcia-Armas Maryam Esmaeli Michael Tu Nicholas Hortiguera Qiuling Xu Robbie Greuner Roger Menezes Sejoon Oh Trung Nguyen Vito Ostuni Yesu Feng.

Integrating Netflix’s Foundation Model into Personalization applications was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: Tail Competition Explains Scaling in Best-of-N Sampling for Verifiable Problems
description:
arXiv:2610.19362v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Best-of-N sampling is a simple inference-time scaling strategy for large language models, yet its behavior under incomplete reward models remains poorly understood. We study Best-of-N as a competition between the extreme reward tails of correct and incorrect responses. This view shows that success depends not only on the probability of sampling a correct response, but also on whether correct responses dominate incorrect ones in the upper tail. Using extreme value theory, we characterize three asymptotic regimes: correct-tail-dominant, incorrect-tail-dominant, and critical explaining both monotonic gains and reward-hacking-induced degradation. We further derive finite-sample scaling laws for representative reward distributions, showing that, under Gaussian rewards, incorrect responses with sufficiently large variance can dominate selection even when their mean reward is lower. Unlike oracle selection, convergence with an incomplete selector can be polynomial rather than exponential. Finally, we propose a lightweight tail-tension criterion to estimate when additional sampling may become harmful. Experiments on synthetic data and real reward model scores are consistent with the theoretically predicted regimes, scaling laws, and diagnostic behavior, suggesting that tail competition provides a unified lens on Best-of-N sampling for verifiable problems.

title: DSABench: Benchmarking Source Discovery, Coordination, and Execution for Multi-Database Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.14700v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Most text-to-SQL benchmarks provide the target database. In a large data catalog, however, choosing the sources is part of the problem: an agent must find every database needed for a request, determine how their results fit together, and execute the resulting workflow. We present DSABench to evaluate these capabilities jointly. Its 815 human-reviewed tasks draw on Spider, BIRD, and LiveSQLBench; 618 require several databases to contribute, and 105 allow more than one interpretation of the required sources. Executable contracts define source participation, cross-source dependencies, and source-local execution, while RouteEnv lets agents inspect public catalog evidence without revealing the gold annotations. In our routing-only study across seven model backends, the highest RA-Set score is 60.55%, compared with a highest RA-Graph score of 34.66% when coordination requirements are included. The gap becomes more pronounced when execution is required. Across four backends, median non-privileged Route+Exec-Graph success ranges from 6.69% to 7.98% without clarification and from 11.44% to 13.25% with one clarification; the best observed clarified configuration reaches 16.99%. On ambiguous tasks, clarification improves exact branch-source recovery by 39.8-43.2 percentage points. These findings illustrate why retrieving plausible databases or producing correct local SQL is not enough: an agent must carry the right information through the entire multi-database workflow.

title: HERO: Harnessing Evidence for Test-time Refinement and Prompt Optimization in Program Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.19184v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Harness optimization improves LLMs by refining reusable prompts and scaffolding, yet requires further adaptation for program generation tasks such as text-to-SQL and text-to-Python. Existing methods often rely on LLM reflectors to propose harness updates, which can fix observed failures but also disrupt previously correct behavior. Text-to-code tasks offer a natural way to mitigate this issue: we can execute generated outputs, allowing us to evaluate and verify the effects of proposed updates directly. Building on this signal, we introduce \textsc{HERO} (\textbf{H}arnessing \textbf{E}vidence for \textbf{R}efinement and \textbf{O}ptimization), which combines offline and test-time harness optimization. At the first stage, \method{} learns reusable prompt updates from execution-verified successes and failures and validates candidate revisions before adoption. At test time, we treat the generated code as an instance-specific harness and refine it using execution feedback. Across four SQL, Cypher, and Python benchmarks, \method{} achieves the best offline performance, improving pass@1 by \(7.6\) points over the initial prompt, while test-time refinement adds another \(2.0\) points and improves execution efficiency.

title: Learning Visual Speech Representations via Cross-Modal Distillation and Joint Face-Lip Modeling
description:
arXiv:2610.19559v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Lipreading remains challenging due to the inherent ambiguity of visual speech cues and their sensitivity to head pose and video resolution. In this work, we propose FLARE, a framework for robust visual speech representation learning via cross-modal distillation and joint face-lip modeling. FLARE leverages semantically rich Whisper representations as the acoustic teacher signal, converting them into discrete distillation targets through a random-projection quantizer and pretraining the model with a masked prediction objective. To capture complementary visual information, FLARE employs a dual-stream architecture that jointly processes lip region-of-interest (ROI) and full-face inputs, where the lip stream captures finegrained articulatory motion and the face stream encodes broader facial dynamics. During pretraining, auxiliary audio input is incorporated to facilitate cross-modal alignment, and modality dropout is applied to encourage robust visual-only representations. For downstream lipreading, FLARE serves as a visual encoder coupled with either a lightweight Transformer decoder or an LLM-based decoder. Evaluated on LRS2, LRS3, and the out-of-domain WildVSR benchmark, FLARE achieves strong lipreading performance, with word error rates of 11.7%, 13.2%, and 34.3%, respectively. A progressive design study confirms the contribution of each major component. Further analyses demonstrate that joint face-lip modeling improves robustness under degraded video resolution and large head pose variation, while yielding more phoneme-discriminative visual representations. Code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/jxzhanggg/FLARE.

title: How to choose the right hosting for your website
description:
When selecting a hosting environment, the choice between shared, VPS, dedicated, or cloud hosting impacts your resource isolation, scalability, and maintenance requirements.

Understanding the trade-offs between managed and unmanaged services is crucial for balancing operational overhead with infrastructure control.

This guide breaks down the essential factors for choosing a provider, from uptime reliability and SSL requirements to the specific needs of Linux vs.

Windows-based environments.

The main types of hospitality

Your choice depends on the needs of your project and the available cost:

  • Shared hosting: The most economical solution, ideal for starting out. Many websites share the same computer. However, if another page hosted on the same computer receives a lot of traffic, the speed of yours may be affected.
  • Virtual Private Server (VPS): You share the main computer with others, but you have your own isolated space and exclusive resources. It's like having your own apartment in an apartment building.
  • Exclusive hospitality: The entire computer belongs exclusively to you. It is the most powerful but also the most expensive option.
  • Cloud Hosting: Your website is hosted on an entire network of computers. It is a very flexible option, as if a problem occurs on one of them, your website can continue to operate using the others.

What to consider before choosing

Before you settle on a company, consider the following points:

  • Availability: It is the most important indicator of whether the provider is reliable. You want your page to remain open for visitors 24 hours a day.
  • Management: In managed hosting, the company takes care of the maintenance and security of the system for you. In unmanaged hosting, you are responsible for all the settings yourself.
  • Specialized packages: Many companies offer WordPress-specific packages that automatically handle tasks like updates and backups.
  • Security: If you are going to have an online store, it is necessary to use a security certificate so that your customer data is encrypted.
  • Additional services: Some companies, such as WP Engine, do not provide email services, so you will have to use another provider for your email.

Switching from one provider to another can be a complex process, so if you're starting out, a good approach is to choose a solution that meets your current needs, knowing that you can upgrade your package later.

title: Your browser agent pays to look at pictures: opencli vs claude-in-chrome token use
description:
We run a lot of clickops through Claude Code: reading dashboards, checking settings, pulling a number out of a web app. There are two ways we do it. claude-in-chrome drives Chrome and can return screenshots. opencli drives the same logged-in Chrome but returns the page as text.

We wanted to know what each one costs in tokens, so we measured it.

What we measured

We went through our own Claude Code session logs: 7,500+ browser tool calls. For each call, we took the token counts the API reported before and after it. The difference is how many tokens that call's result added to the context.

These are real API counts, not character-based estimates.

Screenshots are the bill

claude-in-chrome call type Share of calls Median tokens per call
Returned a screenshot 23% 1,855
Returned text only 77% 373

A screenshot call cost about 5x a text call. The 23% of calls that returned screenshots made up 49% of all claude-in-chrome tokens.

An opencli call had a median of 397 tokens. That is about the same as a claude-in-chrome text call. The difference between the two tools comes from screenshots, not from the text.

Same sites, both tools

Nine websites had at least 10 calls with each tool. Here is the change in median tokens per call when we used opencli instead of claude-in-chrome:

Site claude-in-chrome opencli Change
telegram.org 1,879 275 −85%
github.com 580 336 −42%
cloudflare.com 578 378 −35%
google.com 605 437 −28%
linkedin.com 736 594 −19%
youtube.com 542 470 −13%
lokerdollar.com 432 386 −11%
nvidia.com 363 384 +6%
bing.com 270 353 +31%

opencli won on 7 of the 9 sites, about 27% fewer tokens per call when weighted by call count. The big wins were logged-in web apps like Telegram Web, GitHub and the Cloudflare dashboard. On simple public pages the two tools were even, and on Bing opencli used more. The nvidia.com and bing.com rows have under 30 calls each, so take them loosely.

Our clickops rule now

  1. Use the API or curl when one exists.
  2. Read the page as text with opencli.
  3. Take a screenshot only to check something visual.

Limits of this measurement

The site comparison matches calls by website, not by identical task. We did not run the same task twice with each tool, so this is a field measurement, not a lab A/B. Screenshot results also stay in context and get re-read on later turns. We left that out because session length differed between the tools, so the real cost of screenshots is likely higher than shown here.

title: Five checks before turning an invoice CSV into a follow-up list
description:
An overdue-invoice view looks simple: read a CSV, compare due dates and sort. The awkward bugs live in the details. A worklist can send someone chasing the wrong amount even when its table looks correct.

We used these checks while building Cashflow Check at Xargaar Tools. The examples below are fictional.

1. Work in the smallest currency unit

For the current tool, amounts are plain positive decimals with no more than two decimal places. Convert them to integer cents before arithmetic. An invoice for 1,200.00 with 300.00 paid has 900.00 remaining, not 1,200.00 overdue.

Reject malformed amounts instead of quietly converting them to zero. Check that paid does not exceed the invoice total. Supporting every currency's decimal convention is a separate problem; this tool deliberately limits its input format.

2. Keep currencies separate

USD 900 and EUR 700 are two balances. They are not a meaningful total of 1,600 unless you explicitly choose exchange rates and a valuation date. Our review groups balances by the currency code supplied in the CSV. It does not convert currencies.

3. Validate calendar dates, not just date-shaped strings

A pattern matching YYYY-MM-DD is only the first check. Parse the date and round-trip it back to the same format to catch impossible dates. Use a chosen review date so that a saved worklist states when it was prepared.

An invoice due on the review date is due today, not already a day late. Keep that boundary explicit.

4. Reject duplicate invoice/customer pairs

A duplicate import row can double the amount a dashboard tells someone to chase. Make the key explicit and reject repeats with the input row number. Our current key is the invoice identifier plus customer name; if your source allows reused identifiers, define the right key for that source rather than copying this choice blindly.

5. Treat export as another input boundary

CSV quoting and spreadsheet formula handling solve different problems. Quote fields and double embedded quotes. Separately consider text beginning with formula-like characters such as =, +, - or @ before someone opens the export in a spreadsheet. Test the target spreadsheet's behavior rather than treating a single escape rule as a universal security guarantee.

The same caution applies to the worklist itself: imported payment data can be stale. Check payment records before contacting a customer. A local CSV tool cannot know that money arrived after the export.

Try the workflow

Cashflow Check's free sample runs in the browser without an account or invoice upload. It accepts up to 5,000 rows and a 5 MB CSV, shows remaining balances by customer and currency, and exports a follow-up worklist. It does not connect to a bank or send reminders.

Disclosure: this is our product. The optional one-time $19 review pack adds the offline download, editable review log and weekly workflow. The free tool stays available. It is one part of the Xargaar Tools collection.

title: Imagining Goals with Geometric Horizon Models for Policy Generalization
description:
arXiv:2610.19129v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Training from offline data has allowed for substantial progress in domains such as robotics, leading to general-purpose policies that can be easily applied zero-shot or efficiently finetuned for downstream tasks. However, these policies can still have poor generalization, both due to the choice of modeling objective and from learning from a static dataset. In this work, we focus on the challenging task of zero-shot goal generalization, where a policy is evaluated on unseen tasks that require combining its existing knowledge (compositional generalization). An avenue for improving a policy's generalization is by generating new experience with world models; however, such generation has proven difficult for longer horizons. Thus, to alleviate this issue, we propose TD-Aug, which samples from a geometric horizon model and allows for directly imagining novel outcomes that can be achieved by composing existing knowledge. We demonstrate that training on these future outcomes as goals for goal-conditioned BC policies significantly improves generalization in stitching-based OGBench tasks.

title: KoAGE: Do Large Language Models Know, Learn, and Coin Korean Neologisms?
description:
arXiv:2610.19399v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Korean neologisms arise through diverse mechanisms, a demanding test of language models beyond lexical memorization. To enable systematic evaluation, we introduce NeoTrace, an automated, rerunnable framework that collects and dates neologisms across genres. Its 4,271 entries support KoAGE, a cutoff-aware benchmark with three acquisition and two generation tasks---the latter, to our knowledge, the first to compare model coinages with attested neologisms under their original materials and community context. Across 21 models, lexical recall diverges from contextual inference: in a five-model temporal analysis, models define only 13-30% of cutoff-year words, yet can infer meaning from one usage. However, structural understanding remains limited: even correct definitions barely improve formation analysis of pre-cutoff neologisms. Given word-building materials, single models often follow human formation mechanisms, whereas multi-agent coinage favors abbreviation and depends on interaction framing. KoAGE thus separates what models know, learn from use, and coin.

title: Target-Token Asymmetry Can Masquerade As Depth Specialization
description:
arXiv:2610.19344v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Layer-ablation studies often perturb early or late layers of a language model, compare the damage to prediction on two corpora, and read a larger early-layer effect on one corpus as early-layer specialization for its task. Such a comparison averages over the tokens that each corpus asks the model to predict, and these target tokens differ: math solutions, for example, ask for far more whitespace and numbers than encyclopedia prose. We show that this difference can create the appearance of depth specialization. We split a cross-corpus early--late damage interaction by target-token type and recompute it under a target mixture shared by both corpora. Between GSM8K and Wikitext, a positive interaction replicates across five model instances. In the three fully decomposed models, only whitespace has a positive interaction. Removing whitespace reverses the pooled effect in all three, and matching the full target mixture reverses it in two. The diagnosis holds under position matching, adversarial reassignment of token types, and a continuous readout. The risk can also be anticipated from the tokenizer alone. A screen computed before any model runs places every held-out pair it scored in the region its label predicts, and on the pairs it rates at high or medium risk, removing whitespace reverses every positive pooled estimate. A smaller content-word effect one token ahead follows the share of content targets that the unablated model already predicts. A cross-corpus depth effect therefore supports an interpretation of task specialization only after the target-token mixture is reported, the effect is decomposed by token type, and a mixture-matched summary keeps its sign.

title: Cheap Webhook Task Processing Explained — Node.js SaaS Rate-Limit Retry Backoff
description:
Short answer: for a nightly fintech reconciliation, put the delayed webhook work in a queue and make the worker idempotent. A cron trigger should enqueue a bounded batch, while retries and rate limits live at the worker boundary. That shape is cheap to reason about because the provider's rate limit cannot turn one long cron invocation into a hidden scheduler.

The bill is mostly downstream work, not the timer. Every payment lookup, webhook delivery attempt, and retained message costs attention; a cron job that fires 10,000 calls at once creates a burst of throttled retries. Controlling worker concurrency changes that dominant term. It also gives the team one place to record an idempotency key such as reconcile:2026-09-10:merchant-42:payment-981, so a duplicate delivery cannot post the same ledger adjustment twice.

Bursts hurt.

Suppose the provider allows 20 requests per second and the nightly window contains 2,400 merchants. A cron loop that launches every request immediately will spend its first minutes collecting 429 responses, then create a retry wave that is larger than the original wave. With a queue, the trigger publishes the merchant windows quickly, while workers take 20 tokens per second and attach the same reconciliation key to every attempt. Merchant 17 may fail once and return after a 30-second delay; merchant 18 may succeed on its first call. Those paths do not interfere. The audit row records the provider cursor, attempt count, and final comparison before the message is acknowledged. If the worker dies after the provider accepts the adjustment but before ack, the next delivery still carries the same key, so the database uniqueness check and provider idempotency guard converge on one ledger result. This is the operational reason I care about queue shape more than the timer brand.

There is a retention trade-off. An acknowledged queue message is deleted, and retention tops out at 30 days. I keep the reconciliation result and provider response hash in an audit table before acking; I do not pretend the queue is a replay log. When an auditor asks for a six-month trail, the table is what we query, and the queue's short retention is the deliberate cost of keeping the operational path small.

That boundary is where Infrai can fit: its queue is reachable through a plain REST API, so the nightly trigger and a Python or Node.js worker can share one HTTP contract without an SDK. I would test it for the low-complexity path below, not for workflow orchestration.

Two viable shapes for delayed webhook work

The simple shape is cron plus queue: a nightly trigger finds the reconciliation window, publishes one message per merchant or bounded page, and workers consume at a controlled concurrency. Cron executions are capped at 900 seconds, so long work belongs behind the trigger. The queue's standard delivery is at-least-once; the invariant is that the consumer can safely run the same message twice.

The second shape is a durable workflow engine. Temporal or Airflow can model a multi-step reconciliation with joins, compensations, and a long-lived history. That is the right invariant when a payment run is a graph whose later steps depend on several earlier results. It is more machinery than a single provider sweep needs.

For a small SaaS, I would choose the first shape when the job is “fetch, compare, emit, retry.” Its broader backend surface can also keep storage and scheduling behind the same key, which removes a little integration bookkeeping without changing the queue invariant.

How should Node.js teams model rate limits, retries, and backoff?

Treat a rate limit as state, not as a sleep sprinkled through a cron loop. A worker should reserve a provider token, perform one idempotent operation, and requeue a failed attempt with a bounded delay. Exponential backoff with jitter prevents every merchant from retrying on the same second; Retry-After wins when the provider sends it.

Here is the core decision in Python, kept independent of a vendor client so the behavior is testable:

import requests
import json
import os
import random
import time


def retry_delay(attempt, retry_after=None):
    if retry_after is not None:
        return min(float(retry_after), 604800)
    cap = min(2 ** attempt, 3600)
    return random.uniform(cap / 2, cap)


def reconciliation_key(merchant_id, window_start):
    return f"reconcile:{merchant_id}:{window_start}"


def publish_reconciliation(queue, payload, delay_seconds=0):
    body = {"queue": queue, "message": payload,
            "delay_seconds": delay_seconds}
    headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['INFRAI_API_KEY']}",
               "Idempotency-Key": payload["reconciliation_key"]}
    for attempt in range(5):
        response = requests.request(
            "POST", "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/publish",
            json=body, headers=headers, timeout=20)
        if response.status_code < 400:
            return response.json()
        if response.status_code != 429:
            raise RuntimeError(response.text)
        time.sleep(retry_delay(attempt, response.headers.get("Retry-After")))
    raise RuntimeError("rate limit persisted after five attempts")

Keep delayed messages at or below 604800 seconds, and attach the reconciliation key to the payload. If a write is retried, send the same client id or idempotency key. The platform convention uses an Idempotency-Key header for operations that support it; your application still owns the provider-side idempotency check.

There is no native debounce or throttle primitive, and FIFO deduplication lasts only five minutes. That is a capability boundary, not a failure mode: use a database uniqueness constraint for a longer business window. For one-to-many delivery, publish to separate queues because there is no built-in topic fan-out.

What do queue, cron, and workflow products actually trade?

Option Best fit Retry and rate-limit shape Retention or orchestration caveat
Queue plus cron trigger Delayed webhook batches and ordinary SaaS reconciliation Worker concurrency, requeue, exponential backoff At-least-once; finite retention; no joins
Cloudflare Workers Cron Triggers Short, publicly reachable HTTP trigger You build the queue and retry state A single invocation is capped at 900 seconds
Inngest Event-driven functions with managed retry history Function-level retry and step state More orchestration semantics than a basic queue
Temporal Long-running, branching reconciliation workflows Durable workflow timers and activities Operational and modeling overhead is substantial

The comparison is not a price contest. Cloudflare is compelling when the timer and edge execution are already your platform. Inngest is a better choice when each reconciliation has explicit steps and you want their history attached to the run. Stick with Temporal when you need DAG-like joins or compensation logic. A queue is not suitable when replay across multiple consumer groups is a hard requirement; persist an event log or select a stream system instead.

The small implementation I would ship

Create one queue per independent consumer, publish a bounded batch from the nightly trigger, then let workers claim and ack messages only after the audit row is durable. A failed provider call becomes a delayed republish, with the attempt count and next-attempt timestamp in the message. Keep payloads below 256 KB and delayed work within seven days; a later reconciliation window can be scheduled by the next cron run.

I initially thought a FIFO queue would solve duplicate payments by itself. It does not: the five-minute deduplication window is shorter than a nightly business key, and standard queues can deliver at least once. The invariant belongs in the database and in the provider request, where the same reconciliation_key produces the same result.

One operational wrinkle matters in fintech: cron does not backfill triggers missed while paused, and run output is limited to the first 4 KB. Write a run record as soon as the trigger starts, then store detailed diagnostics in your audit system. Your mileage may vary around provider-specific quotas; confirm the live quota contract before choosing worker concurrency.

Infrai is worth trying for teams that want this queue-centered shape and a plain HTTP integration, especially when the same service already needs several backend capabilities under one key. It is not the right choice for a workflow graph, Kafka-style replay, private push endpoints, or native fan-out. In those cases, use Temporal, Airflow, a stream platform, or a specialist queue that states those guarantees directly.

If this boundary matches your reconciliation job, the queue capability details and runnable examples are at docs.infrai.cc.

  • https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/queue.push_subscribe
  • https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/configuration/cron-triggers/
  • https://www.inngest.com/docs
  • https://docs.temporal.io/workflows
  • https://docs.bullmq.io/guide/retrying-failing-jobs
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110

title: Beyond Time Induction: Structured Conditional Neural Solvers for Parametric Stochastic-Volatility Pricing
description:
arXiv:2610.19254v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Physics-informed neural networks provide a flexible framework for learning parametric PDE solution families without labeled data, yet preserving accurate derivatives across heterogeneous regimes remains challenging. Structured neural solvers offer compact representations, but restrictive conditional parameterizations can limit adaptation across the solution family. We introduce BeTINN, a structured conditional architecture extending time-induced modulation through multi-directional time-parameter conditioning and a joint residual pathway. We evaluate BeTINN on the Heston stochastic-volatility PDE, a demanding parametric problem with mixed derivatives and economically relevant first- and second-order sensitivities. BeTINN improves joint accuracy across normalized option value and key sensitivity metrics relative to our baselines. Controlled ablations characterize the roles of its architectural components. We further find that validation physics loss is informative but does not fully determine differential fidelity, and that accurate solution values can coexist with localized derivative errors. These results support structured conditional adaptation and motivate derivative-aware evaluation when sensitivities are downstream quantities of interest.

title: SceneAE: Scene Generation and Reconstruction in Queryable 3D-Anchored Latent Space
description:
arXiv:2610.19708v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent video world models have increasingly adopted 3D memory mechanisms to integrate historical observations into a lightweight and persistent scene representation. This naturally raises a complementary question: if 3D representations can serve as an effective mechanism for memorizing observed scenes, can they also be directly used as the latent space for reconstructing and generating scenes? Motivated by this idea, we represent a scene as a compact and unstructured 3D-anchored latent space (\textbf{SceneAE}). Each latent combines an
  explicit 3D position with an implicit content feature and is spatially grounded to describe its local scene region, forming a
  sparse latent point cloud. Unlike conventional video-VAE latents that describe how a scene appears from particular viewpoints, our
  representation directly describes the scene itself, making it naturally applicable to both reconstruction and generation. For
  reconstruction, once the scene has been generated, our persistent 3D representation can be projected and decoded into RGB-D observations by different target cameras, without the need to regenerate a video for each new camera trajectory.
  For generation, we leverage the geometry-content separation to first generate camera-controlled 3D geometry and
  then synthesize content conditioned on it, reducing camera-appearance entanglement and improving camera
  controllability. Experiments show that this 3D latent achieves superior generation quality, computational cost, and camera controllability.

title: Exploring Interpretability in Deep Learning-Based Forest Classification - Separating Similar Forest Classes using Sentinel-2 Time Series
description:
arXiv:2610.19270v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The ecological insurance theory posits that diverse forests are more resilient and better able to adapt to changing environmental conditions. Increasing drought and heat stress in Central Europe promotes mixed forests for maintaining ecosystem services. However, a diverse species distribution complicates remote sensing-based species mapping, as distinguishing pure from mixed species compositions at the pixel level remains challenging. We evaluated the potential of recurrent neural networks (RNNs) for tree-species classification from Sentinel-2 time series and investigated the spectral-temporal features underlying class discrimination, with particular emphasis on separating pure from mixed Norway spruce pixels. We compared RNN classification models with Random Forest (RF) and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) and used Integrated Gradients (IG) to quantify feature attributions across spectral bands and time. The best-performing RNN achieved a Macro-F1 score of 0.851 on the test data, outperforming XGBoost by 0.012 and Random Forest by 0.103. Beyond classification performance, the attribution analysis revealed distinct spectral-temporal patterns associated with the separation of pure and mixed Norway spruce pixels. Attribution values increased particularly after approximately day of year (DOY) 125, while B11 showed the strongest contribution during periods of increasing spectral divergence between the two classes. These findings show that recurrent models can provide competitive classification performance while also revealing the phenological periods and spectral regions that are most relevant for distinguishing closely related forest compositions. Combining time-series classification with explainability therefore provides additional insight into the spectral-temporal mechanisms underlying tree-species discrimination and may support more detailed mapping of mixed forest structures.

title: Data-free Multistep Diffusion Distillation
description:
arXiv:2610.19305v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: One-step diffusion distillation achieves strong performance on small datasets but remains insufficient for high-resolution or complex text-to-image settings. Extending to multistep distillation often requires training data, suffers from early-step degradation, inconsistent outputs across sampling budgets, and incurs high computational cost. We identify that these limitations stem from simultaneous training, where a single adapted network approximates multiple score functions of different student distributions at once, causing biased distribution matching and unstable optimization. Therefore, we propose Progressive Multistep Data-free Distillation (PMDD), which assigns a dedicated adapted network per student distribution while avoiding the memory overhead of maintaining multiple adapted networks. Combined with a stage-wise unforget loss to preserve earlier-step generations, PMDD reduces optimization bias in the student, provides faster convergence, and a single unified model that supports multiple inference budgets. Extensive experiments show that PMDD matches or outperforms data-free few-step baselines at every multistep budget, reaches FID 1.99 on ImageNet 64x64 in two steps, below its 512-NFE teacher (2.32), and achieves FID 7.76 on zero-shot COCO 512x512, while requiring 4-5x less training compute than data-free DMDv2 to support three inference budgets.

title: The Silent Failures in Agentic Data Science
description:
arXiv:2610.14115v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models have significantly lowered the barrier to writing code. Naturally, this has also led to the development of data science agents that promise automating the design and execution of data science from task formulation to model development. Existing evaluations of agentic data science (agentic DS) assess downstream predictive performance and code correctness, providing preliminary insight in agentic DS capabilities. We argue that these evaluations overlook the fundamental principles of data science: methodological data science- and domain knowledge. As such, only assessing downstream performance masks methodological failures such as data leakage and inappropriate validation, limiting the development of robust agentic DS systems. In this paper, we evaluate agentic DS beyond accuracy from three different angles: 1) a large-scale analysis of failure modes in common agentic DS frameworks and models across 220 data science tasks, 2) a reusable and extensible test suite with curated data science tasks that test for six specific failures in a controlled manner, and 3) a qualitative assessment of agentic DS pipelines against expert solutions on Kaggle competitions. We find that the majority of agentic solutions contain at least one failure mode despite the complexity of agentic harness or model capacity. Moreover, we identify a positive correlation between the occurrence of data leakage failures and predictive performance, confirming the necessity to evaluate agents beyond accuracy. Our qualitative analysis shows that DS agents generally lack problem solving creativity and domain knowledge, compared to competition-winning data scientists. We believe that principled failure mode analysis, as presented here, should be integral part of agentic DS evaluations, and that the insights we surface will be key in developing trustworthy agentic DS pipelines.
