title: FinGREAT: Evaluating LLMs on Financial Graph-guided Retrieval And Typing
description:
arXiv:2610.19240v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Financial disclosures express the underlying relationships of double-entry accounting through unstructured text. While financial LLM benchmarks predominantly emphasize question answering and classification, schema-guided evidence discovery remains relatively under-explored. We investigate whether open-weight LLMs can extract and classify evidence corresponding to predefined double-entry accounting relationships underlying the text. Using a financial accounting graph comprising 11 nodes (accounts) and 11 edges (transaction types), we evaluate mid-sized models from 5 open-weight families across 1,300 SEC 10-K Item 7 filings spanning 26 years, comparing their extraction performance against three proprietary models. Results reveal substantial differences in extraction volume, edge distributions, and cross-model agreement. Building on this study, we introduce a human-annotated relation classification benchmark comprising 483 passages across three financial accounting categories, evaluating 34 open-weight and 10 proprietary models. The strongest open-weight and proprietary models achieve 84.1\% and 92.8\% accuracy, respectively, with considerable variation across accounting categories. Our findings highlight the importance of evaluating evidence discovery and relation understanding separately, while investigating locally deployable models for scalable, privacy-sensitive financial analysis.

title: Crossing the Gender Binary: Modelling Gendered Reference in Science Fiction and General Fiction
description:
arXiv:2610.19028v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Science fiction is widely credited with unsettling gender. This article asks whether that holds at the linguistic level, in how readily gendered reference gives way to its counterpart, a neutral term, or other social category, and whether it separates the genre from general fiction. It does so by masking man/men, woman/women, and person/people across same-period science fiction and general fiction corpora and classifying RoBERTa's five likeliest substitutes by gender. Retention and displacement are permutation-tested over five resampling rounds, and the underlying sentences are read closely. Both corpora cross the gender binary in both directions, but unequally: where woman is masked, the model predicts a masculine term about twice as often as it predicts a feminine term where man is masked. Each mismatch marks a statistical surprise, a word the corpus did not expect there. Against this shared pattern, science fiction shows greater gender permeability than the general fiction corpus, placing man in feminine contexts more often than general fiction while the reverse rate holds steady. Its degendering tendency is stronger too, drawing both gendered terms toward the neutral. Beyond the binary, a masked woman also draws substitutes naming a social category and no gender far more often than a masked man does. In measuring the gender permeability of man, woman, and person in linguistic distribution and testing whether genre changes it, the study gives science fiction studies linguistic evidence for thematic claims and computational literary studies a pipeline applicable to other category vocabularies, such as race and class.

title: Choosing a WinSCP Alternative: Start With the Job, Not the App
description:
WinSCP already does a lot: SFTP, SCP, FTP/FTPS, WebDAV and S3, plus directory synchronization and Windows scripting. If you’re looking for an alternative, the useful question isn’t “Which app is best?” It’s “Which part of my workflow does WinSCP no longer fit?”

That distinction matters. A tool that works on macOS may not offer WinSCP’s automation, and an SSH terminal with a file browser may not replace a dedicated transfer client.

First, identify the task you need to replace

List what you actually use before comparing apps:

  • Moving files manually: Do you need a two-pane browser, transfer queue, or support for several protocols?
  • Connecting from another operating system: Are you moving to macOS or Linux, where WinSCP doesn’t offer a native desktop app?
  • Working with cloud storage: Do you need S3, Google Drive, OneDrive, or another provider?
  • Administering a server: Do you want a terminal and file browser together, or are you happy using separate tools?
  • Automating transfers: Do existing scripts, scheduled jobs, or .NET integrations depend on WinSCP?
  • Mounting remote files: Do you want remote storage to appear in Finder or File Explorer, rather than opening a transfer client?

These are different needs. A mount tool, a terminal emulator, and an SFTP client aren’t interchangeable just because each can access remote files.

It also helps to check the protocol requirement. SFTP runs over SSH; FTPS is FTP secured with TLS. They’re distinct protocols, so a client supporting one doesn’t necessarily support the other. If you’re weighing transfer options, this SFTP client comparison can help you narrow the category before picking an app.

Shortlist by operating system and workflow

If you want a free, cross-platform file-transfer client

FileZilla Client is a straightforward starting point for FTP, FTPS, and SFTP on Windows, macOS, and Linux. Its standard client is free. Some cloud integrations are part of FileZilla Pro, so check which edition supports the services you need.

It’s a practical choice when your core job is browsing local and remote files and transferring them. It isn’t a one-for-one substitute for WinSCP’s Windows scripting and .NET assembly.

If you need SFTP plus cloud storage

Cyberduck is available for Windows and macOS and supports SFTP alongside a range of cloud storage services. The base app is free and open source. It’s a file and storage browser, not an interactive SSH terminal, and it doesn’t have a native Linux desktop release.

If you’re on macOS

ForkLift offers a Mac-native, two-pane file-manager workflow with remote connections and cloud services. Transmit is another paid Mac option focused on transfers and synchronization. They’re not Linux or Windows replacements, and their licensing differs. Check current platform requirements and terms before buying.

If you want a Windows SSH terminal and graphical SFTP

Bitvise SSH Client combines SSH terminal and graphical SFTP workflows on Windows. It’s a reasonable option if you’ve been using WinSCP alongside a separate terminal client.

MobaXterm is a broader Windows toolbox that includes SSH, SFTP, and tools for other remote-access workflows such as X11. Its free Home edition has limits; check the current edition details if saved sessions, tunnels, or macros matter to you.

If automation is the priority

Don’t switch away from WinSCP just because a different client has a newer interface. WinSCP’s scripting interface and .NET assembly can be important parts of a deployment or backup process. A graphical alternative may not run those jobs, and another command-line tool won’t automatically understand existing WinSCP scripts.

For cross-platform transfer automation, rclone is worth evaluating. It supports SFTP and many cloud backends, but it’s a command-line tool rather than a two-pane file manager. Be especially careful with synchronization: rclone sync can delete files at the destination to make it match the source. Test paths and use a dry run before relying on a new job.

Also distinguish SCP from SFTP when migrating. WinSCP supports both, but many modern workflows use SFTP; this explanation of how SCP and SFTP differ is useful if an old script or server specifically requires SCP.

Migrate without breaking a working setup

Treat a client migration like a small infrastructure change—not just an app install.

  1. Inventory your saved sites. Record hostnames, ports, usernames, protocols, key locations, proxy or jump-host settings, and default remote directories.
  2. Find every automation dependency. Search for scheduled tasks, scripts, and applications that invoke WinSCP. A site you rarely open manually may still be used by a nightly job.
  3. Recreate connections using supported import tools. Don’t assume a destination client can import WinSCP’s settings. An export file can also contain sensitive connection details, so protect it accordingly.
  4. Verify the server’s identity. When the new client first connects, check the host-key fingerprint through a trusted channel. Don’t accept a changed or unfamiliar key just to get past a warning.
  5. Test a harmless transfer. Confirm the remote directory, permissions, file contents, and transfer direction before editing production files or changing a sync job.
  6. Keep a rollback path. Retain the old configuration and scripts until the replacement has passed the real tasks you depend on.

A practical decision rule

If you use Windows and mainly need reliable file transfers or mature WinSCP scripts, staying with WinSCP may be the simplest choice. If you need a native Mac or Linux client, start with a cross-platform transfer tool. If you want a Windows terminal alongside graphical SFTP, evaluate an SSH client that includes both. If repeatable automation is the job, test the replacement’s command-line behavior before migrating production tasks.

The best alternative is the one that covers the specific gap without quietly removing a feature you rely on. If WinSCP still handles your workflow, there’s no technical prize for replacing it.

I originally published a more detailed version of this guide on the SSHFlow blog.

I'm also building SSHFlow — an SSH client where every server gets its own workspace for terminals, SFTP, code, and databases.

title: Frustratingly Easy Agentic RAG via Portable Skills: A Case Study in Customer Support
description:
arXiv:2610.14428v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Enterprise workflow automation typically requires retrieving a complete and accurate set of relevant information from large operational document corpora (SOPs, policy documents) given a specific scenario or request. In customer support (CS), for example, human specialists must determine the correct sequence of resolution steps for each case, a task that demands precise grounding in policy documentation. Meeting this bar in production typically requires complex document chunking, indexing, and retrieval pipelines, often layered with learned re-rankers, query rewriters, and bespoke agentic RAG infrastructure.
  We report a deployment case study of a simpler alternative: a portable skill consisting of a natural-language instruction, lightweight tools (a retrieval API, format-checking scripts), and a corpus enriched with an LLM-generated navigation layer, which is a structured "Wikipedia-style" index over the underlying documents. This agentic RAG approach is straightforward to implement (1-2 engineer days), portable across capable agentic harnesses (e.g., Claude Code), and performs strongly on the challenging task of CS resolution workflow generation, achieving 99.2% procedural equivalence to human-approved ground truth and 83.3% evidence sufficiency. It is also roughly an order of magnitude slower per case than our deployed production assistant (~90 s vs. ~8-9 s), so we claim no latency advantage. Our claim is scoped to that setting: a mature, well-curated corpus, a latency-tolerant workflow, and human review of every case. There, the skill did the work of a complex RAG stack, and maintenance became a matter of editing text and data rather than retraining models.

title: MCP Explained for Frontend Developers: The USB-C of AI Integrations
description:
AI is everywhere today. We have GitHub Copilot writing code, ChatGPT answering questions, and AI agents capable of performing complex workflows. But there is one problem: every AI application needs a different way to connect with tools, databases, APIs, and services.

Imagine buying a laptop that requires a different cable for charging, data transfer, and external displays. It would be frustrating.

That's exactly how AI integrations have looked for a long time.

Enter Model Context Protocol (MCP), a new standard designed to make AI systems communicate with external tools in a consistent way.

In simple terms, MCP is like USB-C for AI applications.

The Problem Before MCP

Let's say you're building a frontend application that allows users to interact with an AI assistant.

Your AI needs to:

Read customer data
Fetch project details
Query a database
Create tickets in Jira
Access GitHub repositories

Without MCP, every integration requires custom implementation.

Frontend App
|
├── Custom GitHub API Integration
├── Custom Jira API Integration
├── Custom Database Connector
└── Custom Internal Service Connector

Every tool has:

Different authentication methods
Different request formats
Different response structures

As the number of tools grows, maintenance becomes difficult.

What is MCP?

Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open protocol that standardizes how AI models communicate with external systems.

Instead of building custom integrations for every tool, developers can expose functionality through an MCP server.

Frontend App
|
▼
AI Agent
|
▼
MCP Server
|
├── GitHub
├── Jira
├── Database
└── Internal APIs

The AI does not need to know how every system works internally.

It simply asks the MCP server for available tools and uses them when needed.

Why Should Frontend Developers Care?

Many frontend developers assume MCP is only for AI engineers.

That's not true.

If you're building:

AI-powered dashboards
Chat interfaces
Internal enterprise tools
Developer portals
Productivity applications

You'll likely interact with MCP-based systems sooner than you think.

For frontend developers, MCP offers three major benefits:

  1. Faster AI Integrations

You don't need to create separate integrations for every backend service.

The AI agent can discover available tools automatically.

  1. Cleaner Architecture

Instead of hardcoding API calls throughout the application, business actions can be exposed through MCP tools.

  1. Better Scalability

As new tools are added, the frontend often requires little or no changes.

The MCP server handles the complexity.

A Real-World Example

Imagine you're building a Project Management Assistant.

A user types:

Show all open bugs assigned to me and create a summary.

Without MCP:

Frontend calls Bug API
Frontend processes responses
Frontend calls AI API
Backend coordinates everything

With MCP:

User submits request
AI discovers available tools
AI calls Bug Tracker Tool
AI receives results
AI generates summary

The process becomes more intelligent and flexible.

MCP Components

There are three main components.

  1. MCP Host

The application where users interact with AI.

Examples:

AI chat applications
IDE extensions
Enterprise assistants

  1. MCP Client

Acts as the bridge between the host and the MCP server.

It sends requests and receives responses.

  1. MCP Server

Provides tools and resources that AI can use.

Examples:

GetUserDetails()
CreateJiraTicket()
FetchSalesReport()
SearchDocumentation()

The AI can discover and use these tools when needed.

Frontend Use Cases
Customer Support Portal

Users ask:

Show all unresolved support tickets from this week.

AI automatically retrieves data from connected systems.

Developer Dashboard

Users ask:

Show all failed deployments in production.

AI can fetch deployment logs through MCP tools.

Knowledge Management System

Users ask:

Summarize architecture documents related to authentication.

The AI retrieves documentation and generates insights.

A Simple Mental Model

Think of MCP as a restaurant.

User → Customer
AI → Waiter
MCP Server → Kitchen
Tools → Chefs

The customer doesn't walk into the kitchen.

The waiter knows which chef can prepare which dish.

Similarly, AI doesn't need direct knowledge of all systems.

It asks the MCP server for available tools and uses them when required.

Benefits of MCP
Reduced Development Effort

Build a tool once and expose it through MCP.

Multiple AI applications can reuse it.

Consistency

Every tool follows a common protocol.

Developers spend less time learning custom integrations.

Better User Experience

AI agents can accomplish tasks rather than just answer questions.

Future-Proof Architecture

As more organizations adopt AI agents, MCP provides a standardized integration layer.

Challenges to Consider

MCP is powerful, but it's not magic.

Security

Giving AI access to tools requires proper:

Authentication
Authorization
Audit logging
Tool Quality

Poorly designed tools lead to poor AI performance.

Monitoring

Track:

Tool usage
Failures
Response times

Just like any other API platform.

My Take

I believe MCP has the potential to become one of the most important standards in the AI ecosystem.

For frontend developers, the biggest shift is this:

We are moving from building applications that only display data to building applications that help users accomplish tasks through AI.

In the next few years, knowing how AI agents interact with tools may become just as important as understanding REST APIs or GraphQL today.

If you're a frontend developer exploring AI, now is a great time to learn MCP.

The earlier you understand it, the easier it will be to build the next generation of intelligent applications.

Final Thoughts

Frontend development has evolved from static pages to SPAs, then to cloud-connected applications, and now to AI-powered experiences.

MCP is another step in that evolution.

Instead of teaching AI about every system individually, we provide a standard way for systems to expose capabilities. The result is simpler integrations, smarter applications, and a better developer experience.

Think of MCP as USB-C for AI: one standard connection that makes everything work together. 🚀

title: GBase Database(GBase 8s) Installation FAQ: 10 Questions Beginners Ask
description:
Installing GBase Database(GBase 8s) for the first time can raise questions about Linux users, environment variables, character sets, network connections, and instance startup. This FAQ answers 10 common installation questions and explains how to troubleshoot typical issues without making risky configuration changes.

Q1: Can I install GBase Database(GBase 8s) as the root user?

Answer: Yes. In a typical GBase Database(GBase 8s) installation workflow, use root to install the database software and perform system-level configuration, then switch to the dedicated gbasedbt account to initialize and run the database instance.

Typical Workflow

Step 1: Install the software as root.

Run the installation program according to the instructions provided with your GBase Database(GBase 8s) installation package.

Step 2: Prepare the database environment.

Verify that the required directories, ownership, permissions, and environment variables are configured correctly for the gbasedbt account.

Step 3: Switch to the database user.

su - gbasedbt

Step 4: Initialize the instance.

Run the documented instance initialization command under the gbasedbt account. For example, oninit -ivy may be used when initializing a new instance, provided this matches the procedure for your version and configuration.

Important: Do not run instance initialization commands against an existing database as a troubleshooting shortcut. Confirm the instance state and follow the appropriate startup or recovery procedure.

Q2: Why can't I connect when sqlhosts contains localhost?

Answer: The cause depends on the connection protocol, server configuration, and how the hostname resolves.

In GBase Database(GBase 8s), the sqlhosts entry specifies the server name, connection protocol, host, and service or port. For TCP connections, an entry may look like this:

gbase01 onsoctcp 192.168.1.100 9088

This is an illustrative example, not a universal configuration. Replace the server name, address, and port with the values used by your installation.

When troubleshooting, verify that:

  • The client uses the expected server name.
  • The host resolves to the correct address.
  • The configured protocol matches the intended connection method.
  • The server is listening on the configured port.
  • Firewall rules allow the connection when connecting remotely.

localhost does not automatically mean a connection will fail. Check the actual sqlhosts configuration and connection error before changing it.

Q3: Can I change the character set after installation?

Answer: It depends on which character set or locale setting you need to change.

GBase Database(GBase 8s) environments may use settings such as DB_LOCALE and CLIENT_LOCALE to control database and client character handling. These settings serve different purposes, and changing a client environment variable does not convert existing database data.

Before making changes:

  1. Identify the database's current locale and the application's expected encoding.
  2. Check the requirements for the specific database and client version.
  3. Test Chinese text insertion and retrieval in a non-production environment.
  4. Back up important data before performing any migration or conversion.

If an existing database must use a different database locale, creating a new database with the intended configuration and migrating the data may be necessary. Confirm the supported migration procedure first.

Do not assume that changing DB_LOCALE or CLIENT_LOCALE alone will convert an existing database. Choose the locale based on the application's requirements and the character sets supported by the installation.

Q4: Why does oninit produce no obvious output?

Answer: Limited terminal output does not necessarily mean that startup has failed.

Start by checking the instance status:

onstat -

Then inspect the relevant environment variables:

echo "$GBASEDBTDIR"
echo "$ONCONFIG"

If the expected environment is configured, inspect the message log. For example, some installations use a log under the database installation's temporary directory:

tail -50 "$GBASEDBTDIR/tmp/online.log"

The actual log location depends on the configuration. Check the configured message-log path if this file does not exist.

Also verify that you are using the correct database account and configuration file. Avoid repeatedly running initialization commands to troubleshoot a startup problem; first determine the instance's current state and read the error messages.

Q5: What is the default port for GBase Database(GBase 8s)?

Answer: Port 9088 is commonly seen in GBase 8s examples, but the actual port depends on the instance configuration.

Check the configured service or port in sqlhosts and the corresponding network configuration. You can inspect listening TCP ports with:

ss -lntp

If you need to change the port, follow the configuration procedure for your version and ensure the client connection settings match the server.

Changing a port may also require updates to firewall rules, monitoring systems, and application connection strings. Do not assume that every installation uses the same port.

Q6: What should I do if dependency installation fails?

Answer: First, identify the missing package or library instead of installing a large, generic list of dependencies.

On a compatible RPM-based Linux system, you can check whether package repositories are available with:

yum repolist

If the installer reports a missing library, check the exact package name and version required by your GBase Database(GBase 8s) release.

Common troubleshooting steps include:

  • Confirming that the operating system version is supported.
  • Checking whether the required repositories are enabled.
  • Verifying package names for the current distribution.
  • Checking library architecture and version compatibility.
  • Using approved offline RPM packages when the environment has no internet access.

Do not assume that packages such as Java, development libraries, or terminal libraries are required for every installation. Follow the prerequisites for your specific release.

Q7: Which operating systems does GBase Database(GBase 8s) support?

Answer: Supported operating systems depend on the product release, package, CPU architecture, and vendor certification.

Before installing GBase Database(GBase 8s), verify the official compatibility information for your exact version. Check:

  • Linux distribution and release
  • CPU architecture
  • Required system libraries
  • Kernel and runtime prerequisites
  • Supported deployment and maintenance configurations

Do not choose an operating system solely because an older installation guide uses it. A distribution that worked for a previous release may not be supported by a newer package.

For production systems, use a supported configuration and confirm the relevant requirements with the official product documentation or vendor support.

Q8: How can I verify that the installation succeeded?

Answer: Verify the instance state, network listener, and database connectivity separately.

Step 1: Check the instance status.

onstat -

Review the output to determine whether the instance is online and operating as expected.

Step 2: Check the network listener.

ss -lntp

Confirm that the expected port is listening. A listening port alone does not prove that database authentication and SQL queries work.

Step 3: Test a database connection.

Use the supported client for your installation, such as dbaccess where available, and connect to the intended database or a designated test database.

Verify that you can execute a simple query with the expected account and permissions.

A successful installation check should cover all three areas: instance status, network connectivity, and an actual database session.

Q9: Where can I download the GBase Database(GBase 8s) installer?

Answer: Start with the official GBase website:

https://www.gbase.cn/

Check the product documentation and download resources available for your version. Access requirements may vary.

Before downloading, confirm the following:

  • The correct GBase Database(GBase 8s) product and release
  • The target operating system
  • The CPU architecture
  • Installation prerequisites
  • Package integrity and any vendor-provided verification instructions

Keep the installer and its corresponding documentation together so that the installation procedure can be repeated consistently.

Q10: How do I configure automatic startup after installation?

Answer: Use the startup mechanism documented for your GBase Database(GBase 8s) release and operating system.

On a system using systemd, database startup may be integrated with a service unit or a vendor-provided startup script. However, the correct service configuration depends on how the instance starts, the required environment variables, and the expected shutdown procedure.

Before enabling automatic startup, verify:

  1. The correct database service account.
  2. The required environment variables and configuration files.
  3. The documented startup and shutdown commands.
  4. Service dependencies and startup ordering.
  5. Behavior after a restart or unexpected shutdown.

Do not copy a generic systemd template into production without validating its ExecStart, ExecStop, process type, and environment settings. An incorrect shutdown command or service definition can interrupt database operations or cause startup failures.

Test automatic startup and shutdown in a non-production environment first, then document the verified procedure for your deployment.

Final Thoughts

Most GBase Database(GBase 8s) installation problems become easier to diagnose when you verify the environment before changing configuration. Check the database account, locale settings, sqlhosts, instance status, and message logs systematically.

For beginners, three habits are especially valuable:

  • Follow the documentation for the exact product version.
  • Verify each installation stage before moving to the next.
  • Diagnose the underlying error before reinstalling or modifying database files.

A careful installation and verification process helps reduce troubleshooting time and makes future deployments more predictable.

title: A Unified Response Framework for Questions and Tutoring Dialogues
description:
arXiv:2610.19532v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Existing student models in educational applications largely focus on student responses to questions. However, as tutoring becomes more accessible at large scale, it is important to analyze dialogues between tutors and students, which may reveal fine-grained evidence on student knowledge. In this work, we propose a unified framework that models both student responses to questions and tutor-posed subtasks during dialogues on a shared item response theory (IRT) scale. We first identify mathematical subtasks in tutoring dialogues, rewrite them into self-contained questions, and identify the correctness of student responses to these subtasks. We then develop an IRT framework that estimates question/subtask difficulty from text, tracks students' evolving abilities across question-answering and dialogue interactions, and a novel method to leverages tutor moves between consecutive subtasks to regularize their difficulty values. We evaluate our framework on two real-world math education datasets containing both human- and AI-tutored dialogues. Results show that our framework outperforms strong baselines on both question difficulty prediction and response correctness prediction.

title: Exact Scaling Laws for a Random-Features Bigram Model
description:
arXiv:2610.19281v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Understanding neural scaling laws is increasingly important for theory and practice, yet first-principles explanations remain limited even in simple settings. In this work, we study capacity-limited scaling in a bottlenecked bigram model with power-law (Zipf) token statistics, viewed as an analytically tractable toy model of a large language model. Fixed random embeddings serve as a proxy for representational capacity and induce an explicit bottleneck of width, allowing us to derive scaling laws for prediction regret as a function of model width, vocabulary size, and the Zipf exponent. Our results complement recent theoretical accounts based on optimization dynamics by isolating scaling due purely to representational constraints. In the appropriate regime, the theory recovers the functional form of classical neural scaling laws and suggests that heavy-tailed language statistics may underlie both optimization- and capacity-driven scaling. Experiments natural language datasets (WikiText2, OpenWebText) closely match the predicted curves.

title: Custom REST API Development: Cost, Process, and How to Hire the Right Developer
description:
Custom REST API Development: Cost, Process, and How to Hire the Right Developer

Every few months, a business owner messages me with the same story. They paid a freelancer a few hundred dollars for a custom REST API development project, and six months later the API collapses under real traffic, has no documentation, and nobody can add a single new endpoint without breaking the mobile app. The routes were the cheap part. Everything around them — authentication, validation, rate limiting, versioning, documentation — was missing.

That is the concrete problem with most API projects: buyers pay for "endpoints" while what they actually need is a stable contract between systems that survives growth, staff changes, and third-party deprecations. This guide explains what custom REST API development really includes, what it costs in 2026, what a production-ready build process looks like, and how to vet a developer before you hand them your project.

What custom REST API development actually includes

A custom REST API is a bespoke HTTP interface — usually JSON over HTTPS — that lets your frontend, mobile app, or partner systems talk to your backend. But the endpoints themselves are maybe 30% of the work. A professional build includes:

  • Resource modelling — deciding what the resources are (orders, users, invoices) and how they relate, so URLs stay clean and predictable.
  • Authentication and authorisation — typically token-based auth (Laravel Sanctum or Passport, JWT, or OAuth2), with per-user permissions, not just a shared API key.
  • Input validation — every parameter checked server-side, with consistent error responses.
  • Rate limiting and throttling — so one abusive client cannot take the whole API down.
  • Versioning — /v1/, /v2/ namespaces so you can evolve the API without breaking existing integrations.
  • Documentation — OpenAPI/Swagger specs or a Postman collection, so another developer can integrate without guessing.
  • Monitoring and logging — request logs, error tracking, and uptime alerts from day one.

If a quote only mentions "CRUD endpoints", you are buying the 30% and will pay for the other 70% later, usually at emergency rates. Ask every candidate what their quote covers beyond the endpoints — error handling, retries, documentation, and handover all matter.

How much does custom REST API development cost in 2026?

Pricing depends on scope, seniority, and region, but these are realistic freelance ranges based on current market data:

  • Single endpoint or third-party integration — $150–$500. One well-built endpoint or a connection to an existing service (Stripe, Twilio, a CRM), with basic documentation.
  • API for a mobile or web app — $500–$2,000. Multiple endpoints with authentication, validation, and testing — the typical MVP backend.
  • Custom API with database and business logic — $2,000–$6,000. Scalable architecture, secure data handling, queued jobs, and full documentation.
  • Ongoing maintenance and support — $1,000–$3,000 per engagement. Monitoring, versioning, performance tuning, and bug fixes as traffic grows.

Hourly rates for freelance API developers range from roughly $15–$45/hour in South and Southeast Asia to $45–$100/hour in North America and Western Europe. The biggest cost driver is not the code itself — it is the layers around each API call: data mapping, error handling, security, testing, and documentation. A vague scope produces a vague price; a developer who prices before asking about rate limits, data quality, and failure handling is guessing.

For context on hiring backend specialists generally, I have written a separate guide on how to hire a Laravel developer without hiring the wrong one — the vetting principles there apply directly to API work too.

The custom REST API development process, step by step

A reliable build follows the same five phases whether it takes one week or two months:

1. Discovery and scoping

The developer maps every system the API must talk to, the exact data each endpoint moves, expected traffic, and what "done" means. Output: an endpoint list and a fixed scope. If this phase is skipped, the project will be re-scoped mid-build — the most common cause of blown budgets.

2. API design

Before any code, the developer designs the contract: resource names, HTTP methods, status codes, request/response shapes, auth scheme, and error format. A good design doc fits on a few pages and can be reviewed by a non-technical founder.

3. Build

Endpoints are implemented with validation, auth, and tests. Database queries are optimised early — N+1 query problems are far cheaper to prevent than to fix in production (fixing SQLSTATE[HY000] [2002] connection refused in Laravel).

4. Testing and hardening

Feature tests for every endpoint, rate-limit checks, auth edge cases, and load testing at 2–3x expected traffic. Documentation is written from the actual implementation, not from memory.

5. Deploy and monitor

CI/CD deployment, error tracking, uptime monitoring, and a documented versioning policy. The developer hands over credentials, docs, and a runbook — not just a zip file.

What a production-ready endpoint looks like

Here is the difference between a tutorial endpoint and one that survives production. First, routes stay thin and versioned, with auth and throttling applied at the group level:

// routes/api.php

use App\Http\Controllers\Api\V1\OrderController;

Route::prefix('v1')->middleware(['auth:sanctum', 'throttle:api'])->group(function () {
    Route::apiResource('orders', OrderController::class);
});

Why it works: versioning (v1) means you can ship breaking changes later without breaking existing clients; auth:sanctum rejects unauthenticated traffic before it reaches your code; throttle:api caps requests per user so one client cannot starve the others.

Second, validation lives in a dedicated Form Request — never inline in the controller:

// app/Http/Requests/StoreOrderRequest.php

namespace App\Http\Requests;

use Illuminate\Foundation\Http\FormRequest;

class StoreOrderRequest extends FormRequest
{
    public function authorize(): bool
    {
        return $this->user()->can('create', Order::class);
    }

    public function rules(): array
    {
        return [
            'customer_id' => ['required', 'exists:customers,id'],
            'items' => ['required', 'array', 'min:1'],
            'items.*.sku' => ['required', 'string', 'max:64'],
            'items.*.qty' => ['required', 'integer', 'min:1'],
        ];
    }
}

Why it works: validation is reusable, testable, and returns consistent 422 responses with structured error messages automatically. The authorize() method keeps permission logic out of the controller.

Third, the controller delegates to a service, wraps writes in a transaction, and returns a proper API Resource with the correct status code and Location header:

// app/Http/Controllers/Api/V1/OrderController.php

public function store(StoreOrderRequest $request)
{
    $order = DB::transaction(fn () =>
        $this->orders->create($request->user(), $request->validated())
    );

    return (new OrderResource($order->load('items')))
        ->response()
        ->setStatusCode(201)
        ->header('Location', route('api.v1.orders.show', $order));
}

Why it works: the transaction guarantees an order is never half-created; the 201 status and Location header follow HTTP semantics so client developers can rely on the contract; the API Resource controls exactly which fields are exposed, so internal columns never leak.

Finally, rate limiting is defined explicitly rather than left at framework defaults:

// bootstrap/app.php (Laravel 11+)

RateLimiter::for('api', function (Request $request) {
    return Limit::perMinute(60)->by($request->user()?->id ?: $request->ip());
});

Why it works: per-user limits are fairer than per-IP limits behind shared NATs, and a named limiter makes the policy visible and adjustable in one place.

5 pitfalls that sink API projects (and the fixes)

  • No versioning. The developer ships /orders and six months later needs to change the response shape — every mobile app in the wild breaks. Fix: namespace from day one (/v1/), even if v2 never ships.
  • Auth as an afterthought. A shared API key in a config file, no per-user scoping. Fix: token-based auth with explicit permissions from the first endpoint.
  • N+1 queries. An endpoint returns 50 orders and fires 200 database queries because relationships are lazy-loaded. Fix: eager load (->with('items')) and check query counts in tests.
  • No documentation. The original developer leaves; the new one reverse-engineers endpoints from the mobile app's network tab. Fix: OpenAPI/Swagger generated from the code, updated with every release.
  • Silent failures. A third-party webhook fails and nobody notices for a week. Fix: structured logging, error tracking, and uptime alerts from launch day — part of the quote, not an add-on.

How to vet a REST API developer before you hire

Ask these five questions. The answers reveal more than any portfolio:

  • "Walk me through how you would version this API when the response shape has to change." (You want: URL versioning, deprecation policy, backwards compatibility.)
  • "How do you prevent N+1 queries, and how would I see the proof?" (You want: eager loading plus query-count assertions in tests.)
  • "What does your error response format look like?" (You want: a consistent envelope — code, message, details — not raw exceptions.)
  • "What is included in your handover?" (You want: docs, credentials, runbook, and a walkthrough — not a zip file.)
  • "How do you handle a third-party API that goes down?" (You want: retries with backoff, queues, idempotency keys, and alerting.)

Red flags: no mention of testing, "we add docs later", .env files committed to the repo, no experience with queues, and pricing given before any scoping questions. If you are hiring more broadly for backend work, the Laravel developer hiring guide covers the full interview process in depth.

Ready to build?

A well-built custom API becomes the foundation your product grows on — new frontends, partner integrations, and mobile apps all plug into the same contract. A rushed one becomes the ceiling. If you are planning an API project and want a senior engineer to scope it properly — endpoints, auth, docs, and a fixed price before any code is written — get in touch through webixyhub.com and we will plan it together.

title: DataJunction as Netflix’s answer to the missing piece of the modern data stack
description:
by Olek Gorajek, Samuel Redai, Yian Shang

Intro

Our Netflix journey from data to dashboards, particularly within the space of the experimentation platform, always presented a unique set of challenges. This blog post aims to illuminate these hurdles and explain how an innovative open-source metric platform became instrumental in overcoming some of them. We’ll showcase the critical role that DataJunction played in streamlining our data workflows and enhancing our ability to derive meaningful insights from our vast datasets.

Metrics are the foundation of data-driven decision-making, but at many organizations, they are scattered, inconsistently defined, and difficult to discover or trust. At Netflix, this challenge first became apparent in our experimentation platform, where reliable metrics are essential for interpreting test results. But the complexity of the original tooling made it very difficult to understand and introspect these metrics both in terms of their definitions as well as their values.

Initial Problem

Scattered metric definitions, redundant datasets, and pipelines are often a natural effect of a fast-moving company with a large and powerful analytical workforce. This is a common problem in big data-driven firms, and it is not easy to solve across multiple departments, which are often governed by somewhat different rules and regulations. An easy-to-use, well-governed, and centralized semantic layer can help with these issues. Our initial problem was most evident in our Experimentation Platform team, where the previous system required:

  • extensive business knowledge
  • familiarity with experimentation conventions
  • and complex engineering practices

This led to metric authoring processes that would take weeks, which was a prohibitive requirement for Data Scientists and Analytics Engineers who wanted to onboard new metrics to the Experimentation Platform.

Enter DataJunction

To address this problem and to set ourselves on the path to a successful semantic layer solution in the future, we looked at several candidates. Among other solutions we evaluated Mando (an internal framework), Minerva (an open source semantic layer from AirBnB), and DataJunction (another open source solution, “DJ” for short). All of them had some strength, but DJ offered one thing that the others did not at the time: a solid SQL parsing and SQL generation engine. At the time of the POC, DJ was also the only open-source solution that stored all its definitions in a connected graph, similar to how relational databases store metadata on their views and queries. Easy “SQL wrangling” with rich metadata was the main feature that convinced us to try it for our immediate use case.

DataJunction originated from a similar internal Facebook project created (around 2015) by the data science and infrastructure (DSI) team, mainly as an answer to the need for metrics portability. During several iterations of the Deltoid project — which was the main experimentation platform at Facebook at the time — users were required to rebuild and repopulate their metrics when they wanted to move to the next version of Deltoid. But after implementing DJ and abstracting all metric definitions the team offered seamless migrations by separating the concerns between the metrics and the stats computation platform. That project was subsequently renamed to MDF (Metrics and Dimensions Factory) and promoted as a generic semantic layer used widely by various departments. In 2021, one of the Facebook engineers (Beto Dealmeida), started the DJ Github project and built out some basic functionality. Then together with some folks at Netflix expanded the scope further, and soon after that the project was introduced at Netflix. Following that introduction, three Netflix engineers (authors of this blog) together with a couple of external contributors, most notably Nick Ouellet, have been building out the remaining features of the platform.

Architecture Decisions

A critical design constraint for building DJ at Netflix was resource scarcity. We refused to compromise on product quality, choosing instead to limit the feature set. Although DJ was clearly capable of addressing many simultaneous problems across diverse use cases, our lack of adequate resources and official support meant we developed it as a side project for over two years. Our hope was that demonstrating its value would eventually secure management attention.

API First, UI and Other Interfaces Later

A metrics platform doesn’t need a flashy front-end to deliver value — its core is the semantic layer, which stores a consistent set of dimensions and metrics and serves this information through a rich API service. You can see below how we structured the main components of DataJunction in the Netflix implementation. Our DJ services (in the middle) interact with the underlying data (on the left) and supply our access layer with the business definitions in the form of SQL w/ metadata or directly with data depending on the client request.

Consistent Graph First, Other Features Later

A complete semantic layer system can seem like an octopus, with its tentacles reaching out into many functional areas and can expand from a basic semantic metadata stored for some datasets to full dashboard functionality. Let’s call out some of them:

  • semantic metadata authoring and management and monitoring
  • metric and dimension query / definition generation
  • metric and dimension data generation (requires a query engine)
  • data visualization and data tracking
  • performance optimization (aka caching or materialization)
  • integration layer with other tools and
  • any / all the above functionality served as: UI, API, client libraries, MCP servers and more.

Of course it is extremely hard to provide the best in class functionality across all these layers, so with our small “unofficial” team we decided to focus on the most important piece: solid semantic layer engine (and API) with the ability to parse SQL as the input to the graph and generate SQL as the serving layer. That is the core of the system and everything else can be added later with less effort and w/o the need to rebuild the core.

Cube as The Perfect Consumption Protocol

Analytical multi-dimensional cubes have been a fundamental concept for decades, with their representation integrated across various data processing and analysis platforms. While definitions and features may vary between tools, they all serve the common purpose of encapsulating, or abstracting, a subset of semantic objects.

In DataJunction, we adopted cubes as first-class features for two main reasons: their familiarity to users and their suitability as a serving interface. They efficiently deliver both the semantic definitions (of metrics and dimensions) and fast data access. See an example of data “flow” graph (dotted lines) and dimensional relationships graph (solid lines) below.

We simplified the creation of basic cubes, allowing them to easily aggregate arbitrary collections of shared metrics and dimensions. Furthermore, accessing, managing, and visualizing these cubes is straightforward for any client integrating with DJ. Custom integrations, such as for Netflix’s internal fast Druid data analysis tool (Data Explorer → see below), became trivial to build, and we also made it easy to materialize these cubes directly in our Druid clusters.

One of DJ’s most powerful client integrations is the ability to link any DJ-originating metric definition back to the DJ ecosystem. This creates a valuable feedback loop: troubleshooting and introspecting business dashboards becomes simple if they display DJ-defined metrics that include links back to the definition source. This link then makes inspecting and running ad-hoc analysis, by modifying existing metrics, a trivial process. This integration is not only possible with our inhouse tools, but also with other well known open-source products, like Superset.

Experimentation at Netflix

Metrics are the backbone of experimentation. They translate data into signals that tell us whether a change is meaningful, safe, and worth scaling. Without trustworthy metrics and dimensions, experiments risk becoming inconclusive or misleading, so a robust metrics layer becomes crucial for data-driven decisions.

At Netflix, the original metrics layer integrated into the experimentation platform was overly complicated. Creating new metrics not only required tribal knowledge of experimentation data artifacts, but also familiarity with complex engineering workflows. This unnecessary friction meant that onboarding a single new metric could take weeks, slowing adoption of new metrics and hindering experimentation.

This is where DataJunction comes in: it provides a central hub for defining metrics and dimensions that can easily be shared and explored via the semantic graph. It also provides flexible, user-friendly interfaces (including a UI, API, and various clients), making it easy for users to author and manage their metrics and other semantic models.

Conclusions

With experimentation domain well supported by DataJunction, we would like to take on next steps to unifying of the general analytics at Netflix and to make it easier for Netflix users to both:

  • find and use metric definitions across verticals (defined in DJ)
  • easily access, modify and experiment with new metrics across Netflix data stack

That will require building out strong integrations between DJ and other tools, but that has been underway and it is one of the most enjoyable parts of this project, where most of the feature exists and we are simply enabling existing systems to exchange information in a structured and reliable way. With a system like DataJunction our internal LLMs can deliver accountable information about the business metrics as well as explanation of how they are defined and used across Netflix.

Related resources:

  • 2023 : DataJunction at Netflix (slide deck)
  • 2025 : DataJunction talk at Data Engineering Open Forum 2025 (video)
  • 2025 : DataJunction: Unifying Experimentation and Analytics (blog)

DataJunction as Netflix’s answer to the missing piece of the modern data stack was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: Accelerating Spatio-Temporal Attention for Video Diffusion on TPUs
description: To address the quadratic latency bottleneck of self-attention in high-resolution video diffusion models, developers implemented Sparse VideoGen (SVG) to dynamically route attention heads to highly structured spatial or temporal sparse masks. Translating this algorithmic sparsity into physical hardware speedups on TPUs required optimizing the Splash Attention kernel by bypassing empty memory tiles, restricting exact coordinate masking strictly to boundary tiles, and permuting token memory layouts into temporal-major order for contiguous access. By aligning these sparse masks with actual hardware tile execution, the combined optimizations significantly reduced wasted matrix operations and achieved up to a 1.69x end-to-end inference speedup for 1440p video generation.

title: Introducing pglifecycle 2.0 beta
description:
I’m pleased to announce the first public release of pglifecycle, an open source schema management tool for PostgreSQL.

pglifecycle keeps your database schema in version control as structured YAML, with one file for each table, view, function, role, and other object. This makes the current schema easy to browse, review, and change without reconstructing it from years of migration files.

With pglifecycle, you can:

  • Pull an existing database into a schema project
  • Build that project into an archive for pg_restore
  • Compare it with a live database and generate the DDL needed to reconcile them

Deployment is plan first. Destructive changes are withheld unless explicitly allowed, making the generated SQL suitable for review in CI.

The companion pglifecycle GitHub Action can detect schema drift and post deployment plans directly to pull requests without applying them.

Version 2 is a Rust rewrite of the original tool, which has managed AWeber’s production schema for more than seven years. The beta release expands PostgreSQL object coverage and improves deployment convergence and safety.

  • Getting Started
  • Documentation
  • GitHub Action

Feedback and real world test cases are welcome as pglifecycle moves toward a stable 2.0 release.

title: Building the MyZubster Metaverse: What We've Shipped and What's Next
description:
Building the MyZubster Metaverse: What We've Shipped and What's Next

From account-linked experiences to distributed abuse protection — an open-source development update.

Over the past development cycle, we've made meaningful progress on the MyZubster Metaverse.

Our goal is not simply to build another virtual environment. We're exploring how a metaverse can connect people, independent projects, digital identities, knowledge, and real-world communities through an open-source ecosystem.

Here's what we've completed, what we've tested, and what still needs work.

✅ What we've completed

1. Account-linked Metaverse experience

The public Metaverse route is available at:

https://www.myzubster.com/metaverse

We have implemented and tested the account-linked flow, connecting the Metaverse experience with MyZubster's broader authentication and user ecosystem.

This provides a foundation for future interactions between digital identity, community participation, and independent projects.

2. Distributed rate limiting

One of our latest milestones is the implementation of MongoDB-backed abuse protection.

The system introduces rate limits for four Metaverse operations:

  • join — entering a session
  • sync — synchronizing session state
  • chat — sending messages
  • emote — submitting interactions

Using a shared MongoDB-backed limiter helps coordinate abuse controls across application instances instead of relying exclusively on individual server memory.

3. Privacy-conscious throttling

We've introduced HMAC-derived identifiers for throttling, rather than storing raw identifiers directly as rate-limit keys.

The implementation also includes:

  • Automatic TTL-based expiration
  • HTTP 429 Too Many Requests responses
  • Retry-After information
  • Protection against spoofed proxy headers
  • Documented privacy and retention boundaries

These measures are intended to reduce abuse while limiting unnecessary retention of identifying information.

4. Fail-closed production behavior

During review, we identified an important issue: if MongoDB became unavailable, the limiter could fall back to local in-memory behavior.

We corrected this behavior so that the production configuration fails closed when the shared rate-limiting dependency is unavailable.

This is an important security trade-off: availability may be reduced during an infrastructure failure, but abuse protection is not silently weakened.

5. Automated testing and GitHub integration

The final development work included:

  • 21 backend test suites passing
  • 125 backend tests passing in the final local verification
  • Clean Git diff checks
  • GitHub pull request review and merge

The distributed abuse protection was merged through:

PR #30 — feat(metaverse): add distributed abuse rate limits

https://github.com/danieldirimini-myzubster/myzubster/pull/30

Merge commit: d911cadd824a1ca00b50cfead7929eb8f80934d0

This represents completed implementation work, not a claim that every production-readiness requirement has been satisfied.

⚠️ What still needs to be completed

1. Dependency security remediation

Our security pipeline continues to flag an existing dependency backlog.

The latest reported audit included:

  • 61 vulnerabilities in total
  • 43 high-severity vulnerabilities
  • 1 critical vulnerability

Some remediation paths involve potentially breaking dependency upgrades, including a major Hardhat migration.

We don't want to hide these findings or blindly apply incompatible updates.

Next step: review production versus development dependencies, assess actual exposure, submit targeted fixes, and rerun the security pipeline.

2. Final production verification

The pull request has been merged, but the final production verification was interrupted before completion.

We still need to verify the deployed commit, production health, and real behavior of the new rate limits.

3. Multi-user and load testing

Passing unit and integration tests is not the same as demonstrating scalability.

We want to validate:

  • Concurrent user sessions
  • Distributed synchronization
  • Chat and interaction throttling
  • MongoDB availability and recovery behavior
  • Performance under realistic traffic

4. Contributor-led testing

We're inviting open-source contributors to test the Metaverse independently, report reproducible bugs, review security assumptions, and improve documentation.

A useful contribution doesn't have to be a large feature.

A clear bug report, a failing test, or a small targeted pull request can move the project forward.

5. Independent infrastructure and decentralization

MyZubster is also exploring interoperability with contributor-owned infrastructure.

Our N4K48 pilot is an early step toward connecting independently managed projects and nodes.

However, an independently hosted VPS is not automatically a decentralized network.

We still need documented interfaces, tested recovery procedures, access controls, and independently reproducible interoperability tests.

This work remains in progress.

🌍 The bigger vision

We want MyZubster to become a place where people can connect their real-world activities, creative work, services, and technical contributions to a shared digital ecosystem.

The Metaverse is one component of that vision, alongside Zorgax, the Marketplace, and the Contributor Passport.

But our immediate priority is simpler:

Make the existing features reliable, secure, understandable, and useful before expanding their scope.

🤝 Join the development

We're looking for contributors interested in:

  • Security and dependency remediation
  • Backend and MongoDB testing
  • Metaverse frontend testing
  • Accessibility and user experience
  • Docker and infrastructure automation
  • Documentation and reproducible test cases

GitHub repository:

https://github.com/MyZubster-Ecosystem/myzubster

Contributor coordination:

https://github.com/MyZubster-Ecosystem/myzubster/issues/1609

Metaverse:

https://www.myzubster.com/metaverse

If you're interested, explore the repository, choose a focused task, and join the discussion.

We're building MyZubster in the open — one verified contribution at a time.

Daniel Ioni (h4x0r)

MyZubster — Open-Source Ecosystem

title: psqlODBC 18.00.0005 released with security fix for CVE-2026-109448
description:
The psqlODBC team has released version 18.00.0005 of psqlODBC, the official ODBC driver for PostgreSQL. This release fixes one security vulnerability and two bugs. All users should upgrade.

Security issue

CVE-2026-109448: heap memory corruption when binding more than 32767 parameters

CVSS 3.1 base score: 5.9 (Medium)

Versions affected: 08.01.0102 through 18.00.0004.

psqlODBC stored the number of bound parameters on a statement in a signed 16-bit field. When an application bound more than 32768 parameters on one statement, the driver wrote zeros outside the memory that holds the parameter bindings. The application could crash, or keep running with corrupted memory. An application is exposed if it lets untrusted input decide how many parameters it binds, for example by building an IN (?, ?, ...) list from user-supplied values.

SQLBindParameter now rejects parameter numbers above 32767 with SQLSTATE 07009. ODBC cannot report more than 32767 parameters, because SQLNumParams and SQL_DESC_COUNT are 16-bit values. No earlier release could run a statement with more than 32767 parameters, so this change does not break any application that worked before.

If you cannot upgrade right away, limit the number of parameters your application builds from external input, or pass long value lists as a single array parameter, for example = ANY(?).

The psqlODBC team thanks Richard Kuesters for reporting this problem.

For more details, see the advisory GHSA-cmfx-rm3r-p2jr.

Bug fixes

  • Statements prepared on the server with 1000 or more parameters could fail with errors such as type "timestam" does not exist. From parameter 1000 on, the driver cut the type name that follows each parameter to fit a fixed-size buffer.
  • Since 18.00.0003, bytea parameters failed with "Type is invalid" when used through Microsoft's OLE DB Provider for ODBC (MSDASQL), for example from ADO.

The Windows packages are now built with OpenSSL 3.5.9.

Download

Windows installers and merge modules for x86, x64 and ARM64 are available from the PostgreSQL download site and from the GitHub release page. The source code is on GitHub.

The full list of changes is in the release notes.

Please report bugs on the psqlODBC issue tracker or the pgsql-odbc mailing list.
