title: How Far Can Coding Agents Go in Visual Generation?
description:
arXiv:2610.19025v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Modern image generation largely relies on specialized generative models that leave the process of image construction implicit in learned parameters. We explore an alternative: general-purpose coding agents that construct images through executable programs. Our study of zero-shot drawing on AgentDrawBench, a 200-prompt benchmark, reveals a distinctive capability profile. Agents excel at preserving structure and satisfying precise visual constraints, achieving competitive results in domains where compositional accuracy matters more than photorealistic appearance, while remaining limited in perceptual richness. Their visual expressiveness varies with the drawing interface, and a qualitative study on reconstruction shows how procedural skills extracted from human demonstrations support different artistic media. We then examine code as an external visual language of thought: a structured, executable representation that agents can construct and inspect. We test it in visual question answering task and find reconstructed visual code retains substantial information for question answering and, in some domains, supports higher accuracy than the original image. These abilities raise a further question: do agents draw on a shared internal representation of scene content beyond a particular drawing program? We explore an internal visual language-of-thought hypothesis, in which a shared, compositionally structured representation supports visual operations across drawing languages. Cross-harness drawings and images assembled from independent single-pixel queries exhibit related layouts and tones. Agents also maintain self-generated room arrangements across viewpoints after visible drawings are removed. These results demonstrate that the coding agent would maintain a consistent and coherent world inside its imagine even before the harness gets involved and the generation starts.

title: React History in Plain Words: What Each Era Took Off Your Plate, and What It Billed You
description:
Here is a component every app has. A user profile: load the user by userId, show their name, and show a green dot while they're online.

I'm going to write it again for most eras of React, from 2013 to today.

Most histories of React go version by version: 0.13, 16.8, 18, 19. You finish reading and you know the dates, but not why any of it happened. I wanted to try a different angle. Every era of React made a deal with you. It took something off your plate, and it sent you a new bill. I'll keep score as I go: what you stopped doing, and what you started paying.

One warning about order. This article follows problems, not dates. Next.js (2016) shows up after hooks (2019), because that's where its problem hurts most.

1. Before React: you are the sync engine

The jQuery version:

$.getJSON(`/api/users/${userId}`, (user) => {
  $('#name').text(user.name);
});

presence.on('change', (id, online) => {
  if (id === userId) $('#status').toggleClass('online', online);
});

It works. Now add a second place that shows the same user, say a header avatar. Then a list of friends with their own dots. Every piece of data lives in two places: in your variables and in the DOM (the browser's live tree of page elements). Every change has to be copied by hand, to every place that shows it. Miss one, and the header says "online" while the profile says "offline".

Backbone, Knockout and AngularJS were already attacking this with data binding. React's answer, open-sourced in 2013, was different. Pete Hunt's Why React post from June 2013 makes the case: stop updating the DOM yourself. Describe what the UI should look like for the current data, and let the library work out what to change.

In plain words: before React you were a waiter who memorizes every table's order and runs to the kitchen with each correction. React gave you an order pad. You write down what the table wants now, and the kitchen works out the difference.

One detail almost nobody mentions: that same 2013 post already lists server rendering as a selling point. Keep it in mind. It comes back later with a different name.

Took off your plate: keeping the DOM in sync by hand.
Billed you: HTML inside JavaScript, and a build step to compile it. JSX looked like heresy in 2013, and a lot of the first year was spent arguing about it.

2. createClass and mixins: sharing logic, badly

Early React components were objects passed to React.createClass. A mixin was a plain object of methods that got copied into every component that listed it. That's how you shared logic:

var Profile = React.createClass({
  mixins: [FetchUserMixin, PresenceMixin], // each one adds state and lifecycle methods
  render: function () {
    if (!this.state.user) return null;
    return <div>{this.state.user.name} {this.state.online && 'online'}</div>;
  },
});

React called every mixin's componentDidMount, so that part worked. The trouble was everything you couldn't see. Which mixin set online? What happens when two mixins both define handleChange? You found out when the page loaded and threw.

React added ES6 classes in 0.13, in March 2015, and classes had no mixins at all. In 2016 Dan Abramov wrote the post that explained why that was a feature, Mixins Considered Harmful. One line from it: "There is no guarantee that two particular mixins can be used together."

So mixins saved you from copy-pasting logic, and charged you in coupling you couldn't see. Rename a method, and the page load told you which mixin had depended on it.

3. Classes: one feature, three methods

Here's the profile as a class (written with class properties, the Babel syntax most teams used):

class Profile extends React.Component {
  state = { user: null, online: false };

  componentDidMount() {
    fetchUser(this.props.userId).then((user) => this.setState({ user }));
    this.unsubscribe = presence.subscribe(this.props.userId, (online) => this.setState({ online }));
  }

  componentDidUpdate(prev) {
    if (prev.userId !== this.props.userId) {
      fetchUser(this.props.userId).then((user) => this.setState({ user }));
      this.unsubscribe();
      this.unsubscribe = presence.subscribe(this.props.userId, (online) => this.setState({ online }));
    }
  }

  componentWillUnmount() {
    this.unsubscribe();
  }
}

(presence.subscribe returns a function that unsubscribes. Both versions in this article rely on that.)

Look at where the presence logic lives. Subscribe in one method, re-subscribe in a second, unsubscribe in a third. One feature, split by when it runs instead of what it does. The fetch is copied twice. Forget the componentDidUpdate branch and the dot keeps showing the previous user.

And there's a race here that's easy to miss: whichever response arrives last wins. Click from user 1 to user 2 quickly. Two requests are in flight. If user 1's response arrives last, setState writes it, and the profile of user 2 shows user 1's name. Nothing in the class shape protects you from that.

Sharing logic got its own problem too. Mixins were out, so the community moved to patterns that wrap one component in another. A higher-order component is a function that takes a component and returns a wrapped one. A render prop is a function you pass as a prop so another component can decide what to render. Both work, but every shared behavior adds a layer. Open the component tree of a 2018 app and you'd scroll through withRouter(connect(withTheme(...))) before reaching your own code.

The React team listed all of this when they introduced hooks. The motivation section reads like a bug report for this exact component: "It's hard to reuse stateful logic between components", complex components where related logic is split across lifecycle methods, and "Classes confuse both people and machines".

Took off your plate: hidden mixin coupling, mostly by not supporting mixins at all.
Billed you: this, logic split across lifecycle methods, and deeply nested wrappers.

4. Hooks: logic grouped by what it does

Hooks were announced at React Conf in October 2018 and shipped in React 16.8, in February 2019. The profile:

function usePresence(userId) {
  const [online, setOnline] = useState(false);
  useEffect(() => presence.subscribe(userId, setOnline), [userId]);
  return online;
}

function Profile({ userId }) {
  const [user, setUser] = useState(null);
  const online = usePresence(userId);

  useEffect(() => {
    let ignore = false;
    fetchUser(userId).then((u) => { if (!ignore) setUser(u); });
    return () => { ignore = true; };
  }, [userId]);

  if (!user) return null;
  return <div>{user.name} {online && 'online'}</div>;
}

The whole presence feature is now one small hook, in one place. Subscribe and unsubscribe sit together (the effect returns its own cleanup), and [userId] re-runs it when the user changes. usePresence is just a function. Any component can call it, and there's no wrapper in the tree.

The race from the class version is fixed with the ignore flag: when userId changes, the old effect's cleanup marks its request as stale. But notice who fixed it: you did. React gave you the place to put the fix and left the fix itself to you.

The new bill is the dependency array. Leave a value out of it, and the effect keeps using the value from the render where it was created. That's a stale closure, and it's the most common hooks bug there is. Lint rules catch most of these bugs, though keeping the linter quiet often means restructuring the code.

Hooks also made "fetch in an effect" the default way to load data. Classes had the same problem, but now it was everywhere. Say the profile shows the user's posts, in a child component that fetches them. The child can't start its request until the parent has fetched the user and rendered it. Then the posts component fetches comments. Each level waits for the one above. That's a waterfall. Libraries like TanStack Query, SWR and Relay helped a lot, but the requests still started in the browser, after the JavaScript arrived.

Took off your plate: this, lifecycle splits, nested wrappers.
Billed you: dependency arrays, stale closures, and cleanup you write yourself.

5. Next.js: render it on the server

Everything in sections 3 and 4 happens in the browser, after the JavaScript bundle (the files the browser downloads) arrives. Until then the user stares at an empty page. Then a spinner. Then another spinner, one per level of the waterfall.

Next.js launched in October 2016, from ZEIT (now Vercel). Its announcement describes where the industry had gone: the pendulum of "'fully server-rendered' swung abruptly to the extreme of 'single page app'". Next.js swung it back with server-side rendering: the page is rendered to HTML on the server with its data, and the browser gets real content right away.

This file-per-page setup is what's now called the Pages Router, to tell it apart from the newer App Router in section 7. At launch the data function was getInitialProps. Since Next.js 9.3 in March 2020, the usual way is getServerSideProps, which runs only on the server:

export async function getServerSideProps({ params }) {
  const user = await fetchUser(params.id);
  return { props: { user } };
}

export default function ProfilePage({ user }) {
  return <h1>{user.name}</h1>;
}

The fetch runs on the server, close to the data. No empty page, no first spinner.

Remember the detail from 2013? Server rendering was already on React's list of selling points. Next.js didn't invent it. It made it the default, so you stopped wiring up the server yourself.

The price is hydration. The server sends finished HTML, and it looks right, but it's dead: buttons do nothing yet. Then the browser downloads the same components as JavaScript and runs them again to wire up the clicks. That wiring step is hydration. You pay for the page twice. If the server and the browser render anything differently (Date.now(), a window check, a locale-formatted date), React throws a hydration mismatch. And data loading lives in one function at the top of the page, so a component deep in the tree still can't fetch its own data on the server.

Took off your plate: the blank page, and setting up server rendering by hand.
Billed you: hydration, hydration mismatches, and page-level data loading.

6. React 18: the era everyone skips

Timelines often jump from hooks straight to Server Components, and React 18 gets less attention than it deserves.

React 18, March 2022, brought three things. I'll take them one at a time.

Concurrent rendering. React can start an update, pause it to handle a click, and come back to it. You opt in through APIs like useTransition.

Suspense. You wrap a slow part of the page, say the user's posts, and React shows a fallback there, like a spinner, until it's ready.

Streaming. On the server, the parts of the page that are ready go out first. The slow part arrives later and fills in its spinner.

In plain words: before 18, the server was a restaurant that brought your whole order at once, so everyone waited for the slowest dish. After 18, starters come out when they're ready, and the steak follows.

There's no new profile code here, and that's the point. This era changed what React can do under the hood, and the next one is built on it.

The bill came from somewhere else. Strict Mode, React's opt-in wrapper for extra checks in development, started mounting every component twice to catch missing cleanup. If your profile fetched twice in dev after upgrading, this is why. Usually the fix was the cleanup function you'd skipped. So 18 took "the whole page waits for the slowest request" off your plate, once a framework wired up streaming for you, and billed you in effects that suddenly ran twice.

7. Server Components: components that never reach the browser

The idea was presented in December 2020, before React 18. It reached most developers through the App Router, Next.js's newer routing system: in beta in Next.js 13 in October 2022, stable in Next.js 13.4, in May 2023. React 19 is when the Server Components APIs were declared stable for frameworks to build on. The 13.4 announcement says the App Router is "built on the foundation of React Server Components and Suspense", the Suspense and streaming that React 18 shipped.

Server Components are not the same as server rendering. With SSR, a component renders on the server and then its code ships to the browser anyway, for hydration. A Server Component renders on the server and its code never ships at all.

The profile, today:

// app/users/[id]/page.tsx: a Server Component
import { PresenceDot } from './PresenceDot';

export default async function ProfilePage({ params }: { params: Promise<{ id: string }> }) {
  const { id } = await params; // Next 15+. In 13 and 14, params was a plain object.
  const user = await fetchUser(id);
  return (
    <>
      <h1>{user.name}</h1>
      <PresenceDot userId={user.id} />
    </>
  );
}

// app/users/[id]/PresenceDot.tsx: ships to the browser, because state and a live subscription only exist there
'use client';
import { usePresence } from '@/hooks/usePresence';

export function PresenceDot({ userId }: { userId: string }) {
  const online = usePresence(userId);
  return online ? <span className="dot" /> : null;
}

The component is async. It fetches its own data with a plain await, on the server, and no useEffect is involved. Any component in the tree can do this, not only the page. The heading and the rest of the page never ship to the browser as JavaScript. Only PresenceDot does, because it's the only part that needs a live subscription.

In plain words: with the Pages Router, the server sent a printed photo of the page, and then the camera too: all the code that built it, so the browser could retake the shot and make it interactive. Server Components send the photo and only the code for the parts that actually move.

The bill is bigger than one line per file. Three costs show up first:

  • 'use client' marks where the browser part starts, and everything that file imports ships with it. Put it on the page instead of on PresenceDot, and you're back in section 4: 
  'use client'; // on page.tsx: the whole profile ships as JavaScript again,
  // the component can't be async anymore, and fetchUser moves back into a useEffect
  • Server files can't use useState, useEffect or context, because there's no browser there to hold state. That's why context providers move down into small client files, and why many third-party UI libraries need a 'use client' wrapper before they work.
  • Props that cross the boundary must be serializable: plain data that can be sent as text. No functions, no class instances.

Then the quieter ones. Waterfalls can come back on the server, as sequential awaits in nested components, so you reach for Promise.all and Suspense boundaries. Next.js caches fetches, routes and navigations in separate layers whose defaults have changed between versions, so "why is this data stale" became a new kind of question. And Server Components need support from the bundler (the tool that packages your code), which in practice means a framework such as Next.js. Your app is tied closer to it than before.

Took off your plate: fetching in effects, the client waterfall, shipping JavaScript for parts that never change.
Billed you: the server/client boundary, caching, and framework lock-in.

8. Today: React 19 and the Compiler

React 19 went stable in December 2024. ref is now a regular prop, so the forwardRef wrapper is on its way out. Actions give you primitives (useActionState, useFormStatus, useOptimistic, <form action>) for the pending states, errors and optimistic updates of a form, the parts you used to build with three useState calls. (An optimistic update shows the expected result right away, before the server confirms it.)

Then in October 2025, React Compiler 1.0. Memoization means caching a result so it isn't recomputed on every render. For years, a fast React app meant doing it by hand:

const onSelect = useCallback((id) => router.push(`/users/${id}`), [router]);
const sorted = useMemo(() => friends.toSorted(byName), [friends]);
return <FriendList friends={sorted} onSelect={onSelect} />; // FriendList wrapped in memo()

The compiler is an opt-in build step that adds that memoization for you. You write the plain version, and it works out what to cache. It can even memoize code after an early return, which manual useMemo can't, because hooks can't be called after a return.

One honest caveat. The docs keep useMemo and useCallback as escape hatches, options for the rare cases where the default isn't enough. The routine was handed off, not deleted.

The compiler also assumes you follow the Rules of React: render is a pure calculation, so props and state aren't mutated and nothing outside changes during render. When it detects a violation, it safely skips that component. A violation it can't detect can make a compiled component misbehave at runtime. Say the profile reads the current theme from a global variable during render: the compiler only sees props and state, so it caches the output, and the profile keeps the old theme after the global changes.

Took off your plate: manual memoization, forwardRef, the boilerplate of form state.
Billed you: the Rules of React, now enforced.

The ledger

Same order as the article. The dates are in each section.

Era Took off your plate Billed you Where you'll see the bill
React itself Keeping the DOM in sync by hand JSX, and a build step Your first webpack/Babel config
createClass + mixins Copy-pasting logic Hidden coupling between mixins A name clash error on page load
Classes Hidden mixin coupling this, lifecycle splits, nested wrappers A wrapper-deep component tree in DevTools
Hooks this, lifecycle splits, wrappers Dependency arrays, stale closures, your own cleanup react-hooks/exhaustive-deps warnings
Next.js The blank page, manual SSR Hydration, mismatches, page-level data loading A hydration error in the console
React 18 Waiting for the slowest request Double-run effects in Strict Mode Effects firing twice in dev
Server Components Effects for data, shipping static UI The client boundary, caching, lock-in A "needs 'use client'" error at build
React 19 + Compiler Memoization, forwardRef, form state The Rules of React, enforced Compiler lint errors, skipped components

Not every era took a chore. React 18 and Server Components mostly added things you couldn't do before. And the bills didn't get smaller. They moved: from your DOM code, to your effects, to the line between server and browser.

Closing

In 2013 the bill was a whole job: you were the sync engine. In 2026 it's knowing which side of one line your code runs on. That's real progress. It just isn't free, and every React release since has moved the cost rather than cancelled it.

Which bill are you paying right now: stale closures, hydration mismatches, or the 'use client' boundary?

title: Filter in ASP.NET Core Web API
description:
Filters in ASP.NET Core Web API
What is a filter?
A filter is code that runs at a specific stage while ASP.NET Core processes a controller action. It can run before or after the action, check access, handle certain exceptions, or inspect the result. This helps you apply common behavior without repeating it in every action. learn.microsoft.com

Types of filters
Filter What it does Main methods
Authorization Checks whether the request can access the action. OnAuthorization
Resource Runs around most of the controller filter pipeline. OnResourceExecuting, OnResourceExecuted
Action Runs around the controller action. OnActionExecuting, OnActionExecuted
Exception Handles certain unhandled exceptions. OnException
Result Runs around execution of the action result. OnResultExecuting, OnResultExecuted
These are the five main controller filter types. ASP.NET Core also has endpoint filters, which run around endpoint handlers and can be used with API endpoints; they are separate from the five-stage controller sequence below. learn.microsoft.com

Order of execution
For a request that is authorized and completes successfully:

HTTP request
↓
Authorization filter
↓
OnResourceExecuting
↓
Model binding
↓
OnActionExecuting
↓
Controller action
↓
OnActionExecuted
↓
OnResultExecuting
↓
Result execution (for example, writing JSON)
↓
OnResultExecuted
↓
OnResourceExecuted
↓
HTTP response
The “Executing” methods run on the way toward the action or result. The “Executed” methods run as those stages finish. Model binding happens after the resource filter starts and before the action filter starts. learn.microsoft.com

Where does the exception filter fit? It is not a regular step in every request. It runs only when an applicable unhandled exception occurs; it does not catch exceptions from every stage of the pipeline. Also, a filter can stop the request early, so the full sequence above will not always run. learn.microsoft.com

Key point for interviews: Authorization → Resource → Action → Result, with the “after” methods running as their surrounding stages finish. Exception filtering is conditional.

title: From Static to Dynamic: Building a Modern Web Experience with Web Components
description:
From Static to Dynamic: Building a Modern Web Experience with Web Components

Web development has evolved from hand‑crafted HTML pages to massive single‑page applications (SPAs) powered by heavy JavaScript frameworks. While frameworks like React, Vue, and Angular dominate the conversation, there’s a quieter revolution happening under the hood: Web Components paired with CSS custom properties (variables). Together they let you write reusable, framework‑agnostic UI pieces that work anywhere—static sites, SPAs, or server‑rendered pages.

In this post we’ll explore why Web Components deserve a spot in your toolbox, walk through a practical example of a custom <user-card> element, and show how CSS variables keep your design system flexible without adding runtime JavaScript bloat. By the end, you’ll have a production‑ready component you can drop into any project, regardless of the stack you’re using.

Why Web Components Matter in 2024

  1. Native Browser Support – All modern browsers ship with the Custom Elements, Shadow DOM, and HTML Templates APIs. No polyfills required for the majority of users.
  2. Framework Agnostic – A component built once can be used in a vanilla HTML page, a React tree, an Angular module, or a Svelte app without adapters.
  3. Encapsulation – Shadow DOM isolates styles and markup, preventing accidental CSS bleed‑through that often plagues large codebases.
  4. Performance – Because the component lives as native DOM, the browser can optimize rendering and layout better than a virtual DOM abstraction.

Despite these benefits, many developers shy away because they think components are “hard to test” or “lack tooling.” The truth is the opposite: modern tooling (Vite, Snowpack, Lit, and even plain ES modules) makes authoring, testing, and bundling a breeze.

Building a Reusable <user-card> Component

Let’s create a small but useful component that displays a user’s avatar, name, and a short bio. We’ll use Lit (a lightweight library that helps work with the Shadow DOM) to keep the code concise, but the final output is just a native custom element.

1. Project scaffolding 

# Create a new directory
mkdir user-card-demo && cd user-card-demo

# Initialize a Vite project (vanilla JS)
npm init vite@latest . --template vanilla

# Install Lit
npm install lit

2. Defining the component (src/UserCard.js) 

// src/UserCard.js
import { LitElement, html, css } from 'lit';
import { property, state } from 'lit/decorators.js';

class UserCard extends LitElement {
  // Public attributes
  @property({ type: String }) name = 'Anonymous';
  @property({ type: String }) avatar = '';
  @property({ type: String }) bio = '';

  static styles = css`
    :host {
      display: block;
      max-width: 280px;
      border: 1px solid var(--card-border, #ddd);
      border-radius: var(--card-radius, 8px);
      overflow: hidden;
      font-family: var(--font-family, system-ui, sans-serif);
      background: var(--card-bg, #fff);
      box-shadow: var(--card-shadow, 0 2px 6px rgba(0,0,0,0.1));
    }
    .header {
      display: flex;
      align-items: center;
      padding: 1rem;
      background: var(--header-bg, #f5f5f5);
    }
    .avatar {
      width: 48px;
      height: 48px;
      border-radius: 50%;
      margin-right: 0.75rem;
      background: var(--avatar-bg, #ccc) no-repeat center/cover;
    }
    .name {
      font-size: 1.1rem;
      font-weight: 600;
      color: var(--name-color, #333);
    }
    .bio {
      padding: 0.75rem 1rem;
      font-size: 0.9rem;
      line-height: 1.4;
      color: var(--bio-color, #555);
    }
  `;

  render() {
    return html`
      <div class="header">
        <div class="avatar" style="background-image:url(${this.avatar})"></div>
        <div class="name">${this.name}</div>
      </div>
      <div class="bio"><slot>${this.bio}</slot></div>
    `;
  }
}

customElements.define('user-card', UserCard);
export default UserCard;

Key takeaways

  • Shadow DOM – The component’s styles live inside static styles, guaranteeing they won’t clash with page styles.
  • CSS Custom Properties – Notice the var(--card-border, #ddd) pattern. The component provides sensible defaults but lets any page override them, keeping your design system fluid.
  • Slots – By exposing a <slot> we let consumers inject richer markup into the bio area if they wish.

3. Using the component (index.html) 

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8" />
  <title>User Card Demo</title>
  <script type="module" src="/src/UserCard.js"></script>
  <style>
    /* Global design tokens */
    :root {
      --card-bg: #fafafa;
      --card-border: #e0e0e0;
      --card-radius: 12px;
      --card-shadow: 0 4px 12px rgba(0,0,0,0.08);
      --header-bg: #fff;
      --name-color: #222;
      --bio-color: #444;
      --font-family: 'Helvetica Neue', Arial, sans-serif;
    }
  </style>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Web Component Showcase</h1>

  <user-card
    name="Jane Doe"
    avatar="https://i.pravatar.cc/150?img=5"
    bio="Frontend engineer who loves CSS art and open‑source."
  ></user-card>

  <!-- Overriding a token for a single card -->
  <user-card
    name="Sam Smith"
    avatar="https://i.pravatar.cc/150?img=12"
    style="--card-bg:#fffbe6; --card-border:#ffd54f"
  >
    <p>Full‑stack developer, coffee addict, and occasional jazz saxophonist.</p>
  </user-card>
</body>
</html>

When you run npm run dev (Vite’s dev server), you’ll see two cards with different looks—thanks to the CSS variables defined at the page level and even per‑instance overrides. No extra JavaScript is required after the initial component registration.

Styling Without Bloat: Harnessing CSS Variables

CSS variables are more than a convenience for theming; they’re a performance win. Because they’re resolved by the browser’s CSS engine, changing a variable (e.g., switching to a dark theme) doesn’t trigger a JavaScript re‑render. In the <user-card> example we:

  • Declared defaults inside the component (var(--card-bg, #fff)).
  • Exposed a global token map in :root that the whole site can update with a single CSS class toggle. 
/* Dark theme toggle */
body.dark-mode {
  --card-bg: #2b2b2b;
  --card-border: #444;
  --name-color: #eee;
  --bio-color: #ccc;
}

Toggling dark-mode on the <body> instantly darkens every card without touching JavaScript.

Testing the Component

Even though the component is native, you still want a solid test suite. Here’s a quick Jest + @testing-library/web component setup:

npm install --save-dev jest @testing-library/dom @testing-library/jest-dom

// tests/UserCard.test.js
import '@testing-library/jest-dom';
import { fireEvent } from '@testing-library/dom';
import '../src/UserCard.js';

test('renders name and avatar', () => {
  const el = document.createElement('user-card');
  el.name = 'Test User';
  el.avatar = 'https://example.com/avatar.png';
  document.body.append(el);

  const nameEl = el.shadowRoot.querySelector('.name');
  const avatarEl = el.shadowRoot.querySelector('.avatar');

  expect(nameEl).toHaveTextContent('Test User');
  expect(avatarEl).toHaveStyle(`background-image: url(${el.avatar})`);
});

Running npx jest confirms the component behaves as expected, and because we’re testing the Shadow DOM directly we avoid flaky CSS selector issues.

Deploying to Production

When you’re ready to ship, Vite’s build command bundles the component into a single, minified ES module:

npm run build

The output dist/assets/user-card.[hash].js can be served via any static host (Netlify, Vercel, Cloudflare Pages). Since the component is an ES module, you can also import it from a CDN like esm.sh or jsDelivr:

<script type="module" src="https://esm.sh/user-card@1.0.0"></script>

This eliminates the need for a build step on the consumer side—a big win for content‑heavy sites that prefer Markdown‑first workflows.

When Not to Use Web Components

  • Heavy state management – If your UI requires a global store (Redux‑style) across many components, a full framework may still be easier.
  • SSR‑first projects – While you can pre‑render custom elements, the ecosystem around SSR for Web Components isn’t as mature as for React or Next.js.

That said, for most UI widgets—cards, modals, tabs, tooltips—Web Components hit the sweet spot of reusability and performance.

Future‑Proofing Your Frontend

The Web Platform continues to mature. Upcoming proposals like CSS Cascade Layers and Declarative Shadow DOM will make component composition even cleaner. By investing in native components now, you’ll be ready to adopt these enhancements without refactoring a massive framework layer.

Recommended Tools

  • SuperCDN – Fast Global CDN with Free Tier – Serve your compiled component assets instantly worldwide. Their free tier is generous enough for hobby projects, and the analytics dashboard helps you track bandwidth usage in real time.

  • CodeSnap – Instant Code Screenshot Generator – Turn any code block into a beautifully styled image for social media or documentation. It supports custom themes, line numbers, and even animated GIFs, making it perfect for showcasing snippets like the ones above.

Happy coding, and may your components stay lightweight and your users stay delighted!

title: Think in Strategies, Act with Tools: Traceable Agentic Optimization for Combinatorial Problems
description:
arXiv:2610.14736v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Optimization by PROmpting (OPRO) directly leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate candidate solutions through natural-language prompting. However, OPRO's optimization process is difficult to track, which prevents LLMs from capturing useful information accumulated over previous iterations, thereby limiting solution quality. To address this limitation, we propose a Tool-Augmented Strategic Agent (TASA) which summarizes and exploits trajectory to improve solution quality. Specifically, TASA plans the strategy for each step based on the optimization trajectory, which decomposes the optimization process into traceable strategy selections. Moreover, we leverage LLM to construct problem-specific tools and introduce a strategy-guided adaptive tool planner, which efficiently utilizes the information of trajectory to update solutions. We establish local convergence under persistent exploration and evaluate the complete framework under a shared candidate-evaluation budget. The results support its solution quality and the traceability of strategy-guided search.

title: Learning What to Keep: Transfer-Aware Personal Skill Learning from User Feedback
description:
arXiv:2610.19380v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: User feedback enables LLMs to refine reusable personalized skills, but often mixes persistent preferences with request-specific corrections. Indiscriminately retaining both risks negative transfer, motivating selective retention at the level of individual requirements. We frame this challenge as selective transfer over atomic rules and propose SkillGrain, a framework for learning reusable personalized skills from user feedback. SkillGrain decomposes feedback into independently actionable rules, predicts their transferability, and retains only those suitable for future requests. To learn these decisions, we combine rubric-guided skill rewards with fine-grained credit assignment that separately evaluates rule content and retention decisions. We further jointly optimize skill induction and skill-conditioned generation through reinforcement learning, ensuring that learned skills support downstream personalization. We construct a benchmark spanning five personalized writing tasks to evaluate cross-request generalization. Experiments across three base models in both in-domain and out-of-domain settings show that SkillGrain achieves the best overall average performance among competing methods.

title: ForkGRPO: Efficient Exploration and Fine-Grained Credit Assignment for Diffusion Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.19408v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) have advanced rapidly, yet strengthening their reasoning through reinforcement learning (RL) remains an open challenge. Any-order generation can suffer from entropy degradation, which narrows the reasoning paths available for exploration. Recent work mitigates this issue by applying standard GRPO with left-to-right generation. However, independently generating every rollout from the input prompt can leave alternative continuations from intermediate states underexplored, while trajectory-level advantages assign uniform credit to all tokens without distinguishing the contributions of individual reasoning segments. We propose ForkGRPO, an RL framework that couples efficient exploration with fine-grained segment-level credit assignment. It samples multiple continuations from high-entropy intermediate states along a reference trajectory, prioritizing textual boundaries and reusing shared prefixes. The continuations provide complementary learning signals: within-state group-relative advantages guide which continuations to reinforce, while Monte Carlo state-value differences indicate which reasoning segments improve expected outcomes. Among the evaluated architecture-preserving RL methods, ForkGRPO achieves the best performance on three of four benchmarks, while improving over the directly comparable JustGRPO by up to 1.2 percentage points and using up to 27.8% fewer generated tokens. ForkGRPO-Fast further achieves a $2.49\times$ training wall-clock speedup with negligible accuracy loss.

title: Designing a Distributed Rate Limiter: Token Bucket, Leaky Bucket, and Sliding Window Counters
description:
title: "Designing a Distributed Rate Limiter: Token Bucket, Leaky Bucket, and Sliding Window Counters"
published: true
published_at: "2026-12-24T09:00:00+05:30"
description: "A practical engineering guide to Designing a Distributed Rate Limiter: Token Bucket, Leaky Bucket, and Sliding Window Counters. Learn core mechanics, production tradeoffs, and best practices."
tags: [systemdesign, backend, redis, architecture]
ai_disclosure_level: some_ai

In modern software development, Designing a Distributed Rate Limiter: Token Bucket, Leaky Bucket, and Sliding Window Counters is a critical subject that every serious engineer must understand. Whether building distributed backend systems, designing scalable databases, or optimizing developer productivity, mastering the underlying mechanics separates junior developers who guess from senior engineers who deliver reliable architectures.

In this deep dive, we break down why Designing a Distributed Rate Limiter: Token Bucket, Leaky Bucket, and Sliding Window Counters matters, examine common failure modes in production, and walk through concrete implementation patterns.

The Problem: Why Naive Approaches Fail

In earlier development workflows or smaller-scale projects, teams frequently overlook the subtleties of system design architectures.

When systems scale, common bottlenecks emerge:

  1. Unpredictable Latency & Resource Starvation: High concurrency and unoptimized execution pipelines exhaust system resources, leading to degraded response times and thread pool stalls.
  2. Hidden Failure Cascades: Unhandled edge cases and lack of defensive invariants create silent data corruption that propagates across microservices.
  3. High Cognitive Overhead: As codebases evolve, poorly structured domain abstractions become difficult to maintain, test, and refactor.

To resolve these challenges, engineering teams must implement disciplined patterns focusing on:

  • Comparing Rate Limiting Algorithms: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Implementing Atomic Sliding Window With Redis Sorted Sets (Zadd: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Zremrangebyscore): Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • And Memory Footprints: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.

Under the Hood: Architectural Overview

Understanding how Designing a Distributed Rate Limiter: Token Bucket, Leaky Bucket, and Sliding Window Counters functions beneath high-level abstractions is essential for diagnosing production anomalies.

+--------------------------------------------------------------+
| System Workflow: System design Architecture                    |
|                                                              |
| [Incoming Workload] ---> [Validation & Boundary Layer]       |
|                                     |                        |
|                                     v                        |
|                     [Optimized Core Execution]               |
|                                     |                        |
|                                     v                        |
|                  [Resilient State / Output Store]            |
+--------------------------------------------------------------+

When designing systems around this pattern, prioritize:

  • Isolation of Concerns: Keep business invariants decoupled from transport protocols and third-party drivers.
  • Deterministic Resource Management: Bound memory allocations, connection pools, and worker concurrency to prevent out-of-memory crashes.
  • Observability & Metrics: Expose granular latency histograms, error rates, and throughput metrics to Prometheus/Datadog.

Practical Implementation

Here is a clean, production-oriented pattern demonstrating these principles in action:

import asyncio
import logging
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Optional

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s [%(levelname)s] %(message)s")
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ExecutionContext:
    task_id: str
    payload: dict
    retries: int = 3

class ResilientProcessor:
    """Production-ready processor addressing: Comparing rate limiting algorithms, implementing atomic sliding window with Redis Sorted Sets (ZADD, ZREMRANGEBYSCORE), and memory footprints."""

    def __init__(self, concurrency_limit: int = 10):
        self.semaphore = asyncio.Semaphore(concurrency_limit)

    async def execute_with_guardrails(self, ctx: ExecutionContext) -> Optional[dict]:
        async with self.semaphore:
            for attempt in range(1, ctx.retries + 1):
                try:
                    logger.info(f"Processing task {ctx.task_id}, attempt {attempt}")
                    result = await self._process_task(ctx)
                    return result
                except (ConnectionError, TimeoutError) as ex:
                    backoff = 2 ** attempt
                    logger.warning(f"Transient error on {ctx.task_id}: {ex}. Retrying in {backoff}s...")
                    await asyncio.sleep(backoff)
                except Exception as ex:
                    logger.error(f"Permanent failure processing {ctx.task_id}: {ex}")
                    raise
            return None

    async def _process_task(self, ctx: ExecutionContext) -> dict:
        await asyncio.sleep(0.05)
        return {"task_id": ctx.task_id, "status": "completed", "meta": ctx.payload}

Production Gotchas to Avoid

When deploying this architecture at scale, keep these three operational realities in mind:

  1. Beware of Unbounded Queues: Always place hard limits on in-memory buffers and connection queues. An unbounded queue simply hides backpressure until the process encounters an Out-Of-Memory (OOM) crash.
  2. Set Aggressive Timeouts: Never make external network or storage calls without explicit connection and read timeouts. A single hanging dependency can exhaust worker pools system-wide.
  3. Ensure Idempotency: Network packets get dropped and clients retry. Ensure that mutating operations can be executed multiple times safely without producing duplicate side-effects.

Summary Checklist

  • [x] Validate at the boundary: Ensure invalid states never penetrate deep domain layers.
  • [x] Enforce bounded resource limits: Protect memory, connections, and CPU threads against unexpected spikes.
  • [x] Log structured telemetry: Attach correlation IDs to log records for rapid root-cause analysis during outages.
  • [x] Design for failure: Always provide graceful fallbacks and fast-failure mechanisms when dependencies degrade.

title: Verify authentication recovery before treating Configuration as the root cause
description:
A return URL containing error=Configuration suggests a configuration mistake. Yet the inspected Auth.js version also produces that destination when a PKCE cookie is missing. The user-facing classification does not identify the cause by itself.

This investigation read SquadNote's recovery implementation and reran tests against its actual Auth.js dependency. It examines rejection, retry navigation, and diagnostic evidence before drawing a causal conclusion.

The source is circle-hub at d116e8a, checked on September 11, 2026. No production authentication logs or user histories were collected. This is an account of recovery code and rerun verification, not proof of a production incident's cause or resolution.

Distinguish the internal error from Configuration

Auth.js's InvalidCheck reference covers PKCE, state, or nonce checks that cannot be performed. Unavailable cookies can produce it, as can configuration issues.

The repository regression test resolves @auth/core through the application's next-auth dependency. It does not substitute a separately installed latest release.

A synthetic callback without its PKCE cookie produced:

Observation Result
HTTP status 302
Redirect destination /sign-in/error?error=Configuration
Internal type passed to the logger InvalidCheck

The fixture deliberately omitted the cookie, so its cause is known. Seeing the same internal type in production would still require investigating why the cookie did not arrive. Expiration, another initiation, and browser behavior cannot be distinguished from that display alone.

First restore a path from failure to a fresh start

The recovery design record and history show the recovery screen in 061a5f2, repeated-submission protection in 2b88c31, and diagnostics in 7f180ad.

The recovery screen presents sign-in and public help without depending on auth() or the database. Displaying an authentication failure does not require successfully repeating the same authentication dependency.

Return destinations are restricted to safe paths on the same origin. Tests preserve invitation-page returns while rejecting external redirection and authentication-page loops. The original callback URL is not reused unconditionally.

Two new initiation requests sent to the actual Auth.js implementation produced different PKCE challenges, S256, and fresh PKCE cookies. However, the initiation fixture uses the internal CSRF-skip option. It does not verify browser CSRF protection or a round trip through the OAuth provider, and no production setting was changed to disable CSRF checks.

Reject a second start before React rerenders

Disabling a button visually can leave a window before React rerenders in which another button can be pressed. The implementation uses a synchronous guard shared by Google and Apple initiation on the same screen:

export function createSubmissionGuard() {
  let submitting = false;
  return {
    acquire() {
      if (submitting) return false;
      submitting = true;
      return true;
    },
    reset() { submitting = false; },
  };
}

Tests against the actual guard reject immediate reacquisition, allow acquisition after the reset used for failure or history restoration, and keep separate instances independent.

Its scope is repeated submission from one screen. It does not serialize initiation across tabs or browsers, nor remove every possible cause of missing cookies.

Correlate how far the flow progressed

The diagnostics investigate initiation and callback boundaries without storing authentication values. The principal events mean:

Event What it establishes
auth.sign_in_started A start request occurred
auth.authorization_redirect Initiation generated a destination
auth.callback_received A callback arrived
auth.sign_in_succeeded Auth.js emitted its signIn event
auth.server_error Failure and diagnostic information were recorded

Initiation and destination generation do not mean authentication succeeded. In particular, the server action's cookiesAfterStart observes the cookie jar at that time. Existing cookies can be present, so presence alone does not establish fresh issuance.

requestId identifies a failing request; attemptId supports correlation with initiation. The latter marker is client-originated diagnostic information and does not authorize authentication. It represents the browser's most recent initiation, so it does not prove the same OAuth transaction across multiple tabs.

Absent, expired, or provider-mismatched markers can prevent correlation. Record why correlation failed instead of rephrasing that as “no initiation happened.”

Add diagnostics without weakening authentication checks

Diagnostic tests verify that synthetic sensitive values, including cookie values, authorization codes, tokens, raw User-Agent strings, and IPs, do not appear in logs. Cookie observations retain only presence for specific names, and paths are restricted to authentication routes.

Tests also check isolation between concurrent requests, preservation of authentication responses when diagnostics or notifications fail, and preservation of the original Auth.js response cookies. The change does not obtain successful logins by relaxing PKCE, state, or nonce requirements.

Alert suppression operates within a Worker instance; it is not a delivery guarantee across all distributed instances. The diagnostic cookie is not a session replacement either. Neither mechanism belongs in the decision that authentication has succeeded.

The 47 tests and the remaining environment checks

The run passed 47 tests across 8 files copied from the fixed commit. It used Node.js v24.15.0, Vitest 4.1.4, Next.js 15.5.15, next-auth 5.0.0-beta.25, and its Auth.js core dependency 0.37.2. The runner and results are preserved.

Some tests invoke the actual Auth.js implementation; others mock route or notification dependencies. Real Google or Apple accounts, Safari or embedded browsers, multiple tabs, and manual browser-cookie deletion were not tested in this run. Historical UI verification documented in the repository is also separate from these rerun results.

Verify the failure classification, fresh initiation, safe return destination, same-screen repeat protection, and the limits of log correlation in order. While the cause remains uncertain, record the conditions for retry and the questions requiring further investigation.

title: Data Density Scaling Laws for Image Self-Distillation
description:
arXiv:2610.19013v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Current scaling law formulations suggest that increasing the number of unique samples in a dataset improves model performance, while repeated exposure to the same samples provides diminishing value. In this work, we examine this assumption for image self-distillation models. Through systematic experiments across diverse datasets, namely Maxar, SATLAS, Waymo, nuPlan, Ego4D, ImageNet, and YFCC15M, we demonstrate that the effects of sample repetition on downstream performance are non-trivial and dataset-dependent. We identify settings where repeatedly training on a smaller random subset can outperform training on a larger set of unique samples. This finding highlights a limitation of existing scaling laws. To address this gap, we propose a modified version of a Chinchilla-style scaling law that explicitly accounts for two factors: the number of unique samples and repetition per sample. This formulation provides a framework for understanding data-compute trade-offs and improves prediction in some regimes where repetition plays a central role, although its benefits are not consistent across datasets. Finally, we examine how subset selection and augmentation affect downstream performance.

title: When POST becomes GET: a redirect bug in a Node.js fetch wrapper
description:
A POST followed a 302 redirect and became a GET. Its body disappeared, but its Content-Type header stayed behind.

That showed up while extending the client comparisons in ssrf-lab, a testing harness I maintain. The affected package was @tak-ps/node-safeurl@1.8.0, a Node.js fetch wrapper that checks URLs and redirect destinations.

This is a functional redirect-conformance bug. The proposed fix is upstream PR #4, submitted and awaiting review as of October 14, 2026. These tests do not demonstrate an SSRF bypass.

The response looked fine. The request told the story.

The comparison uses a small HTTP server on 127.0.0.1. One route returns a redirect; the destination echoes the method, body, and headers it actually receives. That exact local origin is explicitly allowed in the wrapper's configuration.

Both native fetch and the wrapper successfully completed this request:

{
  method: 'POST',
  body: 'hello',
  headers: { 'content-type': 'text/plain' }
}

After a 302 redirect, the destination observed:

Client Method Body Content-Type
Native fetch GET empty absent
node-safeurl 1.8.0 GET empty text/plain

The same difference appeared for 301 POST and 303 PUT. Checking only the final status or whether the fetch promise resolved would miss it.

The Fetch redirect algorithm changes POST to GET for 301/302, and changes methods other than GET/HEAD to GET for 303. When it discards the body, it also removes the request-body headers: Content-Encoding, Content-Language, Content-Location, and Content-Type.

The wrapper already handled the method and body changes. It was missing the corresponding header cleanup.

The fix belongs in the method-rewrite branch

The patch adds Headers to the existing Undici import, then extends the existing switchToGet branch:

if (switchToGet) {
  fetchInit.method = 'GET';
  fetchInit.body = undefined;

  const headers = new Headers(fetchInit.headers);
  for (const name of [
    'content-encoding',
    'content-language',
    'content-location',
    'content-type',
    'content-length',
  ]) {
    headers.delete(name);
  }
  fetchInit.headers = headers;
}

Content-Length is removed as well, because caller-supplied framing for the discarded body should not carry into the GET. It is separate from the standard's four named request-body headers.

Copying through Headers supports object, tuple-array, and Headers inputs without changing the caller's original headers. Unrelated headers survive. The URL validation logic is unchanged.

The condition matters: a 307 or 308 should preserve the method and body, so stripping these headers on every redirect would introduce another bug.

Prove both the fix and the unchanged cases

The upstream regression test records actual incoming requests and checks seven cases:

Redirect cases Before patch After patch
301 POST, 302 POST, 303 PUT All three fail All three pass
307 POST, 308 POST, 301 PUT, 302 PUT All four pass All four pass

It also checks that an unrelated header is preserved and the caller's headers are not mutated. The full patched upstream suite passes 198 tests on each of Node 22.23.3 and 24.21.0, alongside lint and build.

The recorded evidence includes the original failures, fixed tests, full-suite logs, and published-package comparison.

Run the comparison

With Node 22.19 or newer and npm:

git clone https://github.com/roshan-amble/ssrf-lab.git
cd ssrf-lab
git checkout 41659cda6825b2f7e324294d7242ef1b076b6cce
npm ci --ignore-scripts --prefix integrations/community
node integrations/community/check-redirects.mjs

This prints JSON for native fetch and the unmodified published package across five redirect cases. The HTTP comparison stays on the explicitly allowed loopback origin. The broader SSRF suite has separate network-isolation requirements.

The practical testing lesson is to assert what reached the destination: method, body, and headers. A successful response alone cannot establish that a wrapper preserved fetch semantics.

The harness, adapters, and reproduction are in ssrf-lab. Which redirect or URL-handling edge case would you add to this coverage?

AI disclosure: Codex assisted with the investigation, implementation, and test execution, and drafted this article from the linked code and recorded results.

title: Amazon CloudWatch announces log routing and chained log parsers
description:
Amazon CloudWatch now supports conditional log routing and chained parsers via pipelines, giving you more control over how log data is transformed and which CloudWatch log group it's sent to. CloudWatch pipelines is a fully managed service that ingests, transforms, and routes telemetry to CloudWatch without managing infrastructure.

Log pipelines often carry a mix of event types that belong in different places, and individual events can nest one log format inside another. With conditional log routing, you define routes that send each event to a different CloudWatch log group based on conditions evaluated against processed fields, so you can separate events by severity, source, or type and apply the right retention and access controls to each. With chained parsers, you can apply multiple parser processors in sequence, where later parsers consume fields produced by earlier ones. For example, you can parse a JSON envelope first, then apply a Grok parser to a field it extracts. Together, these capabilities let you structure diverse log formats and route them to the right log groups in a single pipeline.

Conditional routing and chained parsers are available in all commercial AWS Regions where CloudWatch pipelines is generally available. You can configure these capabilities using the AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, or AWS SDKs. To get started, see the Amazon CloudWatch pipelines documentation.

title: 40 font-face blocks, 10 files, and the word bold appears nowhere: three typefaces reaching a Next.js site and an Expo app
description:
Munchable uses three typefaces, and each has exactly one job. Fredoka, which is round and friendly, is allowed on the wordmark and hero headlines and nowhere else. Outfit does every other heading. Nunito does body text. The sizes come from a tokens package shared by the website, the phone app and the renderer that produces our video, so a heading is 27/33 in all three.

Two of those consumers load the fonts in completely different ways, and the second one surprised me more than it should have.

The web half, and why it is self-hosted 

const nunito = Nunito({
  subsets: ['latin'],
  weight: ['400', '500', '600', '700'],
  variable: '--font-nunito',
  display: 'swap',
});

Three of those, one per family, each exposing a CSS variable that globals.css consumes through role names rather than family names:

--font-display: var(--font-outfit), ui-sans-serif, system-ui, -apple-system, sans-serif;
--font-body: var(--font-nunito), ui-sans-serif, system-ui, -apple-system, sans-serif;
--font-brand: var(--font-fredoka), var(--font-nunito), ui-sans-serif, system-ui, -apple-system, sans-serif;

--font-brand falling back to Nunito before the system stack is deliberate: if the display face fails, the wordmark should land on the font the rest of the page is already using rather than on whatever Helvetica the device has.

next/font/google downloads the font files at build time and serves them from our own origin. That is a privacy decision before it is a performance one. A <link> to fonts.googleapis.com means every page load reports the visitor's IP address to a third party, and this is a site where the page somebody is reading can be the IBD page or the SIBO page. The URL is a health disclosure. There is no third-party request in the critical path of any page here, and the privacy policy says so, which means the fonts had to come along.

What that actually ships

You can count this yourself on any page of the site. Pull the stylesheet and look at the @font-face blocks:

  • 40 @font-face blocks
  • 10 distinct .woff2 files
  • 3 of the blocks are not web fonts at all

The three odd ones are named Nunito Fallback, Outfit Fallback and Fredoka Fallback. They are synthetic faces pointing at a local system font with adjusted metrics, generated so that the text drawn before the real font arrives occupies close to the same space. That is the mechanism that keeps display: swap from shoving your layout sideways, and it is the main reason to use the font loader rather than hand-writing the @font-face rules.

Forty blocks for ten files because the same file is declared under several weights and several unicode ranges. The browser then fetches only the ones a page actually asks for. On the homepage, in a fresh profile:

performance.getEntriesByType('resource')
  .filter(r => /\.woff2/.test(r.name))
  .map(r => [r.name.split('/').pop().slice(0, 12), r.encodedBodySize]);

Three files, 101,084 bytes in total, all from munchable.app.

The audit this led to

Eleven weights are declared across the three families: four of Nunito, four of Outfit, three of Fredoka.

The public stylesheet contains exactly three numeric weights: 600, 700 and 800. Body copy inherits 400 and never says so. Grep it and that is the whole list, inline SVG demos included.

Which means at least two declared weights are never referenced by the site: font-weight: 500 appears nowhere in the public CSS at all. It appears in exactly one file in the repository, the admin panel's own stylesheet, which is behind authentication and noindexed.

The honest accounting here matters, because it explains why nobody noticed. A declared and unreferenced weight costs a visitor nothing in bandwidth: no rule asks for it, so the file is never fetched. It costs build output, a slightly bigger stylesheet, and a wrong answer to the question "which weights does this product use". It is a one-line fix in each of three calls, and the reason to make it is tidiness rather than speed, which is worth saying out loud instead of dressing it up as a performance win.

The React Native half, where weight is not a number

Here is the part that trips up anybody moving a design system onto React Native. On the web, you ask for a family and a weight and the browser picks a face. In React Native with custom fonts, the weight is part of the family's name:

export const fontMap = {
  Fredoka_600SemiBold,
  Fredoka_700Bold,
  Outfit_500Medium,
  Outfit_600SemiBold,
  Outfit_700Bold,
  Nunito_400Regular,
  Nunito_600SemiBold,
  Nunito_700Bold,
};

Eight named faces, handed to expo-font's useFonts. Then the type scale attaches a family to each variant rather than a weight:

export const typography = {
  brand: { fontFamily: 'Fredoka_700Bold', ...typeScale.brand },
  hero: { fontFamily: 'Fredoka_700Bold', ...typeScale.hero },
  display: { fontFamily: 'Outfit_700Bold', ...typeScale.display },
  h1: { fontFamily: 'Outfit_700Bold', ...typeScale.h1 },
  h2: { fontFamily: 'Outfit_600SemiBold', ...typeScale.h2 },
  title: { fontFamily: 'Outfit_600SemiBold', ...typeScale.title },
  body: { fontFamily: 'Nunito_400Regular', ...typeScale.body },
  bodyStrong: { fontFamily: 'Nunito_700Bold', ...typeScale.bodyStrong },
  label: { fontFamily: 'Nunito_700Bold', ...typeScale.label },
  caption: { fontFamily: 'Nunito_600SemiBold', ...typeScale.caption },
};

fontWeight appears nowhere in the app. Not in the tokens, not in a component, not in a screen. Grep returns nothing, and that is the design: setting fontWeight: '700' on a custom family asks the platform to synthesise a bold, which on Android is a smeared version of the regular face and on iOS is sometimes ignored entirely. Two platforms, two different wrong answers. Naming the face is the only portable instruction.

The ...typeScale.h2 spread is where the two halves meet. The sizes and line heights live in a platform-free package, so h2 is 21/27 on a phone, in the browser build of the same app, and in the rendered video frames, without anybody retyping a number.

One <Text variant="h2"> component reads that table. No screen picks a family, so there is no screen that can pick the wrong one.

Boot, briefly

Fonts block the splash screen, because the app's first screen is a scanner and text reflowing under somebody's thumb in a supermarket aisle is worse than a slightly longer splash. But the gate is fontsLoaded || fontError: a font that fails to load must not hold the app hostage, and the fallback stack exists precisely so that case is merely uglier rather than broken.

Where to see all three

The homepage is the only page with the brand face at full size, so munchable.app is where Fredoka actually earns its place. A content page such as the congee recipe is the ordinary case: Outfit for the headings, Nunito for everything you read, and nothing from a third-party domain in the network panel.

How to Mount Cloud Storage as a Local Drive: 2026 Guide

Mounting cloud storage (Nextcloud, ownCloud, WebDAV, S3, Google Drive, OneDrive) as a real local drive on Windows or macOS used to require either paid tools or fragile hackery. In 2026 the options are mature, but the choice still matters. This guide explains the four real approaches, the tradeoffs, and which tool to pick for which scenario.

Why "mount" instead of "sync"

The naive approach is to sync files locally: a desktop client downloads your cloud to a folder, and changes sync back. That works for one folder at a time, but:

  • Two-way sync conflicts are confusing when you have multiple devices
  • You need to pre-allocate disk space for the entire cloud
  • You cannot use OS-native tools (Spotlight, Quick Look, Time Machine) on the remote files

A true mount, on the other hand, makes the cloud appear as a drive letter (Windows) or /Volumes/xxx (macOS). Files stream on demand, with no sync, and you use them like local files.

The four approaches (and which tools use which)

  1. Kernel filesystem driver — installed at OS level, catches all file I/O. Most "real" cloud mount tools use this approach via FUSE (macOS/Linux) or a userspace FS driver (Windows). Examples: Mountain Duck, ScsDriver, RaiDrive, ExpanDrive.

  2. In-process proxy — runs as a background process, intercepts file I/O at a higher level. Faster to develop, less reliable under heavy load. Examples: NetDrive (older versions), Air Live Drive.

  3. Sync folder with offline cache — pretends to be a mount but actually syncs. Examples: Google Drive desktop, Dropbox, OneDrive. Not a true mount, but often mislabeled as one.

  4. Protocol-specific client — only works for one protocol (WebDAV, SFTP, etc.) and does not appear as a real drive. Examples: Cyberduck (WebDAV/SFTP), FileZilla (FTP), mountainduck-cli (SFTP).

For a true "cloud as a local drive" experience, you want approach 1 or 2.

Protocol matrix: which tool supports which

Tool WebDAV S3 SFTP OneDrive Google Drive
ScsDriver ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅
Mountain Duck ✅ ❌ ✅ ✅ ✅
RaiDrive ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅
ExpanDrive ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅
Cyberduck ✅ ✅ ✅ ❌ ❌

ScsDriver: the 2026 sweet spot

ScsDriver is a Windows userspace FS driver that supports WebDAV, S3, SFTP, OneDrive, and Google Drive. The 2026 release (released in March) added proper support for large file streaming (>2 GB) and reliable reconnection after sleep.

Pricing (overseas)

  • $1.5 / month
  • $5.5 / year
  • $5.5 lifetime (limited-time offer, was $9.99)

CN users: the lifetime price in China is ¥20, separately listed on the official site.

My testing (Windows 11 24H2, 1 TB Nextcloud)

Operation ScsDriver Mountain Duck RaiDrive Free
1.2 GB ISO copy 4 min 12 s 5 min 30 s 6 min 50 s
Reconnect after sleep <3 s 6 s 8 s
Listing 10k files 8 s 9 s 22 s
Concurrent uploads 8 4 4 (free) / 16 (pro)

When to use what

  • ScsDriver — best overall, especially if you mix multiple cloud backends. Best price ($5.5 lifetime).
  • Mountain Duck — if you only need WebDAV/SFTP and want the most polished UI. $49/year.
  • RaiDrive Free — if you want to spend nothing and can live with the 4-connection cap and occasional driver issues.
  • ExpanDrive — if you are on macOS and need S3 + WebDAV + SFTP in one tool. $49.99/year.
  • Cyberduck — if you just need a one-off file transfer, not a mount.

How to set up ScsDriver in 10 minutes

  1. Download the installer from https://scsoi.com/
  2. Run as administrator
  3. Click "Add Connection" → pick WebDAV (or any of the 5 protocols)
  4. Enter your server URL, username, password
  5. Pick a drive letter (e.g. Z:)
  6. Open File Explorer — your cloud is now Z:

The whole setup takes about 10 minutes, including restarting Explorer.

FAQ

Q: Does ScsDriver work on macOS?
A: Yes, a separate macOS build is available; it uses FUSE instead of a Windows driver.

Q: Can I mount multiple Nextcloud accounts at once?
A: Yes, each connection gets its own drive letter.

Q: Does the $5.5 lifetime include future updates?
A: Yes, lifetime includes all 2026.x and 2027.x updates.

Q: What about iOS / Android?
A: Not currently — ScsDriver is Windows + macOS only.

Disclaimer: I bought all licenses at full price. The ScsDriver pricing link above is the public page.
