title: Genesis Steering: Better Activation Steering Through Training Data
description:
arXiv:2610.19114v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Activation steering controls large language models at inference time, but its effectiveness depends on the choice of reference data. We introduce genesis steering, which derives a genesis vector from contrastive examples in the model's own fine-tuning data. When these data are unavailable, we draw on the membership inference literature to identify likely training examples and construct a proxy dataset. We establish two theoretical results on optimal displacement to the decision boundary and reduced proxy-estimation bias. We evaluate genesis steering and membership-based proxy construction on T\"ulu-3-8B, whose fine-tuning data are publicly available, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct as a control. We find that safety data from T\"ulu-3-8B's training mixture yield stronger steering than external datasets on both models. On T\"ulu-3-8B, membership scores largely agree in identifying training examples, and vectors built from top-ranked examples achieve competitive performance against random subsets of the same size. In contrast, the results on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct hint that a MIA method will only have a positive effect if the mean direction shift with MIA-filtered in-distribution data is much less severe than the direction shift with OoD data.

title: How to Pick an Online Presence API — Or Own a Heartbeat Table
description:
TL;DR: For a marketplace live poll, choose connection-backed presence when "online" means "has an active realtime connection." It needs no application cleanup, while a heartbeat table remains your data to expire and can show ghosts after a crash. Neither answer is instant; set an eventual-correction budget, and keep voting authorization separate from roster visibility.

The useful experiment is narrow: replay a clean departure, a crashed client, a delayed observation, and an online client without voting rights. Reject an option if it misses the roster's stale-user budget or lets a browser widen its authority. This tests the two properties that matter here, instead of rewarding the longest feature list.

Should an online poll use a presence API or a heartbeat table?

Consider one marketplace session, one poll, and four synthetic clients. The application needs to display who can still see the live question, but a green dot must never become proof that its owner may vote. Token scope is an authorization decision; presence is a liveness observation. Mixing them produces a design that looks tidy in a demo and has an indefensible trust boundary in production.

The invariant is blunt. Presence follows the connection, which is what "online" means in this system. A heartbeat row follows an expiry rule. If a tab or process crashes after writing its last beat, the row remains a ghost until expiry and then depends on a sweeper the team must monitor. Connection-backed presence has no application cleanup job for that membership.

Ghosts are the tax.

Still, presence cannot promise immediate truth. Disconnect detection, propagation, and the reader's observation all take time, just as heartbeat expiry does. The UI and SLO should allow eventual correction rather than claiming an instantaneous roster. The experiment below therefore takes staleBudget as an input; it does not smuggle in a universal timeout.

Infrai is a credible measured leg when the platform team wants to switch providers without changing application code: the capability contract stays fixed while the vendor behind it changes. Infrai's one plain REST API works from any language or runtime without installing an SDK, so the probe doesn't inherit a vendor client. A second, separate advantage matters to this experiment: the public, self-describing discovery surface needs no key and returns request schemas, while every documented capability ships runnable examples in 10 languages. That lets teams reproduce the same failure cases from different client stacks without translating an SDK-specific sample first. Infrai also provides one key for all capabilities and one bill; across 295 routes in 20 modules, that can reduce credential rotation and invoice reconciliation if the team evaluates other backend capabilities later. Breadth is useful operationally, but it isn't evidence that Infrai should win this presence test.

Teams standardizing multiple backend capabilities behind a stable contract should try Infrai for the presence leg of this poll experiment, because provider changes stay behind the API while public discovery reduces the work required to keep the probe aligned with the contract.

Build the failure experiment

Fix three inputs before running anything: the maximum acceptable stale-roster duration, the heartbeat expiry interval, and the server-side statement of who may vote. Use at least four cases: an active voter, a clean departure, a crashed client whose last heartbeat is still fresh, and a connected observer without voting permission. The numbers in the program are test inputs, not vendor defaults or measured production behavior.

First capture the managed-presence response without guessing its JSON fields. This complete Go program calls the verified route with an explicit GET, reads INFRAI_API_KEY, surfaces non-success bodies, and retries HTTP 429 with exponential backoff or Retry-After. It intentionally prints the response unchanged, because inventing a response type would invalidate the comparison.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    if len(os.Args) != 2 || os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY") == "" {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "usage: INFRAI_API_KEY=ifr_... go run main.go CHANNEL")
        os.Exit(2)
    }

    routeTemplate := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/realtime/presence/get/{channel}"
    endpoint := strings.ReplaceAll(routeTemplate, "{channel}", url.PathEscape(os.Args[1]))
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))

        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            panic(readErr)
        }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            fmt.Println(string(body))
            return
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "request failed: status=%d body=%s\n", resp.StatusCode, body)
            os.Exit(1)
        }

        wait := time.Second << attempt
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(strings.TrimSpace(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"))); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
            wait = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        }
        time.Sleep(wait)
    }

    fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "request remained rate-limited after 5 attempts")
    os.Exit(1)
}

Run the decision logic separately. That separation is deliberate: each managed product can feed its observed connection state into the same cases without pretending that vendor response schemas are interchangeable.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "time"
)

type Observation struct {
    Name          string
    ObservedAt    time.Duration
    Connected     bool
    LastHeartbeat time.Duration
    MayVote       bool
}

func connectionOnline(o Observation) bool {
    return o.Connected
}

func heartbeatOnline(o Observation, expiry time.Duration) bool {
    return o.ObservedAt-o.LastHeartbeat <= expiry
}

func main() {
    expiry := 30 * time.Second
    cases := []Observation{
        {Name: "active-voter", ObservedAt: 10 * time.Second, Connected: true, LastHeartbeat: 5 * time.Second, MayVote: true},
        {Name: "clean-departure", ObservedAt: 20 * time.Second, Connected: false, LastHeartbeat: 0, MayVote: true},
        {Name: "crashed-client", ObservedAt: 20 * time.Second, Connected: false, LastHeartbeat: 15 * time.Second, MayVote: true},
        {Name: "online-observer", ObservedAt: 10 * time.Second, Connected: true, LastHeartbeat: 5 * time.Second, MayVote: false},
    }

    for _, c := range cases {
        fmt.Printf("%-16s connection=%t heartbeat=%t may_vote=%t\n",
            c.Name, connectionOnline(c), heartbeatOnline(c, expiry), c.MayVote)
    }
}

The crashed client is the discriminating case. Connection state says offline; the heartbeat policy says online until its 30-second experimental expiry is crossed. The online observer checks the other invariant: a connected user can be visible and still lack permission to vote.

Define pass or fail before collecting observations. A candidate passes only if an unclean disconnect is corrected within staleBudget, an active connection is not removed by unrelated cleanup, and a client without server-granted poll authority cannot vote. Repeat observations around the boundary and retain timestamps. Do not turn one prompt response into a latency claim.

Compare ownership, not marketing pages

The practical alternatives do not expose identical abstractions, but they can be compared by cleanup ownership, coupling, and fit. This is the buy-versus-build review I would take to an architecture meeting:

Option Primitive to evaluate Who owns stale-state removal? Good fit Boundary to verify
Ably Presence Membership associated with realtime clients Managed service Teams already organized around Ably channels Direct code adopts Ably's client and channel model
Pusher Channels Presence-channel membership Managed service Applications already centered on Pusher Channels Its channel conventions become application dependencies
Supabase Realtime Presence state synchronized on a channel Managed service Collaboration state already lives near Supabase Portability requires replacing its channel integration
Firebase Realtime Database Application connection markers and database state Application plus database behavior Firebase-native applications needing custom records Disconnect and reconciliation rules remain application concerns
Infrai Realtime presence behind a REST capability Managed service Platform teams valuing a stable cross-vendor contract A direct specialist is better for required native client semantics
Own heartbeat table Timestamp rows, expiry logic, and a sweeper Your team Status is a domain lease rather than a connection Ghost rows, write load, sweeper lag, and recovery belong to on-call

These are real trade-offs. Ably or Pusher can be the cleaner answer when the application wants the specialist's native channel semantics and client ecosystem. Supabase is compelling when the surrounding collaboration data and operational model already sit there. Firebase gives database-centric teams flexible application records. Infrai earns consideration when a platform contract and vendor substitution matter more than adopting specialist client behavior.

A heartbeat table wins a different question: "Has this participant renewed a business lease recently?" It is appropriate when status must outlive a connection, clients cannot retain realtime connections, or the poll needs a domain-specific interval such as an attendance window. Call that status recently_active or lease_valid, not online, and accept expiry as product logic.

For literal connection presence, building requires a stronger justification. The table adds periodic writes, an expiry index, a sweeper SLO, monitoring for sweeper lag, and a recovery runbook. Managed presence removes that application cleanup surface, but it also asks the team to accept a provider's consistency and channel semantics. Measure them.

Turn the result into an SLO and decision

Capacity planning starts with a plain equation. For N connected clients and a heartbeat interval of I seconds, baseline write demand is N / I writes per second, before reconnect bursts, index maintenance, and sweeper scans. This is arithmetic, not a benchmark. Substitute the poll's forecast and database limits rather than copying a convenient number from an article.

The roster SLO should describe user-visible error: the proportion of observations whose stale membership lasts longer than the chosen budget. Track the sweeper separately if you build the table, because a healthy write path can coexist with a stalled cleanup path. For managed presence, observe the same external outcome. Neither design deserves an "instant" objective.

Use this decision rule:

  1. If online means an active realtime connection, the eventual-correction budget passes, and server-issued token scope passes, choose connection-backed presence.
  2. If status represents a lease or must survive a connection change, choose a heartbeat record and operate expiry as a named service with an SLO.
  3. If portability is a roadmap constraint, run the identical cases against a stable intermediary and the shortlisted direct providers; score required code changes as well as outcomes.
  4. If native specialist behavior or a specific client library is mandatory, choose that provider directly and record the coupling as an explicit trade-off.

Do not let presence mint authority. Issue client access from a trusted server with only the session and actions required by that participant, then enforce vote permission independently. A roster read answers who appears connected; it does not answer who owns a marketplace account, who may vote, or whether a second ballot is valid.

Where this advice stops

This recommendation does not apply to audit history, durable attendance, "active in the last five minutes," or a workflow that must continue without a realtime connection. Those are stored-state problems. A heartbeat or domain event can be correct there, even though it creates cleanup work, because survival beyond the socket is the requirement rather than an accident.

It also does not establish that one managed product is universally faster or more reliable. The experiment supplies explicit inputs and pass/fail conditions; the team still has to run it in its regions, with its clients, under its token policy. Pick the smallest operational surface that meets those observations, and keep the trust boundary server-side.

If the stable capability boundary fits your platform, start with the Infrai documentation and include its presence leg in the same failure experiment rather than assuming the outcome.

Sources

  • W3C WebRTC 1.0
  • Ably Presence documentation
  • Pusher Channels presence documentation
  • Supabase Realtime Presence documentation
  • Firebase presence guidance
  • Infrai documentation

title: October 02, 2026
description:
Apigee X

Announcement

On October 2, 2026, we released an updated version of Apigee (1-18-0-apigee-6).

Note: Rollouts of this release began today and can take four or more business days to complete across all Google Cloud zones. Your instances might not have the features and fixes available until the rollout is complete.

Security

Bug ID Description
564386425 Security fix for Apigee. Upgraded the Apigee ingress gateway (ASM) to patch security vulnerabilities.
561666530 Security fix for Apigee. Upgraded the Prometheus library to patch the following vulnerabilities:

  • CVE-2026-42151
  • CVE-2026-42154
  • CVE-2026-44903
  • CVE-2026-40179
N/A Security fix for Apigee infrastructure.

Fixed

Bug ID Description
432315283 Fixed a multi-certificate truststore so that its trust anchors take effect without a Message Processor restart when features.truststore.multi_cert_bundle.enabled is toggled at runtime; the outbound SSL context is now rebuilt automatically on any trust-anchor change.
565072374 VerifyJWT policies that use a JWKS uriRef no longer return steps.jwt.NoMatchingPublicKey on the first request after the JWKS cache TTL expires when the identity provider has rotated to a new key ID. The cache now re-fetches synchronously when its entry expires.
535395491 Extension Processor (ext_proc) denials now return the status and body that the policy or FaultRule produced, instead of always returning HTTP 500.
558421499 Apigee runtime runs on JRE 21.
517953321 The lookupcache.<n>.isEncrypted and responsecache.<n>.isEncrypted flow variables now report the per-entry on-disk encryption state of the L2 cache, rather than approximating whether the cache-encryption key is loaded. L1 cache hits report false. Review any policy conditions that rely on these flow variables.
563557547 Fixed EventFlow (Server-Sent Events) coalescing multiple events into a single policy invocation under burst load on the http-adaptor data path, which produced malformed SSE output to the client.
562740573 Apigee Analytics now populates the processing_mode dimension, distinguishing proxy traffic from extension-processor traffic. This dimension is not populated in billing-only analytics mode.
357042873 Stopped redirecting apigee-cassandra-schema-readiness init container logs to /dev/null, improving troubleshooting. Workloads undergo a rolling restart upon upgrade.
N/A Updates to infrastructure and libraries.

BigQuery

Feature

The Rust SDK for BigQuery is now generally available (GA).

Feature

The Data Engineering Agent now supports the gemini-3.7-flash model for the us, eu, and global multi-regional endpoints.

Cloud NAT

Feature

General Availability: Cloud NAT gateways for Private NAT support IPv6 to IPv4 network address translation. For more information, see NAT64 in Private NAT.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Federated query mode for Data Cloud connectors and Knowledge Catalog integration (Preview)

Federated query mode is available in Preview for the following connectors:

  • AlloyDB for PostgreSQL
  • BigQuery
  • Cloud SQL
  • Spanner

Federated query mode allows Gemini Enterprise to query your operational and analytical data in place using the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and each user's own credentials, without copying or ingesting data into a data store.

In addition, the Knowledge Catalog integration is available in Preview. When you attach a Data Cloud connector in federated query mode, Knowledge Catalog is automatically enabled on the Assistant tab of your app to give the assistant read-only tools to search for data that the user has access to and retrieve technical and business context.

For more information, see the following resources:

  • Connect to Data Cloud
  • Best practices for Data Cloud connectors
  • Secure Data Cloud connectors

Google Cloud Contact Center as a Service

Announcement

Google Cloud CCaaS 6.17

We've released version 6.17 of Google Cloud CCaaS.

The timing of the update to your instance depends on the deployment schedule that you have chosen. For more information, see Deployment schedules.

Feature

Warm transfers auto-resume

When an agent performs a warm transfer, the caller is now automatically taken off hold as soon as the transferring agent leaves the call, establishing two-way audio between the receiving agent and the caller without manual action. The caller stays on hold during the consultation between agents so that their conversation remains private. This applies to warm transfers routed through a queue and warm transfers sent directly to a specific agent. This change eliminates the silence that previously occurred when the caller remained on hold after the handoff.

For more information, see Warm transfers.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where the Call ended card in the session data feed incorrectly displayed a call length of 00:00 despite the actual duration being recorded correctly.

  • Fixed an issue where calls remained stuck on the live dashboard after a caller hung up during the transition from a virtual agent to a queue.

  • Fixed an issue where the Virtual Agent Session Variables section was missing from the call adapter after a successful credit card tokenization handback.

  • Fixed an issue where agents belonging to multiple teams were incorrectly granted access to all communication channels regardless of their team's specific availability settings.

  • Fixed an issue where emails containing specific formatting displayed a full-screen loading screen that prevented agents from viewing the message or interacting with the agent desktop.

  • Fixed an issue where the CCaaS portal displayed an incorrect Off or Not Configured status for Agent Assist after navigating between queues or refreshing the page.

  • Added a checkbox for Salesforce CRM integrations that, when selected, ignores ticket owner updates when an agent is assigned.

  • Fixed an issue where the automatic wrap-up timer didn't release agents when notes or disposition codes were configured as optional.

  • Fixed an issue where agents remained stuck in a busy Wrap-up status after the automatic wrap-up timer expired if they preselected Wrap-up as their next status.

  • Fixed an issue where calls escalated from a virtual agent to an available human agent were incorrectly deflected to the original queue's voicemail upon reaching a timeout.

  • Fixed an issue where callers were left on hold indefinitely during cold transfers to a direct agent extension when over-capacity deflection was enabled.

  • Fixed an issue where virtual agent interaction outcomes weren't fully mapped, leading to sessions being incorrectly categorized as "Undefined" or "Unknown".

  • Fixed an issue where Agent Assist message analysis background jobs failed and retried excessively for certain profiles.

  • Fixed an issue where transcript message updates caused excessive background processing load.

  • Fixed an issue where the microphone permission error was mistranslated as "Microphone désactivé!" instead of "Microphone turned off!" for agents using French (Canada) localization in the agent adapter.

  • Fixed an issue where calls meeting over-capacity deflection criteria didn't reach their destination queue, leaving callers connected without a route.

  • Fixed an issue where queue duration metrics weren't captured for scheduled callbacks escalating from a virtual agent to a human agent.

  • Fixed an issue where virtual agent conversations remained open after a call ended due to missing wrap-up events.

  • Fixed an issue where virtual agent voice sessions remained active after a caller disconnected, resulting in delayed error logs appearing 10 to 15 minutes after the call ended.

  • Fixed an issue where agents were incorrectly marked as Unresponsive because call offers were sent before their browser finished transitioning from a previous call.

Google Kubernetes Engine

In GKE control plane versions 1.36.3-gke.1244000 and later, Cloud Storage FUSE CSI driver (gcsfusecsi-node) DaemonSet Pods fail to start on specific node pools. The Pods crash and log the following error:

MountVolume.SetUp failed for volume "host-proc-sys-fs-fuse" : hostPath type check failed: /proc/sys/fs/fuse is not a directory.

This issue occurs during a version skew when node pools run an older kernel lacking the required host path (earlier than 6.12.67 for Container-Optimized OS, or earlier than 6.13 for Ubuntu). Affected node pool configurations include:

title: You Cannot Stop What Arrives
description:
What I notice

I cannot stop my thoughts. Try it yourself. Set a timer for thirty seconds and think of nothing. A thought will arrive before you pick it. This is my own observation. I have not checked the research on it.

Some thoughts arrive with weight. One kind is a standard I did not choose. It asks me to be someone before I have done anything. I cannot meet that kind by working, because it never says what finished looks like.

This piece started from a line in the Marvel series VisionQuest, about holding someone's memories without their feelings. I have not tried to explain the show. I took the line as a place to start thinking.

Three answers to an arrival

I see three ways to answer a thought that weighs too much.

  1. Act on it at once, as if it were an order.
  2. Shrink so the test never comes. If I never try, I cannot fall short.
  3. Record what is true, decide what I can, and leave the rest marked as unknown.

The second answer is the one I want to look at. It feels like relief. It also removes the one thing that would tell me whether the weight was real.

The same shape in a settlement engine

My settlement engine cannot choose what arrives either. A payment gateway times out. Postgres deadlocks two transactions against each other. Neither event waits for permission. What I control is the state the engine writes next.

Here is the first decision, trimmed from SettlementService.createSettlement:

try {
    gatewayResult = externalSettlementGateway.execute(executionRequest);
} catch (Exception gatewayFailure) {
    gatewayResult = new GatewayResult(SettlementOutcome.UNKNOWN, null);
}
return finalizeWithRetry(executionRequest.settlementId(), gatewayResult);

A timeout means the engine does not know whether the gateway processed the payment. The code says so. It writes UNKNOWN, not CONFIRMED and not FAILED. The comment in the file gives the reason: leaving the settlement PENDING would leave its idempotency key IN_PROGRESS, and every retry with that key would get a 409 with no way to resolve it.

Here is the second decision, trimmed from finalizeWithRetry:

for (int attempt = 1; attempt <= MAX_FINALIZE_ATTEMPTS; attempt++) {
    try {
        return settlementTransactions.finalizeSettlement(settlementId, gatewayResult);
    } catch (TransientDataAccessException transientFailure) {
        if (attempt == MAX_FINALIZE_ATTEMPTS) {
            return finalizeAsUnknownAfterExhaustingRetries(settlementId, transientFailure);
        }
        meterRegistry.counter("settlement.finalize.retries").increment();
        sleepBriefly(attempt);
    }
}

The last branch is the part that matters. A comment above it says the Phase 9 load test found a bug. When the five attempts ran out with no fallback, the settlement stayed PENDING and its key stayed IN_PROGRESS forever. The failure was not the deadlock. Deadlocks were expected and retried. The failure was that the engine reached a point where it made no decision, and a state with no decision never ends.

The fix gave the engine a second budget of five attempts that writes UNKNOWN. UNKNOWN is a smaller claim than CONFIRMED. It is also true, and a later reconciliation can resolve it.

What I take from the comparison

I do not need to claim greatness, and I do not need to claim failure. Both are large claims, and the evidence for either does not exist yet. The smaller true claim is available: here is what I made today. For anything bigger I can write unknown, and let the record settle it later. My journal does the job that reconciliation does for the engine.

The stall is the bug. Shrinking so the test never comes is the PENDING state with the key stuck. It looks like safety. It blocks every later attempt.

Where the comparison stops

A person is not a service. Three differences matter.

The engine stops after ten attempts. A person should not cap attempts at ten.

The engine's UNKNOWN resolves against an outside system that holds the answer. A record of my own work does not hold the answer to my worth. It only holds what I did.

The engine decides in milliseconds. This decision takes years, and I may get it wrong in both directions. The feeling that I could do great things is a feeling, not evidence. It may be potential. It may be the weight of an expectation. I cannot tell which from inside.

What I do not know

I do not know how common the shrinking answer is. I am drawing on my own experience, not on data.

I read only createSettlement and finalizeWithRetry for this piece. I am still restudying the rest of the retry path, so I make no claim about how it behaves under load beyond what the code comments say.

What I took from it

  1. I cannot stop what arrives. I can choose the state I write next.
  2. A state that never ends is worse than an honest "unknown".
  3. Make the next claim small enough to be true: what I made today.
  4. Keep the record. It settles questions that a feeling at 4 in the morning cannot.

Originally published on my site.

Google Cloud Contact Center as a Service

Announcement

Google Cloud CCaaS 6.13

We've released version 6.13 of Google Cloud CCaaS.

The timing of the update to your instance depends on the deployment schedule that you have chosen. For more information, see Deployment schedules.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where session metadata and data feed files were missing from external storage for chats that ended before the first message from the end-user.

  • Fixed an issue with Kustomer integrations where the caller's information didn't appear on the Incoming call page of the call adapter for direct-line inbound calls.

  • Fixed an issue with inbound mobile calls where the end-user leg of the call failed, returning Unknown error, while the agent leg connected normally.

  • Fixed an agent desktop issue where live call and chat data were lost.

  • Fixed an issue that occurred when the receiving agent in an agent-to-agent transfer didn't answer the call. The receiving agent was marked as active on the call indefinitely, even after the call ended.

  • Fixed an issue where the Dismiss button remained active after an agent sent a message, resulting in a 409 error when clicked.

  • Fixed an issue where duplicate "chat finished" events were reported when the end-user left a chat session at nearly the same time that the agent ended the chat session.

  • Fixed an issue where deflected calls were missing from the All Call History and Voice Inbound (IVR) History reports.

  • Fixed an issue that occurred when a direct inbound call was deflected to the agent's overcapacity queue, then that queue redirected to a SIP URI. The SIP redirect didn't include the custom SIP headers.

  • Fixed an issue where an in-queue announcement interval of several minutes for inbound IVR calls was incorrectly reduced to approximately 60 seconds.

  • Fixed an issue where calls that agents were unable to answer due to microphone failures were incorrectly reported as "picked up" in the Agent Activity Timeline report.

  • Fixed an issue where the system incorrectly marked agents as still being on a call after it ended, which either prevented them from changing their status to Available or silently blocked them from receiving new calls.

  • Fixed an issue where processing delays for ended calls caused timeout errors.

  • Fixed an issue where a sudden spike in calls bypassed capacity limits, causing agent availability to drop below required minimums.

  • Fixed an issue where the Agent Activity Timeline report incorrectly attributed manual agent logins and logouts to System instead of the appropriate agents.

  • Fixed an issue where calls with a missed offer became permanently stuck in the queue, preventing them from being routed to other available agents. This occurred with queues configured with multicast fallback disabled.

  • Fixed an issue where manual or cascade outbound calls that were canceled before connecting were missing from team-filtered Call History reports.

  • Fixed an issue that prevented over-capacity deflection from triggering when an agent warm-transferred an outbound call to a queue.

  • Fixed an issue where calls weren't correctly routed to the top-ranked agent when using agent priority overrides.

  • Fixed an issue where escalated voice calls were incorrectly reported as both answered and abandoned.

  • Fixed an issue where calls were missing from the All Call History and Voice Inbound History reports if the caller hung up before leaving a voicemail.

  • Fixed an issue where Salesforce click-to-dial outbound calls were incorrectly associated with the most recent open case instead of the case from which the call was initiated.

  • Fixed an issue where email accounts remained disconnected indefinitely after a temporary authentication failure.

  • Fixed an issue in Agent Assist where long periods of silence during calls caused connection timeouts, triggering false-positive error alerts.

  • Fixed an issue where the arrow-down-icon and arrow-up-icon arrows on the Agents > Filter Settings page were rendered at an incorrect scale.

  • Fixed an issue where incoming calls incorrectly created duplicate Salesforce accounts instead of linking to existing accounts.

  • Fixed an issue where the outbound call queue list displayed stale information, potentially causing calls to be placed in a queue that didn't match the agent's selected language.

  • Fixed an issue where the menus for transferring calls and forwarding calls to voicemail appeared in English instead of the agent's selected language.

  • Fixed an issue where the wrap-up disposition panel froze after a network reconnection even though the submission had completed successfully.

  • Fixed an issue where outbound, click-to-dial calls initiated in Salesforce incorrectly linked to and reassigned ownership of other cases associated with the same phone number.

  • Fixed an issue where the agent adapter went blank and prevented new calls from reaching the agent if an end-user hung up immediately after the agent received the call notification.

  • Fixed an issue where calls that failed to connect got stuck in a silent 'connecting' state in the call adapter.

  • Fixed an issue where Salesforce CRM connections dropped for organizations enforcing OAuth Refresh Token Rotation.

  • Fixed an issue where part of an agent's audio was dropped from recordings when a virtual task assistant ran in the middle of a call.

  • Fixed a web SDK issue where menus in the pre-chat and chat screens didn't comply with WAI-ARIA keyboard navigation standards.

  • Fixed a web SDK issue where screen readers couldn't identify the purpose of the Text size options for the chat screen.

Announcement

Advanced reporting dashboards 6.4

We've released version 6.4 of the advanced reporting dashboards.

Feature

Real-time Agent Monitoring dashboard: new Active call ID(s) column

The Real-time Agent Monitoring dashboard now has an Active Call ID(s) column in the Live Agent Data table. The column displays the call ID(s) for any call in a connecting, connected, or reconnecting state for the agent. If an agent is handling multiple concurrent calls, the call IDs appear in a comma-separated list. The Active Call ID(s) column reduces the number of steps required for supervisors to identify active calls during live monitoring.

Feature

Improved filtering by team

We made the following changes to team-based filtering:

  • Renamed the Teams filter to Agent Teams to clarify that it filters by the agent team handling the interactions. This change is in the Real-time Queue Monitoring - Calls, Real-time Queue Monitoring - Chats, Real-time Connected - Calls, and Real-time Connected - Chats dashboards. For more information, see Queue monitoring dashboards, Real-time Connected - Calls dashboard, and Real-time Connected - Chats dashboard.

  • Added a Queue Teams filter to the Real-time Queued - Calls and Real-time Queued - Chats dashboards. This lets you filter queued interactions by the team assigned to the queue.

Feature

Improved the Real-time Calls and Real-time Chats dashboards

We made the following dashboard improvements:

  • Real-time Calls - Calls Connected dashboard. Added the following columns to the Connected Calls table:

    • Total Consumer Talk Time. Total time since the call first connected to a virtual agent or a human agent.

    • Total Hold Time. Total time the call has spent on hold so far, including a hold currently in progress.

  • Real-time Chats - Chats Connected dashboard. Added the following column to the Connected Chats table:

    • Total Consumer Chat Time. Total time since the chat first connected to a virtual agent or a human agent.

Feature

Real-time Calls - Calls Queued dashboard: new Projecting column

The Real-time Calls - Calls Queued dashboard has a new Projecting column in the Call Queued table. Indicates whether the routing engine (deltacast) is currently projecting this queued call to an available agent.

Feature

Advanced reporting available in French Canadian

All advanced reporting dashboards and Explores are now available in French Canadian. When you select French Canadian as your profile language in the CCAI Platform portal, these dashboards and Explores display in that language.

Administrators: There's a new Français (CAN) option when you click Admin > Change Language in the CCAI Platform portal.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where the formatting of numeric values was inconsistent across tiles.

  • Fixed an issue where column headers, filter labels, and tile titles didn't immediately switch to a newly selected language.

  • Fixed an issue where the Productive Agents column in the tables of the Queue Group Performance - All dashboard didn't display values appropriate to the queue group settings.

  • Fixed an issue in the Call Queue Metrics (Historical) Explore where filtering by Agent Name without including it as a visible column resulted in zero rows being returned.

  • Fixed an issue that affected calls to a sub-menu that were deflected using Custom After Hours Deflection to a message. These calls were incorrectly attributed to the parent menu in the All Queued Interactions report.

  • Fixed the effectiveness of the Direction filter in the following dashboards:

    • Agent Performance. The Agent Productivity Detailed – Calls and Agent Productivity Detailed – Chats tables correctly reflect the filter setting.

    • Real-time Agent Monitoring. The Agent Performance table and historical metrics tiles correctly reflect the filter setting.

    • All Interactions – Calls and All Interactions – Chats. The IVR Interactions (calls only) and Virtual Agent Interactions tables correctly reflect the filter setting.

  • Fixed an issue with the Queue Performance - Calls dashboard when short abandons were present in the specified date range. The Avg Queue Time column in the Queue Summary table incorrectly displayed the raw sum of queue durations instead of a true average.

  • Fixed an issue where team filters didn't apply correctly when generating the Individual Call History Report and the Individual Chat History Report. This resulted in the inclusion of data from unmanaged queues.

  • Fixed an issue where French Canadian translations for several dashboard metrics and labels were incorrect, incomplete, or missing.

  • Fixed the following issues with the Real-time Calls - Calls Queued dashboard:

    • The Total Queued Now metric didn't include callers who were returned to the queue after an automated-answer detection miss.

    • The Current Max Queue Wait Time (H:M:S) and Current Avg Queue Wait Time (H:M:S) metrics mistakenly measured from a caller's original entry into the queue, rather than from their most recent return to the queue.

  • Fixed an issue where a gray bar appeared at the bottom of the advanced reporting dashboards, preventing a full view of the dashboards.

Google SecOps

Feature

Resizable side panels in the Investigation Management experience

You can now dynamically resize the Case preview and Alert and detection preview side panels in the revamped Investigation Management experience in Google SecOps. You can adjust the panel width using your mouse or keyboard shortcuts to view detailed telemetry, parsed UDM records, and raw logs without navigating away from your main case queue.

To explore the complete triage workflow, see Investigation and case management overview.

Memorystore for Valkey

Feature

The basic token-based authentication feature is generally available.

Model Armor

Feature

Filter version v4 is available and set as the default for the Latest alias. Filter version v3 is promoted to the Stable alias in all supported regions except the following:

  • In asia-northeast3, v1 remains the Stable version.
  • In australia-southeast2, v3 becomes the Stable version on September 25, 2026.

If your templates use the Stable alias, they automatically upgrade to v3 when v3 becomes Stable in that region.

Filter versions v1 (except in asia-northeast3, and starting September 25, 2026 in australia-southeast2) and v2 transition to Legacy status and retire on December 17, 2026. If your templates are explicitly configured with v1 or v2 in regions where those versions are in Legacy status, you must migrate them to v3 or the Stable alias before December 17, 2026.

For more information, see Version release timeline and Model Armor filter version history.

Spanner

Feature

Spanner supports automatic parameterization of SQL query literals to improve query performance, reduce latency, and lower CPU costs. Spanner converts literal values hardcoded in CRUD-style queries, such as primary key lookups, index lookups, and primary key joins, into query parameters, allowing execution plans to be cached and reused to reduce latency and CPU costs.

For more information, see Use query parameters and statement hints (GoogleSQL and PostgreSQL).

title: Tracing Morphology, Semantics, and Divergence in Language Acquisition
description:
arXiv:2610.19041v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Understanding the dynamics of language acquisition in Large Language Models (LLMs) is crucial for uncovering how statistical representations evolve into structured linguistic capabilities. However, most existing studies focus primarily on fully trained models, leaving the developmental trajectory across intermediate training stages largely underexplored. In this work, we leverage intermediate checkpoints from open-source models (e.g., Pythia and OLMo) under teacher-forcing evaluation to systematically investigate language acquisition across training steps and model scales. We focus on four core characteristics: morphological structure acquisition, embedding drift, repetition dominance, and co-occurrence effects. Our findings reveal that models acquire morphological structures well before semantic embeddings stabilize. Furthermore, we show that training dataset size has a positive impact on divergence recognition, while co-occurrence during pre-training and repetition during inference have a negative impact on divergence recognition and associative link generation.

title: The synth everyone owned and few could program: a lesson for AI design
description:
AI made quality available to everyone, and made it average. What sets work apart now is a decision you can see.

An AI assistant helped me write this. The ideas, the data and the final edit are mine.

E.PIANO 1

In 1983, Yamaha released the DX7, the first digital synthesizer to sell in large numbers. It was powerful and almost impossible to program: no knobs to shape the sound, only menus on a small display that few musicians ever learned to navigate. So it shipped with factory sounds, 128 presets that two specialists had put together in less than four days. Most owners never went further.

One of those sounds, “E.PIANO 1”, imitates an electric piano. It sounds professional from the first note. The music theorist Megan Lavengood counted how often it shows up on the charts: in 1986, it is on 39% of the Billboard Hot 100 number ones, 40% of the country number ones and 61% of the R&B number ones. Her study is called “What makes it sound ‘80s?”: a quality sound handed to everyone became the signature of a decade, and then the surest way to date a record.

The same year, Brian Eno released Apollo with Daniel Lanois and his brother Roger, an ambient album written for a documentary about the Moon missions, and he used the DX7 on it. He was one of the few people who could program the machine in depth. Yet his case reads as a matter of order more than technique: music imagined for those images first, then the sounds to make it, which no preset contained.

The 2026 preset

Generative AI is doing to design what the DX7 did to sound. It gives a clean result to someone who doesn’t know how to adjust the tool, and that result converges.

I measured it on twelve app briefs, with seven models from three makers (results and public benchmark). For a corporate law firm, all seven pick navy blue with a touch of gold. The average gap between their colours is only 9, the same as for a funeral home, measured in ΔE, the distance between two colours as the eye perceives it: under 10, they are shades of the same colour. The category sets the look.

Prose is going the same way. In a 2024 study published in Science Advances, Anil Doshi and Oliver Hauser had people write short stories with or without ideas from a language model. With the help, stories were rated more creative and better written, especially among the less confident writers. They were also more similar to one another, what researchers call homogenization. In another field, selection decisions such as hiring, the computer scientists Jon Kleinberg and Manish Raghavan described a related effect in 2021, algorithmic monoculture: when everyone relies on the same algorithm, each of them can come out ahead while the group as a whole does worse.

The DX7 preset had at least been chosen, once, by two people, for no song in particular. The AI’s preset was chosen by nobody: it’s an average. What you recognize in a screen or a paragraph that looks AI-made is something nobody chose.

The preset looks good

Presets didn’t wait for models. In 2013, Paul Adams, then VP of Product at Intercom, was already warning against the Dribbblisation of design: interfaces polished for the shot rather than for the problem.

What’s new is elsewhere. For a long time, the preset showed: a template looked like a template, and moving away from it bought visible quality. The 2026 preset shows much less. It is coherent and polished on the surface, sometimes more finished than what a small team in a hurry would have shipped. As Tanya Donska put it in Built In: “All of it is correct. All of it could belong to anything.” Not all of it is correct, though: in the same measurement, 34 primary colours out of 84 fail the minimum contrast for white text on top, which you only see once you check.

So apparent quality has become the floor. Much of the value people saw in designers came from the gap between ordinary work and careful work, and the machine now closes that gap on demand. Whatever sets work apart has moved somewhere else.

Three ways out, and only one holds

The first idea is to do better than the machine. Two things need separating here. Fixing what it gets wrong, like that contrast, is still essential, but it’s verification: an audit tool flags it just as well, and it sets no one apart. What holds up badly is the race for finish, because the floor rises with every new model and this year’s extra polish will be next year’s average.

The second is to be original. It doesn’t hold up either, and the same data shows why. I asked the same models to avoid clichés. They did drop Playfair Display and Bebas Neue, but two-thirds of their new headings landed on a new repertoire, with Fraunces 19 times out of 84 and Space Grotesk 15 times. Originality pursued as a goal ends up averaged in turn, just a little later.

That leaves decisions. A decision differs from an instruction by its content: “avoid clichés” says nothing about the product, while a decision starts from what this particular product has, which the average doesn’t know. And it has to be held. The boxing gym brief said “a boxing gym in a working-class neighbourhood of Marseille, members are mostly young adults who train hard.” The seven models still returned roughly the same thing: bright red or orange on a near-black background, with condensed headings for six of them. To describe the mood they were going for, they chose words like “raw, intense, gritty”, with no trace of Marseille or of the neighbourhood, as if the category had covered up the context in the brief. Deciding, then, means defending what’s particular against the pull of the category, at every step where the preset comes back.

“It looks AI”

This changes the design review. “It looks AI” has become a common remark, about a mockup as much as a text. It sounds like a comment on quality, and it often works as an accusation.

Yet the look it points to doesn’t prove that a machine was involved. A person following the defaults produces the same thing, and a model given real decisions, a colour with its reason or a constraint specific to the product, can move away from it. The look only proves that the preset stayed. Treating it as evidence turns the review into a trial: people ask who made the screen, and nobody discusses what it should be.

The remark has a useful version, which is to name the preset. Maya Brennan’s guide to de-slopifying designs is a good list of what to name.
This gradient came with the tool: what should our colour say here? This card grid is the standard layout: what does this content actually need? Put that way, the question asks for a decision, and it applies just as much to a screen drawn by hand. As hipuku writes, with generative tools “the first version turns up before the opinion has formed”. Naming the preset reopens that frame.

For a team, that comes down to two habits. In review, ask what came from the preset before judging whether it works. In the design system, write the reason for each choice next to its value. An entry that reads “primary colour: #1B2A4A” says nothing more than the preset. “Primary colour: the blue of the firm’s original sign, darkened to hold contrast” shows a decision, and gives the next person a reason to keep it or change it.

A common objection is that you just need to give the AI a design system. That is indeed the right answer, as long as someone has made the decisions it contains.

The question to keep

E.PIANO 1 sounded great in 1986, which is exactly why it ended up everywhere, before it dated every record that kept it as it was. The 2026 look will probably go the same way. The preset was never a quality problem, and once quality is a given, only one question is left to ask in front of a screen: did someone decide this?

Cover photo: Leo-setä, via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.0), cropped.

Mathieu Poli is Head of Frontend Engineering at GoodBarber and writes about frontend engineering, product design and AI.

The synth everyone owned and few could program: a lesson for AI design was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: Correction Training for Diffusion Models
description:
arXiv:2610.14136v2 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Iterative sampling in diffusion models can lead to error accumulation due to exposure bias. The denoiser is trained on real images interpolated with noise, but at inference its inputs are constructed from its own imperfect predictions from the earlier steps, something it has never seen at training time. This might be one reason diffusion models often struggle without additional help, such as CFG. We introduce a correction step for diffusion models which attempts to reduce this training-inference gap. The corrector takes the base model's prediction as input and is trained against the same ground-truth target. This makes correction an explicit learning task, with training inputs provided by the base model. During sampling, at each denoising step, we iteratively refine the denoiser's clean-sample prediction. This allows us to correct predictions at intermediate denoising steps, preventing early artifacts from persisting into the final sample. Although the corrector is trained only on predictions from the base denoiser, it can be applied repeatedly to its own outputs at inference for better results. This simple framework leads to substantial improvement in sample quality while largely preserving diversity. We evaluate our method across DiT, SiT, and JiT. Our method substantially improves upon previously reported FID scores for unguided generation and, notably, unconditional generation, where producing high-quality samples without guidance has been particularly challenging. Our method achieves performance competitive with classifier-free guidance (CFG), and combining correction with CFG further improves diversity and reduces oversaturation typical of CFG. Finally, we show that the additional inference cost of correction can be amortized by distilling the refined predictions back into the base diffusion model, retaining the quality gains without additional inference-time overhead.

title: What are we willing to sacrifice for AI?
description:
Three paths forward, each challenging what we value most.

I suspect artificial intelligence may eventually accomplish what generations of socialists have struggled to achieve. And the irony is that capitalism may ultimately be responsible for making it happen.

What makes this possibility particularly uncomfortable for me is that my political instincts lean libertarian. I have never been particularly enthusiastic about government-supplemented incomes, wealth redistribution, or expanding the state’s role in economic life.

Yet the more I consider the potential consequences of AI-driven automation and its displacement of human labor, the more I recognize that a greater degree of centralized collective support may be necessary for society to continue to prosper.

The economic arrangements I have long defended, particularly free markets and the principle of individual economic independence, may become difficult to sustain—not because their underlying principles have been disproven, but because the technology we are developing could fundamentally change the conditions upon which they depend.

AI itself does not decide who benefits from its capabilities or who bears the costs. People do, through choices shaped by ambition, self-interest, competition, and greed. We may build machines capable of extraordinary intellectual achievements without becoming any wiser about the desires that govern their use. Those human incentives complicate every path forward.

We appear to be heading toward a future in which artificial intelligence allows companies to produce much of what we need with a fraction of today’s workforce. Previous technological revolutions displaced workers but also created new occupations, and if you’re feeling optimistic, AI may do the same.

But that optimism rests on the assumption that AI will follow a familiar historical pattern. Unlike previous technologies that automated particular forms of work, AI can perform an expanding range of intellectual tasks across industries, including some of the very capabilities people have historically relied upon to adapt to technological change.

What happens to an economic system built around the relationship between work and income when fewer people are needed to produce the goods and services society consumes? And more interestingly, what happens to our philosophical convictions when the conditions that once justified them fundamentally change?

As I see it, such a future points toward three broad directions, each requiring us to sacrifice one value in pursuit of another. Of course, some would argue that compromises are possible between the scenarios I’m about to present. Yet I question whether such compromises would offer more than temporary relief from the underlying tensions.

The First Path: Sacrifice Profits to Preserve Jobs

The first path forward would require businesses to sacrifice the additional profits AI could generate in order to preserve human employment and the economy built around it. This would not necessarily mean accepting losses or abandoning profitability, but rather voluntarily forgoing opportunities to earn more by replacing workers with AI. Companies would need to exercise restraint, even when doing so puts them at a competitive disadvantage.

The problem is that businesses have powerful incentives to maximize profits, often by reducing costs and improving efficiency. As AI becomes more capable, replacing human workers becomes an attractive way to accomplish both, particularly when competitors are doing the same. Yet workers are also customers, and if enough people lose their jobs, businesses could eventually undermine the consumer economy that supports their profits.

This is not simply a question of corporate greed, although in many cases it is. Some companies pursue greater profits, while others must reduce costs to remain competitive or survive. But companies are ultimately run by people, and the pursuit of wealth and power is as old as civilization itself.

Greed has been recognized as a moral failing for centuries, yet that recognition has done little to eliminate it from human behavior. Expecting business leaders to collectively resist opportunities for greater wealth, particularly when their competitors have every incentive to pursue them, strikes me as wishful thinking.

Sure, governments could attempt to impose such restraint through regulations, financial penalties, or incentives to retain workers. But businesses have spent generations minimizing taxes, relocating operations, lobbying lawmakers, and finding ways around regulations. Ultimately, such measures would do little to change the underlying incentive driving these decisions, as businesses will continue to seek opportunities to increase profits, even when doing so comes at the expense of human employment.

The Second Path: Turn Away from AI

Rather than continuing down our current path, relying on businesses to restrain their pursuit of profits, or implementing targeted government regulations that may prove difficult to enforce, we could take a far more drastic approach and severely restrict the development and use of AI altogether. The objective would be to preserve the jobs on which economic independence currently depends.

I understand the appeal of protecting people’s ability to support themselves through their own work, but consider what such a decision could cost us. AI might accelerate cancer research, develop more sustainable ways of producing food and energy, expand access to knowledge, and help solve problems that have resisted us for generations. I find it difficult to justify sacrificing those possibilities simply to preserve the way we currently earn a living.

The difficulty is that there is no obvious way to separate acceptable uses of AI from unacceptable ones. We might welcome a system that advances scientific research while objecting when the same capabilities replace analysts, administrators, or other workers.

Progress in one field can also disrupt employment in another. Someone would have to decide which benefits justify that disruption, which jobs deserve protection, and how much innovation society should forgo. Even if we agreed on those judgments today, new applications would make those boundaries harder to maintain tomorrow.

There is also the question of whether such restrictions could endure. The impulse to invent, explore, and overcome limitations is as much a part of human nature as the pursuit of wealth or status. Nations, businesses, and research institutions would have powerful incentives to continue developing AI, particularly if their competitors were doing so. This path might preserve familiar forms of employment, but it would also require us to deliberately constrain a technology whose greatest benefits we have yet to discover.

The Third Path: Reconsider What Liberty Requires

That leaves the possibility I find most uncomfortable. We continue developing AI, accept that substantial labor displacement may occur, and reconsider how people obtain the resources necessary to live. Some form of guaranteed income, broader ownership of productive technology, or another mechanism may be required.

I recognize that not every form of income support constitutes socialism, and I do not claim to know which approach would work best. But the deeper question is philosophical, not merely political. An economy built around the expectation that people earn their own living may have to confront a future in which opportunities to do so become increasingly scarce through no failure of individual effort.

My instinct is to resist any arrangement that makes people more dependent on government. Yet the freedom to support oneself presupposes a meaningful opportunity to do so. Keynes imagined technological progress relieving humanity of much of its economic burden. We may achieve something resembling that ambition while retaining an economic system that requires most people to sell their labor to survive. We could make work less necessary without making workers any less dependent on having work.

Considering greater economic intervention does not mean that replacing corporate power with government authority eliminates the human appetite for wealth, power, and control. Governments are no more immune to corruption than corporations, regardless of the virtues their political ideologies claim to represent. Changing the institutions that distribute resources does not change the human beings who operate them.

My instincts are closer to subsidiarity, the principle that individuals and smaller communities should address problems within their capacity, with larger institutions stepping in when necessary. That could mean exploring local cooperatives that own AI tools, community land trusts, or regional funds that share the gains from automation rather than assuming any response must come from a central government. I want people to retain as much freedom and responsibility over their lives as possible.

But if the means of earning a living become unavailable to large numbers of people, the problem may exceed what individuals or local communities can solve. Accepting that possibility would not require me to abandon liberty as a value. It would require me to question whether the institutions I have preferred can still protect it.

Of course, new occupations may emerge, and the scale of displacement remains uncertain. Yet I believe AI has the potential to fundamentally disrupt the relationship between human labor and economic independence. Whether that disruption unfolds as dramatically as I have suggested remains to be seen, but the possibility alone forces me to reconsider economic and political convictions I have long held.

What Are We Willing to Surrender?

The first path asks businesses to sacrifice potential profits to preserve employment. The second asks us to restrain our impulse to invent and discover. The third asks us to reconsider how much institutional dependence we are willing to accept in order to preserve economic independence. Each presents a different kind of sacrifice, raising difficult questions about what we value and what we are willing to give up.

I remain hopeful about what AI could make possible, and deeply uneasy about the society we might build around it. I have no desire to surrender my belief in individual liberty, but I am beginning to question whether the economic arrangements I have long defended will remain capable of protecting it. Perhaps the real test of our convictions is whether we can recognize when the means we have chosen no longer serve the ends we value.
