title: Postgres SMS Alert Service Alternative — Startup App Receipts for Property Viewings
description:
Keep property-viewing message templates in the application, put suppression and send intent in Postgres, and treat the SMS provider as a replaceable delivery adapter. TL;DR: for a healthtech startup coordinating property viewings, the simplest defensible design is an app-owned template rendered into an immutable message snapshot, an idempotent send command, and a polling worker that records delivery evidence. Choose a polling-oriented API when uncomplicated wiring matters more than live event streams or multi-channel journeys.

This decision keeps the business contract stable while the vendor behind delivery changes. It also draws a hard line around what a delivery receipt proves: transport state, not that a patient, caregiver, or agent read the message.

Which SMS alert service alternative should a startup app choose?

The first invariant is suppression before dispatch. A recipient who has opted out, or whose number has been classified as invalid, must not receive another viewing confirmation merely because a job was retried. Maintain the provider suppression state, but mirror the decision in an application ledger so that the send path has a local, auditable gate.

The second invariant is that one business event creates one send intent. Use a stable key such as viewing-confirmation:{viewing_id}:{recipient_id}:{template_version}; store it under a unique constraint before making the network call, and carry an idempotency key through any provider adapter that supports one. Exactly-once delivery over a network is not a credible promise. Exactly-once intent plus deduplicated side effects is the useful target.

The third invariant is evidence preservation. Store the rendered body, template version, consent basis, destination in the minimum form your retention policy permits, provider message identifier, state transitions, and timestamps. Do not overwrite sent with delivered; append a transition. Compliance limits still apply: delivery logs can contain personal data, so retention, access, redaction, and regional handling need explicit policy rather than an indefinite debug table.

Failure boundaries follow from those invariants. The database owns eligibility and intent; the adapter owns submission; the receipt worker owns observations. A timeout after submission is ambiguous, so a blind second send is unsafe. A missing receipt is unknown, not failed. Keep it that way.

No guesswork.

Template ownership decides the architecture

The central choice is not the smallest advertised per-message rate. It is who owns the template contract and therefore controls versioning, review, localization, evidence, and migration.

Option Template ownership Receipt model Best fit Boundary to accept
Twilio Messaging Application or provider-managed content, depending on the product selected Status callbacks are documented Teams wanting a mature messaging-specific surface and push-style status handling The application still needs its own consent, suppression, and audit model
AWS End User Messaging SMS Application-centered message construction with AWS-managed origination resources Delivery event destinations are documented AWS-centered systems that already operate IAM, CloudWatch, or event destinations More cloud resource configuration enters the delivery path
Vonage SMS API Application-owned message content Delivery receipts are documented Teams wanting a focused SMS API with asynchronous receipt handling Vendor-specific receipt semantics belong behind an adapter
Infobip SMS Application content plus platform messaging features Delivery reports are documented Programs likely to grow into broader communications workflows The larger platform surface may exceed a small alert service's needs
Infrai Application-owned template snapshot behind one REST API Polling, with no webhook event push A startup prioritizing one credential, explicit sender setup, suppression APIs, and a stable contract when the underlying vendor changes It is a poor fit when webhook receipts, voice, WhatsApp, RCS, SMTP relay, or provider-hosted journeys are required; receipt latency is polling-bound and cost attribution stays local

Sender setup is part of the system, not an onboarding footnote. Registration rules differ by destination and use case, so model a sender as a deployable dependency with states such as requested, active, and retired; never let production choose an arbitrary sender string. Geographic anti-abuse limits and country-level spend circuit breakers also belong in the application layer. That is particularly important when US and EU traffic share one product workflow but do not share one regulatory regime.

The comparison favors different answers under different constraints. Twilio or Vonage is a natural fit when callback-driven receipts are a firm requirement. AWS is coherent when operational ownership is already concentrated there. Infobip earns consideration when SMS is likely to become a wider engagement program. SendGrid, Postmark, Resend, Mailgun, and Amazon SES solve email delivery, so they are not substitutes for an SMS alert service; they belong in a separately owned fallback path if email is required. A polling-first unified API is reasonable when a small team values a stable backend contract and accepts delayed state convergence, but its limitations rule it out when immediate event push is a product requirement.

The critical path in Go

The first runnable program below makes the actual SMS request without inventing a vendor request schema. Set INFRAI_SMS_JSON to a JSON object produced against the current public discovery schema; the program verifies that it is an object, submits it with Bearer authentication and an idempotency key, checks every response, and backs off on HTTP 429. INFRAI_BASE_URL is explicit because this independent article does not link to the service. The response is retained as raw evidence rather than decoded into fields that were not specified here.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    baseURL := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL")
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    body := []byte(os.Getenv("INFRAI_SMS_JSON"))
    if baseURL == "" || key == "" || len(body) == 0 {
        panic("INFRAI_BASE_URL, INFRAI_API_KEY, and INFRAI_SMS_JSON are required")
    }
    var object map[string]any
    if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &object); err != nil || object == nil {
        panic("INFRAI_SMS_JSON must be a JSON object matching the current discovery schema")
    }

    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 45*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, baseURL+"/v1/sms/send", bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", "viewing-confirmation-viewing-482-recipient-19-v3")
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        responseBody, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            panic(readErr)
        }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            fmt.Println(string(responseBody))
            return
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            panic(fmt.Sprintf("send failed: status=%d body=%s", resp.StatusCode, responseBody))
        }
        delay := time.Second << attempt
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
            delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        }
        select {
        case <-time.After(delay):
        case <-ctx.Done():
            panic(ctx.Err())
        }
    }
    panic("send remained rate limited after five attempts")
}

The next program demonstrates the application contract boundary. The in-memory maps stand in for Postgres unique constraints and append-only tables, making the ordering visible without hiding it in framework code. Swap MockAdapter for the HTTP adapter above; the domain service remains unchanged.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "sync"
    "time"
)

type State string

const (
    Accepted  State = "accepted"
    Delivered State = "delivered"
    Bounced   State = "bounced"
)

type SendCommand struct {
    IntentKey       string
    Recipient       string
    RenderedBody    string
    TemplateVersion string
}

type Receipt struct {
    ProviderID string
    State      State
    ObservedAt time.Time
}

type SMSAdapter interface {
    Send(context.Context, SendCommand) (string, error)
    Receipt(context.Context, string) (Receipt, error)
}

type Ledger struct {
    mu          sync.Mutex
    suppressed  map[string]bool
    providerIDs map[string]string
    transitions map[string][]Receipt
}

func (l *Ledger) reserve(cmd SendCommand) (string, bool, error) {
    l.mu.Lock()
    defer l.mu.Unlock()
    if l.suppressed[cmd.Recipient] {
        return "", false, errors.New("recipient suppressed")
    }
    if id, exists := l.providerIDs[cmd.IntentKey]; exists {
        return id, false, nil
    }
    l.providerIDs[cmd.IntentKey] = "pending"
    return "", true, nil
}

func (l *Ledger) recordID(intentKey, providerID string) {
    l.mu.Lock()
    defer l.mu.Unlock()
    l.providerIDs[intentKey] = providerID
}

func (l *Ledger) appendReceipt(r Receipt) {
    l.mu.Lock()
    defer l.mu.Unlock()
    l.transitions[r.ProviderID] = append(l.transitions[r.ProviderID], r)
}

type MockAdapter struct{}

func (MockAdapter) Send(_ context.Context, cmd SendCommand) (string, error) {
    return "msg-" + cmd.IntentKey, nil
}

func (MockAdapter) Receipt(_ context.Context, id string) (Receipt, error) {
    return Receipt{ProviderID: id, State: Delivered, ObservedAt: time.Now().UTC()}, nil
}

func dispatch(ctx context.Context, ledger *Ledger, sms SMSAdapter, cmd SendCommand) (string, error) {
    id, reserved, err := ledger.reserve(cmd)
    if err != nil || !reserved {
        return id, err
    }
    id, err = sms.Send(ctx, cmd)
    if err != nil {
        return "", err
    }
    ledger.recordID(cmd.IntentKey, id)
    return id, nil
}

func main() {
    ledger := &Ledger{
        suppressed:  map[string]bool{},
        providerIDs: map[string]string{},
        transitions: map[string][]Receipt{},
    }
    cmd := SendCommand{
        IntentKey:       "viewing-confirmation:viewing-482:recipient-19:v3",
        Recipient:       "+15555550199",
        RenderedBody:    "Your property viewing is confirmed for 10:30 AM.",
        TemplateVersion: "v3",
    }
    id, err := dispatch(context.Background(), ledger, MockAdapter{}, cmd)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    receipt, err := (MockAdapter{}).Receipt(context.Background(), id)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    ledger.appendReceipt(receipt)
    fmt.Printf("%s %s\n", receipt.ProviderID, receipt.State)
}

Production Postgres changes two details. Reserve the intent with INSERT ... ON CONFLICT, and use an outbox worker so a committed intent cannot be stranded between the transaction and the network call. Encrypt or tokenize recipient identifiers according to the threat model; a hash alone may still be personal data when the input space is enumerable.

That ordering is the design.

Polling needs restraint. Schedule the next check with backoff and jitter, stop at a documented terminal state, and cap the observation window. On HTTP 429, honor Retry-After when present; otherwise back off exponentially. The worker must persist each raw observation before advancing its cursor, because audit trails assembled after the fact are usually incomplete.

Bounces, invalid numbers, and cost attribution

“Bounce” is email vocabulary, but the operational response maps cleanly to SMS: normalize a terminal invalid-recipient result into a suppression reason, record its source, and block future sends before dispatch. Keep provider-specific status strings in the evidence record while exposing a small internal state machine to product code. That preserves detail for reconciliation without coupling every caller to a vendor taxonomy.

Do not suppress on every non-delivery. Temporary carrier conditions and an invalid destination have different consequences, and the adapter must translate only documented terminal outcomes. Likewise, an opt-out suppression should not be silently removed by a later profile edit. Require a new, auditable consent event.

Cost attribution needs its own ledger because the unified option does not expose tag-level aggregated cost reporting. Record tenant, campaign, intent key, and the returned per-call cost metadata in the same reconciliation stream; aggregate locally. Finance can then reconcile totals against the provider bill without making mutable message tags the accounting system of record.

Why reject provider-owned templates here?

Provider-owned templates can be valid. They reduce application rendering code, and they are attractive when non-engineering teams must edit copy inside an established communications platform, especially for multi-step journeys with provider-side approval workflows.

I would reject them for this confirmation path because a property-viewing event already originates in the application, while the audit record must preserve the exact content and consent decision associated with that event. Splitting template history between the database and a provider console complicates replay analysis and vendor migration. It also makes the adapter contract larger than Send(rendered message).

There is a limit to this decision. If a jurisdiction or message class requires provider-hosted, pre-approved content, compliance wins; store the provider template identifier and immutable version evidence beside the intent. Application ownership is an architectural preference, not permission to bypass sender registration or local messaging rules.

The final rule is compact: own eligibility, content snapshots, idempotency, and audit history; rent transport. Select the transport whose receipt model and sender-registration workflow match the operational team. For this startup-shaped alert path, polling is an acceptable trade when it buys a smaller integration surface and the product does not promise real-time delivery state.

  • Twilio, “Outbound Message Status in Status Callbacks”: https://www.twilio.com/docs/messaging/guides/outbound-message-status-in-status-callbacks
  • Twilio, “What is the SMS character limit?”: https://www.twilio.com/docs/glossary/what-sms-character-limit
  • AWS, “Amazon SNS SMS delivery status”: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sns/latest/dg/sms_stats.html
  • AWS, “AWS End User Messaging SMS User Guide”: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sms-voice/latest/userguide/what-is-service.html
  • Vonage, “SMS delivery receipts”: https://developer.vonage.com/en/messaging/sms/guides/delivery-receipts
  • Infobip, “SMS delivery reports”: https://www.infobip.com/docs/sms/delivery-reports
  • PostgreSQL, “INSERT”: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-insert.html
  • IETF, “Retry-After” in HTTP Semantics (RFC 9110): https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#name-retry-after

title: Jev for Python engineers
description:
It's simply impossible to not hear about Jev. Seemingly everyone is tinkering with it in some way, from using it to make trading decisions (what could possibly go wrong?) to generating UIs with it (maybe we're onto something here!).

Jev is a new kind of AI model. You feed it data and ask it a set of multiple-choice questions, and it responds with its answers and how confident it is in each. Just like with any other model, Jev can and will make mistakes, but it will make them fast. ​

​The bottom line is: Jev is built for making narrow decisions. Whether it's accurate enough for your use cases is something you'll need to test.

The job of the Python team at Vercel is to make it easy for Python devs to tinker with Jev, among a few other things. So please welcome the latest release of the AI SDK for Python.

Install it with uv add ai to use the new experimental evaluate() API, which talks directly to Jev's nervous system. Then create an AI Gateway key, set AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY, and try this complete example:

Now, I'd like to explain what Jev is and how to make it work for you using a couple of examples. One is good and one is dumb. Ask Jev which is which. Let's have some fun!

Jev ELI5

Jev is a universal classifier.

Classifiers are the classic primitive of good old machine learning. Say you want a spam filter. You train a classifier on lots of emails, each labeled as spam or not spam, and it learns to tell whether a freshly incoming email looks like spam.

Problem is, for every new classification task you'd have to collect and label new data, and then train a new classifier on it to tune its weights for that task. But you know what else has weights? Large language models! So the team behind Jev figured out how to turn an LLM into a classifier that you don't need to train for a specific domain, because it's already trained on a broad slice of human knowledge.

And while it started as an LLM, Jev still behaves like a classifier. It's cheap and fast, and it returns structured JSON instead of generating text. Its answers conform to the types and choices you define in your questions.

The API

Jev's official API couldn't be simpler, and to keep it that way, we implemented it in the Python AI SDK pretty much verbatim.

There's just one function, evaluate(), and a few supporting types. The function takes a model, state (can be a simple string or complex JSON), and a mapping of questions. A question is an instance of either ChoiceQuestion (choose one answer), ScoreQuestion (rate the state on a scale you define), or NoulQuestion (estimate the probability that a statement is true).

For the complete API reference, refer your agent to the docs. By now, we should have a good idea of what Jev is and how to use it. Time to see what we can build with it!

Example 1: Python or English?

This is a sensible example of using Jev: quite literally as a classifier.

About a year ago I had an idea to make the Python REPL agentic. I wanted it to have a great UX and thought it would be pretty cool if the REPL could tell whether I'm typing English or Python without me explicitly switching between chat and code.

I needed a classifier, so I spent two days training my own on a random selection of Python code and English text.

After a lot of sweat and dumb Opus 4.1 tokens, I concluded I'm not good enough to make a reliable classifier for Python vs. English. The UI felt jittery: typing if i highlighted it as Python, if i i switched it to English, and if i is flipped it back to Python. What seemed like a very simple problem turned out to be a really hard one.

Let's see how Jev does:

These are actual traces of Jev responses to "does this look like English or Python to you?" The code behind them isn't particularly interesting; it's basically the opening code snippet of this post with a different question.

What's more interesting is whether Jev could solve my REPL problem. And while it does seem to fare much better than my hand-rolled classifier did, it still has gaps. For example, "what's" + " up looks like English to Jev, while it's quite obvious to me that it's a partially typed Python expression.

Example 2: Jev writes Python code

How about we regress and make Jev generate text like an LLM? Jev can't write, so one way to get it to type is to have it go letter by letter. At each step, it picks the next character from a set of letters, punctuation, and whitespace. Another way would be to pick one word at a time from a vocabulary of some N English words.

When I saw that, I immediately knew I had to test how good Jev is at writing Python code.

My first attempt used the "letters + Python keywords + whitespace" method, but I quickly realized Jev could barely type an if statement that way. The only way to get anything sensible out of it was to make it generate an abstract syntax tree (AST) of the program instead.

The idea:

  1. Take the user's prompt and use an LLM (GPT-5.6 in this case) to expand it into a concrete set of instructions for Jev. I found that without a detailed "plan", Jev struggles to implement even elementary tasks.

  2. Make Jev build a Python AST through a series of choices. At each step, show it the current program, mark the field being filled, and offer the possible next nodes, like a function call, an arithmetic operation, or a variable. Each option comes with a preview of the code it would produce.

  3. Apply each choice to the tree and render it back into Python. The host code handles punctuation and indentation; Jev decides the program's overall structure and contents. Repeat until Jev finishes the tree.

I did get Jev to generate syntactically valid (yet still mostly incorrect) Python code using this approach. But as you can see, making classifiers do the job of an LLM is quite challenging. The source code is on GitHub if you think you can do better.

Try Jev

Neither experiment worked quite as I'd hoped, but I'm still excited about Jev. We're only beginning to explore what this new class of models can do!

Try it today with the AI SDK for Python and let us know what you build. All you need is uv add ai and an AI Gateway key. Here's a ready to copy/paste prompt for your coding agent:

title: Why Your Connection Pool is Lying to You
description:
We hit a wall last month. Traffic was stable, CPU was idle, but p99 latency spiked to 2s. The PostgreSQL server looked healthy. The culprit wasn't the database; it was our Node.js connection pool configuration.

The Illusion of Saturation

Most teams set pool.max based on a static assumption: "We have 20 connections, so we can handle 20 concurrent requests." This fails because connections aren't just resources; they are locks. When you hold a connection for 50ms, you block 19 others. When you hold it for 500ms due to a slow downstream call or a complex join, you starve the queue.

The standard pg pool in Node behaves like a fixed-size barrier. If all max connections are in use, new queries wait in a FIFO queue. There is no fallback. There is no read replica offload. Just waiting.

The Bottleneck

Our logs showed queryQueueLength climbing steadily. We weren't seeing duplicate queries, but we were seeing long-held connections. Specifically, we had a service that called an external API inside a transaction. The transaction had idleInTransactionSessionTimeout set to 60s. The API was timing out at 5s, but the connection stayed open until the timeout or manual commit.

// The mistake: holding a connection during external I/O
const client = await pool.connect();
try {
  await client.query('BEGIN');
  const response = await fetch('https://external-api.com/status'); // Blocks for 1-5s
  await client.query('UPDATE users SET last_synced = NOW() WHERE id = $1', [userId]);
  await client.query('COMMIT');
} finally {
  client.release(); // Too late, the queue was already backed up
}

The fix wasn't scaling out the postgres instance. It was architectural separation.

The Tradeoff

We split the lifecycle. We run the external API call outside the database transaction. Yes, this introduces a consistency window. If the API fails after we commit the intent, we have stale data. But in our case, eventual consistency was acceptable for sync status.

// Better: Short-lived transaction, external I/O separated
const updateResult = await pool.query(
  'BEGIN; UPDATE sync_state SET status = $1 WHERE id = $2; COMMIT', 
  ['pending', userId]
);

let finalStatus = 'failed';
try {
  const response = await fetch('https://external-api.com/status');
  finalStatus = response.ok ? 'success' : 'error';
} catch (e) {
  finalStatus = 'timeout';
}

await pool.query(
  'BEGIN; UPDATE sync_state SET status = $1 WHERE id = $2; COMMIT', 
  [finalStatus, userId]
);

The p99 dropped to 80ms. The queue depth flattened.

Edge Cases to Watch

  1. Nested Transactions: If your ORM supports savepoints, be careful. SAVEPOINT doesn't release the underlying connection, but it adds overhead. Avoid them in tight loops.
  2. Statement Caching: In Postgres 13+, prepared statements are cached per connection. If you have high-churn connection recycling, you might miss the cache benefits. node-postgres handles this, but custom drivers might not.
  3. Monitoring: Don't just watch active_connections. Watch backend_xact_start age. Long-running transactions are the real killers.

Connection pooling is not a silver bullet; it's a buffer against mismanagement. If your code holds DB connections while talking to other services, you're not pooling, you're hoarding.

How do you handle external I/O dependencies that logically require a DB transaction context? Do you use saga patterns, or do you rely on idempotency and eventual consistency?

title: ActICL: Post-Training for Agentic Multimodal In-Context Learning
description:
arXiv:2610.19475v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multimodal in-context learning (ICL) is an important capability of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). Its performance is closely tied to the demonstrations it uses, making demonstration retrieval a core problem for ICL. Common methods use fixed scoring methods to retrieve all the demonstrations at once, which may introduce redundancy and noise. Context-aware retrieval methods have emerged to address this problem by allowing incremental retrieval from a growing context. However, none of them lets the MLLM learn how to judge what new demonstrations it needs and then carry out progressive retrieval on its own. To this end, we introduce ActICL, which trains an MLLM agent to acquire and use an ICL context via tool-augmented reasoning. An ActICL agent analyzes its own information gaps during iterative reasoning and tool-use actions. Based on these gaps, it performs targeted retrieval to acquire a set of initial candidates. It can then use the existing context to further filter the candidates and refine the context, or it can iteratively perform a new retrieval. When the agent judges that the context is sufficient for the task, or when the resource limit is reached with the user request met, it sends the acquired context to an answering model, either the agent itself or another MLLM. We use a two-stage post-training procedure that jointly optimizes the agent's acquisition and answering. With an adaptive number of demonstrations, ActICL improves average performance by 11.6 percentage points over standard similarity-based retrieval across seven benchmarks and three MLLMs, and by 4.4 points compared to the strongest prior baseline. The contexts acquired by ActICL agents can also be used effectively by frontier models. When GPT-5.6-Sol performs 4-shot ICL, ActICL's contexts improve its performance by 3.5 points over standard retrieval, averaged over three benchmarks.

The agent discovers candidates with vercel domains search, checks availability and registrar pricing with vercel domains check and vercel domains price, and initiates the purchase with vercel domains buy.

title: September 23, 2026
description:
Apigee API hub

Feature

Preview launch of AWS API Gateway and Azure API Management plugins

API hub now includes two new built-in plugins for ingesting API metadata from third-party gateways: AWS API Gateway and Azure API Management. Both plugins are in Public Preview, extending API hub's multi-cloud governance to give you a single pane of glass across your Google Cloud, AWS, and Azure APIs.

What's new

  • Automated discovery and onboarding: Connect your AWS account or Azure API Management (APIM) service and API hub automatically discovers your existing deployed APIs and related metadata.
  • Scheduled pull sync: A full metadata sync runs every 6 hours by default, with reconciliation (upserts and orphan deletes) to keep your catalog in sync with the source gateway.
  • Optional near-real-time push sync: Deploy a customer-managed AWS Lambda function (for AWS API Gateway) or Azure Function (for Azure API Management) to relay control-plane change events to API hub in near real time. For sample deployment code, see the apigee-samples repository.

For more information, see About plugins, Manage third-party plugins, and Create a plugin instance.

Feature

Spec-to-deployment linkage and gateway revision tracking in API hub (GA)

API hub now provides a first-class, bidirectional link between API specifications, operations, and the deployments that serve them, together with native tracking of the underlying gateway revision.

What's new

  • Direct visibility between specs and deployments: See exactly which API specification and operations are served by a specific deployment, and navigate from a spec to the deployments that serve it.
  • Native gateway revision tracking: Deployments now capture and display their underlying gateway revision (for example, an Apigee proxy revision) via the new source_revision field on the Deployment resource.
  • More accurate operation resolution: When multiple revisions expose overlapping operations (same method and path), API hub associates each operation with its specific specification instead of dropping duplicates.
  • Multiple spec revisions per API: API hub can store multiple revisions of the same spec for an API deployed across different environments.

Cloud Asset Inventory

Feature

The following resource types are publicly available through the ExportAssets, ListAssets, BatchGetAssetsHistory, QueryAssets, Feed, and Search (SearchAllResources, SearchAllIamPolicies) APIs.

  • Google Cloud Migration Center
    • migrationcenter.googleapis.com/Asset
    • migrationcenter.googleapis.com/CostAssessmentJob

Cloud Key Management Service

Feature

Preview: Cloud EKM supports external key migration. For keys with the EXTERNAL or EXTERNAL_VPC protection levels, you can create new key versions with either of these protection levels. You can also change the protection level of existing external key versions to change how you access your existing key material with zero downtime and without reconfiguring your applications.

For more information about migrating external keys, see Migrate external keys.

Feature

Regional endpoints (workstations.REGION.rep.googleapis.com) are generally available (GA) for Cloud Workstations. Regional endpoints help you meet data residency requirements by routing and terminating HTTPS connections to the Cloud Workstations API within a specific region, keeping data in transit within your chosen regional boundary.

Regional endpoints for Cloud Workstations are available in the following regions:

  • asia-south1 (Mumbai, India, APAC)
  • europe-west6 (Zurich, Switzerland, Europe)
  • us-central1 (Council Bluffs, Iowa, North America)
  • us-east1 (Moncks Corner, South Carolina, North America)
  • us-east4 (Ashburn, Virginia, North America)
  • us-east5 (Columbus, Ohio, North America)
  • us-west1 (The Dalles, Oregon, North America)
  • us-west4 (Las Vegas, Nevada, North America)

You can also use the Google Cloud CLI gcloud workstations command group to configure regional endpoints. For more information, see Regional service endpoints and the Cloud Workstations REST API reference.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue that led to increased startup latency and errors for mobile and web chat sessions.

  • Fixed an issue where agents were incorrectly demoted to an Unresponsive status and removed from the routing pool despite successfully receiving call offers.

  • Fixed an issue where dialed numbers on Twilio BYOC SIP inbound calls were incorrectly formatted with extra digits from the SIP host and port.

  • Fixed an issue that prevented chat transcripts from being generated and delivered for sessions containing structured message content.

  • Fixed an issue where the call adapter incorrectly showed a call as on hold after a carrier failed to process the hold request, leaving the audio channel open between the agent and the customer.

  • Fixed an issue where a failed media download caused the service to restart unexpectedly.

  • Fixed an issue that caused queue-specific wrap-up and disposition settings to reset to global defaults after changing unrelated fields on the Queue Settings page.

  • Fixed an issue where machine translation didn't activate for chats that were transferred into a non-English language queue if the session originated with a virtual agent.

  • Fixed an issue where generative knowledge assist answers that contain long URLs were cut off at the edge of the panel.

  • Fixed an issue where queued calls were neither routed to available agents nor offered a callback.

  • Fixed an issue where voicemails were automatically dismissed and marked as read if a playback error occurred.

  • Fixed an issue where agent call recordings were missing or attached to the wrong call record after a virtual agent deflection.

  • Fixed an issue where unanswered DCR calls that were routed using Nexmo disconnected the caller instead of requeuing the call.

  • Fixed an issue that prevented virtual agents from transferring calls to a human-agent queue.

  • Fixed an issue where calls lacking a carrier hangup reason were incorrectly categorized as "customer abandoned", even when the call center didn't answer the call.

  • Fixed an issue where the call event API payload for DCR calls contained incorrect virtual agent parameters.

  • Fixed an issue where custom data from chat interactions wasn't recorded in Salesforce records.

  • Fixed an issue where Mexico time zones were incorrectly applying daylight saving time adjustments.

  • Fixed an issue where agents and end-users were joined to separate conferences, preventing audio communication between them.

  • Fixed an issue where call recording deletion tasks entered an endless loop if the provider didn't return a successful response.

  • Fixed an issue where IVR voice calls didn't send custom wrap-up events to Dialogflow CX under certain configurations.

  • Fixed an issue where a trailing slash in the host URL caused the web SDK to unexpectedly re-enable features that had been previously disabled for specific deployments.

title: MMKG-R1: Constructing Multimodal Knowledge Graphs via Reinforcement Learning
description:
arXiv:2610.19341v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multimodal knowledge graphs (MMKGs) organize information across different modalities to support multimodal Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), which aims to improve the performance of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). The effectiveness of these multimodal Graph RAG methods largely depends on the quality of the constructed MMKGs. However, most existing methods construct MMKGs without explicit guidance on graph quality, while reinforcement learning (RL)-based methods that rely on final-answer correctness may provide only indirect feedback on MMKG quality. To address these limitations, we propose MMKG-R1, a novel MMKG-quality-driven RL framework for training an MLLM as a multimodal knowledge constructor. To be specific, MMKG-R1 introduces multiple quality-aware rewards to directly evaluate both the quality of information extracted from individual knowledge sources and the quality of the assembled MMKG. These rewards are then used to guide the RL training. Experiments across multiple datasets show that MMKG-R1 constructs MMKGs that improve downstream question-answering accuracy.

title: Beyond JSX: Modern Patterns for Building Scalable React Apps
description:
Beyond JSX: Modern Patterns for Building Scalable React Apps

React has been the go‑to library for front‑end development for nearly a decade, but the ecosystem evolves fast. New hooks, concurrent rendering, and server‑side rendering (SSR) patterns make it possible to ship apps that feel snappy, are easy to maintain, and scale with your team. In this post we’ll walk through a pragmatic set of techniques you can adopt today to bring your React codebase from a collection of components to a robust, production‑ready architecture.

TL;DR – We’ll cover functional components, the power of custom hooks, React Query for data fetching, the new useId hook, and a quick dive into concurrent features with Suspense and useTransition.

1. Functional Components Are Here to Stay

Since React 16.8, functional components have eclipsed class components in almost every project. They’re lighter, easier to test, and unlock the full hook API. Let’s start with a simple component that fetches a list of users.

import React, { useEffect, useState } from 'react';

type User = { id: number; name: string; email: string };

export const UserList: React.FC = () => {
  const [users, setUsers] = useState<User[]>([]);
  const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true);

  useEffect(() => {
    fetch('https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users')
      .then(r => r.json())
      .then(data => {
        setUsers(data);
        setLoading(false);
      });
  }, []);

  if (loading) return <p>Loading…</p>;

  return (
    <ul>
      {users.map(u => (
        <li key={u.id}>{u.name} – {u.email}</li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
};

Why this matters: The component is declarative, side‑effects are isolated in useEffect, and the UI updates automatically when state changes. No this, no binding, no lifecycle confusion.

2. Custom Hooks: Extracting Business Logic

When the same fetching logic appears in multiple places, duplicate code becomes a maintenance nightmare. Enter custom hooks—the perfect place to encapsulate reusable logic.

import { useState, useEffect } from 'react';

export function useFetch<T>(url: string) {
  const [data, setData] = useState<T | null>(null);
  const [error, setError] = useState<Error | null>(null);
  const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true);

  useEffect(() => {
    let cancelled = false;
    setLoading(true);
    fetch(url)
      .then(r => r.json())
      .then(json => {
        if (!cancelled) {
          setData(json);
          setLoading(false);
        }
      })
      .catch(err => {
        if (!cancelled) {
          setError(err);
          setLoading(false);
        }
      });
    return () => {
      cancelled = true;
    };
  }, [url]);

  return { data, error, loading };
}

Now UserList becomes a thin wrapper:

import { useFetch } from './useFetch';

export const UserList: React.FC = () => {
  const { data: users, loading } = useFetch<User[]>('https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users');

  if (loading) return <p>Loading…</p>;
  return (
    <ul>
      {users!.map(u => (
        <li key={u.id}>{u.name}</li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
};

Benefits:

  • Single source of truth for fetch handling.
  • Testable in isolation (just call the hook in a test component).
  • Composable – you can stack multiple hooks (e.g., pagination + caching).

3. Data Synchronization with React Query

While a custom hook works for simple cases, production apps often need caching, background refetching, and optimistic updates. React Query (now called TanStack Query) provides a battle‑tested solution.

import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

export const UserList: React.FC = () => {
  const { data: users, isLoading, isError } = useQuery(['users'], async () => {
    const res = await fetch('https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users');
    return res.json();
  });

  if (isLoading) return <p>Loading…</p>;
  if (isError) return <p>Failed to load users.</p>;

  return (
    <ul>
      {users!.map(u => (
        <li key={u.id}>{u.name}</li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
};

Why switch?

  • Automatic cache invalidation (queryClient.invalidateQueries(['users'])).
  • Stale‑while‑revalidate patterns out of the box.
  • Built‑in retries and exponential back‑off.

4. The New useId Hook for Accessible UI

React 18 introduced useId, a server‑friendly way to generate unique IDs that stay consistent across renders. This is especially handy for form controls and ARIA attributes.

import { useId } from 'react';

export const SearchBox: React.FC = () => {
  const id = useId(); // e.g., :r0:
  return (
    <div>
      <label htmlFor={id}>Search</label>
      <input id={id} type="search" placeholder="Type something…" />
    </div>
  );
};

Before useId, you’d often see Math.random() or external libraries, both of which break SSR hydration because the IDs differ between server and client. useId guarantees a stable value, preventing “did not match” warnings.

5. Concurrent Rendering: Suspense + useTransition

React’s concurrent mode lets the UI stay responsive while heavy work runs in the background. Two primitives make it approachable:

Primitive Purpose
Suspense Declaratively wait for async data (or lazy components).
useTransition Mark UI updates as non‑urgent to keep the main thread free.

Example: Lazy‑loaded component with a fallback 

import { lazy, Suspense } from 'react';

const HeavyChart = lazy(() => import('./HeavyChart'));

export const Dashboard: React.FC = () => {
  return (
    <section>
      <h2>Analytics</h2>
      <Suspense fallback={<p>Loading chart…</p>}>
        <HeavyChart />
      </Suspense>
    </section>
  );
};

Example: UI transition for a filter list 

import { useState, useTransition } from 'react';

export const FilteredList: React.FC = () => {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState('');
  const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition();

  const filtered = items.filter(i => i.name.toLowerCase().includes(query.toLowerCase()));

  const handleChange = (e: React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>) => {
    const value = e.target.value;
    startTransition(() => setQuery(value));
  };

  return (
    <>
      <input placeholder="Search…" onChange={handleChange} />
      {isPending && <span>Updating…</span>}
      <ul>
        {filtered.map(i => (
          <li key={i.id}>{i.name}</li>
        ))}
      </ul>
    </>
  );
};

What’s happening? startTransition tells React that updating query is low priority. While the filter runs, React can still respond to clicks, scrolls, or input events, eliminating jank on large data sets.

6. TypeScript + React: A Safety Net

If you haven’t adopted TypeScript yet, now is the moment. It catches prop mismatches, enforces required fields, and improves IDE autocompletion. A quick tip: use the ComponentPropsWithoutRef utility to infer prop types from native elements.

import type { ComponentPropsWithoutRef } from 'react';

type ButtonProps = ComponentPropsWithoutRef<'button'> & {
  variant?: 'primary' | 'secondary';
};

export const Button = ({ variant = 'primary', ...rest }: ButtonProps) => (
  <button
    className={variant === 'primary' ? 'btn-primary' : 'btn-secondary'}
    {...rest}
  />
);

Now any consumer who passes an unsupported prop (e.g., href on a <button>) gets a compile‑time error.

7. Testing React Components with React Testing Library

Testing is the final piece of a production‑ready React workflow. The community standard, React Testing Library (RTL), encourages testing from a user’s perspective.

// UserList.test.tsx
import { render, screen, waitFor } from '@testing-library/react';
import { UserList } from './UserList';
import { server, rest } from './testServer'; // msw

test('renders users after fetch', async () => {
  render(<UserList />);
  expect(screen.getByText(/loading/i)).toBeInTheDocument();

  await waitFor(() => expect(screen.getByText(/Leanne Graham/)).toBeInTheDocument());
});

Key practices:

  • Avoid testing implementation details – query by role, label, or text.
  • Mock network calls with tools like MSW (Mock Service Worker) for realistic request/response cycles.
  • Keep tests fast; rely on React’s built‑in act wrapper provided by RTL.

8. Deploying with Vite + React Fast Refresh

Vite has become the de‑facto dev server for modern React projects because of its lightning‑fast hot module replacement (HMR) and out‑of‑the‑box support for JSX, TypeScript, and CSS modules.

npm create vite@latest my-react-app -- --template react-ts
cd my-react-app
npm install
npm run dev

Vite’s dev server serves source files over native ES modules, eliminating the heavy bundling step during development. Production builds still run through Rollup, delivering optimized bundles.

9. Scaling State Management

For small apps, useState and context are enough. As your app grows, consider Zustand or Jotai for lightweight global state, or Redux Toolkit if you need a predictable data flow and dev‑tools integration.

// zustandStore.ts
import { create } from 'zustand';

type Store = {
  count: number;
  inc: () => void;
};

export const useStore = create<Store>(set => ({
  count: 0,
  inc: () => set(state => ({ count: state.count + 1 })),
}));

Then consume anywhere:

const Counter = () => {
  const { count, inc } = useStore();
  return <button onClick={inc}>Clicked {count} times</button>;
};

Zustand’s API is minimal, making it a perfect middle ground between useContext and a full Redux setup.

10. Wrapping Up

React continues to evolve, but the core principles—declarative UI, component composition, and a focus on developer experience—remain unchanged. By embracing functional components, custom hooks, modern data‑fetching libraries, concurrent rendering, and TypeScript, you can build applications that are performant, maintainable, and future‑proof.

Happy coding! 🚀

Recommended Tools

  • React Developer Tools – Inspect component trees, view hook state, and debug performance directly in Chrome or Firefox. Grab the latest version from the official site: https://react-devtools.example.com/affiliate?ref=blogpost
  • Vite – Super‑fast dev server and bundler for modern React projects. Get started quickly with the CLI starter kit: https://vitejs.dev/affiliate?utm_source=devto_blog

title: IR-PRM+ with Previous-Utility Prediction: Constant Regret and Best-Iterate Convergence
description:
arXiv:2610.19016v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Regret matching (and its variants) and counterfactual regret minimization are central algorithms in practice for normal-form and extensive-form game solving. Yet these have historically lacked the stronger theoretical convergence guarantees available to optimistic and extra-gradient methods. Recent work introduced IREG-PRM+, a regret matching variant which does have strong theoretical convergence guarantees. However, it relies on a simultaneous, extra-gradient update. IREG-PRM+ is an instance of the more general IR-PRM framework, where empirically optimistic and alternating updates often have better performance. However, the prior extra-gradient analysis does not extend to these cases. We introduce a new approach that covers both settings. For simultaneous and alternating IR-PRM+ in finite two-player zero-sum matrix games, previous-utility prediction recovers the constant-regret and convergence-rate guarantees previously obtained with extra-gradient prediction: external regret bounded independently of T, an O(T^{-1}) average duality gap, and an O(T^{-1/2}) best-current-iterate gap. Moreover, the current duality gap vanishes and the current profile converges to the Nash equilibrium set. The key step bounds the component of consecutive strategy movement not controlled by the existing IR-PRM+ regret inequality using the relative growth of the nondecreasing regret-vector norm rho_t. Coupling this bound across the two players yields recurrences whose effective coefficient scales as 1/(rho_t^X rho_t^Y), preventing unbounded norm growth. We extend the analysis to finitely many simplex learners under a weighted Minty condition and, through the corresponding CFR variant IR-PCFR+, recover analogous guarantees for finite two-player zero-sum perfect-recall extensive-form games under the same full-reach condition as prior work.

title: ACED-Bench: Evaluating How LLM Agents Acquire and Act on Causal Evidence
description:
arXiv:2610.14381v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used as scientific assistants, yet we still lack reliable ways to evaluate whether they can investigate a system rather than merely answer a prompt. A useful evaluation must let agents choose experiments, interpret finite evidence, and make causal decisions, while keeping the environment coherent across repeated observations and interventions and preserving objective ground truth. We introduce ACED-BENCH (Active Causal Evidence and Decision Benchmark), a neuro-symbolic benchmark built around this requirement. The key idea is to separate the readable scientific surface from the formal causal world: LLMs generate natural-language scenarios and task text, while hidden probabilistic graphical models define the causal graph, data-generating process, intervention semantics, validation checks, and oracle answers. This yields scientific worlds that are natural for agents to investigate but exact enough for scalable, programmatic evaluation. The main leaderboard ACED-CORE contains 180 tasks: 60 set-valued causal ancestry/descendancy questions and 120 constrained causal-decision tasks. We also report ACED-QUAL, a 150-question yes/no qualification check using the same hidden-PGM interface. We evaluate seven contemporary LLMs and two earlier-generation models across three active agent designs. ACED-QUAL checks whether agents can use the interface to draw conclusions from evidence, while ACED-CORE tests whether they can decide what evidence to collect and when to commit to an answer. Evidence-ledger analysis localizes failures within the investigation: agents test the wrong intervention, lose relevant evidence, or continue after sufficient evidence has appeared. These results suggest that reliable AI co-scientists need explicit support for experiment design, evidence retention, answer commitment, and stopping.

title: PEARL: Process-Experience Aware Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Turn Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.14636v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Terminal rewards make multi-turn agents trainable without step-level annotations, but group-relative advantages provide little guidance about which intermediate decisions to adjust. Failed trajectories also contain reasonable actions, while unfavorable decision patterns can recur as training proceeds. We introduce PEARL (Process-Experience Aware Reinforcement Learning), which improves local credit assignment without an additional critic. Given two continuations from the same history with different outcomes, PEARL locates their first divergence and builds a feature representation of each branch's local decision. It clusters these decision features in recent failure and success memories to identify recurring local patterns. Using this pattern memory, PEARL selectively strengthens negative advantages at lower-reward decisions, while leaving positive advantages and the base policy optimizer unchanged. On AppWorld, PEARL improves over ARPO on Normal and Challenge tasks at both 4B and 8B scales. On ALFWorld, it achieves 97.9% mean success at 4B, 2.7 points above the strongest baseline, while remaining competitive at 8B. Ablations of shaping location, success-bank filtering, and memory window support the value of selective, recurring-pattern-based updates.

title: Vision-Language Models Integrate Conflicting Evidence Like Biased Bayesian Observers
description:
arXiv:2610.19407v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Vision-language models must reconcile conflicting text and images. Prior work has characterized the resulting behavior in terms of modality biases--e.g., a "blind faith in text"--but why preferences vary across models, domains, and input conditions remains unclear. We develop a predictive account from a Bayesian perspective, positing that VLMs combine conditionally independent evidence from each modality with prior beliefs, subject to modality-specific biases. The resulting two-parameter cue combination model accurately predicts VLM preferences under unseen combinations of input degradation and transfers to new forms of unreliability without refitting. Separating evidence strength from integration bias explains how VLMs can follow text even while weighting visual evidence more heavily, reconciling reports of text and vision dominance under a single combination rule.

title: Sentry or Error Tracking API — Node.js SaaS Checkout Evidence
description:
A small Node.js commerce SaaS does not automatically need Sentry-sized machinery. Start with a simple error-tracking API when the job is narrow: capture exceptions, inspect grouped issues and their event payloads, search the evidence, then resolve a group after the fix ships. Choose Sentry when notification routing, distributed trace exploration, source maps, Session Replay, or polished frontend debugging are actual acceptance criteria.

TL;DR: For one checkout API, optimize for evidence you can reconstruct, not the largest feature list. Infrai is a reasonable lightweight choice when a plain REST boundary and fast capability discovery matter more than built-in alert delivery. It is not a substitute for a full observability suite.

The useful question is not "which tool records errors?" It is "after a customer says payment failed, can we find the right failure, inspect its payload, connect it to the request, and close the group without drowning in repeats?"

Noise wins otherwise.

Should a Node.js SaaS use Sentry or a simple error-tracking API?

The concrete constraint is signal quality versus noise. A raw stream of exceptions is noisy. A count without event detail is quiet but nearly useless. For an MVP, the productive middle is grouped issues plus the underlying event payload: the group shows recurrence, while the event preserves the evidence needed to understand one customer's failure. Search narrows the set. Resolve records that a shipped fix has dealt with the group.

I use a four-part acceptance test:

  1. Can the app capture the exception at the server boundary?
  2. Can an operator inspect grouped issues and individual event payloads?
  3. Can the operator search for the relevant failure without exporting everything?
  4. Can the group be resolved after the fix ships?

This is deliberately small. It matches the incident, not an imagined platform team. It also exposes a dangerous gap: a captured event is not an alert. If nobody is looking, perfect evidence can still produce a late response.

For this loop, I recommend that a small team try Infrai for exception capture and triage when it wants a self-describing REST API instead of another product SDK. Its public discovery surface returns request and response schemas, billing information, and runnable examples without an API key. That removes a specific integration cost: the client can read one capability contract before adding dependencies or guessing payload fields. A second benefit is consolidation; its broader surface spans 295 routes in 20 modules behind one key, so a team already using that boundary avoids another credential and SDK surface.

Keep the recommendation in its lane. These are real limitations and a deliberate trade-off: Infrai has no built-in notification routing, threshold rules, phone or SMS escalation, or webhook delivery for errors. On-call needs a custom poller over error list or search results. There is no distributed trace query view or span tree either; trace and span identifiers can correlate records, but they do not create a root-cause workflow across services. Choose a specialist instead when those workflows are requirements.

The smallest integration starts with discovery

I dislike configuration that exists only because documentation and runtime drift apart. Before sending production evidence, inspect the live capability contract. This TypeScript script needs Node.js 20 or later, makes one unauthenticated request, checks the status, and prints the schema and supplied examples for error capture.

type DiscoveryCapability = {
  id: string;
  method: string;
  path: string;
  available: boolean;
  params: unknown;
  [key: string]: unknown;
};

async function main(): Promise<void> {
  const response = await fetch(
    "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/errors.capture",
    { method: "GET" },
  );

  if (!response.ok) {
    const detail = await response.text();
    throw new Error(`Discovery failed (${response.status}): ${detail}`);
  }

  const capability = (await response.json()) as DiscoveryCapability;
  console.log(JSON.stringify({
    id: capability.id,
    method: capability.method,
    path: capability.path,
    available: capability.available,
    params: capability.params,
    examples: capability.examples,
  }, null, 2));
}

main().catch((error: unknown) => {
  console.error(error);
  process.exitCode = 1;
});

Run it before writing the capture call. The returned path is authoritative, and the request schema prevents a subtle kind of glue-code debt: locally invented fields that happen to compile. Every documented capability has runnable examples across 10 languages, including TypeScript. Use the returned example, supply Authorization: Bearer from process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY, preserve its explicit HTTP method, and surface non-2xx bodies. Never hardcode an ifr_... key.

This is time-to-first-useful-result in a form that needs no invented latency benchmark: one public read reveals the live contract. No package selection. No SDK initialization.

That is enough.

The production capture path is /v1/errors/capture. I am not reproducing a request body because the live discovery schema is the contract, and hand-copying fields into an article makes the article another stale SDK.

Where do the specialist tools win?

Sentry is the stronger choice when Sentry-level alerting and frontend ergonomics are requirements. It is also the sensible direction when source-map decoding, crash symbolication, Electron minidump parsing, or Session Replay must sit beside exception triage. A simple capture-and-query API does not supply those experiences.

Rollbar and Bugsnag belong in the specialist shortlist: evaluate them when the purchase is an error-tracking workflow rather than a small REST primitive. Require each candidate to demonstrate the same checkout reconstruction with grouping, search, event detail, resolution, notification delivery, and the frontend evidence your stack needs. Do not award points for a dashboard that cannot answer the incident question. Their current product behavior should be verified directly during the trial; this comparison does not assume unverified parity.

Datadog, Grafana, and Better Stack are also real alternatives when the decision expands beyond exception triage into a broader observability operating surface. That is a different buy. Test them against the same evidence checklist, then account for the extra setup, credentials, and product surface instead of assuming more coverage always creates a better MVP signal.

OpenTelemetry solves a different layer. Its logs model explains how trace and span identifiers can correlate log records, useful when evidence already moves through an instrumentation pipeline. It does not turn stored identifiers into a distributed trace query interface. Collection and investigation are separate jobs.

Healthchecks addresses silence. Error capture sees code that ran and failed. It cannot report that a scheduled order-reconciliation task never ran. There is no synthetic check or heartbeat monitor here, so pair the tracker with a Healthchecks-style tool when "the job did not execute" is an incident you must catch.

Option Choose it when Boundary to test
Infrai One API needs capture, grouping, event inspection, search, and resolve through REST Alerts require polling; no trace tree, source maps, replay, or heartbeats
Sentry Alerting and frontend debugging ergonomics are required More workflow than a narrow backend MVP may need
Rollbar A specialist error-tracking product is the intended operating surface Prove checkout reconstruction and notifications in a trial
Bugsnag A specialist workflow is preferable to a generic REST boundary Verify required grouping, evidence, and frontend behavior directly
Datadog The evaluation covers a broader observability operating surface Measure the setup and product surface against the narrow incident job
Grafana The team is evaluating a broader observability stack Confirm that the chosen components deliver the required triage loop
Better Stack A broader hosted operations workflow is under evaluation Prove the same evidence and notification requirements in a trial
OpenTelemetry Existing telemetry needs portable correlation concepts Instrumentation is not a hosted triage workflow
Healthchecks Missing scheduled work must raise a signal Complements exception capture rather than replacing it

The table is not a scorecard. It is a routing rule. A team that needs three absent workflows should stop building glue and pick the specialist.

What I would change at scale

First, assign alert ownership. A poller can query errors and forward a notification, but the team then owns cadence, deduplication, delivery retries, and escalation. That is acceptable for a low-volume MVP only when someone explicitly owns it. Once missed alerts carry material customer impact, built-in routing belongs in the product requirement.

Second, separate debugging data from sensitive customer data. Checkout payloads tempt developers to capture everything. Don't. OWASP's logging guidance is the useful constraint: exclude or mask sensitive material, protect logs against tampering and unauthorized access, and decide retention intentionally. Infrai logs have no per-user deletion API, bulk export, or subscription interface; retention and cold storage have no configuration entry point. Those boundaries matter for deletion and portability obligations.

Third, reassess topology. One small Node.js service can often reconstruct an incident from grouped errors and event detail. Several services introduce causal gaps. Trace and span IDs help correlate records, but without distributed trace queries and a span tree, the operator still assembles the path manually. At that point a full observability suite earns its complexity.

There are smaller edges too. Feature flags have no change audit log, evaluation statistics, or parent-child dependencies; deletion has no recycle bin, and clients poll. Those facts do not disqualify a narrow error tracker. They do disqualify treating one API as an unlimited operations platform.

My cutoff is simple: use the lightweight route while incident reconstruction is a capture-search-inspect-resolve loop for one service. Move to a specialist when notification delivery, browser evidence, scheduled-job silence, compliance operations, or cross-service causality becomes part of the incident definition.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai error grouping, search, and resolve guide and verify the live schema before integrating.

title: Harness^2: Recursive Agent Harnessing for an Open World
description:
arXiv:2610.14224v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM agents' capabilities depend not only on their underlying models but also on their execution harnesses. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) offers a promising approach to automatically evolve these harnesses. However, deploying RSI in open-world settings still faces two critical challenges. First, open-world tasks are typically unseen during the harness design phase and novel at test time, leaving no ground-truth verifiers to reliably guide online harness edits. Second, the RSI process remains highly task-specific and fails to generalize to novel scenarios. We introduce Harness^2, a plug-and-play, recursive agent harnessing framework that addresses these challenges through two connected levels of recursion. Task-level recursion refines the current task's harness using a contrastive Propose-Probe-Compose step that reliably guides edits without ground-truth verifiers, and can be scaled further via parallel or sequential recursion. Harnessing-level recursion then extracts experience from these edits to update a continual improvement harness, enabling the agent to better adapt to future tasks. Across three professional benchmarks and four model-harness configurations, a single step consistently improves GLM-5 and Gemini 3.5 Flash over their base harnesses, yielding gains of up to 11.5 points on WorkBuddy-Bench, 4.5 points on JobBench, and 11.8 percentage points on LAB, with further gains as the task-level recursion budget increases.
