title: Decoupling Knowledge Forgetting and Refusal Learning in MLLM Unlearning
description:
arXiv:2610.14605v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Current evaluations of multimodal unlearning typically focus on whether a model stops outputting target information. This surface-level criterion, however, masks two critical failure modes. First, knowledge suppression techniques often induce confabulation, leading the model to hallucinate facts about the unlearned subject. Second, refusal training merely alters observable behavior without erasing the underlying knowledge; such models might decline open queries but still identify correct answers under multiple-choice probing. To overcome these limitations, we propose Forget-Aware Self-Distillation (FASD). This method is designed to achieve honest ignorance, a state where the model genuinely loses the target knowledge and learns to acknowledge its absence. FASD separates these goals into two complementary channels. The behavior channel distills appropriate refusals from an ignorance-prompted copy of the model itself. Crucially, target tokens are masked from the teacher distribution to avoid accidentally reteaching the forgotten concepts. Simultaneously, the knowledge channel directly suppresses ground-truth answer spans independently of the model's generated responses. Experiments demonstrate that FASD successfully unlearns target knowledge, prevents information leakage in open-ended tasks, and preserves performance on retained data. The resulting model not only forgets the specified information but accurately recognizes the boundaries of its own knowledge. Code and data will be released upon publication.

title: Engineering a Modern Vehicle-Rental Marketplace: Architecture, Search, and UX Challenges
description:
Introduction

Vehicle-rental platforms sit at the intersection of e-commerce, geospatial search, and logistics coordination. Unlike standard retail marketplaces where a product sits in a centralized warehouse, a mobility marketplace deals with distributed, heterogeneous assets managed by independent local providers.

The software challenge lies in synchronizing search, listing information, dynamic availability, transparent pricing, and booking workflows into a seamless user experience. For travelers navigating unfamiliar terrain, the system must abstract away provider fragmentation while remaining strictly honest about what data is verified versus what is assumed.

Designing a Useful Vehicle-Discovery Experience

A robust discovery engine must filter vehicles by geographical constraints, vehicle categories, rental durations, and practical requirements. When engineers design the catalog interface, treating motorcycles, scooters, and cars as interchangeable entities leads to poor UX.

Listing components must dynamically render attributes relevant to the chosen category—such as engine displacement and luggage capacity for motorcycles or seating capacity and transmission type for cars. Platforms specializing in motorcycle rental Colombia must ensure that filtering parameters reflect the technical and logistical realities of the region, helping users quickly distinguish between light city commuters and heavy touring rigs.

Building Location-Aware Search

Geospatial queries form the backbone of any travel mobility platform. Travelers searching for transport require location-aware filtering that adapts to different urban and regional contexts.

Consider three distinct operational hubs across Colombia:

  • Bogotá: High-altitude urban commuting, dense traffic patterns, and frequent suburban departures require reliable filtering for city-appropriate scooters and versatile cars.
  • Medellín: Nestled within an Andean valley, the terrain demands precise categorization for riders looking for agile machines suited to steep inclines and winding mountain roads.
  • Cartagena: Coastal conditions and flat coastal highways favor lightweight scooters and comfortable cars for regional exploration.

Engineers must optimize spatial indexes (such as PostGIS extensions or Elasticsearch geo-queries) to ensure fast radius searches around specific pickup points, transit hubs, or neighborhoods. Implementing intuitive search filters for pickup locations, rental dates, and provider details minimizes user friction and reduces bounce rates during the initial discovery phase.

Supporting Different Vehicle Categories

Different vehicle classes serve fundamentally distinct travel intentions. Grouping them incorrectly in the database schema or UI creates confusion.

For instance, urban commuters looking for a scooter rental Colombia require agile, fuel-efficient transport with simple storage solutions. Conversely, travelers planning extended coastal drives or urban commuting in major business centers rely heavily on car rental Medellin or general car rental Colombia listings.

Product teams must design modular database schemas that allow vehicle attributes to scale independently. A motorcycle listing requires fields for helmet inclusion, luggage racks, and engine specs, while a car listing requires details on doors, AC, and transmission. Emphasizing these distinctions prevents booking errors and ensures renters select equipment matching their actual operational needs.

Making Listing Information Transparent

Trust in a rental marketplace is directly proportional to data transparency. Ambiguous pricing, hidden fees, or unclear pickup instructions cause immediate user drop-off and support overhead.

Engineering systems must enforce strict data contracts for listing pages, displaying:

  • Granular vehicle specifications and maintenance notes.
  • Exact rental duration calculations and time-zone-aware pickup/return windows.
  • Transparent total pricing, itemizing base rates, taxes, and applicable deposits.
  • Provider information, verified compliance badges, and required documentation (such as valid driver's licenses and international permits).
  • Clear cancellation policies and insurance terms.

A well-architected marketplace distinguishes confirmed provider-supplied data from assumptions, guiding users directly to official terms without hiding restrictions behind opaque UI patterns.

Trust, Verification, and Booking Workflows

Building a resilient booking workflow requires careful state machine design. A reservation typically moves through distinct states: draft, pending_provider_review, confirmed, active, and completed.

Provider verification should be handled as a data attribute rather than an absolute safety guarantee. Platforms must avoid over-promising; verification simply means identity and documentation checks have met baseline platform standards.

From a frontend perspective, UX principles dictate clear error boundaries, idempotent payment processing steps, immutable confirmation screens, and secure handling of PII (Personally Identifiable Information). If a payment gateway times out or inventory status changes mid-checkout, the state machine must gracefully roll back without leaving orphaned reservations or charging users twice.

Supporting Adventure Travel and Tours

Long-distance journeys and organized excursions introduce unique technical and logistical requirements. Explorers planning extensive itineraries often seek specialized options, such as an adventure motorcycle rental Colombia or curated motorcycle tours Colombia, when organizing a multi-day motorcycle road trip Colombia.

From a product standpoint, supporting adventure travel means integrating rich content blocks, itinerary maps, and explicit pre-trip checklists. Platforms must prompt users to verify their rider eligibility, international licensing credentials, protective gear availability, and regional weather or road restrictions. Encouraging travelers to consult official transport authorities and local providers ensures safety compliance beyond what software can automate.

A Practical Marketplace Engineering Checklist

  1. Define Journeys: Map clear user journeys for both renters and independent local providers.
  2. Modular Schema: Design scalable database schemas for distinct vehicle categories and location filters.
  3. Data Integrity: Keep listing data synchronized and flag unverified fields clearly.
  4. Transparent Pricing: Display itemized totals, deposits, and cancellation terms upfront.
  5. State Management: Implement robust state machines for booking confirmation and payment handling.
  6. Data Privacy: Encrypt and secure personal information and payment tokens.
  7. Mobile Optimization: Test responsive layouts extensively on mobile devices used by on-the-go travelers.
  8. Friction Analytics: Monitor search-to-booking conversion funnels using privacy-conscious analytics tools.
  9. Feedback Loops: Collect structured user feedback to refine confusing checkout or search workflows.

How MotoShare.co Fits Into the Travel-Mobility Landscape

Platforms like MotoShare.co exemplify how localized marketplaces connect travelers with independent vehicle providers across Colombia. By focusing on transparent discovery for motorcycles, scooters, and cars, the platform aligns with core marketplace architecture principles: clear categorization, location-driven search, and straightforward provider coordination without unnecessary booking friction. Keeping listings transparent and decentralized allows local providers to manage their own fleet details while giving users a unified discovery interface.

Conclusion

Building a successful vehicle-rental marketplace requires more than just a searchable database. It demands rigorous data modeling, transparent pricing UX, reliable state management, and clear communication of rental terms. By prioritizing data accuracy and user-centric design, engineering teams can build resilient platforms that simplify mobility for travelers and empower local providers alike.

title: Stop exporting JSON tokens and use CSS variables instead
description:
A designer tagged me in a Figma comment on Tuesday morning. They wanted to know if we could start exporting our brand tokens as deeply nested JSON files. They had just read an article about complex token pipelines. I just stared at my screen for a minute. We are a web team building a React application. We do not need a massive parsing engine just to read a blue hex code.

This happens all the time in our industry. Teams get obsessed with the idea of a universal format. They build massive configurations to transform JSON into something the browser can actually use. It feels like everyone is overcomplicating the simplest part of frontend development.

The pipeline trap

I see this pattern everywhere. A team decides they need a design system. They set up a pipeline that exports something like this from Figma.

{
  "color": {
    "brand": {
      "primary": {
        "value": "#0052cc",
        "type": "color"
      }
    },
    "background": {
      "base": {
        "value": "#ffffff",
        "type": "color"
      }
    }
  }
}

Then the web developers have to write a script to flatten this object. They have to map it to their styling solution. Maybe they are using Tailwind. Maybe they are using styled-components. Either way, it adds a completely unnecessary layer of complexity.

If a colour breaks in production, you cannot just inspect it easily. You have to trace the error back through your build script. You have to figure out if the JSON was malformed or if your parser failed. That is a lot of wasted time for a background colour.

The browser already solved this

CSS variables are the only token format that actually matters for the web. You do not need a build step to use them. You just load the file and the browser understands it immediately.

Look at how much cleaner the CSS approach is.

:root {
  --color-brand-primary: #0052cc;
  --color-background-base: #ffffff;
}

You can inspect this directly in Chrome DevTools. You can change the values on the fly to test new designs. You can scope them to specific components. JSON cannot do any of that natively.

Theming is where CSS variables really show their power. If you want to add a dark mode using JSON, you usually have to output multiple files. Then you have to write JavaScript logic to swap those themes in your application. With CSS variables, the browser does all the heavy lifting for you.

[data-theme="dark"] {
  --color-brand-primary: #4c9aff;
  --color-background-base: #111111;
}

You just toggle a data attribute on your HTML tag. The browser updates every single component instantly. There is no JavaScript required. There is no complex state management. It just works.

What about native apps?

This is always the counter-argument I hear. People say you need JSON so iOS and Android can consume the exact same tokens.

That is technically true if you work at a massive tech company with dedicated mobile teams. But most teams are web-first. Even if you do have mobile developers, forcing the web team to parse JSON just to appease iOS is backwards. Let the mobile teams compile what they need. The web should just get CSS. You should optimise for the platform where your users actually spend their time.

A better workflow

We stopped doing the JSON dance months ago. Now we just push CSS variables straight from Figma to our repository.

The designer updates a colour in Figma. A pull request automatically appears in our GitHub repository with the raw CSS file. The developer reviews the visual diff and merges it. The pipeline is entirely transparent. There are no build scripts to maintain.

This is exactly why I built Design System Sync. I got incredibly tired of writing parsing scripts for different teams. I wanted a tool that respects how the web actually works. It exports your Figma variables directly to GitHub or Bitbucket as ready-to-use CSS variables. It handles the formatting automatically.

You can check it out at https://ds-sync.netlify.app?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=bot or grab the plugin directly from the Figma Community at https://www.figma.com/community/plugin/1561389071519901700?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=bot.

It also supports W3C formats if you really need them. But honestly, you probably just need CSS.

Are you still maintaining custom build scripts to parse JSON tokens for your web application?

title: Behind the Scenes: Evolving Netflix’s Ads Event Pipeline for Live — Part II
description:
By Yogesh Nagarur

Introduction

In Part 1 of this series, we shared how Netflix built the Ads Event pipeline and approached it as a system design problem: replacing fragmented pipelines with a centralized collection, enrichment, and a standard data contract. The result was Ads Event Publisher, the system that collects ad telemetry from client devices, enriches it with the context of the ad that was actually served, and publishes a single, unified stream of ad events to every downstream consumer: frequency capping, metrics, billing, measurement partners, and reporting. Any member viewing or account details that move through this pipeline end-to-end are encrypted and handled in accordance with Netflix’s strict privacy and security practices to safeguard member PII.

If ad serving is the “brain” and ad events are the “heartbeats” that feed it, then enrichment is what gives each heartbeat its meaning, turning a bare “[Somebody] watched an ad to completion” signal into “this campaign, this creative, at this price, for this break.” Part 1 described that enrichment step as a single box in the architecture. This post is about what was inside that box, and why we rebuilt it.

Part 1 ended with a look at what was on the horizon: ads on live streams, de-duplication, and richer data signals. A single project delivered all three by rebuilding the Ads Event Publisher around stateful stream processing. We replaced a database lookup with a real-time streaming join in Apache Flink, which let the system scale for Live, took a dependency off the critical path, and replaced the engine of a high-traffic pipeline without downtime.

Let’s dive in.

A quick recap: enrichment and the Metadata Registry

When an ad is served, the ad server knows everything about it: the campaign, the creative, the price of the impression, the targeting context, and the tracking URLs that measurement partners expect us to fire. The client device, by contrast, knows almost nothing: just an opaque token and when to send each event. Enrichment is the act of reuniting the two.

In the architecture from Part 1, that reunion happened through the Ads Metadata Registry, a Key-Value store:

  • When the ad server made a decision, it wrote the metadata for that impression into the registry.
  • It encoded only reference identifiers into the opaque token returned to the device, keeping the token small.
  • Later, when the client fired an event carrying that token, the Ads Event Publisher decoded the token, looked up the metadata in the registry, and stitched the two together into an enriched ad event.

This design served us well. The registry was globally replicated, which gave us a useful property almost for free: an event arriving in any region could find its metadata regardless of where the ad was decided. It future-proofed the token against ever-growing metadata, and it carried us through the first phase of Netflix’s advertising growth.

But as we looked ahead, especially to ads on live streams, the limits of this design became clear.

Why we needed to evolve

The forcing function was Live. Netflix’s live slate has grown rapidly, from NFL games to blockbuster fight nights to the FIFA Women’s World Cup 2027, and viewership keeps growing. That traffic looks nothing like Subscription Video on Demand (SVOD): a single event can surge toward tens of millions of concurrent viewers within minutes, then drain just as fast when it ends. Building the ad pipeline for Live meant building for that trajectory.

To see why the old design could not get there, let’s put some numbers on it. When Netflix streamed the Jake Paul vs. Mike Tyson fight to more than 100 million viewers, a single ad break at that scale would generate an enormous volume of ad events. Serving those ads in the old design would have meant writing metadata for each of them to the Metadata Registry and waiting for acknowledgment before the ads could serve: millions of must-succeed database writes per second on the ad-serving critical path. That pattern created three core problems at Live scale:

  1. It was a scaling bottleneck. Every ad and every ad break is a write. Multiply that by tens of millions of concurrent viewers, keep it non-lossy (a dropped write is a dropped ad, and lost revenue), add Live’s spiky on/off pattern, and the write load becomes enormous. But you cannot safely scale the registry up once the event starts. Adding nodes reshuffles data across the cluster to rebalance it, and doing that in the middle of a live event could slow or even fail the very writes you are adding capacity for. That leaves one safe option: pre-scaling for the peak in advance and hoping the forecast is accurate.
  2. Fewer dependencies on the critical path. Serving an ad meant a synchronous, must-succeed write to the registry, followed by a wait for its acknowledgment. Every system on the critical path is one more thing that can stop an ad from serving, and the metadata registry had no fallback, so an unhealthy registry meant serving stopped. Taking hard dependencies off that path was the goal, and the registry was the biggest one we could remove.
  3. It put event freshness at risk. If writing slowed down under load, or lookups timed out, events spilled into retries and dead-letter queues, and enriched ad events were delivered late. Some systems might be fine, but others, such as frequency capping, cannot. It needs events under a strict SLA to decide whether the next selected ad can run without breaking policies.

So we asked a simple question: the ad server already knows and logs everything about the ad it served. Does it really need to write that to a database on the hot path? Can we match that against the downstream Kafka stream of client events, which is always there, after the fact?

The write leaves the critical path entirely; no shared datastore outage can stop serving, and enrichment becomes something we scale elastically with Live rather than a cluster we babysit.

Matching two streams after the fact is a streaming join, and that is where Flink comes in.

Why Flink

We chose Apache Flink because near-real-time, stateful stream processing is exactly what it is built for, and because it has deep, production-tested platform support at Netflix. Just as important, we already knew how to run it. As Part 1 noted, our Ads Sessionizer is a large stateful Flink job, so operating one at scale, tuning state, checkpoints, and recovery under production load, was familiar ground for the team. Enrichment on Flink was built on that experience rather than starting from scratch.

The new architecture

At its core, the new Ads Event Publisher is built as an Apache Flink streaming job. Each event moves through a handful of stages:

  1. Normalize. Client events arrive from several sources, including SVOD, live, playback, and embedded ad breaks, each with a slightly different shape. We first normalize them into a common form.
  2. Re-route. Client events and response events may appear in different regions; we inspect and reroute them to the correct job-processing region for a successful join.
  3. Join. The heart of the job: we match each client event to the ad-serving response for the same impression, enriching it with the full serving context using a KeyedCoProcessFunction
  4. Deduplicate. Revenue-bearing events are de-duplicated, so nothing is counted twice.
  5. Publish. We extract measurement beacons for our partners and route the enriched ad event to its downstream consumers.

The join is the interesting part. Client events and ad serving responses arrive on separate streams at different times, so the job holds recent responses in memory and matches events against them over a 60-minute window. Three things can happen:

  • The response is already there when an event arrives → we enrich it on the spot.
  • The event arrives first → we hold it for a configuration duration (currently set to 60 minutes) until the matching response shows up, then enrich it.
  • No response arrives within the window → we mark the event as unmatched for later recovery.

We built the join as a custom Flink operator (a KeyedCoProcessFunction) rather than a built-in windowed join. We do not need a windowed join ordering and time-window semantics, since downstream consumers handle ordering; we simply match each client event to its response by key. Owning the operator at its lowest API form lets us control the matching state directly, including how long we hold it and what we do with an event that never matches. This allows us to tune retention per stream or persist unmatched events to a durable store later without rewriting the join. Our goal is always to build a strong base to reap the benefits later as we scale.

To make that concrete, picture a member watching a live game. When the ad server decides which ad to show, it logs its response, and a few seconds later, the member’s device fires a “first quartile” event carrying the opaque token. Both arrive at the job keyed to the same impression, and because the response is already waiting, the event is enriched on the spot with its campaign, creative, price, and tracking URLs, then published downstream in near real-time.

Why 60 minutes? Almost all events, roughly 99.999% of them, reach the job well before that, so extending the window further would only grow the state store and lengthen checkpoints for a vanishingly small gain. The remaining 0.001% still matters for precise billing and reporting, and we recover those events via a separate path described later on.

Cross-region: matching events where their data lives

The Metadata Registry handled cross-region enrichment for us because it was built on a globally replicated key-value store: a client event could land in any region and still find its ad’s metadata. Global replication was a feature the platform provided (see Netflix’s Key-Value Data Abstraction Layer), so serving an ad in one region and enriching its events in another was simply not something we had to think about.

A streaming join does not come with that convenience, and here the two sides of the join live in different places. The ad serving response stays in the region where the ad was served. The client event, though, is fired by the device, and the device can be anywhere: a member might start an ad on home wifi and switch to mobile data partway through, and that network change can route the event to a different region than the one that served the ad. So a client event is routed to a region that does not have the matching serving response.

The tempting fix is to stream every region’s serving responses into every other region so that each region can match any client event locally. We rejected it: that would mean every region storing every serving response worldwide, the vast majority of which will never be used in the join, which is wasteful in both cost and compute.

Instead, we treat this as a routing problem and route the client event rather than replicating the response. We encode the serving region into the ad token, so when a client event arrives in the wrong region, we forward it to the region that owns its response. For example, an ad is served in us-east-2, the member’s device switches from wifi to mobile data mid-ad, and the resulting event arrives in us-east-1. That region reads the token, sees the ad belongs to eu-west-1, and forwards the event back there, where its serving response is waiting. Only the small trickle of genuinely cross-region events pays for the extra hop.

Catching the long tail of late-arriving events

Sixty minutes covers the vast majority of events, but not all of them. A device may have been offline, an ad paused, or an engagement event delayed by hours. Rather than drop these stragglers, we set them aside and recover them through a companion path: an hourly Spark batch job, orchestrated by Maestro, Netflix’s workflow orchestrator, re-pairs each straggler with its serving response from our data warehouse (which has a far longer retention than our in-stream window) and publishes it through the same downstream sinks. This keeps the streaming job’s memory bounded while still catching the long tail.

This also lets us support event types that arrive well after the 60-minute window, including certain tracking-related events, while keeping the door open to extending the system to additional event types down the line and improving our match rate as needed. We also designed this offline job with reuse in mind: it can replay dead-letter queues and backfill historical data, giving us a single mechanism for both long-tail recovery and operational recovery.

What was hard

Beyond the architecture itself, three things took real work, and together they are what made the pipeline stable, correct, and safe to switch on.

Keeping the core lean.

Operating a stateful streaming join at live-event scale took real tuning, and most of our hard-won lessons come back to one idea: the job’s only job is matching events. Anything else we were tempted to bolt on, such as external lookups or incidental side-processing, was better moved off the hot path, or it eventually showed up as instability under load. Getting this right was the difference between a job that comfortably kept pace with live traffic and one that fell behind. It is unglamorous work, and it is most of the work.

De-duplicating Events

Duplicates are a fact of life here in an event processing pipeline. A client may retry an event, and our upstream delivery is at-least-once so that the same event can arrive more than once. For revenue-bearing events, the ones that feed billing, nothing should be counted twice.

The solution here is a simple and idempotent key. For each event, we compute a stable ID by hashing a few fields that uniquely identify it, such as the ad ID, the event type, and, for repeatable events, an offset or timestamp. The same underlying event always hashes to the same ID, so if we have seen an ID before, we drop the repeat.

What changed with Flink is where we remember those IDs. The previous design kept them in an external key-value store and did a check-and-write over the network for every event; Flink lets us keep that state local to the job instead. We key the stream by event ID, which routes every copy of a given event to the same place, and a local state store with a short time-to-live remembers the IDs we have recently seen. Keying by ID also removes the race the external store had to guard against, since a given ID is handled in only one place at a time, with no network hop on the hot path. Multiple improvements here alone.

We are deliberate about the guarantee: at-least-once delivery with best-effort de-duplication, not exactly-once. In-stream dedup removes the vast majority of duplicates within its window. However, a few can still slip past, for instance, through a cross-region reroute, a late-arriving recovery, or a restart that replays recent events. So we also carry the event ID through to the enriched ad event itself, which lets consumers who need exact counts, such as billing, run their own idempotent de-duplication over their own, longer windows.

Production Rollout

This was the most challenging part of the project. For a system that feeds billing and frequency capping, “trust me, the new one is correct” is not good enough, so we ran the Flink pipeline alongside the legacy one and made it earn its traffic.

Both pipelines continuously processed the full event stream, allowing us to compare them in real time: we published their outputs side by side. We ran automated audits that alerted us when the two drifted apart. Those audits earned their keep, surfacing subtle discrepancies we would never have caught from dashboards alone.

How do we know the enrichment logic between the two systems was equal for the audits to make sense? Early in development, we extracted that logic into a shared module that both the legacy service and the Flink job depend on, so any change to how an event is enriched is applied to both at the same time. A failure in the audits, therefore, pointed to a real difference in the pipeline mechanics.

Cutover was a separate question from comparison, and this is the part that warrants precision. We could not simply send a random percentage of events to each pipeline, because the same event landing in both would be double-counted downstream. Instead, the split was deterministic: a stable key on each event decided which pipeline was responsible for publishing it, so every event was published exactly once, even though both pipelines saw all of them. Raising the threshold moved events from the legacy pipeline to Flink a slice at a time, and we could dial it back instantly if anything looked off.

By the time we fully cut over, the two pipelines agreed on well over 99.99% of events, and we rolled it out region by region rather than all at once. Then came the satisfying part: we turned off the ad server’s writes to the Metadata Registry, and decommissioned the legacy service and the registry itself. The single point of failure on the ad-serving critical path is simply gone. One of the oldest ad serving components at Netflix was deleted.

Operating the Flink platform

Operating a large stateful streaming job in production is its own job, and we did not build that muscle alone. We leaned heavily on Netflix’s Flink platform team. Early on, the job’s checkpoints were slow and heavy. The first checkpoint in particular took a long time, and we were holding more state in memory than we needed. Working with the platform team, we trimmed the state, reduced checkpoint durations, and validated the gains in load tests. That is what keeps the job from stalling during Live bursts.

The same team also gave us operational scaffolding we did not have to invest in, including continuous delivery and canary deployments, so we could ship and roll out the Flink job with the same guardrails and confidence as the rest of our production systems. Netflix operates more than 25,000 Flink jobs (see Building a Scalable Flink Platform at Netflix), and that maturity is what we have to build on. We layered on custom canary metrics that catch issues before a release, CI/CD that lets us stagger rollouts, and a deploy flow that keeps the old job running until the new one has detected healthy checkpoints, so we never destroy a working job before the new job gives us the green light.

The results

  • Enrichment is off the critical path for ad serving. The ad server no longer performs a synchronous, must-succeed database write to serve an ad. It logs and moves on, and an entire class of “the lookup store is down, so ad serving is down” failures no longer exists.
  • Fewer systems, fewer schemas, fewer hops. We retired both the legacy service and the Metadata Registry.
  • Built for Live, and continuously tested for it. An ad break is what this service is designed to handle, so during our journey, we also ran large-scale load tests to simulate real-life traffic. In our latest load test, a single AWS region handled one ad break for a large concurrent audience, processing hundreds of thousands of events per second, joining the large majority of them against their serving responses in real time, and outputting enriched ad events at a comparable rate, all with negligible timeouts and errors. We test this throughout development and keep doing so as live audiences grow, and we are not at the ceiling yet.
  • We delivered the Part 1 roadmap. Live-stream ad events, in-stream de-duplication, and richer real-time enrichment all shipped on this foundation.

Key takeaways

  • Take the database off the hot path when you can. Our biggest win wasn’t raw performance — it was blast radius. Trading a synchronous write-and-wait for a fire-and-forget log plus a downstream join removed an entire failure mode from ad serving.
  • Match events where their data lives. Real-time joins beat global replication by routing events to their data rather than copying the data everywhere.
  • Earn the cutover. Running both systems in parallel and diffing their output on live traffic was slower than a flag-day switch — and it’s the only reason we trust the result.

What’s next

We have an exciting list of projects on the horizon: scaling the live path for the next tier of concurrent audiences, bringing the remaining delayed engagement events fully into the streaming world, reducing the Flink state size we need to manage, working on bringing even more resilience to the eventing processing pipeline, and continuing to add new event types and richer signals for our downstream consumers.

Re-architecting the engine of a running, revenue-critical pipeline in place was a real multi-team effort. If building real-time systems at this kind of scale sounds like your thing, Ads Engineering is hiring.

Acknowledgements

This was a multi-team effort across Netflix. Thank you to everyone who designed, built, validated, and operated the new pipeline:

Ads Engineering: Yogesh Nagarur, Kinesh Satiya, Jeet Mehta, Nitin Saini, Persis Shah, Guangyu Chen, Jimmy Liu, Riley Berton, Simon Spencer, Aadesh Patel

Ads Data Engineering: Eugene Yusim, Brandon Nicklas, Indu Narayan

Ads SRE: Max Michaels, Kevin Chung, Carlos Avalos, Brian Christie

Data Movement: Mark Cho, Herbert Wang, Shraddha Ladda, Nikhil Sulegaon, James Lubin, Daniel Trager

title: From Copying to Composition: How Language Models Develop In-Context Learning
description:
arXiv:2610.19113v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In-context learning (ICL) allows language models to adapt their behavior from instructions and demonstrations in a prompt, but accuracy alone does not reveal how contextual information controls their predictions. We study the acquisition and trainability of ICL with a controlled diagnostic that separates copying a nearby demonstration from integrating information across the prompt. Across 17 models, about a third prefer the copied answer, a few are undecided, and the rest prefer the rule-consistent answer, which goes with higher accuracy and with control by the requested value rather than the closest conflicting example. Checkpoint analyses show that models begin prioritizing task-relevant prompt tokens over conflicting examples long before their accuracy improves beyond chance level. In matched training experiments, synthetic documents that define endings and then query them shift models toward compositional responses on the controlled diagnostic, whereas fine-tuning on definition exercises built from rewritten real documents improves accuracy when prompts reassign label meanings. The results suggest that ICL is not acquired as a single, uniform capability. Instead, prompt control, answer preference, construction without candidates, and transfer can develop along distinct trajectories.

title: Running Apache Spark experiments in my sleep (and on a plane)
description:
By Prashanth Gedde Narayanaswamy

As one of Netflix’s largest and critical data pipelines, member-sessionizer consolidates tens of billions of hourly client events, encompassing user taps, playbacks, and engagement signals, into individual viewing sessions per profile.

A quick two-week tuning effort spiraled into two months when standard approaches hit a wall. Because the failures only happened at full production scale, each test took hours, limiting me to just three or four attempts daily. The turning point was changing the goal: instead of trying to speed up a single run, I built a way to run and monitor multiple tests at once and track every result.

That mindset led to an unconventional setup: kicking off five Spark jobs at once and monitoring them over spotty inflight Wi-Fi during a day-long trip home, while cloud servers handled the actual heavy lifting. This post covers how I set up that loop, along with the Spark bottlenecks and memory quirks I uncovered along the way.

The Scale Dilemma: Small Samples Don’t Catch Scale Bugs

Standard engineering wisdom says that you should isolate bugs on small datasets to iterate quickly. That works for standard software bugs, but it fails completely for big data performance bottlenecks.

While upgrading our sessionization pipeline from a legacy logging architecture to a modern platform, the new job hit critical failures, including executor Out-Of-Memory (OOM) errors, severe shuffle spillage, and thousands of stage retries. None of these issues could be reproduced using sampled data. The failures only triggered at full production scale because of data skew: an idle Netflix tab left streaming overnight generates tens of thousands of telemetry events, while a typical session only produces a handful. A standard 1% sample misses these extreme long-tail sessions entirely.

To catch the real bugs, every test run had to execute against a full hour of unsampled production data, along with all the deployment overhead that came with it.

The Strategy: Branch-Driven Isolation

The biggest win came from a feature in Dataflow, Netflix’s command-line tool for building, testing, and deploying data pipelines. It supports branch-driven development: our workflows run on Maestro (Netflix’s workflow orchestrator), which schedules and executes the jobs, and they already use a sanitized branch name (the ${dataflow.sanitizedbranch} placeholder). So if I push a branch like pgn/cap-experiment, then the deployed workflow, its tables, and its run namespace all get tagged with that branch name. This eliminates collisions with team members or between my own concurrent runs.

With that isolation in place, the model was simple: one branch is one independent experiment. I parameterized the scheduler (cap size, shuffle partitions, heavy-device threshold, feature flags) and gave each variant its own branch and output table. Instead of queuing five sequential tests over 10 hours, I fired off five variants simultaneously against the same time window. Total execution time dropped from the sum of all runs to just the length of the single slowest job.

Managing per-branch tables added zero overhead. Dataflow provisions and updates tables automatically from declared schemas without manual DDL. Whenever I modified the event bag structure between experiments, the table schema updated seamlessly, no CREATE TABLE or ALTER TABLE required.

The only real constraint was cluster contention. Because these heavy Spark jobs shared resources with the rest of the company, peak hours sometimes limited me to two concurrent runs instead of five. But even running two or three jobs in parallel was a massive improvement over single-threaded debugging.

The key takeaway: don’t focus on making a single multi-hour run faster, build a setup where you can run many experiments simultaneously without them stepping on each other.

While the previous chart shows the time savings, the architecture that enables this isolation looks like below:

How an AI Agent Helped

Running five parallel experiments gets messy fast. Tracking instance IDs, configs, memory spills, and stage failures across variants makes it easy to lose track.

This is where an AI agent stepped in, not to write clever code, but to handle operational grunt work. I described variants in plain English, and the agent updated scheduler configs, deployed to the branch, triggered jobs, and polled metrics. Once complete, it compared spill and failure counts across variants in a summary table, allowing me to ask, “Which run is closest to OOM-free at peak load?” and get an immediate answer.

The value wasn’t deep Spark expertise, but operational memory. It turned tedious Spark UI cross-checks into a single prompt.

Eventually, I packaged this workflow into a reusable agent skill (.agents/skills/sandbox-deploy-and-run/) run via /sandbox-deploy-and-run <module> <scheduler-file> [PARAM=value]. It handles the full lifecycle—preflight, deploy, background polling, auto-diagnostics, and re-entrant resume <instance_id> support—turning multi-hour experiments into a single command.

Why tmux Mattered

All of this ran on Workbench, Netflix’s cloud dev environment, using my laptop as a thin terminal. Without session persistence, an SSH drop or sleeping laptop would kill multi-hour Spark runs mid-flight.

tmux running directly on Workbench solved this. Every experiment lived in a named cloud session: I could close my laptop, reattach hours later, and pick up where I left off. Combined with branch isolation, this made "start five and walk away" possible.

This is now my default setup: a local terminal (Ghostty), dedicated git worktrees per branch, and persistent tmux sessions on Workbench. The local laptop is disposable—closing it or losing network never interrupts the jobs.

That setup turned a long travel day into active iteration time. I kicked off batches at the gate, checked results via AI agent over spotty inflight Wi-Fi, and squeezed 4–5 full experiment cycles into a single 24-hour flight.

What All Experiments Uncovered

The root cause came down to a single operator: collect_list. Because Spark buffers each full event bag in memory, long-session OOMs were driven by individual bag size, not total dataset volume. The legacy pipeline handled identical row counts without crashing, proving that each event in the new bag had grown significantly heavier.

Two factors inflated event weight:

  • Field types and Option boxing: The session ID changed from an 8-byte Long to a UUID string. Worse, wrapping fields in Scala Option forced Spark to deserialize typed Datasets into JVM objects (Some wrappers), driving up object allocation and GC pressure across tens of thousands of events per session.
  • Bloated string attributes: Low-value fields (e.g., referrer URLs, test allocations) added several hundred bytes per event. Multiplying these strings across collect_list wasted terabytes per hour, even though downstream tasks rarely used them.

The Fixes:

  1. Unboxed primitives: Removing Option wrappers from non-nullable fields dropped peak executor memory from 112% to 58% of the slot with zero disk spill.
  2. Slimmed event bags: Dropped unused per-event attributes and hoisted session-invariant metadata (app version, country) up to the session header.

Takeaway: Reducing individual event weight delivered far better stability than throwing more cluster memory at the problem.

Two Experiments That Changed My Mind

Out of dozens of runs, two findings completely overturned my assumptions about Spark memory management:

  • Finding 1: Narrowing rows can trigger faster OOMs. Slimming our table dropped its size below Spark’s auto-broadcast threshold, prompting the query planner to switch from shuffle joins to broadcast joins. Because broadcast joins pin build-side tables directly into executor memory, narrower rows actually increased total memory pressure.
  • Finding 2: Broadcast hash joins were silently draining memory. Adaptive Query Execution (AQE) rewrote nine sort-merge joins into broadcast hash joins at runtime. While each join stayed under our 400 MB broadcast limit individually, AQE pinned ~3.1 GB of cumulative data simultaneously in a single executor, pushing containers over the edge.

The Surgical Fix: Instead of disabling broadcast joins globally, I lowered only AQE’s runtime threshold (spark.sql.adaptive.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold) to 10 MB while leaving the compile-time threshold untouched. That single change freed up ~3.1 GB of executor memory without impacting initial query planning.

Takeaway: Broadcast joins speed up queries, but pinned memory isn’t free. Watch accumulated broadcasts in your execution plan, not just dataset sizes.

Keeping a Single Experiment Log

When running dozens of parallel tests, the biggest risk isn’t job failure, it’s losing track of what you’ve already tried or confusing which JAR and config produced a result.

To solve this, I scaffolded the AI agent to append a row to a repository Markdown table after every run:

  • Run # | Jar ver | Change vs. Previous Run | Config | Key Metrics (Spill, Failed Tasks, Peak Memory, Duration)

If a run yielded a key finding, the agent added a short note explaining what the result proved or disproved.

Key Takeaways:

  • Single source of truth: It created an auditable history for the entire investigation.
  • Forced discipline: Requiring “Change vs. Previous Run” forced me to isolate variables. Whenever I bundled multiple changes, I couldn’t isolate the root cause and had to rerun the test — a mistake the log format immediately exposed.

A secondary doc (events-join-spark-tuning.md) captured the distilled findings as a quick "symptom-to-knob" lookup, so teammates didn't have to wade through the full chronological history.

A Mistake I Learned From: The Fix That Only Worked Off-Peak.

To cap session size, I added row_number().over(Window...) and filtered for the first N events. It passed off-peak tests cleanly, but crashed with OOMs at peak load.

The issue was structural: Spark’s Window operator buffers an entire session in memory before evaluating row numbers and filtering. The cap trimmed output downstream, but it didn't limit memory usage during buffering, so a single skewed session overwhelmed executor memory.

The Fix & Lesson: We moved truncation ahead of the Window stage to cap events before buffering occurs.

Takeaway: Test fixes against worst-case input skew. Off-peak runs hide structural bottlenecks that peak scale will immediately trigger.

The final fix

Pulling it together, four changes shipped, each isolated to a single experiment before it landed:

  • Unboxed the never-null fields from Option to plain primitives. Peak executor memory dropped from about 112% of the slot to about 58%, with zero spill.
  • Slimmed the event bag. Dropped per-event fields nobody used, and hoisted session-invariant fields (versions, country, connection type) to the session level so they are stored once per session, not once per event.
  • Capped session size before the Window stage. Dropped oversized sessions ahead of the buffering, and truncated the bag to the cap rather than dropping whole sessions.
  • Lowered AQE’s runtime broadcast threshold. Set spark.sql.adaptive.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold to 10 MB, leaving the compile-time threshold untouched.

The Unresolved Bottleneck

While these fixes made the pipeline run cleanly, they didn’t solve the underlying scaling issue: aggregating an entire session’s event bag into a single row has a hard ceiling. As our upstream telemetry source evolves and adds new attributes, each event in the bag becomes heavier, meaning this memory pressure will eventually return without a single line of code changing on our end.

Slimming and unboxing bought us headroom, but they didn’t change the fundamental data shape. The biggest takeaway from this effort is that tuning buys time, not infinite scale. If your underlying data model allows unbounded row growth, tuning alone won’t save you , eventually, the architecture itself has to change.

Summary

  • If the bug only appears at scale, stop trying to sample. Build a way to run many full-scale runs in parallel instead.
  • If your scheduler can use the branch name, then one branch becomes one isolated experiment, and running many at once becomes easy.
  • Use an AI agent to run the operation, not only to write code. Deploy, poll, pull metrics, compare variants: this is where most of the time goes.
  • Once a loop repeats, package it as a skill. The deploy-run-watch-diagnose cycle becomes one command.
  • Use tmux for long runs. The run must survive you closing the laptop.
  • Keep one single experiment log, and make every entry state the one change from the previous run. The format itself forces you to change one variable at a time.
  • For memory problems, look at the per-row width first, not only at the total data volume. Bigger field types, Option boxing, and fat unused strings all add up inside a collect_list bag.
  • Tuning buys headroom, not a new ceiling. If the data shape can grow without a bound, the design has to change eventually, tuning alone will not save you.

Running Apache Spark experiments in my sleep (and on a plane) was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: SPECTRA-VLA: Base-Fine Hyperspectral Token Transfer at Frozen Vision-Language-Action Interfaces
description:
arXiv:2610.19651v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Hyperspectral imaging distinguishes RGB-similar objects, but a pretrained vision-language-action model needs a state its frozen decoder can use. SPECTRA-VLA provides a native-width spectral upgrade without retraining the visual encoder or action decoder. A learned continuous residual enriches each target token through its own normalized false-color reference; projection, norm control and validation-calibrated injection regulate the change. Across 86 held-out acquisitions, category balanced accuracy rises from 0.812 to 0.883. With identical residuals and scale, own-token addition improves reuse of an external category-derived probe on frozen decoder logits: 0.701 versus 0.590 with pooled replacement, at similar image-disjoint recognition. Five grouped tests covering the same 86 acquisitions recover within-category spectral shape with $R^2=0.802/0.337$ from continuous and posterior-code states. Category-matched spectral swaps further show that own-token composition approximately doubles the target-specific recovery increment after frozen decoding. Spectral enrichment and receiving-token preservation thus work together at the pretrained interface.

title: Cross-Modal Latent Influence: Patch-Level Training Sample Attribution for Vision-Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.14190v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Explaining a vision--language model (VLM) prediction requires tracing training-example influence to the multimodal evidence that mediates it, yet existing attribution methods largely operate only at the sample level. Recent latent-mediated influence methods provide feature-level attribution in language models, but lack the multimodal and spatial structure needed to ground influence in VLMs. We introduce MOSAIC (Multimodal Orthogonalized Sparse Autoencoders for Influence Characterization). It learns a shared sparse image--text latent space whose concepts are 1) sparse within each modality, 2) supported on contiguous image regions, 3) aligned to the phrases that describe them, and 4) approximately decorrelated. It then applies EK-FAC to decompose training-example influence through these concepts and localize their contributions to specific text phrases and image regions. We evaluate MOSAIC on Qwen and Gemma across captioning, chest X-ray understanding, and visual question answering. The learned features are more localized and coherent without degrading task behavior, and ablating influence-ranked latents changes model outputs more than ablating latents ranked by activation or frequency. We find that visual evidence can substantially reorganize training-data attribution while preserving more of the shared latent structure. MOSAIC thus connects where model behavior comes from with what multimodal evidence carries that influence.

title: Reliable GPU compute for large training & inference jobs
description:
Authors: Nick Rutigliano, Argha C, Samartha Chandrashekar

How we detect failing GPUs and network fabric, remediate machines automatically, and let long-running jobs survive hardware loss.

Open Netflix, and the home screen is assembled for you: which rows appear, the order they appear in, the titles within them, and the artwork for each title are chosen by machine learning models trained on how hundreds of millions of members watch. Personalization is one of the most widely used things we build, and members feel it every time they open the app. Like a growing share of Netflix, it runs on GPUs, which train those models and increasingly serve them live.

Those GPUs have to stay healthy for that experience to hold up, and keeping them healthy is harder than it sounds. A single large training job can run for weeks across hundreds of GPUs spread over many machines. It runs as a gang: the ranks move in lockstep, exchanging data every step, so the job advances only as fast as its slowest participant and stops entirely if one participant dies. Every GPU, every high-speed network adapter, and every interconnect must keep working throughout the run. At the scale at which modern machine learning runs, individual GPUs and network links can fail during a run, so the underlying platform must be prepared for this and handle it without a person in the loop.

This post describes how we keep our GPU infrastructure healthy for training and inference. We cover how we detect failing hardware before and during jobs, how we automatically remediate a bad machine, and how we let a long job survive the loss of a machine. These training workloads run on our modern Kubernetes-native Compute platform.

Why GPU reliability matters

Netflix aims to entertain the world, and machine learning has been part of how we do that for years, from the recommendations that help members find something to watch to the systems that help produce and promote titles. As generative AI advances, we are investing in it on both sides of the business: for members, through better recommendations and higher-quality promotional assets; and for storytelling, through creative tools for our production partners.

All of this runs on GPUs, for both training and inference, and GPU capacity is among the fastest-growing and most expensive parts of our infrastructure. That makes reliability a business concern on two fronts. — -

  • Availability: a training run that loses a machine, or an inference service that cannot get healthy capacity, delays work that members and creators depend on.
  • Cost efficiency: a GPU sitting idle behind a slow neighbor, or a whole machine pulled from the pool because one device is degraded, becomes capacity we paid for and are not using. Higher reliability and higher utilization mean more useful work per GPU, which is equivalent to spending less to do the same work.

Inference is a growing share of that GPU footprint as more of these AI features reach members, so the reliability and efficiency that matter for multi-week training runs increasingly matter for always-on serving too.

Why basic health checks are not enough

We start from the baseline provided by the cloud provider. Cloud providers run instance status checks on virtual machines: a system status check for the underlying host’s power, network, and hardware reachability; an instance status check to verify that the operating system is up and reachable; and a check on attached storage. It emits scheduled maintenance events when it plans to retire or reboot a host, and it can automatically recover an instance that becomes impaired. We use all of these, and the maintenance events feed one of our own checks. They catch a machine that is down, unreachable, or slated for maintenance, and they stop at the instance level. They confirm the box is up and reachable. They do not verify that each GPU, its on-chip memory, its interconnect, and its network fabric are healthy enough to support distributed training.

The next step most teams take is a GPU-level check to confirm that the driver responds and that the GPUs are visible. That catches a dead or missing GPU, but misses the cases that take the most time.

  • A GPU can answer a status query and still be faulty once a workload touches it. A fault in on-chip memory or in the firmware that manages the device can remain invisible until a job allocates memory or runs sustained compute, at which point the job fails or slows.
  • A high-speed network adapter may be present but show fewer links than expected. Collective operations still run, at a fraction of the bandwidth, so the job does not crash. It crawls, and the cause is easy to miss.
  • A check can fail in ways that leave a faulty machine looking healthy. The diagnostic tool can hang when the driver hangs, and a naive check that waits on it hangs too. A binary that the check depends on can go missing after a driver upgrade, causing the check to stop running and report nothing. A check that can silently stop running is worse than no check, because it gives false confidence while the machine keeps working.

Because a job runs as a gang, any one of these on any one machine can degrade or stop the whole job, and none of them shows up in an instance-level check or a driver-responds check. The health system has to assume the hardware can lie and the tools that inspect it can break.

Our approach

We treat reliability as four layers, each catching what the layer below cannot:

1/ Node and hardware health: find bad GPUs, network adapters, interconnects, memory errors, and thermal issues, then taint or recycle the machine.

2/ Scheduler and platform: retry at the task & job level, validate a machine before it takes work, and drain & recycle machines safely.

3/ Training loop: checkpoint and use elastic workers so a job survives losing a machine.

4/ Observability: metrics, service-level objectives, and failure attribution across the other three.

The first two layers keep hardware problems away from jobs. The third accepts that some loss is unavoidable and makes it cheap. The fourth tells us whether the first three are working.

How the health checks work

Checks run in two tiers. Device-level checks look at each GPU. A node-level agent, built on the open-source Kubernetes node-problem-detector, runs on every GPU machine every 30 seconds and turns check results into conditions on the Kubernetes node, the same mechanism Kubernetes uses to mark a node NotReady. Controllers watch those conditions and decide whether the machine can take on work.

GPU device checks are built on NVIDIA’s DCGM for driver-reported error codes, uncorrectable memory errors, interconnect integrity, and thermal state, and networking adapter checks inspect the host state for the count and link state of the Elastic Fabric Adapter interfaces that carry cross-machine traffic. A few of these checks deserve detail.

  • Failing closed: if the driver or the diagnostic tool is unresponsive, the check times out and marks the machine unhealthy. A check that cannot reach the hardware reports a problem rather than passing, so a wedged driver takes the machine out of rotation rather than letting it hide behind a hung tool.
  • A fallback path: driver error codes are the strongest signal that a GPU has faulted, but the tool that reads them can itself be broken in certain failure modes! When it does, we read the kernel log dmesg directly for those codes, so no Xid or SXid errors are missed.
  • Our own fatal-error map: vendor driver error catalogs lag newer GPU generations and do not always match what we see in production, so we keep our own mapping of which codes are fatal for each GPU family. A code that means reset-the-GPU in one generation can be benign in another, and one GPU generation emits a burst of normally-fatal code on every healthy boot, which we learned to treat as noise rather than drain fresh machines.
  • No silent no-ops: a check fails when a required dependency is missing. This one came from an upgrade that dropped a binary the network-adapter check relied on. The check quietly stopped running, and machines with the wrong number of adapters shipped for days before the slow jobs were traced back to them. Now a missing dependency fails the check.

Turning a bad machine into healthy capacity, automatically

When a check fails, the machine’s node condition changes, and controllers take over. We distinguish two levels. A problem condition blocks new work from landing while jobs are running, because pulling a job off a machine is disruptive, and many problems clear on their own. If the condition persists beyond a tolerance window, it escalates to a failure condition, which evacuates the machine, drains its tasks (overriding the normal disruption limits to move quickly), terminates it, and replaces it.

Karpenter node auto-repair is used on our compute stack. We have customized it with a policy and a controller that maps each node condition to the duration we tolerate it before acting, so a fast-fatal error is actioned within minutes. At the same time, a flaky signal gets a longer window, and a cap limits how much of a cluster we will disrupt at once, so a bad rollout of the checks themselves cannot cascade into tearing down a whole cluster. We plan to upstream this feature to all Karpenter users.

Not every fault requires a full replacement, and replacement is the slowest way to restore capacity. We match the action to the fault. Killing the offending job clears a software wedge. Resetting a single GPU clears many transient device faults. Rebooting the machine clears the firmware state that has drifted over a long uptime. Terminating and replacing is reserved for hardware that fails a test we trust. For that last case, we record the GPU’s immutable hardware identifier, which stays with the physical device across reboots and relaunches even when the instance changes, report it to the cloud provider, and keep our own list, so a device that fails repeatedly does not quietly rejoin the pool under a new instance.

One subtlety sits between detection and scheduling. A freshly checked machine was handed to the scheduler just as its checks were still settling, so a job could land on it a moment before a slow check flagged it. We now hold capacity until the checks have run and settled, which closed that window.

Validating a machine before it takes work

A machine that just booted is not trusted until it proves itself. Before we release its capacity, it passes system checks, confirms the GPUs and their topology are present, and runs a round of GPU diagnostics. We then wait for the health checks to run twice, because the longer checks, such as counting network adapters, take more than one cycle to fire, and releasing after a single pass would let work land before those checks are reported. Only then do we remove the startup taint. On teardown, we run deeper diagnostics and record the GPU identifiers, which feed the same bad-hardware list, so hardware that failed once does not silently cycle back into service.

Letting long jobs survive machine loss

Even with all of the above, some machines are lost mid-job, so we make that cheap. Jobs checkpoint their state, and on a lost machine, they resume from the last healthy checkpoint rather than restarting from the beginning of a multi-week run. Workers are elastic and retryable, and the scheduler automatically retries platform-caused failures.

Attribution is what makes automatic retries safe. If we retried every failure, we would mask genuine bugs in a job and burn GPU hours looping on an error the platform cannot fix, so we classify each failure as platform or application before retrying. One example of why this matters: a class of timeouts in NCCL, the collective communication library GPUs use to exchange data, appeared to be a network fault and was traced to data-loading stalls at high worker counts. The GPUs and the network were fine, and the fix was in the data pipeline. Treated as hardware failures, those timeouts would have cycled healthy machines without fixing the cause.

Measuring whether it works

We track GPU reliability along three service-level objectives, each split by cause, so a miss points at the layer responsible:

  • Availability: the amount of GPU capacity available for scheduling at any given moment.
  • Job-start success: whether a job starts promptly once its capacity is available.
  • Job success: whether a job finishes without a platform-caused failure.

Each objective is split into hardware, driver, platform, and user causes. Hence, an availability dip from bad hardware reads differently from one caused by a scheduler change or a user misconfiguration. We optimize for goodput, the useful work the fleet completes, because a job held back by one slow GPU can look healthy on an uptime chart while getting almost nothing done. Specific targets for each objective are provided here for illustrative purposes.

A closed remediation loop

These pieces form a loop. Hardware is validated at allocation, before a job starts, with a short collective communication run and pairwise network tests. Hence, any machine that fails within the first minute fails before the job is admitted. During the job, we watch passively for driver errors, memory errors, thermal events, and more. We view each job as a distributed system, which lets us identify a single slow rank dragging the rest, rather than only whole-machine failures. When something is wrong, remediation is automatic and graded. The loop is the same whether a job runs through our batch scheduler, Kueue, or Ray.

Sharing GPUs safely

Not every workload needs a whole GPU, and leaving small inference jobs on dedicated GPUs wastes capacity. We partition GPUs with MIG for memory-level isolation between tenants, so a fault or a memory hog in one partition does not affect another. We also reconfigure those partitions without restarting the machine, so that a pool can shift between many small slices and a few large ones as demand changes. GPU and network adapter allocation is device-plugin-based today, to move to Kubernetes Dynamic Resource Allocation once it is supported in Karpenter. This matters because a GPU talking to a network adapter or working with a CPU on the wrong PCIE root of the machine incurs a bandwidth penalty.

Device-level allocation also changes how we handle a single bad GPU. With DRA support, instead of losing the whole machine, we could isolate the one faulty device and keep the others serving, which matters most for inference, where many small jobs share a machine. And because allocation is expressive, a job can request the capabilities it needs, such as memory or tensor-core support, and the platform matches a suitable GPU type, so users are not pinned to a model they had to choose in advance.

Results

Moving from basic checks and manual draining to layered checks and automatic remediation changed two things users feel. More of the GPU fleet is available for scheduling at any time because bad machines are caught and cycled quickly, rather than sitting in the pool or waiting on an on-call engineer. And fewer jobs fail due to platform issues because most faults are caught before a job lands, and the rest are automatically remediated and retried. Graded remediation also returns capacity in minutes for faults that only require a job kill, a GPU reset, or a reboot, rather than the longer wait for a replacement machine.

Since the above improvements have landed, we’ve seen:

  • Consistently achieving >99.95% availability of our GPU nodes
  • Job success rate has gone from ~98% to above 99.5%

What is next

We are extending active checks to cover additional failure modes under load, widening burn-in so more classes of failures can be cleared before a user encounters them, and making remediation more granular so more error types are cleared in place rather than requiring a full node replacement loop for certain Xid errors. Additionally, we want to do more periodic diagnostics between jobs.

We are working to make placement more topology-aware using Kubernetes Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) once it lands in Karpenter, for example, by aligning on Compute/IMEX Domains, PCIe roots, and NUMA nodes.

More on the performance side for multi-GPU training, we plan to run a custom Linux scheduler built on sched_ext. Firstly, we can prioritize processes during collective coordination, such as when GPUs exchange results before the next round of compute, thereby reducing overall GPU idle time by establishing a fleet-wide priority for these tasks. The effect is small on one machine but grows across hundreds of machines, where a few percent of throughput amounts to a large amount of capacity. Secondly, we can prioritize data-loading processes to minimize the bottleneck that sometimes occurs when data is not loaded onto GPUs quickly enough to maintain steady progress.

While we already monitor throttling events, GPUs do not have to report throttling for it to hurt a job. One running ten to fifteen degrees hotter than its peers, even within healthy limits, sets the pace for the gang, so we can treat a large temperature gap as a fault, stop the job, and move it to cooler GPUs.

Additionally, we plan to expand our NCCL RAS (reliability, availability, serviceability) monitoring to identify NCCL issues sooner, such as mismatched collectives or hangs, to more quickly resume work.

Closing

Hardware fails, and at this scale, it fails often enough that the platform has to treat failure as normal. Detecting problems before and during jobs, automatically remediating machines, and allowing long jobs to resume after a loss lets teams run large-scale training and inference without babysitting the hardware. If you like these kinds of problems, we are hiring.

Reliable GPU compute for large training & inference jobs was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
