title: Dimension-Free Scaling Laws for Size Generalization: An Exponential Separation
description:
arXiv:2610.19279v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Modern machine learning models increasingly operate on variable-size structured data, such as sets and graphs. A central requirement is \emph{size generalization}: the ability of a model trained on inputs of one size to generalize to inputs of a different, potentially much larger, size. Classical statistical learning theory, however, primarily considers fixed input domains, and its guarantees often deteriorate with input dimension. Although extensive work has established when models on sets and graphs can be transferred across input sizes, such results do not characterize the statistical cost of doing so: the sample complexity of size generalization, and its relationship to classical in-domain learning, remain largely unknown. We develop a statistical learning theory of size generalization and establish a sharp exponential separation in sample complexity. Letting $n$ denote the number of training samples, we show that polynomial source decay is insufficient for efficient size generalization: while it yields error $n^{-\Theta(1)}$ and hence polynomial sample complexity for in-domain learning, size-generalization error decays only as $(\log n)^{-\Theta(1)}$, yielding an exponential separation. Thus, polynomial in-domain sample complexity can become exponential across sizes. We then identify an exponential source condition under which size generalization achieves error $n^{-\Theta(1)}$, recovering polynomial sample complexity. These guarantees are independent of input dimension and depend only on the number of training samples, yielding dimension-free scaling laws. We also provide matching minimax lower bounds, establishing optimality. To our knowledge, this work provides the first dimension-free minimax theory of size generalization and a rigorous characterization of when, and at what statistical cost, learning can transfer across input sizes.

title: Following the Flow the Law Requires: Training Voice Agents to Transfer to Unseen Regulated Procedures in Debt Collection
description:
arXiv:2610.18881v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Voice agents built on large language models (LLMs) now handle customer calls, but in regulated applications completing the task is not enough: the agent must follow a conversational flow set by law. In debt collection, it must confirm it is speaking to the debtor before mentioning the debt, identify itself and the creditor, state the amount, and avoid prohibited language. Every creditor turns these rules into its own procedure and revises it. We ask whether a small, self-hosted policy can be trained once and then follow regulated procedures it has never seen. One machine-readable specification per deployment, FlowSpec, generates the policy instruction, gates the tools, supplies the supervision and defines the tests; the agent speaks only approved catalogue sentences. We fine-tune a 9-billion-parameter model on 2,506 conversations from 297 randomized procedures and evaluate a Thai outbound-call agent on four unseen deployment procedures (three debt collection, one non-debt), one from a wholly withheld lineage. Documented checks, fixed by the procedure, rise from 67--71 percents to 93--100 percents, while grounded checks, fixed by the conversation, already pass at 97--100 percents before training; scenario pass rate rises from 15/43 to 40/43. An audit of the shared specification finds 11 defects, 3 of which its own metric did not expose.

title: "4200subscribers": the content said "black" and the renderer believed it
description:
Our numerical reasoning practice shows you source material (a table, a bar
chart, a line graph) and asks you questions about it. The content that drives
those charts carries a unit alongside each value, because "4200" on its own
means nothing and "4200 subscribers" does.

For a while, several of our charts rendered that as:

4200subscribers

Which is the single most recognisable bug in the genre. Here is the code that
produced it, and if you have written a dashboard you have written this line:

<span className="font-semibold">
  {hasValue ? `${value}${unit}` : '-'}
</span>

Template literal, value, unit. Correct for 45 and %. Wrong for 4200 and
subscribers. And the fix is not "add a space", because then you get:

4200 %
£ 286000

Worse, the currency case is not a spacing problem at all. A pound symbol is a
prefix, so gluing it on in either direction gives you 286000£, which is not
how anyone writes money in English.

Three shapes, one function

The unit strings in our content fall into three groups, and they want three
different treatments:

shape examples rendering
currency £, $, £m symbol leads, remainder trails
symbol or one letter %, k, % per year attach directly
word or multi-letter hours, MWh, thousand households space between

So the concatenation became a function. All 32 lines of it, docstring included:

/**
 * Join a data value to the unit a question bank gives for it.
 *
 * Bank units come in three shapes, and gluing them straight on reads wrong for
 * two of them: "4200subscribers", "£4200" rendered as "4200£".
 */
export function formatWithUnit(value: number | string, unit = ''): string {
  if (!unit) return String(value);

  if (/^[£$€]/.test(unit)) {
    const symbol = unit[0];
    const rest = unit.slice(1);
    const n = typeof value === 'number' ? value : Number(value);
    // "-£5", not "£-5".
    return Number.isFinite(n) && n < 0
      ? `-${symbol}${Math.abs(n)}${rest}`
      : `${symbol}${value}${rest}`;
  }

  if (unit.startsWith('%') || unit.startsWith(' ') || unit.length === 1) {
    return `${value}${unit}`;
  }

  return `${value} ${unit}`;
}

Some notes on the decisions in there, because every branch is a judgement call
someone will want to argue with.

Currency is split, not matched whole. The unit £m is a symbol plus a
magnitude, and they go on opposite sides of the number: £12m. Taking
unit[0] as the symbol and unit.slice(1) as the remainder handles £, $m
and €bn with one branch.

Negative numbers move the sign outside the symbol. £-5 is the kind of
output that makes a reader stop and squint at a chart, which in a timed practice
test is a cost I am imposing on them for nothing. Three lines to produce -£5.

% per year attaches, per year would not. The rule is "starts with %",
not "is %", because a percentage of something still wants the sign tight
against the number: 2.5% per year.

length === 1 catches k and m without a list. Any one-character unit
attaches directly. It is a heuristic and I am comfortable with it: there is no
single-letter unit in English that wants a space.

A unit that already begins with a space is left exactly as written. This is
the escape hatch. If a piece of content needs spacing this function would not
give it, the content can say so and the function will not second-guess it.

The test file is all cases, which is the right shape for a pure function like
this:

expect(formatWithUnit(4200, 'subscribers')).toBe('4200 subscribers');
expect(formatWithUnit(1840, 'MWh')).toBe('1840 MWh');
expect(formatWithUnit(2.5, '% per year')).toBe('2.5% per year');
expect(formatWithUnit(12, '£m')).toBe('£12m');
expect(formatWithUnit(-5, '$')).toBe('-$5');
expect(formatWithUnit(7, ' units')).toBe('7 units');
expect(formatWithUnit('n/a', '')).toBe('n/a');

That last one is why the signature takes number | string. A value is not
always a number; sometimes a table cell says n/a, and Number('n/a') is NaN,
which is how you end up shipping a chart that reads "NaN%".

Two components were doing their own concatenation across five call sites, and
both now call this instead. The interesting part was not writing the function,
it was that the same mistake had been written twice independently, because
${value}${unit} looks so obviously right that nobody reviews it.

The same bug wearing a different hat

In the same commit, this:

const SHAPE_COLORS: Record<KFLogicalShape['color'], string> = {
  red: '#ef4444',
  blue: '#3b82f6',
  green: '#22c55e',
  yellow: '#eab308',
  black: '#1f2937',
};

Four of those are colours. The fifth is a role. Red means red, but "black"
means ink, and #1f2937 is a very dark grey that was effectively invisible
against the dark card those shapes are drawn on. In dark mode, the item that
the content called black was the one you could not see.

  // "Black" is the ink colour, so it follows the theme's foreground: a fixed
  // #1f2937 vanished into the dark card the frames sit on.
  black: 'currentColor',

With className="text-foreground" on the SVG, so currentColor resolves to
whatever the theme says text is. One word in a lookup table, and the shape is
dark on light and light on dark.

The thing both bugs have in common

Our content banks store descriptive strings: a unit, a colour name, a label.
Both of these bugs came from a renderer taking one of those strings literally.
unit was treated as a suffix because it usually is. black was treated as a
hex value because it usually is. In both cases the right move is for the
renderer to interpret the string as a declaration of intent rather than as
output.

That is an easy sentence to write after the fact and an annoying one to act on
in advance. The practical version: when a data field's name is a noun from the
problem domain rather than from the view layer, do not pipe it into the view
unexamined.

Both fixes are on live pages if you want to look at them. The charts and tables
that carry these units are what
numerical reasoning practice
is made of, the tabbed source documents are listed on
Aon's practice page, and the abstract shape
sequences whose "black" is now ink are the Elements Logical test on
Korn Ferry's. Each page says which of
its tests are free.

title: ISC Stormcast For Thursday, October 15th, 2026 https://isc.sans.edu/podcastdetail/10138, (Thu, Oct 15th)
State of agent skills
description:
In seven months, the skills.sh registry grew to one million agent skills and recorded nearly 280 million installs.

A skill gives an AI agent reusable instructions for a particular job. Agents are capable but generic; they can do many jobs, but they don't know how a specific person, team, or company does them. A skill supplies that missing context and can be as simple as a file written in ordinary language.

Anthropic introduced Agent Skills in October 2025, and Vercel launched the skills.sh registry three months later.

Using aggregate data from the registry, this report follows a new market through its first million skills: what people teach agents, what gets installed, and where the value is heading.

Skills turn expertise into software

To write a skill, some of the judgment behind a job has to be made explicit, like the steps to follow, what good looks like, and how to evaluate the result. The agent and its tools already supply much of the underlying capability, so the skill only has to provide the judgment and instructions specific to a job.

This makes skills faster and easier to create than conventional software.

skills.sh reached one million skills in seven months. GitHub took 27 months to reach one million repositories. Apple's App Store took just over five years to get to one million apps. npm took more than nine years to reach one million packages.

Far more people can describe how work should be done than program a computer to do it. And once a skill is written, it can be distributed and installed without being rewritten for each agent. Skills pair a much larger pool of creators with software’s capacity for reuse, driving the explosive growth of the ecosystem.

What people are teaching agents

We classified the registry's most-installed skills by the kind of work they help agents do. Together, these skills account for more than four-fifths of all installs. Published listings show supply: what authors have made available to agents; installs show demand: what people want their agents to learn.

Supply leans technical. More than half of listings teach software engineering, agent workflows, data, infrastructure, or security, with software engineering alone accounting for about a quarter.

Demand is more distributed. There's isn't a single category with more than a fifth of installs. Software engineering remains the largest at 18%, followed by agent workflows at 15%, then business operations and writing at nearly 11% each.

To see how each category performs for its size, we also compared its installs per listing with the average.

Business operations, writing and documents, and cloud and infrastructure get the most installs per listing. Demand for that work is split across fewer skills, so each one carries more of it. The average business operations skill draws 74% more installs than the average, writing and documents 50% more, cloud and infrastructure 42% more.

Software engineering, education and productivity, and research are oversupplied. The average software engineering skill draws about 30% fewer installs than average, education and productivity 39% fewer, research 55% fewer.

To write a skill, you need to understand a job. To install one, you need only want the job done. Most skills are technical because they began in developer tools. Installs cover a much broader range of work because agents are useful in every part of a company.

Skills that improve how agents work are among the most installed

Agent workflows and automation account for 14.8% of installs in the classified dataset, second only to software engineering. Among listings with at least 100,000 installs, agent workflows are the largest category.

Agent workflow and automation skills teach agents how to plan, route work, use tools, and automate browsers, abilities that apply across many jobs. A contract-review skill applies to contracts, but a planning skill applies to any job the agent takes on, contracts included.

People are using agents to improve agents. And because agents also help write skills, the catalog grows by improving the very machinery used to build it.

A few skills capture most installs

Install activity is highly concentrated. Nearly half of all skills were installed exactly once. At the other end, 375 skills, or 0.04% of the registry, account for 62% of installs, and the top 1.2% account for 94% of installs.

For all that concentration, there's no single winner. Even the most-installed skill accounts for less than 1% of all installs.

Skills compete within jobs and accumulate across them. Once a team chooses an expense-report skill, it has little reason to install another expense-report skill. But it can use that skill alongside others for spreadsheets, research, and presentations. Each job crowns its own winner, and the winners together carry most of the installs.

Seven in eight installs go to skills any industry can use

We also classified each skill by whether its work was shared across industries or specific to one. Tasks such as cleaning up a spreadsheet or deploying a website recur at banks and hospitals, law firms and restaurants. These cross-industry skills account for 66% of classified skills and 87.5% of installs. On average, they receive 3.6 times as many installs per listing as industry-specific skills.

The advantage is portability, whether a skill reaches across jobs, like agent workflows, or across industries. The skills installed most are the ones the most people can use.

The next generation of skills

The first million skills taught agents what everyone knows. The next million will teach your agents what only you know.

Public skills and better models are making general expertise available to every team, which will turn it into the baseline rather than any kind of advantage. More of the differentiating value will move to company-specific judgment. For example, when a customer gets a refund or what can ship without another review.

The measure of a skill will also shift from popularity to effectiveness. Today, the best signal of a skill's quality is its install count. As models improve, the bar rises, because a skill justifies itself only if the agent does the job better with it than without it. Skills will get tests and benchmarks that measure exactly that.

Skills have already turned expertise into software. The public catalog will continue to grow as supply catches up to demand. And organizations will build on top of it, writing down the knowledge only they have and maintaining it the same way they now maintain code.

Explore the first million, or add to the next, at skills.sh.

About this report

This report uses aggregate skills.sh data. A few notes on measurement:

  • Catalog totals count unique registry listings.

  • Install figures use aggregate registry counters. They do not represent unique people or necessarily independent choices.

  • Function and industry findings describe a classified sample rather than the full catalog.

  • Each analysis uses the latest complete data available. Figures may be revised as the underlying data and methodology improve.

title: FireGraphNet: Sub-daily wildfire spread prediction with directed graph neural networks
description:
arXiv:2610.19191v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Wildfire decisions are made in hours, yet most learned spread models predict daily on targets including burned area. We propose FireGraphNet which formulates 12-hour growth as node classification on directed H3 graphs, with candidates ahead of the front and wind alignment, terrain, fuel continuity and barriers on edges. On satellite perimeters it achieves average precision 1.7-1.9x the strongest distance baseline on test California fires and 1.62x out of state. We show this skill comes from message passing rather than cell features or the aggregator, is highest on young fires in state, is carried deep along the wind by its edges, and is hidden by pooling. A convolutional network matches this ranking once trained on new growth, at worse calibration, so candidate construction, target definition, and aggregation shape conclusions about model skill. Editing fuel and barrier attributes reduces predicted spread more under guided than random placement, extending FireGraphNet to operational intervention analysis.

title: Vercel Marketplace database browser now supports Redis
description:
You can now run Redis commands, browse keys, and inspect values directly in the Vercel dashboard using the Marketplace database browser.

Both the Redis and Upstash for Redis integrations in Vercel Marketplace are supported, so you no longer need redis-cli or a separate database UI.

From your project, open Infrastructure > Storage and select a Redis database. The database page now includes two new tabs:

  • CLI: Run Redis commands and inspect the results. Run multiple commands by separating them with newlines or semicolons, with support for MULTI/EXEC transactions.

  • Browser: Browse keys in a flat list or grouped by prefix, and filter them by type or pattern. Select a key to inspect its value and metadata, including its type, TTL, encoding, and size. Supported value types include string, JSON, hash, list, set, and sorted set.

These tabs are currently available only to team members with the Owner role. Learn more in the Marketplace storage documentation.

title: Mapping Arctic Polynyas from Sea Ice Concentration Data Using Hierarchical Partitioning and Differentiated Region Growing: Sensitivity to Threshold and Product Choices
description:
arXiv:2610.19647v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Accurately delineating Arctic coastal polynyas from sea ice concentration data remains challenging because of complex coastal geometry and spatially heterogeneous ice conditions. We develop a daily sea ice concentration (SIC) mapping framework based on hierarchical partitioning, connected-component analysis, and differentiated region growing for polynya and open-water regions. Applied to September-May ice seasons from 2002/03 to 2024/25, the framework achieves a mean overall accuracy of 96.74% and a mean kappa coefficient of 0.93 in the 63-scene visual assessment. Sensitivity experiments reveal a consistent pattern: the absolute magnitude of SIC-defined polynya extent is strongly configuration-dependent, whereas major temporal features are comparatively more stable. Relative to a 75% upper SIC threshold, seasonal extent integrals differ by 13.48%, 32.47%, and 65.04% at thresholds of 80%, 85%, and 90%, respectively, while the broad interannual structure remains recognizable. The response is also strongly regional and seasonal, with the largest threshold sensitivity in the Central Arctic Ocean, very weak sensitivity in the Gulf of St. Lawrence, and greater pan-Arctic curve separation from January onward. At an 80% threshold, product-comparison MAPE is 68.19% between the 6.25 and 25 km products and 11.47% between the 12.5 and 25 km products under their respective comparison periods and reference definitions. Regional product disagreement is likewise heterogeneous. Together, these results show that reproducible long-term polynya monitoring requires a fixed and explicitly documented combination of SIC product, threshold, and spatial classification rules, while broad temporal patterns can remain informative even when absolute extent differs substantially.

title: At-Least-Once Queue Retries Explained (and 1 Idempotency Key That Stops Duplicate Digests)
description:
If you just want the weekly digest to stop landing twice in the same inbox, don't go shopping for a better broker. Standard queue delivery is at-least-once, so a duplicate reminder is ordinary traffic rather than an incident — every broker worth running will replay a message when a worker dies mid-job. What stops the second copy is a send ledger: one uniquely-keyed row per user, per reminder, per scheduled run, written by the consumer before the email leaves the building.

That's it. One row.

The rest of this is the stuff that bites afterwards — how to pick the queue, how to write the worker in Node.js, and which three counters tell you the dedupe is doing anything at all.

Where the second copy of a fintech digest comes from

Picture the Friday 06:00 job at a payments company. A cron trigger fans out one message per active customer — call it 40,000 of them — and a pool of Node.js workers drains the queue, renders the week's balance and transaction summary, and hands it to the mail API. Ten messages per batch, roughly sixty seconds of work each. Nothing exotic.

Now kill one worker between "mail accepted" and "ack sent".

The broker has no idea the mail went out. Its visibility timeout expires, the message becomes visible again, a second worker claims it, and a customer receives their account summary twice. At a fintech that lands differently than a duplicate newsletter: support has to establish that the customer got two copies of one statement and not one copy of two settlement runs, and that conversation costs more than the send ever did.

Deploys do the same thing, quietly. Roll the worker pool during the run and every message in flight goes back on the queue — correct behaviour, duplicate processing, same outcome.

FIFO queues help less than the marketing suggests. Content-based or explicit deduplication ids are real, but they cover a window of about five minutes, and the retry that hurts is the one that arrives after a crash loop, a redeploy, or a mail provider that took ninety seconds to answer. Past the window, the broker has forgotten. Your consumer has not, if you gave it somewhere to remember.

There's a cost axis hiding in here too. You can shrink the duplicate window by acking earlier, which trades a risk of losing a digest entirely for lower latency, or you can run fatter batches with fewer workers, which trades wall-clock time for a smaller bill. Both dials move duplicates around. Neither removes them.

Which queue setup should I use if the same reminder message gets sent twice to users?

Pick on two questions: does the platform remember completed work for you, and do you already run the infrastructure it needs. Nothing in the table below makes consumer idempotency optional — it changes how much of the ledger you write yourself.

Option Delivery model Dedupe you get for free Where the send ledger goes
BullMQ on Redis at-least-once, in-process workers job ids are unique while the job is retained your Postgres, or a Redis key with a TTL
Inngest at-least-once with step memoisation completed steps are not re-run on retry the platform, for step results
Temporal at-least-once activity execution none — activities must be idempotent by contract your own activity guard
Upstash QStash at-least-once HTTP delivery optional deduplication id per publish your own store
Infrai queues at-least-once, FIFO dedupe over a 5-minute window an Idempotency-Key convention on writes your own store, behind one REST API and one key

BullMQ is the default pick when Redis is already in the stack and you want the worker to be a Node.js process you can attach a debugger to. The catch is that Redis persistence becomes part of your delivery guarantee, which is a conversation with whoever owns the Redis budget.

Inngest earns its keep when the digest is a flow rather than a send — fetch balances, wait for a reconciliation event, then mail — because step memoisation means a retry resumes instead of restarting. Temporal is the heavier version of that answer, and it's the right one when the workflow spans days and you can staff a cluster. Neither is a good fit if all you have is one queue and one worker.

QStash suits serverless deployments with no long-lived process to drain a queue; it pushes to your HTTP endpoint instead.

Infrai fits the narrower, very common shape of this job: a cron trigger, a queue, and an email send that all belong to the same weekly run and would otherwise mean three signups, three keys, and three invoices to reconcile at month end. One REST API covers the lot, which is mostly a procurement and on-call convenience rather than a technical one — but on a two-person platform team, it's the difference between one runbook and three. It doesn't support DAG-style orchestration or fan-in joins, so if the digest needs a real workflow graph, stick with Temporal or Inngest.

A Node.js worker that claims the reminder before it sends

The ordering matters more than the storage engine. Claim, send, ack — and if any step throws, don't ack, because the message coming back is the behaviour you want.

import { Pool } from "pg";
import { sendDigest } from "./mail.ts";

const BASE = process.env.INFRAI_API_BASE!;   // API root for your queue provider
const KEY = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY!;
const QUEUE = "weekly-digest";

const db = new Pool({ connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL });

type DigestJob = { user_id: string; reminder_id: string; scheduled_at: string };
type QueueMessage = { message_id: string; receipt: string; body: DigestJob };

async function call(path: string, payload: unknown, idempotencyKey?: string): Promise<Response> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 5; attempt++) {
    const res = await fetch(`${BASE}${path}`, {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        authorization: `Bearer ${KEY}`,
        "content-type": "application/json",
        ...(idempotencyKey ? { "Idempotency-Key": idempotencyKey } : {}),
      },
      body: JSON.stringify(payload),
    });
    if (res.status !== 429) return res;
    const retryAfter = Number(res.headers.get("retry-after") ?? 0);
    await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, retryAfter > 0 ? retryAfter * 1000 : 2 ** attempt * 250));
  }
  throw new Error("rate limited five times in a row; leaving the batch for the next tick");
}

function sendKey(job: DigestJob): string {
  return `${job.user_id}:${job.reminder_id}:${job.scheduled_at}`;
}

// One row per (user, reminder, scheduled run). The unique index is the idempotency.
async function claim(job: DigestJob): Promise<boolean> {
  const { rowCount } = await db.query(
    "insert into digest_sends (send_key, claimed_at) values ($1, now()) on conflict (send_key) do nothing",
    [sendKey(job)],
  );
  return rowCount === 1;
}

export async function drainOnce(): Promise<number> {
  const res = await call("/v1/queue/consume", { queue: QUEUE, max_messages: 10, visibility_timeout: 120 });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`consume returned ${res.status}: ${await res.text()}`);

  const { data } = (await res.json()) as { data: { messages: QueueMessage[] } };
  let suppressed = 0;

  for (const msg of data.messages) {
    const first = await claim(msg.body);
    if (first) await sendDigest(msg.body, sendKey(msg.body));
    else suppressed++;

    const ack = await call("/v1/queue/ack", { queue: QUEUE, receipt: msg.receipt });
    if (!ack.ok) console.error("ack rejected", ack.status, await ack.text());
  }
  return suppressed;
}

Three details carry the whole thing. The claim happens before the send, so a crash after the insert leaves a row that suppresses the retry rather than a customer with two statements. The same sendKey is passed to the mail call as its idempotency key, so the provider gets a second chance to catch what your database missed. And the ack only runs after the send returns, which is the part people invert when they're chasing throughput.

rowCount === 1 is doing a lot of work in that function, so give the table a unique index on send_key and a claimed_at column you can prune on. Thirty-five days of retention is plenty for a weekly job.

If storing raw account identifiers in a send table is awkward for your data classification, hash the tuple with HMAC (RFC 2104) and store the hex output. Uniqueness survives; the identifiers don't leak into a second table.

Three counters that prove the dedupe is doing something

I teach this as a before/after, because the ledger is invisible until you count it.

Count suppressed claims — the else branch above. A healthy weekly run shows a small non-zero number, usually a handful out of tens of thousands. Zero across several runs means either your workers never crash (possible) or the ledger isn't actually on the send path (more likely, and worth a lunchtime investigation). A number climbing past one percent of the run says the visibility timeout is shorter than your real handler latency, and the fix is the timeout, not the ledger.

Second, track age of the oldest unacked message during the run. That's your real duplicate exposure window: everything older than the visibility timeout is a candidate for redelivery. It's also the honest latency metric for a digest — not how fast one send is, but how long the tail takes to clear.

Third, count sends per send_key from the mail provider's own logs, not yours. Your ledger says the worker behaved. The provider's log says the customer's inbox agrees. Those two disagreeing is the only evidence worth paging someone about, and I'd wire that one to an alert rather than a dashboard nobody opens on a Friday.

What this design doesn't cover

The ledger is now a dependency of sending. If the database is unreachable, the correct move is to let the worker throw and the message return on its visibility timeout — sending blind is how you get the duplicates back.

Two platform limits are worth checking before you commit. Ack usually deletes the message, and retention caps out well short of a log-structured broker, so if replaying last month's digest run is a requirement, stick with Kafka or a stream you control rather than a work queue. Delayed delivery is also bounded — seven days on hosted queues is a common ceiling, which is fine for a weekly cadence and useless for an annual renewal reminder.

Long fan-outs need the same care. A scheduled trigger that runs a single HTTP handler will hit a hard execution ceiling — 900 seconds on some platforms — so the trigger should enqueue and return, and the workers should do the sending. Forty thousand renders inside one cron invocation is a timeout waiting to happen, and a timeout mid-run is exactly the retry that duplicates.

I'm not certain the HMAC step is worth it for every team; if your send table already lives inside the same compliance boundary as the customer record, it's ceremony. The claim row, though, is not optional. At-least-once is a promise the broker keeps by sending twice — idempotency is how your consumer keeps it once.

References

  • Google Cloud Pub/Sub overview (at-least-once delivery semantics): https://cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/overview
  • Amazon SQS FIFO queues, deduplication ids and the 5-minute interval: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/FIFO-queues.html
  • Stripe API: idempotent requests and idempotency keys: https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests
  • BullMQ documentation: https://docs.bullmq.io/
  • Temporal documentation on activity idempotency: https://docs.temporal.io/activities
  • Inngest step memoisation and retries: https://www.inngest.com/docs/learn/inngest-steps
  • Upstash QStash deduplication: https://upstash.com/docs/qstash/features/deduplication
  • RFC 2104, HMAC keyed-hashing for message authentication: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2104

title: VideoHarness-SRSI: Structured Recursive Self-Improvement for Video Understanding Harness
description:
arXiv:2610.19424v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM system capabilities depend not only on model parameters but also on the executable harnesses that organize information acquisition, tool use, reasoning, and memory. Recursive harness evolution can automate their design, but how it can reliably discover generalizable systems from limited, noisy, and repeatedly reused feedback remains unclear. We study this question in agentic video understanding, where rich multimodal evidence and coupled mechanisms make harness optimization challenging. We first introduce VideoHarness-BRSI, a recursive self-improvement framework that evolves video harnesses around a frozen vision-language model. Analyzing over 4,000 evolved candidates, we find it competitive with hand-engineered systems but identify three interconnected failure modes: validation overfitting, search-budget dilution, and the early-experience trap. We trace all three to a common root: the same imperfect validation evidence drives both harness revisions and the proposer's search strategy. We therefore propose VideoHarness-SRSI, an evidence-governed framework in which every search decision rests on evidence that is transferable, sufficient, and gathered before the search commits. It restricts the proposer to content-free feedback, informs exploration with instrumented warm-up experiments, and develops mechanisms in isolated probe-race branches before factorial composition and joint refinement. Across four video understanding benchmarks, VideoHarness-SRSI improves the equally weighted mean held-out score by 6.2% relative to VideoHarness-BRSI and reduces the mean validation-test gap by 37.9%. Reliable harness evolution thus depends on how search is organized and informed, not only on how well it optimizes validation performance.

title: Good Onboarding Starts Before Sign-Up: My Take on AviorSwap
description:
As a developer, I often think about onboarding as something that happens after registration.

There’s a welcome screen, maybe a checklist, and a few tooltips explaining where to click.

But as a user, I start forming my understanding much earlier. The homepage is already teaching me how to think about the product.

That’s what I appreciate about AviorSwap’s presentation: it gives me a straightforward introduction to what the platform is for and how to get started.

Give me a direction first

When I explore a new service, I don’t need to understand every feature immediately. I need a useful starting point.

AviorSwap makes deposit and swap actions visible early in the experience. For me, that establishes a clear direction.

I can identify the main activities without first learning a complicated navigation structure.

This is a design decision I respect because it requires prioritization. Every product has multiple things it could highlight. Choosing the actions that best explain its purpose helps a new visitor get oriented.

Let curiosity be part of the experience

I don’t always arrive at a platform ready to perform a specific action. Sometimes I just want to explore.

AviorSwap’s market sections, including popular assets and daily movers, give that curiosity somewhere to go.

I like this combination: a clear path for task-focused users and an entry point for people who are still getting familiar with the service.

It reminds me of good documentation. Sometimes I need a specific command. Sometimes I need an overview that helps me decide what to investigate next.

Both are valid ways to begin.

Explain the sequence in everyday language

One part of the public website I appreciate is the FAQ’s description of the onboarding process.

It outlines the progression from creating an account to setting up a wallet, depositing cryptocurrency, and exchanging assets.

Knowing the sequence helps me build expectations. I can understand how one step connects to the next before entering the workflow.

As developers, we spend so much time inside our products that we can forget how valuable this basic explanation is.

A new user shouldn’t need to reverse-engineer the journey from button labels.

Make the important topics easy to find

AviorSwap also puts pricing and fees near the center of its messaging.

I see that as a positive presentation choice. Costs are naturally part of how someone evaluates an exchange, so they deserve a visible place in the introduction.

When I design interfaces, I try to ask: what question is the user likely to have at this point?

Putting relevant information near the moment that question appears is one of the most useful things an interface can do.

What I’d bring into my own work

My impressions come from exploring AviorSwap’s public website. The aspect that stands out to me is how its presentation introduces the service through recognizable actions and short explanations.

It’s a useful reminder that onboarding includes everything a user sees while deciding whether a product makes sense to them.

For my own projects, I’d carry forward three ideas:

Make the primary action easy to recognize.

Give curious visitors something meaningful to explore.

Explain the overall process before asking users to navigate it.

That’s why AviorSwap’s approach appeals to me. It brings attention to the early moments when a visitor is becoming a user—and those moments deserve thoughtful design.

What’s the best onboarding decision you’ve borrowed from another product?

title: How I Shipped a Java Library to Maven Central, Solo
description:
The dual-write problem shows up wherever a service needs to update its database and notify the outside world as one atomic step. The write succeeds and the publish fails, or the reverse, and two systems that were supposed to agree quietly stop agreeing. The usual fixes are heavyweight: two-phase commit, or a CDC pipeline like Debezium reading the database's transaction log.

I built oncebox to solve it without either. The event is written to an outbox table in the same transaction as the business write, then polled and published separately, safely, even with several instances polling the same table at once. I started on October 11, 2025. A year later it's on Maven Central at v2.0.0, with signed releases and a test suite I'm proud of. This is what went into that.

What it does

oncebox guarantees a database write and a message-broker publish either both happen or neither does, with no two-phase commit and no CDC tooling watching the binlog. You call publish() (or annotate a method with @OutboxPublish) inside your existing @Transactional method. The event is written to an outbox table in that same transaction, and a poller picks it up and publishes it to Kafka or RabbitMQ, retrying with backoff. Anything that keeps failing moves into a dead letter queue, which has its own REST API for inspecting and replaying failed events. On the receiving side there's an inbox that dedupes on the event's id, so a redelivered message doesn't get processed twice. Postgres, MySQL, and Oracle on the write side; Kafka and RabbitMQ as brokers. You pick one of each.

A year, alone

As of today it's 13 Maven modules and 602 Java files, more than half of them tests. Five released versions so far: v1.0.0, v1.1.0, v1.1.1, v1.1.2 and v2.0.0.

There was no team to split this with, which meant no one to unblock me either. Every dialect quirk, every CI failure, every "why does this pass on Postgres and hang on MySQL" moment was just me and the logs. The upside of solo is that nothing shipped that I didn't fully understand. The downside is that everything took longer than it would have with a second set of eyes to catch the mistake I was too close to see.

Shipping is its own project

The polling logic was one job. Getting it onto Maven Central as something a stranger could <dependency> into their pom.xml and trust was another: GPG signing so releases are verifiable, the Sonatype/Central publishing flow, javadoc.io rendering usable docs instead of a wall of bare method signatures, and Codecov and CodeFactor wired up so the README badges report something real.

None of that touches the outbox logic, but it's what separates a repo I pushed from a library someone can depend on in production. The config is split into oncebox.outbox.* and oncebox.inbox.*, so a service can run only the side it needs. There are ready-made Grafana dashboards and a Postman collection for the DLQ API, because "read the source to figure out the metrics" is not documentation. Each of those was a small decision on its own.

Where the engineering lived

The core trick is SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED. It lets several instances poll the same outbox table in parallel, each locking a disjoint batch of rows without blocking the others. Event IDs are UUIDv7 instead of random UUIDs, so inserts land at the tail of the primary-key index instead of scattering writes across it under load. Polling is adaptive: exponential backoff toward a max delay while the table is empty, back to a fast poll as soon as events show up, so idle instances don't hammer the database. Event types are polled independently, in parallel, on a library-managed thread pool.

Supporting three databases with one concurrency primitive turned out to be a project of its own. Postgres and Oracle behave. On MySQL, InnoDB's default REPEATABLE READ makes that same locking clause take gap locks, so concurrent pollers deadlock instead of grabbing disjoint batches, unless the outbox datasource runs at READ COMMITTED. That one deserves its own post. Oracle diverges differently: it can't express FETCH FIRST ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED the way Postgres batches it in a CTE, so the batch size is capped at the JDBC level with PreparedStatement#setMaxRows. One concurrency primitive, three implementations.

The failure paths got the same attention as the happy path. If an instance dies mid-publish, its events are left IN_PROCESS. A separate recovery worker sweeps those back to PENDING without touching the retry count, so a crash doesn't cost an event its remaining retries. Anything that exhausts its retries moves to the dead letter queue in one transaction (lock the batch, insert into the DLQ table, delete from the outbox, commit) instead of two separate writes that could disagree if the process dies in between.

v2.0.0 is a breaking release. The structure is now named by mechanism, outbox and inbox, rather than by the role of the service. Every timestamp is set by the database clock instead of the JVM, so instances in different time zones agree on it. And each captured batch now carries a lock token, which fences it against a poller that no longer owns it.

Why I went overboard on tests

With no one reviewing my PRs, tests were the only thing between me and shipping a race condition to users I'd never meet. 346 of the 602 Java files in the repo are test sources, split across tiers that each catch a different kind of failure. Unit tests cover logic, integration tests run against real databases, and a concurrent tier hammers the SKIP LOCKED polling path with multiple real threads to catch races a mock never would. A classpath-isolation job checks the library still works when only one database dialect's jar is on the classpath, catching accidental hard dependencies between modules that should be independent. End-to-end tests run across a 3-database × 2-broker matrix, and Gatling load tests run against dockerized infrastructure on every release tag.

For a library one person maintains, that's a lot of test infrastructure. It's also the only way I could say with any confidence that a release won't deadlock someone's production database.

Try it

oncebox is Apache 2.0, on Maven Central as io.github.dmitriy-iliyov:oncebox-*, and the source is at github.com/dmitriy-iliyov/oncebox. If you have a dual-write problem and don't want to stand up a CDC pipeline to solve it, I'd like to know whether this works for you. Issues, PRs, and stars all help when it's one person deciding whether to keep going.

Written 2026-10-15, against oncebox v2.0.0. Repo stats are current as of this post; check the README for anything that has moved since.

title: 6 Common GBase Database(GBase 8s) oninit Startup Failures and How to Troubleshoot Them
description:
Running oninit -ivy only to see GBase Database(GBase 8s) fail to start? Before reinstalling the database, check the environment variables, configuration files, port availability, directory permissions, shared memory settings, and disk space.

Here are six common causes of GBase Database(GBase 8s) startup failures and how to investigate them on Linux.

1. Cannot Find the onconfig File

Possible cause: ONCONFIG is unset, references the wrong configuration file, or the file is missing.

Check the environment:

echo "$GBASEDBTDIR"
echo "$ONCONFIG"
ls "$GBASEDBTDIR/etc/onconfig."*

Verify that ONCONFIG matches the intended configuration file and that the file exists in the expected directory. Correct the environment according to your installation before retrying startup.

2. Cannot Bind to the Database Port

Possible cause: The configured port is already in use or the listener configuration is incorrect.

Check the port:

ss -lntp | grep ':9088'

Replace 9088 with the port configured for your instance.

Identify the process before taking action. Do not terminate unrelated services blindly. If a port conflict exists, resolve it or select an available port and update the relevant server and client configurations consistently.

3. Permission Denied

Possible cause: The database operating system account cannot access required configuration, storage, or diagnostic directories.

Inspect directory ownership and permissions:

ls -ld /opt/GBASE/gbase_data

Check the relevant parent directories and files as well. Confirm that the database service account has the permissions required by your installation.

Avoid applying recursive ownership or permission changes to an entire directory tree without understanding its contents. Incorrect changes can introduce additional security and operational problems.

4. Not Enough Shared Memory

Possible cause: Available system resources or shared memory configuration do not meet the instance requirements.

Start by inspecting the system setting:

cat /proc/sys/kernel/shmmax
free -h

Review the actual startup error and compare the current system configuration with the requirements for your GBase Database(GBase 8s) version and workload.

Do not apply arbitrary shared memory values from online examples. The appropriate settings depend on the operating system, database configuration, and available resources.

5. No Space Left on Device

Possible cause: A filesystem used for database storage, temporary files, or diagnostic logs has run out of space.

Check available capacity:

df -h
df -i

Check both disk space and inode availability. Review the relevant storage locations and database logs to identify the affected filesystem.

Free space only after confirming which files can safely be removed. Never delete database storage files or logs blindly to make the startup error disappear.

6. sqlhosts Configuration Problems

Possible cause: The connection configuration file is missing, unreadable, or contains an incorrect server entry.

Check the configured path and contents:

echo "$GBASEDBTSQLHOSTS"
cat "$GBASEDBTSQLHOSTS"

Verify that the file exists, the database account can access it, and the server name, protocol, hostname, and port match the intended connection configuration.

A sqlhosts problem may primarily affect client connectivity rather than instance startup, so use the exact error message to determine whether it is relevant to the current failure.

Quick oninit Diagnostic Script

This basic script checks several common environment and system conditions:

#!/bin/bash

echo "=== GBase Database(GBase 8s) Startup Diagnostics ==="

echo
echo "1. Environment"
echo "GBASEDBTDIR=${GBASEDBTDIR:-unset}"
echo "ONCONFIG=${ONCONFIG:-unset}"
echo "GBASEDBTSQLHOSTS=${GBASEDBTSQLHOSTS:-unset}"

echo
echo "2. Configuration file"
if [[ -n "${GBASEDBTDIR:-}" &&
      -n "${ONCONFIG:-}" &&
      -r "$GBASEDBTDIR/etc/$ONCONFIG" ]]; then
    echo "onconfig file found and readable"
else
    echo "Check ONCONFIG and the configuration path"
fi

echo
echo "3. sqlhosts file"
if [[ -n "${GBASEDBTSQLHOSTS:-}" &&
      -r "$GBASEDBTSQLHOSTS" ]]; then
    echo "sqlhosts file found and readable"
else
    echo "Check sqlhosts path and permissions"
fi

echo
echo "4. Disk space"
df -h

echo
echo "5. Inode availability"
df -i

echo
echo "6. Shared memory setting"
cat /proc/sys/kernel/shmmax 2>/dev/null ||
    echo "Unable to read shmmax"

echo
echo "7. Recent startup logs"
if [[ -n "${GBASEDBTDIR:-}" &&
      -r "$GBASEDBTDIR/tmp/online.log" ]]; then
    tail -30 "$GBASEDBTDIR/tmp/online.log"
else
    echo "Check the diagnostic log location for your installation"
fi

Save the script as check_oninit.sh and run it in the appropriate database environment. The diagnostic log location may differ depending on your installation.

This script identifies potential configuration issues; it does not replace reviewing the actual oninit error messages.

Final Thoughts

Most GBase Database(GBase 8s) startup investigations should begin with the exact error message and the database diagnostic logs. Check the environment and configuration first, then investigate ports, permissions, system resources, and storage.

The key takeaway: Avoid changing multiple settings at once. Identify the failing component, make one controlled change, and verify the result before proceeding.

A systematic troubleshooting process makes GBase Database(GBase 8s) installation and Linux database administration easier to maintain.

title: LLM-jp-4 Technical Report
description:
arXiv:2610.19331v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: This paper presents LLM-jp-4, a family of Japanese sovereign large language models (LLMs) developed with an emphasis on transparency, reproducibility, and practical usability. LLM-jp-4 comprises an 8B dense model and a 32B-A3B mixture-of-experts model, both trained from scratch on approximately 12 trillion tokens. To support independent verification and reproduction, we establish explicit criteria for selecting training data, external models, and software, and make the development process publicly available. Evaluation results demonstrate substantial improvements over previous LLM-jp models and competitive performance against open-weight models of similar scale. By documenting the development principles, training procedures, and empirical findings of LLM-jp-4, we aim to provide a reference for future sovereign AI development.

title: Push images to Vercel Container Registry from GitHub Actions
description:
You can now push container images from GitHub Actions to Vercel Container Registry (VCR) without storing long-lived registry credentials.

The new vercel/vcr-action/login action authenticates your workflow using GitHub OIDC. It exchanges the workflow’s OIDC token for a short-lived Vercel access token, then uses that token to log in to vcr.vercel.com. When the job ends, the action logs out and revokes the Vercel token.

To start:

  • Create an OIDC policy on your Vercel team that matches the GitHub repository and workflow, and grants read-write access to VCR.

  • Store your Vercel team ID as a GitHub repo variable, for example VERCEL_TEAM_ID, along with the team slug, project slug, and repo name used in the image tag.

  • Give the workflow or job id-token: write permission.

Then add the login step before you build and push and the image:

The action authenticates Docker by default. Pass engines to use Podman or Buildah instead.

After VCR finishes preparing a linux/amd64 image, you can use it as a custom Vercel Sandbox image. Within the same project, reference it as <repository>:<tag>.

Learn more in the VCR documentation and the GitHub Actions guide.

title: ANASSA: From High-Level Framework to Low-Level Architecture for Spatial Agentic AI
description:
arXiv:2610.14382v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agentic AI systems operating over geospatial data require more than autonomous reasoning and tool use; they must also support explicit orchestration, spatial validation, governance, provenance, failure handling, and human decision authority. Prior work introduced ANASSA, an agentic AI orchestration framework for spatial intelligence that established high-level components and responsibility boundaries for governed agentic execution (arXiv:2609.14824). However, the framework did not specify how those high-level responsibilities should be systematically decomposed into an implementation-facing low-level architecture. This paper addresses that gap by applying Design Science Research (DSR) to refine the ANASSA framework from high-level architectural (HLA) responsibilities into a low-level architecture (LLA). The resulting design preserves the responsibility boundaries of the foundational framework while translating them into executable architectural structures, including 47 logical roles, versioned task graphs, capability-based agent selection, typed contracts, explicit runtime states, spatial validation mechanisms, governance controls, failure and recovery paths, and provenance records. The architecture is demonstrated through an end-to-end execution trace and analytically evaluated for requirements traceability, internal consistency, responsibility preservation, and technology independence. The resulting high-level-to-low-level design provides an implementation-facing bridge between the ANASSA framework and future system implementations, defining how governed spatial agentic workflows can be made inspectable, reconstructable, and testable without binding the architecture to a specific AI model, geospatial platform, communication protocol, or deployment environment.

title: Show HN: Pulse Local, a Mac budgeting app whose AI models run on your machine
description:
Hi HN, I'm Niz. Pulse Local is a budgeting app for Mac (Apple Silicon, beta) that answers questions about your spending with models that run on your machine. Local mode needs no account. The ledger and your questions stay on the machine, and the app sends no analytics or crash logs.

I felt there are not enough consumer apps that run locally with no calls to the outside world that help us manage sensitive corners of our lives. This app in its local variant only downloads a couple of models and occasional updates, it does not send any analytics nor data.

Features-wise, Pulse local is a complete budgeting app that offers an assistant built on top of a fine-tuned model and thousands of rules embedded in the code itself. I'm sharing it for free with options to help me continue experimenting with fine-tuning and expanding along this direction.

How it works: you import a CSV from any bank, in any currency. When you ask a question, a tuned Qwen3 0.6B model reads it into a structured query, and code, not the model, does the money math against the ledger. A 4B checker model double-checks each money answer; when the two readings disagree, the app says it is not sure instead of guessing. That change took wrong answers from about one in five to 5 in 494 questions across our last three tests. The write-up covers how we test, the designs that failed, and the limits of the claim: https://pulseos.finance/pulse-local/writing/agree-or-not-sur...

The tuned weights are on Hugging Face (PulseOS/pulse-local-qwen3-0.6b).

Limitations: the first start downloads about 2.9 GB of models. With the checker on, a money answer takes 12 to 14 seconds (you can turn the checker off). Small models can still misread an open-ended question. The app answers in English. Mac only for now; Windows is next.

The app is free. An optional Connected mode (Sync Pass, $29/year) syncs US banks through Plaid; transactions pass through our server's memory and are not stored.

Feedback welcome, especially on wrong answers and on questions it should handle but does not.

title: TRACER: Trace-Regularized Training Against Indirect Prompt Injection
description:
arXiv:2610.19133v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Indirect prompt injection uses untrusted retrieved content, tool outputs, or agent messages to override an LLM's intended behavior. We show that defense robustness is channel-conditioned: the same attack succeeds 18% of the time as a follow-up message but 53% when placed in retrieved context. We propose TRACER (Trace-Regularized Adversarial Channel Exposure with Reward-shaping), a channel-aware adversarial training method that samples presentation wrappers and combines an answer-anchored, evidence-gated reward with ATRC, which aligns attacked reasoning with clean evidence when an injection is invalid. On GSM8K with Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, TRACER reduces RAG-framed ASR from 65.5% to 6.1% while preserving 78-82% clean accuracy. Joint RAG+tool training achieves 13.9% average ASR across framings at 3B scale, while a single epoch at 7B reaches 9.4%. These results demonstrate that robust defenses must explicitly train and evaluate across deployment channels.

title: Big Tech Is on Track to Spend $800B on AI in 2026. Can the Economics Hold?
description:
One hot inflation report. A sell-off in AI infrastructure stocks. And a question the whole industry can no longer dodge.

For the last few years, the AI conversation has mostly been about capability.

Can a model write code? Can it answer questions? Can it generate images? Can it browse the web? Can it act like an agent?

Those are important questions. But in October 2026, another question has become impossible to ignore:

Can the AI industry turn massive spending into sustainable, measurable value?

This is no longer only a technology question. It is now a business, energy, infrastructure, policy, and investment question. And the answer will shape which companies lead the next decade.

⚡ TL;DR (save this)

  • Markets wobbled. AI and AI-infrastructure stocks fell after hotter-than-expected US inflation data.
  • The spending is enormous. The largest US hyperscalers are on track for about $800B of capex in 2026 and around $1.1T in 2027.
  • There is a gap. An Axios-reported analysis found a ~$1T gap between AI-related spending since 2024 and AI revenue so far.
  • Power is a hard limit. Data-center electricity demand grew 17% in 2025 versus about 3% for overall demand.
  • The next winners will not simply spend the most. They will deliver trustworthy execution.

📉 The Market Just Sent a Warning

This week, major AI and AI-infrastructure stocks fell after the United States released hotter-than-expected inflation data.

Why does inflation matter to AI? Because AI at scale is capital-intensive.

Building and running AI systems requires:

  • Advanced GPUs and specialized chips
  • Large data centers
  • High-speed networking
  • Massive storage systems
  • Reliable electricity
  • Cooling infrastructure
  • Skilled engineering teams
  • Continuous model training and inference capacity

Many companies fund this buildout through debt, future revenue expectations, and investor confidence.

When inflation rises, markets begin to expect higher interest rates. Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive. When borrowing becomes more expensive, every large infrastructure project becomes harder to justify.

That is why AI stocks reacted sharply.

Reuters reported that shares of debt-heavy AI infrastructure companies fell as investors became more concerned about the financing of the industry's massive buildout. CoreWeave, Nebius, Oracle, and Dell were among the companies affected.

This does not mean AI is failing. It means the market is asking a fair question:

Is the spending producing enough real value to justify the cost?

💰 The Scale of AI Spending Is Enormous

To understand why this matters, look at the numbers.

Goldman Sachs has estimated that the largest US hyperscalers are on track to spend about $800 billion on capital expenditure in 2026. Consensus expectations suggest this could rise to around $1.1 trillion in 2027.

Capital expenditure, or capex, means money spent on long-term assets such as:

  • Data centers
  • Servers
  • GPUs
  • Networking equipment
  • Land and buildings
  • Power infrastructure
  • Cooling systems

This is not ordinary software spending. This is industrial-scale investment.

Alphabet, for example, reported $80.6 billion in capital expenditures during the first half of 2026 and guided to $195-205 billion for the full year.

That is an extraordinary amount of money being committed to compute, data centers, and AI infrastructure.

At the same time, an analysis reported by Axios found a gap of nearly $1 trillion between hyperscaler AI-related spending since 2024 and the AI revenue generated so far.

This does not mean AI companies have "lost" $1 trillion. It means there is a difference between:

  • Money invested in AI infrastructure
  • Money earned from AI products and services

That difference matters. Investors can support long-term investment when they believe future revenue will arrive. But if spending keeps rising faster than revenue, confidence can weaken.

🏗️ AI Is Becoming an Infrastructure Industry

AI used to feel like a software industry. Now, it increasingly looks like an infrastructure industry.

Why? Because modern AI depends on physical resources: electricity, land, water, fiber networks, chips, cooling systems, data centers, and power grids.

A powerful model is not just an algorithm. It is an algorithm running on expensive hardware, inside a data center, connected to a power grid, supported by supply chains, and maintained by engineers.

This changes the conversation. The question is no longer only:

"How smart can the model become?"

It is also:

  • "Can we power it?"
  • "Can we cool it?"
  • "Can we afford it?"
  • "Can we deploy it responsibly?"
  • "Can it create value for customers?"

AI is becoming similar to railways, electricity grids, telecom networks, and cloud computing. Infrastructure industries create enormous value, but they also require enormous capital, planning, and discipline.

🔌 Electricity Is Becoming a Core AI Constraint

One of the most important facts in this debate is energy.

According to IEA data cited in recent reporting, data-center electricity demand grew by 17% in 2025, while overall electricity demand grew by around 3%.

That is a major difference.

AI data centers need continuous power. They cannot simply switch off during peak hours. Training large models and serving millions of users requires stable, high-capacity electricity around the clock.

This creates several challenges:

1. Power availability

Many regions already face grid constraints. Adding a large data center is not as simple as buying land and installing servers. It requires access to sufficient electricity capacity.

2. Grid upgrades

New data centers may require new transmission lines, substations, and grid upgrades. These projects can take years to approve and build.

3. Energy costs

If data centers increase demand faster than supply, electricity prices can rise for nearby communities and businesses.

4. Environmental impact

AI infrastructure affects carbon emissions, water usage, land use, and local communities.

5. Public policy

Governments are beginning to ask who should pay for the infrastructure required to support AI growth.

In the United States, the House passed a bipartisan bill designed to encourage state utility regulators to protect consumers from rising energy costs linked to large data centers. The bill still needs further approval to become law, but the direction is clear.

In Europe, regulators are preparing stricter disclosure requirements for data centers, including water use, clean-power adoption, and energy efficiency.

The message is simple:

AI growth must be matched by responsible energy planning.

🎯 The Shift From Demos to Business Outcomes

The first phase of enterprise AI was about experimentation.

Companies asked:

  • Can we build a chatbot?
  • Can we connect an LLM to our documents?
  • Can we create a proof of concept?
  • Can we show leadership an AI demo?

That phase was necessary. But demos do not pay for data centers. Business outcomes do.

The next phase is about production AI:

  • AI that reduces manual work
  • AI that improves decision-making
  • AI that accelerates customer response
  • AI that automates repeatable workflows
  • AI that improves quality and compliance
  • AI that creates measurable ROI

This is where agentic AI becomes important.

An AI agent is not just a chatbot. It is a system that can understand a goal, plan steps, use tools, interact with systems, and complete a task.

For example, instead of asking:

"What is our leave policy?"

An employee may ask:

"Apply for two days of leave and confirm my balance has updated."

An agent may need to:

  1. Understand the request
  2. Find the correct application screen
  3. Fill in the required details
  4. Submit the request
  5. Verify the outcome
  6. Report success or failure with evidence

This is much more valuable than a simple question-and-answer system. But it is also more demanding. An agent that takes action must be accurate, safe, observable, and accountable.

🛡️ Why Agentic AI Needs Governance

As AI agents become more autonomous, governance becomes essential.

A chatbot that gives a wrong answer is frustrating. An AI agent that submits the wrong form, sends the wrong email, updates the wrong record, or triggers the wrong workflow can create real business damage.

That is why enterprises need:

Human approval for high-risk actions

Not every action should be automatic. Deleting records, making payments, changing production configurations, or sending external communications may require human confirmation.

Least-privilege access

An agent should only have the permissions required for its task. It should not automatically receive broad access to every system.

Audit trails

Every important action should be logged: what the agent saw, what it decided, what it did, and what evidence supports the result.

Clear success and failure states

A good AI system should say:

  • "Task completed successfully."
  • "Task failed because of a product defect."
  • "Task could not be completed because a required screen or precondition was unavailable."

It should not pretend everything is fine when it could not verify the outcome.

Monitoring and observability

Teams need to monitor agent behavior in real time, detect unusual actions, and stop an agent if needed.

This is especially important as agents move from answering questions to operating inside business systems.

🏆 The Real Competitive Advantage: Trustworthy Execution

Many people think AI competition is only about who has the biggest model. That is no longer the full picture.

The next competitive advantage will come from trustworthy execution.

A company may have access to a powerful model, but if it cannot connect that model safely to its data, workflows, permissions, and business processes, the value remains limited.

The companies that win will be those that can deliver:

  • Reliable AI systems. The system should work consistently, not only in a demo.
  • Measurable ROI. Every AI initiative should answer: What time, cost, risk, or quality improvement did we create?
  • Safe automation. AI should automate the right tasks, with the right controls, in the right environments.
  • Evidence-based results. Users should be able to see why the AI reached a conclusion or completed an action.
  • Responsible infrastructure. AI growth should consider power, water, emissions, and community impact.
  • Human-centered design. AI should assist people, not confuse them or remove accountability.

🏢 What This Means for Businesses

For business leaders, the message is clear: do not evaluate AI only by model benchmarks. Evaluate it by business impact.

Ask questions like:

  • Which workflow are we improving?
  • How much time or cost are we saving?
  • How are we measuring quality?
  • What happens when the AI is wrong?
  • Who approves high-risk actions?
  • How do we audit decisions?
  • What data does the AI access?
  • How do we protect customer information?
  • What is the total cost of ownership?
  • How does this affect our energy and infrastructure needs?

AI strategy should not be "adopt AI everywhere." AI strategy should be:

Adopt AI where it creates clear, measurable, responsible value.

👩‍💻 What This Means for Engineers

For AI engineers, developers, and architects, the skills that matter are changing.

It is no longer enough to know how to call an LLM API.

The most valuable engineers will understand:

  • System design
  • Retrieval and context management
  • Tool use and function calling
  • Agent orchestration
  • Evaluation and testing
  • Observability
  • Security and permissions
  • Cost optimization
  • Human-in-the-loop workflows
  • Production deployment

The best AI systems will not be built by prompt engineering alone. They will be built by combining models, data, tools, policies, tests, monitoring, user experience, and business understanding.

That is where real engineering value lies.

🚀 What This Means for Startups

For startups, this is actually good news.

When AI becomes expensive, companies cannot afford vague experiments. They need focused solutions that solve specific problems.

The best startup opportunities will be in areas such as:

  • AI quality assurance and testing
  • Agent governance and auditing
  • AI cost optimization
  • Enterprise workflow automation
  • Domain-specific AI assistants
  • Data readiness and governance
  • AI security
  • Model evaluation
  • Human-in-the-loop review tools
  • Industry-specific automation

A startup does not need to build a foundation model to create value. It can build the layer that makes AI usable, safe, measurable, and trustworthy inside real organizations.

🔭 The Bigger Picture

AI is not disappearing. It is maturing.

The first phase was about possibility. The next phase is about responsibility.

The first phase asked: "What can AI do?"

The next phase asks: "What should AI do, at what cost, with what safeguards, and for whose benefit?"

That is a healthier phase. Because real transformation does not come from hype. It comes from systems that work reliably in the real world.

AI will create enormous value, but only when companies treat it as more than a trend. They must treat it as:

  • A product
  • A system
  • An infrastructure investment
  • A business process
  • A governance responsibility
  • A long-term commitment

The companies that understand this will build durable advantage. The companies that only chase demos may find that the cost of AI is much easier to measure than its value.

💡 Final Thought

The AI race is no longer only about who can build the most powerful model. It is about who can build the most useful, efficient, safe, and economically sustainable AI systems.

The next winners will not simply spend the most.

They will convert compute into clarity.

They will convert automation into accountability.

They will convert data into decisions.

And they will convert AI into measurable business value.

The future of AI belongs to those who can make it work in the real world.

💬 Your turn

What will matter more in the next phase of AI: model capability or practical, trustworthy execution?

Tell me in the comments. If this helped you think about AI beyond the hype, a reaction and a share help other engineers and leaders find it. Follow for more on AI systems, agents and the economics behind them.

title: Do You Want Your Web App to Feel Like a Native App?
description:
You can give your Codename One web app the same desktop theme family as your users' operating system: Aqua on macOS, Fluent on Windows, or Adwaita on Linux. Menus can sit above the app in HTML, with commands such as File and View visible instead of tucked into a mobile overflow menu.

What is Codename One? Codename One is an open-source framework for building native iOS, Android, desktop, and web apps from a single Java or Kotlin codebase. Learn more at codenameone.com.

That gives you a browser version of your app that fits more comfortably on a desktop. The JavaScript port now supports both choices, and the same theme work reaches the Certificate Wizard you use to sign your apps.

Follow the operating system, or choose a theme

Set these in the Settings app's Build Hints:

nativeTheme=native
javascript.titleBar=html

In codenameone_settings.properties, use codename1.arg.nativeTheme and codename1.arg.javascript.titleBar instead. Desktop browsers select Fluent for Windows, Aqua for macOS, and Adwaita for Linux and the remaining desktop systems. Phones and tablets keep the mobile theme selection. The browser detection treats an iPad as a tablet even when it reports a Mac browser.

These are Codename One themes drawing the controls. They are not the operating system's native widget toolkit embedded in the page.

The Settings app demonstrates the three desktop theme families now available to browser apps. Click to compare the controls at full size.

You can pin a desktop theme when the application's design calls for it:

javascript.desktopTheme=fluent

The other explicit choices are aqua, adwaita and none. none keeps mobile themes on desktop browsers. Leave the value at auto to follow the operating system. The broader nativeTheme=modern setting has different behavior: it selects the modern mobile families, including on desktop browsers. Use native when desktop family selection is what you want.

Put commands above the app

The default javascript.titleBar=toolbar keeps the themed Toolbar inside the app. With html, the page supplies title and menu bars instead. The title follows the current form; commands group into menus using the same Command.setDesktopMenu() hint used on the desktop ports.

For example, inside an initialized app:

com.codename1.ui.Form form = new com.codename1.ui.Form("Notes");
com.codename1.ui.Command refresh = new com.codename1.ui.Command("Refresh") {
    public void actionPerformed(com.codename1.ui.events.ActionEvent event) {
        form.setTitle("Notes refreshed");
    }
};
refresh.setDesktopMenu("View");
form.getToolbar().addCommandToOverflowMenu(refresh);
form.show();

Commands without a menu hint go into a Commands menu. The HTML bars follow the selected appearance and the browser's light or dark preference. They do not have fake minimize, maximize or close buttons: the page does not own the browser window. The browser tab title remains the application's display name.

The source is in JavaScriptDesktopChrome, with build-hint and page behavior documented in the JavaScript guide.

Keep navigation inside your browser app

We do not support additional native Window surfaces in the JavaScript port. Popup blockers and the browser's window ownership make that a different promise from drawing a menu inside the current page. Windows browsers are supported; extra OS windows are the unsupported feature. Dialogs and navigation within the app remain the appropriate model.

There are renderer limits too. For example, the full lifted-lens optics from Sunday's iOS article are not implemented in the browser. Try the actual controls and effects your app uses rather than assuming a theme name proves complete renderer parity.

The build prunes theme resources it can prove the app will not reach. If your code constructs resource names dynamically, set javascript.pruneThemes=false; otherwise a theme loaded only through that constructed name may be missing.

Use the same desktop styling when you sign your app

A gallery of buttons cannot tell us whether an application works comfortably with a desktop theme. The Certificate Wizard has longer forms, tables, dialogs and instructions that people must actually read to finish a task.

PR #5916 adopts the native desktop themes there, continuing the work we did in Settings. Its current source uses @DesktopBuild(themeMode = "native", titleBar = DesktopTitleBar.NATIVE, ...), with interactive scrollbars. Fluent, Aqua and Adwaita now provide the surrounding control styles instead of a separate wizard-specific desktop imitation.

title: Gemini 4 Argon: Built to solve your hardest problems
Spectral-MoE: Heterogeneous Per-Layer Expert Utilization in Dense-to-MoE Conversion
description:
arXiv:2610.19232v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models impose substantial memory demands and arithmetic costs during inference. Dense-to-mixture-of-experts (MoE) conversion is a model optimization technique that aims to reduce these arithmetic costs. Dense-to-MoE conversion partitions pretrained feed-forward network (FFN) neurons into experts and selects a subset for each token. Leading methods fall into two categories: analytic methods produce a converted model quickly using heuristics, while learning methods produce a model much more slowly by optimizing via gradients. Both approaches, however, fix the same active expert count, or "utilization," at every layer. We introduce Spectral-MoE, which learns to allocate a utilization budget heterogeneously across layers. Its name draws a metaphor between separating a dense FFN into experts and separating a light beam into its spectrum. Spectral-MoE consists of two distinct approaches: a static approach that uses a single per-layer scalar which is shared across tokens, and a dynamic approach which emits a per-token schedule. We demonstrate that both allocators improve performance over uniform on both the analytic-based and learning-based SOTA dense-to-MoE methods. At 25% FFN utilization, dynamic allocation reduces WikiText-2 perplexity relative to uniform by 1.04, 2.96, and 2.71 points on the learned base for Llama-2-7B, Llama-3-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B, respectively. The corresponding reductions on the analytic base are 2.45, 6.26, and 2.17 points. On the learned base, dynamic allocation improves six-task mean accuracy over uniform by an average of 1.5, 4.2, and 3.6 percentage points across the three models at FFN utilizations of 12.5%, 25%, and 50%, respectively. These results establish per-layer expert utilization as a novel optimization axis in dense-to-MoE conversion.
