title: Inverse Reasoning Models for Efficient Post-Training and Verification from Answer-Only Data
description:
arXiv:2610.18878v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Post-training reasoning LLMs often requires making a tradeoff between costly supervision and compute inefficiency: supervised finetuning typically requires reasoning traces, which is data inefficient since in many applications one only has prompt-answer tuples and lacks the groundtruth chain-of-thought (CoT) sequence. On the other hand, reinforcement learning (with verifiable rewards, for example) can operate without CoT data but it is much more compute-inefficient since it requires multiple autoregressive completions per optimization step, none of which are guaranteed to give a non-zero policy gradient. In this work we explore a middleground, a self-distillation technique that uses answer-only data, treating CoT as latent variables. This relies on training a partner ``inverse reasoning LLM" that generates the original's reasoning traces conditioned on the answer. The inverse model is trained once and reused across incoming batches of answer-only data, with all generation happening offline and up front, making the approach particularly suited to continual post-training. Using Qwen3-0.6B on the Countdown and GSM8K tasks, we show that after GRPO training has saturated, a single offline distillation round from the inverse model roughly doubles pass@1 on hard prompts and, on Countdown, outperforms rejection-sampling self-distillation on every hard-tail metric at every mix ratio (with smaller gains on GSM8K); rejection sampling by construction has no signal on problems the model never solves on its own. Continued GRPO on the fresh data retains an edge at hard pass@1 but trails distillation at pass@8 and pass@32 while regenerating rollouts at every step. As an added bonus we see that the inverse model has a second application as an accurate verifier of correctness. When used for best-of-$n$ selection at test time, it raises selection accuracy on Countdown from 0.753 (majority voting) to 0.969.

title: I Built a Faceless Video Factory That Remembers Which Content Actually Pays
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle

My side hustle is faceless short-form video. The problem with every tool I tried: they're script runners. Same topic list, same output, run after run. Nothing learns. So I built one that does — a factory that remembers what earned money and steers the next video toward it.

The loop nobody closes

Here's the insight that made this worth building. A faceless-content pipeline has two halves, and everyone only builds the first:

  1. Produce a video from a topic (script → render → post)
  2. Learn which topics paid, so the next one is better

Half 2 is where the money compounds, and it's the half everyone skips. This factory closes it with Backboard's persistent memory:

   recall what paid ──▶ [Brain] ──pick topic──▶ [Script] ──▶ [Assemble] ──▶ [Cashier]
        ▲                    (local LLM +        (local)     (FFmpeg)       (revenue)
        │                     recalled facts)
        └──────────────────── remember the outcome ───────────────┘

Before each video, the brain asks Backboard "what earned money before?" and
lets that steer the pick. After each video, the revenue result is written back
to memory. Run it twice and the second run is measurably smarter than the first.

Why Backboard + a local model

Backboard's memory is the differentiator — facts persist across runs and
sessions, so the factory compounds instead of resetting. But its hackathon
credit covers Memory + RAG, not LLM chat. So generation runs on a local
llama.cpp model on my own machine.

That split isn't a workaround, it's the whole side-hustle thesis: Backboard
supplies the long-term memory that makes the factory smarter; the local model
keeps the per-video cost at zero. No cloud token bill eating the margin.

The learning, measured

I ran the brain cold, then seeded two outcomes, then ran it warm. Here's what
changed:

Run Memory state Topic picked Why
1 (cold) 0 facts recalled What I learned monetizing 40 short videos No history — picked blind
2 (warm) 4 facts recalled The side hustle nobody talks about: faceless video Steered by the $61.30 earner in memory

The seeded facts the brain learned from:

Past video Views Revenue Signal
"Building an income stream that works while you sleep" 14,200 $61.30 🟢 high earner
"From keyword to video in under five minutes" 3,100 $3.10 🔴 underperformed

And the rendered output it produces each run — a real 1080×1920 vertical MP4:

Property Value
Resolution 1080×1920 (9:16)
Codec h264 + aac
Narration espeak-ng (on-device)
Background FFmpeg gradient (generated, not downloaded)

The revenue model behind the cashier is real math, not a mock — YouTube Shorts
RPM, TikTok Rewards RPM, and an affiliate conversion model, all documented and
editable in one file.

What's actually local-first

The whole point of a side hustle is margin, so nothing here phones home for
the expensive parts:

  • Scripts → local llama.cpp on :8080 (falls back to a template if the server's down, so the pipeline never blocks)
  • Narration → espeak-ng on-device
  • Background → FFmpeg gradients filter, generated locally
  • Memory → Backboard (the one cloud call, and it's the free Memory + RAG tier)

Try it 

git clone https://github.com/Reggiebro/faceless-video-factory && cd faceless-video-factory
bash demo.sh        # cold start -> seed -> warm run, the learning in one script
python3 orchestrator.py   # full pass: brain -> script -> video -> cashier

The repo is MIT. The brain (backboard/brain.py) is ~150 lines and readable
end to end — recall, pick, record. That's the whole idea.

Has anyone else used persistent memory to make a content pipeline compound
rather than just repeat? I'm curious whether the recall-steers-the-pick loop
holds up at scale, or whether it starts chasing its own tail after a few dozen
runs. What would you add to the feedback signal beyond revenue?

title: The Anatomy of Harness Engineering: How to Evaluate, Iterate, and Guard AI Coding Agents
description: While end-to-end benchmarks like SWE-bench provide broad performance scores for AI agents, they are often expensive, slow, and lack the root-cause diagnostics needed to explain exactly where an agent's logic broke down. To solve this, developers should adopt behavioral evaluations—fast, local, unit-style tests that assert on discrete intermediate actions, such as verifying specific tool calls or file modifications rather than final string equality. By building these inexpensive micro-checks alongside macro benchmarks, engineering teams can confidently iterate on system prompts and upgrade models without the risk of regressions.

title: FDE-Bench: Evaluating End-to-End Delivery from Underspecified Real-World Business Requests
description:
arXiv:2610.14539v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Real-world business requests often leave key requirements unstated because frontline practitioners struggle to articulate rules they know from experience. Forward-deployed engineers (FDEs) must elicit these requirements through dialogue and iteratively optimize solutions until they meet customer acceptance criteria. Existing optimization benchmarks typically start from explicit objectives, while clarification benchmarks often introduce information gaps into existing tasks. We introduce FDE-Bench, the first benchmark built from real customer projects to evaluate agents on end-to-end delivery tasks that require interactive requirement clarification and iterative optimization. Its 49 cases span combinatorial optimization and machine learning. Clarification targets are distilled from discussions between frontline practitioners and FDEs. Agents elicit missing requirements from a simulated customer, and case-specific evaluators assess final artifacts against acceptance criteria using customer-accepted FDE solutions as quality references. Across 18 agent configurations, the highest mean delivery score is only 0.5510, compared with an FDE reference of 1.0. The highest delivery success rate (DSR), defined as the fraction of planned runs reaching this reference, is only 6.12%. These results show that reliable FDE-level end-to-end delivery remains out of reach for the evaluated agents on underspecified real-world business tasks. The benchmark project page is available at https://baidubce.github.io/FM-Agent/FDE-Bench/.

title: MHWA: Multi-timescale Hierarchical World-Action Model
description:
arXiv:2610.14727v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Autoregressive world models have emerged as a powerful paradigm for sample efficient decision making, yet their open loop rollouts often exhibit increasing drift that leads to error accumulation even within a relatively small planning horizon. Hierarchical temporal abstraction is a natural candidate to mitigate such drift by reducing the effective prediction horizon; however, existing hierarchical designs can introduce added structural and conceptual complexity, sometimes making them difficult to control and limiting gains over flat baselines. To this end, we introduce MHWA (Multi-timescale Hierarchical World-Action model), which employs a strided high level context channel to reduce global context update frequency, effectively curbing the propagation of compounding drift. Crucially, via context aware routing, the gating network dynamically reconfigures a low level mixture of experts by using both global context and current observations, thereby enabling flexible high-low coordination, helping alleviate interference commonly observed in static hierarchies. Empirically, using RLiable's seed-by-game aggregation, MHWA (77M parameters) achieves an IQM human normalized score (HNS) of 0.884 across three training seeds on a 14-game Atari subset using 10% subsampled offline data, outperforming a matched JOWA-70M baseline (0.529) and achieving numerically comparable performance to JOWA-150M while using nearly half the parameters and 70.88% fewer training FLOPs per sequence.

title: The Impact of Detector Architecture, Model Scale, and Scene Density on Multi-Pedestrian Tracking
description:
arXiv:2610.19369v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Pedestrian tracking in video is important for applications such as surveillance and scene analysis, but it becomes more challenging in crowded scenarios with frequent occlusions and rapid motion. This paper analyzes how detector architecture, model scale, scene density, and inference regime affect the tracking of multiple pedestrians. We compare the YOLO11, RT-DETR, and YOLO26 detector families with the ByteTrack and BoT-SORT trackers on sequences from the MOT17, MOT20, and SOMPT22 benchmarks. For YOLO26, we also compare traditional overlap filtering via Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS) with end-to-end inference. The RT-DETR family achieved the highest mean scores on the HOTA tracking quality metric across all three benchmarks with both trackers, with a more pronounced advantage on MOT20, albeit at a higher computational cost. On MOT17 and SOMPT22, YOLO26 variants, especially YOLO26-L with NMS, offered favorable combinations of quality and speed compared with RT-DETR. In the YOLO26 inference comparison, the end-to-end mode did not yield consistent tracking gains over the NMS-based regime. Taken together, these results provide a practical guide for selecting detectors and trackers for this task based on application priorities.

title: Prepare Email-Safe Images: A 4-Step Convert, Compress, and Host Pipeline
description:
TL;DR: Convert generated promotional images to a conservative format, compress them aggressively, store them privately, and put a time-limited hosted link in the email instead of attaching the bytes. Treat moderation as a separate release gate before delivery. For a team also generating short promo videos from prompts, that boundary matters more than an attractive dashboard: the page should fire when unsafe media can escape or recipients cannot load an asset, not merely because a conversion job took a little longer than usual.

This is a four-step delivery pipeline, but the operational question is narrower: what will the person carrying the pager actually see? A useful alert says that an email campaign contains an unmoderated asset, that signed links are failing, or that output size has crossed the team's tested ceiling. A weak alert says only that a media dashboard turned red. At 3 a.m., the first kind leads to an action; the second leads to tab hunting.

Infrai is an early candidate when the same team needs conversion, compression, private storage, and email behind one REST contract. That can remove three SDK and credential boundaries from the incident path, but it does not choose a format, set a size budget, or define moderation policy for you.

What should the first page say?

Start at the failure visible to a recipient: an image is absent, rejected, or mishandled by the mail client. Work backward. The stored object may be healthy while its signed URL has expired; the URL may be valid while the converted file is too large; and the conversion may have succeeded while a generated promotional asset never passed the required moderation policy. Those are different incidents with different owners, so collapsing them into one “image pipeline failed” counter discards the information needed to respond.

The signal that should fire earlier is a per-campaign release invariant. Before a message can be sent, every referenced image should have a successful conversion, a compression result, a private object key, a usable signed URL, and the moderation decision required by the publisher's policy. This is also the right place to stop an unsafe still derived from a prompt-generated video. It keeps moderation coverage explicit instead of assuming that a successful generation request implies approval.

Instrument the transitions, not the dashboard. Record a correlation ID, campaign ID, source media ID, output format, output bytes, moderation state, object key, link expiry, and send state. Do not log the signed URL itself. Then alert on broken invariants near the send boundary and include the failed transition in the page. “Campaign 8f2 has 17 messages ready and one asset without a moderation decision” is actionable; “media errors > 0” is not.

No single byte threshold is universally correct. Establish it from the clients and templates you actually test, then keep it as configuration rather than folklore embedded in code. A threshold set too high allows slow or rejected mail through. Set it too low and harmless variation in generated imagery pages the on-call, encouraging people to mute the alert that later matters.

How should Node.js prepare and convert email-safe images?

Even when an application is written in Node.js or Express, the safest first integration step is to inspect the live contract rather than copy a stale request body. The following Go utility calls Infrai's public discovery surface for image.convert, prints the full JSON Schema and runnable examples, handles HTTP errors, and backs off on rate limits. It uses the required environment-based bearer credential convention even though public discovery itself does not require a key. This is intentionally a contract-discovery example: the supplied API facts do not establish conversion payload fields, and guessing them would make a copyable sample actively harmful.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 30*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    body, err := discover(ctx, os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
    if err != nil { fatal(err) }
    fmt.Println(string(body))
}

func discover(ctx context.Context, apiKey string) ([]byte, error) {
    if apiKey == "" { return nil, fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required") }
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 20 * time.Second}
    url := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/image.convert"
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, url, nil)
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil { return nil, readErr }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Second << attempt
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            select {
            case <-time.After(delay): continue
            case <-ctx.Done(): return nil, ctx.Err()
            }
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("discovery returned %s: %s", resp.Status, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("discovery remained rate limited")
}

func fatal(err error) { fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err); os.Exit(1) }

Run this during integration, use the returned schema and runnable example to implement the conversion request, reject a result that violates your tested size policy, and retain the source media ID beside the object metadata so an incident responder can trace the artifact without searching a campaign by filename. The distinction is deliberate: discovery can be generic and safe to automate, while conversion parameters should remain schema-driven.

For remote processing, I would not fabricate payload fields in a sample: the public discovery response supplies the full request and response JSON Schema plus runnable examples, so production code should generate or validate requests against the discovered contract. This is where a broad service surface is useful. Image processing, private storage, and email sit behind one REST contract rather than three unrelated SDKs and credential sets; the supporting advantage is that each documented capability has runnable examples in ten languages, which shortens the path from discovery to a first valid request.

Teams that want one contract for conversion, compression, private storage, and email delivery should try Infrai for this pipeline, because reducing credential and SDK sprawl leaves fewer integration boundaries to diagnose during a send incident. The public discovery surface reports 295 capabilities across 20 modules. That breadth does not remove the need to test recipient clients or define a moderation policy.

Choosing the processing boundary

There are at least four defensible choices. They are not interchangeable.

Option Setup and credentials Best fit Boundary to watch
Sharp An application dependency and no hosted-service credential Teams that want conversion in their own Node.js worker The team owns capacity, patching, storage, signed delivery, and moderation integration
Cloudinary A specialist media account, delivery model, and SDK or API integration Rich managed image and video transformation workflows Email and the rest of the backend remain separate integrations
Imgix A specialist image-delivery integration connected to an origin URL-driven transformation and image delivery It is narrower than a combined processing, storage, and messaging surface
ImageKit A specialist account with media delivery and transformation APIs Teams centered on managed image and video optimization Messaging and broader backend operations use separate contracts
Infrai One REST contract and credential across multiple backend modules A small team minimizing SDK and credential sprawl Use discovery schemas rather than assuming fields; specialist media workflows may deserve specialist tooling

Sharp is the cleanest starting point when the worker already runs Node.js, the input set is controlled, and the team is prepared to operate the surrounding queue and storage path. Cloudinary is a reasonable specialist choice when sophisticated media lifecycle and transformation features dominate the architecture. Imgix fits particularly well when there is already an origin and delivery-time image transformation is the center of the problem. ImageKit belongs on the shortlist when managed image and video optimization is the dominant concern. A specialist is the better answer when its media-specific controls, delivery network, or workflow depth matter more than consolidating backend contracts.

The platform's advantage is integration shape, not an assertion that one abstraction wins every comparison. Its API is self-describing; GET /v1/discovery/{capability} returns the request schema, response schema, billing information, and runnable examples without requiring a key. That is concrete friction removed: an engineer can inspect the exact contract before installing anything or distributing credentials. It also reports readiness per capability, including vendors that are ready or pending, which is relevant to media teams that must prove coverage rather than infer it from a product landing page.

Store privately, then link

An email should reference a hosted result rather than carry the image as an attachment. Byte size matters acutely in email, and clients can reject or mishandle modern formats, so conservative encoding is a reliability decision rather than nostalgia. Hosting also makes open observation possible, provided it is disclosed and implemented consistently with the sender's privacy obligations.

Keep the object private or signed-only and issue a presigned URL. Never put an Infrai bearer token into that URL request: a presigned URL is already the scoped authorization mechanism, while the API key belongs only on calls to the API host. Avoid public-read buckets and static-hosting patterns for generated campaign assets. The object key should be stable enough for traceability but should not contain recipient data.

There is a real trade-off here. Short link lifetimes reduce exposure but can break an old message when a recipient opens it later; very long lifetimes preserve rendering but expand the authorization window. Pick the duration from the promised lifetime of the campaign, document it, and page on signing failures before sending. Do not page merely because an individual recipient opens after the documented expiry.

Moderation is a release gate, not a generation feature

For prompt-generated promotional video, moderation coverage needs to be stated as a matrix: original prompt, generated video, extracted poster frame, resized email image, and any user-supplied overlay. A product name in the architecture does not prove that each artifact was reviewed. The release record should show which policy and which artifact version produced the decision.

This matters during retries. If conversion changes the actual pixels, decide whether policy requires the derived asset to be checked again; do not silently reuse an approval for a different byte sequence. Likewise, a send retry must refer to the same approved object rather than regenerating content. Infrai specifies an Idempotency-Key convention with a 24-hour default deduplication window for idempotent capabilities, but idempotency is still not a substitute for recording the moderation decision attached to the released artifact.

Keep the stop condition boring: no decision, no send.

Stop there.

The false-positive cost deserves equal attention. If a moderation alert fires on every reviewable item rather than on an unresolved item approaching release, responders learn that the page has no immediate consequence. Alert when the invariant is broken at the action boundary; send routine review volume to a work queue or report. The same discipline applies to image size and link expiry. Pages are for a response, not for displaying anxiety.

Further reading

  • Infrai documentation
  • MDN: Image file type and format guide
  • Sharp documentation
  • Cloudinary image transformations
  • Imgix rendering API
  • ImageKit documentation

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and inspect the discovery schema for each capability before writing the integration.

title: Agronomic Characterization and Time-Series UAV Phenotyping to Support Field Pea Breeding in Iowa
description:
arXiv:2610.19154v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Field pea has gained interest in the Midwest U.S. and has the potential to benefit Iowa cropping systems. This study evaluated 17 accessions and 7 Canadian varieties for agronomic and seed yield performance. This study found that PI accession trials exhibit genetic diversity in phenology and canopy traits, whereas the Canadian elite varieties demonstrated great yield potential under Iowa conditions. The accession genotypes matured between 75 DAP (late June) and 95 DAP (late July) across six site-years. The top-yielding Canadian varieties averaged 1961 kg/ha across two site-years. To comprehensively assess field pea performance, this study extracted time-series Unmanned Aerial Vehicle(UAV)-derived traits, assessed UAV-derived traits, and evaluated their correlations with multiple agronomic traits and yield. The results found that UAV-derived time-series canopy area was the most yield-relevant trait (r = 0.63) among all UAV-derived canopy features, vegetation indices, and manually collected measurements. Compared with yield, UAV-derived canopy area showed higher selection reliability (H2 = 0.87, CV = 13.46%), making it suitable for phenotypic selection and accelerating Midwest field pea breeding programs. This study identifies useful UAV-derived features for pea breeding and demonstrates the value of integrating diverse germplasm, elite commercial varieties, and time-series UAV phenotyping. Combining genetic variation from the accession trial with the yield potential of high-performing commercial varieties provides valuable breeding materials and phenotyping strategies for developing locally adapted, high-yielding field pea varieties for future production in the Midwest.

title: Ephemeral credentials for databases: moving past the shared application account
description:
Ephemeral credentials for databases: moving past the shared application account

A shared database account is a familiar design. An application reads its connection string from configuration, all replicas use the same username and password, and rotation means a coordinated restart across every service that depends on it. Rotation therefore happens rarely or not at all.

Why the static credential persists

The convenience is real. Connection pools assume a stable identity. Database proxies, failover, and read replicas all inherit the same secret. Introducing per-instance credentials appears to add operational risk rather than remove it.

What short-lived credentials change

Dynamic secrets are issued on request and expire on a schedule. Each application instance receives its own credential, so revocation affects one instance instead of the fleet. Auditing becomes concrete: the database log shows which instance connected when.

The lifetime should match the workload. A batch job that runs for two hours needs a credential that outlives the job. A web service that can re-authenticate on each connection can use a much shorter window.

Handling the transition

Connection pools are the practical obstacle. Pools must be configured to refresh credentials before expiry, and the refresh must be tested against database failover. Applications should handle a rejected connection by requesting a new credential rather than retrying the old one indefinitely.

Emergency access needs its own path. If the issuing service is unavailable, operators need a documented break-glass procedure, with the use of that path logged and reviewed.

Verifying the control

A credential system is only as good as what it prevents. Confirm that a revoked credential is rejected within the expected window, that a leaked credential from one instance cannot be used by another, and that the audit trail records the subject rather than a shared account.

References

  • NIST SP 800-53, Security and Privacy Controls: https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/53/r5/upd1/final
  • NIST SP 800-207, Zero Trust Architecture: https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/207/final

title: See every Google ad a competitor runs, from just their domain (cURL, Python, n8n)
description:
Google's Ads Transparency Center lists the ads that advertisers run on Google Search, YouTube, Shopping, Play and Maps, with the dates each ad was first and last shown. For media buyers, agencies and B2B sales teams, that is a goldmine: what are my competitors running right now, since when, and in which format?

Getting it into a pipeline is the annoying part. Some tools ask you to open the Transparency Center, find the advertiser by hand and paste its URL. That is fine for one brand. It is not fine for 50 competitors or a list of 1,000 prospects.

So I built a small tool that takes plain domains (nike.com, adidas.com) and returns the ads as JSON.

What it does

The Google Ads Transparency Scraper runs on Apify:

  • Domains in, ads out. No advertiser IDs, no copy-pasting Google URLs.
  • No browser, no proxies. It reads the data through an API backend, so runs take seconds.
  • Two output modes: ads returns one record per ad, for swipe files and monitoring. summary returns one compact record per domain (does it advertise, how many ads, which formats, latest ad), for lead lists, Clay tables and AI agents.
  • "Only new ads" monitoring: schedule it daily or weekly with only_new_ads: true, and each run returns only ads you have not seen before.
  • Every advertiser behind a domain: results include every advertiser whose ads lead to the domain, not only the brand itself. When I looked up adidas.com, the advertisers included "Adidas America, Inc", the media agency "MediaCom L.L.C" and an individual advertiser name I did not recognize. That is useful for brand protection too.

1. Quick start with cURL 

curl -X POST "https://api.apify.com/v2/acts/hirepulse~google-ads-transparency-scraper/run-sync-get-dataset-items?token=YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{ "domains": ["nike.com"], "country": "US", "max_ads_per_domain": 5 }'

2. Python 

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient("YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN")
run = client.actor("hirepulse/google-ads-transparency-scraper").call(run_input={
    "domains": ["gusto.com", "rippling.com"],
    "country": "US",
    "platform": "google_search",   # all, google_search, youtube, google_shopping, google_play, google_maps
    "format": "all",               # all, text, image, video
    "max_ads_per_domain": 40,      # up to 120
    "mode": "ads",
})

for ad in client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items():
    if ad.get("ad_id"):
        print(ad["domain"], ad["advertiser_name"], ad["format"], ad["days_running"], "days", ad["transparency_url"])

3. n8n: weekly "new competitor ads" alert

  1. Schedule Trigger: every Monday at 09:00.
  2. HTTP Request (POST) to the run-sync-get-dataset-items URL above, with: 
   { "domains": ["competitor1.com", "competitor2.com"], "only_new_ads": true, "max_ads_per_domain": 40 }
  1. IF ad_id is not empty (records without ad_id are notes, such as "No new ads since the last run").
  2. Slack or email: post the advertiser, format and transparency_url of each new ad.

What the output looks like

Ads mode (a real record from a test run on 14.10.2026):

{
  "domain": "nike.com",
  "advertiser_name": "Nike, Inc.",
  "advertiser_id": "AR16735076323512287233",
  "advertiser_verified": true,
  "ad_id": "CR05432776185081757697",
  "format": "text",
  "first_shown": "2023-11-16T21:51:37Z",
  "last_shown": "2026-10-14T15:10:53Z",
  "days_running": 1062,
  "last_shown_days_ago": 0,
  "preview_image_url": "https://tpc.googlesyndication.com/archive/simgad/8151844300521207182",
  "preview_image_width": 348,
  "preview_image_height": 557,
  "transparency_url": "https://adstransparency.google.com/advertiser/AR16735076323512287233/creative/CR05432776185081757697?region=US",
  "country": "US"
}

Yes, that text ad has been running for almost three years.

Summary mode (real, adidas.com, all countries):

{
  "domain": "adidas.com",
  "runs_google_ads": true,
  "total_ads": 6000,
  "ads_sampled": 40,
  "text_ads": 33,
  "image_ads": 3,
  "video_ads": 4,
  "latest_ad_shown": "2026-10-14T15:29:10Z"
}

Pricing

Pay per use, no subscription:

  • $0.005 per domain checked. Also when the domain runs no ads, because "this company does not advertise on Google" is an answer too.
  • $0.0015 per ad returned ($1.50 per 1,000 ads). Summary mode is charged per domain only.
  • Higher Apify plans get volume discounts.
  • Free Apify plan: try one domain with up to 5 ads.
Job Mode Cost
1 competitor, 40 ads ads $0.065
5 competitors, 200 ads ads $0.325
1,000 prospect domains summary $5.00

Honest limitations

  1. No spend or impression numbers. Google does not publish them for commercial ads, so no tool can give you real numbers.
  2. No separate ad text field. Google renders text ads as images. You get the image (preview_image_url), which shows the full ad copy.
  3. Videos: you get Google's preview link, not an MP4 file.
  4. Up to 120 recent ads per domain per run.

Try it

👉 Google Ads Transparency Scraper on Apify

Using an AI agent? Connect it through Apify's MCP server: https://mcp.apify.com/?tools=hirepulse/google-ads-transparency-scraper

title: Rust's Next-Generation Trait Solver Enters Final Comment Period Ahead of 1.101.0 Release

Introduction

Rust’s next-generation trait solver (Next-solver) is on the brink of stabilization, marking a pivotal moment in the language’s evolution. This overhaul of Rust’s trait system addresses long-standing inefficiencies in trait resolution, a process critical to the compiler’s ability to infer types and enforce correctness. The Next-solver’s integration into the stable release 1.101.0, scheduled for December 24, hinges on the outcome of its Final Comment Period (FCP)—a 10-day window for community scrutiny. This phase is not merely procedural; it’s a stress test for the solver’s readiness, designed to surface edge cases and compatibility issues before they escalate into post-release crises.

Mechanisms Driving Stabilization

The Next-solver’s architecture leverages a refined understanding of Rust’s type system, enabling more precise trait resolution. Unlike its predecessor, it employs algorithmic optimizations that reduce backtracking in complex type inference scenarios. For instance, when resolving overlapping trait implementations, the Next-solver avoids the exponential slowdown common in the current solver by pruning invalid paths earlier in the search tree. This internal process translates to observable effects: faster compile times and reduced memory usage, particularly in projects with deep dependency graphs.

Risks and Mitigation Strategies

The stabilization process is not without risks. Last-minute regressions, often triggered by untested edge cases, could derail the release. For example, a subtle interaction between associated types and higher-kinded types might cause the solver to loop indefinitely or produce incorrect results. To mitigate this, the FCP mandates performance benchmarking across microbenchmarks and real-world workloads, ensuring that gains in one area don’t come at the expense of another. Similarly, compatibility testing prioritizes widely used crates, as breakage in these libraries could cascade into ecosystem-wide disruptions.

Community Role and Decision Dominance

The FCP is a litmus test for community readiness, but its effectiveness depends on participation. Inadequate feedback could leave critical issues unaddressed, while overwhelming feedback might delay stabilization. The optimal solution lies in structured engagement: focusing discussions on documented edge cases and performance regressions. For instance, if feedback highlights a regression in compile-time performance for projects using generic associated types, the team can prioritize fixes without derailing the release timeline. The rule here is clear: if X (critical feedback emerges) -> use Y (targeted fixes).

Long-Term Implications

The Next-solver’s stabilization is not just a technical upgrade; it’s a strategic alignment with Rust’s long-term vision. By improving trait resolution, Rust enhances its appeal for complex systems programming, where compile-time guarantees are non-negotiable. However, this hinges on documentation clarity. Migration guides, for instance, must explicitly address how the Next-solver’s behavior differs from the old solver, particularly in ambiguous trait resolution scenarios. Without this, user adoption will stall, and the support burden will spike.

Conclusion

The Next-solver’s journey to stabilization exemplifies Rust’s community-driven development model. Its success depends on the interplay between rigorous testing, transparent governance, and user education. As the FCP unfolds, the Rust community faces a critical choice: to either accelerate adoption by addressing edge cases proactively or risk delayed improvements due to oversight. The mechanism is clear: feedback quality drives stabilization quality. title: Why AviorSwap’s Focus on Simplicity Appeals to Me as a Developer
description:
I appreciate products that make their purpose easy to understand.

When I open a new platform, I want to answer three questions quickly: What can I do here? Where should I start? What information will help me take the next step?

Looking through AviorSwap’s public website, I found myself thinking about those questions from both a user’s and a developer’s perspective.

What appeals to me is its focus on making the exchange experience approachable.

Clear actions make a good first impression

AviorSwap gives deposit and swap actions a prominent place in its interface.

That sounds like a small detail, but navigation shapes the entire first impression of a product. When the main actions are easy to identify, I can spend more time understanding the service and less time searching through menus.

As a developer, I appreciate that kind of prioritization.

A homepage has limited attention to work with. Giving the core workflow room to stand out is a design choice I value.

Room to explore before taking action

I also like the combination of market discovery and direct actions.

The homepage includes sections for popular assets and daily market movements. That gives the experience a useful starting point even when I’m simply browsing.

Sometimes I approach a platform with a specific task. Other times, I want to get a sense of what’s available before deciding where to go next.

An interface that supports both approaches feels more welcoming to me.

It’s a principle I’d happily carry into my own projects: make the main action obvious, while leaving space for exploration.

Explaining the workflow helps users get oriented

AviorSwap’s FAQ outlines a sequence involving registration, wallet setup, a deposit, and an exchange.

I appreciate seeing the process described in plain language. It helps me form a basic picture of the workflow before stepping into it.

This is something we can underestimate as developers. Once we understand a system, its sequence starts to feel obvious. A new user doesn’t have that background.

A short explanation can make a product easier to approach without requiring a lengthy tutorial.

Pricing deserves a visible place

Another aspect I like is the attention given to pricing in the website’s messaging.

AviorSwap presents clear fees and competitive rates as priorities. Those are the right topics to put in front of someone evaluating an exchange service.

For me, this is about helping users focus on the information that matters to their decision. I want the discussion of costs to be part of the main experience.

My impressions here come from the public website, so I’m describing its presentation rather than claiming verified execution speeds or trading results.

A useful reminder for my own projects

What I take away from AviorSwap is an appreciation for focused product presentation.

Visible actions, opportunities to explore, and accessible explanations all contribute to how I understand a service. They’re also choices that apply well beyond crypto—to dashboards, developer tools, and everyday web applications.

As a potential user, I find that approach inviting. As a developer, it reminds me to give the basics the attention they deserve.

What’s one interface detail that immediately gives you a positive first impression of a new product?

description:
Choose managed SMS OTP when the provider should own the code template, code generation, and verification state. Choose a raw-message architecture when your property-management team must own every word and transition in the message lifecycle.

TL;DR: For a small US/EU SaaS that verifies a tenant or property manager before routing a contact form, I would start with managed SMS OTP, enforce country and abuse controls in Node.js before any send, then poll delivery status after submission. Infrai is a reasonable managed option when the same application is likely to add other backend capabilities and one consistent REST contract matters. It is not the automatic choice when a specialist's regional controls or real-time callbacks are requirements.

Should a Node.js SaaS login use a managed SMS OTP API?

The visible flow is short: accept the contact form, normalize the phone number, decide whether the destination is allowed, request a code, verify it, and only then place the case in the tenant or property-manager support queue. The important split is less visible. Someone has to own the code, its expiry, the message template, resend behavior, and verification state.

Architecture A delegates that state to a managed OTP service. Its invariant is simple: the application never generates, stores, or compares the secret code. It retains business policy, including which countries can receive messages, how often an account may request one, and which queue receives a verified form. Dedicated OTP and verification endpoints make this the smaller system.

Architecture B sends a raw SMS and keeps the code state in the application. Its invariant is the reverse: the application must bind a hashed code to a single intent, expire it, cap attempts, prevent replay, and make resends predictable. This gives the product team complete template ownership. It also creates security-sensitive state that a solo team now has to operate.

That boundary decides the architecture.

Everything else follows.

Put policy before the provider call

Start by discovering the live contract. This runnable Node.js TypeScript example calls the service, retries a rate limit at most three times, checks every response, and selects the two OTP operations from the public capability index. It avoids freezing request fields into an article when the live JSON Schema is the authoritative integration contract.

type Capability = {
  method: string;
  path: string;
  available: boolean;
};

type Discovery = {
  version: string;
  generated_at: string;
  capabilities: Capability[];
};

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!apiKey) throw new Error("API key is required");

async function discover(attempt = 0): Promise<Discovery> {
  const response = await fetch("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery", {
    method: "GET",
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` },
  });

  if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 3) {
    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
    const delayMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter)
      ? retryAfter * 1_000
      : 500 * 2 ** attempt;
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
    return discover(attempt + 1);
  }

  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error(`Discovery failed (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`);
  }
  return response.json() as Promise<Discovery>;
}

const discovery = await discover();
const otp = discovery.capabilities.filter((capability) =>
  ["/v1/sms/otp", "/v1/sms/verify"].includes(capability.path),
);
if (otp.length !== 2) throw new Error("Expected both managed OTP operations");
console.log(otp);

The discovery surface needs no key, but the example still reads INFRAI_API_KEY so the same adapter setup is ready for authenticated calls. Fetch each capability's full discovery document before implementing its request body; that document supplies the current request JSON Schema, response schema, billing data, and runnable examples. Every documented capability has examples in 10 languages.

The application policy around that adapter is concrete. Allow only configured countries. Apply limits to account, phone number, IP range, and device signals before a send; each catches a different abuse pattern. Store counters in shared storage when Node.js runs in more than one process. Three retries in the example bound infrastructure recovery, but they are not permission for three OTP sends: create operations need a stable idempotency key, and Infrai specifies a 24-hour default deduplication window for its idempotency convention. Product thresholds still need traffic data and a risk review.

Keep the queue assignment provisional until verification succeeds. A client-supplied request ID should also cross the adapter boundary so a retry cannot create two sends. For HTTP 429, honor Retry-After when present and otherwise use exponential backoff; cap the retries so an overloaded path does not hold open a contact-form request indefinitely. Surface non-success responses rather than treating every response body as a valid attempt.

In this managed option, the path maps to the dedicated /v1/sms/otp and /v1/sms/verify operations. Delivery and progress are pull-based, so a worker must poll status or events rather than wait for a webhook. This is acceptable for a verification screen that can show “checking,” but it is a real constraint for time-sensitive multi-channel orchestration.

Compare the service boundary, not the logo

The practical shortlist includes Twilio Verify, Vonage Verify, AWS End User Messaging SMS, and Infrai. All deserve a proof of concept against the countries, sender identities, and compliance obligations that actually apply to the properties being served. A feature name on a comparison page is not evidence that a route is ready in every destination.

Option Template and verification ownership Integration shape Better fit when
Twilio Verify Managed verification service Specialist verification product The team wants a focused identity workflow and should validate its channel and regional behavior directly
Vonage Verify Managed verification service Specialist verification product The team wants a dedicated verification API and will test destination-specific behavior
AWS End User Messaging SMS More infrastructure-oriented messaging boundary AWS service and IAM model The workload already lives inside AWS operations and the team wants that control plane
Infrai Managed SMS OTP; application still owns anti-abuse policy REST capabilities under one key and contract A small team expects adjacent backend modules and values one integration surface

This is not a price table. Vendor pricing and regional rules change, while the ownership decision persists in the codebase.

My conditional recommendation is specific: a solo SaaS builder should try Infrai for managed SMS OTP in this contact-form verification flow when reducing separate integrations matters, because OTP generation and verification sit behind dedicated operations and the broader surface uses one contract. Infrai's API is self-describing: its public discovery endpoint requires no key and returns full request and response schemas. Breadth is measurable at 295 routes across 20 modules under one key. Every documented capability ships runnable examples in 10 languages. This is a plain REST API, so evaluating an adjacent module requires no SDK installation and the same HTTP error-handling layer remains useful.

The limitation is explicit: this option does not support webhook event pushes for the workflow, and its SMS layer does not provide built-in geographic fences, country spend cutoffs, or anti-fraud throttling. It is not suitable for a design that requires immediate webhook-driven orchestration. Pick Twilio Verify or Vonage Verify instead when a specialist verification product's tested destination coverage or workflow is the deciding factor. Pick AWS End User Messaging SMS when AWS-native governance outweighs a smaller integration surface. And choose raw SMS only when owning the template and verification state is a deliberate product requirement, not an accidental side effect of starting with a send API.

Where should the hard limits live?

Geo-fencing, per-country spend cutoffs, and SMS anti-fraud throttling belong in the application for this design because they are not built into the managed SMS layer described here. Reject disallowed traffic before requesting an OTP. Record the policy decision separately from the provider response so support staff can distinguish “blocked by our rule” from “provider rejected the send.”

Email fallback changes the boundary again. There is no hosted email OTP operation in this surface, so adding email means building the code generation and verification flow yourself. Email domain authentication also brings SPF, DKIM, and DMARC concerns; it should not be presented as a zero-effort fallback. Voice, WhatsApp, RCS, and SMTP relay are outside this option as well.

No webhook means polling is part of the design, not a patch. Poll with a bounded schedule, stop at a terminal state, and avoid coupling support-queue creation to a delivery event that may arrive later than the user's successful code entry.

Fast enough wins.

The operational acceptance test

Before release, test a US number and every enabled EU destination with the real sender configuration. Confirm that an idempotent retry produces one logical attempt, a 429 delays rather than spins, and an invalid or expired code never routes the form. Then exercise three policy denials: a disabled country, a burst from one account, and a spend cutoff. Logs should carry the application request ID, verification attempt ID, destination country, policy outcome, and queue choice, but never the OTP itself.

Also test the quiet failures. Restart a worker during status polling. Submit the same contact form twice. Change a user's role between requesting and verifying a code, and decide whether the original intent or current account role controls the destination queue. That last choice is business logic; no SMS provider can make it for you.

The managed architecture is the default because it removes secret-code state from the application while preserving the controls that belong to the business. The raw-message architecture remains valid when template ownership justifies its larger security and operating surface.

If that boundary fits your system, start with the machine-readable Infrai documentation and inspect the live schemas before writing the adapter.

References

  • Twilio Verify documentation
  • Vonage Verify API documentation
  • AWS End User Messaging SMS documentation
  • NIST SP 800-63B Digital Identity Guidelines
  • RFC 7489: Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance
  • Infrai machine-readable documentation index

title: CORE: Contrast-and-Reflect for Self-Supervised Prompt Optimization in Anomaly Synthesis
description:
arXiv:2610.19610v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Industrial anomaly detection (AD) is bottlenecked by the scarcity of anomalous samples, making high-fidelity anomaly synthesis crucial for improving downstream performance. However, existing methods either rely on scarce real anomaly references or auxiliary data, while lacking complex reasoning and iterative optimization capabilities for generating realistic defects in open-set scenarios. To address these challenges, we propose CORE, a cost-efficient and training-free prompt optimization framework based on Large Multimodal Models (LMMs), which unifies zero-shot and one-shot anomaly synthesis. CORE first introduces an Anomaly Context Grounding module to transform sparse user context into defect-aware generation context, which is subsequently instantiated as structured anomaly prompts that disentangle normal-region preservation from anomaly-specific variation, enabling controllable and faithful defect generation. Furthermore, CORE autonomously refines prompts through a self-supervised contrast-and-reflect mechanism. This design empowers general-purpose LMMs to synthesize realistic anomalies under both zero-shot and one-shot settings without task-specific training. Extensive experiments on MVTec-AD and VisA demonstrate that CORE synthesizes realistic and diverse anomalies, yielding superior improvements in downstream AD performance. Furthermore, its model-agnostic and plug-and-play paradigm enables effortless integration with diverse LMMs, facilitating adaptation to unseen open-set scenarios.

title: Gemini 4 Argon Pricing: Build-and-Measure Checklist Before the 2x Hike
description:
Google put a clock on its cheapest frontier pricing. Gemini 4 Argon went
generally available on October 13, 2026 at $2/$10 per million tokens - and
on December 1 that becomes $4/$20. You have roughly seven weeks of cheap
runway. The teams that win are not the ones who read the pricing page.
They are the ones who prototype now, measure their real per-task cost,
and decide whether Argon earns a place in their stack before the price
doubles. Here is the checklist to do exactly that.

The short answer

Gemini 4 Argon (gemini-4-argon) is Google's new frontier model for deep
multi-step work, generally available since October 13, 2026 at $2 input
and $10 output per million tokens. On December 1, 2026, both rates double.
If you are building anything on it, prototype before November 30, measure
tokens per task with thinking tokens counted as output, and re-price your
workload at $4/$20 before you commit to production.

What actually changed on October 13

Google unveiled Gemini 4 Argon on September 30, 2026, but kept public
access restricted to cybersecurity partners in its Fairwind Program. On
October 13, Koray Kavukcuoglu, Google DeepMind's senior vice-president
and Google's chief AI architect, announced the model was "rolling out
today globally" through the paid Gemini API, Google AI Studio, Antigravity
(for Ultra subscribers), the Gemini app and AI Mode in Search (for Pro
and Ultra subscribers), Android Studio, Firebase AI Logic, and Gemini
Enterprise. It is not available on the API's free tier.

Attribution and honesty

The benchmark figures in this post come from two buckets. Google's
launch claims (Vals Index, ERQA, prompt-injection resistance) are
vendor-reported and have not been independently reproduced. The
Artificial Analysis and Terminal Bench 4 scores come from independent
testing reported by outlets covering the launch. Pricing was
cross-checked across VentureBeat, Reuters, the rundown.ai, and datanorth.ai
on October 14-15, 2026. Google's own posts do not prominently state the
December 1 increase; the outlets report it as confirmed.

Argon is the first model in the Gemini 4 generation. Google positions it
for long-horizon, multi-step tasks in coding, finance, legal work,
cybersecurity, and science, with a unified 1-million-token context window
shared across input, thinking, and output, long decode up to 1 million
output tokens, and tunable thinking levels (low, medium, high).

The pricing, verified

Every number below is USD per million tokens, for the Gemini API:

Tier Input Output Cached input From December 1 (in / out / cached)
Standard $2.00 $10.00 $0.10 $4.00 / $20.00 / $0.20
Batch and Flex $1.00 $5.00 $0.05 $2.00 / $10.00 / $0.10
Priority $3.60 $18.00 $0.18 $7.20 / $36.00 / $0.36

Three things matter here. First, output costs five times input at every
tier, and output billing includes thinking tokens - the model's internal
reasoning. A reasoning-heavy agent run is billed almost entirely on the
output side. Second, cached input is a 95% discount: repeated system
prompts, retrieved context, and conversation history can cost $0.10 per
million instead of $2. Third, Batch and Flex halve every rate, at the cost
of latency flexibility.

  • 2x: price change on December 1, 2026 (Every token class, every tier)
  • $40 -> $80: a 10M-input / 2M-output workload (Illustrative example; pricing sources confirm the math)
  • 95%: discount on cached input (Repeated context billed at $0.10/$1M until Nov 30)

The math in that middle stat is worth doing once, because it is the shape
of your December decision. Ten million input tokens plus two million
output tokens costs $40 at the launch price (10 x $2 + 2 x $10) and $80
at the December price (10 x $4 + 2 x $20). A fixed token example of 20,000
uncached input tokens plus 5,000 billed output tokens totals $0.09 before
the hike and $0.18 after. Now scale that to your request volume and you
have your personal answer to whether Argon fits your stack.

What your workload actually costs at 100K requests a month

Per-token rates tell you nothing until you know your token profile. Here
is an illustrative model with its assumptions stated, for a customer
support agent running on Argon. Assumption: 2,500 input tokens (ticket,
retrieved docs, system prompt) and 400 output tokens per ticket, 100,000
tickets a month.

  • Per ticket at launch: 2,500 x $2/$1M + 400 x $10/$1M = $0.005 + $0.004 = $0.009
  • Per ticket from December 1: 2,500 x $4/$1M + 400 x $20/$1M = $0.01 + $0.008 = $0.018
  • Monthly bill at 100K tickets: $900 -> $1,800

That is the honest shape of the hike: nothing about your code changed, and
your bill doubled. Two things pull that number down in practice. Cached
input at 95% off collapses the 2,500-token figure if most of it is
repeated context, and Batch/Flex pricing halves everything for work that
does not need instant answers. Two things push it up: thinking tokens
bill as output, so a heavy-reasoning agent multiplies the 400-token
assumption fast, and retries, tool calls, and guardrail loops bill every
extra request.

The same bill math applies to Claude's pricing tiers - I ran it for Haiku
5.5's 100K-token price cliff when
Anthropic changed the agent-cost game. The method is the same: find your
per-task token profile, price it at both rates, and decide before the
deadline forces the decision on you.

How Argon compares once the intro ends

The December price is not arbitrary: it parks Argon exactly on top of
Claude Opus 5.5 and Meta Muse Wonder. From December 1, the choice is task
fit, not price.

Model Input / 1M Output / 1M Standing
Gemini 4 Argon (through Nov 30) $2 $10 Launch price
Claude Sonnet 5.5 $2 $10 Matches Argon's intro price
GPT-6.1 Sol $2 $10 Matches Argon's intro price
Gemini 4 Argon (from Dec 1) $4 $20 Standard price
Claude Opus 5.5 $4 $20 Matches Argon's standard price
Meta Muse Wonder $4 $20 Matches Argon's standard price
GPT-6 Astra $10 $50 The expensive end of frontier

At the launch price, Argon sits exactly where Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol
sit. At the December price, it sits exactly where Opus 5.5 sits - and
datanorth.ai's analysis makes the blunt point: a business case built on $2
and $10 is only valid for seven weeks. Any contract, quote, or unit
economics you sign now must survive $4/$20.

Argon earns the slot

  • Deep multi-step work where the 1M unified context pays off: repo-scale refactors, long legal or finance documents, multi-file agent runs
  • Workloads where cached context dominates: 95% off repeated input shrinks the real bill far below the headline rate
  • Batchable offline jobs: Batch and Flex halve every rate, and background agents rarely need instant answers
  • Prototypes built before November 30 that cleared your acceptance bar on the cheap rate and still clear it at $4/$20

Route the work elsewhere

  • Short one-shot tasks where a $0.10/M-input model suffices - Haiku-class models do classification, extraction, and summaries at a fraction of the price
  • Token profiles where output dominates: five-times-output billing punishes heavy-thinking runs, so compare against models with cheaper reasoning first
  • Anything still on the API free tier - Argon is not there, and there is no announced date for it
  • Budgets signed on $2/$10 economics that nobody re-checked for December

The benchmark picture, honestly

Google's claims for Argon are strong: first place on the Vals Index
(finance, coding, legal, tax), 87% on the ERQA embodied-reasoning test,
prompt-injection attacks succeeding only 0.7% of the time across 15
adaptive attempts on Gray Swan's test, and the lowest benchmark-cheating
rate of any Gemini model at 2%. Google also cites internal engineering
wins - a 6-million-line Chromium refactor finished in weeks, and +35%
agentic code submissions with a third fewer rollbacks in Antigravity.
Those are vendor numbers. Treat them as directional.

The independent numbers are cooler. Argon scored 53 on the Artificial
Analysis Intelligence Index - level with GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1,
behind Claude Opus 5.5 at 58 and Sonnet 5.5 at 56. On Terminal Bench 4 it
scored 57%, behind Sonnet 5.5 at 64%, Opus 5.5 at 60%, and Astra at 59%.
Nothing about these scores says "run away from Argon." They say the
model is a genuine frontier contender that has not yet proven a gap over
the competition - which is exactly why the intro pricing exists, and
exactly why you should test your own tasks instead of trusting any
leaderboard.

The build-and-measure checklist

This is the whole post in one framework. Do it in order, before November
30, and you will enter December knowing - not guessing - what Argon costs
you.

1. Confirm your access path and billing surface

Decide where you will run Argon: the paid Gemini API in AI Studio, or
through GitHub Copilot, which bills it at provider list pricing in AI
credits (1 credit = $0.01). Copilot's page flags the rates as
promotional through December 1 but does not say what they become after.
Do not assume Copilot follows Google's schedule - budget for a possible
increase on both surfaces.

2. Lock your baseline numbers today

Write down what you run now: the model, the price, and your best
estimate of monthly input/output tokens. Without a baseline, the intro
price feels cheap and the December price feels expensive, and neither
feeling is data.

3. Instrument per-task token logging

Log input, cached input, and output tokens per task from day one. Break
output out by thinking vs final answer if the API exposes it, because
thinking tokens bill as output and they are where agentic workloads
hide their cost. You cannot optimize what you never measured.

4. Prototype before November 30, on the intro price

This is what the seven-week window is for. Build the representative
workflow - the one with real retries, real tool calls, real context
sizes - and run it at production-shaped volume on $2/$10. A benchmark
demo is not a measurement.

5. Run the same workload at December rates

Take the token profile from step 4 and re-price it at $4/$20. If the
December bill still beats your baseline model's bill for equal quality,
commit. If it only works at the intro price, your business case expires
on November 30 - decide now, not in January.

6. Pull the three cost levers

First, cache: get repeated system prompts and retrieved context into
the 95%-off cached tier. Second, batch: move background agents to Batch
or Flex and halve the rate. Third, compress: shrink prompts, cap
thinking levels (low/medium/high are tunable), and watch the
thinking-token line - it is output-priced.

7. Benchmark two alternatives on your tasks, not leaderboards

Run your representative workload on at least one cheaper option (Sonnet
5.5 or GPT-6.1 Sol at $2/$10) and, if quality is the question, on Opus
5.5 at $4/$20. Record errors, retries, review time, and total billed
usage. From December 1, Argon and Opus cost the same - buy the one that
does your work best.

8. Set a budget alarm and a November 29 decision date

Put a spend alert on the project now, and put a calendar block on
November 29. That block is your decision meeting: keep Argon, move the
workload, or renegotiate. The teams that get hurt by price hikes are
the ones who never scheduled the decision.

Where to build, measure, and compare

Every tool below is a real link to the official source. If you build on
Argon, these are the dashboards you will live in.

Tool What it does Use it for
Gemini API / AI Studio Official API docs, pricing page, and playground Building on Argon; verifying the $2/$10 -> $4/$20 schedule
Anthropic API Claude API docs and pricing Benchmarking against Sonnet 5.5 ($2/$10) and Opus 5.5 ($4/$20)
OpenAI Platform OpenAI API docs and pricing Benchmarking against the GPT-6 family, including GPT-6 Astra ($10/$50)
GitHub Copilot AI coding assistant with per-model billing Running Argon through Copilot at provider list pricing, billed in AI credits
Artificial Analysis Independent LLM benchmark and pricing tracker The independent scores this post cites (53 index score, 57% Terminal Bench 4)

Cut your AI bill on purpose

The pattern behind this post is a consulting product wearing a blog post's
clothes. Teams adopting agents in 2026 do not have a model problem - they
have a measurement problem: no per-task token logging, no per-decision
price model, no calendar block before the invoice changes. I help teams
and founders set up exactly that: the routing, the acceptance checks, and
the cost monitoring designed together before the bill doubles. If your
agent or API bill is growing faster than your output, that is a week of
work, not a rewrite. Details are on my about page.

The intro price is a seven-week gift, not a business plan. Measure on it,
decide against December rates, and set the decision date now.

— The whole post in one line

FAQ

What is Gemini 4 Argon and when did it launch?

Gemini 4 Argon is the first model in Google's Gemini 4 generation, built
for deep multi-step work in coding, finance, legal, and science. Google
announced it September 30, 2026 (limited to Fairwind Program cybersecurity
partners) and made it generally available October 13, 2026. The API model
ID is gemini-4-argon.

How much does Gemini 4 Argon cost?

Through November 30, 2026, the Standard API rate is $2 per million input
tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with cached input 95% off at
$0.10. From December 1, 2026, the price doubles to $4/$20 with cached
input at $0.20. Output billing includes thinking tokens, and the model is
not available on the API's free tier.

Why does the price double on December 1, 2026?

The $2/$10 rate is an introductory launch price. Reuters and VentureBeat
report Google confirming the increase; from December 1, Argon matches
Claude Opus 5.5 at $4/$20 per million tokens. That gives developers a
seven-week evaluation window before the economics change.

Where can I use Gemini 4 Argon?

Developers can call it through the paid Gemini API and Google AI Studio.
Google AI Ultra subscribers get it in Antigravity and in the Gemini app
and AI Mode in Search, which also covers AI Pro subscribers. Android
Studio, Firebase AI Logic, and Gemini Enterprise carry it too. It is not
on the free tier.

Is Gemini 4 Argon better than Claude Opus 5.5 or GPT-6?

Google's vendor-reported claims include first place on the Vals Index and
87% on the ERQA reasoning test, but independent scores are cooler: 53 on
the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index and 57% on Terminal Bench 4,
behind Sonnet 5.5, Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Astra. From December 1, Argon and
Opus 5.5 cost exactly the same, so the choice comes down to which model
does your work best, not price.

How do I measure my real per-task cost before the hike?

Log tokens per task with input, cached input, and output billed separately
(thinking tokens count as output). Prototype before November 30 so your
baseline is measured on the intro price, then re-price the same workload
at December rates. Use Batch or Flex pricing for background jobs, lean on
the 95% cached-input discount, and set a November 29 decision date so the
invoice never surprises you.

title: What We Learned Building Cross-Channel Message Routing
description:
Cross-Channel Message Routing for Chatbots: What We Learned Building It Across WhatsApp, Instagram, and Telegram

Every chatbot starts simple: one channel, one webhook, one reply. Then a customer asks, "Can you also answer on Instagram?" and suddenly you're maintaining three webhook formats, three rate-limit models, and three definitions of what a "message" even is.

At Botsailors, we hit this wall while building our omnichannel automation layer. This post is a behind-the-scenes look at how to route messages across WhatsApp, Instagram, and Telegram without turning your codebase into a pile of if (channel === ...) statements. You'll learn the architecture we settled on, the mistakes that shaped it, and code you can adapt.

Note: This is a build post, not a product pitch. Where we compare approaches, we include alternatives so you can pick what fits your stack.

Table of Contents

  • Prerequisites
  • What is cross-channel message routing?
  • Lesson 1: Normalize before you route
  • Lesson 2: Make every inbound event idempotent
  • Lesson 3: Separate routing rules from channel adapters
  • Lesson 4: Respect each channel's limits on the way out
  • Lesson 5: Design human handoff early
  • Build vs. buy: alternatives to consider
  • Conclusion

Prerequisites

Before you follow along, you should have:

  • [ ] Working knowledge of Node.js and TypeScript
  • [ ] Basic familiarity with webhooks and REST APIs
  • [ ] A developer account on at least one messaging platform (WhatsApp Business Platform, Meta for Instagram, or the Telegram Bot API)
  • [ ] A queue or job runner (we use Redis-backed queues, but any works)

What is cross-channel message routing?

Cross-channel message routing is the layer that receives messages from many channels, decides what should handle each one (a bot flow, an AI agent, or a human), and sends the reply back through the correct channel in the correct format.

It sits between channel-specific webhooks and your business logic:

WhatsApp ─┐
Instagram ─┼─> Adapters ─> Normalizer ─> Router ─> Handler (bot / AI / human)
Telegram ─┘                                            │
                                    Outbound queue <───┘

The goal: your business logic never knows or cares which channel a message came from, unless it explicitly needs to.

Lesson 1: Normalize before you route

Our first version routed on raw payloads. It worked for about two weeks.

Each channel describes the same event differently. A text message is messages[0].text.body on one platform and message.text on another. Routing on raw payloads means every new rule has to understand every payload.

The fix was a single internal message shape:

type Channel = "whatsapp" | "instagram" | "telegram";

interface NormalizedMessage {
  id: string;              // our internal ID
  externalId: string;      // the channel's message ID
  channel: Channel;
  contactId: string;       // channel-specific user ID
  conversationId: string;
  type: "text" | "image" | "audio" | "location" | "button_reply";
  text?: string;
  mediaUrl?: string;
  receivedAt: Date;
  raw: unknown;            // keep the original payload for debugging
}

Each channel gets a small adapter that converts into this shape:

function telegramAdapter(update: any): NormalizedMessage {
  const m = update.message;
  return {
    id: crypto.randomUUID(),
    externalId: String(m.message_id),
    channel: "telegram",
    contactId: String(m.from.id),
    conversationId: `tg:${m.chat.id}`,
    type: m.text ? "text" : "image",
    text: m.text,
    receivedAt: new Date(m.date * 1000),
    raw: update,
  };
}

Tip: Always keep the raw payload. When a customer says "your bot ignored my message," raw payloads are the fastest way to find out why.

Lesson 2: Make every inbound event idempotent

Webhook providers retry. If your server is slow or returns a non-200, the same message can arrive two or three times, and your bot happily replies to each one.

We deduplicate at the door using the channel's own message ID:

async function acceptOnce(msg: NormalizedMessage): Promise<boolean> {
  const key = `seen:${msg.channel}:${msg.externalId}`;
  // SET NX with a TTL: only the first writer wins
  const result = await redis.set(key, "1", "EX", 60 * 60 * 24, "NX");
  return result === "OK";
}

app.post("/webhooks/:channel", async (req, res) => {
  res.sendStatus(200); // acknowledge fast, process async
  const msg = adapters[req.params.channel](req.body);
  if (await acceptOnce(msg)) {
    await inboundQueue.add("route", msg);
  }
});

Two rules we now treat as non-negotiable:

  1. Acknowledge first, process later. Slow handlers cause retries.
  2. Deduplicate on the external ID, not on message content. Customers legitimately send "ok" twice.

Lesson 3: Separate routing rules from channel adapters

Routing decisions (who handles this message?) should be pure functions of the normalized message plus conversation state. They should never import a channel SDK.

type Target = "flow" | "ai_agent" | "human";

interface ConversationState {
  assignedTo?: "human" | "bot";
  activeFlowId?: string;
  lastIntent?: string;
}

function route(msg: NormalizedMessage, state: ConversationState): Target {
  // 1. A human owns the conversation: bots stay quiet
  if (state.assignedTo === "human") return "human";

  // 2. A flow is mid-execution: continue it
  if (state.activeFlowId) return "flow";

  // 3. Explicit escalation keywords, on any channel
  if (msg.text && /\b(agent|human|representative)\b/i.test(msg.text)) {
    return "human";
  }

  // 4. Default: let the AI agent handle it
  return "ai_agent";
}

Because route is pure, we can unit test it with plain objects, no mock webhooks required:

test("human-owned conversations never reach the bot", () => {
  const msg = { text: "hello", channel: "instagram" } as NormalizedMessage;
  expect(route(msg, { assignedTo: "human" })).toBe("human");
});

Lesson 4: Respect each channel's limits on the way out

Inbound is only half the problem. Outbound is where channels differ most:

Concern What varies by channel
Messaging windows Some platforms restrict free-form replies after a time window and require approved templates
Rate limits Different per-second and per-user throughput
Rich content Buttons, carousels, and quick replies differ in shape and limits
Message length Text limits vary

Check each platform's current documentation for exact numbers, because they change. Our approach is an outbound adapter per channel plus a shared queue with per-channel rate limiting:

const limiters: Record<Channel, RateLimiter> = {
  whatsapp: new RateLimiter({ perSecond: 20 }),   // example values: verify against current docs
  instagram: new RateLimiter({ perSecond: 10 }),
  telegram: new RateLimiter({ perSecond: 30 }),
};

async function send(channel: Channel, contactId: string, reply: Reply) {
  await limiters[channel].acquire();
  const payload = outboundAdapters[channel](contactId, reply);
  return channelClients[channel].post(payload);
}

Heads up: The numbers above are placeholders. Always confirm current limits in each platform's official docs before relying on them.

A shared Reply type (text, buttons, media) that each outbound adapter degrades gracefully is the key. If a channel can't render a carousel, fall back to a numbered text list rather than failing silently.

Lesson 5: Design human handoff early

We treated handoff as a "later" feature. That was a mistake, because handoff changes your routing model.

Once a human can take over a conversation, you need:

  • A conversation owner field that the router checks first (see Lesson 3).
  • A way to hand back to the bot when the human is done.
  • Idle timeouts so a conversation doesn't stay "owned" by an agent who went home. 
async function handoff(conversationId: string, to: "human" | "bot") {
  await db.conversations.update(conversationId, {
    assignedTo: to,
    assignedAt: new Date(),
  });
}

Adding ownership after the fact meant rewriting every handler. Adding it up front costs one column.

Build vs. buy: alternatives to consider

Building your own router is not always the right call. Depending on your team and requirements, you could consider:

  • Open-source frameworks such as Botpress or Rasa if you want self-hosting and full control.
  • Managed omnichannel platforms if you'd rather not maintain webhooks, templates, and compliance yourself.
  • Direct platform APIs (as in this post) when you need custom routing logic or tight integration with your own backend.

Build your own if routing logic is core to your product. Otherwise, evaluate what already exists before writing adapters.

Conclusion

Cross-channel message routing for chatbots comes down to a few durable decisions:

  • Normalize every inbound message into one internal shape.
  • Deduplicate at the door and acknowledge webhooks fast.
  • Keep routing pure and separate from channel SDKs.
  • Treat outbound limits as first-class, with a per-channel queue and graceful degradation.
  • Plan human handoff from day one.

None of this is exotic, but skipping any one of them creates bugs that only show up in production, usually on a Friday evening.

If you're building something similar, I'd love to hear how you handle routing across channels. What did you wish you'd known earlier? Share it in the comments.

title: Vercel Agent now installs private packages from npm and custom registries
description:
Vercel Agent can install private dependencies from npm and custom registries using credentials stored as shared environment variables on Vercel. npm, pnpm, and classic Yarn running in Agent sessions authenticate as they do in Vercel builds.

To get started, add a shared environment variable for Development or Preview:

  • Use NPM_TOKEN for private packages hosted on registry.npmjs.org.

  • Use NPM_RC to configure custom or multiple registries.

Vercel Agent reads only team-shared variables, not project-scoped ones. Credential values stay outside the sandbox, so the agent cannot read them.

Learn more in the private dependencies docs.
