title: EffectCraft: The Open-Source Motion Graphics Powerhouse Built in Rust!
description:
Quick Summary: 📝

EffectCraft is an open-source motion graphics and compositing tool written in Rust, aiming to be a clean-room reimplementation of Adobe After Effects. It offers features like Lottie import/export, scriptability, and a readable project file format, making it suitable for creating animated titles, motion graphics, and visual effects.

Key Takeaways: 💡

  • ✅ EffectCraft is a free, open-source, Rust-based clean-room reimplementation of Adobe After Effects.

  • ✅ It offers a familiar UI with extensive features like 306 effects, 3D support, and cross-platform compatibility (including browser).

  • ✅ Developers benefit from built-in Lottie support for web/app animations and human-readable JSON project files for version control.

  • ✅ The entire application is scriptable, enabling powerful automation and custom workflow integrations.

  • ✅ Its pure Rust video/audio codecs ensure efficiency and minimal external dependencies.

Project Statistics: 📊

  • ⭐ Stars: 6363
  • 🍴 Forks: 3283
  • ❗ Open Issues: 298

Tech Stack: 💻

  • ✅ Rust

Hey fellow developers! Ever felt the pinch of proprietary software when diving into motion graphics or visual effects? Or wished for a more developer-friendly, open-source tool that lets you create stunning animations without breaking the bank or wrestling with opaque file formats? Well, prepare to get excited, because I just stumbled upon a GitHub project that's poised to revolutionize the game: EffectCraft!

Imagine having a tool that mirrors the power and flexibility of industry giants like Adobe After Effects, but is completely free, open-source, and built from the ground up in pure Rust. That's exactly what EffectCraft is aiming to be. It's a clean-room reimplementation, meaning it's not just a clone, but a fresh take on motion graphics, designed with modern development practices in mind. This isn't just a passion project; it's a rapidly evolving, already usable application for creating animated titles, complex compositions, and dazzling visual effects.

EffectCraft embraces the core concepts you'd expect: compositions, layers, keyframes for precise animation control, and a massive library of 306 effects. It even includes layer styles, expressions, and full 3D camera and light support, culminating in a robust render queue. What's truly impressive is its native availability across macOS, Windows, and Linux, and yes, even in the browser! This cross-platform versatility alone is a huge win for any developer or artist.

Now, let's talk about why EffectCraft is a game-changer for us developers. First off, it boasts built-in Lottie import and export. For anyone working on web or mobile applications, this is massive! No more clunky plugins or conversion headaches; your animations go straight from EffectCraft to your apps and websites seamlessly. This feature alone makes it incredibly appealing for front-end and UI/UX developers.

But wait, there's more! EffectCraft's project files are readable JSON (.ecproj). This is a huge deal for collaborative teams and version control. Imagine being able to git diff your animation projects! This level of transparency and integration with standard developer workflows is practically unheard of in this space. Furthermore, every single action within EffectCraft is scriptable. Whether you want to automate tasks via the command line, control it through a JSON channel, or integrate it with an agent-based system, the possibilities for automation and custom workflows are endless. And as a final cherry on top, it uses pure Rust for all video and audio decoding and encoding, ditching FFmpeg for a lean, efficient, and dependency-minimal approach.

EffectCraft is young and moving fast, but it's already incredibly powerful and brimming with potential. It offers a familiar interface for those coming from other tools, but with a foundational architecture that's built for the future. If you're into motion graphics, animation, or just curious about what's possible with Rust in the creative space, you absolutely need to check out EffectCraft. It's truly exciting to see such a robust and developer-friendly tool emerge in this domain. Go give it a star and join the community!

title: Can LLM Agents Efficiently Identify Appliance Faults? Insights From Diagnosing a Simulated Appliance
description:
arXiv:2610.19291v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In so-called "Industry 4.0," integrated sensors, analytics tools, and other digital technologies supplement industrial workflows, potentiating enhanced visibility and automation. Prognostics and health management (PHM) and natural language processing (NLP) practitioners alike have explored the application of large language models (LLMs) to industrial asset management, but many prior works' focus on exam-like benchmarks has limited their assessment of LLMs' ability to automate practical operations. Herein, we introduce CoffeeBench, a fault diagnostics task for LLM agents, using a simulated appliance. The LLMs we evaluate struggle to consistently identify faults from the sensor information alone, but the best-performing ones can iteratively refine the fault-option space to eventually obtain a successful diagnosis. Our subsequent analyses, therefore, focus on: differentiating models by diagnostic efficiency (RQ1); examining the lagging performance of the three worst models (RQ2); and identifying viable heuristics for selective prediction (RQ3), including that initial diagnostic uncertainty and LLM-judged soundness of reasoning are high-signal predictors of diagnostic success. In addition to our benchmark results (Section 3.1), we provide practical insights for improving the performance of the open-weight models on CoffeeBench, such as by explicitly tracking episode state on their behalf to reduce timeouts (Section 3.2) or applying a deliberation loop to refine diagnostic hypotheses (Section 3.3).

title: Qt, GTK, Flutter, Electron? No: a graphics engine from scratch, entirely in Rust
description:
Llimphi draws every pixel of tawasuyu, even inside an operating system that boots with no Linux underneath. Why it exists, how it works and how true that “from scratch” really is.

Every time you open an application, something has to draw every button, every letter and every window on your screen, dozens of times per second. That something is a graphics engine, and almost nobody builds their own: most of the world’s software is painted with Qt, GTK, Flutter or Electron. Tawasuyu, the software suite with Quechua names being written in the Gioser workshop, chose not to borrow one.

Its engine is called Llimphi, which in Quechua means color, shine, pigment. It draws the whole suite: the desktop, the editor, the video player, the control panels and the interface of the project’s own operating system. Today 276 pieces of the suite are painted with Llimphi.

Fifteen and a half seconds of Llimphi. Everything on screen is drawn by the engine, frame by frame: the controls, the cosmos sky, the supay corridor, the infinite voxel world and the hand.
Why not use one that already exists

Until May 2026, tawasuyu was drawn with GPUI, the engine behind the Zed editor. On May 26 it was removed entirely, and not on a whim: the project has its own operating system, wawa, which boots straight on the hardware, with no Linux underneath. No existing engine knows how to draw there.

Qt, GTK and Flutter take a conventional operating system for granted, with its window manager, its installed fonts and its memory management. Llimphi was designed from day one to paint both in a desktop window and in the video memory of a kernel that has just powered on. That requirement forced it to be written from scratch.
What “from scratch” means

It is worth being precise, because it is the question every programmer asks. Llimphi did not reinvent every piece. Just as Flutter relies on Skia and GTK on Cairo, Llimphi uses four free projects from the Rust community for the most specialized jobs. Everything else is its own: the way an application describes its screen, how it reacts to each click, the components and the paths that lead to the pixels.

Talking to the graphics card: wgpu · community
Drawing curves and fills with antialiasing: vello · community
Working out where each box goes (flexbox and grid): taffy · community
Shaping text: Arabic, Chinese, emoji, ligatures: parley · community
The life cycle of each application: Llimphi
Components, themes, animation, accessibility: Llimphi
Painting without a graphics card, inside the kernel: Llimphi
Isolating an application and painting its drawing from outside: Llimphi

The four community pieces are written in Rust too. That is why the headline says “entirely in Rust”, and stands by it.
How a Llimphi application thinks

Llimphi follows the Elm architecture, named after a language known for applications that almost never crash. The idea is simple: the application does not modify the screen, it describes it. Every time something happens, the engine goes through six steps:

input: A click, a key or a gesture arrives.
update: The application computes its new state.
view: It describes how it should look in that state.
layout: The engine works out the position of each box.
raster: It turns that description into pixels.
present: It shows the finished frame.

Since nothing touches the screen directly, no two parts of the program fight over the same button. It is the same reason this style became popular on the web with React, except here it runs natively, with no browser in between.
One brush, four paths to your screen

The most unusual part of Llimphi is that the same drawing can reach the screen by completely different paths, depending on where the application runs. “Looks about the same” was not good enough: each path was put side by side with the others and the pixels were counted.
With a graphics card

The everyday path on the desktop. It is the reference everything else is measured against.
CPU only

The one the wawa kernel uses, since it has no video driver.
Subscribe to the Medium newsletter

Fills and layers identical bit for bit. Accented text may differ, because the kernel only ships three fonts.
By message

An isolated application doesn’t touch the screen: it sends its drawing as a message and the system paints it on its behalf.

0 pixels of difference across the four test scenes.
For phones

A path that works on mobile graphics chips without general-purpose compute, such as the Mali-G57.

No pixel differs by more than 1/255 out of 19,200.

The “by message” path coming out with zero difference has a practical consequence: an application can live locked away, with no permission at all to touch the screen, and still look exactly the same. Security that costs nothing in appearance.
What it already ships

Close to eighty components: buttons, tables, text editors with multiple cursors, node graphs, panel splitters, calendars and more.
Eleven modules that combine components into complete application pieces.
Real text: right-to-left writing, Chinese characters, emoji, ligatures and input methods for Asian languages.
Accessibility: every element can declare what it is and what it is called, and the tests query it the way a screen reader would.
Image-based tests: a screen is compared with its approved version, and any unexpected change makes the test fail.
A 3D voxel engine that mounts inside the same interface, as just another component.

What it doesn’t do yet

An engine that promises too much loses the trust of whoever tries it, so it is worth saying what is missing too:

The phone path has been tested on real hardware, but no published application uses it yet. The current Android builds take another path that doesn’t work on every chip.
Outside its three built-in fonts, text may look different in the kernel and on the desktop. The cause is known: with no operating system underneath, there is nowhere to get more fonts from.
Part of Llimphi is already published on crates.io, Rust’s official registry, but the release is incomplete and some recent pieces haven’t been uploaded yet.

How to try it

For Rust programmers, the way in is a single package:

cargo add llimphi

The package bundles the core, the themes and the 3D engine. For the rest, the best demonstration is tawasuyu itself: every window in the suite is a Llimphi application.

Originally published at https://gioser.net on October 12, 2026.

title: A Gradient-Regularized Deep Learning Method for Restoring Image in Myopic Vision
description:
arXiv:2610.19218v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Myopic vision degrades the quality of human vision due to spherical eye defocus aberrations that impair the perception of fine spatial details. To address this limitation, this work proposes a deep learning-based approach to computationally design transformed images that allow individuals with myopia in fixed distance to perceive scenes with enhanced clarity. The method trains a neural network to counteract defocus aberrations modeled using the second-order Zernike polynomial $Z_2^0$. The approach employs a U-Net architecture trained with a loss function combining reconstruction error minimization with spatial difference structural preservation through $\ell_1$ regularization. Training is carried out exclusively on the KITTI dataset, while testing is performed on DIV2K and ImageNet datasets, demonstrating generalization across diverse image distributions. Under myopic conditions modeled by $Z_2^0$, baseline performance shows visual degradation with PSNR values ranging from 19.47 to 27.42 dB across datasets and severity levels. The proposed gradient-regularized method achieves consistent improvements, delivering PSNR gains ranging from 1.48 to 7.34 dB and significantly lower perceptual compared to classical baselines.

title: October 05, 2026
description:
Agent Platform Workbench

Change

20261004.00_p0 Release

Change

Installed latest packages from upstream dependencies.

Change

The BigQuery JupyterLab plugin is now enabled independently of the Dataproc plugin: it is enabled by default and can be turned off with the new disable-bigquery instance metadata key, while disable-mixer now controls only the Dataproc plugin.

Change

20261004.00_p0 Release

Change

Installed latest packages from upstream dependencies.

Apigee Edge for Public Cloud

Security

Security fixes for the integrated portal and API specs in the Apigee Edge management UIs.

The Apigee Edge UIs for managing integrated portals and API specs were updated to patch vulnerabilities in underlying libraries and serving components. Functionality is unchanged, but some pages might show minor styling differences.

BigQuery

Feature

Iceberg external tables and Iceberg managed tables now support flexible column names by default. This feature is generally available (GA).

Feature

The gemini-embedding-2 model works well for embedding long strings, including multilingual and unstructured data. It supports a mix of text, images, audio, video, and PDF files. You can use this model in the AI.EMBED, AI.SIMILARITY, and AI.GENERATE_EMBEDDING functions. This model is generally available.

Cloud Load Balancing

Feature

External IPv6 addresses are now supported for Standard Tier. For more information, see IPv6 subnet ranges.

This feature is in Preview.

Compute Engine

Feature

Generally available: Z3 machine types that have 8 to 44 vCPUs can use Hyperdisk Balanced High Availability volumes to synchronously replicate data across two zones.

For more information, see About Hyperdisk Balanced High Availability.

Feature

Preview: External IPv6 addresses are now supported for Standard Tier. For more information, see IPv6 subnet ranges.

Confidential Space

Announcement

A new Confidential Space image (260900) is available.

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Fixed

CodeMender updates (v0.12.0)

This release introduces updates to CodeMender:

  • Hidden file scanning: Added the --include-hidden flag to cm find (or include_hidden under scan in config.yaml) to include hidden directories and files, such as .github/ and .config/, in vulnerability scans.
  • Larger file support: Raised the default file discovery size limit (max_file_size_kb) from 500 KB to 2 MiB so cm find no longer skips large source files. Existing configurations that use the previous 500 KB default are upgraded automatically, and --deep and --diff scans can now read beyond the inline preview of files larger than 64 KB.
  • Report output for every scan mode: cm find --output now writes the scan report for standard, --deep, --parallel, and --diff scans.
  • Scoped fixes: cm fix now prevents the agent from modifying CI/CD pipelines, static analysis configurations, build definitions, and repository configuration files that are outside the scope of the vulnerability being fixed.
  • Accurate session token usage: cm now reports the total token usage across all turns of a session, instead of only the final turn, so token counts in cm stats and session exports match billed usage.
  • Bug fixes:
    • Fixed duplicate findings in cm report and cm stats, and stopped merging distinct vulnerability types reported on the same line.
    • Fixed database is locked errors during cm find --deep scans with multiple workers.
    • Reduced false positives by requiring a concrete, viable exploit before reporting a finding with high confidence.
    • Included sessions from cm find --deep and cm find --diff workers in cm stats.
    • Fixed cm verify resolving relative finding and exploit artifact paths against the current working directory instead of the project root.

For more information, see the CodeMender documentation.

Google Kubernetes Engine

Deprecated

Starting on July 1, 2026, Identity Service for GKE is deprecated in GKE version 1.36 and earlier. This feature is also unavailable in organizations that were created on or after July 1, 2025. GKE version 1.37 and later don't support Identity Service for GKE. Before you upgrade clusters to 1.37 and later, disable this feature and migrate to Workforce Identity Federation.

For more information, see Identity Service for GKE deprecation.

Feature

GKE support for using the c4-standard-* machine types (up to 192 vCPUs) as Confidential GKE Nodes with Intel TDX is generally available. For more information, see the following pages:

  • To use this feature with GKE , see Encrypt workload data in-use with Confidential GKE Nodes.
  • To learn more about the feature from Compute Engine, see Confidential VM overview.
  • To see supported configurations, including machine support, see Supported configurations and its "Machine types, CPUs, and zones" section.

Google SecOps

Feature

[Spotlight Feature] Terraform and client libraries for multiple features using Chronicle API

Terraform providers and Google Cloud client libraries are now available for several Google SecOps features using Chronicle API including Feeds, Parsers, Rules, Findings Refinements, Retrohunts, Dashboards, Data Tables, Watchlists, Custom Lists, Environments, Environment Groups, Data Export, SOAR Domains, and SOAR Networks. For more information, see Terraform reference.

Terraform providers enable programmatic provisioning and management of Google SecOps resources as code, while Client Libraries enable developers to build custom integrations and automate Google SecOps workflows in their preferred programming languages. For more information, see Client libraries.

Guest Environment

Feature

Version 20260921.00 of the guest agent is now available for all supported operating systems. This version introduces the following features:

  • The managed workload identity certificate refresher is now a locally bundled extension. For more information, see Managed workload identities overview.
  • The guest telemetry extension is updated to version 1.1 and polls every 15 minutes instead of every 24 hours. However, it will only send data to the API every 24 hours, unless it detects a change in the system since the previous poll. The extension supports the following capabilities:
    • Running a command as the user associated with a discovered process.
    • Configuring regular expressions to match against the version command output.

Fixed

Version 20260921.00 of the guest agent is now available for all supported operating systems. This version introduces the following fixes:

  • The NetworkManager setup now no longer reloads the primary NIC when it applies changes to the network configuration of secondary NICs, unless necessary.
  • If the core plugin successfully rolls back any configurations, then it force-reloads the configurations to make sure that the instance re-obtains DHCP leases for secondary NICs.
  • The core plugin now respects the address-manager configuration flag and the corresponding metadata attribute.
  • The extensions manager now ignores install and remove requests from ACS for the core plugin and locally bundled extensions.
  • The extensions manager no longer logs that there are no local plugins to install when it's installing local plugins.
  • The metadata script runner now respects the sysprep_specialize configuration flag.

Knowledge Catalog

Feature

Data products in Knowledge Catalog now support Looker (Google Cloud core) assets. You can package, govern, and share Looker (Google Cloud core) dashboards, dashboard elements, Looks, Explores, and LookML projects, models, and views in a data product using Google Group mirroring and IAM access controls. For more information, see About data products and Create data products.

title: I’ve Been Building a Student Hub, and I’d Love Some Feedback
description:
Hey everyone!

This is my first post on DEV.to, so I thought I'd start by sharing something I've been working on.

I'm currently a Psychology student from the Philippines. Before switching programs, I spent three years studying Computer Engineering. I still enjoy programming, though, so I've been continuing to learn on my own and working on different projects whenever I have the chance.

One of those projects is Unified Student Hub.

It's a web app I've been building to help students keep track of their schoolwork, organize their study materials, and figure out when to study.

It's far from finished, but I wanted to share it here and see what other people think.

Why I started working on it

Being a student means dealing with a lot of different things at once.

Sometimes assignments are posted in group chats. Other times they're on a school platform. Lecture slides end up in random folders, and important PDFs get buried somewhere in your downloads.

Then there's the problem of actually finding time to study, especially when multiple deadlines are coming up.

I know there are already plenty of productivity apps out there, but I wanted to try building something myself that combines the things I personally find useful.

At first, it was mostly about keeping deadlines organized. Then I started adding other features, and the project slowly grew into something bigger.

What I've built so far

Right now, the app lets you add assignments, exams, and other deadlines, then organize them by subject.

There's also a weekly planner. You can set the hours you're available, add your classes or other commitments, and estimate how much time you need to finish your tasks.

The app uses that information to put together a study schedule.

It isn't AI-powered or anything. It's just scheduling logic that I've been working on and improving.

I've also added a few other things along the way:

A place to store PDFs, PowerPoints, documents, and other study materials

A PDF reader with highlighting and drawing tools

A study timer with customizable breaks and cycles

Calendar and syllabus imports

Optional reminders

Some offline features, including access to locally saved materials

I also worked on Canvas and Moodle imports, although those depend on what each school allows.

Not everything is as polished as I'd like, but the main features are there.

Here's a screenshot

The design is still changing. I've been trying to make the interface less cluttered and easier to understand, especially for someone opening the app for the first time.

What I'm using

For anyone curious about the stack:

React and Vite for the frontend

FastAPI for the backend

PostgreSQL for the hosted database

SQLite for local development

I've learned quite a bit while working on this, especially about connecting the frontend and backend, handling user accounts, and getting everything deployed.

I still have a lot to learn.

Since I'm studying Psychology now, most of my programming practice happens during my free time. Building projects has been one of the ways I keep learning.

Sometimes I spend more time figuring out why something isn't working than actually writing the feature, but I guess that's part of it.

The parts I'm still working on

One problem I've run into is that I keep thinking of new things to add.

At some point, I realized the app was starting to become confusing even to me.

There were too many sections, settings, and buttons competing for attention.

So I'm trying to focus less on adding features for now and more on making the existing ones easier to use.

I want someone to be able to open the app, add their schoolwork, set their available hours, and understand their study plan without needing a tutorial for every little thing.

There are also bugs I haven't found yet, and some features still need more testing.

I'm not going to pretend it's ready for everyone to rely on. It's an early version, and I'm still figuring things out.

I'm looking for people to try it

I figured I should probably start getting feedback instead of just deciding everything myself.

If you're a student, I'd love to know whether something like this would actually be useful to you.

And if you're a developer, feel free to look through the code. Suggestions and criticism are welcome.

Here are the links:

Try the app:
https://unified-student-hub-vg2s.vercel.app/

GitHub:
https://github.com/cabauatanhans47-cyber/unified-student-hub

I'd recommend trying it with sample assignments first since it's still in beta.

I'm especially curious about whether the interface makes sense when you first open it. Is it obvious what to do? Are there features that seem unnecessary? Is anything broken?

Even if you only spend a few minutes exploring it, I'd appreciate hearing what you think.

I'll probably share more updates as I continue working on it.

Anyway, that's what I've been building lately. Thanks for reading!

title: From Qualitative Text to Integrated Evidence: The Parallel-Then-Integrated (PTI) Procedure
description:
arXiv:2610.19164v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Mixed methods research offers established strategies for integrating qualitative and quantitative evidence, but less guidance for integrating two computational representations of the same qualitative corpus. This methodological study introduces Parallel-Then-Integrated (PTI), a four-step procedure for explicit and traceable integration. We present PTI using 1,203 interview paragraphs from 29 mothers in Nepal. The two representations were ontology-guided Patient Voice (PV) coding with PVminer and data-driven themes generated through non-negative matrix factorization (NMF). A theme-complete crosswalk documented convergence, divergence, and preprocessing-sensitive differences. Depression status, based on Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) scores, served as a secondary external anchor for exploratory association checks. PTI provides a structured approach for integrating computational representations of qualitative text within mixed methods research.

title: DUALVIEW: Leveraging Broad and Output-Specific Evidence for LLM-based Multi-Output Text Regression
description:
arXiv:2610.19206v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: While work on LLM-based regression has largely focused on scalar prediction, multi-output text regression remains less explored. We present DualView, a parameter-efficient approach to leverage LLMs for multi-output text regression. \method{} first extracts broad and output-specific representations from a frozen LLM, then uses a dual-branch architecture to produce the full score vector. Across five heterogeneous regression tasks and eight LLMs (up to 122B), DualView outperforms seven supervised regression baselines while requiring 82--1842 times fewer fitted parameters than the three strongest baselines. These improvements extend across individual output dimensions and persist even with limited training data. Notably, DualView using a smaller open-weight LLM can outperform unsupervised prediction with Gemini 3.1 Pro. Controlled ablations show that broad and output-specific evidence provide complementary predictive benefits, while lightweight shared predictors achieve strong performance with fewer trainable parameters.

title: INTACT: Inducing Latent Reasoning on a Frozen Backbone
description:
arXiv:2610.19568v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Latent reasoning replaces natural-language chains of thought with compact continuous "soft-token" representations, reducing the number of intermediate tokens that must be decoded autoregressively. We use a small external encoder to induce latent reasoning in a frozen backbone model. The encoder iteratively maps the backbone's hidden states to new latent blocks, constructing a latent reasoning prefix, after which the frozen model writes its remaining reasoning and its answer as text. Our method, INTACT, trains this encoder through distillation to reproduce the effect of written reasoning steps while keeping the model's behavior close to that of the frozen backbone, and then reinforces it on answer correctness. Across four frozen backbones from 1B to 8B, INTACT improves both GSM8K and average out-of-domain accuracy, including GSM8K gains from 75.8% to 79.3% on Llama-3.2-3B and from 77.6% to 79.7% on Qwen2.5-3B. It also reduces end-to-end latency per problem by 19% on Llama-3.2-3B and outperforms the evaluated latent-reasoning baselines at the 3B and 8B scales. Beyond the mathematics setting, the same recipe trained on a multi-domain corpus improves the frozen backbone on twelve evaluation benchmarks spanning mathematics, science, and commonsense, without task-specific adaptation.

title: Nobody wants your AI app
description:
The people buying AI are blunt about the fact that the future is intelligence that disappears into existing platforms. Everyone wants it invisible and under their total control at the same time.

We are all racing to build AI apps that nobody wants to open.

Specifically, the standalone AI app, the thing you download, log into, and go to, is a worse idea than almost anyone building in the space wants to admit.

The numbers are brutal. According to RevenueCat’s analysis of more than 115,000 apps, AI apps are fantastic at getting you to sign up and terrible at getting you to stay. They convert free users to paid faster than regular apps, then lose them roughly a third faster.

A year in, only about one in five subscribers is still paying.

The pattern is simple and a little embarrassing. People try the AI app, get their “wow,” and then just stop opening it, because, often, it was just a novelty experience. Venture firm Bessemer has started warning that even business AI tools are heading for the same cliff unless they get themselves embedded into something people already use every day.

This is basically the same problem people had with Google+ (remember that?). Google got hundreds of millions of people to sign up, and then 90 percent of sessions lasted under five seconds.

You can build a gorgeous destination, pour a fortune into it, and get everyone to sign up once, and it still dies if nobody comes back.

Nir Eyal called what these app are missing the Hook Model, that products become habits through a loop of trigger, action, reward, and investment, each pass making the next one more likely. A novelty AI app nails the middle of that loop, you act, you get your clever reward, once, but there’s nothing pulling you back tomorrow and nothing that costs you to simply walk away from it. The loop never closes, so a habit never forms.

On the enterprise side, the rejection is blunter and faster. I’ve lost count of how many times I’ve heard large companies insist they are not taking on yet another tool. At this point, they often already have their own internal AI product and don’t want a new destination, a new login, a new thing for their people to remember to visit.

They want the capability dropped inside the systems they already use, where the work already happens. Snyk, a security firm, studied more than 3,000 enterprise environments and found exactly that. Companies are stitching AI into their existing stack, not buying standalone products to use in parallel.

This is bigger than a retention problem.

The destination is dying. Not AI, AI is everywhere and growing. The app is dying.

The idea that you deliver intelligence by building a place for people to come get it is over. The future is no app at all, intelligence woven invisibly into the tools people already live in, surfacing when it’s useful and getting out of the way when it isn’t.

While that may sound clean, it isn’t. The same companies that want the AI invisible also want it completely under their control. They want it to disappear into the workflow and they want a dashboard, an audit trail, a record of every time it ran and what it touched.

Invisible to the user, totally visible to the owner.

Those two desires are at war, and whoever satisfies both at once is going to win the next decade of AI products.

We need to take stock of why the app model is collapsing, what the people buying AI actually want instead, why “invisible” is so much harder than it sounds, and where the real work, and the real careers, are moving.

The companies still pouring money into beautiful standalone AI apps are building tollbooths on a road people have already started to abandon.

The app everyone downloaded and nobody kept

Surprise, it’s not Quibi!

Malika Aubakirova and Anjney Midha at a16z, working with OpenRouter, analyzed more than 100 trillion tokens of real-world AI usage. Stickiness, they found, doesn’t depend on your product’s interface or features, but rather on the capabilities of the underlying model.

The same study found that fewer than one in ten weekly ChatGPT users ever bothers to try a competing assistant, despite there being zero cost to do it. People plant themselves in one big AI and stay.

They will not leave ChatGPT. They will drop your ChatGPT wrapper in a week. Stickiness lives with the model and churn lives with the destination you built on it.

People aren’t loyal to your app. They’re loyal to the intelligence inside it, and that intelligence is for rent, to everyone, including you.

This is why the AI app graveyard is filling up so fast. Character.AI lost roughly 60 percent of its user base in a year.

Jasper, one of the early AI-writing darlings, watched more than half its revenue evaporate.

Google+ had hundreds of millions of accounts and almost no one who came back. A gorgeous destination nobody had a reason to visit twice.

Yupp, an AI startup that raised thirty-three million dollars and signed up 1.3 million users, shut down anyway, with its founders explaining that the models underneath improved so fast that they never found a durable reason for anyone to keep coming back.

Over a million people used the product and it still wasn’t a business..

If that pattern feels familiar, it should. This is basically the MoviePass story with better branding (and I worked on MoviePass!).

Millions signed up overnight. There was no durable business underneath, and it collapsed in a heap. A lot of AI apps are basically following this same model.

MoviePass got millions of people to sign up almost overnight for something that felt like a cheat code, and the spectacular sign-up numbers meant nothing once it turned out there was no durable business underneath. Massive adoption, a value proposition that dissolved on contact with reality, and a collapse that happened faster than anyone expected.

A lot of today’s AI apps are doing the exact same thing.

Brian Balfour, the founder of Reforge and former head of growth at HubSpot, calls this “product-market fit collapse.” In normal software, customer expectations rise slowly, so a product that nails its market can coast for a while. In AI, he points out, expectations reset almost instantly.

Every time a new model drops, users recalibrate what “good” even means, and dropping your app for whatever is newer, or for the raw model underneath it, costs them nothing. You are not building toward a stable finish line because the finish line keeps moving away from you every few months.

We have a category with astonishing sign-up rates, near-zero switching costs, expectations that reset on a monthly basis, and no loyalty to anything except the model you don’t own.

That same body of research points, almost accidentally, at the way out. The a16z study describes what it calls a “glass slipper” effect. When a user’s actual workflow fits a particular model so precisely that it creates real inertia, a cost, finally, to leaving. The apps that retain are the ones that have wedged themselves so deeply into something a person does every day that walking away would actually hurt.

The answer is quite simple. Stop building a place for people to visit and start building something they can’t easily remove.

What the people buying AI actually want

Larger companies say they aren’t adding another AI tool the way someone declines a second helping at a dinner they’re already full from. These are organizations that have spent two years drowning in AI pilots, logins, dashboards, and Chrome extensions, and they have hit a wall.

Companies do not want another destination. They want the capability, the actual intelligence, dropped inside the systems their people already use, where the work already happens.

The most striking version of it I’ve heard is that you shouldn’t even have to know you’re using a different product. You should just know that the thing you were doing got better.

That is a remarkable thing for a company to say about a product it is paying for, and it is becoming the default expectation rather than the exception. The same instinct shows up outside the enterprise too. A news organization I talked with recently had no interest in building another app for people to download. They wanted their journalism to show up where people already are, in a text message, inside the AI assistant someone is already talking to, with no new place to go.

This is where the measurable center of gravity has already moved, and the infrastructure numbers show it.

The Model Context Protocol (MCP), the open standard that lets AI reach into the tools and data a company already uses, went from a developer curiosity to something closer to 97 million downloads a month and production use inside roughly 40 percent of technical organizations. Gartner expects that by the end of the 2026, 40 percent of enterprise applications will ship with task-specific AI agents built in.

The designers paying attention have already clocked what this does to the job. Patrick Neeman puts it bluntly, that chat was only ever an interface, and agents are something else entirely.

The design work, he argues, has moved to the contract underneath the product, the rules and handshakes that let one system quietly hand a task to another and get a trustworthy answer back. When the interface disappears, the thing you’re actually designing is the behavior.

Think about what “invisible utility” has always looked like once a technology matures. Mark Weiser, the Xerox PARC scientist who coined the term “ubiquitous computing,” put it in a line that has aged remarkably well. “The most profound technologies are those that disappear. They weave themselves into the fabric of everyday life until they are indistinguishable from it.”

Mark Weiser called it in 1991. “The most profound technologies are those that disappear.” He was describing the future of the interface before most of us had one. AI is finally proving him right.

Nobody opens an app to use electricity. You don’t launch a program to get water out of the tap. The most important technologies succeeded precisely by disappearing, by becoming something simply present in the walls, available the instant you need it and invisible the rest of the time.

That is the shape AI is racing toward, and the companies building beautiful standalone AI destinations are, in a sense, trying to sell you a generator and a trip to the well at the exact moment everyone else is wiring the building.

The holy grail is a world where one AI simply calls another. Google’s Agent-to-Agent protocol, now governed by the Linux Foundation and adopted across more than 150 organizations, exists precisely so that one company’s AI can hand a task to a specialized capability elsewhere and get a usable answer back, with no human opening a separate product to make it happen.

The interface vanishes completely into the workflow. It’s genuinely hard to build well, and the infrastructure is still young, but the direction is set. The companies that understand it are to disappear.

That sounds like a potential answer. Make the intelligence invisible, embed it in the workflow, and, BOOM, you win. The problem is that the people who want it invisible want something else at the very same time, something that pulls in the exact opposite direction, and that contradiction is where most of this is going to get stuck.

Nobody has figured out invisible, but watched

The answer seems to be to make AI invisible. Embed it, dissolve it into the workflow, let it work without anyone having to go anywhere. Simple.

Except it isn’t, and the reason is entirely stuck in humanity. The same companies that demand the AI be invisible to their employees demand that it be completely visible to them.

They want it to disappear into the workflow, and they want a dashboard showing every time it ran. They want it to act without being summoned, and they want an audit trail of everything it touched. They want it woven invisibly into the fabric of everyday life, to borrow Weiser’s phrase, and they want a kill switch they can reach in half a second, a demand that turns out to be mostly aspirational.

In a Writer’s enterprise survey, more than a third of employees said they couldn’t immediately pull the plug on a rogue AI agent even if they needed to. Invisible to the user, yet totally visible to the owner.

The same leaders who tell me they want our capability to vanish into their systems will, ten minutes later, ask how they’ll track exactly who used it, how often, and what it returned, so they can prove the ROI to their own bosses. One large company essentially wanted the product to be invisible to its workforce and fully instrumented for its executives at the same time.

A recurring, hard stop in these conversations is data. More than one major brand has told me, flatly, that they will not feed their proprietary information into an outside tool, no matter how good it is, and that any vendor has to guarantee the model underneath isn’t quietly learning from what they put in.

Invisible is fine. Ungoverned is a non-starter.

Security researchers now treat this as table stakes.

Becky Brooks describes how organizations need to be able to answer basic questions about every AI action, which tools it called, what data passed through, whether any of it was proprietary, and most of them can’t.

The data behind that fear is genuinely alarming. The Verizon 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report, the most-cited study in enterprise security, found that employee use of unapproved AI tools tripled in a single year, to 45 percent of the workforce, with two-thirds of those people using personal accounts outside any corporate control.

Cyberhaven’s analysis found the average employee now feeds sensitive data into an AI tool about once every three days.

IBM’s Cost of a Data Breach report found that a growing majority of breached companies had no governance in place to manage AI or even detect its unapproved use.

The AI already has disappeared into the workflow.

It gets starker when you look at the actual network traffic. Infrastructure company Kong examined enterprise AI usage running through its systems and found that fewer than 1 percent of organizations had any AI-specific governance controls in place.

Meanwhile, almost 98 percent of their AI requests were flowing out to third-party proprietary services, every one of them carrying prompts, context, and often sensitive data outside the company’s own walls.

OutSystems found 94 percent of organizations worried that AI sprawl is piling up complexity, technical debt, and security risk, while only around 12 percent have any centralized way to manage it. Everyone feels the car accelerating. Almost nobody has their hands on the wheel.

There’s an old piece of political wisdom that fits this moment better than it has any right to. “Trust, but verify.” The companies buying AI have landed in exactly that posture, except the technology has made the two halves nearly impossible to hold at once.

The whole appeal of invisible AI is that you don’t have to watch it. The whole fear of invisible AI is that you can’t.

A thing designed to operate without your attention is, by definition, a thing operating outside your attention, and that is a terrifying property to hand a system that can touch your data, your customers, and your decisions.

This is the actual product problem of the next decade. The winning AI products will be the ones that pull off the paradox of being genuinely invisible to the person doing the work, and genuinely transparent to the person who owns the risk.

Disappear for the user. Light up like a control room for the owner. The teams that treat “invisible” as the whole goal are going to build things no serious company will deploy, because they solved for elegance and ignored accountability. The teams that bury everything in dashboards and approval gates will build something so visible and so clunky that it’s just another tool nobody opens, which puts us right back where we started.

Enterprises want the AI invisible to their people and lit up like this for themselves: every action logged, every data path visible. Invisible to the user, accountable to the owner. Almost nobody has built both.

Getting both right is brutally hard. It’s also the only version of this that actually wins.

Move Up the Stack or Get Buried in It

If you design or build products for a living, this could read like a eulogy for your job. It isn’t. The app dying is not the same as the work dying.

The work moved, and the people who notice where it went are going to be fine. The people who keep polishing the thing that’s going away are the ones who should be nervous.

Nielsen Norman Group has been studying how people actually use software since before most AI founders could type, put it about as plainly as it can be put, AI didn’t kill UX, it moved where the value lives.

The interface, the screen, the thing we used to spend all our time perfecting, is becoming a commodity. You can generate a competent one in an afternoon now. What you cannot generate in an afternoon is the judgment about what the system should do, when it should speak up, when it should stay quiet, what it’s allowed to touch, and how a human stays in control of something built to run without them.

Patrick Neeman has a sharp way of framing the trap we have to design our way out of. The reason everyone reached for chat, he argues, is that conversation is good enough at standing in for everything that it can hide the real product rather than reveal it.

The thing that feels like the answer, a text box you talk to, is often the thing keeping you from building what the moment actually needs.

The designer’s job used to be drawing the screen. Now it’s deciding the behavior, the rules and handshakes underneath, the contract between systems that no user will ever see but every user will feel.

The hardest, highest-value version of that work is the paradox from a minute ago, made real.

Mangus Eriksen lands on the exact tension this whole piece has been circling. Invisible AI only works if people trust it, and trust requires transparency and real control, without burying that control three menus deep. Read that next to the governance data from earlier and you have the entire job description for the next decade of product work.

Make it disappear for the person using it. Make it accountable to the person who owns it. Hide the machinery, surface the controls. That is a genuinely hard design problem, and it is nothing like designing a prettier chat window.

Think about what happened to the switchboard operator. In the early 20th century, connecting phone calls by hand was one of the most common jobs for young women in America. Then AT&T automated it, and the economists James Feigenbaum and Daniel Gross documented what followed. Once a city switched to dial, the operator jobs didn’t shrink, they vanished, dropping 50 to 80 percent and never coming back.

The need underneath, connecting people reliably, didn’t vanish at all. It moved up the stack, into switching systems and the engineers who design them, and it got more valuable. The part that matters is this: the women who were operators mostly didn’t make that jump.

The function moved up, and a lot of the people defined by the old version of it got left behind. The ones who thrived were the ones who moved to the layer underneath before they were forced to.

This connects to something that’s becoming ubiquitous in AI. Nobody is coming to hand you the next version of your job. Not in the broad economy, and not in our corner of it.

The people who make it through every one of these shifts are the ones who stop defending the thing they were good at and start building the thing the new world actually needs, before they’re forced to. In this case, that means letting go of the beautiful destination and getting good at the invisible, accountable system underneath it.

The future of AI is the intelligence woven so completely into the tools people already use that they stop noticing it’s there, with a clean pane of glass that lets whoever is responsible see exactly what it’s doing. Invisible to the user. Accountable to the owner. Almost nobody is building for both yet, which is precisely why it’s the opportunity.

The companies still pouring money into gorgeous standalone AI apps are building elegant tollbooths on a road people have already started to leave. The winners are somewhere else entirely, down in the plumbing, making the intelligence disappear into the work and handing the owner the keys to watch it.

The destination is dead. The infrastructure is where everything now lives.

References and further reading

Why the app model is collapsing

Malika Aubakirova, Anjney Midha, Alex Atallah, Chris Clark, Justin Summerville, State of AI: An Empirical 100 Trillion Token Study. Stickiness depends on the underlying model, not your interface; fewer than 10% of users switch despite zero cost.

RevenueCat, 2026 State of Subscription Apps Report. AI apps churn 30 to 36 percent faster than non-AI apps; only about 1 in 5 subscribers remains after a year.

Bessemer Venture Partners, Seven Product Strategies to Prevent Churn for B2B AI App Leaders. Even B2B AI tools face the churn cliff unless embedded in a daily workflow.

Brian Balfour (Reforge), on product-market fit collapse. In AI, customer expectations reset almost instantly and switching is trivial.

Google+ (Wikipedia). The destination that signed up hundreds of millions and became a ghost town, with 90 percent of sessions under five seconds.

MoviePass (Wikipedia). Spectacular sign-ups, no durable business underneath, fast collapse.

What the buyers actually want

Snyk, State of Agentic AI Adoption. Across 3,000-plus enterprise environments, organizations are embedding AI into their existing stack rather than buying standalone tools; the real AI footprint is roughly 3x the model list.

The Enterprise MCP Guide. The Model Context Protocol’s near-vertical adoption, roughly 97 million monthly downloads and production use in about 40 percent of technical organizations.

Gartner, via OutSystems research. 40 percent of enterprise applications will ship with task-specific AI agents by the end of the year.

Patrick Neeman, Headless AI Will Make Every Product a Platform. The design work has moved to the contract underneath the product.

Mark Weiser (Wikipedia). The father of ubiquitous computing: “The most profound technologies are those that disappear.”

Google’s Agent-to-Agent protocol (via FifthRow). The Linux Foundation standard that lets one AI hand a task to another, adopted across 150-plus organizations.

Invisible, but watched

Writer, 2026 Enterprise AI Adoption Report. A third of employees say they couldn’t immediately pull the plug on a rogue AI agent.

The MCP and AI Governance Gap (Techstrong). Enterprises need to answer basic questions about every AI action, and most can’t.

Verizon, 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report. Employee use of unapproved AI tools tripled in a year to 45 percent of the workforce, two-thirds via personal accounts.

Cyberhaven, shadow AI analysis. The average employee feeds sensitive data into an AI tool about once every three days.

IBM, Cost of a Data Breach Report. A growing majority of breached companies had no governance to manage or detect AI use.

Kong, enterprise AI governance research. Fewer than 1 percent of organizations have AI-specific governance controls; almost 98 percent of AI requests go to third-party services.

OutSystems, State of AI Development. 94 percent worry about AI sprawl; only about 12 percent have centralized management.

Where the work goes

Nielsen Norman Group, on AI-native UX. AI didn’t kill UX, it moved where the value lives; the interface is becoming a commodity.

Patrick Neeman, Designing for AI Means Designing Like It’s 1999. Conversation is good enough at standing in for everything that it can hide the real product.

UXmatters, The Era of the Invisible User Interface. Invisible AI works only if people trust it, which requires transparency and real control.

James Feigenbaum and Daniel Gross, Answering the Call of Automation (Quarterly Journal of Economics). When switchboards automated, the job vanished and the incumbents mostly did not move up with the work.

Nobody wants your AI app was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: AWS HealthOmics introduces resource fallback order for Nextflow workflows
description:
Today, AWS HealthOmics introduces the resource fallback directive for tasks in your Nextflow workflows, enabling you to define an ordered list of preferred accelerator types, including an option to fallback to CPU instances. Researchers and bioinformaticians can use this directive to reduce time spent diagnosing and resubmitting runs due to accelerator constraints and keep production workflows running. AWS HealthOmics is a HIPAA-eligible service that helps healthcare and life sciences customers accelerate scientific breakthroughs at scale with fully managed bioinformatics workflows. 

With resource fallback for Nextflow workflows, you can prioritize your preferred accelerator for your task. When your preferred accelerator is unavailable, HealthOmics automatically moves through your specified alternatives in the fallback without resubmission. Each accelerator profile has a configurable timeout, giving you control over how long HealthOmics searches for that accelerator before moving to the next. Shorter timeouts help you move quickly through the fallback order, while longer timeouts increase the probability of reserving your preferred accelerator. You can also include a CPU profile as a final fallback to increase the likelihood of your task reserving an instance. 

You can now use resource fallback for Nextflow workflows in all AWS HealthOmics Regions: US East (N. Virginia, Ohio), US West (Oregon), Europe (Frankfurt, Ireland, London), Israel (Tel Aviv), and Asia Pacific (Seoul, Singapore, Tokyo). To learn more, visit the advanced resource configuration and Nextflow specifics documentation.

title: Building a reading ruler that floats over every Android app: touch pass-through, Android 12's opacity cap, and masks
description:
I make ReadFocus+, a small Android app that floats a translucent strip (a "reading ruler") over the screen, mainly for people with dyslexia or ADHD who lose their place in long text. It has to work on top of any app: ebooks, PDFs, browsers, news apps. So it is built on a SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW overlay. These are the parts that took the most time.

Layout: one strip, two masks, one control panel

  • The strip: one window, MATCH_PARENT wide with adjustable height. TYPE_APPLICATION_OVERLAY (TYPE_PHONE below API 26), PixelFormat.TRANSLUCENT.
  • Line highlight mode: a View inside the strip painted with a GradientDrawable in the theme colour; the View's alpha sets the strength. No custom onDraw.
  • Reading mask mode: two separate windows, a solid View pinned to Gravity.TOP and one to Gravity.BOTTOM, with the gap between them as the reading window. When you drag the strip, both masks follow.
  • Control panel: another window holding the mode switch and the lock button.

Letting touches through to the app underneath

(The code below is simplified for the article.)

A reading ruler is only useful if you can keep scrolling the app under it.

int flags = WindowManager.LayoutParams.FLAG_NOT_FOCUSABLE
          | WindowManager.LayoutParams.FLAG_NOT_TOUCH_MODAL
          | WindowManager.LayoutParams.FLAG_LAYOUT_IN_SCREEN;
if (locked) flags |= WindowManager.LayoutParams.FLAG_NOT_TOUCHABLE; // locked = touches pass through
  • The default is locked (touch pass-through). To move the strip you unlock it from the panel, then drag the strip itself with ACTION_DOWN/MOVE/UP and updateViewLayout on params.y.
  • When toggling FLAG_NOT_TOUCHABLE, I remove the window and add it again rather than only updating the flags.
  • y is clamped between the status bar and the navigation bar, using WindowInsets (statusBars, navigationBars, systemGestures, displayCutout).

Android 12: the opacity cap on pass-through windows

From Android 12 (API 31), an overlay that lets touches pass through to another app has a maximum opacity. Go above it and the system blocks the touches instead (the "untrusted touches" protection).

float maxAlpha = 1f;
if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= 31) {
    InputManager im = getSystemService(InputManager.class);
    maxAlpha = (im != null) ? im.getMaximumObscuringOpacityForTouch() : 0.8f;
}
params.alpha = maxAlpha;

So the window alpha is pinned to that ceiling, and the visible strength comes from the inner View's alpha and the theme colour. This is also why the mask can never be fully black.

Display cutouts

On phones with a notch, the top mask must not leave a gap above it:

  • API 30+: LAYOUT_IN_DISPLAY_CUTOUT_MODE_ALWAYS
  • API 28–29: LAYOUT_IN_DISPLAY_CUTOUT_MODE_SHORT_EDGES

On rotation, onConfigurationChanged re-clamps the strip and redraws the masks. Every window also has FLAG_KEEP_SCREEN_ON, so the screen doesn't go dark mid-page.

Staying alive and coming back after process death

  • A foreground service with foregroundServiceType="specialUse" (FOREGROUND_SERVICE_SPECIAL_USE) and a low-importance, ongoing notification.
  • Besides START_STICKY, the overlay is restored on app launch, on process restart, and by a WorkManager watchdog every 15 minutes.
  • Users can revoke the overlay permission at any time, and adding a window after that throws BadTokenException, so Settings.canDrawOverlays() is checked before every addView.

The permission flow

ACTION_MANAGE_OVERLAY_PERMISSION with a package: URI → retry without it → fall back to ACTION_APPLICATION_DETAILS_SETTINGS. The guide screen checks canDrawOverlays() in onResume and returns as soon as it's true.

Wrapping up

Most of the work was in small details that let the overlay sit on top without getting in the way. If you're building an overlay of your own, I hope this saves you some time. The app is here (there's a Windows version too):

  • Google Play: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.codedac.readfocus
  • Website: https://codedac.com/apps/readfocus.html

title: Did the LLM Answer the Question? A Semantic Reconstruction Game for Jailbreak Evaluation
description:
arXiv:2610.19306v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Jailbreak attacks against large language models (LLMs) are evaluated using attack success rate (ASR), which depends on correctly identifying responses that fulfill prohibited requests. Existing evaluators can mistake refusals or topically related responses for successful attacks. We show that changing only the judge LLM can alter reported ASR by up to $82$ percentage points. We introduce the semantic reconstruction game, a training-free evaluator that decomposes compliance judgments into constrained semantic comparisons. Given only a response, an LLM reconstructs the request answered by its substantive content, excluding information merely repeated or refused. The game compares this reconstruction against similar decoy requests to determine whether it matches the original request, allowing abstention when neither candidate matches. Across three off-the-shelf LLM judges, the game achieves the lowest mean error against human labels among evaluated methods and reduces variation in reported ASR. It prioritizes avoiding false positives, even at the cost of missing some successful jailbreaks.

title: Your Swap Screen Is Showing the Wrong Number
description:
A month ago I wrote about what a crypto app should do before you press "Send". There's one more thing that happens before that button, and most swap interfaces still get it wrong: the number they put in the biggest font.

Usually it's the exchange rate. 1 XMR = 0.12 ETH. Clean, comparable, easy to sort.

It's also the least useful figure on the screen.

What lands in the user's wallet is an amount. Between the rate and that amount sit several costs the rate doesn't show.

One quote, four costs

Cross-chain swaps make this easy to see, because each leg has its own costs. Take Monero to Ethereum. CoinMarketCal recently published a breakdown of XMR to ETH exchange fees and counted four separate costs behind a single quote:

XMR network fee   → paid by the user, from their own wallet
Provider fees     → trading fees charged by liquidity sources
Spread            → gap between the market price and the offered rate
ETH payout fee    → gas to send ETH to the user's address

Only the first one is under the user's control. The Monero fee depends on network load and transaction size, not on the amount sent, and wallets let you choose from four priority levels. Everything else is decided by the provider.

The Ethereum side has its own formula. According to ethereum.org, a transaction costs gas units multiplied by the base fee plus a priority fee. A plain ETH transfer uses 21,000 gas. The base fee can move by up to 12.5% per block with demand, so the same payout can cost noticeably more at a busy moment.

None of this shows up in "1 XMR = 0.12 ETH".

Better rate, worse result

Here's a simple case. Two quotes for a 2 XMR swap (the numbers are illustrative):

  • Quote A shows a rate of 0.12000 ETH, charges a 0.1% trading fee, and takes a 0.002 ETH withdrawal fee afterwards.
  • Quote B shows 0.11925 ETH, with every cost after the deposit already included.

Sort by rate and A wins. Now compute what actually arrives:

function rankByReceived(quotes) {
  return quotes
    .map((q) => ({
      name: q.name,
      received: Number(
        (q.amountIn * q.rate * (1 - q.tradingFee) - q.fixedFees).toFixed(6)
      ),
    }))
    .sort((a, b) => b.received - a.received);
}

rankByReceived([
  { name: "A", amountIn: 2, rate: 0.12, tradingFee: 0.001, fixedFees: 0.002 },
  { name: "B", amountIn: 2, rate: 0.11925, tradingFee: 0, fixedFees: 0 },
]);
// [ { name: "B", received: 0.2385 }, { name: "A", received: 0.23776 } ]

B pays out more. The gap is small here, but a UI that ranks by rate picks the wrong option every time this pattern appears. And it appears a lot, because "no fees" usually means the fees moved into the spread or into a step that comes later.

The rate wasn't lying. It answered a question the user didn't ask.

Small swaps hurt the most

Network fees are roughly fixed per transaction. They don't scale with the amount, so their share grows as the swap gets smaller.

const feeShare = (receivedEth, fixedFeesEth) => fixedFeesEth / receivedEth;

feeShare(0.24, 0.002); // ≈ 0.0083 → 0.8%
feeShare(0.03, 0.002); // ≈ 0.0667 → 6.7%

Same fees, eight times the impact. This is also why providers set minimum amounts: below a certain point, fees eat most of the order. A screen that shows only the rate hides this completely. A screen that shows the received amount makes it visible the moment someone types a small number.

What the quote object should carry

If I were designing the API behind a swap screen, the response would put the received amount first and say what's inside it:

{
  "amountIn": { "value": "2.0", "asset": "XMR" },
  "amountOut": { "value": "0.2385", "asset": "ETH" },
  "rateMode": "floating",
  "includedInQuote": ["spread", "provider fees", "ETH payout fee"],
  "paidSeparately": ["XMR network fee"],
  "expiresAt": "2026-10-15T12:00:00Z"
}

amountOut is the headline. Anyone who wants the rate can derive it.

includedInQuote and paidSeparately matter more than they look. Two quotes are only comparable if they cover the same costs. Without these fields, the frontend has no way to tell whether it's comparing like with like.

rateMode tells the user what kind of promise they're getting. A floating quote follows the market until execution and can land slightly above or below the estimate. A fixed quote locks the amount for a limited window, usually with a small buffer priced in for volatility. Both are fine. Hiding which one it is isn't.

expiresAt is there for fixed quotes. A locked amount with no visible deadline is a support ticket waiting to happen.

Thin liquidity widens the gap

For pairs with deep markets, the difference between the rate and the received amount stays small. For thinner pairs it grows, and Monero is a good example. Kraken stopped XMR trading and deposits for clients in the European Economic Area from October 31, 2024. Fewer venues usually means wider spreads, and the spread is exactly the cost a rate-first screen never shows.

So the less liquid the asset, the more misleading the headline rate gets. That's the opposite of what users need.

A short checklist for swap screens

  • Lead with the amount the user will receive.
  • Say whether that number is an estimate or a guaranteed amount, and for how long.
  • List what's already included and what the user still pays.
  • Flag amounts close to the minimum, where fixed fees dominate.
  • Compare quotes by received amount, never by rate.

None of this needs new infrastructure. The provider already calculates every one of these numbers to build the quote. The only question is whether the interface passes them on.

People spend what arrives in their wallet. The screen should start there.

title: The 8 tests I ship in a starter kit (and why I stop at 8)
description:
Most starter kits ship with one test: test_that_true_is_true. It's the Laravel default, and almost nobody replaces it. When I started packing my SaaS kit for other developers, I decided the test suite had to earn its place — a buyer should be able to run php artisan test, watch green, and trust that the auth layer they just bought actually works.

So the kit ships tests/Feature/AuthTest.php with eight real tests. Here's what they cover and why each one exists.

The register tests. test_register_returns_token_and_user posts to /api/auth/register and asserts a 201 with a user object (shaped through the API resource) and a token. It also asserts the database row was created with role => 'user' — because the register endpoint hardcodes the role. Which leads to the second test: test_register_cannot_self_assign_admin_role. You can POST role: admin all day; you still get created as a user. That's a security property, and security properties are exactly the things that deserve tests — they're the ones that silently regress when someone "refactors" the controller six months later.

The login tests. test_login_returns_token_and_user creates a user via the factory and asserts a 200 with the token and user. test_login_with_wrong_password_returns_401 asserts the failure shape: 401, message Invalid credentials. Testing the sad path matters more than the happy path here — frontend devs build their error UI against the exact status code this endpoint returns.

The contract tests. test_me_requires_authentication hits /api/auth/me with no token and expects a 401. test_me_without_accept_header_returns_json_401 is the sneaky one: it checks that even without an Accept: application/json header, you get JSON back, not a redirect to a login page that doesn't exist. If you've ever debugged a SPA that got HTML back from an API and choked, you know why this test exists. It's a one-line regression test for a bug I hit on a real client project.

The authorization tests. test_non_admin_cannot_list_users and test_admin_can_list_users — a regular user gets 403 on the user index, an admin gets 200. Two tests, the entire role system proven end to end.

And here's the deliberate part: I stop at 8. There is no test for password reset, no test for email verification, no test for Stripe webhooks — because the kit doesn't ship those features. I won't write tests for code that doesn't exist to make the suite look bigger. A starter kit is a foundation, not a framework, and its tests should mirror its actual scope. What it does ship, it proves.

All eight run against a fresh database (RefreshDatabase), take a couple of seconds, and are written against the public API of the app — routes and JSON — not internals. That means a buyer can refactor my controllers freely and the tests still guard the contract their frontend depends on.

If you want the whole thing — Sanctum auth, role middleware, the admin user management loop, and these 8 tests proving it all works — I packed it into the Laravel + React SaaS Starter Kit, $19 one-time. Skip the three days of wiring and start on the part that's actually yours.

title: Do Perturbation Predictors Learn Gene Interactions? Diagnosing Extrapolation in Agentic Screening
description:
arXiv:2610.18880v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: High-throughput perturbation screens increasingly use machine-learning models to predict the effects of gene combinations that were never measured. A difficult case arises when both genes in a test pair were seen individually during training, but their combination was not. In this setting, standard OOD methods often fail because neither gene appears unfamiliar on its own. We therefore compare each model prediction with a simple additive prediction obtained by summing the two observed single-gene effects. The difference between them, which we call additive disagreement (AD), measures how much extra interaction effect the model introduces for an unseen combination. Across eight prediction methods and three Perturb-seq datasets, specialised neural predictors do not consistently outperform this simple additive baseline. More importantly, predictions with larger deviations from the additive baseline tend to have larger errors. Conventional output-based and embedding-based confidence signals are inconsistent across datasets and models, whereas AD remains informative across all evaluated compositional settings. We further study how this signal can guide decisions in an agentic perturbation-screening workflow. The code is available at https://github.com/zygao930/OOD.

description:
Posted by Paul Feng, VP of Product Management, Google Play, Google Play


Today, we shared how we’re taking our “More than a store” vision into its next chapter. From You tab—now a personalized home base for your favorite apps and content—to Play Games Sidekick connecting over 2 billion players, Google Play is meeting users wherever they are. [1] 

For developers, our goal is to help you connect with your audience and build a sustainable business. Below is a checklist to optimize your apps for our latest discovery features, new tools to deepen player engagement, and updates to our quality programs that reward great user experiences with lower service fees.

Reach the right users on Google Play and in the Gemini app

Earlier this year, we shared how new tools are transforming app and content discovery. Now, we’re expanding these features to make it easier for people to find your app.   

  • App comparisons on Ask Play: Ask Play already helps users find the right app through natural conversation, understanding context and adapting to follow-up questions. Now, it can generate dynamic, side-by-side app comparisons directly in search results. When a user compares details like subscription models or offline capabilities, Ask Play summarizes your store listing and user reviews to help them choose your app with confidence.
  • Game finder: Tailored by each player’s gameplay habits, favorite mechanics, and community reviews, Game finder explains why a title is recommended and highlights what similar players and profiles you follow are enjoying. It begins rolling out to English-language users in the US today. 
  • Play in Gemini: People are increasingly discovering apps directly through conversations in Gemini—driving over 6 million app installs in just two months since launch. [2] When someone describes a specific need, such as organizing family recipes or finding a collaborative task manager, Gemini matches their request to your store listing and key features, so they can evaluate and install your app with a single tap. And now, with Gemini Live, they can get these same app recommendations through voice conversations. 

To make sure your app is represented accurately everywhere users discover content—from Ask Play and Game finder to the Gemini app and Collections on home screens—review the following checklist: 

  1. Keep store listings and promotional events fresh: Regularly update your descriptions, tags, and events in Play Console to highlight new features, seasons, and timely offers.
  2. Upload high-resolution media assets: Use clean images and video previews that look great across different screen sizes and devices.
  3. Validate deep links in Play Console: Use the new built-in deep link emulator to preview and test your links without needing a physical device.
  4. Integrate Engage SDK: Bring users back to your app by delivering personalized content across surfaces, including Apps Home, You tab, and Android tablets—now supporting 9 categories, including Education and Health & Fitness.

Deepen player engagement with social competitions and rewards

Once players find a game they love, recognizing their progress and connecting them with a community keeps them coming back. We’re introducing new ways for players to share their favorite moments, compete with friends, and earn rewards: 

  • Playbacks in Sidekick: With Sidekick—our in-game overlay now reached over 285M users—we bring Quests, Leagues, Sprints, and community features just a tap away.[3]


  • Sprints: Building on Leagues, which turn in-game leaderboards into month-long competitive seasons, Sprints are fast-paced, 48-hour challenges that match 2 to 5 players of similar skills. It gives players an exciting reason to jump back into your game throughout the week.


  • Quests: Beyond competing on leaderboards, players want their time and progress rewarded. We’re expanding Quests beyond Play Points to include in-game rewards like character skins, performance boosters, and valuable currencies. 

You can turn on these competitive and social features by integrating Game Stats and Play Games Rewards:

  • Game Stats: By sharing basic gameplay event signals—such as match completions, score thresholds, or key milestones—your games can show daily Streaks and become eligible for platform-wide competitions like Leagues and Sprints. Game Stats connects seamlessly with your backend data , giving you access to our engagement mechanics without rebuilding matchmaking or leaderboard systems.
  • Play Games Rewards: Now generally available, you can set up ongoing in-game rewards that celebrate achievements and sync with Play Points. This helps you grow loyal players and keep them coming back.

Accelerate business growth with the Apps Experience and Level Up program

These new discovery and engagement tools help you deliver a better user experience while growing your business. For developers looking to go even further, our quality programs - Apps Experience and Level Up reward standout apps and games with lower service fees. 

Titles integrating Level Up guidelines, like Summoners War, PUBG MOBILE, and Fruit Ninja are already seeing strong results by polishing graphics performance, integrating Game Stats, and launching Leagues and Quests. For example, PUBG MOBILE drove 22% uplift in new installs from high-value players, and achieved a 62% uplift in spend per buyer among engaged players.[4]

Both programs are now available in Australia, Japan, the EEA, UK, and US, and will roll out to Korea by the end of the year.  We've also made it easier to submit and manage your program enrollment directly in Play Console.  

Explore these new tools in Play Console today—where you’ll also start seeing a visual refresh rolling out this month to streamline your everyday workflow. Please keep sharing your feedback with us as we build the future of Google Play together.
