title: Your line of business web does not need a framework
description:
A new business app starts with a question: React, Vue or Angular? The question that rarely gets asked is whether it needs one at all. For a page that lists orders, edits a customer and shows a few figures, the browser now does most of what we once picked a framework for.

This article walks through what frameworks were for, what the browser has taken over, and what is still missing. Then it builds a working order page in one HTML file, with no framework and no build step.

The habit

You start a project. You pick a framework, then a component library for that framework, then a state library, a router and a form library that fit both. By the time the first page shows a table, you have five dependencies that must agree with each other, and each will ship a breaking major version on its own schedule.

None of that is wrong. A framework gives a team one way to do things, and every developer you hire has used one. But it is a choice made by reflex, and the reasons it was the right reflex ten years ago have mostly gone away.

What a framework was for

Frameworks filled holes in the browser. Look at what those holes were, and what fills them today:

You needed a framework for The browser has
Your own reusable tags Custom elements
Knowing when a component appears and disappears connectedCallback and disconnectedCallback
Modals that trap focus and close on Escape <dialog>
Dropdowns that float above everything The Popover API
Form validation Constraint validation: required, min, pattern, :invalid
Numbers, amounts and dates per locale Intl
Code split into modules ES modules, loaded straight from a URL

The big remaining selling point is reactivity: change a variable and the page follows. That solves a real problem in an app where a hundred things depend on each other. A business page is rarely that app. It shows records, lets you change one, and shows the result. The places that change are few, and you know which they are.

What is still missing

The browser has no table that sorts and pages. No tabs, no tree view, no chart. That is what a business page is made of, and it is the real reason teams reach for a framework and its component library.

So that is the gap I filled with @relax.js/components: tables, tree views, tabs, menus, dialogs, charts and meters for business pages. Not a framework. Each one is a plain custom element, and where the browser already has the part, it uses it: the table is a native <table>, menus use the Popover API, the dialog is a <dialog>.

A page with no framework

Save this as a file and open it. No npm install, no bundler:

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="utf-8">
    <title>Orders</title>
    <link rel="stylesheet" href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@relax.js/components@2.0.0/dist/theme.css">
    <style>
        body { font-family: system-ui; background: var(--surface-bg); color: var(--text-primary); }
    </style>
</head>
<body>
    <r-stat-tile label="Orders"></r-stat-tile>
    <button id="add">New order</button>

    <r-table page-size="10">
        <r-column field="number" sortable>Order</r-column>
        <r-column field="customer" sortable>Customer</r-column>
        <r-column field="total" sortable>Total</r-column>
    </r-table>

    <r-dialog id="new-order" heading="New order">
        <template>
            <form method="dialog">
                <label>Customer <input name="customer" required></label>
                <label>Total <input name="total" type="number" min="1" required></label>
                <button value="save">Save</button>
            </form>
        </template>
    </r-dialog>

    <script type="module">
        import 'https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@relax.js/components@2.0.0/+esm';

        const orders = [
            { number: 'SO-10001', customer: 'Fjällbo AB', total: 12400 },
            { number: 'SO-10002', customer: 'Kvarnen HB', total: 860 },
            { number: 'SO-10003', customer: 'Ekdahl & Son', total: 3150 },
        ];

        const table = document.querySelector('r-table');
        const tile = document.querySelector('r-stat-tile');
        const dialog = document.querySelector('#new-order');

        function show() {
            table.rows = orders;
            tile.setAttribute('value', orders.length);
        }

        dialog.addEventListener('submit', (event) => {
            const form = new FormData(event.target);
            orders.push({
                number: `SO-${10001 + orders.length}`,
                customer: form.get('customer'),
                total: Number(form.get('total')),
            });
        });

        document.querySelector('#add').addEventListener('click', async () => {
            if (await dialog.open() === 'save') {
                show();
            }
        });

        show();
    </script>
</body>
</html>

You get a figure, a sortable table with grouped numbers and a pager, and a modal form. The form refuses to save without a customer or with a total below 1. That is the browser, not my code and not a library.

Now count what is not there. No state store. No virtual DOM. No compiler. No component tree to keep in your head. The data is an array, and show() is the whole rendering strategy: when the data changed, you tell the page.

"But who keeps the page in sync?"

You do, and that is the point. A framework re-renders when it decides something changed. When it gets it wrong, you debug the framework: why did this render twice, why did that not render at all.

Each component here redraws when you change its attributes, its properties or its content, and at no other time. There is no base class, no reactivity and no hidden scheduler. The lifecycle is the one on MDN. If the table shows old rows, you forgot to set rows, and a breakpoint on that line tells you so.

One rule trips everybody up: records go in a property, not an attribute. Attributes are strings, and a list in an attribute is a JSON string the component would have to parse and keep in sync with the property. So rows, columns and chart data are set from code, and scalars like page-size are attributes.

"But it needs Relax.js core"

Yes. The components have one peer dependency, @relax.js/core, and the jsDelivr link pulls it in for you.

That does not sneak a framework back in. A framework calls your code: it owns the lifecycle, the rendering and the state. Core is a set of libraries your code calls, and you use only the parts you need: typed form reading, routing, dependency injection, translations. The components themselves call it for four things:

  • translating the words they show (No data, Next)
  • reporting errors through one channel
  • formatting values
  • letting the router open a dialog, and only for a dialog you give a name

When the page above grows into an app with several pages, those same libraries give you a router and typed forms. You add them when you need them, not on day one.

Already on React or Vue?

Then the components still work, because every framework renders HTML and a custom element is HTML. The property rule above is all you need to know. React 19 assigns rows={orders} as a property. In Vue you write :rows.prop="orders" and tell the compiler that r- tags are not Vue components. Events are plain DOM events.

It is a way out as much as a way in. The table you use in React today is the same table in the page that replaces it.

The takeaway

Frameworks were the right answer to a browser that could not do much. The browser caught up. For a page that lists, edits and summarizes records, what is missing is the business components, not a framework. Add those as plain custom elements, write the updates yourself, and you have nothing left to migrate away from.

Next in the series: server-side paging and sorting, with one async function.

title: WorldMemBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Memory of Video World Models
description:
arXiv:2610.19063v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As video models enable longer and more realistic interactive experiences, maintaining a world consistent with its history becomes essential. This requires both preserving previously observed content and ensuring coherent world evolution over time. World memory is a critical capability to evaluate alongside visual fidelity and video duration. We introduce WorldMemBench, a benchmark for systematically evaluating world memory in video world models. Across 260 test cases, it assesses static memory through the retention of human identity and appearance, object appearance and geometry, and environmental content and geometry, and dynamic memory through event progression and state persistence. Using controlled camera departures and multi-revisit trajectories, the benchmark evaluates static content against fixed initial references and dynamic events against expected state transitions. It combines appearance and geometry metrics with event-specific assessments, and reports video quality and camera-following accuracy as complementary diagnostics. Evaluation of nine representative models shows that strong static retention does not imply reliable dynamic state evolution, while repeated revisits reveal memory degradation beyond the first return. Human studies support the alignment between our automatic evaluations and human judgments. WorldMemBench provides a systematic testbed for diagnosing memory failures and guiding the development of persistent, temporally coherent video worlds.

title: SAT-RL: Training Language Models for Logical Reasoning with Symbolic Solvers
description:
arXiv:2610.14402v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance in mathematical and logical reasoning, yet they still suffer from the curse of complexity and struggle as problem difficulty increases with the number of constraint interactions and the size of the search space. In contrast, satisfiability solvers such as Z3 provide scalable and verifiable reasoning through constraint solving under formal theories, but lack the flexibility to interpret natural-language problem descriptions. In this work, we propose SAT-RL, a reinforcement-learning (RL) framework that trains LLMs to interact with symbolic solvers through multi-turn tool execution. SAT-RL leverages synthetic data generation with verifiable solutions, supervised warm-up on solver-augmented traces, and solver-grounded reinforcement learning with tool-aware rewards. Experiments show that SAT-RL substantially improves symbolic reasoning with tools on both in-domain and out-of-domain logic tasks. Our code is available on https://github.com/sunjia72/SAT-RL.

title: Lag: A Mean-Field Optimal Policy for Online Assignment with Reusable Resources
description:
arXiv:2610.19038v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study online task assignment with reusable resources. This problem arises in peer reviewer assignment, skill-based call routing, rideshare matching, emergency dispatch, and crowdsourcing: Tasks arrive according to a geometric process and must be immediately assigned to servers that become temporarily busy, yielding rewards that depend on the task-server pair. The goal is to maximize long-run average reward.
  We cast the problem as a contextual restless multi-armed bandit (CRMAB). We derive an occupancy-measure LP (OCC-LP) that upper-bounds the reward of any work-conserving policy. From its dual we obtain Lag, a closed-form index policy. We introduce a scaling regime in which the number of copies of each server and the number of arrivals per step grow together. This regime yields the first deterministic fluid limit for a contextual bandit. In it, Lag is asymptotically optimal.
  Finally, we evaluate our algorithms on peer review datasets and call center routing. The Lagrangian index achieves 83-99% of the LP upper bound across all load levels. Moreover, the Lagrangian index policy significantly outperforms the natural greedy assignment scheme, improving reward by up to 12.3% on journal data and 36% on structured synthetic instances.

title: Running Hermes Agent on Cursor and Google Antigravity Without Third-Party Proxies
description:
Most developers using autonomous agent harnesses like Hermes Agent already have developer subscriptions: Cursor Pro for coding and Google Antigravity for Gemini/Claude access. But pointing an external agent at them usually means either paying twice for metered API keys, or piping session tokens through third-party reverse proxies.

I built two open-source plugins that drive the official local CLIs instead:

  • hermes-antigravity-oauth (wraps Google's agy CLI)
  • hermes-cursor-acp (wraps Cursor's agent acp server)

Here is how both work and the engineering problems they solve.

1. Cursor ACP: Tool Fencing and Call Recovery

Cursor doesn't expose a chat completions API, but the Cursor CLI includes an ACP server (agent acp).

Connecting Hermes to it required three fixes:

A. The Security Fence

Cursor's CLI has native tools (Read, Write, Shell, WebFetch). When running an external agent harness, Hermes must control all file and shell execution under its own approval rules.

Without intervention, Cursor's native Read can read any file on disk. The plugin creates a private workspace at $HERMES_HOME/cache/cursor-acp-workspace and rewrites .cursor/cli.json every turn:

{
  "permissions": {
    "allow": [],
    "deny": [
      "Read(**)", "Read(/**)", "Write(**)", "Write(/**)",
      "Shell(*)", "WebFetch(*)", "Mcp(*:*)"
    ]
  }
}

This forces Cursor to refuse its internal tools and emit tool calls through Hermes instead.

B. Tool-Call Parser Fixes

Hermes injects tool schemas into the prompt and expects <tool_call>{...}</tool_call> blocks in the output. Standard regex parsers break when:

  1. The model mentions <tool_call> in conversational prose before the actual block.
  2. The model outputs a flat {"name": "...", "arguments": {...}} object instead of a nested function call.

Our parser scans each tag, decodes JSON using raw_decode, and normalizes both shapes so Composer and GPT calls execute reliably.

C. Compression Preservation

Cursor returns no token counts over ACP. If a plugin reports 0 tokens, Hermes assumes real usage has completed and stops proactive compression. Emitting usage=None tells Hermes the provider is usage-less, preserving context compression.

2. Antigravity OAuth: Keychain and Claude Tool Bridging

For Google Antigravity, hermes-antigravity-oauth talks to the agy binary:

  • No Token Handling: The plugin never touches Google credentials. hermes auth add antigravity-oauth runs agy's browser sign-in, and credentials remain in the OS Keychain.
  • SOUL.md Delivery: The Hermes persona is written to GEMINI.md in the private workspace, which agy respects as top-level instructions.
  • Claude Native Tool Re-routing: Claude models on Antigravity often emit native run_command or view_file calls. The plugin intercepts these and re-issues them as Hermes terminal and read_file commands, preserving user approvals.

3. One-Command Setup

Both plugins ship with npx installers:

# Cursor models
npx hermes-cursor-acp
hermes --provider cursor -m claude-opus-5-5

# Google Antigravity models
npx hermes-antigravity-oauth
hermes --provider antigravity-oauth -m gemini-3.8-flash

Links & Provenance

Both are MIT licensed, covered by CI unit tests, and published to npm with GitHub Actions OIDC provenance:

  • hermes-cursor-acp: GitHub · npm · Catalog PR #138835
  • hermes-antigravity-oauth: GitHub · npm · Catalog PR #126041

title: Testing a Retro Text Generator as Two Different Products
description:
A text-image generator can look like a single form: enter a phrase, choose some visual settings, generate, and download. From a product-engineering perspective, however, a logo route and a poster route do not have the same success criteria.

This article shows how to turn those two creative intentions into observable UI contracts. It is a black-box test plan based on public-facing workflow language, not an analysis of private source code, model architecture, API design, or performance.

Start with intent, not the Generate button

A successful server response tells us very little about whether the result is useful. A logo-oriented user needs a compact identity asset that survives repeated use. A poster-oriented user needs a headline that works inside a one-off information hierarchy.

That suggests two top-level contracts:

Surface Primary user question Failure that matters most
Logo route Is the name still recognizable across contexts? The word shape collapses at small size or depends on one background
Poster route Can the viewer find the message in the intended layout? The headline overwhelms the date, place, or call to action

The public Fontify retro workflow describes short text entry, font color and background choices, image-size selection, preview or generation, and image download. Those are useful observable stages. They should not be confused with guarantees about trademark distinctiveness, production-ready vectors, accessibility, or an installable font file.

Model only states a user can observe

Keep the test model deliberately modest:

type CreativeIntent = 'logo' | 'poster';

type ObservableState =
  | { kind: 'editing'; text: string }
  | { kind: 'generating'; requestId?: string }
  | { kind: 'preview-ready'; intent: CreativeIntent }
  | { kind: 'download-ready'; formatLabel: string }
  | { kind: 'recoverable-error'; messageVisible: boolean };

This is a proposed test vocabulary, not a claim about the product’s implementation. Its value is that bug reports become reproducible. “The tool failed” turns into “after editing a completed preview, a second Generate action left the old image visible without a progress or error state.”

Also test what happens when intent changes. If a person moves from a square logo exploration to a wide poster composition, are the prior text and settings intentionally preserved, intentionally reset, or silently mixed? Any of those behaviors can be valid, but the interface should make the outcome understandable.

Define a logo-specific matrix

Use the Retro Font Logo Generator as the logo-focused entry point and prepare inputs that reveal recognition problems:

  • a short name with repeated letters;
  • a name containing a narrow and a wide character;
  • mixed case, if the current interface accepts it;
  • a name near the apparent input boundary;
  • light, dark, and transparent-background attempts when those options are available.

For each case, review the preview at three scales: the editor size, a compact card, and a favicon-like thumbnail. The automated check can confirm that a preview exists and that an enabled download action follows. Human review still has to answer whether letters merge, internal counters close, or an important terminal is cropped.

Do not encode guessed DOM selectors into the article as if they were stable product contracts. A real automation suite should inspect the live accessible roles and labels first. An illustrative Playwright skeleton might look like this:

test('logo journey exposes a reviewable result', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto(LOGO_ROUTE);
  await page.getByRole('textbox').fill('MOONROOM');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /generate/i }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('img')).toBeVisible();
  // Project selectors, completion signals, and download assertions
  // must be verified against the current live UI before use.
});

Define a poster-specific matrix

The Retro Poster Font Generator needs scenarios that expose hierarchy and canvas problems rather than only glyph problems:

  1. A two-word event name in a wide composition.
  2. A long headline that may wrap.
  3. A date containing numbers and punctuation.
  4. A high-detail uploaded background, if the live page currently permits one.
  5. A mobile viewport where controls and preview compete for space.

The critical visual assertions are not merely “image exists.” Check safe margins, wrapping, cropping, foreground-background contrast, and whether a changed ratio is reflected in the newest preview and downloaded asset. When pixel-diff testing is used, keep tolerance and baseline updates under review; generative output may not be deterministic enough for strict full-image comparison.

A more durable split is to automate workflow invariants and reserve aesthetic judgment for a review checklist. Workflow invariants include input persistence, visible loading or error feedback, prevention of accidental duplicate actions, and consistency between selected settings and the export metadata visible to the user.

Test failure and recovery paths

Creative tools are often tested only on the happy path because the preview is the exciting part. Recovery deserves its own matrix:

  • empty or whitespace-only input;
  • unsupported or unrendered characters;
  • network interruption during generation;
  • a second click while work is in progress;
  • changing text after a preview is ready;
  • navigating back from a download-ready state;
  • retrying without losing the creative brief.

For each failure, record whether the message identifies the problem, preserves recoverable input, and presents a clear next action. Avoid inventing a character-support promise: verify behavior with the current interface and document the result.

Keep the product boundary visible

QA can verify that a route accepts input, exposes settings, produces a reviewable result, and offers a download path. It cannot certify that a generated logo is legally unique or that a poster is effective for every audience. Commercial projects also require a current license check, and teams should distinguish a rendered text image from an editable font family.

The main engineering lesson is simple: do not let a shared component erase distinct user intent. The same generator shell can support multiple creative surfaces, but each surface needs its own fixtures, visual-review questions, and release criteria. Test the job, not just the button.

title: AgriJev: Efficient Agricultural Candidate Scoring with Multi-Scale Adapted Models
description:
arXiv:2610.19478v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agricultural systems make decisions over heterogeneous entity types, textual judgments, and knowledge-question options. Generating a textual answer adds decoding and extraction steps to decisions that ultimately require a candidate choice. We introduce AgriJev, a family of adapted Qwen3.5 models at 0.8B, 2B, 4B, and 9B. A shared interface conditions on agricultural text, a judgment question, and candidate definitions, returning scores and relative probabilities in one forward call. We prepare source-aware training records and frozen evaluations from existing agricultural resources, retaining original groups and annotation provenance. Comparisons include original Qwen3.5 models and matched agricultural SFT models, both evaluated through native answer generation. Across 17 external test views, AgriJev-9B reaches 75.44% mean accuracy, exceeding the original and SFT generators by 5.89 and 3.79 percentage points. It outperforms the original generator on 13 views and narrows the mean gap to hosted Jev 1.13.0. On a fixed A100 workload, its median scoring latency is approximately half that of same-scale answer generation. Task-dependent gains and failures characterize a practical choice among agricultural model weights and inference contracts.

title: Rebuilding the Among Us Floor Plan From the Game's Own Collision Data
description:
I train Among Us bots in a simulator of the game. A crew walks the ship doing tasks and votes out suspects in meetings. Hidden impostors kill, travel through vents (tunnels only impostors can use) and sabotage the ship, including shutting a room's doors for 10 seconds. The bots learn by self-play in leagues, each league a roughly ten-hour training run that starts from the bots the previous league ended with.

The simulator decides where players can stand with a grid of 126 by 70 tiles. The grid comes from the map file of an open-source web clone of the game, MIT-licensed and written by a third party. I used it because it was there and it matched the ship's layout room for room. It is also wrong, in a way I only saw once the replays were drawn on the real game's art: a crewmate jogging along the top of a corridor with its feet on the corridor's back wall. Measured against the game's own collision data, the clone's floor is 1.75 times too big.

Where the real floor comes from

Among Us is a Unity game, and the 2018 Android build ships its levels as Unity asset files inside the APK (the Android app package). The ship is a single prefab (a saved Unity object tree) called ShipStatus. Alongside the artwork, it carries the colliders the physics engine uses to stop players walking through things. I read them out of the APK with UnityPy, a third-party Python library for Unity asset files, without running the game. There are 79 wall outlines, which are edge colliders along the edge of every room and corridor. There are also 33 solid obstacles: the Cafeteria tables, the MedBay beds, the engines, Navigation's chairs and a few task consoles.

The player prefab supplies the other number that matters. A player is a 0.7-scaled object with a circular collider of radius 0.2234 at its feet. So the centre of a player's feet can never get closer than 0.156 units (Unity's unit of distance) to a wall or an obstacle. One unit is 2.646 of my simulator's tiles (from aligning a render of the ship with the clone's map), which makes the clearance 0.41 tiles.

The rebuild draws every outline and obstacle into a grid eight times finer than the simulator's tiles. It flood-fills the inside of the ship from a known floor point, then removes everything within the foot clearance of a wall or obstacle. A tile is walkable if its centre survives. Two details mattered. The outlines had to be drawn three sub-cells thick, because two outlines meeting at a corner can leave a gap finer than one sub-cell; the first version's flood fill escaped through one and filled the outside of the ship. And 56 tiles of floor that were not connected to the rest were dropped. The build would also force each of the 14 vent grilles onto the floor, since the game snaps a player's feet onto a grille to enter it, but in the final build none needed it.

How wrong the old floor was

walkable tiles
the clone's map 3,314
the game's colliders 1,894
on both 1,867
on the clone's map only 1,447
on the game's colliders only 27

Every room shrank, unevenly. Eight of the 21 rooms and corridors, the worst and best by the ratio of old to new walkable tiles:

room old real old / real
O2 98 32 3.06
Weapons 180 78 2.31
Shields 133 58 2.29
Upper Engine 110 48 2.29
Cafeteria 658 351 1.87
MedBay 142 105 1.35
central hall 253 196 1.29
Storage 162 147 1.10

The pattern is what the replays suggested. In a corridor, the clone's map counts the whole drawn height as floor. That includes the band of wall panels along the top, which the game draws as the back wall, so a corridor loses that band plus the foot clearance on each side. Rooms full of furniture lose the furniture; on the clone's map you could walk straight across the Cafeteria tables. Storage, an open room with crates mostly along its edges, barely changed.

Before switching, I checked that nothing the simulator depends on fell off the new floor. All 14 vents are on walkable tiles. Every task station moved by at most 3 tiles, to the nearest real floor in its own room. Each of the 7 rooms with doors still cannot be walked into from outside while its doors (13 in all) are shut. Impostors can still vent into some of them, as in the game.

How much it changed the game

I do not know precisely, which is the honest answer. The bots were trained on the old floor and played on the new one without retraining. I played 40 games on each floor with the bots from my fourth league, 15 players and 3 impostors, using a fixed random seed so the run repeats exactly:

floor crew wins tasks done kills per game vents per game
clone's map 36 of 40 69% 5.8 3.3
game's colliders 34 of 40 65% 6.0 3.6

Two games in 40 is within what a different seed could produce. But an earlier unseeded test, also 40 games each, with the same league's bots taken at an earlier checkpoint and an earlier version of the simulator, measured the crew at 78% on the old floor and 68% on the new one. Forty games cannot separate a 2-point effect from a 10-point one, so the effect is somewhere in that range. Either way it is far smaller than a factor of 1.75 in walkable floor suggests. My guess at why is that the bots decide between rooms rather than between tiles. A room's neighbours, its vents and the walking distance between rooms are close to unchanged, so the floor mostly changes where a player stands inside a room rather than where it goes.

I switched anyway. The simulator is meant to model the real game, and the old floor was visibly wrong in every replay, whatever it did to the win rate. Training since then has used the real floor, and the old one remains available for comparison with older runs. My fifth league, the first to train on the new floor, later collapsed for reasons I could not separate from the floor change, which is a separate post.

The simulator, the extraction and the rebuild were written by Claude Code at my direction, and the corridor wall-walking was something I spotted in the replays. The code is not public, and the extracted game data and art stay on my machine. The figures above come from the rebuild script's output and a seeded comparison script; anyone with the 2018 APK and UnityPy can read the same colliders.

What I take from it is that a simulator can be wrong by a factor of 1.75 in a quantity that sounds fundamental and still produce similar outcomes. Outcome metrics are a poor check on whether a simulator is faithful. The check that found this was looking at the picture.

title: Towards Training and Inference of Graph Neural Networks in Graph Databases
description:
arXiv:2610.19142v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Graph Neural Networks on large graphs commonly rely on in-memory graph storage with ad hoc data processing pipelines for both training and inference. Graph databases provide scalable storage and efficient traversal for graphs that can evolve over time, but their applicability in GNN training and inference are rarely studied. We show that graph DBs can be used in GNN training and inference directly, executing sampling, feature retrieval, and even the full forward pass. We show different GNN training pipelines can perform on-the-fly sampling and retrieval in graph DBs using Cypher. We further provide optimisations that speed up the training process by \~2.5x while maintaining the same accuracy. We illustrate that fully in-DB inference is possible, independent of how the GNNs are trained. Our inference setup can be >10x faster than cold loading the graph into RAM with no extra memory overhead on real-world graphs. Our work lays the foundation for in-graph-DB GNN training and inference.

title: Escape Analysis: How Can a Compiler Eliminate a Heap Allocation Without Changing Your Code?
description:
Consider this Java method:

double distanceBetween(double x1, double y1, double x2, double y2) {
    Point a = new Point(x1, y1);
    Point b = new Point(x2, y2);
    return Math.sqrt(
        Math.pow(b.x - a.x, 2) + Math.pow(b.y - a.y, 2)
    );
}

Two Point objects are created, used in a calculation, and then discarded. The source code calls new, which in Java means heap allocation, object initialization, and eventually garbage collection. But if you look at this from a different angle: both objects are born at the start of the method, used for arithmetic, and are completely useless after the return statement. Nothing outside the method ever sees them. No other thread can observe them. They exist solely to hold two doubles each.

Does the runtime actually need to allocate heap memory for them? That question is what escape analysis is designed to answer.

What It Means for an Object to Escape

Before a compiler can eliminate an allocation, it needs to prove that the allocation can be eliminated. The key concept is whether an object escapes its local scope.

An object escapes when a reference to it can be observed from outside the context in which it was created. There are several ways this happens:

Return. A method that returns a reference to a locally created object immediately causes it to escape. The caller now holds a live reference, so the object must exist somewhere accessible after the method returns. Stack frames are discarded on return, which means the object cannot safely live in one.

Shared state. Storing a reference in a field of an object that outlives the current scope, or in a static field, allows code anywhere in the program to observe the object. The compiler must assume the object could be read at any time.

Opaque callees. When a method passes an object to another function and the compiler cannot fully analyze what that function does with the reference, it must conservatively assume the object might escape. If the callee stores the reference in a field or returns it to its own callers, the assumption would be violated.

Non-escaping objects are those where the compiler can prove that every reference to the object stays within a bounded scope. It is created, used, and the last reference to it disappears, all within a region the compiler can reason about.

The Point objects in the opening example are non-escaping. The references a and b are local variables. They are never returned, never stored in any field, never passed to an opaque method. The compiler can trace every use of them.

How the Compiler Reasons About References

Escape analysis is not a single yes-or-no check. It is a data flow analysis that the compiler runs over the program's intermediate representation, tracking how references to each object propagate through the code.

The classic formulation, and the one underlying HotSpot's C2 compiler, builds a connection graph: a representation of the relationships between object references, the fields through which they flow, and the boundaries across which they might cross. Each object in the graph carries an escape state. HotSpot's C2 uses three states: NoEscape, for objects whose references are entirely contained within the method; ArgEscape, for objects passed as arguments but not observed to escape further; and GlobalEscape, for objects accessible from outside the method or thread.

The analysis is conservative. If the compiler cannot prove that a reference stays local, it assumes it might escape. Conservative analysis is safe: it never eliminates a necessary allocation. But it also means some allocations that a human could see are unnecessary will be retained because the compiler's model of the code is not complete. Inlining is one of the most important enablers of escape analysis. When a callee is inlined into the caller, the compiler gains full visibility into what the callee does with every argument, which allows escape states to be refined. HotSpot's C2 requires inlining to occur before scalar replacement can work. If a method is not inlined because it is too large or was not compiled at the right optimization tier, the analysis may classify its arguments as escaping, even if they do not.

The Optimization: Scalar Replacement

The natural first guess is that escape analysis moves objects from the heap to the stack. For some compilers and runtimes, that is exactly what happens. The Go compiler does this: if it proves that a value will not outlive the current function, it allocates the value in the goroutine's stack frame rather than on the heap. You can observe this directly with go build -gcflags="-m", which annotates each allocation decision.

HotSpot's C2 JIT takes a different path. According to the OpenJDK wiki: "C2 does NOT replace a heap allocation with a stack allocation for non globally escaping objects." Instead, C2 performs scalar replacement.

Scalar replacement decomposes an object into its constituent fields and eliminates the object itself. Rather than allocating a block of memory and storing field values in it, the compiler treats each field as an independent local variable. The object never materializes as a contiguous region of memory. No allocation happens. No garbage collector ever needs to reclaim it.

The transformation for the Point example looks conceptually like this. Before scalar replacement:

// What you wrote
Point a = new Point(x1, y1);
double ax = a.x;
double ay = a.y;

After scalar replacement, the compiler replaces all field accesses with synthetic local values:

// What the compiler works with internally
double a_x = x1;  // scalar substitute for a.x
double a_y = y1;  // scalar substitute for a.y

The Point object never exists. The field reads (a.x, a.y) become references to local values that can be kept in registers. Aleksey Shipilëv's JVM Anatomy Quarks describes this precisely: HotSpot "does not do stack allocations per se, but it does approximate that with Scalar Replacement."

From there, register allocation can place those scalar values in CPU registers for the duration of the computation. The two doubles that would have been heap-allocated objects end up as register values, with no allocation, no initialization overhead, and no GC involvement.

A Concrete Walk-Through

Take the full distance method from the opening:

double distanceBetween(double x1, double y1, double x2, double y2) {
    Point a = new Point(x1, y1);
    Point b = new Point(x2, y2);
    return Math.sqrt(
        Math.pow(b.x - a.x, 2) + Math.pow(b.y - a.y, 2)
    );
}

For scalar replacement to apply, C2 needs to:

  1. Inline the Point constructor so it can see that no reference to the new object leaks out of the construction.
  2. Determine that a and b have escape state NoEscape: no return of the references, no field stores into external objects, no passing to opaque methods.
  3. Replace new Point(x1, y1) with two scalar variables a_x = x1, a_y = y1.
  4. Rewrite every a.x and a.y access to use those scalars.
  5. Eliminate the allocation instruction entirely. After this transformation, the method compiles to arithmetic on four double values, none of which requires heap memory. The behavior observed by any caller is identical: they receive the same double result. The only change is internal to the representation of the computation.

Lock elimination is a related optimization that escape analysis enables. If an object is non-escaping, no other thread can hold a reference to it, so any synchronized blocks on that object are unnecessary. The compiler can remove them.

Where the Analysis Fails

Escape analysis has hard limits, and understanding them is as important as understanding what it can do.

The most common barrier is an opaque method call. If distanceBetween passed a to any method that C2 has not inlined, the compiler would have to assume the reference might escape. The Point would remain heap-allocated. This is why HotSpot's OpenJDK scalar replacement documentation explicitly lists non-inlined methods as a case where scalar replacement is prevented.

Interface dispatch is a related problem. When a method is called through an interface, the compiler cannot always determine which concrete implementation will run, which makes it impossible to inline the callee. Without inlining, the escape state of the argument is unknown.

Some operations are identity-sensitive. Java's == operator on objects tests reference identity. If the compiler replaces an object with scalars, two allocations that previously produced distinct references might appear identical or might behave incorrectly if the program depends on them being different objects. The compiler must verify that no code in scope depends on the object's identity before it can safely decompose it.

Synchronization presents a harder constraint. If code synchronizes on an object that the compiler is considering for scalar replacement, the semantics of Java's memory model require that the lock be observable. Lock elimination is sound only when the object is genuinely non-escaping, so the compiler must be certain before removing it.

Conservative analysis also means that HotSpot will retain an allocation if any uncertainty exists. The analysis can handle many cases that appear complex in source code, but it cannot analyze beyond what it can observe. Dynamic loading of classes, reflection, and native code are all effectively opaque.

The Performance Picture

Removing allocations reduces pressure on the garbage collector by producing fewer objects that need to be tracked and collected. In throughput-sensitive code that creates many short-lived objects in tight loops, this can meaningfully reduce GC pause frequency and time spent in allocation paths. Keeping data in registers rather than memory also reduces memory traffic.

That said, allocation in modern JVMs is fast. HotSpot's thread-local allocation buffers (TLABs) allow most allocations to complete with a simple pointer bump. The cost of a single allocation is small. The benefit of elimination comes from the aggregate effect over many allocations, particularly in hot loops, and from the downstream reduction in GC work.

Whether scalar replacement improves a specific workload depends on the compiler's ability to apply it, the allocation rate of the relevant code, and the GC configuration. Profiling with allocation-aware tools is the right way to measure this, not inference from source code alone.

The Developer's Relationship With This Optimization

The existence of escape analysis and scalar replacement changes what source-level object creation actually means. Writing new Point(x, y) in Java does not guarantee that a heap allocation will occur at runtime. Whether one does depends on the JIT compiler's escape analysis, whether the relevant methods were inlined, and the escape state the analysis assigned to the object.

This is intentional. The language specification defines what the program must compute and what observable side effects it must produce. It says nothing about whether intermediate objects need physical representation. The JIT compiler is free to choose any implementation that preserves observable behavior.

Several practical points follow from this:

Write code that is clear and correct. Avoiding allocation for its own sake by using awkward data structures or manual field decomposition will not necessarily produce faster code and will make the compiler's job harder if it disrupts inlining.

Measure before concluding. Allocation sampling profilers can show which allocations actually reach the heap at runtime. An allocation that appears in source code may not appear in profiles if scalar replacement has already eliminated it.

Do not assume Java and Go behave identically. Go's escape analysis operates at compile time and makes stack-allocation decisions that are baked into the generated machine code. HotSpot's analysis operates in the JIT compiler and uses scalar replacement rather than stack allocation. The mechanisms, the triggering conditions, and the diagnostics are different.

Check compiler output when it matters. Go's -gcflags="-m" flag reports escape decisions. HotSpot's -XX:+PrintEliminateAllocations flag reports scalar replacement. These are the ground truth; source code is not.

The Deeper Insight

Escape analysis reflects a broader principle in compiler design: a language's specification describes the required observable behavior of a program, not its required internal representation. The compiler is free to transform how data is stored, how operations are sequenced, and how objects are physically represented, as long as anything the program is permitted to observe remains consistent with the specification.

A heap allocation is a mechanism for giving data a lifetime that outlives a function call. When the compiler can prove that a particular datum does not need that extended lifetime, the allocation is unnecessary. The datum can be represented as local values, stored in registers, and discarded the moment the function returns. The program computes the same result. The method's caller observes the same returned value. Nothing that any correct program could observe has changed.

What the compiler has changed is what never needed to exist in the first place.

Sources

  • OpenJDK HotSpot Escape Analysis Wiki — authoritative description of C2's escape analysis algorithm and its explicit statement that C2 does not perform stack allocation.
  • Aleksey Shipilëv: JVM Anatomy Quarks #18 — Scalar Replacement — detailed technical explanation of scalar replacement in HotSpot C2.
  • HotSpot Escape Analysis and Scalar Replacement Status (OpenJDK) — analysis of escape analysis coverage and limitations in C2.
  • Oracle Java Magazine: Escape Analysis in the HotSpot JIT Compiler — accessible explanation with GC log evidence.
  • Segment Engineering: Allocation Efficiency in High-Performance Go Services — practical explanation of Go's stack-allocation-first approach and escape analysis flags.
  • Go compiler escape analysis flags — go build -gcflags="-m" documentation.

title: Add S3 uploads to Vercel apps without storing long-lived AWS keys
description:
A Vercel app can accept a file upload and store the object in Amazon S3 without putting a long-lived AWS access key in source code or deployment variables. Vercel’s Amazon S3 Marketplace integration now connects an S3 resource to a Vercel project, supplies connection details as environment variables, and authenticates with short-lived OIDC credentials. The practical work remains yours: authorize the uploader, choose the object key, validate the file, and decide who can read it.

This guide walks through the setup boundary, the server-side upload path, and the security decisions that still matter after credentials are handled. It is for a team adding file uploads to a Vercel-hosted application, especially one that already uses AWS and wants its storage flow near the project configuration.

Choose the integration for the workflow you have

Amazon S3 and Vercel Blob solve overlapping but different setup problems. Vercel Blob is a storage service for files in a Vercel app, with Vercel-managed delivery features. The S3 Marketplace integration is a fit when the application already depends on AWS, when the team wants S3 resources visible beside its Vercel project, or when its storage workflow uses S3-specific services such as S3 Tables or S3 Vectors.

The Marketplace path keeps project setup together: create or connect the resource in the Vercel dashboard, then use the values made available to the project. A linked AWS account has an important constraint: the Vercel flow supports buckets created through Vercel, rather than attaching an arbitrary pre-existing bucket. If an application already writes to a bucket that was created elsewhere, check the current setup path before planning a migration. Do not assume “connect an AWS account” means every bucket in that account is selectable.

The integration also does not remove the need to understand AWS permissions. OIDC changes how the application obtains credentials; the IAM role still determines which AWS actions those credentials can perform. Treat the role policy, project environment, and upload route as separate controls.

Connect the S3 resource to the project

Start in the Vercel Marketplace from the project that will run the upload route. Create an S3 resource through the guided flow or link the AWS account you intend to use. Review the environment variables that Vercel adds and the project environments to which the connection applies. Keep production and preview behavior deliberate; a preview deployment should not automatically inherit broader access than it needs.

Vercel’s integration uses short-lived OIDC credentials instead of storing static AWS keys in the application. That means you do not paste an IAM user’s long-lived access key into an environment variable or commit it in a local file. The application still needs ordinary configuration such as the bucket name and region, and AWS still needs a role with a trust relationship for the intended Vercel project and environment.

For new integrations, inspect the connection details and the resulting IAM access before sending real user files. Confirm the role can write only to the bucket and key prefix the application requires. If a function only stores user uploads, it should not receive broad permissions to list every bucket or alter bucket policy. Keep any administrative bucket operations outside the request path.

Build a server-side upload route

The Vercel changelog’s example uses createS3 from @vercel/aws, then sends an AWS SDK PutObjectCommand from a route handler. The outline is small:

// lib/s3.ts
import { createS3 } from "@vercel/aws";

export const s3 = createS3();

// app/api/upload/route.ts
import { PutObjectCommand } from "@aws-sdk/client-s3";
import { s3 } from "@/lib/s3";

export async function POST(request: Request) {
  // First authenticate the user and verify upload permission.
  const formData = await request.formData();
  const file = formData.get("file");

  if (!(file instanceof File)) {
    return Response.json({ error: "A file is required." }, { status: 400 });
  }

  // Apply application-specific size and content checks here.
  const objectKey = `uploads/${crypto.randomUUID()}`;

  await s3.send(new PutObjectCommand({
    Bucket: process.env.S3_BUCKET_NAME!,
    Key: objectKey,
    Body: Buffer.from(await file.arrayBuffer()),
    ContentType: file.type || "application/octet-stream",
  }));

  return Response.json({ key: objectKey });
}

An existing AWS account can be linked; buckets provisioned through the Vercel connection are new buckets. The older buckets shown remain untouched.

This is a route shape, not a complete production policy. The example deliberately leaves authentication and validation as explicit steps because they depend on the application. A successful AWS write does not prove that the requester is allowed to upload for the account identified by the URL or form.

The object key should be generated on the server. Do not accept a bucket name or unrestricted key from the browser: a user could otherwise choose another tenant’s path or overwrite an object the app treats as authoritative. Use an opaque identifier for the storage key and save the original filename as display metadata after normalizing it. Scope each upload to the authenticated user or tenant, and ensure the IAM policy and application checks agree about the allowed prefix.

Set upload limits before reading an entire file into memory. Check the declared MIME type, but do not trust it as proof of file contents; inspect or decode the bytes when the file type matters. Restrict accepted formats, cap size, and rate-limit requests. For larger uploads, design a multipart or direct-to-storage flow separately, including how a client receives narrowly scoped authorization and how unfinished uploads are cleaned up.

Decide who can read each object

Storage access is a product decision. A profile image meant to be public and an invoice or user export should not share the same read path. Keep private objects behind application authorization, and return a short-lived download mechanism only after checking the caller’s access. If a file is intentionally public, make that choice explicit and avoid placing sensitive content in that bucket or prefix.

The Marketplace S3 connection uses short-lived OIDC credentials rather than static AWS keys for the upload flow; the scene is conceptual, not a Vercel or OTF integration screen.

Do not rely on an unguessable object key as the authorization rule. Random identifiers reduce accidental discovery, but the app still needs to check ownership before returning a download URL or proxying bytes. Consider whether a user can replace a file, whether each replacement should create a new version, and how deletion requests propagate to S3 and the app’s metadata store.

Think through consistency as well. An upload can succeed in S3 while a database write fails, or the reverse if the application records an object before storage confirms it. Store the object key and upload state in a way that supports retries and cleanup. Make the route safe to retry where possible, and avoid returning a success response until the application has enough proof to show the file to the user.

Test the full path before opening it to users

Use a small, non-sensitive file in a development or preview environment. Verify the route rejects an unauthenticated request, a missing file, an oversized file, and a file type the product does not accept. Then upload an allowed file and confirm that the generated key uses the intended tenant prefix and that an authorized user can retrieve it.

Test the negative cases, too: a user from another tenant should not be able to overwrite or read the object; a preview project should not gain production access by accident; and a failed metadata write should not leave a misleading success state. Check the Vercel function logs and AWS-side audit trail without logging file bytes, user credentials, or temporary tokens.

Finally, test the deployment environments that matter. A route that works locally can still fail if the project is not connected to the S3 resource in Preview or Production, if the bucket region is wrong, or if the AWS role trust policy does not match the project and environment. Keep a short runbook with the resource owner, bucket and region, allowed prefixes, expected environment variables, and a safe way to rotate or narrow permissions.

Where an app template fits

Adding S3 is a storage integration task; it does not create the rest of the product around it. If the same team also needs an editable SaaS application shell, the OTF SaaS Dashboard template is an optional $99 starting point with a Vite and Hono app, sign-in, projects, teams, and sample analytics screens. It does not include Amazon S3 or configure this Marketplace integration. Keep the storage connection in the application’s own Vercel and AWS setup.

For an example of how a small Hono backend can be deployed on Vercel’s alternative serverless platform, see our guide to running a Hono backend on AWS Lambda. Use that as a separate deployment discussion; it is not a prerequisite for the Vercel Marketplace path described here.

Sources

  • Amazon S3 joins the Vercel Marketplace — October 14, 2026. Marketplace setup, environment variables, OIDC credentials, upload example, linked-account limits, and S3 versus Blob use cases.
  • SaaS Dashboard template and pricing — checked October 15, 2026. The kit is $99 and does not include this S3 integration.

title: How to Build an Inventory Management Solution That Prevents Stock Drift
description:
A warehouse dashboard can show 120 units available while the picking team finds only 93. The discrepancy may come from delayed order reservations, duplicate webhook events, unrecorded returns, or concurrent updates from multiple sales channels. The result is overselling, failed fulfilment, and replenishment decisions based on incorrect data.

An Inventory Management Solution needs to do more than store stock quantities. It must preserve consistency across receiving, picking, order allocation, returns, and stock adjustments, even when multiple services update inventory simultaneously.

The architectural challenge is deciding which component owns the stock balance, how transactions are applied, and how failed integrations recover without creating duplicate movements. In this guide, we will design a practical inventory workflow using Node.js, PostgreSQL, and asynchronous messaging. For broader warehouse architecture considerations, explore inventory and warehouse management solutions.

Context and Setup

An Inventory Management Solution typically receives updates from e-commerce applications, ERP systems, warehouse management software, and third-party logistics providers. Each system may report a different event, but the inventory service must maintain one consistent view of available stock.

Consider a SKU with 100 units on hand and 15 units already reserved for unfulfilled orders.

The system should calculate:

  • On-hand quantity: 100 units physically recorded in stock.
  • Reserved quantity: 15 units allocated to existing orders.
  • Available quantity: 85 units eligible for new allocations.

A common implementation mistake is storing only a single mutable quantity. Without reservation tracking and transaction history, it becomes difficult to explain why stock changed or safely reverse an operation.

Research published in Management Science by DeHoratius and Raman in 2008 examined nearly 370,000 inventory records across 37 stores of one retailer. The researchers found that 65% of the records were inaccurate. This historical study demonstrates why inventory accuracy must be supported by operational controls rather than assumed from database values alone.

Prerequisites

The example assumes:

  1. Node.js with an asynchronous PostgreSQL driver.
  2. PostgreSQL tables for stock balances, reservations, and inventory movements.
  3. A stable order identifier for deduplicating incoming events.
  4. Database transactions and row-level locking.
  5. A background worker for retrying failed downstream notifications.

Designing an Inventory Management Solution With Transaction Safety

The central design principle is to treat inventory changes as transactions, not independent quantity updates.

Step 1: Define the Inventory Data Model

Store physical stock, reservations, and movement history separately. This provides an auditable record of receiving, dispatches, returns, and adjustments.

A simplified schema could contain:

  • inventory_balance: SKU, warehouse, on-hand quantity, reserved quantity, version.
  • inventory_reservation: order ID, SKU, quantity, reservation status.
  • inventory_movement: movement ID, SKU, quantity delta, reason, reference ID, timestamp.
  • processed_events: event ID and processing status.

Use a composite key on (sku, warehouse_id) to prevent multiple balance records for the same product and location.

The movement table should be append-only for normal operations. Corrections should create compensating movements instead of silently rewriting historical transactions.

Step 2: Apply Stock Changes Atomically

A stock check followed by an independent update creates a race condition. Two checkout requests could both read the same available quantity and reserve more stock than exists.

The following PostgreSQL statement performs a conditional reservation. It assumes inventory_balance contains the SKU's current on-hand and reserved quantities.

-- Why: update only when sufficient unreserved stock exists.
UPDATE inventory_balance
SET reserved_qty = reserved_qty + $1,
    version = version + 1
WHERE sku = $2
  AND warehouse_id = $3
  AND on_hand_qty - reserved_qty >= $1
RETURNING sku, on_hand_qty, reserved_qty, version;
-- No returned row means the reservation was rejected.

Execute this statement inside a database transaction alongside reservation creation, event deduplication, and movement recording. Commit all changes together or roll them back.

The application must also validate that the requested quantity is positive and that the event has not already been processed.

Step 3: Make Event Processing Idempotent

Payment confirmations, order cancellations, and shipping notifications can be delivered more than once. An idempotent consumer ensures that replaying the same event does not apply the same inventory movement twice.

Use a unique constraint on the event identifier and insert the deduplication record within the same database transaction as the stock update.

async function reserveInventory(db, event) {
  const client = await db.connect();

  try {
    await client.query("BEGIN");

    // Why: a unique event ID prevents duplicate processing.
    const result = await client.query(
      `INSERT INTO processed_events (event_id)
       VALUES ($1)
       ON CONFLICT (event_id) DO NOTHING
       RETURNING event_id`,
      [event.id]
    );

    if (result.rowCount === 0) {
      await client.query("ROLLBACK");
      return { duplicate: true };
    }

    // Why: the conditional update prevents overselling.
    const stock = await client.query(
      `UPDATE inventory_balance
       SET reserved_qty = reserved_qty + $1,
           version = version + 1
       WHERE sku = $2
         AND warehouse_id = $3
         AND on_hand_qty - reserved_qty >= $1
       RETURNING sku`,
      [event.quantity, event.sku, event.warehouseId]
    );

    if (stock.rowCount === 0) {
      throw new Error("Insufficient stock");
    }

    // Persist the reservation and movement here,
    // using the same transaction and client.
    await client.query("COMMIT");
    return { reserved: true };
  } catch (error) {
    await client.query("ROLLBACK");
    throw error; // Let the caller retry or handle rejection.
  } finally {
    client.release();
  }
}

This is a simplified reservation example, not a complete production service. Production code must validate payloads, handle database connection failures, distinguish permanent business rejections from transient errors, and ensure reservation and movement records are committed in the same transaction.

Step 4: Separate Database Commits From External Notifications

Do not call a shipping API or publish a message while holding a database transaction open. External requests can time out after the remote service has already processed them.

Instead, use the transactional outbox pattern:

  1. Save the inventory changes and an outbox event in one database transaction.
  2. Let a background worker publish committed outbox events.
  3. Retry transient failures with exponential backoff.
  4. Deduplicate messages at the receiving service.
  5. Monitor outbox age, retry counts, and dead-letter events.

A direct message publish after a database commit is simpler, but a process crash between those operations can lose the notification. The outbox adds storage and worker complexity while making recovery more reliable.

Real-World Application

At Oodles, an inventory implementation should begin by identifying where stock is created, reserved, consumed, and reconciled across connected systems. The appropriate design depends on the existing ERP, warehouse workflows, transaction volume, and integration contracts.

For example, consider a multi-channel retail workflow in which orders arrive through an online store while warehouse staff receive and dispatch stock through a separate system. A suitable implementation would centralize inventory movements, use transactional reservations, deduplicate inbound events, and reconcile warehouse quantities against system balances.

Measure the outcome using baseline and post-deployment data rather than assuming a performance improvement. Useful indicators include reservation failure rate, duplicate movement count, inventory record accuracy, API latency at the 95th percentile, and the time required to recover failed messages.

No verified Oodles project metrics were supplied for this article, so specific before-and-after improvements should be reported only after they have been measured in an actual deployment. You can explore Oodles for more information about its Inventory Management Solution software engineering and integration services.

Conclusion: Key Takeaways

  • Separate stock concepts: Track on-hand, reserved, and available quantities independently.
  • Enforce consistency in the database: Use conditional updates, transactions, and appropriate constraints.
  • Design for duplicate delivery: Make event processing idempotent using stable event identifiers.
  • Recover from integration failures: Use a transactional outbox, retries, and dead-letter handling.
  • Measure operational correctness: Track inventory discrepancies, reservation failures, and recovery times.

1. What is an Inventory Management Solution?

An Inventory Management Solution is software that tracks stock quantities, reservations, receipts, transfers, dispatches, and adjustments across warehouses or sales channels. It helps businesses maintain accurate stock records and coordinate replenishment and order fulfilment.

2. How do you prevent overselling in an inventory system?

Inventory Management Solution Prevent overselling by checking available stock and updating reservations atomically within a database transaction. Use conditional SQL updates or row-level locking, enforce quantity constraints, and ensure concurrent requests cannot reserve more units than are available.

3. Should inventory updates use synchronous APIs or message queues?

Synchronous APIs are useful when an operation requires an immediate reservation decision. Message queues are suitable for downstream notifications, warehouse events, and asynchronous integrations. A transactional outbox can connect committed database changes to reliable event publication.

4. How does an Inventory Management Solution handle duplicate webhooks?

It stores a stable event identifier under a unique database constraint and processes that event within the same transaction as the inventory changes. If the event has already been committed, the consumer skips the duplicate instead of applying the stock movement again.

5. Which metrics should developers monitor in inventory software?

Developers should monitor inventory record accuracy, reservation rejection rates, duplicate event counts, API latency, outbox processing delays, and failed-message retries. These metrics reveal whether the system maintains correct stock balances and recovers effectively from integration failures.

Let's Discuss Your Inventory Architecture

How does your current system handle concurrent reservations, duplicate order events, or inventory reconciliation across warehouses? Share your implementation challenges and questions in the comments.

If you are planning an Inventory Management Solution, discuss your requirements with the Oodles team, including your existing ERP, warehouse workflows, integration points, and consistency requirements.

title: AWS Security Hub now supports resource criticality for prioritization
description:
Today, AWS Security Hub adds resource criticality to exposure prioritization, helping central security teams focus on the exposures that threaten their most business-critical resources.

You can set criticality with an automation rule, for example marking every compute resource in a specific account as Very High. title: RASSG: Repair-Aware Semantic Survival Gating for Streaming Tool Execution
description:
arXiv:2610.14659v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Streaming speech assistants can launch tools before users finish speaking, overlapping execution with incoming speech to reduce user waiting time. However, subsequent self-corrections can invalidate apparently stable arguments, causing stale execution whose irreversible effects persist even after the final call is corrected. We propose Repair-Aware Semantic Survival Gating (RASSG) to jointly control tool launch and cancellation during streaming speech. RASSG launches a tool when three consecutive speech recognition results arrive with identical nonempty arguments, then combines calibrated argument invalidity risk with execution costs to decide cancellation at the last feasible opportunity before effects become irreversible. Evaluation on ReCAST, FDB-v3, and Audio2Tool uses a controlled execution clock with fixed tool runtimes and cancellation parameters. On ReCAST's prospective-repair subset, RASSG reduces the stale execution rate from LocalAgreement-2's 50.00% to 3.15%, with a mean delay of 3.676s across successful trajectories. The stale reduction also holds against every early-execution baseline on both public speech datasets. Ablations with identical initial launches support active cancellation, showing the value of controlling ongoing calls before their effects become irreversible. Code and data are available at https://github.com/daijinhu/RASSG.

title: Apple's on-device model called our iPhone 17 "not eligible", so we tested everything except the model
description:
The first time I asked the on-device model whether it could run on a real phone, SystemLanguageModel.default.availability answered .unavailable(.deviceNotEligible). The device was an iPhone 17 on iOS 26.6, which is new enough for Apple Intelligence. It was also bought in mainland China, where Apple Intelligence isn't offered, and as far as I can tell that is the whole reason.

That was a problem. It was the night before I submitted an AI menu for CapScribe, my caption app: keyword emphasis, title suggestions and emoji, all generated on device. The one phone I own will never run it. The simulator can't run it either.

So the honest version of this post is: here is how we shipped a Foundation Models feature we could not run, and what we tested instead.

The gate has more than two states

availability isn't a Bool. When it's unavailable you get a reason, and the reasons deserve different copy:

switch SystemLanguageModel.default.availability {
case .available:
    return .available
case .unavailable(let reason):
    switch reason {
    case .deviceNotEligible:
        return .unavailable("Device not eligible for Apple Intelligence")
    case .appleIntelligenceNotEnabled:
        return .unavailable("Apple Intelligence not enabled in Settings")
    case .modelNotReady:
        return .unavailable("Model is downloading or not ready")
    @unknown default:
        return .unavailable("Model unavailable")
    }
}

Only one of those is permanent. "Not enabled" is a trip to Settings. "Not ready" usually means the model is still downloading and will sort itself out. Collapse them into a single "AI unavailable" string and you tell the user with a fixable problem that they're stuck, while the user with an ineligible phone learns nothing.

My first instinct was to hide the menu whenever the model isn't there. I didn't. A missing button looks like a bug to anyone who read the release notes, and a hidden menu can't explain itself. What shipped: the menu always appears, the three actions are disabled, and a disabled row at the bottom says which case you're in.

A seam so the fallback can be tested

The service takes an optional model behind a one-method protocol:

public protocol AssistantModel: Sendable {
    func respond(to prompt: String) async throws -> String
}

If a model is injected, the service sends it the prompt and decodes the JSON it returns. If not, it checks availability and either opens a LanguageModelSession with a @Generable output type or throws .unavailable(reason). The real path is short on purpose. The less code that only runs on hardware I don't have, the better.

Unit tests inject a mock that records the prompt. That's where the input cap gets checked: transcripts are cut to 3,000 characters before they reach the model, and a test feeds a much longer string and asserts nothing past the cap made it into the prompt.

UI tests can't inject anything, so there's a DEBUG-only launch argument:

#if DEBUG
public static func makeFakeIfNeeded() -> OnDeviceAssistant? {
    guard ProcessInfo.processInfo.arguments.contains("-uitest-fake-assistant") else { return nil }
    return OnDeviceAssistant(model: FakeAssistantModel())
}
#endif

The fake returns fixed JSON: a couple of keywords, three titles, one 🎬. With the flag set, a UI test runs all three actions in the editor. It checks that keyword emphasis gets switched on in the style panel, that three title rows appear, and that the emoji really lands at the end of the caption text. Without the flag, a second UI test opens the same menu in the simulator, where Foundation Models reports unavailable, and asserts the actions are disabled and the reason row exists and isn't empty.

That second test is the one I care about most. On my own phone the unavailable path is the only path, and for plenty of users it will be too.

What this doesn't cover

The real model. Prompt quality, latency, whether @Guide(.count(3)) really yields three titles every time on a real device: none of that has run on hardware we own. The App Review notes spell out the device requirement, and real-model verification sits on our roadmap as blocked until we get an eligible phone.

I went back and forth on shipping like that. What tipped it was proportion. The code that only runs on eligible hardware is a handful of lines handed straight to Apple's framework. The code that decides what everyone else sees runs on every build.

If you're adding Foundation Models to an app, two things are worth doing on day one. Give each unavailability reason its own message, and put a protocol between your feature and LanguageModelSession, so the fallback path gets tested in the simulator, where it's the default anyway.

I build CapScribe, an on-device caption app for iOS. The menu in question is in the editor: https://apps.apple.com/app/id6801041856?utm_source=devto

title: MontageFlow: Physically Valid High Fidelity EEG Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.14507v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generative modeling offers a promising solution to the scarcity of labeled clinical electroencephalography (EEG) data under strict privacy constraints. Although recent generative models report substantial improvements in generation fidelity, we show that these gains conceal a categorical failure. EEG is not an arbitrary multichannel signal: each channel records the voltage difference between two scalp electrodes. So, real recordings satisfy exact linear identities among their channels. Current generators invariably violate these identities, yet this has gone unnoticed. We therefore propose MontageFlow, a flow-matching model that enforces these identities by restricting its output to signals that satisfy them. We find that ensuring validity improves fidelity too. Furthermore, to retain the EEG characteristics that oversmoothing washes out, we also condition the model on a physiological state vector encoded from the whole EEG window. For generation, this vector is drawn from a prior fitted in latent space. Across 3 large-scale benchmarks, our model improves TS-FID by 1.6-3.6$\times$ over the closest rival while ensuring validity.

title: Retrieve What Helps, Only When It Helps: Agentic Reinforcement Learning for Selective Retrieval-Augmented Machine Translation
description:
arXiv:2610.19528v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Retrieving external knowledge can improve large language model (LLM) translation by providing supplementary information such as idiom interpretations and terminology. However, existing retrieval-augmented machine translation systems typically apply predefined retrieval strategies uniformly across all inputs. We argue that translation operates in a partial-evidence regime: LLM's parametric knowledge suffices for many inputs, while external evidence benefits a subset and usually supports rather than directly provides the desired translation. This creates two challenges: deciding when to retrieve and what evidence to acquire. We introduce Selective Retrieval-Augmented Translation (SRAT), an agentic reinforcement learning framework that learns when to translate directly or retrieve, what to retrieve, and how to integrate these decisions by optimizing final translation quality. To align evidence retrieval with downstream translation quality rather than simple semantic similarity, we further develop joint Plackett--Luce optimization and translation-quality contrastive training for retriever-training. Experiments on idiom, knowledge-intensive, and document-level translation with offline or online retrieval show that SRAT consistently outperforms never- and always-retrieve baselines, and quality-aligned retriever training provides further gains when similarity-based retrieval is insufficient. The results demonstrate the benefit of treating retrieval as a learnable translation action rather than fixed preprocessing.
