title: Eloquent vs Query Builder in Laravel: When to Use Each
description:
Use Eloquent when you are working with individual records that have behavior: validation rules, casts, relationships, events, soft deletes. Use the query builder when you are working with rows as data: reports, joins, aggregates, bulk writes and large exports. That rule covers most cases, but the details are where bugs come from, because the two do not behave the same on updates, deletes and inserts. I ran both against a 50,000-row MariaDB table using the real framework code (Laravel 13.35.0) to measure the cost and to check every claim below.

They are the same engine

An Eloquent builder is a wrapper around the query builder. The same fluent methods exist on both, and the SQL is nearly identical. The only difference in this example is the soft delete condition the model adds on its own:

DB::table('posts')
    ->where('status', 'published')
    ->orderByDesc('id')->limit(5)->toSql();
// select * from `posts` where `status` = ? order by `id` desc limit 5

Post::where('status', 'published')
    ->orderByDesc('id')
    ->limit(5)
    ->toSql();
// select * from `posts` where `status` = ? and `posts`.`deleted_at` is null order by `id` desc limit 5

So the choice is not about SQL features. It is about what happens to the rows before you see them and when you write them back.

What Eloquent adds, and what it costs

The query builder returns plain stdClass objects with the values exactly as the database driver gives them. Eloquent turns every row into a model: it applies casts, attaches the original attributes for dirty tracking, fires a retrieved event and registers the model with its relations. In the test, the same row looked like this from each side:

Column DB::table() Model
meta (JSON) string: '{"tags":["a","b","c"],"score":1}' array (cast)
published_at string: '2026-10-14 13:38:00' Carbon instance (cast)
Row type stdClass Post

That convenience has a price, and it shows when you load many rows. I loaded all 50,000 rows with each approach, in a fresh PHP process each time, three runs per row, taking the median:

Approach (50,000 rows, all columns) Time Extra memory
DB::table('posts')->get() about 160 ms 59 MB
Post::get() about 980 ms 103 MB
Post::get() then reading the casts on every row about 1,900 ms 105 MB
Post::query()->toBase()->get() about 200 ms 60 MB
DB::table() with select('id', 'title') about 65 ms 28 MB
Post::select('id', 'title')->get() about 880 ms 76 MB
DB::table()->chunkById(1000) about 180 ms 2.3 MB
Post::chunkById(1000) about 1,200 ms 4.2 MB
DB::table()->cursor() about 255 ms 8.4 MB
Post::cursor() about 2,900 ms 9.4 MB

Hydrating 50,000 models took about six times longer than reading the same rows as plain objects, and used less than twice the memory. Selecting only the columns you need helps both sides, but does not remove the hydration cost. Nobody renders 50,000 models in one request, so this matters for exports, reports and background jobs, not for a paginated page of 25 rows. The numbers are from one machine with MariaDB on localhost; a network hop would add the same cost to both sides, which would shrink the percentage gap but not the absolute one.

Two practical notes from the table. First, toBase() is the bridge: it keeps your model's query scopes and gives you plain rows. Second, cursor() keeps memory flat but is the slowest option for models. The Laravel documentation also notes that PDO still buffers the raw results, so for very large result sets it recommends lazy(), and chunkById when you update the column you are filtering on.

Three places where they behave differently

This is the part that causes production bugs. I ran each operation inside a transaction and rolled it back, with listeners registered on the model:

Operation Model events Result
$post->update([...]) saving, updating, updated, saved updated_at changed
Post::where(...)->update([...]) none updated_at changed
DB::table('posts')->where(...)->update([...]) none updated_at unchanged
$post->delete() (soft deletes on) deleting, deleted Row kept, deleted_at set
Post::where(...)->delete() none Row kept, deleted_at set
DB::table('posts')->where(...)->delete() none Row permanently deleted
Post::insert([...]) none created_at is NULL
Post::create([...]) saving, saved (the create events fire as well) Timestamps filled

Read it as three rules:

  1. A mass update or delete through Eloquent fires no model events. The Laravel documentation says this directly: the models are never retrieved, so events such as updating and deleting are not dispatched. If you have an observer that clears a cache, writes an audit log or syncs a search index, a Post::where(...)->update() silently skips it. Load the models and save them, or accept that the observer will not run.
  2. The query builder ignores soft deletes. DB::table('posts')->delete() removes the row for good, while the same intent through the model only sets deleted_at. Counts differ too: on my data Post::count() returned 49,000 while DB::table('posts')->count() returned 50,000. A report built on DB::table() will include soft-deleted rows unless you filter them yourself.
  3. Bulkinsert()does not set timestamps, even on a model. Post::insert() goes straight to the query builder, so created_at and updated_at stay NULL unless you supply them. Post::upsert() is different: as documented, it sets the timestamps. In my test it updated updated_at, while DB::table('posts')->upsert() left it untouched.

Mass assignment follows the same split. A model only fills attributes you allow ($fillable in my test; the 13.x documentation shows a Fillable attribute for the same job), and extra keys are silently discarded. In my run, Post::create() with id and an unknown key ignored both, whereas DB::table()->insert() with an unknown column failed with a QueryException. The query builder does protect against SQL injection through parameter binding, but the documentation warns that PDO cannot bind column names, so never let user input pick a column or an order by field.

Which one to use

Task Use Why
Show, create or edit one record in a form or API Eloquent Casts, validation flow, mass-assignment protection, events
Anything with relationships (with(), whereHas()) Eloquent Relationships are the main reason to have models
Rules that must always run (observers, soft deletes, global scopes) Eloquent The query builder skips them
Reports, dashboards, joins across several tables, groupBy aggregates Query builder You want rows and numbers, not objects
Exporting or processing tens of thousands of rows Query builder, or toBase() with chunkById or lazy Roughly 6x faster here, with less memory
Inserting thousands of rows insert() or upsert() Next section
Changing one column on many rows (increment, status flips) One mass update query Next section

Mixing them safely

You rarely need to choose one for a whole application. These patterns use each where it fits.

Read big sets as plain rows but keep the model's scopes (soft deletes included):

Post::query()
    ->where('status', 'published')
    ->toBase()                       // stdClass rows, no model hydration
    ->orderBy('id')
    ->chunkById(1000, function ($rows) {
        foreach ($rows as $row) {
            // $row->title, $row->views ...
        }
    });

Write a report with the query builder and filter soft deletes yourself:

$top = DB::table('posts')
    ->join('users', 'users.id', '=', 'posts.user_id')
    ->whereNull('posts.deleted_at')
    ->groupBy('users.id', 'users.name')
    ->selectRaw('users.id, users.name, count(*) as posts, sum(posts.views) as views')
    ->orderByDesc('views')
    ->limit(20)
    ->get();

Insert in bulk and fill the timestamps yourself:

$now = now();

foreach (array_chunk($rows, 1000) as $chunk) {
    Post::insert(array_map(fn ($r) => $r + ['created_at' => $now, 'updated_at' => $now], $chunk));
}

The speed difference is large. Inserting 5,000 rows took about 2,700 ms with Post::create() in a loop (5,000 queries), and about 120 ms with Post::insert() in chunks of 1,000. Updating the same 5,000 rows one model at a time took about 3,000 to 3,200 ms; one Post::where(...)->increment('views') query took about 15 ms. On a remote database each saved round trip is worth more, so the gap grows. The trade is the one from the table above: the fast version skips events, so only use it where nothing depends on them.

Frequently asked questions

Is Eloquent slow?

Not for normal page work. In my test, loading models with get() cost about 0.02 ms per row, including the query itself. It becomes a problem when you load tens of thousands of rows, or run thousands of single-row queries in a loop, which is more often an N+1 or batching problem than an Eloquent problem.

Can I mix Eloquent and the query builder in one project?

Yes, and most mature Laravel apps do. Keep models for your domain objects and use DB::table() or toBase() for reporting and bulk work. Just remember the three differences above.

Does the query builder protect against SQL injection?

Values are bound as PDO parameters, so you do not need to escape them. Column names and order by fields cannot be bound, so whitelist them if they come from user input.

References: Laravel: Eloquent ORM and Laravel: Query Builder.

Originally published on DEV Talk.

title: Measuring the Impact of Personalized Recommendations
description:
By Kevin Zielnicki, Guy Aridor, Aurélien Bibaut, Allen Tran, Winston Chou, and Nathan Kallus

Introduction

Personalization is everywhere on the internet. It shapes the products we discover, the stories we read, the music we hear, and the movies and TV shows we watch. At Netflix, personalization has been central to the member experience for decades — from the Netflix Prize to our modern recommender system that helps members navigate a large and constantly changing catalog.

But personalization is not only an algorithmic problem, it is also a measurement problem. How do we know how much value personalization creates? More precisely, how do we separate the appeal of a title from the value created by recommending that title to the right member at the right time?

In a new article in the International Journal of Industrial Organization — which we are also presenting at this year’s ACM Conference on Economics & Computation (EC ‘26) — we develop a model of member behavior, title choice, and personalized recommendations. The model lets us estimate how recommendations affect both whether members choose to watch and, if so, which titles they choose. In this post, we summarize our approach and main findings.

The Measurement Challenge

A natural first attempt at valuing recommendations is to ask: what share of viewing comes from titles that were recommended? This is an intuitive metric, but it fails to answer the causal question at hand.

The problem is that recommendations are not randomly assigned. A title appears on a member’s homepage precisely because the recommender system predicts that the member might want to watch it. If a member watches that title, was it because the recommendation caused the member to watch it? Or would she have watched it anyway because of her underlying preference for that kind of title? This is the core measurement challenge: recommendations are targeted to demand, so viewing a recommended title combines the effect of personalization with the member’s underlying preferences.

One way to solve this would be to run a large experiment that replaces Netflix’s personalized experience with an unpersonalized one. That would create clean variation — but it would also be a poor member experience. Personalization is a central part of how members locate valuable titles in a large catalog, so turning it off broadly is not an acceptable measurement strategy.

Instead, we take a hybrid approach. We build a behavioral model that separates members’ underlying preferences from the incremental effect of recommendations. The model uses the natural variation in the recommendation system, for example due to algorithmic exploration, to estimate how recommendations affect choice. Then, to validate the model predictions about title substitutability, we use small-scale A/B tests that “nudge” the salience of a handful of titles exogenously, generating ground-truth substitution patterns for a subset of titles. This lets us combine the scale and richness of modeling with the credibility of experimental evidence.

A Model of Member Choice

To measure the value of personalization, we need a model of what members would watch under different recommendation systems. Our model treats Netflix viewing as a day-by-day choice process. On each day, a member chooses among the titles available in the catalog, or she chooses not to watch anything. This gives us a concrete target to estimate: the probability that a member watches each title on a given day, as a function of their preferences, their viewing history, and the recommendations they see.

A simple version of this model would be too restrictive. It might assume, for example, that removing one title from the catalog shifts viewing toward all other titles in roughly proportional ways. But that isn’t how member choice works. If a member is considering a romantic comedy, the closest substitutes are likely other romantic comedies, not every title on Netflix equally. For similar reasons, two members may react very differently to the same recommendation.

To capture this complexity, we use a low-rank choice model. The model learns a representation of each title and a corresponding representation of each member’s current preferences. These representations are not limited to manually specified features like genre, cast, or language. Instead, they are learned from viewing behavior itself, allowing the model to capture nuanced similarities between titles that may be difficult to describe with coarse features, such as genre or release date, alone.

Member preferences are dynamic. What someone wants to watch today depends on what they have watched recently. A member who just finished a crime thriller may be in a different preference state than the same member after watching a stand-up special or a kids’ movie. Rather than estimate a fixed preference vector for each member, the model summarizes each member’s past viewing history into a current preference state. This lets us capture heterogeneous and time-varying tastes while also scaling to millions of members.

The key component for our purposes is that the model explicitly parameterizes the effect of recommendations. When a title is recommended, the model gives it an additional recommendation effect, or “bonus,” that increases its probability of being chosen. This bonus is a reduced-form way to capture two related mechanisms. First, recommendations can create awareness by helping members discover titles they may not have known about. Second, recommendations can provide information by signaling that a title is likely to be a good match.

Once estimated, the model becomes an engine for predicting counterfactuals. We can ask what would happen if a title were not recommended, if a different set of titles were recommended, or if the current recommender system were replaced with simpler alternatives. Because the model separately represents member preferences, title appeal, and recommendation effects, it lets us estimate not only how recommendations affect total viewing, but also how they change which titles are watched.

The model is only useful, however, if it captures real substitution patterns. The next step is therefore validation: comparing the model’s predictions to randomized experiments that directly perturb, on a small scale, the visibility that each title receives.

Validating the Model with Randomized Experiments

The model relies on an important assumption. After conditioning on the member, title, and state information available to the recommender system, we treat the remaining variation in whether a title is recommended as if it were randomly assigned. In our setting, this assumption is reasonable: we observe all of the information available to the recommender system, so we should be able to model its behavior accurately. But it is still an assumption. A useful model should not only fit historical viewing patterns; it should also predict what happens when recommendations change for external reasons.

Thus, to validate the model, we used randomized experiments that introduce variation in title visibility exogenously. These experiments mirror the kinds of variation that occur routinely when recommendation algorithms are updated: some titles receive more impressions, while others receive fewer. The key difference is that, in the validation experiment, this variation was prespecified so that we could estimate clean experimental benchmarks.

Specifically, we randomly assigned members to treatment arms that slightly nudged recommendations towards and away from different categories of titles. This let us measure diversion ratios: when a set of titles becomes less visible, how much viewing shifts to other titles, and how much shifts out of Netflix viewing altogether?

We then asked whether the model could reproduce those experimentally measured substitution patterns. We estimated the model on the control group, simulated the same recommendation changes, and compared the model-implied diversion ratios to the experimental ones. The agreement was strong: the model’s predicted diversion ratios had a correlation of 0.86 with the experimental estimates and an R-squared of 0.73.

This validation gives us confidence that the model captures counterfactual substitution patterns accurately. Subsequently, we ask what would happen under more dramatic changes, such as different recommender systems.

Counterfactuals: Aggregate Consumption and Diversity

With a validated model in hand, we can move from measurement to counterfactuals. Instead of asking only what happened under the current Netflix experience, we can ask what would have happened if members had seen recommendations generated by a different system.

We compare the current recommender system to three baselines:

  1. The first is random recommendations: every member receives titles selected uniformly at random from the catalog. This is not intended as a realistic product experience, but it helps isolate the value of having recommendations that are relevant.
  2. The second is popularity-based recommendations: every member receives broadly popular titles. This is a natural non-personalized benchmark.
  3. The third is a basic matrix factorization model, a classic personalized recommendation approach and a useful baseline for older generations of recommender systems.

In each counterfactual, we replace the recommended titles while keeping the rest of the choice environment fixed. This lets us estimate how much viewing would change if the recommendation policy changed, holding constant the catalog, members, and model of member choice.

The results show that the current recommender system generates substantially more engagement than each benchmark. Relative to the current system, random recommendations reduce engagement by 16%, popularity-based recommendations reduce engagement by 12%, and matrix factorization reduces engagement by 4%. These are large differences at Netflix scale. Even the comparison to matrix factorization — a personalized baseline — suggests that continued improvements in personalization translate into meaningful gains in how effectively members find titles they want to watch.

Engagement is only part of the story. A recommender system could increase viewing while concentrating attention on a narrow set of already-popular titles. That would be a worse experience for members whose tastes are not well represented by those titles, and it would make poorer use of a broad catalog.

We therefore also examine consumption diversity: how broadly viewing is distributed across titles. The current system performs well on this dimension too. Popularity-based and matrix-factorization recommendations both substantially increase concentration, meaning that fewer titles receive meaningful viewership. Random recommendations produce slightly more diversity, as expected, but at a large cost to engagement.

Taken together, these counterfactuals show that the value of personalization is not just that members watch more. It is also that members are matched to a broader set of titles. The current recommender system increases engagement while preserving a wide distribution of viewing, reflecting the diversity of member tastes across the Netflix catalog.

Decomposing the Impact on Titles

The aggregate counterfactuals show that personalization increases engagement while maintaining broad consumption across the catalog. We can also use the model to ask a more granular question: why does a recommended title get watched?

There are three conceptually distinct channels:

  1. The first is exposure: simply showing a title to a member can increase the probability that the member watches it. This captures the basic value of surfacing a title that may otherwise have been hard to find.
  2. The second is selection: recommended titles are shown to members who already have a relatively high baseline probability of watching them. This channel doesn’t lead to incremental engagement, but it can smooth the discovery experience and help users feel that the recommender system understands their preferences.
  3. The third is targeting: the recommender system may identify members for whom the recommendation itself is especially effective, meaning members who are much more likely to watch the title when it is recommended than when it is not.

The distinction matters because not all recommendation-driven viewing should be interpreted the same way. If recommendations worked only through exposure, then any reasonably visible surface could generate much of the same value. If they worked mostly through selection, then recommendations would mainly be finding members who were already likely to watch a title. Targeting is different: it captures whether the system is placing titles in front of members for whom the recommendation changes the decision.

Our model lets us estimate these channels title by title. For each title, we can compare the predicted probability that a targeted member watches it when recommended to the probability that an average member watches it when not recommended. We then decompose that difference into selection, exposure, and targeting.

We first show that exposure is meaningful: showing a title to an average member roughly triples its consumption probability relative to the baseline. Exposure is not the main driver of differences in consumption, as mechanical exposure explains only about 7% of the gap under the current recommender system, while selection and targeting account for the vast majority of the difference and the targeting effect is nearly seven times larger than the exposure effect.

This pattern is especially informative when compared with simpler recommendation systems. Random recommendations are dominated by exposure because they do not personalize: differences in consumption mostly reflect differences in what titles are shown. Matrix factorization changes this by making recommendations personal, reducing the role of exposure and leaving exposure, selection, and targeting to contribute nearly evenly to consumption differences. The current recommender system goes further: its gains come less from mechanical exposure, but more from targeting the right titles to the right viewers.

Targeting is also not uniform across the catalog. It is strongest for mid-popularity titles: titles with enough potential audience to be broadly relevant, but not so much mass appeal that everyone already knows about them. Very popular titles need less help from targeting, while very niche titles may have too small an audience to target effectively. The largest gains come from the middle of the catalog, where personalization helps connect specific titles with specific member tastes.

Conclusion

Personalized recommendations are valuable because they help members navigate a large catalog and find titles they want to watch. They are also valuable to Netflix because they make the service more useful, more engaging, and better able to serve a wide range of tastes.

But measuring that value is not straightforward. Recommendations are targeted by design, so we cannot simply compare recommended and non-recommended viewing. At the same time, turning off personalization at scale would create a worse member experience.

Our approach combines a large-scale model of member choice with true experimental validation. The model lets us separate underlying title preferences from the incremental effect of recommendations, and the experiments verify that the model captures real substitution patterns.

Using this framework, we find that personalization affects both how much members watch and which titles they watch. The value of recommendations comes not just from exposure, but from matching the right titles to the right members.

Measuring the Impact of Personalized Recommendations was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

Regular expression matchers in host and route rules in URL maps are now generally available (GA).

You can now use regular expressions (regex) matchers to configure more flexible and precise traffic routing rules within URL maps for Application Load Balancers. This feature allows you to leverage the power of RE2 syntax for matching on:

  • HTTP Headers: Using the regexMatch field within headerMatches in routeRules.

CodeMender updates (v0.14.0)

This release introduces updates to CodeMender:

  • Better pull request scans: cm find --diff now catches removed security controls and gives large files more time (configurable with --diff-job-timeout).
  • Unified sessions: --deep and --diff scans now appear as a single session in cm session list, cm report, and cm stats.
  • Moved code in cm verify: cm verify now finds code that moved since cm find and updates the finding's location.
  • Guided activation: cm now opens the activation page and waits for activation instead of exiting.
  • New cm find flags: --deep-max-turns limits exploratory steps per file in --deep scans, and --enable-bash allows shell commands during scans.
  • Improved detection: More distinct findings per file and more precise CWE classification for weak hashing and randomness.
  • Bug fixes:
    • Fixed scans of repositories reached through nested symbolic links.
    • Fixed findings for nonexistent files and over-merged findings.
    • Shell scripts created by cm verify are now executable.

For more information, see the CodeMender documentation.

Fixed

The following issues were fixed in 1.35.600-gke.140:

  • Fixed vulnerabilities listed in Vulnerability fixes.
  • Fixed an issue where audit-proxy retried audit log exports indefinitely on permanent errors, generating excessive audit logging traffic.
  • Fixed an issue where the Kubernetes preflight health check scanned all namespaces in the admin cluster instead of the target cluster's namespace, causing cluster upgrades to fail if an unrelated cluster had stale reconciling resources.
  • Fixed an issue where user clusters repeatedly alternated between reconciling and running states if the management cluster configured a different pod density configuration than the user cluster.

Google Distributed Cloud (software only) for bare metal

Announcement

Google Distributed Cloud (software only) for bare metal 1.35.600-gke.140 is now available for download. To upgrade, see Upgrade clusters. Google Distributed Cloud for bare metal 1.35.600-gke.140 runs on Kubernetes v1.35.8-gke.100.

After a release, it takes approximately 7 to 14 days for the version to become available for installations or upgrades with the GKE On-Prem API clients: the Google Cloud console, the gcloud CLI, and Terraform.

If you use a third-party storage vendor, check the listing of our previously-qualified storage partners.

Fixed

The following issues were fixed in 1.35.600-gke.140:

  • Fixed vulnerabilities listed in Vulnerability fixes.
  • Improved containerd resilience against state corruption if a node reboots while unpacking container images.
  • Fixed an issue where the periodic configuration drift health check failed with a version not supported error while a cluster upgrade or rollback was in progress.
  • Fixed an issue where audit-proxy retried audit log exports indefinitely on permanent errors, generating excessive audit logging traffic.
  • Fixed an issue where the Kubernetes preflight health check scanned all namespaces in the admin cluster instead of the target cluster's namespace, causing cluster upgrades to fail if an unrelated cluster had stale reconciling resources.
  • Fixed an issue where upgrading or recreating a node during maintenance mode could proceed before storage volumes finished detaching, resulting in orphaned CSI VolumeAttachment resources or I/O errors. After the fix, node drain verifies that kubelet unmounts all host volumes and that CSI VolumeAttachment resources detach before completing the drain.
  • Fixed an issue where Certificate Authority (CA) rotation failed for self-managing clusters (admin, hybrid, and standalone). The failure occurs during the final phase of the rotation when attempting to move management resources back from the temporary bootstrap cluster to the self-managing cluster, which can leave the cluster in an unmanageable state. You must upgrade your clusters to version 1.35.600-gke.140 before you rotate your CAs.
  • Fixed an issue where BareMetalMachine status conditions prematurely reported nodes as ready and available during maintenance mode transitions.
  • Fixed an issue in clusters using bundled BGP load balancing where control plane upgrades or configuration updates could cause up to 20 seconds of API server connection failures while a control plane node restarted. After the fix, failover to a healthy control plane node completes in approximately 4 seconds.
  • Fixed an issue where user clusters repeatedly alternated between reconciling and running states if the management cluster configured a different pod density configuration than the user cluster.

title: Fantastic Metrics and How to Find Them: Meta-Evaluating Metrics for Multi-lingual Style-Personalized Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.19166v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Meta-evaluation of text generation metrics and LLM-judges is primarily conducted using metric-human correlations. However, prior work has shown that correlation is not an appropriate estimate of a metric's evaluation capability and can be unstable across evaluation settings, such as different datasets or languages. Therefore, we propose a regression-based meta-evaluation of metrics that learns on calibrated metric outputs to predict human ratings. We ground this measurement relative to a trivial constant-mean baseline and human agreements to provide a comparable measure of metric capability across evaluation settings. To test our meta-evaluation framework, we developed a large-scale multi-lingual style-personalized text generation (SPTG) benchmark, collecting multiple annotations across 10 topologically diverse languages and four evaluation dimensions, each with varying degrees of subjectivity. We meta-evaluated 32 metrics from three style evaluation paradigms (string-based, embedding-based, and LLM-judges) and their ensembles over these 40 evaluation settings. Our analysis revealed that even simple string- and embedding-based measurements can match strong LLM-judges when calibrated to human ratings. We also identified characteristics of human annotations that determine metric performance, as well as conditions under which a metric ensemble outperforms its individual constituents.

title: Retrieval Architecture for Candidate Search: Bounded Fallbacks and Audit Trails
description:
Recruiting search has a hard constraint that a demo tends to hide: an answer assembled from a slow or unauthorized source is worse than a narrower answer that a recruiter can verify. Short answer: use staged retrieval with explicit collections, bounded queries, and source context that remains attached to every candidate claim. Treat each fallback as a contract with a deadline, an access check, and an audit event.

I approach this like a ledger boundary. A candidate profile is an indexed fact, a ranking decision is a derived fact, and a citation is the receipt that lets somebody reconstruct the decision later. The system should never imply exactly-once retrieval, because networks retry and sources change; it should make each stage idempotent and make duplicate evidence harmless.

Start with a retrieval contract

Before choosing a vector engine, map the user-visible answer to fields the pipeline can actually retrieve. For “find backend candidates who have shipped payment reconciliation,” the contract might require a candidate identifier, an access scope, the matching excerpts, their source identifiers, and a freshness timestamp. A result that has a high similarity score but no source identifier is incomplete, even if its prose sounds convincing.

Preserve tenant and access-control metadata on every indexed item. Put those attributes beside the chunk, not in a separate cache that can drift. At query time, apply the tenant and authorization predicates before ranking or generation. This is where many fallback designs quietly leak data: the primary index filters correctly, then the lexical fallback searches a shared table without the same predicate.

The contract also defines failure semantics. An empty stage means “try the next permitted stage,” while a denied stage means “stop and record the denial.” A timeout is not permission to broaden scope. That distinction belongs in the audit trail with a request ID, stage name, query limit, and selected source IDs.

Three words matter: bounded, attributable, repeatable.

It failed closed.

How should fallbacks shape retrieval architecture for recruiting candidate search?

Use a narrow-to-broad sequence, with explicit budgets at every hop:

  1. Search the tenant’s candidate collection with semantic retrieval and a small top-k.
  2. If recall is insufficient, run a lexical query over the same authorized corpus, preserving the original filters.
  3. If the corpus is stale or lacks a required document, consult an approved web-backed source, but return its URL or document identifier as context rather than silently blending it into a profile.
  4. If all bounded stages fail, return a partial answer that says what was searched and what was unavailable; do not fabricate a match.

Each stage gets its own timeout and retry budget. A 300 ms semantic query followed by a 300 ms lexical query is a product decision, not an implementation detail. Retries must use exponential backoff for rate limits, and a consumer that receives the same event twice must be idempotent. In payment systems I would call this the exactly-once mindset: execution may happen more than once, but the recorded effect and the explanation remain stable.

Web-backed context deserves extra skepticism. Scrape or search results can be stale, duplicated, or outside the recruiter’s authority. Store the returned URL or document ID, the retrieval time, and the policy decision that allowed it. A reviewer should be able to remove that source and see which part of the answer changes.

Collection boundaries and auditability

Separate collections by tenant and, where policy requires it, by document class such as resume, portfolio, and public posting. Collection deletion should be an explicit administrative event; deleting a vector without recording why creates an audit gap. Keep a tombstone with the candidate ID, actor, timestamp, and replacement status so a later reconciliation can distinguish “never indexed” from “intentionally removed.”

The same discipline applies to updates. Use a deterministic document key derived from tenant, candidate, and source revision. Upserting that key can be retried without creating a second profile chunk. Query responses should carry source identifiers into the generation prompt and into the final response metadata. This is the practical bridge between retrieval-augmented generation research and a recruiting workflow: the model gets context, and the recruiter gets evidence.

Here is a small Go adapter for one bounded semantic stage. It calls Infrai through plain HTTP, keeps the key in the environment, and treats a rate limit as a signal to wait rather than a reason to flood the service. The payload fields are the stage contract owned by this application: collection, tenant, query, and limit.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func querySemantic(ctx context.Context, tenant, query string, limit int) ([]byte, error) {
    payload, err := json.Marshal(map[string]any{
        "collection": "candidate-content",
        "tenant":     tenant,
        "query":      query,
        "limit":      limit,
    })
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    baseURL := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL")
    if baseURL == "" {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_BASE_URL is required")
    }
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 300 * time.Millisecond}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, baseURL+"/v1/vector/query", bytes.NewReader(payload))
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * 100 * time.Millisecond
            if retryAfter := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"); retryAfter != "" {
                if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); parseErr == nil {
                    delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
                }
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("vector query returned %s: %s", resp.Status, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("vector query remained rate-limited after retries")
}

The caller records the stage name and error before moving on, then deduplicates by (tenant, candidate_id, source_id). That key is more useful than a similarity score when a recruiter asks why two excerpts appeared twice.

Comparing engines without losing the policy layer

The engine is replaceable; the retrieval contract is not. These options have different operational shapes, so the right choice depends on where the team wants to own policy and scaling work.

Option Useful fit Trade-off for candidate search
Elasticsearch Teams already operating a search cluster and needing lexical plus vector features in one system More cluster and mapping responsibility; tenant filters and audit fields remain your design
OpenSearch Organizations preferring an open-source distribution and self-managed deployment choices You own upgrades, capacity, and the consistency of security filters across fallback paths
Pinecone A managed vector-first service when semantic retrieval is the central workload Lexical fallback and evidence storage usually require another system, increasing reconciliation surface
Infrai A plain REST boundary is useful when a polyglot service should call vector capabilities without installing an SDK Validate collection tenancy, retention, and export requirements against your governance policy before standardizing

Infrai’s relevant advantage here is the plain REST API: any service that can send HTTP can call it, with no client library version to maintain. Its broader single-key surface can also reduce the number of authentication boundaries in a small pipeline, but that is an integration convenience, not proof that its retrieval ranking fits every corpus.

The discovery surface is public and self-describing, with 295 routes across 20 modules. Infrai’s one key, one bill convention means the same credential can cover the vector stage and adjacent backend calls. For a recruiting platform that also needs storage or scheduled reconciliation, that broad capability surface and uniform map can reduce adapter work while leaving the ranking policy in your code.

The catch is ownership. A team that needs custom analyzers, on-prem residency, or deep cluster-level tuning may be better served by Elasticsearch or OpenSearch. A team that wants a managed vector service and already has a separate evidence store may prefer Pinecone. Do not choose on a unit-price screenshot; choose on filter correctness, deletion semantics, and the evidence a reviewer can inspect.

Rollout and reconciliation checklist

Start with shadow traffic: run the new semantic stage beside the current search, compare candidate IDs and source coverage, and log every divergence without changing recruiter-visible results. Then enable the first fallback for a small tenant set. Define a maximum end-to-end deadline, a maximum number of returned excerpts, and a clear partial-answer status.

At launch, monitor four audit measures: the share of results with source IDs, authorization-filter failures, duplicate evidence keys, and timeout frequency by stage. Reconcile index contents against the source-of-record on a schedule. When a candidate is deleted or access is revoked, remove its vectors and verify that no fallback collection still returns the old source.

Your mileage may vary: a public portfolio may be acceptable for one recruiting workflow and prohibited for another. Keep that policy outside the ranking model, version it, and record the decision with each retrieval event. That is how a fallback becomes a controlled path instead of an accidental data boundary.

References

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/dense-vector.html
  • https://opensearch.org/docs/latest/search-plugins/knn/
  • https://docs.pinecone.io/guides/get-started/overview

title: TimeSeries Tiered Storage Journey: Kafka/Flink Streams to Native Cassandra Cold Reads
description:
By Oleksii Tkachuk, Rajiv Shringi, Chris Lohfink, Abe Ratnofsky, Kartik Sathyanarayanan

Introduction

In an earlier post, we introduced the TimeSeries Abstraction, our high-throughput, low-latency platform designed to store and query temporal event data at scale. It has since become the operational backbone for Netflix’s largest datasets, which now span multiple petabytes.

However, managing such large datasets in hot storage, tuned for low-millisecond latency access, is not cheap. At Netflix, cost-efficiency is a continuous discipline rather than a temporary initiative. This post shares two solutions that significantly reduce storage costs by continuously moving older, less frequently accessed data into cheaper object storage:

  • Solution 1: Uses Apache Kafka and Flink to stream data directly to S3
  • Solution 2: Leverages Cassandra backups in S3 and pluggable Memtables to read data directly from S3

We’ll start with the Kafka/Flink-based design, then describe how we evolved to a native Cassandra-based cold tier.

Challenges

As Netflix’s TimeSeries datasets have expanded, we’ve encountered several compounding challenges:

  • Growing retention demands: Users often push for increasing data retention to serve a broader range of use cases, which in turn increases the storage costs.
  • Escalating costs: Maintaining massive, dense clusters for infrequently accessed historical data is prohibitively expensive.
  • Sparse historical access: Most queries target recent events, but older data must remain readily available for occasional audits and investigations.
  • Operational strain: High storage density on hot nodes complicates scaling, deployment, and cluster stability.
  • Latency requirements: Even historical data sometimes requires sub-second query performance for internal tooling and analysis.

This creates a clear opportunity: keep the most recent data on fast storage and migrate older, rarely read data to cheaper storage while preserving a consistent API. Done well, this can meet user and operational needs while greatly reducing our infrastructure spend.

TimeSeries Abstraction

Before we dive into the cold storage solutions, here is a quick recap of how TimeSeries partitions its dataset into multiple tables, each covering a window of time we call Time Slices.

This enables several key optimizations, most notably allowing a table to become immutable once it crosses the write boundary, which lets us safely apply further optimizations. For more details, refer to our previous post.

This slice information is critical and is maintained in a dedicated metadata table:

Creating new Time Slices and maintaining their metadata is a primary responsibility of the TimeSeries control plane. The TimeSeries data plane uses this information to correctly route the read and write traffic to the provisioned tables.

With that background, let’s look at the different solutions we built for data tiering.

Solution 1: Streaming with Apache Kafka and Flink

Our first solution followed a familiar streaming pattern using Apache Kafka and Flink, where we streamed data to S3 in realtime while simultaneously persisting it to Cassandra.

Getting Data Into S3 Efficiently

To optimize data streaming to S3, the system hash-partitions Time Series IDs into buckets. This partitions the stream and lets dedicated Flink tasks handle each bucket, ultimately batching and reducing the write throughput to S3. Flink workers batch events into Parquet files grouped by event time within the hour. These files are great for high-throughput streaming writes, but not for low-latency reads.

Enter the Compaction job.

Compaction Job to Optimize Reads

The compaction job runs daily and merges small Parquet files into a single, optimized daily Parquet file per namespace.

The job further optimizes the Parquet files in the following ways:

  • Small Row Groups: Creates small (4–8 MB) row groups to minimize lookup cost. We can then use the Parquet Java library to perform range reads of row groups from S3. This is intentionally well below Parquet’s recommended row group floor — smaller groups were better because our reads are dominated by point/range lookups rather than full scans.
  • Event Sorting: Sorts events within a row group by time, eliminating brute-force scans when querying for a time range.
  • Bloom Filters: Caches Bloom filters and file metadata in EVCache, allowing the TimeSeries query planner to efficiently skip unnecessary reads from S3.

Once the compaction job completes, all compacted files per partition are recorded in the TimeSeries control plane, and the hot storage slices can now be truncated!

On some of our largest datasets, this job typically takes about 12 hours, prioritizing lower compute costs over execution speed.

Streaming Cold Tier Read

Once compacted files are optimized in cold storage, they are ready to be read. The TimeSeries data plane fans out a given query across both the hot and cold tiers and merges their result. The users still use the same query interface:

The Cold Tier Data Plane uses compaction metadata for aggressive planning and pruning, which dramatically reduces the S3 query fan-out. As a result, retrieving a full day of data requires at most three sequential S3 reads, even in the uncommon case where an ID spans two row groups. This yields a p50 latency of ~150 ms and a p99 latency of ~500 ms per read.

At the time of writing, the streaming cold tier implementation was processing up to 1,250 reads per second from cold storage globally:

Why not stop here?

The streaming cold tier has delivered real savings, shrinking both Cassandra’s EBS footprint and the Cassandra backup footprint in S3. But the streaming infrastructure itself is expensive and adds moving pieces that widen the team’s on-call scope:

We wanted to improve this further and asked ourselves:

  • Can we avoid streaming data into the object store and the associated data transfer costs?
  • Can we reduce the compute and operational overhead of new components?

That led to a more radical question: Can we read directly from existing Cassandra backups in S3?

Solution 2: Cassandra Cold Storage for Immutable Data

At Netflix, we back up Cassandra data into S3 at regular intervals for disaster recovery. The idea for tiering is simple:

Read directly from these S3 backups instead of paying a separate data transfer cost to S3.

Once TimeSeries marks a hot Time Slice as ready for cold storage, we can customize Cassandra to read directly from its backups, allowing us to delete the on-disk data copy. This would also incur minimal changes to the TimeSeries read path!

To make this viable in production, we had to answer a series of “How…?” questions.

How Can We Read the Backups Efficiently?

We introduced a new compaction strategy in Cassandra, which we call ReadOnlyCompactionStrategy (ROCS). Here is how it works:

Once a time slice crosses the user-configured cold-tier boundary, TimeSeries stops accepting writes for that time slice making it immutable. This immutability unlocks significant optimization opportunities:

  • SSTable overlap: Standard strategies (LCS, TWCS) often produce SSTables that overlap in the token space, and so a single partition key may exist across multiple files.
  • Read fan‑out: Because a read must touch every SSTable covering the key’s token range, this overlap turns a single point-read into multiple lookups, increasing latency across all tiers.

ROCS re-compacts all SSTables once, aligning them precisely with token ranges:

ROCS applies more broadly to all TimeSeries use cases, driving tail latency down on all storage tiers by reducing the SSTable fan-out during read operations:

Once the immutable Time Slices have been optimized, it is time to trigger backups.

How Would We Leverage Backups?

Cassandra backs up every node in the cluster, organizing each backup on S3 as a declarative manifest, along with the SSTables backing the keyspace’s tables:

 {bucket}/
  └── {prefix}/                             ← cluster identity (env_backup/hash_app)
      └── {token}/                          ← node identity (ring token)
          ├── META_V2/                      ← manifests, one per snapshot
          │   ├── {snapshotInstantMs}.json
          │   ├── {snapshotInstantMs}.json
          │   └── ...
          └── SST_V2/                       ← actual SSTable files
              └── {backupTimestamp}/        ← snapshot timestamp
                  └── {keyspace}/
                      └── {table-with-uuid}/ 
                          └── {compression}/
                              └── {encryption}/
                                  ├── {component-file}
                                  └── ...

The backup manifest orchestrates the backup, listing the paths to all its SSTables:

manifest.json
  ├── info
  │   ├── appName              "cass-cluster"
  │   ├── region               "us-east-1"
  │   ├── snapshotInstantMs    1748908800000
  │   ├── backupPathPrefix     "prod_backup/1234_cass/token"
  └── data[]
      └── [0]
          ├── keyspaceName     "ks"
          ├── columnfamily     "tbl-a1b2..."
          └── sstables[]
              └── [0]
                  └── components[]
                      ├── na-1-big-Data.db
                      ├── na-1-big-Index.db
                      ├── na-1-big-Filter.db
                      ├── na-1-big-Statistics.db
                      ├── na-1-big-Summary.db
                      ├── na-1-big-CompressionInfo.db

Alongside the large Data.db file, backups include a compact set of index, metadata, and integrity files. This structure allows us to quickly locate, validate, and restore specific partitions or data ranges without scanning the entire dataset. Furthermore, since the manifest catalogs every S3 path, we can download most of these components directly to the Cassandra node (excluding the Data.db file) where they occupy negligible space. These local components enable efficient query planning before any data is read from S3.

How Would Cassandra Read From Backups?

Cassandra reads typically pull data from two sources: the Memtable, which holds recent unflushed writes, and flushed SSTables on durable storage. As of Cassandra 4.1, we can leverage pluggable Memtables to redirect reads from “cold” tables directly to the backup storage in S3.

-- create table for a given Time Slice
CREATE TABLE data_20260616_00_04 (
    ...
    ...,
    PRIMARY KEY ((time_series_id, time_bucket, event_bucket), event_time, event_id, key)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (event_time DESC, event_id DESC, key DESC)
    ...
    AND compaction = ...
    AND compression = ...
    AND memtable = 'backupmemtable:timestamp=1781953200000' ← Custom memtable
    ...

The timestamp marks the point at which the backup is guaranteed to cover the full table, and the table is guaranteed to be immutable.

Opening a backup Memtable kicks off a state-machine initialization that pulls the index data from S3 onto the node once:

This process ensures all SSTable components are downloaded reliably through several resilience mechanisms:

  • Retries and backoff: All S3 operations and file-system cache writes use retries with exponential backoff.
  • Resource isolation: Initialization runs on a dedicated thread pool, isolated from normal Cassandra operations.
  • Partial download protection: If a downloaded component’s size doesn’t match the manifest, it is deleted and re-downloaded.
  • DDL change protection: A .timestamp file marks completed initialization and ties it to the backup timestamp. If the table’s backup timestamp changes, this file is removed and initialization restarts for the new timestamp.
  • Read protection: Memtable initialization is asynchronous; reads to an initializing memtable block for at most half the read RPC timeout.

Once initialization has pulled every SSTable component (except Data.db) from S3 onto the local disk, the Memtable is ready to serve reads. Here is what the read process looks like:

To minimize latency, the system parallelizes S3 reads across requests, SSTables, and individual chunks. A shared cache deduplicates fetches and prefetches data, so chunks are ready before they are needed.

We further optimize cluster and table settings to reduce the number of S3 calls:

  • Larger compression chunks: Reduce S3 calls per partition by reading fewer, larger chunks (accepting some over-fetch on small reads).
  • Read repair disabled: Avoid expensive, unnecessary repair traffic against immutable, pre‑repaired backup data.
  • Speculative retries disabled: Prevent S3’s higher latency from triggering redundant, overlapping reads.

How Would We Know When It Is Safe To Read From Backups?

However, before the Memtable can point to a backup, we must confirm two things across the whole ring, and we use Cassandra Virtual Tables to do that.

First, that ROCS re-compaction succeeded:

cqlsh> SELECT * FROM netflix_views.cluster_view                                                                                                                                                          
       WHERE keyspace_name = 'system_views' AND table_name = 'sstable_tasks';

keyspace_name | table_name    | host     | value                                                                                                                                                        
--------------+---------------+----------+------------------------------------------------
system_views  | sstable_tasks | 10.0.0.1 | [{"table_name":"<.>","kind":"compaction", ...}]
system_views  | sstable_tasks | 10.0.0.2 | [] <---- no active compactions
system_views  | sstable_tasks | 10.0.0.3 | []

And second, that backups were fully captured (denoted by uploaded=True):

cqlsh> SELECT * FROM netflix_views.complete_backups                                                                                                                                                      
       WHERE keyspace_name = 'my_ks' AND table_name = 'my_table';

keyspace_name | table_name | timestamp     | num_tokens | num_uploaded | uploaded                                                                                                                       
--------------+------------+---------------+------------+--------------+----------
my_ks         | my_table   | 1765211400000 |          3 |            3 |     True
my_ks         | my_table   | 1765213200000 |          3 |            2 |    False

How Would We Automate This Entire Flow?

The TimeSeries control plane automates the entire transition as slices cross the immutable boundary:

Each slice can be in any lifecycle stage at any time without impacting system availability, and the system remains resilient to delayed backups or lagging compactions.

How Would Cassandra Handle The Additional Load?

Serving data from S3 is much more CPU-intensive than reading from local storage. A sudden spike in read requests can overwhelm the Cassandra cluster and affect the hot path, turning a cost-saving feature into a reliability risk.

To avoid this, cold reads can optionally run on a separate Cassandra cluster that points its backup Memtables at the hot cluster’s backups:

The cold Cassandra cluster must match the original cluster in topology but need not match it in hardware! We can run the cold cluster on much smaller, cheaper, storage-light instances.

Real World Performance

Cassandra Cold Tier was rolled out to the most storage‑intensive TimeSeries Abstraction clusters. It currently stores over 15 PB of compressed data in Cassandra cold storage and has allowed us to cut attached storage significantly on all affected clusters:

At the same time, it serves thousands of reads per second from cold tier storage in any given region:

Cassandra Cold Tier improves p90 latency by ~30% over the previous cold storage implementation, thanks to more efficient S3 access patterns and smaller read sizes, while keeping p99 latency under ~500 ms. Cassandra already handles bursts of cold reads gracefully via its chunk cache, so this design preserves that same resilience for the S3-backed cold tier:

Acknowledgements: Special thanks to our stunning colleagues who contributed to the TimeSeries Abstraction’s success and collaborated with us on the cold storage solutions: Kaidan Fullerton, Matt Lehman, Sumanth Pasupuleti, Carlos Matias Herrero, Nick Pavlakis, Bryan Keller, Francesco Di Chiara

TimeSeries Tiered Storage Journey: Kafka/Flink Streams to Native Cassandra Cold Reads was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

Cloud Billing

Feature

Spend cap budgets are now generally available for a limited set of services

For eligible services, you can configure a spend cap budget to automatically pause usage when your estimated spend exceeds the budget amount you set. You can manage spend cap budgets in the Budgets page in the Google Cloud console and using the Cloud Billing Budget API.

Spend caps are a cost control mechanism. A spend cap is enforced when usage costs exceed your budget target amount. When enforced, any new request to the eligible services, within the specified project, are paused and no further usage costs are accrued until the spend cap is lifted. You can manually lift an enforced spend cap, or wait until the start of the next month when the spend cap is automatically lifted.

Spend caps use gross, estimated costs to trigger the alerts and caps, enforcing a cap much faster than the actual costs are processed and appear on billing reports. Even though faster than reports, the enforcement of spend caps isn't instant and any cost overages are billed as normal.

More information about spend cap budgets

For managing spend cap budgets in the Google Cloud console, see:

  • How spend cap budgets work to help you control spend

Announcement

Google Cloud CCaaS prerelease notes 6.22

Here are the pre-release notes for what we expect to be the next version of Google Cloud CCaaS. When we release this version, we expect the new capabilities to be as shown here.

Feature

Campaign-based scheduled callbacks

Agents can now schedule a callback during an outbound campaign call. The callback belongs to the campaign, not to an individual agent, and the dialer calls the consumer back in the time slot they chose. Administrators set slot length, capacity, booking window, and expiry for each campaign, and supervisors can track upcoming, completed, and expired callbacks from the campaign list.

Feature

Transcript separation for chat

You can now configure Google Cloud CCaaS to deliver a separate transcript file for each participant segment in a chat, instead of one combined transcript per session. Under Settings > Chat > Chat Transcript, select Per Segment in Transcript Separation to generate individual transcript files for each agent, virtual agent, or supervisor who joins the chat—helpful for identifying which participant handled each part of a transferred or escalated conversation. Your consumers still receive a single, full-chat transcript regardless of this setting.

By default, this capability is inactive. Contact Google Cloud Support to turn it on for your instance.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where direct access point (DAP) greeting messages played twice when a call was deflected to an internal phone number due to queue overcapacity.

  • Fixed an issue where session metadata for top-level menu paths and selected menus was incorrectly displayed in English instead of the user's configured language.

  • Fixed an issue where a failed Salesforce lookup was incorrectly treated as having no matches, which resulted in the creation of duplicate records.

  • Fixed an issue where inbound transfer restrictions remained in force even after being hidden in the administrator interface, causing queues to become silently unreachable for transfers.

  • Fixed an issue where hold music continued to play throughout a call recording after a warm transfer was completed.

  • Fixed an issue where outbound virtual agent audio was prematurely truncated during multi-message turns.

  • Fixed an issue where the Real-time Monitoring Queues report didn't accurately count skill-matched agents for skills-based queues, often displaying zero available agents despite their availability.

  • Fixed an issue where calls deflected to an external phone number after entering a queue were incorrectly recorded as abandoned by the customer.

  • Fixed an issue where the credit card tokenizer was missing from the SmartActions menu during outbound callback calls.

  • Fixed an issue where mandatory call dispositions were discarded if an agent's voice connection dropped but their session remained active.

  • Fixed an issue where the text resize menu in the chat widget wasn't scrollable at 400% browser zoom, which prevented users from accessing all available text size options.

  • Fixed an issue where the system incorrectly prevented saving automatic call redirection settings when the target was a virtual agent-operated queue.

  • Fixed an issue where duplicate call records were created for a single inbound call, causing incorrect wait times to appear in the real-time queue view.

  • Fixed an issue where empty data attributes caused an error in the agent interface during call connections.

  • Fixed an issue where the Transfer Restrictions destination picker provided no feedback when a queue was ineligible, making it indistinguishable from a typo or search error.

  • Fixed an issue where incoming calls were rejected with a SIP 603 error due to high database latency and connection timeouts.

  • Fixed an issue where the documentation for the Apps API and call session metadata schema didn't define the top-level parentId and finishReason fields.

  • Fixed an issue where certain inbound call failures were incorrectly reported as a busy signal.

  • Fixed an issue where the event processor service crashed during scaling or rebalancing of the system.

  • Fixed an issue where the conversation ID was missing from chat events during active sessions.

  • Fixed an issue where report exports didn't download or remained stuck in a processing state indefinitely.

  • Fixed an issue where agents could transfer calls to queues that were already closed if their transfer list was loaded while the queue was still open.

  • Fixed an issue where queued chats were assigned to agents after the end-user had become unresponsive without being prompted to check in.

  • Fixed an issue where voice calls cold-transferred to an over-capacity queue generated duplicate reporting records and incorrect queue wait times if the callback leg failed.

  • Fixed an issue where direct inbound calls deflected to voicemail during after-hours played three separate audio prompts sequentially.

  • Fixed an issue where a single call was simultaneously assigned to two different agents if the pickup coincided with the cascade timer expiry.

  • Fixed an issue where direct inbound calls weren't projected to agents in a breakthrough-enabled status if another call was already waiting in their queue.

  • Fixed an issue where a gray empty area appeared below the chat container in the agent adapter when the iframe width was narrower than 449px.

  • Fixed an issue where several Kubernetes and Google Cloud service accounts were granted overly broad permissions, which could have allowed for unauthorized privilege escalation.

  • Fixed an issue where an agent's status sequence was recorded in the incorrect order following a brief connection loss during an active chat.

  • Fixed an issue where selecting a contact during a native campaign call didn't automatically open the corresponding record in the CRM.

  • Fixed an issue where AI-generated Smart Disposition suggestions were inconsistently displayed for outbound calls during the wrap-up period.

  • Fixed an issue where call recordings became distorted or garbled when multiple holds were placed during a call.

  • Fixed an issue where audio uploads were accepted based on the file extension rather than the actual file content, which caused call disconnections when incompatible formats were played.

  • Fixed an issue where the call duration timer in the external call adapter didn't match the In-call status timer in the agent desktop for inbound calls.

  • Fixed an issue where the sentiment score was incorrectly displayed in the call adapter for calls escalated from a virtual agent, even when the Sentiment Analysis setting was disabled.

  • Fixed an issue where duplicate reporting rows were generated for call and wrap-up durations due to concurrent system events.

  • Fixed an issue where agents couldn't sign in or refresh their status if their account was linked to a deleted or unknown status.

  • Fixed an issue where the Manager API documentation for agent activity logs omitted 17 chat routing and activity values, leading to incomplete reporting data for customers.

  • Fixed an issue where a supervisor's name didn't appear in the chat widget when joining a conversation using the monitor then barge workflow.

title: Spectral World Renderer: Unified 3D Hyperspectral Unmixing
description:
arXiv:2610.19520v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Cameras and the foundation models built on them recognize what a 3D scene contains, but not what it is made of: surfaces of the same colour can be different materials. Hyperspectral unmixing explains each spectrum as a mixture of material signatures, yet in 3D it is applied to rendered images after the views are composited, or tied to slow implicit fields, and no multi-view data with known composition exist to check the result. We present the Spectral World Renderer (SWR), which unifies world generation and unmixing. A coding agent builds executable 3D worlds that are rendered with measured spectra, so every hyperspectral image comes with exact labels and sub-pixel proportions; the resulting SWR-Bench provides eight indoor and outdoor worlds in which decompositions can be verified. SWR then unmixes inside rendering: each Gaussian of a compact 3D representation is decoded into material abundances before compositing, so one render yields spectra and material maps, and any surface can be queried by material name, a clicked pixel or a reference spectrum. Without material labels, SWR identifies materials best in all eight worlds, has the best mean PSNR on real captures, trains 3.7-12.9x faster than unmixing baselines, renders 34.9 labelled views/s and separates same-coloured materials.

title: Beyond Corrected Actions: Training LLM Agents on Textual Critiques
description:
arXiv:2610.19367v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for multi-turn agentic tasks that require interactions with users and environments over extended sequences of actions. A common approach to improving LLM agents is to use more capable expert models to provide training supervision, either by behavior cloning the expert's trajectories or by using the expert to correct the actions in trajectories generated by the weaker student model. However, expert LLMs can provide richer supervision than actions alone: they can directly generate textual critique that explain why specific actions are incorrect. We study whether training on such feedback benefits LLM agents and propose Critique-Augmented Agentic Fine-Tuning (CAFT), a framework that elicits textual expert feedback on student-generated trajectories. For each incorrect action, the expert yields both a corrected action and a textual critique explaining the student's mistake--which we then use as the training target for fine-tuning. Across four student models from the Nemotron 3 and Gemma 4 families on the agentic domains $\tau^2$-Bench Airline+Retail and WebShop, adding critiques to action-level supervision improves performance by 8% on average over action-only distillation. Additionally, CAFT checkpoints can also provide a better warm start for reinforcement learning than expert-trajectory distillation. Our results demonstrate that textual critiques can strengthen supervision for multi-turn LLM agents.

title: Are Multimodal Benchmarks Really Useful? Item-Level Multimodal Benchmark Diagnosis via Structure-Response Co-Calibration
description:
arXiv:2610.14542v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multimodal benchmarks are central to evaluating whether models can reason over information from multiple modalities. However, existing literature has revealed that some benchmarks may contain shortcut items that can be answered from a single modality or from answer-option regularities alone, thus failing to reflect models' true cross-modal inference ability. Existing methods for assessing benchmarks typically rely either on intrinsic item structure or extrinsic model response behavior, which are not adequate for a comprehensive diagnosis. To fill in this gap, we propose SRCoD, a structure-response co-calibrated diagnosis framework for item-level diagnosis of modality dependence in multimodal benchmarks. SRCoD estimates sample-wise multimodal information structure from benchmark content and target answers, and uses this signal as a soft structural anchor for modality-conditioned item response modeling. The learned model produces a calibrated item-level diagnostic profile that reflects how strongly an item depends on different forms of modality evidence, enabling fine-grained benchmark analysis beyond aggregate accuracy. SRCoD also provides interpretable attribution of the diagnosis results. Extensive experiments under two complementary protocols, i.e., benchmark-refinement oriented validation and human-labeled item validation, demonstrate that SRCoD outperforms state-of-the-art benchmark diagnosis methods.

title: AegisVox: Factorized Privacy and Clinical Preservation for Long-Form Speech
description:
arXiv:2610.14643v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Clinical speech reveals identity through both spoken identifiers and voice, yet its pauses, delivery, and speaker roles can also carry useful clinical evidence. Protecting that speech therefore requires more than preserving its words. We present AegisVox, a factorized framework that assigns consistent surrogate voices and edits identifier-bearing turns using document-consistent replacements. Across 390 public simulated or non-patient conversations totaling 63.6 hours, a matched comparison of two speech renderers separates replacement realization from retained identifiers, speaker linkage, and clinical preservation. Text-to-speech rendering realizes 535/601 planned replacements versus 453/601 for the codec-based speech editor. However, similar aggregate clinical preservation conceals more model-labeled contradictions, and conversation-wide speaker scores conceal greater edited-speech linkage under a score-direction sensitivity analysis. Fresh transcription of original audio provides a reference for interpreting the clinical measurement chain; an independent judge tests sensitivity to model-based assessment. Better replacement realization can therefore coexist with worse clinical or speaker-linkage measurements. AegisVox supports use-specific evaluation of those tradeoffs, not a guarantee of identifier removal or clinical safety.

title: Refactoring a Distributed Cache for Strong Reads When Eventual Consistency Fails
description:
we hit a subtle bug in our order‑service after a recent traffic surge: occasional duplicate invoices appeared in the admin UI. the root cause? a cache layer that was designed for eventual consistency but was being used for read‑after‑write scenarios.

The Problem

our stack uses a Node.js API gateway, a PostgreSQL write store, and a Redis cluster as a read‑through cache. writes go through a transaction, then an async job publishes an order.updated event to a Kafka topic. the consumer updates the Redis entry. under low load the latency between the DB commit and the cache refresh is negligible, but under load the lag grows to several seconds. the UI, which reads directly from Redis for latency reasons, sometimes shows stale data, leading to duplicate processing downstream.

Why Not Just Switch to Strong Consistency?

we could have forced every read to hit the DB, but that defeats the purpose of the cache. another option is to use Redis' wait command to block until replicas acknowledge the write, but that only helps with replication lag, not with our asynchronous event pipeline. the real challenge is to preserve the low‑latency read path while guaranteeing that any read immediately after a write sees the latest state.

A Pragmatic Refactor

instead of treating the cache as a fire‑and‑forget layer, we turned it into a write‑through store for critical entities. the API now performs the DB write and updates Redis in the same request, using a transaction‑like pattern. we still keep the async Kafka flow for eventual propagation to other services, but the cache is now authoritative for the write‑through path.

// write‑through helper – keeps DB and Redis in sync
async function updateOrder(id: string, payload: Partial<Order>) {
  // 1️⃣ start DB transaction
  await db.transaction(async trx => {
    await trx('orders').where({ id }).update(payload);
    // 2️⃣ update Redis inside the same logical unit
    const cacheKey = `order:${id}`;
    const fresh = { ...(await trx('orders').where({ id }).first()), ...payload };
    await redis.set(cacheKey, JSON.stringify(fresh));
  });
  // 3️⃣ fire async event for downstream consumers
  await kafka.produce('order.updated', { id, ...payload });
}

Trade‑offs & Edge Cases

  • Latency vs. Consistency – the write‑through path adds a few milliseconds to the request, but the UI now reads correct data.
  • Cache Invalidation – if another service updates the order directly in the DB (bypassing the API), the cache can become stale. we mitigated this by adding a TTL of 30 seconds and a background poller that reconciles mismatches.
  • Failure Scenarios – if Redis is unavailable, the transaction still commits to the DB, but we must decide whether to fail the request or proceed without caching. in our case we fail fast, returning a 503, because a stale cache is worse than a brief outage.
  • Memory Pressure – keeping a large write‑through cache can increase memory usage. we tuned Redis maxmemory-policy to volatile-lru and scoped the cache to only high‑traffic entities.

The Takeaway

by moving from an eventual‑only cache to a write‑through model we regained strong read guarantees without sacrificing overall performance. the pattern does introduce extra complexity around failure handling and cache hygiene, but those concerns are manageable with clear contracts.

how do you handle read‑after‑write consistency in your high‑traffic services, and what patterns have you found most sustainable?
