title: Contextual Credit Policy Optimization
description:
arXiv:2610.19103v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Group-based reinforcement learning enables large language model agents to learn from sparse outcome rewards in long-horizon tasks. Recent methods derive step-level credit by comparing observation-matched experiences across trajectories. However, identical observations can occur in different contexts, and matched peers are not equally informative for a given decision. Moreover, favorable terminal outcomes can obscure redundant actions or detours within successful trajectories. To address these two challenges, we propose Contextual Credit Policy Optimization (CCPO). For the first, CCPO weights observation-matched peers from other trajectories by contextual similarity, computed from frozen LLM representations and accumulated trajectory statistics, allowing peers from similar contexts to contribute more to a step's baseline. For the second, CCPO pairs historical credit, which compares the realized return against the weighted peer baseline, with future credit, which measures the change in contextual outcome value over a short realized continuation. A step is thus credited for the progress it makes, not only for its trajectory's eventual outcome. Both credits are computed in hindsight from rollouts already collected for training, enabling CCPO to address these challenges without an auxiliary value critic. Across two Qwen2.5-Instruct backbones (1.5B and 7B), CCPO achieves up to 97.4% success on ALFWorld and 79.4% on WebShop and outperforms GRPO by up to 21.6 and 18.5 points. Ablations show that contextual weighting outperforms uniform weighting, and that historical and future credit serve as complementary learning signals.

title: How Much Does It Cost to Build an AI App?
description:
An AI app has two costs: a one-time build and a monthly running bill that grows with every use of its AI features. Clutch reports an average AI development project of $120,594.55 (updated September 21, 2026), and vendors in the GoodFirms survey (updated September 28, 2026) say adding AI raises a software project's cost by up to 30%. The running bill depends on which AI features the app has, and you can estimate it from published per-use prices before you build.

This article covers apps with AI features: chat, search over your own documents, text generation, reading images and documents, image generation and transcription. For agents that plan and take actions, see how much an AI agent costs. For the cost of the app around the AI, see what a SaaS MVP costs. All prices were read on October 5, 2026.

What does it cost to build an AI app, according to published data?

Clutch's review data puts the average AI project at $120,594.55 and the most common budget at $10,000 to $49,999. No public dataset separates AI apps from other AI projects, so each figure below is labeled with what it measures.

Source What it measures Figure Date
Clutch AI Pricing Guide Client reviews of AI development companies Average project $120,594.55; most common band $10,000 to $49,999; typical timeline 10 months Updated September 21, 2026
Clutch, same guide Hourly rates of AI development companies listed on Clutch Most charge $24 to $49 an hour Updated September 21, 2026
GoodFirms cost survey What more than 100 software companies say adding AI does to a project "AI Integration alone can result in a 0-30% increase in cost" Updated September 28, 2026
GoodFirms, same survey Post-launch upkeep "an average of 10–20% annually on post-launch maintenance, bug fixes, and updates" Updated September 28, 2026

Two cautions apply. Clutch's average includes large projects, and its most common band is far below the average. GoodFirms collected its answers from vendors "between September and October 2025", so the figures are what sellers say they charge.

How do the build cost and the run cost of an AI app differ?

The build cost is paid once and depends on scope and engineering time. The run cost is paid every month and depends on how many people use the AI features and which models serve them.

In most software, an extra user costs little to serve. In an AI app, every chat reply, summary, scan or generated image is a paid call to a model, priced per token, per image or per minute. A feature that is cheap in testing can become the largest line on the bill once thousands of people use it daily.

The run cost also moves without any change to your app. Stanford HAI's 2025 AI Index reports that "the inference cost for a system performing at the level of GPT-3.5 dropped over 280-fold between November 2022 and October 2024." Prices can rise too. Google lists Gemini 3.8 Flash at $0.75 per million input tokens "through December 31, 2026" and $1.50 from January 1, 2027, on its pricing page last updated October 1, 2026. And Anthropic's pricing page notes that the tokenizer in Claude 4.7 and later models "produces approximately 30% more tokens for the same text." Plan to re-check the run cost whenever you change models.

What does each AI feature cost to build and run?

Each AI feature has its own build work and its own unit of charge. The table lists the main features, what the build involves and one published price for the run side.

AI feature What the build involves Run cost is charged per Published price (October 5, 2026)
Chat assistant Prompt design, conversation storage, guardrails, a test set of real questions Input and output token Claude Haiku 4.5: $1 input, $5 output per million tokens (Anthropic)
Search over your documents Ingestion, chunking, embeddings, a vector index, permission filtering Embedding token, plus vector database storage and reads text-embedding-3-small: $0.02 per million tokens (OpenAI); Pinecone Standard: "$50/month min. usage" (Pinecone)
Text generation (drafts, summaries) Templates, length limits, a review step before anything is sent Mostly output token Same per-token prices as chat
Reading images and scans Image resizing, an extraction schema, human review of low-confidence results Image token A 1000×1000 image is 1,296 tokens, "about $1.30 USD per thousand images" on Claude Haiku 4.5 (Anthropic vision docs)
Image generation Prompt templates, moderation, storage, labeling of AI-generated output Generated image Gemini 3.1 Flash Image: "$0.067 per 1K image" (Google)
Transcription Audio capture, upload handling, speaker labels, correction tools Audio minute gpt-transcribe: $0.0045 per minute (OpenAI)

Search is the feature whose run cost is mostly fixed. Embedding text is cheap, so the vector database's monthly minimum usually dominates at low volume. Image generation and transcription are the opposite: each use has a fixed price, and prompt caching does not reduce it.

Image size matters for the reading feature. Anthropic's vision documentation says "High-resolution images can use up to roughly three times more visual tokens than the same image on a standard-tier model", so resizing images before sending them is a cost decision as well as a speed one.

How do you estimate the monthly run cost of an AI app?

List each AI feature, estimate its monthly volume, multiply by the unit price, and add the fixed minimums. Then replace the assumptions with numbers measured on a prototype.

Worked example: An app has 5,000 monthly active users. Each user sends 30 chat messages, makes 4 document scans, generates 2 images and transcribes 20 minutes of audio a month. Each chat call carries 4,000 input tokens (instructions, retrieved passages and history) and returns 300 output tokens. The volumes are assumptions for illustration. The prices are those listed on October 5, 2026.

Feature Monthly volume Unit price Monthly cost
Chat on Claude Haiku 4.5 150,000 calls: 600M input, 45M output tokens $1 / $5 per million tokens $825
Document search 150,000 queries embedded (4.5M tokens) on text-embedding-3-small; vector database minimum $0.02 per million tokens; $50 a month minimum $50
Document scans on Claude Haiku 4.5 20,000 images at 1,296 tokens, plus 300 output tokens each $1 / $5 per million tokens $56
Image generation on Gemini 3.1 Flash Image 10,000 images at 1K $0.067 per image $670
Transcription with gpt-transcribe 100,000 minutes $0.0045 per minute $450
Total $2,051, or about $0.41 per user

Embedding the document library itself is a one-time cost here: 100 million tokens at $0.02 per million is $2.

Three things stand out. Model choice moves the chat line from $82.50 a month on OpenAI's gpt-6-luna ($0.10 / $0.50 per million tokens) to $1,650 on Claude Sonnet 5.5 ($2 / $10), so the same app costs between about $1,309 and $2,876 a month. Image generation and transcription together cost $1,120, more than the chat line on Claude Haiku 4.5. And features that do not need an instant answer can use batch pricing: Google lists the same image model at "$0.034 per 1K image" in its batch tier, and Anthropic's Batch API gives "a 50% discount on both input and output tokens."

Hosting for the app itself, error monitoring and AI request tracing come on top. Our article on reducing LLM API costs covers caching, model routing and batch processing in detail.

What drives the build cost of an AI app?

Five things drive it beyond the ordinary app work: data preparation, evaluation, guardrails, compliance and the review interface.

Data preparation

Search over your documents is only as good as the documents. Cleaning them, splitting them into passages, keeping the index current and enforcing who may see what make up much of a retrieval build.

Evaluation

An AI feature needs a test set of real inputs with expected results, run every time a prompt or model changes. Without it, a model switch that cuts the run cost can quietly lower quality.

Guardrails

Any feature that reads outside content can be manipulated by it. The OWASP Gen AI Security Project's 2025 entry on prompt injection says "Indirect prompt injections occur when an LLM accepts input from external sources, such as websites or files." It recommends to "Implement human-in-the-loop controls for privileged operations to prevent unauthorized actions."

Compliance

Apps offered in the EU carry disclosure duties. Article 50 of the AI Act, as published by the European Commission's AI Act Service Desk, requires that generated "audio, image, video or text content" be "marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated." The Commission's AI Act page, last updated August 3, 2026, says the Act "became applicable on 2 August 2026" and that its transparency rules took effect that month.

Review interface

Features that act on uncertain output, such as extracted invoice fields, need a screen where a person can check and correct results. It is ordinary product work, and it is often left out of first estimates.

How can you lower the cost of an AI app?

Start with one AI feature, measure it, and size the rest from real usage. The levers below come from the providers' own pricing terms.

  1. Use the smallest model that passes your tests. In the example above, the chat line differs 20-fold between two models.
  2. Cache stable prompt text. Anthropic prices a cache read at "0.1x base input price" for most models, so instructions repeated on every call cost a tenth as much after the first.
  3. Batch work that can wait. Overnight summaries, bulk scans and catalog images do not need instant answers.
  4. Resize images and limit output length. Both cut tokens on every call.
  5. Meter AI use per customer from launch. Then pricing and plan limits can follow real costs.

See LLM cost optimization for applying these to an app that is already live.

Key takeaways

  • An AI app has a build cost and a run cost, and the run cost grows with every use.
  • Published AI build figures center near $120,000, with a common band of $10,000 to $49,999, and vendors say AI adds up to 30% to a software project.
  • Each AI feature has its own unit of charge: tokens, images or minutes.
  • In the worked example, 5,000 users cost about $2,051 a month, or $0.41 each, and the chat model alone moves the total between about $1,309 and $2,876.
  • Data preparation, evaluation, guardrails, compliance and review screens drive the build beyond ordinary app work.

Frequently asked questions

How much does it cost to add AI to an existing app?

Vendors in the GoodFirms survey say AI integration adds 0 to 30% to a project's cost. The run cost is extra and depends on usage. In the worked example above, it is about $0.41 per active user a month.

How much does an AI app cost to run per month?

It depends on the features, the volume and the models. The example app with 5,000 users, chat, document search, scans, image generation and transcription costs about $2,051 a month at prices listed on October 5, 2026, before hosting and monitoring.

How long does it take to build an AI app?

Clutch reports 10 months as the typical timeline for AI development projects in its reviews, as of September 21, 2026. That covers all AI projects. An app with one well-scoped AI feature usually takes less, and no public source gives timelines for AI apps alone.

Is it cheaper to host my own model than to pay per token?

At low and medium volume, per-token APIs usually cost less, because self-hosting adds a fixed monthly cost for servers whether or not anyone uses them. Hosting your own model starts to pay at high, steady volume or when data must stay on your own infrastructure. See private LLM deployment.

Will AI running costs go down over time?

Per-token prices have fallen sharply: Stanford HAI's 2025 AI Index reports a 280-fold drop for GPT-3.5-level performance between November 2022 and October 2024. Individual prices can still rise, as Google's scheduled 2027 increase for Gemini 3.8 Flash shows, and newer models can use more tokens for the same text.

Easital Technologies Ltd. designs, builds and runs AI apps. Its own product StepVideo combines language and speech models in one media pipeline. See AI development services, generative AI development, RAG development, LLM cost optimization and our work.

Sources

All sources were opened and checked on October 5, 2026.

Clutch, "AI Pricing Guide", Anna Peck, updated September 21, 2026. https://clutch.co/developers/artificial-intelligence/pricing
GoodFirms, "Custom Software Development Cost 2026", updated September 28, 2026. https://www.goodfirms.co/resources/custom-software-development-cost-survey
Stanford HAI, "The 2025 AI Index Report", 2025. https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-index/2025-ai-index-report
Google, "Gemini Developer API pricing", last updated October 1, 2026. https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/pricing
Anthropic, "Pricing", Claude API documentation, read October 5, 2026. https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing
Anthropic, "Vision", Claude API documentation, read October 5, 2026. https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/vision
OpenAI, "Pricing", OpenAI API documentation, read October 5, 2026. https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/pricing
Pinecone, "Pricing", read October 5, 2026. https://www.pinecone.io/pricing/

title: Building a Multi-Tenant RAG in 8GB RAM: Why I Ditched Qdrant and Kafka (Phase 0)
description:
I have 8 GB of RAM and 6 vCPUs. With those specs, I'm building and running a full production-ready RAG system.

I’m not self-hosting the LLM. I’m not spinning up Qdrant. I’m not adding Kafka.
Those aren't my personal preferences—they are constraints strictly dictated by the hardware. When you run a JVM alongside a Python AI worker on an 8 GB machine, every megabyte counts.

Today, I’m starting to build Corpus in public: a document chat platform where every answer strictly cites its sources, and each organization's data remains completely isolated from the rest (strict multi-tenancy).

The Stack (100% Dockerized)

  • Backend API: Java 21 + Spring Boot 4
  • AI & Embeddings Service: Python + FastAPI
  • Storage & Vector DB: PostgreSQL (pgvector) + Redis
  • Frontend: React

Why this architecture?

  • PostgreSQL + pgvector over Qdrant/Milvus: Maintaining a dedicated vector database alongside a relational DB in 8 GB of RAM is overkill. Keeping relational metadata and vector embeddings in the same engine simplifies transactions and saves precious memory.
  • Redis over Kafka: I need asynchronous processing for document ingestion, not a massive distributed event-streaming cluster eating up heap memory.

Current Status: Phase 0

All 5 services spin up cleanly with a single docker compose up, and the core system design is locked in the repository. There is no live demo yet.

Next step: The ingestion pipeline—turning raw PDFs into queryable vector chunks without triggering the Linux OOM killer.

I’ll be documenting every architectural trade-off and every failure along the way.

🔗 GitHub Repository: aletgdev/corpus-rag

Looking for advice from the community 👇

For those of you who have built something similar under tight resource constraints: How would you handle local embedding generation within an 8 GB RAM budget while guaranteeing strict multi-tenant isolation in pgvector? (e.g., Row-Level Security vs. schema-per-tenant vs. metadata filtering).

Any war stories or tips are more than welcome in the comments!

title: One Block Ahead: Promoting Sampler State in Diffusion Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.19510v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Block-diffusion language models denoise a whole block of token positions in parallel so each forward pass can emit many tokens. However, blocks are still denoised in strict sequence, a cost that within-block acceleration leaves untouched. Here, we investigate decoding blocks concurrently and propose One Block Ahead (OBA), a training-free decoding algorithm that denoises the next block alongside the current one. We demonstrate that for uniform-state diffusion LMs, where a block's denoising progress is not visible in its intermediate tokens, concurrent decoding is advantageous if the next block's tokens are promoted together with the corresponding sampler state, including the self-conditioning signal and the denoising time. We also derive a break-even criterion that relates the benefit of OBA to the relative cost of a paired-block forward pass. On DiffusionGemma, a state-of-the-art diffusion LM, OBA increases the tokens per forward pass by 42.3% (from 15.64 to 22.25) and the single-request denoising throughput by 16.3%, averaged over ten benchmarks, with a small accuracy regression.

title: Robust Real-Time Monocular Human Pose Estimation with Insole-Based Sensor Fusion
description:
arXiv:2610.19494v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Real-time monocular human pose estimation is an important sensing component for human-centered intelligent systems. While recent camera-based methods have achieved impressive accuracy, fundamental challenges persist, particularly when visual observations are incomplete, such as during lower-body occlusion or short out-of-frame intervals. In these challenging but common scenarios, vision-only systems often struggle to reconstruct physically plausible lower-limb motion and reliable foot-ground contact. Due to the highly unobtrusive and wearable nature of smart insoles, this paper investigates whether simple plantar pressure and acceleration sensors can effectively resolve these visually induced limitations. To systematically investigate this, we first collect a synchronized multimodal dataset and then propose a part-decoupled temporal fusion framework. The proposed model fuses foot-sensing features into the lower-body branch to compensate for incomplete visual evidence, while a lightweight coordinator exchanges information between the upper- and lower-body temporal representations to maintain whole-body consistency. The framework is evaluated with three representative real-time visual backbones based on 2D keypoints, 3D landmarks, and SMPL-based human mesh recovery. We evaluate our framework on three representative real-time visual backbones. Quantitative experiments demonstrate that incorporating simple foot sensors consistently improves pose accuracy, motion smoothness, and gait-related measurements over vision-only baselines, with the most significant gains observed under occlusion and short visual-dropout conditions. Ultimately, our results demonstrate that unobtrusive foot sensing provides vital and complementary physical observability when camera observations are temporarily unavailable.

title: Why Is My Kubernetes Job Still Pending? Tracing Kueue Admission with Headlamp
description:
You submit a Kubernetes Job and wait for its Pods to appear. A minute passes. Then another. The Job is still suspended, there are no application logs, and there may not even be a Pod to inspect.

In a cluster managed by Kueue, this can be completely normal. Kueue may still be deciding whether the Job can use the requested resources. The useful question is not only “Why is the Pod pending?” It is first “Has Kueue admitted the Workload?”

The Kueue plugin for Headlamp brings that investigation into the Headlamp UI. Instead of reconstructing the admission path from several commands and large YAML objects, you can begin with the Workload, read its condition message, and follow links through the LocalQueue, ClusterQueue, ResourceFlavor, and Cohort.

This article follows that Headlamp-first path. The command line appears only in a short optional section for reproducing the example.

Before you begin

You need a Kubernetes cluster with Kueue installed, a Headlamp installation, and the 0.1.0-alpha Kueue plugin. Your Kubernetes identity must be allowed to read the Kueue resources used in this article.

The alpha release provides read-only views for Kueue v1beta2 Cohorts, ClusterQueues, LocalQueues, ResourceFlavors, and Workloads. It does not add its own create, edit, stop, resume, or delete workflows. Headlamp still provides its standard YAML and resource actions where your permissions allow them.

First, separate admission from Pod scheduling

Kueue and the Kubernetes scheduler answer different questions.

  • Kueue admission: Should this Workload start now, considering queue policy, quota, ResourceFlavors, admission checks, and other waiting Workloads?

  • Pod scheduling: After the Workload is admitted and the Job resumes, which nodes can run its Pods?

That boundary changes the investigation. If the Workload is not admitted, stay in the Kueue section of Headlamp. If it is admitted but its Pods are still Pending, move to Headlamp's normal Job and Pod views and inspect scheduler events.

The Headlamp-first troubleshooting path

The quickest investigation starts with the Workload, not with a shell.

Step 1: Open the Workloads view

In Headlamp, open Kueue → Workloads. Select the namespace that contains the Job, then find the Workload created for it.

Kueue creates a Workload to represent the resource request and admission state of a Job. In the alpha plugin, owner references are shown as Kind/name text but are not yet clickable. The Workload name normally contains the Job name, so the namespace filter and table search are the simplest ways to locate it.

Before opening the detail page, the list already gives you a useful first scan:

  • LocalQueue

  • priority and priority class

  • active state

  • admitted state

  • completion state

  • a readable current status such as Admitted, Finished, or Inadmissible

  • age

If there is no matching Workload, check three things before going further: the selected namespace, whether the Job was submitted to a LocalQueue, and whether your Kubernetes account can list Workloads. The plugin performs permission checks and displays an access message when the current identity cannot read a resource.

Step 2: Read status, conditions, and events

Open the Workload. Start with its current status and conditions, not with the full YAML.

For admission troubleshooting, the most important condition types are QuotaReserved and Admitted.

  • Admitted=True means Kueue has admitted the Workload. The Job can resume, so any remaining Pending Pods belong to the scheduling branch of the investigation.

  • QuotaReserved=False with a reason such as Pending means Kueue has not reserved quota. The condition message explains what prevented the reservation.

  • An Inadmissible status means the Workload currently cannot fit the available queue configuration. A missing covered resource, unsuitable ResourceFlavor, stopped queue, or admission check can all lead you here.

For example, a condition message may report that Kueue could not assign a ResourceFlavor because the ClusterQueue has insufficient CPU quota. That message is the first real answer to “Why is my Job still pending?” The rest of the Headlamp journey explains the configuration behind it.

Also check the Events section. Conditions describe the current state; events help show what recently changed or what Kueue attempted.

Step 3: Compare the Workload's request with its assignment

Stay on the Workload detail page and inspect the PodSets and resource requests. The plugin shows the requested Pod count, CPU, memory, and other resources that Kueue evaluates together.

This matters because a Job with parallelism: 3 and a one-CPU request per Pod asks Kueue for three CPUs in total. Looking at only one Pod's template would underestimate the Workload.

If quota has already been reserved, the same page also shows the assigned ClusterQueue, ResourceFlavors, and admitted resource usage. If those admission assignments are absent, the Workload has not reached that point yet.

In our example, the Workload requests:

  • three Pods

  • three CPUs in total

  • 600 MiB of memory in total

The next question is where that request entered Kueue.

Step 4: Follow the linked LocalQueue

Use the LocalQueue link on the Workload detail page. A LocalQueue is the namespace-level entry point used by the Job. It connects namespaced Workloads to a cluster-scoped ClusterQueue.

The LocalQueue page shows:

  • its namespace and connected ClusterQueue

  • stop policy and current status

  • pending, reserving, and admitted Workload counts

  • Kueue conditions and Kubernetes events

  • related Workloads in the same namespace

This page answers two practical questions: Did the Job enter the queue you expected, and is it the only Workload waiting there?

If the LocalQueue is inactive or stopped, that may already explain the wait. If it is active, follow the linked ClusterQueue to inspect the capacity behind it.

Step 5: Inspect ClusterQueue capacity and usage

A ClusterQueue represents the cluster-level quota and admission policy available to one or more LocalQueues.

On its Headlamp detail page, compare the Workload request with:

  • covered resources

  • nominal quota for each ResourceFlavor

  • current reservations and usage

  • borrowing and lending limits

  • pending, reserving, and admitted Workload counts

  • queueing strategy and stop policy

  • preemption, fair-sharing, flavor-fungibility, and admission-check settings

  • Kueue conditions and Kubernetes events

For the example in this article, the ClusterQueue provides a nominal quota of two CPUs and two Pod slots. The Workload asks for three of each. The condition message and the ClusterQueue page now tell the same story: the Workload does not fit, so Kueue leaves the Job suspended.

This is an admission-capacity problem. It is not evidence that kube-scheduler failed to find a node.

Step 6: Check ResourceFlavor and Cohort when needed

Quota is not always a single pool. A ResourceFlavor can represent a class of compute through node labels, taints, tolerations, or topology settings. Use the ResourceFlavor link from the ClusterQueue when the condition mentions flavor assignment or when the Workload requires a particular hardware class, such as GPU nodes.

If the ClusterQueue belongs to a Cohort, follow that link too. Cohorts let ClusterQueues share unused quota. The Headlamp page shows parent and child Cohorts, member ClusterQueues, referenced ResourceFlavors, resource groups, borrowing and lending limits, and fair-sharing information.

These pages help answer a more subtle question: Is the Workload blocked because the queue has no quota of its own, because it cannot borrow enough, or because no suitable flavor can be assigned?

What we learned without leaving Headlamp

For the sample pending Job, the UI gives us a complete explanation:

  1. The Workload is not admitted.

  2. Its QuotaReserved condition is false and the message points to insufficient quota.

  3. The Workload requests three CPUs and three Pod slots.

  4. Its LocalQueue is active and points to the expected ClusterQueue.

  5. The ClusterQueue provides only two CPUs and two Pod slots.

  6. Kueue therefore keeps the Job suspended until quota becomes available or the queue configuration changes.

The important part is not that Headlamp invents a new status. It reads the same Kubernetes API objects as other clients, then places the related resources and human-readable values in one connected investigation.

If the Workload is admitted, switch views

Suppose the Workload detail page shows Admitted=True, but the application is still not running. Kueue has completed its part of the decision. Continue in Headlamp's standard Kubernetes views:

  1. Open Workloads → Jobs and inspect the Job state and events.

  2. Open Workloads → Pods and filter by the Job name or namespace.

  3. Select a Pending Pod and read its Events section.

At this stage, look for scheduler concerns such as insufficient node capacity, node affinity, taints and tolerations, topology constraints, persistent-volume binding, or image-pull failures.

This handoff is the most useful troubleshooting rule in the article:

  • Not admitted: investigate Kueue resources in Headlamp.

  • Admitted, but Pods are Pending: investigate Job, Pod, node, and scheduler information in Headlamp.

A repeatable Headlamp checklist

When the next Job does not start, use this short path:

  1. Open Kueue → Workloads and select the correct namespace.

  2. Find the Workload associated with the Job.

  3. Check the readable status, Admitted, and QuotaReserved conditions.

  4. Read the condition message and recent events.

  5. Compare PodSet resource requests with any admission assignments.

  6. Follow the LocalQueue link and confirm its status and ClusterQueue.

  7. Follow the ClusterQueue link and compare quota, reservations, usage, and policy.

  8. Inspect ResourceFlavor or Cohort details when the message points to flavor selection or shared quota.

  9. If admitted, move to Headlamp's Job and Pod views.

What Headlamp replaces during this investigation

The plugin does not replace kubectl or kueuectl for scripts, exact object output, or changes. It replaces the repetitive UI-less navigation needed during an interactive investigation.

Question Headlamp path Command-line equivalent
Is the Workload admitted? Kueue → Workloads → status and conditions kubectl describe workload <workload-name> -n <namespace>
Which LocalQueue did it enter? Workload → linked LocalQueue kubectl get localqueue <localqueue-name> -n <namespace> -o yaml
Which ClusterQueue provides quota? LocalQueue → linked ClusterQueue kubectl get clusterqueue <clusterqueue-name> -o yaml
Which flavor or shared quota matters? ClusterQueue → ResourceFlavor or Cohort kubectl get resourceflavor <flavor-name> -o yaml or kubectl get cohort <cohort-name> -o yaml
What happened after admission? Workloads → Jobs and Pods → events kubectl describe job <job-name> -n <namespace> or kubectl describe pod <pod-name> -n <namespace>

For scripts and GitOps workflows, the command line remains the right tool. For a person asking “why is this waiting?”, the linked Headlamp path is usually faster to read.

Optional: reproduce the pending scenario

The plugin repository includes sample Cohort, ClusterQueue, LocalQueue, ResourceFlavor, and Job manifests for local testing. Apply those examples to a cluster where Kueue is installed, then open the Kueue section in Headlamp.

To reproduce the specific quota mismatch used in this article, configure a ClusterQueue with two CPUs and two Pod slots, then submit a three-Pod Job that requests one CPU per Pod. The Job enters its LocalQueue, Kueue creates a Workload, and the Workload remains pending because the combined request is larger than the available quota.

Keeping this setup separate from the main walkthrough is intentional: once the resources exist, the investigation itself should happen in Headlamp.

Current alpha limitations

The 0.1.0-alpha release is an initial read-only view of the Kueue admission path.

  • The plugin does not add its own create, edit, pause, resume, or delete flows.

  • Workload owner references are displayed as text and are not currently navigable.

  • The UI depends on the Kubernetes permissions of the identity used by Headlamp.

  • Metrics and a visual relationship map are possible follow-up areas rather than features of this release.

These limits are useful to state clearly: the plugin's current purpose is to make admission state and resource relationships easier to inspect.

Developed during LFX Mentorship

The plugin was developed during CNCF LFX Mentorship 2026 Term 2 using TypeScript, React, Kubernetes APIs, and Headlamp's plugin system.

Utkarsh Raj implemented the plugin with guidance and review from René Dudfield (@illume) and Kevin Hannon (@kannon92). Feedback from the Headlamp and Kueue communities shaped the resource views, status presentation, navigation, documentation, tests, and first alpha release.

Try it and share feedback

Explore the plugin source and README, read the 0.1.0-alpha release documentation, or share feedback in the release issue.

If a pending Workload is still difficult to explain after following the Headlamp path, that is exactly the kind of feedback that can improve the plugin.

title: Create complex UI with a class library in PHP
description:
Despite the rise of JavaScript frameworks like React and Angular, building the UI on the backend is still a common feature in many web applications. This is generally done with a template library, like Twig, Blade or Latte, and often using a different language which is close or related to the main application language. A template engine then converts the template code into the application language, and generally caches the generated code for further reuse.

In the PHP ecosystem, there are many attempts to build application UIs using a class library.

Some of the most popular complements a template library. spatie/html extends Laravel Blade with functions to build HTML elements. Symfony Forms and Nette Forms can build forms, then validate and process their values.

Less known and less used, there are other PHP packages whose purpose is to build an application UI using a class library. ATK UI, Viewi, ui-awesome/html, danielescherzer/html-builder and Sirius HTML are a few examples of such libraries.

However, they don't match the advanced features of template libraries like Blade or Twig. Even when providing a fluent API, generally those libraries can only create chunks of HTML or individual HTML components, without being able to tie them together into a complete UI block. The user then needs to complement them with a template engine or plain PHP calls for string concatenation, iterative or conditional rendering.

The HTML Builder library

HTML Builder is a PHP library that provides classes to represent the HTML components, as well as an API to build UIs using those classes. A UI is built using a call tree, where each component receives its children as parameters. HTML tags are created by calling methods named after the tags, while attributes are set using methods named set followed by the attribute name in PascalCase.

    $this->html->div(
        $this->html->div(
            $this->html->label($this->html->text('Collation'))
                ->setFor('collation')
        )->setStyle('width: 30%;'),
        $this->html->div(
            $this->html->select(
                $this->html->option('(collation)')
                    ->setValue('')
                    ->setSelected(true),
                $this->html->each($collations, fn(array $groupCollations, $group) =>
                    $this->html->list(
                        $this->html->when($group === '', fn() =>
                            $this->html->each($groupCollations, $this->html->option(...))
                        ),
                        $this->html->when($group !== '', fn() =>
                            $this->html->optgroup(
                                $this->html->each($groupCollations, $this->html->option(...))
                            )->setLabel($group)
                        )
                    )
                )
            )->setName('collation')
        )->setStyle('width: 70%;')
    )->setStyle('display: flex; justify-content: space-between;')

This is the same template, built with Twig.

<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between;">
    <div style="width: 30%;">
        <label for="collation">Collation</label>
    </div>
    <div style="width: 70%;">
        <select name="collation">
            <option value="" selected>(collation)</option>
            {% for group, groupCollations in groups %}
                {% if group == '' %}
                    {% for collation in groupCollations %}
                        <option>{{ collation }}</option>
                    {% endfor %}
                {% else %}
                    <optgroup label="{{ group }}">
                        {% for collation in groupCollations %}
                            <option>{{ collation }}</option>
                        {% endfor %}
                    </optgroup>
                {% endif %}
            {% endfor %}
        </select>
    </div>
</div>

The virtual components

What actually makes the HTML Builder library as powerful as a template library, is its virtual components.

A virtual component takes application data as input, and generates zero, one or more components as output. It generates no additional HTML tag, so its output is only composed of those of the generated components.

There is a bidirectional relation between virtual and real components. A real component can contain either real or virtual components as children, and a virtual component can generate a collection of real and virtual components.

Virtual components enable the HTML Builder library to generate HTML elements dynamically, a feature not available in the libraries mentioned above.

The types of virtual components

The HTML Builder library provides 5 types of virtual components.

Note: a closure passed to a virtual component must return a single component, which can be real or virtual.

The When component

The When component mimics the if clause of template languages. It takes a boolean condition and a closure as parameters, and calls the closure only when the condition is true.

    $this->html->when($user->isLoggedIn,
        fn() => $this->html->div($this->html->text($user->email)));

The List component

The List component groups a set of components into a single one. It then allows to pass a list of components in places where a single component is expected, for example as the return value of a function.

    $this->html->when($user->isLoggedIn,
        fn() => $this->html->list(
            $this->html->b($this->html->text('Welcome ')),
            $this->html->div($this->html->text($user->email))
        );

The Pick component

The Pick component mimics the PHP switch clause. It takes multiple When components as input, and calls the closure provided by the first true condition.

    $this->html->pick(
        $this->html->when($user === null,
            fn() => $this->html->html('Welcome')),
        $this->html->when($user->isAdmin,
            fn() => $this->html->html("Welcome <b>{$user->name}</b>")),
        $this->html->when(true,
            fn() => $this->html->html("Welcome {$user->name}"))
    );

The Each component

The Each component takes an array of items and a closure as parameters, and calls the closure with each item in the array. It then generates the same number of components, each of which can be either real or virtual.

    $this->html->select(
        $this->html->option('(Default)')->setValue(0),
        $this->html->each($choices,
            fn($choice) => $this->html->option($choice->label))
    );

The Each component can also take an iterator or a generator as parameter, and the closure also accepts the array key value as second parameter.

    $this->html->select(
        $this->html->option('(Default)')->setValue(0),
        $this->html->each($choices,
            fn($choice, $id) => $this->html->option($choice->label)->setValue($id))
    );

The Loop component

The Loop component is the same as the Each component, but its second parameter is a LoopItem object, which provides various information about the current loop.

    $this->html->select(
        $this->html->option('(Default)')->setValue(0),
        $this->html->loop($choices,
            fn($choice, $loop) => $this->list(
                $this->when($loop->current->group !== $loop->prev?->group,
                    fn() => $this->html->option($loop->current->group)
                        ->setClass('group-title disabled')),
                $this->html->option($choice->label)->setValue($id))
            )
    );

Note: The Loop component was inspired by this article on Twig.

Comparison with template engines

The HTML Builder library combines a fluent PHP API with a lightweight, object-oriented approach to HTML generation.

Its virtual components support dynamic content while deferring the execution of closures until rendering. This keeps UI construction entirely within PHP, using a consistent fluent API from start to finish, without requiring a separate template compilation step.

The combination of regular and virtual components provides the building blocks needed to implement the main features commonly found in template engines, including conditional rendering and iteration, while preserving the fluent API. Combined with PHP's object-oriented features, such as inheritance, traits, method overloading, and composition, this approach offers a flexible way to structure and reuse UI code.

Like template engines, HTML Builder can also be extended with custom functions to meet application-specific needs.

Why use HTML Builder?

When using the HTML Builder library, the application UI is organized as a library of PHP classes rather than a collection of template files. This makes the UI independent of any particular application framework and eliminates the need for a separate template engine.

UI classes can accept structured objects and domain-specific data types instead of relying solely on simple arrays. This allows the interfaces between the UI and other application components to be defined more explicitly, improving separation of concerns and making dependencies easier to understand.

A class-based UI can also benefit from familiar software engineering practices, including encapsulation, inheritance, code reuse, and unit testing. For applications where the UI is maintained as part of the codebase, this approach can make the code easier to organize, maintain, and test.

What changes with HTML Builder?

Template engines commonly compile templates into PHP code and cache the compiled result for reuse. This reduces the overhead of processing templates repeatedly and can provide a performance advantage over an object-based approach to HTML generation.

HTML Builder instantiates objects for HTML components and makes use of features such as magic methods, closures, and method calls to compose the final output. These mechanisms introduce some runtime overhead compared with executing precompiled PHP code.

However, performance depends on the implementation, the structure of the UI, and the amount of work involved in rendering it. The trade-off is an approach that emphasizes object-oriented composition, extensibility, and code reuse rather than minimizing runtime overhead.

Some template engines also provide a sandbox that allows untrusted templates to be executed with restricted capabilities, improving security. Developers can define which functions templates are allowed to call. This feature is particularly useful when an application needs to render templates provided by third parties.

HTML Builder does not provide a sandbox, as it is designed to build HTML directly from PHP code rather than to execute untrusted templates. Its UI classes are intended to be part of the application's codebase, not to serve as a restricted execution environment for externally supplied templates.

The UI Builder library

The UI Builder library extends the HTML Builder library with functions for creating UI components based on CSS frameworks. It provides a set of primitives for creating components such as buttons, cards, tabs, pagination, and more, as well as configuring their properties.

The UI Builder library is currently used to build the UI of the Jaxon DbAdmin application, and the example below is taken from its codebase.

    $this->html->build(
        $this->html->buttonGroup(
            $this->html->button(
                $this->html->text($this->trans->lang('Columns ')),
                $this->html->when($columnCount > 0, fn() =>
                    $this->html->badge("$columnCount")->primary())
            )->outline()
                ->secondary()
                ->fullWidth(),
            $this->html->button(
                $this->html->text($this->trans->lang('Filters ')),
                $this->html->when($filterCount > 0, fn() =>
                    $this->html->badge("$filterCount")->primary())
            )->outline()
                ->secondary()
                ->fullWidth(),
            $this->html->button(
                $this->html->text($this->trans->lang('Order ')),
                $this->html->when($sorterCount > 0, fn() =>
                    $this->html->badge("$sorterCount")->primary())
            )->outline()
                ->secondary()
                ->fullWidth()
        )->fullWidth()
    );

The UI Builder library is separated into multiple PHP packages.

The lagdo/ui-builder package provides the BuilderInterface interface, which defines the functions that each builder must implement. It also provides base classes for UI components and implements a common set of functions shared by the different builders.

Each supported CSS framework has its own package, which implements the Builder class and the corresponding UI component classes. Each component class defines how the component's HTML is generated for the target framework, using the functions provided by the lagdo/ui-builder and lagdo/html-builder packages.

The framework-specific Builder class extends the AbstractBuilder class provided by the UI Builder package and only needs to specify the names of the component classes it uses.

The following CSS frameworks are currently supported:

  • Bootstrap 5
  • Bootstrap 4

The Bootstrap 3 package is deprecated.

The packages for Tailwind CSS and Bulma are under development and will be available soon.

Closing thoughts

Generating an application UI entirely in PHP has always been challenging. PHP libraries designed for this purpose have traditionally lacked many of the features offered by template engines, often requiring developers to supplement them with a template engine or direct PHP calls.

Thanks to its virtual components, the HTML Builder library bridges this gap. Its fluent API and methods named after HTML tags make it easier to build complex application UIs entirely in PHP.

The UI Builder library takes this approach a step further by extending the HTML Builder library with higher-level UI components, such as buttons, cards, tabs, and pagination. Framework-specific packages generate the corresponding HTML for CSS frameworks such as Bootstrap, Tailwind CSS, and Bulma.

title: CISA Urges Immediate Ivanti Connect Secure Updates as Honeypots Log 105 Exploit Attempts
description:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Tuesday urged organizations to take steps to immediately update their Ivanti Connect Secure (ICS) appliances and deployments to the latest version following the disclosure of an actively exploited vulnerability.

The security flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-104935 (CVSS score: 8.6), is a case of authentication bypass impacting ICS
